encountered in terms of how it might 
prime stereotypes. What sorts of inter -
pretations would you expect people to

to limit the extent to which news stories

to counteract the effects of the auto-

2.2: BLACK CRIMINALITY 3.0: THE 
CENTRALITY OF STEREOTYPES IN 
THE 21ST CENTURY
Travis L. Dixon
By the early 2000s, scholars and lay people alike 
suggested overt racism was a thing of the past 
(Devine, 1989). The Civil Rights movement and the 
Obama presidency even led some to argue that we 
had entered a post-racial society in which race and 
racism played a diminished role in our collective 
lives (Anderson, Goins, & Howard, 2015). Those 
myths came crashing down with the election of a 
president who campaigned proudly on his racism.
Donald Trump’s presidency (2017–2021) relied 
on race, gender, and religious stereotypes to guide pol-
icymaking. His first campaign speech singled out Mex-
ican immigrants for bringing crime to America through 
illegal immigration. His terrorism policy revolved 
around a travel ban affecting largely Muslim countries. 
He called African and Caribbean nations s***hole 
(or perhaps s***house) countries (Kiely, 2018; Vitali, 
Hunt, & Thorp, 2018), and White supremacists very 
fine people (Gray, 2017). The President relied on cable 
news, rather than daily security briefings (Parker & 
Costa, 2017; Smith, 2016), which may have fueled his 
conviction that these stereotypes represent reality.
The author provides social scientific evidence 
demonstrating that stereotypical news portrayals 
shape perceptions of stigmatized groups. Mediated 
stereotypes reinforce news viewers’ false concep-
tions of various racial groups and the roles they 
occupy in society. Social media only make things 
worse.

20 Audiences
Moreover, his core base includes avid consumers 
of ideological information sources such as FOX News 
and Breitbart.com. After Trump lost his re-election 
bid, that base, driven by conspiracy theories and overt 
racism, attempted a coup at the US capital on Janu-
ary 6, 2021 (Jacobson, 2021). Insurrectionists grasped 
the most dramatic US symbol of racism and intoler-
ance, the Confederate Flag, while threatening to lynch 
vice-president Pence for not overturning a free and fair 
election.
One reason Trump was not re-elected in 2020 
may have been his handling of the COVID-19 pan-
demic (Hart, 2021). The virus first appeared in Wuhan, 
China, in November 2019. Worried that it would affect 
his re-election, Trump downplayed the need to com-
bat the virus and again relied on racial stereotyping, 
calling it the “China-virus” and the “kung-flu” (Man, 
2020).
Stereotypical media consumption fueled both the 
storming of the capital and a spike in anti-Asian vio-
lence driven by pandemic propaganda, demonstrating 
the centrality of stereotypical media in our politics and 
social reality.
I will provide an overview of research into the 
content and effects of media stereotypes, primarily 
regarding African Americans but also Latinos and 
Muslims. Then I’ll discuss how the changing nature of 
news in the digital age exacerbates the effects previ-
ously observed with legacy media.
Race in News Portrayals
My work, and that of other scholars, has found that 
news consistently misrepresents African Ameri-
cans as the primary perpetrators of crime (Dixon & 
Linz, 2000a; Entman, 1992, 1994; Gilliam & Iyengar, 
2000). In one of my earliest studies, Blacks were 
twice as likely as Whites to be portrayed as perpe-
trators of crime on local television news (Dixon & 
Linz, 2000a) and six times more likely to be depicted 
as perpetrators than as officers. Blacks were over -
represented as criminals on the news (37%) com-
pared to crime reports (21%).
This contrasts starkly with how Whites appear 
on local news (Dixon & Linz, 2000a, 2000b). Whites 
appear as officers twice as often than as criminals and 
are overrepresented (69%) compared to employment 
records (59%). Whites appear as victims twice as 
often as Blacks do and are overrepresented as victims 
(43%) compared to crime reports (13%), a pattern also 
found in network news (Dixon, Azocar, & Casas, 2003). 
These and other studies show that the news associates 
African Americans with criminality when compared to 
Whites, for both adults and juveniles (Dixon & Azocar, 
2006).
In addition, the news highlights Black and Brown 
criminals who harm White victims (Dixon & Linz, 
2000b; Heider, 2000; Romer, Jamieson, & de Coteau, 
1998); negative pretrial publicity appears more often 
on TV with Black or Brown suspects accused of vic-
timizing White people (Dixon & Linz, 2002). The mes-
sage about African American and White people in 
crime news has been clear: Black people are criminals 
and suspects, whereas White people are victims and 
officers.
These findings paint a bleak picture of stereotypi-
cal portrayals and race in the news, although they raise 
some questions. Have things changed recently, and if 
so, how? Most of these studies have focused on crime 
news—are the portrayals the same when we change 
the context? What about other stigmatized groups?
I re-examined representations of race on local 
news programming 15 years after my earlier studies 
(Dixon, 2017a), to assess whether the same distortions 
of Black people as criminals and White people as vic-
tims/officers seen in the 1990s and early 2000s con-
tinued. Some things had changed, but others had not. 
Surprisingly, Blacks were no longer overrepresented as 
criminals or underrepresented as officers and victims. 
Instead, the news accurately represented Black people 
in each of these roles. This appears to be an improve-
ment. At the same time, White people remained over-
represented as homicide victims (35%) compared to 
their representation in crime reports (13%). Similarly, 
news programs overrepresented White people as 
officers (73%) compared to employment records 
(53%). Therefore, although the portrayal of Black char-
acters improved, White people continued to dominate 
the news as victims and officers.
These findings (as well as others described below) 
left me wondering about the role of context in the por-
trayal of race and crime. Many of our studies sampled 
only crime stories. What would we find in other news 
topics or contexts? We investigated this by considering 


Media Effects 21
how family was discussed in news and opinion media. 
The sample reflected the range of sources from which 
people now get their news, including legacy media 
(e.g., CNN) and digital opinion media (e.g., Breitbart.
com). We sampled over 800 news stories that prom-
inently mentioned family (e.g., mother, family, father), 
to assess how family might be discussed based on the 
race of the family members.
We found significant and large differences. First, 
criminality and Black people returned to the forefront. 
Black family members were overrepresented as crim-
inal suspects in the news (37%) compared to arrest 
records (26%). The opposite was true of White fam-
ily members (28% associated with crime in the news, 
70% of criminal suspects according to crime reports). 
Second, Black families were often overrepresented as 
being both poor and welfare recipients compared to 
official reports. Finally, Black fathers were consistently 
depicted as absentee dads, which did not match with 
official studies of Black father interactions with their 
kids. Thus, we found that context matters. When we 
focus on families, we find both classic stereotypes of 
Black criminality and additional stereotypes of pov-
erty and Black father abandonment. These findings 
were evident both in conservative opinion media such 
as the Blaze and legacy sources such as ABC News.
In another context, Mastro, Blecha, and Atwell 
Seate (2011) analyzed The New Y ork Times, The Los 
Angeles Times, and USA Today. Black criminal athletes 
were overrepresented compared to the percentage 
of Black athletes in their respective sports. Coverage 
included explicit details about the crimes committed 
by Black but not White criminals, was more accusatory 
toward Black than White athlete criminals, and left the 
impression that White athletes were less responsible 
for their crimes than Black athletes.
Although much of my work compared African 
Americans and Whites, I have also considered the por-
trayal of other groups, especially the depictions of Lati-
nos. My investigation of Latinos in crime news (Dixon &  
Linz, 2000a, 2000b) found that Latinos were largely 
underrepresented as perpetrators (29% on the news 
vs. 47% in crime reports), officers (10% on the news vs. 
25% in employment records), and victims (19% on the 
news vs. 54% in crime reports), appearing to replicate 
the conclusions of other scholars who had examined 
Latino depictions in entertainment media (Mastro, 
2009; Mastro & Greenberg, 2000). Latinos occupied 
little space in English-language media and tended to 
be invisible no matter what role was examined.
When I studied the depiction of Latinos during 
my more recent analytical update of Los Angeles news 
stations, I found that their portrayal had shifted. Latinos 
were now accurately depicted as perpetrators on TV . 
However, they continued to be underrepresented as 
homicide victims in news programs (10%) compared 
to crime reports (50%) and as police officers (16%) 
compared to employment records (30%).
Similar to the African American crime portrayals 
mentioned above, context may also matter when we 
consider Latino portrayals. We examined the immi-
grant status of suspects accused of crime on national 
broadcast and cable news coverage of immigration 
(Dixon & Williams, 2015). We found that Latino immi-
grants were overrepresented as criminals (97%) com-
pared to official reports (47%). We also found that 
TV news overrepresented the percentage of undoc-
umented Latinos (99%) compared to official reports 
(75%). The mainstream legacy news media contribute 
to the misplaced notion that Latinos are bringing crime 
and drugs to the US.
This study also examined the depiction of Mus-
lims and terrorism, finding that the news media con-
sistently associated terrorism with Islam. News media 
greatly overrepresented Muslims as US terrorism sus-
pects (81%) compared to official reports (6%). In fact, 
the media often struggle to present White supremacist 
militia extremists as responsible for most US-based 
terrorism. Instead, many of these White terrorists tend 
to be framed as simply mentally ill.
The Effects of Stereotyping on Social 
Reality Perceptions
Despite the slight updates and changes in news 
portrayals, the media tend to promote gross stere-
otypes of various racial groups. Black people are 
associated with crime, poverty, and social instability. 
Latinos are framed as undocumented immigrants 
involved with crime. Muslims are terrorist suspects. 
Whites appear as victims and officers and not ter -
rorism suspects. These portrayals have significant 
implications for media audiences’ understandings 
of various minoritized groups.

22 Audiences
Many scholars interested in the effects of dis-
torted racial portrayals have used cognitive acces-
sibility and priming to explain what happens after 
exposure (Dixon, 2020). Cognitive accessibility sug-
gests that people use mental shortcuts to make rele-
vant social judgments. So, someone encountering an 
individual linked to a stereotype (e.g., a Muslim) might 
make a judgment about that person based on repeated 
exposure to the stereotype (e.g., seeing Islamic terror-
ists on TV). For example, because Latinos are repeat-
edly shown as undocumented immigrants in the news, 
news exposure to Latinos may activate the cognitive 
linkage between Latinos and criminal immigration. 
This linkage may then be used in race and crime 
judgments (e.g., increased support for deportations). 
Research has shown that cognitive accessibility leads 
viewers exposed to Muslim terrorism to support civil 
restrictions and other policies that harm Muslims 
(Saleem, Prot, Anderson, & Lemieux, 2017), and that 
exposure to undocumented immigrant Latinos leads to 
increased notions of immigrant threat (Atwell Seate & 
Mastro, 2017).
Our own research has uncovered the effect of 
stereotype accessibility in multiple experiments. In a 
series of studies (Dixon, 2006a, 2006b; Dixon & Azocar,  
2006), we exposed participants to a news clip pre-
senting Black suspects, unidentified criminals, White 
criminals, or non-crime stories. Participants exposed 
to Black suspects tended to view a subsequent Black 
criminal suspect as guilty of his alleged offense, espe-
cially if participants watched a lot of news. In addition, 
participants exposed to Black suspects were more 
likely than those exposed to non-crime stories to 
believe that the world was a dangerous place, espe-
cially if they watched a lot of news. Given that African 
Americans are linked with criminality so often in news, 
exposure to crime news devoid of racial identifiers still 
elicited unfavorable thoughts about Blacks. When pre-
sented with illegal activity committed by unidentified 
suspects, audiences still linked African Americans with 
criminality and inferred that the perpetrators were 
African American (Devine, 1989; Shrum, 2002).
Although experiments allow us to determine 
causality, they are by necessity contrived and do not 
represent actual media content in a natural viewing 
environment. So, I undertook a pair of surveys, asking 
how often respondents watched local (Dixon, 2008a) 
and network news (Dixon, 2008b) programs. I also 
asked questions designed to uncover the extent to 
which respondents held certain stereotypical views of 
Black people. Because I had examined how often var-
ious news programs portrayed Black people as crim-
inals, I could calculate how often various local news 
viewers were exposed to this stereotype. Viewers who 
watched local news shows portraying the worst crim-
inal stereotypes endorsed the view that Black people 
were violent. Heavy local news viewers exposed to a 
Black or unidentified criminal were more likely than 
those exposed to a White criminal to believe that he 
could not be reformed, and those exposed to network 
news programs tended to endorse explicit racism 
against Black people. These findings indeed appear 
to complement and extend our earlier experimental 
results. Exposure to racialized crime news reinforces 
stereotypes of Black people, through a process of cog-
nitive accessibility. However, do new media make this 
situation better or worse?
New Media Pitfalls and Opportunities
People’s increasing reliance on digital resources 
for news (Pew Research Center, 2013) presents 
both opportunities and pitfalls. Most people follow 
sources that reinforce their opinions and political 
leanings and algorithms map users’ behavioral pat-
terns and give people more of what they had previ-
ously liked. Therefore, there are fewer opportunities 
to confront and challenge our biases (Dixon, 2017b). 
I have argued that this reinforces the cognitive acces-
sibility problems laid out above and lays the ground-
work for increased stereotyping of racial groups. I 
have described this pattern using a construct I call 
the Socially Mediated Stereotyping Model (SMSM). 
The SMSM suggests that stereotype reinforcement 
can be driven by the affordances and algorithms of 
social media designed to encourage ingroup iden-
tification. Thinking about how we began this chap-
ter, discussing the Jan. 6 attack on the US capital, 
early indications suggest that many of the Trump 
supporters had been caught in a right-wing media 
bubble or silo. This silo contained multiple reinforc-
ing stereotypes about racial and political groups that 


Media Effects 23
increased stereotype accessibility and helped rein-
force ingroup nationalist identity (Dixon, 2020).
On the other hand, people who use digital 
media to challenge their own and other’s stereotypes 
might actually reduce racial bias. We can use tech-
nology to resist prejudice and stereotyping, making 
the media message less potent (Devine, 1989; Liv-
ingston & Brewer, 2002). In some of my ongoing 
work, I demonstrate that heavy social media users 
with a strong activist orientation rejected the idea 
that Blacks have a propensity toward crime and 
embraced police reform compared to non-so-
cial media activists. This demonstrates that social 
media has many pitfalls but some opportunities to 
reverse negative stereotyping as well.
We must remain aware and critical of our 
media content, whether digital or legacy media. 
Y ou should read and watch the news, but you 
should consider the credibility and potential biases 
of these news sources, especially online sources. 
Approach crime news with a critical eye. As cit-
izens, consider becoming involved and advocat-
ing for more balanced coverage of topics. Twitter, 
email, and digital messaging have made it rela-
tively easy to reach out to media outlets. Above 
all, remember that the media do have an effect and 
that we all play a part in dealing with it.

2.3: POSITIVE MEDIA PSYCHOLOGY: 
THE ROLE OF UPLIFTING MEDIA IN 
ENCOURAGING SOCIAL GOOD
Mary Beth Oliver, Bingbing Zhang, and 
Magdalayna Drivas
As you will see throughout this book, researchers 
have long explored the negative effects of media 
In this overview of media effects, the authors look at 
something you might not yet have considered: how 
media can uplift us and help us become our higher 
and better selves.


Media Effects 25
when it comes to race, class, gender, and sexuality. 
This focus is for good reason; we must understand 
how media can affect stereotyping, prejudice, and 
diminished self-esteem. However, if we can envi-
sion how media may cause harms, we can also 
envision how media may be harnessed for social 
good. Over the last decade, we (first author Oliver, 
with colleagues) have studied the meaningful and 
positive sides of media, looking at how media might 
uplift people, cause us to want to be our “higher and 
better” selves, help us see the good sides of human 
nature, and enhance our feelings of connectedness 
with broader and more diverse groups of people 
(Oliver et al., 2021; Raney et al., 2021). Here, we 
describe how positive media psychology employs 
the concepts of eudaimonic and self-transcendent 
responses, discuss what research tells us about how 
often people consume inspiring content and the 
types of portrayals that appear to evoke this reac-
tion, look at the outcomes associated with uplift-
ing media and how those outcomes are related to 
issues of social good, and discuss some challenges 
present in this line of scholarship.
Hedonic versus Eudaimonic Media 
Gratifications
Early in the scholarship of media psychology, 
researchers realized that audiences are not passive. 
When we consume most types of media, we often 
do so for a reason. How are we feeling when we want 
to watch a sitcom? What was our day like when we 
want to watch a thriller rather than a romance? 
Scholars from a uses and gratifications perspective 
argue that to understand how media affect viewers, 
we must also understand what motivates people in 
their media selections and what gratifications they 
experience from media consumption (Palmgreen  
et al., 1985). Some people may need information 
and use the media to gain insights into current hap-
penings, others may be lonely and use the media for 
companionship, and yet others may be feeling stress 
and turn to media to unwind or kick back at the end 
of the day.
Building on this tradition of looking at people’s 
motivations for media consumption, Zillmann and  
Bryant (1985) argued that even if people are not aware 
of why they consume different media offerings, their 
media behaviors are predictable. Namely, in introduc-
ing the concept of mood management, these research-
ers argued that one of the primary motivations for 
our media selections is to manage our moods. In 
particular, they reasoned that we fundamentally oper-
ate as hedonists – motivated to maximize pleasurable 
moods and to minimize negative moods. What does 
this mean? Consider returning home from a stressful 
day. Do you watch a suspenseful thriller? A nail-biting 
sports event? From a mood management perspec-
tive, you may watch these types of genres, but you are 
probably more likely to turn to content that is soothing, 
relaxing, and that helps ease your stress.
The assumption that we are hedonists makes 
intuitive sense, but the picture becomes cloudy when 
we think about different types of narratives. Consider 
movies such as Schindler’s List or Hotel Rwanda. It is 
difficult to imagine that people watch these mov-
ies to feel pleasure. In thinking about why a person 
might choose to view these types of heart-wrenching 
media experiences, we first considered that at times, 
people might actually like to feel sad (Oliver, 1993). 
Phrases such as “having a good cry” are frequently 
used to capture these feelings. However, the more we 
thought about this, the more we began to consider 
that perhaps people use these types of content not 
to experience sadness per se but to experience mean-
ing. In shifting our focus (Oliver & Raney, 2011), we 
were reminded of Aristotle’s (trans. 1961) distinction 
between hedonic well-being (pleasure) and eudaimonic 
well-being (human flourishing). Eudaimonia refers to 
gratifications and states that may not be pleasurable 
per se but are experienced as deeply meaningful, such 
as self-realization, insight into life’s purpose, and per-
sonal development (Waterman, 1993). We reasoned 
that media entertainment can address both hedonic 
and eudaimonic concerns and that these concerns 
are not necessarily mutually exclusive. For example, 
many people find the film The Shawshank Redemp-
tion both enjoyable and meaningful. Consistent with 
this reasoning, our research showed that people  
tend to report greater enjoyment of media content that 
evokes feelings of thrill and humor but greater appre-
ciation of content that grapples with questions such 
as purpose in life or the human condition (Oliver & 
Bartsch, 2011).

26 Audiences
Media and Self-transcendence
As we continued to study meaningful media, we 
broadened our conceptualization of user responses. 
In particular, we shifted our focus somewhat from 
studying eudaimonic gratifications to looking at 
how media can elicit self-transcendent responses 
(Oliver et al., 2018). Unlike eudaimonic gratifica-
tions, feelings of self-transcendence shift attention 
away from one’s own personal or egoistic concerns 
toward a recognition of other people, of nature, or 
even the universe at large. In shifting our attention 
outwardly, we also have a tendency to recognize our 
interconnections with others, realizing that although 
we may come from different cultures, countries, or 
experiences, we share common hopes, dreams, and 
concerns (Yaden et al., 2017).
There are a many types of self-
 tr
anscendent 
responses, some of which have received more 
research attention than others. One commonly stud-
ied response is elevation – the feelings that arise when 
we witness others display exemplary acts of “moral 
beauty” such as kindness, generosity, or compassion. 
When we feel elevated, we may experience tears, 
a lump in the throat, or even chills (Algoe & Haidt, 
2009). A related concept is kama muta – a Sanskrit 
word referring to feeling moved by witnessing com-
munal sharing, such as family members reuniting 
and sharing hugs at the airport after a long separa-
tion (Fiske et al., 2017). Finally, some scholars have 
increasingly begun to explore the self-transcendent 
emotion of awe. Many things may elicit awe, including 
vast landscapes, the stars above, or a rainbow span-
ning the horizon. In general, researchers suggest that 
experiencing awe involves feeling that the self is small 
compared to the vastness of nature or the universe, 
and needing to reframe our perspective to make 
sense of such vastness (Keltner & Haidt, 2003).
How Common Are Uplifting Media 
Experiences?
Thus far, we have described how media can evoke 
eudaimonic and/or self-transcendent states, but how 
often do people actually experience these types of 
responses? To examine this question, we have con-
ducted a variety of studies looking at how frequently 
people are inspired by media, user traits that predict 
exposure, and the types of media content that people 
often experience as inspiring.
To get a broad picture of how often people are 
inspired by media, we conducted two national sur -
veys of U.S. respondents (Janicke-Bowles et al., 2021; 
Raney et al., 2018). We found that the vast majority 
of people have experienced inspiration from media, 
including music, film, books, television, and social 
media. We also found that some personality traits 
(spirituality, empathy, and gratitude) are associated 
with greater consumption of inspiring media.
We have also conducted content analyses to 
study the types of content that tend to elicit inspiration. 
We analyzed Y ouTube videos tagged as “inspirational” 
and found that the most typical portrayals depicted 
hope, appreciation of beauty and excellence, and grat-
itude (Dale et al., 2017). In another study, we looked 
at inspiring versus non-inspiring New Y ork Times news 
stories that were frequently shared (Ji et al., 2018). We 
found that words related to awe, elevation, hope, and 
gratitude were more frequently included in inspira-
tional than non-inspirational stories. Researchers have 
expanded this research to include contemporary types 
of content that may evoke inspiration. For example, 
Rieger and Klimmt (2019) studied memes associated 
with the hashtags #inspirational and #meaningful 
to see what additional hashtags were present. Their 
findings mirrored those of our work, with the target 
hashtags associated with hashtags such as #love, 
#beautiful, #happy, #peace, and #wisdom.
Outcomes of Inspiring Media 
Experiences and Implications for Race/
Class/Gender
Thus far, we have identified how media may pro-
vide individuals with meaningful and experiences 
(including eudaimonic and self-transcendent 
responses), and we have presented evidence that 
these are common experiences while consuming a 
variety of media content. In this section, we discuss 
additional outcomes associated with meaningful 
media experiences and then turn to what they may 
imply about issues related to race, class, and gender.
In general, research in positive media psychology 
shows that inspiring media experiences have a host 


Media Effects 27
of prosocial outcomes. Sometimes, these outcomes 
are simply positive motivations such as desiring to 
be a better person. Other times, though, studies have 
observed actual changes in behavior such as work-
ing for a charity, donating money, or helping others 
with tasks (see Schnall & Roper, 2012). This body of 
research also shows that the experience of inspiration 
can affect perceptions of other people and our con-
nections, including increasing beliefs that people are 
generally good-hearted and that we are all intercon-
nected and part of the same human experience (Oliver 
et al., 2021). Overall, this research implies that there 
may be a host of prosocial outcomes related to race, 
class, and gender, although most of the research in this 
area has focused on race and sexuality.
One of the hallmarks of racism and prejudice is 
seeing different racial and ethnic groups as out-group 
members (Tajfel & Turner, 1986). When people per-
ceive members of other racial and cultural groups as 
different and distant from themselves, they tend to per-
ceive their own group members as superior to those 
in other groups. Importantly, if media can elicit expe-
riences of elevation and inspiration, the resulting feel-
ings of heightened connection with others could play a 
role in reducing racism.
In an early study, we tested this by having White 
participants view one of three types of short videos 
that are often encountered on Y ouTube or social 
media: videos that were uplifting, videos that were 
humorous but not particularly inspiring, or a control 
video (Oliver et al., 2015). We found that elevation in 
response to the uplifting videos increased perceptions 
that humans are basically good and interconnected. 
These perceptions were associated with more favora-
ble attitudes toward multiple non-White groups (e.g., 
African Americans, Asians, Latinos). We found simi-
lar results in a later study where watching videos of 
human kindness led to greater intentions to interact 
with diverse others in the future (Krämer et al., 2017).
In terms of sexuality, we are aware of only few 
experiments examining how inspiring media may 
reduce negative attitudes toward members of the 
LGBTQ+ community. As with our research on racial 
attitudes, one early study compared how neutral, 
amusing, or inspiring videos would affect prejudicial 
attitudes toward gay men (Lai et al., 2014). Although 
the effects were small, the inspiring videos did reduce 
negative attitudes. However, other studies have failed 
to find similar effects (Bartos et al., 2020), so additional 
work is needed to help us understand when these 
types of media materials will be effective.
So far, the research we have reviewed on inspir-
ing media and prejudice reduction has focused on 
attitudes. However, reporting more positive attitudes is 
different from actually engaging in prosocial behaviors. 
It can be quite easy to say that one intends to interact 
with another person or to help another person, but it 
is quite different to actually do the behavior. Neverthe-
less, some studies suggest that inspiring media can play 
a role in affecting behavioral support for oppressed 
groups. For example, Freeman et al. (2009) found that 
exposure to inspiring media encouraged greater char-
itable giving to a Black-oriented cause (The United 
Negro College Fund) – particularly among people who 
were otherwise least likely to give.
Challenges in Using Inspiring Media for 
Social Good
Overall, current and ongoing research in positive 
media psychology paints a hopeful picture in terms 
of using media for social good. However, there are a 
number of challenges and gaps in the literature that 
we need to consider.
First, as mentioned previously, most of the 
research in this area has focused on race and, to a 
lesser extent, sexuality. In contrast, how inspiring 
media may play a role in terms of gender is almost 
non-existent. In many respects, this lack of research 
is surprising because touching or uplifting content is 
generally more heavily consumed by women than 
men. However, if we re-conceptualize “inspirational” 
media to mean “motivational” (rather than eudai-
monic or self-transcendent), then we see a great deal 
more research, and particularly as it relates to body 
image. Much of this research has focused on “fitspira-
tion” on social media sites such as Instagram in which 
influencers try to motivate others to be more healthy 
and physically fit. However, experimental research 
suggests that rather than serving as reassuring moti-
vator for young women, exposure to fitspiration posts 
can actually increase negative body image (Dignard 
& Jarry, 2021; Rounds & Stutts, 2021). Similar effects 
have been found among men (Fatt et al., 2019; Y ee 

28 Audiences
et al., 2020). Clearly, more work is needed in this area 
because “inspiring” content may, under some circum-
stances, have unintended detrimental effects.
Likewise, research is sorely lacking in terms of 
issues related to social class, although numerous exam-
ples of “random acts of kindness” videos are presumed 
to be inspiring. For example, media that depict over-
coming poverty often focus on either the sheer hard 
work of the impoverished person (suggesting that pov-
erty is an individual problem) or the generosity of some 
individual in providing resources or money. In the latter 
case, one might feasibly suggest that such generosity 
may be inspiring or elevating to viewers, motivating 
them to be generous in turn. However, as Conrad-Pérez 
et al. pointed out, such “charity savior” narratives may 
reinforce the characterization of impoverished peo-
ple as “needy victims who can only be saved through 
acts of charity” (2021, p. 3973) while ignoring the need 
for structural changes (e.g., government programs) to 
address systemic inequality. Further, although research 
on moral emotions confirms that exemplary acts of 
kindness and generosity may elicit elevation, some 
research suggests that under some circumstances, it can 
also elicit feelings of pity (Bartsch et al., 2018).
In terms of race, anecdotal evidence suggests 
that under some circumstances, media content that 
may be intended to inspire may be perceived as crass 
or even offensive. In 2017, Pepsi aired a television 
commercial featuring Kendall Jenner as a heroic fig-
ure in a social protest mirroring a Black Lives Matter 
event. Rather than seeing the ad as inspirational, many 
viewers expressed outrage, posting comments such as 
“Who knew a can of Pepsi could solve centuries of 
systemic discrimination and abuse. Tone deaf does not 
even begin to describe this...” . As a result, Pepsi pulled 
the ad after only one day. Likewise, many motion pic-
tures that may have been intended to be moving in 
their portrayals of race (e.g., Blind Side, The Help) are 
often characterized as “White savior films” (see Ash, 
2017). Such films cast White characters as heroic in 
helping people of color, suggesting that any successes 
that people of color experience are due to the kind-
ness and warm-hearted help of White people. Thus, in 
attempting to employ inspiring media to reduce racial 
prejudice, we should keep in mind that inauthentic or 
demeaning depictions may be perceived as negative 
or offensive in some circumstances.
Looking Toward the Future
This overview of the role of inspiring media and its 
intersection with issues related to race, class, and 
gender generally suggests the hopeful possibility that 
media can lead to greater feelings of compassion, 
increased altruistic behaviors, and lessened feelings of 
disdain or prejudice. However, given that this is a rela-
tively young area of research among media psycholo-
gists, we are now seeing that some types of “inspiring” 
media may have no effects or, in some circumstances, 
have an opposite effect than intended. As we move 
forward in this line of research, we are excited not 
only to become more nuanced in our theorizing but 
also to explore the myriad ways that positive media 
may lead us to reach our higher, better selves.

2.4: BODY IMAGE AND ADOLESCENT 
GIRLS’ SELFIE POSTING, EDITING, AND 
INVESTMENT
Jennifer Stevens Aubrey and Larissa Terán
Some argue that selfies or photographic self-por -
traits uploaded to social media websites are tools of 
empowerment that allow users to control how they 
are seen by others (e.g., Simmons, 2013). Reflecting 
this thinking, in 2014 the Dove Self-Esteem Project 
released a short film called Selfie, in which selfies 
were presented, through the perspectives of adoles-
cent girls, as an empowering way for “them to rede-
fine beauty one picture at a time” (Moss, 2014). In 
the video, teen girls and their mothers were trained 
to take a good selfie and were encouraged to accept 
diverse bodies and appearances, especially their own. 
It is a heartwarming story of mothers and daughters 
listening to each other’s appearance insecurities and 
learning how to overcome them together.
At the same time, these girls and their mothers 
focused on particular body parts and appearance 
attributes that were deemed most appealing to oth-
ers, and how to present themselves in ways others 
will appreciate. At the end of the video, the girls hang 
selfies in an art gallery, while observers attach post-it 
notes to the pictures, noting their success in presenting 
particular body parts in an appealing manner.
Selfies provide opportunities to scrutinize one’s 
appearance from an outsider’s perspective and to 
verify others’ approval (or lack thereof) of one’s 
appearance. When people apply this perspective to 
the self, they are likely to learn to view themselves 
as objects to be looked at by others, a tendency 
called self-objectification (Fredrickson & Roberts, 
1997). This is a concern for adolescent girls’ mental 
and behavioral health because self-objectification 
is related to low interoceptive awareness (dimin-
ished ability to detect one’s body signals), dimin-
ished capacity to achieve optimal concentration in 
a given task, and increased appearance anxiety and 
body shame (Moradi & Huang, 2008). In turn, these 
consequences put girls and women at risk for eating 
disorders, depression, and sexual dysfunction. Thus, 
one could think of self-objectification as a gateway 
to the dark side of adolescence, leading to some of 
the most prevalent health concerns adolescents, 
especially girls, face.
In light of these perspectives, it is important 
to examine the role of selfies in female adoles-
cents’ body image. Are selfies a tool of empower -
ment or a detriment to adolescents’ experiences? 
To answer this question, we conducted a survey of 
female adolescents (ages 14–17) that was designed 
to assess different facets of selfie activities, self-
 
objectific
ation, and both negative and positive sub-
jective evaluation of one’s appearance.
Selfie Culture
In 2013, Oxford Dictionaries declared the word 
selfie the word of the year. In 2017, a Y ouGov poll 
of American adults showed that 94% were familiar 
with the term, and 69% had taken at least one selfie 
(Bame, 2017). In light of its popularity, this phenom-
enon has garnered scholarly interest from both the 
qualitative and quantitative perspectives.
The authors surveyed adolescent girls to see 
whether selfie activities are related to the girls’ 
self-
 objectific
ation, appearance anxiety, and 
body esteem.


Media Effects 31
Qualitative research, which undertakes in-depth 
investigations of people’s experiences, has generated 
differing perspectives of selfies. On the one hand, self-
ies are seen as self-therapeutic. They can create an 
image of the self that is in opposition to the demands 
of a consumer culture that prescribes narrow con-
ceptions of attractiveness (Kedzior & Allen, 2016). 
Although selfies can feel empowering to the individ-
ual, they simultaneously reproduce and contribute to a 
sexually objectifying culture and maintain social hier-
archies based on appearance (Kedzior & Allen, 2016). 
Additionally, adolescent girls perceive that sexualized 
selfies garner more likes, but the reaction to this obser-
vation varied greatly (Davidson & Ribak, 2017). Some 
teen girls defended the practice as an expression of 
their self-identity, whereas others found it problematic, 
signaling a lack of self-confidence.
Quantitative research, which uses numerical data 
to draw statistically supported conclusions, has tended 
to suggest that selfies are disempowering. Based on a 
nationally representative sample of U.S. social media 
users, Fox and Vendemia (2016) found that women put 
more effort into presenting a socially desirable physi-
cal appearance online by editing photos, and women’s 
body image and tendency to compare themselves neg-
atively to ideal others drove this behavior. Additionally, 
selfie behaviors were associated with adolescent girls’ 
over-evaluation of shape and weight, body dissatisfac-
tion, dietary restraint, and internalization of the thin 
ideal (McLean, Paxton, Wertheim, & Masters, 2015).
In light of the findings from both qualitative and 
quantitative researchers, it is clear that engaging with 
digital and social media is consequential for adoles-
cent girls (McLean et al., 2015). Throughout a complex 
system of media messages from multiple platforms, 
girls are reminded that their appearance is a vital crite-
rion on which their value is based and that they should 
make sexiness a priority (Ward & Aubrey, 2017). At the 
same time, adolescents experience increased pres-
sure to conform to culturally sanctioned gender roles 
(Hill & Lynch, 1983). Pubertal changes, alongside new 
experiences with dating, create expectations that girls 
behave in more feminine, sexually attractive ways.
Another key developmental hallmark of 
adolescence is egocentrism. As adolescents’ 
brains develop, they start to conceptualize their 
own thoughts and the thoughts of others, which 
represents major cognitive development (Elkind, 
1967). However, they fail to differentiate between 
their own mental preoccupations and what others 
are thinking about. Thus, they tend to believe that 
other people are as obsessed with their behavior 
and appearance as they are, a phenomenon known 
as imaginary audience beliefs. Social media use is 
related to imaginary audience ideation (Cingel & 
Krcmar, 2014), likely because adolescents use social 
media to control the way their imagined audience 
sees them.
Research Questions and Procedure
For this study, we took inspiration from objectifica-
tion theory (Fredrickson & Roberts, 1997). Because 
selfies allow users to present themselves to others in 
their social network and to consider their network’s 
evaluations of their appearance, we reasoned that 
selfie activities would be associated with self-
 
objectific
ation. Further, we examined the relation-
ships between selfie activities and adolescent girls’ 
subjective evaluations of their appearance, both 
from a negative (e.g., appearance anxiety) and from 
a positive (e.g., body esteem) point of view. We dis-
tinguished between three types of selfie activities: 
frequency of selfie posting, editing selfies, and one’s 
investment into selfies (McLean et al., 2015). Edit-
ing and investment imply that users scrutinize their 
appearance before and after posting selfies; thus, 
we reasoned that they should be examined sepa-
rately from the sheer frequency of posting selfies. 
We posed three research questions.
RQ1: Are selfie activities related to adolescent girls’ 
self-objectification?
RQ2: Are selfie activities related to adolescent girls’ 
appearance anxiety?
RQ3: Are selfie activities related to adolescent girls’ 
body esteem?
We wanted to explain the unique relationships 
between selfie behaviors and body image. Therefore, 
it was important to control for other variables that 
could explain adolescent girls’ body image. Doing 
so is a rigorous way to test these links because it 
rules out the possibility that the associations are 

32 Audiences
simply spurious, or attributable to some other third 
variable. In our study, we controlled for participants’ 
body mass index (BMI), age, race, frequency of 
social media use, and imaginary audience beliefs.
We addressed these research questions using a 
cross-sectional survey of adolescent girls. This sam-
ple was recruited through a private survey firm. Adults 
who had a daughter between the ages of 14 and  
17 were contacted to see if their daughter would like 
to participate in the survey for a small amount of 
monetary compensation. If the parent consented and 
the daughter assented, the adolescent completed a 
20-minute online survey. Of the 296 participants who 
completed the survey, 18 participants were dropped 
from the analyses because they failed attention checks. 
Thus, the final sample consisted of 278 adolescent girls 
ages 14–17 (M
age = 15.57, SD = 1.11, 64.4% White/
European American, 10.4% Black/African American, 
8.3% Latina, 16.7% other).
We measured selfie-posting frequency, selfie edit-
ing, and selfie investment. First, participants were pro-
vided with a definition of selfies and asked to report 
how often on a 6-point scale they post selfies (0 = 
Never, 1 = Very Infrequently, 5 = Very Frequently). 
For selfie editing we asked how often participants used 
eight editing techniques on their selfies before posting 
(e.g., getting rid of red eye) on a 5-point scale (1 = 
Never, 5 = Always). For selfie investment, we asked 
three questions that assessed how much participants 
were preoccupied with their selfies before posting. 
Participants indicated on a slider scale from 0 to 100 
where they fell between two extremes (e.g., “I don’t 
care what photos I post” versus “I carefully select the 
best photo to post”).
For the body image variables, we used established 
and validated scales. To measure 
 s
elf-objectification, 
participants filled out the Self-Objectification Beliefs 
and Behaviors Scale (Lindner & Tantleff-Duncan, 
2017). Example items included “looking attractive to 
others is more important to me than being happy with 
who I am inside” and “I choose specific clothing or 
accessories based on how they make my body appear 
to others” (1 = Strongly Disagree, 5 = Strongly Agree). 
Participants also completed the Social Appearance 
Anxiety Scale (Hart, Flora, Palyo, Fresco, Holle, & 
Heimberg, 2008). Example items included “I get tense 
when it is obvious people are looking at me” and “I 
am uncomfortable when I think others are noticing 
flaws in my appearance” (1 = Definitely Disagree,  
5 = 
 Definit
ely Agree). Participants completed the 
Appearance Evaluation Subscale of the Body-Esteem 
Scale (Mendelson, Mendelson, & White, 2001). Exam-
ple items included “I like my looks just the way they 
are” and “I like the way I look without my clothes”  
(1 = Strongly Disagree, 5 = Strongly Agree).
BMI was calculated from participants’ self-
 
r
eported height and weight. Race was treated as a 
dichotomous variable (1 = White, 0 = all other). Partic-
ipants reported on a 6-point scale how often they used 
social media (0 = Never, 5 = Very Frequently). Finally, 
participants completed the New Imaginary Audience 
Scale (Goossens, Beyers, Emmen, & van Aken, 2002), 
consisting of 23 items assessing how often the adoles-
cents imagined themselves in different situations (e.g., 
“being admired for being cool,” 1 = Never, 4 = Often).
Findings: It Is a Matter of How 
Adolescents Approach Selfies
To answer our research questions, we conducted 
multiple regression analyses. This is a technique 
that allowed us to test the relationship between the 
selfie behaviors and the three self-image variables 
while simultaneously controlling for the other var -
iables that might be related to body image. In the 
following, we will report the results of three regres-
sion models, one for each body image variable. In 
the models, we report whether a control variable 
and each of the selfie behaviors are statistically sig-
nificant (i.e., is not due to statistical chance). The 
index of the relationship is represented by a beta (β) 
coefficient, which can be negative (i.e., one variable 
is related to a decrease in the other) or positive (i.e., 
one variable is related to an increase in the other). A 
β near 0 means that there is no relationship between 
the variables; a β of around .10 is a small relation-
ship, .30 is medium, and .50 is strong.
Overall, the model for RQ1 explained a sta-
tistically significant amount of variance in self-
 
objectific
ation, F(8, 206) = 16.28, p < 0.001, adjusted 
R2 = 0.37. The only control variable associated with 
self-
 objectific
ation was imaginary audience beliefs 
(β = 0.43, p < 0.001). Of the selfie variables, selfie edit-
ing (β = 0.21, p = 0.001) and selfie investment (β = 0.13, 


Media Effects 33
p = 0.039) were associated with self-objectification, but 
selfie frequency was not (β = 0.05, p = 0.510).
The model for RQ2 explained a significant 
amount of variance in appearance anxiety, F(8, 206) =  
17.10, p < 0.001, adjusted R2 = 0.39. In this model, 
adolescents’ BMI (β = 0.19, p = 0.001) and imag-
inary audience beliefs (β = 0.34, p < 0.001) were 
positively associated with appearance anxiety. Sim-
ilarly, selfie editing (β = 0.28, p < 0.001) and selfie 
investment (β = 0.22, p < 0.001) positively predicted 
appearance anxiety, but selfie frequency did not 
(β = −0.13, p = 0.089).
The model for RQ3 explained a significant 
amount of variance in body esteem, F(8, 206) = 
6.02, p < 0.001, adjusted R
2 = 0.17. Of the control 
variables, only BMI was statistically significant, 
negatively predicting body esteem (β = −0.35, p < 
0.001). Selfie investment negatively predicted body 
esteem (β = −0.24, p = 0.001). Neither selfie editing 
(β = −0.06, p = 0.444) nor selfie posting (β = 0.11, 
p = 0.224) was related to body esteem.
Taking Stock of Selfies
The notion that selfies are tools of self-empowerment,  
at least in terms of body image, is challenged by 
these results. But an important caveat is that ado-
lescent girls’ approach to selfies matters. The 
frequency of posting selfies was unrelated to adoles-
cents’ body image outcomes. Rather, the investment 
in selfies and editing of selfies are the activities that 
have disempowering potential. Two patterns of find-
ings support this contention. First, selfie investment 
was associated with all three body image variables, 
in the disempowering directions. Selfie invest-
ment was positively related to self-objectification  
and appearance anxiety, whereas selfie investment 
was negatively related to body esteem. All three 
of these relations were statistically significant, but 
the size of the relations varied from small (self-
 
objectific
ation) to small-to-medium (appearance 
anxiety and body esteem). Second, selfie edit-
ing was positively related to self-objectification 
and appearance anxiety. These were both medi-
um-sized relationships. Thus, selfie investment and 
editing represent an approach to selfies that sig-
nals the acknowledgment that one’s appearance is 
scrutinized by social media audiences. To the extent 
that adolescent girls apply these self-scrutinizing 
activities to their selfies, they are more likely to 
experience negative body image.
Girls who self-objectify tend to think of them-
selves as objects for others’ consumption and evalu-
ation (Fredrickson & Roberts, 1997). Selfies provide 
a salient way for adolescent girls to see (and control) 
how others see them. Thus, it makes sense that girls 
who self-objectify would take more pains to ensure 
that their selfies are appealing to others. Another 
premise of objectification theory is that girls are more 
likely to self-objectify than boys because their value 
and worth are more related to their appearance. Thus, 
investment in one’s selfies can be seen as a way of pro-
tecting one’s worth.
The results further suggested that girls who edit 
their selfies feel anxious about their appearance. If one 
were fearful of others’ appearance evaluations, using 
selfie-editing tools to make the photos more appeal-
ing would be a reasonable way to deal with such an 
anxiety. Indeed, this finding is in line with research on 
eating disorders that has shown that body monitoring, 
which is essentially invited from others when one posts 
a selfie, is a maintaining factor for body dissatisfaction, 
a key indicator of eating disorder pathology (Shafran, 
Fairburn, Robinson, & Lask, 2004). Girls who are pre-
occupied with how they look tend to become more 
vigilant and critical about their appearance, far from 
the empowerment that the Dove Self-Esteem Project 
would like consumers to believe (e.g., Simmons, 2013).
Finally, to test whether selfie activities were 
related to an empowering dimension of body image, 
we examined participants’ positive appearance eval-
uation, one facet of body esteem. The results showed 
that being fastidious about choosing the perfect photo 
was actually associated with lower body esteem. Thus, 
it is possible that girls feel pressure to post selfies 
because they are a normative social media practice, 
but their time, attention, and worry about choosing the 
right one are indicative of feeling not great about their 
appearance.
Although our findings illustrate adolescents’ 
experiences with the social media practice of self-
ies, we note that the study design does not allow us 
to make conclusions about the causal order between 
the variables. Posting selfies could result in adolescent 

34 Audiences
girls’ appearance anxiety, for example, as they receive 
and interpret feedback from their social networks on 
their appearance. Additionally, girls who are anxious 
about their appearance might use selfie-editing tools 
to make themselves appear appealing to others. In 
reality, the direction of influence probably goes both 
ways, in a reinforcing spiral (Slater, 2007), but further 
research is needed to sort out the causality.
Importantly, it is worth repeating that posting 
selfies is not harmful as an activity in and of itself. To 
be sure, selfies can be a fun way to document and 
share experiences with friends and family. However, 
peer approval and attention in the form of likes, fol-
lows, and comments can be intoxicating, especially 
in adolescence when imaginary audience ideation 
ramps up. For girls who are socialized to prioritize their 
appearance over most other characteristics, selfies 
can quickly turn into a platform of self-objectification. 
Obsessing about selfies and engaging self-scrutiny 
through selfie manipulation are practices that should 
be discouraged among adolescent girls. In the matter 
of selfies, it is not the frequency of posting, but rather 
an appearance-obsessive approach to posting selfies, 
that can backfire on adolescent girls’ body image.

2.5: SOCIAL MEDIA USE AND WELL-
BEING: A COMPARISON BETWEEN 
THE GENERAL POPULATION AND US 
MILITARY VETERANS
Marina Krcmar, Habiba Ahmed, and Frank T . 
Robinson, Jr.
Although research documents both positive and 
negative influence of social media use (SMU) on 
users’ health and well-being, little attention has been 
paid to identifying the impact of SMU on US mil-
itary veterans, who are active social media users. 
Our goal is to better understand how SMU relates to 
veterans’ well-being. We surveyed both the general 
population and veterans. Comparing these popula-
tions allows us to consider general well-being indi-
cators (e.g., loneliness, anxiety) linked with mental 
health and to highlight mental health outcomes par-
ticularly relevant to veterans (e.g., PTSD). Quantita-
tive data allow us to make statistical comparisons 
of the two groups. We also qualitatively analyzed 
veterans’ open-ended responses to questions about 
their experiences with social media.
Social Media Use and Well-Being
Research shows that some kinds of social media 
use result in negative well-being outcomes, whereas 
other kinds are associated with positive outcomes. 
Multiple studies have found an association between 
SMU and depression (e.g., Shensa et al., 2018), with 
public posts or social comparisons specifically influ-
encing depression (Faelens et al., 2021). Stress and 
anxiety are also associated with SMU. Time spent 
on Facebook was associated with increased stress 
(Bevan et al., 2014), but Shaw et al. (2015) found 
symptoms of anxiety associated with SMU only 
when passively used (e.g., scrolling and browsing). 
Even research showing that SMU is correlated with 
loneliness suggests that the effect is bi-directional 
(Clark et al., 2018), meaning that when people 
engage in SMU, they often do so out of loneliness, 
but unfortunately, SMU can increase loneliness.  
Perhaps SMU undermines feelings of social con-
nection by offering a mere illusion of connection or 
by taking time away from potentially more fulfilling 
offline connections.
Still, SMU can be associated with positive out-
comes; it can increase social connectedness or the 
feeling of belonging and relatedness with others (e.g., 
Ahn & Shin, 2013). Image-based social media allows 
for more intimacy, immediacy, and emotional connec-
tion (Pittman & Reich, 2016). SMU may also relate 
to social support (Nabi et al., 2013). In contrast, find-
ings on life satisfaction are mixed, depending largely 
on how social media are used (Krcmar et al., 2020). 
Facebook use is generally associated with lower life 
satisfaction (Stieger, 2019), and comparing oneself to 
others online is a consistent harbinger of lowered life 
satisfaction (Faelens et al., 2021).
Veterans’ Well-Being and SMU
Given the high levels of negative well-being out-
comes among veterans, looking at SMU and well- 
being among veterans is vital. We know that many 
veterans who actively use social media also suffer 
from depression, PTSD, and anxiety (Pedersen et al.,  
2015). Although in-person social contact among 
veterans lowered the risk of developing depression 
(Teo et al., 2018), social contact through Facebook 
did not affect the risk of depression or PTSD (Teo 
The authors investigated how social media use 
relates to military veterans’ well-being, and found 
that social media use can be both harmful and 
 beneficial – de
pending on how it is used.

36 Audiences
et al., 2019). Perhaps, much like the general pop-
ulation, the link between SMU and specific well- 
being outcomes for veterans depends on how social 
media are used. In other words, passively scrolling, 
socially comparing, and connecting with strangers 
are likely to have one set of outcomes, whereas 
direct communication with family and looking at 
images of close connections have another.
As noted, direct communication with family 
and friends may provide social connectedness for 
veterans. Benefits may extend from mere connection 
to alleviating loneliness or providing social support. 
Social connectedness and support may act as a buffer 
to negative well-being outcomes because both face-
to-face and mediated social connections can reduce 
loneliness (Rohrer et al., 2018) and increase social 
support (Asante & Castillo, 2018), and those are both 
connected to overall well-being. Furthermore, if SMU 
is used specifically for direct communication and com-
municating about emotions, social connectedness 
could be improved, especially among veterans who 
may be geographically distant from other veterans and 
others who may understand and help with their situ-
ations. If the ultimate goal is to decrease depression, 
there is reason for optimism – if social media are used 
in beneficial ways.
This research explores whether there are dif-
ferences between veterans and non-veterans in their 
SMU. We also explore the relationship between vari-
ous SMU behaviors and well-being indicators in these 
groups.
We administered an IRB-approved online ques-
tionnaire to adults, with efforts made to sample vet-
erans. The final sample of 164 included 58 veterans 
and 106 non-veterans. The veterans were mostly male 
(79%) and ranged in age from 31 to 80 (average = 59). 
They identified as 36% White, 62% Black or African 
American, and 1% other. The general (non-veteran) 
population sample identified as 41% male and 59% 
female, with ages ranging from 18 to 62 (average about 
27). They identified as 59% White, 23% Black or  
African American, 2% American Indian or Alaska 
Native, 8% Asian, and 6% Latinx.
Besides demographic information, we asked about 
SMU. These are combined into dimensions, listed in 
Table 2.5.1. The table presents the means and stand-
ard deviations of each dimension for the total sample, 
allowing us to see which SMU behaviors are more or 
less commonly used for the entire sample and broken 
down by sex and race. Because of the sample distri-
bution, we collapsed the race category into White and 
non-White.
We also measured negative well-being indicators 
(depression, stress, PTSD, anxiety, loneliness, and 
social disconnectedness) and positive well-being indica-
tors (life satisfaction and perceived social support). We 
asked the veteran sample open-ended questions about 
their online social comparison and emotional sharing.
What Did We Find?
The means in Table 2.5.1 show us that there are 
some differences in SMU by race and sex. Due to 
the small sample size, we compared only men vs. 
women and Whites vs. non-Whites. From this, pat-
terns suggested that although all groups used broad-
casting at about the same levels, Whites and females 
as compared to non-Whites and males engaged in 
more browsing, image creation, and social compar-
ison, as well as direct communication and engag-
ing with family and friends. Emotional sharing and 
self-presentation on social media were also used by 
females more than males; differences by race did 
not emerge for these behaviors.
After reviewing the relative usage of each type of 
SMU for the total sample and then based on race and 
sex, we turn to our statistical comparisons. Because of 
the sample size and distribution, we compare veterans 
and non-veterans, without further dividing the sam-
ples by race and sex. First, we compared veterans and 
non-veterans in their SMU across all uses (e.g., scroll-
ing, posting, social comparison) using a MANOV A, 
which allows us to look at differences between veter-
ans and non-veterans on many dependent measures 
at once. We controlled for age and sex because there 
are many more males than females in the veteran sam-
ple, and veterans were slightly older than non-veterans. 
We found a significant difference (F[5], 141 = 5.099,  
p < 0.001, Wilks’ Λ = 0.847). Compared to the general 
population, veterans engaged in less direct communica-
tion (M = 3.82, SD = 1.003, vs. M = 3.2, SD = 0.92), 
relied less on friends and family (M = 3.45, SD = 0.73 vs 
M = 2.87, SD = 0.79), and engaged in less social com-
parison (M = 2.37, SD = 1.04; M = 1.64, SD = 0.806).


Media Effects 37
As presented below, we then ran partial correla-
tions to look for relationships between various SMU 
and well-being outcomes while controlling for age and 
sex. Because age and sex are related to the other var-
iables, removing those effects allows a clearer picture 
of the relationship between SMU and outcomes. We 
did this for the total sample, and given our interest in 
veterans, for the veterans only.
Relationships between SMU and Well-Being 
Outcomes (Total Sample)
For the total sample (Table 2.5.2), direct commu-
nication resulted in significantly more perceived 
social support, less loneliness, and less social 
disconnectedness. Communicating with friends 
and family (as compared to strangers) was  
significantly related to more perceived social sup-
port, less social disconnectedness, and less lone-
liness. Thus, direct communication online has 
beneficial outcomes.
We also found negative outcomes. Browsing with-
out engagement was related to less life satisfaction. 
Social comparison was associated with more social 
disconnectedness, depression, loneliness, and anxiety, 
and less life satisfaction. Emotional communication 
was related to significantly more depression, but other 
research suggests that emotional communication can

ing depression.
These results help us see what harms (browsing 
and social comparison) and what helps (direct com-
munication, communicating with family and friends) 
well-being.
Relationships between SMU and Well-Being 
Outcomes (Veterans Only)
Next, we examined SMU and well-being among 
veterans only (Table 2.5.3). We supplement these 
quantitative data with some qualitative responses. 
Unlike the many significant differences found in 
our quantitative data, no clear race or sex patterns 
emerged in the qualitative responses. Thus, example 
comments supplement the quantitative data with-
out calling further attention to sex or race. Because 
of the small sample size, we discuss both significant 
results (p < 0.05) and those that approached signif-
icance (results that are telling, even if not strictly 
significant, p < 0.10), noting when the latter was the 
case.
The positive outcome for veterans is that com-
municating with family and friends is associated with 
greater life satisfaction. As one veteran said, “if my chil-
dren lived in the same state as I do, I would have no 
use for social media at all.” Another explained: “I like 
connecting to friends and family that I might not see. 
It’s uplifting, especially if you’re home bound a lot like I 
am.” When we looked at social connectedness, which 
has been found to be vital to veteran well-being, we 
also ran a standard multiple regression. This kind of 
analysis allows us to look at several variables at once 
as they relate to one dependent variable, in this case, 
social disconnectedness. We found that social media 
direct communication (B = −.519, p  = 0.003) and 
emotional communication (B = −0.590, p  = 0.007) 
both individually and taken together resulted in signifi-
cantly lower social disconnectedness (F [2, 38] = 6.342, 
p = 0.004, R
2 = 0.250) among veterans. Thus, using 
social media to communicate and share emotions 
offers benefits for veterans, perhaps especially when 
done with family and friends.
However, negative outcomes were also common. 
Browsing was significantly related to more depression 
and less life satisfaction but, oddly, less stress. Perhaps 
depression and loneliness spark the chain of online 
browsing, and although it cannot alleviate depression, 
it may help relieve stress when used to relax. Emo-
tional communication was related to more depres-
sion (p < 0.10), loneliness (p < 0.10), and significantly 
more anxiety. It is not clear whether sharing emotions 
online is a cause or result of, say, loneliness, but the 
qualitative comments are interesting, and especially 
consistent among male veterans. At least half of the 
males expressed similar sentiments. As one said, “It’s 
that ‘black-hole’ feeling. If I reveal or expose myself 
where would it go? Who would see it? How would 
they (whoever they are) view me? I didn’t want that 
‘exposed’ feeling. Especially having a military back-
ground, experiencing what I experienced, I had to 
be careful not to reveal. If I revealed, then I wanted 
to self-diagnose myself to reel the exposure back in.” 
Another expressed similar reluctance to share emo-
tions online: “I’ve shared emotions on social media.  
It’s a feeling that I feel like I’m revealing and expos-
ing myself. After I’ve done it, I’ve questioned myself 
whether I’ve shared too much, opened too much…. 
After still I feel like I’ve opened myself up to not only 
my friends (will they look at me different?) and worst 
yet, to people I don’t even know but I’ve ‘befriended.” 
On the other hand, some veterans expressed positive 
feelings about sharing online, stating that they were 
encouraged by “seeing the response of others [and 
that] motivates me to keep striving to be that positive 
example or light” or “I might post a feeling just to get a 
little feedback or encouragement without sharing too 
much.”
Finally, social comparison affected not only life 
satisfaction but was also associated with more social 
disconnectedness, more depression, loneliness, and 
anxiety. The qualitative comments reflected this. One 
veteran said that he did less social comparing as he got 
older, but recalled, “The experience felt challenging as 
if I was measuring myself up against someone… The 
thoughts I would have (at that time) could be com-
pared to running on a tread mill. Trying and never get-
ting anywhere. I recall feeling incomplete afterward.” 
Another stated, “I felt less than because someone  
I knew was prospering more than me. I felt like I should 
be in a better place or ahead of them.” Despite most 
reporting social comparison as a negative, some said 
it motivated them.

Media Effects 41
Implications for Veterans and SMU
We’ll focus our discussion on veterans, who were 
our primary focus. Again, our qualitative analysis 
didn’t reveal patterns of sex or race differences, 
so we focus on our quantitative results. Veterans 
were less likely than non-veterans to engage in the 
SMU behaviors of direct communication, friends/
family, use of images, social comparison, self-
 
pr
esentation, browsing, and emotional communi-
cation. Differences in well-being between veterans 
and non-veterans were not large but are important. 
Everyone may experience depression, loneliness, 
stress, anxiety, and life satisfaction, but veterans 
experienced less social support and social con-
nectedness than our non-veteran sample did. That 
may shed light on the lingering mental health prob-
lems for veterans.
It is also possible that there is stigma around men-
tal health among veterans, particularly after they have 
been honored and discharged. Our qualitative results 
showed that veterans experiencing poor well-being 
such as emotional stress must constantly overcome 
military stigma to seek treatment and help. Given that 
attention to veterans’ mental health care and their abil-
ity to access adequate services continues to be a low 
priority for government and given self-stigma (Rossler, 
2016), veterans may lack both access and willingness 
to get help. Veterans’ challenges may be even larger 
than shown here. Our sample voluntarily participated 
in a survey, suggesting a relatively high-functioning set 
of skills.
That said, findings related to SMU remain inter-
esting. First, browsing and broadcasting were problem-
atic for veterans, related to depression, loneliness, and 
lower life satisfaction. Social comparison was related 
to an even larger number of negative outcomes for 
veterans: lower life satisfaction, and more social dis-
connectedness, depression, loneliness, and anxiety. 
All of these factors are significantly related to PTSD. 
Although we cannot argue from our data that social 
media influences the outcome of PTSD, there appears 
to be a constellation of problematic outcomes related 
to media use such as social comparison online.
When examining social (dis)connectedness 
among veterans, we found that two forms of SMU 
were beneficial: direct communication and emotional 
communication. Social disconnectedness was also 
related to increased loneliness, stress, anxiety, and 
depression, and decreased life satisfaction. All of these 
problematic outcomes are related to PTSD.
Thus, we see that SMU may both harm and offer 
a source of support for veterans as they navigate their 
communicative lives. The main takeaways here seem 
to be that how social media are used is key and that 
especially for veterans, social media can be used to 
buffer against some of the negative well-being factors 
often associated with life after military – but only occur 
if social media are used in ways associated with posi-
tive outcomes.

2.6: EXAMINING INFORMATION 
GATHERING FOR SOCIALLY 
VULNERABLE POPULATIONS
Cory L. Armstrong and Anna Grace Usery
As the Diaz-Greene family sifted through the rub-
ble that used to be their mobile home, they couldn’t 
help but ask, “Why me?” They were new to the area 
and didn’t know about the impending weather. The 
tornado siren could be heard only faintly in their 
trailer park. The family looked for anything – clothes, 
coins, pictures – they could cling to for comfort after 
a powerful tornado ripped through the area. This is 
an unfortunate reality that many vulnerable popula-
tions face each time a natural disaster occurs.
This scenario, although fictional, is a stark reality 
for many socially vulnerable people. Severe weather 
unfolds quickly, and anyone can be in the path of 
destruction as a storm steamrolls through the area. 
People need information to save their lives and pro-
tect their property; this study analyzes how socially 
vulnerable populations gather information and utilize 
mass media related to severe weather, specifically 
tornadoes.
Socially vulnerable populations are those that 
are especially at risk during emergencies (natural 
or other disasters; disease outbreaks). Increased 
risk or vulnerability is associated with a number 
of factors, including age, education, being a per -
son of color, and residing in a rural area (see Stein, 
Dueñas-Osorio,  & Subramanian, 2010; Cahyanto, 
Pennington-Gray, Thapa, Srinivasan, Villegas, Mat-
yas, & Kiousis, 2014). Further, research about social 
The authors study how people of different socially 
vulnerable populations (unemployed, rural, minor-
itized, less well-educated, women) use media to 
learn about impending weather events.

vulnerability shows that these groups seek informa-
tion differently than do others without those pres-
sures; information-seeking differences have been 
found across topics including but not limited to
