We focus our analysis on weather (tornado-related 
information-seeking, and study groups based on 
gender, race, education, employment, and location 
(rural or urban).
Social Vulnerability during Severe 
Weather Events
When residents have economic, social, or physical 
barriers that keep them from taking precautionary 
action against impending severe weather events, 
they are classified in academic research as being 
socially vulnerable (Flanagan, Gregory, Hallisey, 
Heitgerd, & Lewis, 2011). Vulnerability, as defined 
by Cutter et al. (2009), is “the susceptibility of a given 
population, system, or place to harm from expo-
sure to the hazard and directly affects the ability to 
prepare for, respond to, and recover from hazards 
and disasters” (p. 2). The social aspects of vulner -
ability focus specifically on those who face accen-
tuated circumstances during impending weather. 
For example, social vulnerability increases with 
age (Andrew, Mitnitski, & Rockwood, 2008). Also, 
Black and Hispanic families are disproportionately 
affected when severe weather hits, in part because 
of lack of resources and geographical barriers 
toward taking precautions (Fothergill, 
 Maest
as,  & 
Darlington, 1999).
Recent research in this area indicates that 
women, minoritized people, and those who are less 
educated often seek more information than other 
social groups to become prepared when severe 
weather is present (e.g., Armstrong, Hou & Towery, 
2020). Thus, the lack of information is an additional 
barrier toward preparation because, even if they 
determine they should prepare or evacuate the area, 
they may still lack the economic resources to ade-
quately prepare or recover from the event. Research 
also shows that people less likely to evacuate dur -
ing impending weather are those with low income, 
less education, women, and minoritized people 
(see Stein, Dueñas-Osorio, & Subramanian, 2010). 
Where areas are situated physically – such as flood-
prone areas (Tate, Rahman, Emrich & Sampson, 
2021) – can create social vulnerability, but certain 
geographical locations also suffer heightened social, 
economic, and educational disparities, especially in 
urban areas (Cutter & Finch, 2008).
Differences in gender do not escape the 
social vulnerability index. Reisig, Pratt, and Holt-
freter (2009) found that men and women pre-
pare for impending weather differently. For 
example, 
 Llor
ente-Marrón, Díaz-Fernández, Mén-
dez-Rodríguez, and Gonzalez Arias (2020) found 
negative outcomes of severe weather (e.g., prop-
erty damage) were intensified when households 
were headed by a woman. Further, individuals who 
are unemployed are more likely to be vulnerable 
because they lack money to buy food and prepara-
tory items or funds to travel out of the area before 
a storm (Cutter, 2017). Also, research from China 
found those who are unemployed, or are poor, rural 
farm workers, are much more vulnerable to weather 
disasters (Chen, Cutter, Emrich & Shi, 2013).
When one is considered socially vulnera-
ble within the context of these characteristics, it 
impacts human resilience to many factors. Research 
shows social vulnerability affects how communities 
bounce back from weather-related disaster and can 
cause more deaths than in communities that are 
economically, socially, and politically advantaged 
(Flanagan et al., 2011). No matter the corner of 
the world, social vulnerability exists and can hin-
der the quality of human life. When these factors 
are present, individuals can be negatively influ-
enced in their quality of life or in things we do to 
feel safe and secure as humans (Khaksar, Khosla,  
Chu, & Shahmehr, 2016).
From a weather standpoint, safety and secu-
rity represent a home in a geographic location 
that can withstand the impending storm. This 
scenario could include having a solid insurance 
plan, a storm shelter, and food and supplies to 
withstand a power outage for several days. From 
an information-seeking standpoint, this represents 
a well-established network of support (friends, 
family, co-workers) to rely on for information 


Media Effects 45
when disaster strikes. Socially vulnerable peo-
ple often miss some of that support by lacking 
money, transportation, or resources to help them 
prepare effectively. They may also have language 
or comprehension barriers, which could limit the 
use and availability of general mass media notifi-
cation channels. They may also have geographic 
limitations or live in low-lying or rural areas, which 
are more difficult to reach during severe weather 
events. The social and economic factors listed 
above contribute to knowing how a person will 
prepare for imminent weather. Although these fac-
tors help explain some disparities and vulnerabil-
ities when severe weather is imminent, and they 
are the ones we focus on here, research is not lim-
ited to these factors.
Information-Seeking during Impending 
Severe Weather
This study seeks to better understand how different 
mass media channels and methods of communica-
tion aid in weather preparedness for different peo-
ple. Although research has shown that social and 
economic factors influence weather preparedness, 
we know little about how people learn about severe 
weather, and what differences exist across the mul-
tiple contributors to social vulnerability discussed 
above.
Our study is guided by two research ques-
tions: (1) What types of mass media do people 
use to learn about impending tornadoes? (2) Are 
there differences in media use based on demo-
graphics related to social vulnerability? The mass 
media outlets we studied included both legacy 
media (newspapers, radio, and television) and dig-
ital media (Facebook, Twitter, general Internet, or 
other social media).
To answer our questions, we conducted an 
online survey from the coverage area of the National 
Weather Association in Memphis, TN, which includes 
55 counties across Tennessee, Missouri, Arkansas, 
and Mississippi. This geographical location is a 
good choice for our research because tornados are 
frequent in these regions. The area comprises both 
rural and urban locations and is home to a diverse 
population, including people of color (especially 
African Americans and Hispanics). The population 
contains a notable number of unemployed people, 
and it reflects both the highly educated and the less 
educated.
Using a private research firm, 679 responses 
were collected from April 27 to May 28, 2021. 
About half of the respondents (364) live in urban 
areas. The sample was majority female (481) and 
White (504). The median age was 36 to 45 years. 
About half (355) of the sample was employed, and 
about three-fifths (395) had at least a high school 
education. Thus, our sample provides an appropri-
ate range of people to support comparisons based 
on the variables we are using to reflect differences 
in social vulnerability.
We asked respondents about seven media 
types (listed above and also included in Table 
2.6.1). We asked from which of the sources they 
generally received tornado watch and warning 
information, reported on a scale of 1 (never receive) 
to 5 (always receive). We also asked for demo-
graphic information, which we used to conduct 
statistical tests to determine whether the groups 
exhibited significant differences. We used t-tests – 
 st
atistical tests comparing the average answers of 
the two groups to see whether the groups differed 
by more than would be expected by chance – to  
compare the use of each media type by race 
(White/non-White), gender (male/female), edu-
cation (high school education or lower/more than 
high school education), employment (full or part-
time employment/not employed), and location 
(urban/rural).
The core of our results can be found in Table 
2.6.1. Our first research question asked about peo-
ple’s use of various media to learn about impend-
ing tornados. The column on the left of Table 2.6.1 
presents the means and standard deviations of 
each media type’s use for the sample as a whole. 
This reveals that television is the predominant 
source for information during tornados (3.6 out 
of 5) – 
 r
egardless of group – followed by radio 
(including weather-specific radios). This supports 
prior research, which has consistently suggested 
 t
elevision as a key information source during 

46 Audiences
weather events. The least-employed media for 
weather information in this sample were newspa -
pers and Twitter.
The rest of the table addresses our second 
research question, which looks for differential 
media use by people in demographic groups 
related to social vulnerability. We found few sta-
tistically significant differences related to gender, 
except that women use Facebook for weather-
 
r
elated information more than men do. Regard-
ing race, our findings indicated that non-White 
respondents were significantly more likely to use 
newspapers, television, Twitter, Internet, and 
social media to gather information than their 
White counterparts. Those who are more educated 
used Twitter, the internet, and other social media 
to gather information more often than the less 
educated did. Those who were at least part-time 
employees were more likely than the unemployed 
respondents to use all media for information gath-
ering, except 
 t
elevision. Geographic location was 
only significantly 
 diff
erent for other social media, 
which found that urban residents use it more than 
rural residents.
Although we didn’t find widespread differences 
in media used or getting weather-related informa-
tion based on the variables we used, it is worth not-
ing that unemployed respondents reported using 
less media in all categories, except television, and 
that less-educated respondents reported using 
less digital media than well-educated respondents. 
These findings contradict prior research findings 
and makes us wonder whether some socially vul-
nerable people may not be receiving the message 
about impending weather events. Maybe those 
respondents are getting their information else-
where, but maybe they’re not getting the informa-
tion at all.
Other noteworthy findings suggest that tele-
vision and social media reach a large portion of 
social groups, but clearly not everyone is using 
these mass media to get information. Non-White 
respondents reported using media for severe 
weather alerts more frequently than White 
respondents did. Although some prior research 
has suggested that socially vulnerable populations 
tend to rely on media more heavily during severe 
weather, our research contradicts that, finding 
instead that people of color employed both televi-
sion and radio more than White respondents did. 
This finding suggests that social vulnerability is a 
complex concept – as is reliance on media types 
– and not all social groups may respond in the 
same way when confronted with severe weather. 
For example, while interesting, the lack of differ -
ences in information-seeking between men and 
women could indicate coverage is more inclusive. 
Similarly, the lack of difference between urban and 
rural areas (except for general social media use) 
also shows equal efficacy of these media in terms 
of reaching mass populations.
One of the limitations of this study is that we 
focused exclusively on information-seeking on 
mass media (broadly defined). That is, we looked 
only at where people went for information after 
deciding they wanted information. We didn’t look 
at how people responded to information being, 
in essence, pushed to them by various sources. 
Future research could expand our work to investi-
gate people’s awareness of and response to emer -
gency warning and alert systems of all types, from 
tornado sirens to the Emergency Alert System, 
to Wireless Emergency Alerts. Are there differ -
ences in socially vulnerable populations for these 
alerts? To what extent do the alert systems reach 
socially vulnerable groups and generate an appro-
priate response? Overall, our findings suggest that 
information gathering through media use during 
tornado outbreaks varies across certain socially 
vulnerable populations – particularly among race, 
employment, and education demographics. It is 
paramount that when severe weather hits, no one 
is overlooked in the alert system. Therefore, work 
is needed to verify that critical weather emer -
gency warnings reach all residents of an affected 
area.
Note
Data for this project were provided through a 
$15,000 grant from the Cooperative Program for 
Operational Meteorology, Education and Training 
(COMET®) Outreach Program through the Univer-
sity Corporation for Atmospheric Research.


Media Effects 47

2.7: WHO DESERVES A BREAK? HOW 
RACE AND CLASS SHAPE SUPPORT FOR 
THE CHILD TAX CREDIT
Alina Renee Oxendine
During 2021, millions of American families 
received an enhanced child tax subsidy or “Child 
Tax Credit,” which was part of the American Res-
cue Plan. Extension of the program was debated 
in Congress, but because negotiations have been 
It’s Your Turn. What Do You Think? What 
Will You Find?
 1.
 Sear
ch for media coverage of a recent 
natural disaster, and then for a natural 
disaster about 25 years ago. Who is por-
trayed as having been affected by the 
events? How did the information they 
have (or didn’t have) help prevent harm 
or fail to prevent harm? What changes 
do you see over time?
 2.
 T
alk with your friends and family about 
where they get their information about 
natural disasters, disasters caused by 
human actions, or disease outbreaks. 
How do information-seeking behav-
iors differ across the different types of 
events? What specific information needs 
do people have for weather events such 
as tornadoes or hurricanes?
 3.
 If
 you were a reporter, what could you do 
to disseminate weather-related informa-
tion most effectively to socially vulner -
able populations? Consider all options 
for reaching people, including but not 
limited to the ones we studied.
In this survey experiment, the author analyzes sup-
port for the Child Tax Credit (2021) and whether 
race and class shape perceptions of whether recip-
ient families are deserving of government support.

48 Audiences
unsuccessful, families no longer receive payments 
(Gupta, 2021). Although short-lived, this policy pro-
vides insights into public support for similar kinds of 
near-
 uni
versal programs providing benefits to fam-
ilies at vastly different socioeconomic levels. With 
so many different types of families eligible, does it 
matter which ones are highlighted in the media? 
Do race or class shape Americans’ perceptions of 
whether recipient families are deserving of the Child 
Tax Credit? In this project, I analyze American per-
ceptions of the Child Tax Credit using a survey and 
a 3 × 2 embedded experiment that analyzes differ -
ent types of American families benefiting from the 
policy. The conditions feature families that differ in 
terms of both race (Latinx vs. Black vs. White) and 
class (affluent vs. poor).
Interplay of Race, Class, and Policy 
Attitudes
Americans have complex and conflicting beliefs 
about government programs and the people 
who benefit from them. An important question is 
whether policies should target the people most 
in need or be universal and inclusive, benefiting 
most people. Many Americans like the idea of 
targeted benefits because it seems most efficient, 
but means-tested programs tend to have higher 
administrative costs in determining who quali-
fies. They also enjoy less widespread support and 
can become associated with stigmatized groups, 
decreasing their popularity even further (Gilens, 
1999). Universal programs, in contrast, tend to be 
more robust, sustainable, politically popular, and 
successful in redistributing resources from the 
rich to the poor (Jacques & Noël, 2018; Korpi & 
Palme, 1998).
It is interesting to analyze what happens to 
public support for policies if middle class or even 
affluent Americans are described in the media 
as receiving benefits. When the race and class 
of beneficiaries vary, which characteristics are 
most beneficial or harmful for public support? 
Research on American public opinion reveals 
that racial attitudes influence how people think 
about many public policies and social programs 
(Gilens, 1999; Winter, 2008). Americans tend to 
underestimate how much they benefit from public 
programs (Mettler, 2011) and overestimate how 
much “others,” particularly Black Americans, ben-
efit (Gilens, 1999). Racial resentment is a power -
ful predictor of opposition to means-tested social 
welfare programs, especially when White peo-
ple envision Black beneficiaries (Federico, 2006; 
Gilens, 1999). But to what extent does race matter 
for a universal program for families, such as the 
Child Tax Credit?
Survey Experiment: Do Race or Class 
Matter?
My research explores what Americans think 
about the Child Tax Credit and whether the race 
or class of recipient families influences support 
for the policy. A controlled, pretest–posttest sur -
vey experiment allows me to measure whether 
and to what extent recipient characteristics mat-
ter. Respondents answered a set of pretest sur -
vey questions, read a news article (one of seven 
versions that were assigned randomly), and com-
pleted a set of posttest questions. The pretest and 
posttest included items evaluating support for the 
Child Tax Credit with a question that captures the 
level of support with a seven-point Likert scale 
(“What do you think of the Child Tax Credit, which 
includes monthly cash payments for American 
families with children?”) and a question measuring 
support with a 100-point slider (“Using a scale of 
0 to 100, to what extent do you support the U.S. 
Child Tax Credit?”).
In between the pretest and posttest, respond-
ents read a news article about the Child Tax Credit 
or an unrelated news story about an archeological 
stone tool excavation, which was the control con-
dition. The stories, based on Gupta (2021), Liacko 
(2022), Swenson and Torbati (2021) and Ritter 
(2020), are described below.
The article using the working-class frame 
(experimental conditions 1–3) presents facts about 
the Child Tax Credit and discusses a family struggling 


Media Effects 49
with unemployment. The family uses Child Tax 
Credit payments to cover the cost of preschool 
and limited extracurriculars for their son, but can-
not cover preschool for the younger daughter. The 
three conditions contain the same text and type of 
photograph but feature families with different racial 
backgrounds: condition 1 features a Black family, 
condition 2 a White family, and condition 3 a Latinx 
family. The upper-class frame (experimental condi-
tions 4–6) presents the same facts about the Child 
Tax Credit and the same types of photograph as in 
the working-class frame but discusses an affluent 
family running a small business that, even though it 
took a hit during the COVID-19 pandemic, remains 
financially stable. In this condition, the family uses 
Child Tax Credit payments to “cover childcare, ren-
ovate their kitchen, and put some money back into 
their family business.” As above, these three con-
ditions feature families with different racial back-
grounds: condition 4 (Black), condition 5 (White), 
and condition 6 (Latinx). Finally, the control condi-
tion is a real news story about an archeological exca-
vation (Ritter, 2020).
After performing a manipulation check to con-
firm that the stories reflected the desired differences 
in terms of social class, I recruited adult workers living 
in the United States using Amazon Mechanical Turk 
(MTurk).
A group of 700 MTurk workers completed 
the survey in January 2022. The sample was 46% 
female and 54% male. Respondents resided in 48 
different states and reported ages ranging from 20 
to 79. About 81% of respondents were White/Cau-
casian, and 19% were Black, Hispanic, Asian, Amer-
ican Indian, or some other race, and 64% reported 
having children. Respondents represented a range 
of socioeconomic backgrounds, with 45% reporting 
household incomes under $50,000 and 55% report-
ing incomes equal or greater than $50,000. Educa-
tion also varied but was relatively high: about 12% 
had graduate degrees, 62% had bachelor degrees, 
and 26% had an associate’s degree or less. Political 
ideology varied, although the group skewed slightly 
left with 45% liberal, 32% conservative, and 23% 
moderate.
The Pretest Survey: Americans Support the  
Child Tax Credit
In my pretest (or baseline) survey, most respondents 
were in favor of the Child Tax Credit. About 66% 
reported that they either supported or strongly sup-
ported the policy, about 9% of respondents opposed, 
and 8% were neutral. On a scale of 0 (no support 
for the Child Tax Credit) to 100 (full support), the 
average score was 68. There was a statistically sig-
nificant difference in support between liberal and 
conservative respondents (p < 0.01), with liberals 
averaging 71 and conservatives averaging 65.
Linear regression helps us learn whether ide-
ological differences hold up when controlling for 
other factors. It is a tool for isolating which demo-
graphic and political characteristics are associated 
with support for the Child Tax Credit. I analyzed the 
dependent variable with the question “On a scale 
from 0 to 100, to what extent do you support the 
U.S. Child Tax Credit?” and tested for a relationship 
between Child Tax Credit support and several inde-
pendent variables (including the number of children, 
education, income, gender, age, race, political party, 
and ideology). In this model [F(8, 692) = 3.16, p < 
0.001, R
2 = 0.035], I found that the most influential 
variables were the number of children (more chil-
dren boosted support, β = 2.44, p < 0.01), political 
ideology (conservatives were less supportive, β = 
−2.10, p < 0.01), and political party (democrats 
were more supportive, β = 1.08, p < 0.10). Other 
characteristics (income, race, gender, age, and edu-
cation) were not statistically significant.
I found similar results when I analyzed the same 
independent variables but with a seven-point Likert 
scale measuring the level of Child Tax Credit oppo-
sition (“What do you think of the Child Tax Credit, 
which includes monthly cash payments for Amer -
ican families with children?”). In this model [F(8, 
688) = 7.15, p < 0.001, R
2 = 0.077], opposition was 
lower among respondents with children (β = −0.25,  
p < 0.01) and with democrats (β = −0.088, p < 
0.05), and higher among conservatives (β = 0.12, p 
< 0.01). In this model, older (β = 0.012, p < 0.01) 
and higher income (β = 0.066, p < 0.05) respond-
ents were more strongly opposed to the policy. As 

50 Audiences
with the first model, race, gender, and education 
were not influential.
The Experimental Manipulation: Race and 
Class Intersections Are Influential
Using the experiment embedded in the survey, we 
can analyze whether respondents are more or less 
supportive of the Child Tax Credit after reading their 
assigned news story. Focusing on the question that 
measures support with the 100-point slider, I sub-
tracted posttest scores from pretest scores. Overall, 
the results suggest that respondents are no more likely 
to support the Child Tax Credit if 
 w
orking-class, 
rather than affluent, families are depicted. I used 
a one-way ANOV A to evaluate whether groups’ 
average scores differ significantly from one another. 
Although respondents became more supportive of 
the Child Tax Credit after reading the news articles, 
there were no statistically significant differences 
when comparing the working class, affluent, and 
control conditions.
Even though differences fail to emerge with 
social class alone, I found interesting differences 
when race and class intersect. Across the seven 
conditions, the most pronounced pretest–posttest 
increase in support for the Child Tax Credit was 
4.47 points in the group reading the story featuring 
a struggling, working-class Latinx family. In con-
trast, the smallest increase (1.03 points) was in the 
group reading the story featuring a White affluent 
family. An independent-samples t-test revealed 
a statistically significant difference between the 
means of these two groups (p  < 0.05). After the 
working-class Latinx family, the next largest 
increase in support was 3.73 in the group read-
ing about the Black affluent family. And after the 
White affluent family, the next lowest increase 
(1.55) was in the group who read about the Black 
working-class family.
Overall, the race–class intersection seems par-
ticularly harsh for poor Black families. Respondents 
reading about White or Latinx families had more Child 
Tax Credit support for working-class than for affluent 
families. But the pattern is reversed for respondents 
reading about Black families; they expressed higher 
Child Tax Credit support for the affluent family than 
for the working-class family. An independent-samples 
t-test confirms that respondents find the working-class 
Latinx family more sympathetic than the working-class 
Black family (p < 0.05).
Who Is Deserving? Respondents React to  
the Families
After respondents read the news story featured in 
the experiment, I asked some open-ended ques-
tions to evaluate how carefully they read and to 
analyze their perceptions of the family featured in 
the article. I asked, “Do you think that the family 
featured in the news story is deserving of gov-
ernment aid? Explain briefly why or why not.” 
Although more than half did not answer or wrote 
“N/A” because they were in the control condition, 
220 respondents gave reasons why the family was 
deserving, and 55 gave reasons why the family was 
undeserving.
Respondents who thought the family was 
deserving said things such as “all families deserve 
help” and “at least they are trying their best.” Some 
respondents equated work with deservingness: 
Both of those parents work, but they still can’t 
meet all of their needs. Even though they could 
cut down on some expenses that sound like 
luxuries, they deserve more help from the gov-
ernment than families that aren’t really trying to 
find work or actually working.
About 75% of the respondents who thought the 
family was undeserving provided either a brief “no” 
or a neutral response. Most of these responses 
referred to the affluent families. As one respond-
ent said, “no, they look like a very well off family 
that does not deserve to be helped.” Another said, 
“...if they were grossing more than 100k in their 
business during 2019 and had rental properties, I 
don’t find it likely that they really needed [the Child 
Tax Credit].”
In contrast, about 25% of responses in the 
“undeserving” group were negative and judgmen-
tal. These critical comments were about equally 


Media Effects 51
divided between the working-class Black family 
and the working-class Latinx family. They consist-
ently critiqued the families’ life choices, citing poor 
planning, or criticized how families spent the Child 
Tax Credit. For example, after reading the article 
in the Black working-class condition, a respondent 
said: 
No, I don’t think that they should be given the 
child tax credit. If you lose your jobs, then 
you need to prioritize expenses. If you can’t 
afford preschool or extracurricular activities 
for your preschoolers, then you no longer do 
those activities. Money from taxes shouldn’t be 
used to send to people for these types of frivo-
lous expenses. Food vouchers or gift cards for 
school items should be a better use of govern-
ment tax dollars. 
In the working-class Latinx condition, a childless 
respondent also took aim at the parents’ spending 
priorities and life choices:
Absolutely not. They are using it for ballet 
lessons??? Are you kidding me? I won’t have 
kids because I know that I do not have enough 
money for them and I could live at least a year 
or more if I was fired on my own with no help 
with what I have in savings. These are not 
poor people in a bad situation, they put them-
selves there and should be putting some of that 
money in savings.
A few respondents, often without children, 
expressed frustration with the broader policy and 
attacked the working-class family: “If I’m not getting 
$300 per month for doing nothing, neither should 
they, it’s blatant discrimination to be giving people 
that much when all I get is the bill for it.” Another 
respondent echoed:
No, your kids don’t get to go to soccer practice 
when you decide to quit your job. The govern-
ment and other taxpayers should not have to 
pay for you to have ‘breathing room.’ If you 
want breathing room, it’s up to you to make 
that happen.
Although most of the criticism was directed toward 
working-class families, some negative, visceral com-
ments were directed at the Black affluent family: 
No, even in their worst they still made lots of 
money. I think they are greedy and making 
lots of money and don’t know how to budget. 
I think they are taking advantage of the system 
to get more money. How is it my fault they had 
a bunch of kids?
Race, Ideology, and Self-Interest Drive 
Support for the Child Tax Credit
Despite negativity from a minority of respondents 
about the Child Tax Credit and the families who 
have benefited, most respondents were supportive 
and believed that American families needed help. 
Respondents who were moderate or liberal in terms 
of ideology comprised the majority of my survey 
sample, and they were more likely than their conserv-
ative counterparts to endorse the program. Qualita-
tive and quantitative evaluations also revealed a clear 
dichotomy between respondents with and without 
children. Support from respondents who are parents 
may stem in part from self-interest and a nuanced 
understanding of the difficulties of raising children.
When considering demographic backgrounds 
of families receiving aid, the intersection of race and 
class also made a difference. Respondents expressed 
particularly low support, both quantitatively and 
qualitatively, for the Black working-class family. This 
evidence of racism, combined with self-interest, 
suggests the need for more universal than means-
 
r
elated public policies. Even though family-friendly 
policies may not apply directly to non-parents, we 
can design them to benefit most families. Inclusive 
programs tend to be more effective in reducing stig-
matization of beneficiaries, better funded, and more 
successful than means-tested programs (Jacques & 
Noël, 2018; Korpi & Palme, 1998).
Cross-national studies reveal that American 
parents are more discontented than parents in 
countries with family-friendly public programs like 
childcare subsidies and paid time off. Research 
also suggests that extensive family-friendly policy 

52 Audiences
packages improve life satisfaction for the entire pop-
ulation, not just parents (Glass, Simon & Andersson, 
2016). Because of this, news outlets, organizations, 
and public interest groups supporting family-friendly 
programs might benefit from emphasizing the col-
lective, expansive benefits of these programs and 
counteract negativity from citizens who think they 
may not benefit personally.
References
Federico, C. (2006). Race, education and individualism revis-
ited. The Journal of Politics, 68 (3), 600–610.
Gilens, M. (1999). Why Americans hate welfare: Race, media 
and the politics of antipoverty policy. University of Chi-
cago Press.
Glass, J., Simon, R. W., & Andersson, M. A. (2016). Parent-
hood and happiness: Effects of work-family reconcilia-
tion policies in 22 OECD countries. American Journal of 
Sociology, 122 (3), 886–929.
Gupta, A. (2021). ‘A blessing and a relief:’ How four fam-
ilies used the Child Tax Credit. New Y ork Times. 
https://www.nytimes.com/2021/12/21/well/family/
child-tax-credit-families.html
Jacques, O. & Noël, A. (2018). The case for welfare state 
universalism, or the lasting relevance of the paradox of 
redistribution. Journal of European Social Policy, 28 (1), 
70–85.
Korpi, W. & Palme, J. (1998) The paradox of redistribution 
and strategies of equality: Welfare state institutions, ine-
quality, and poverty in the Western countries. American 
Sociological Review 63 (5): 661–87.
Liacko, A. (2022). What the end of the child tax credit 
means for families. Denver7 News. https://www.theden-
verchannel.com/news/national-politics/the-race/
what-the-end-of-the-child-tax-credit-means-for-families
It’s Your Turn: What Do You Think? What 
Will You Find?
 1.
 Ha
ve half the class go to news sources 
that are read or viewed more frequently by 
American conservatives (e.g., FOX News, 
the Wall Street Journal) and have the other 
half go to news sources that are utilized 
more often by liberals (MSNBC, HuffPost, 
New Y ork Times). Use keywords “child 
tax credit” to search for stories about this 
policy. What facts are presented? Do the 
stories discuss the policy in a way that is 
positive, negative, or neutral? How does 
this framing affect the quality or the con-
tent of the story? Discuss differences that 
you see between the news sources, and 
how you think such differences might 
affect viewers’ evaluations of the policy.
 2.
 Select f
ive stories about the Child Tax 
Credit (or any other government bene-
fit such as the Supplemental Nutrition 
Assistance Program or Temporary Assis-
tance for Families) from outlets iden-

3.1: ARGUING OVER IMAGES: NATIVE 
AMERICAN MASCOTS AND RACE
C. Richard King
Native American mascots, once accepted icons, 
have become controversial symbols over the past 
quarter century. Increasingly, they raise troubling 
questions. Does the continued use of American 
Indian symbols and nicknames in sports honor or 
insult Native Americans? Do mascots like Chief 
Wahoo of the Cleveland Indians (retired 2018) or 
gestures such as the tomahawk chop perpetuate 
racist stereotypes? Does it matter whether names 
such as the Atlanta Braves, the Chicago Black-
hawks, or the Washington Redskins (retired 2020) 
are intentionally offensive or merely happened to 
offend many Native Americans? Answers to these 
queries have much to tell us about race. In obvious 
and invisible ways, critics and defenders invaria-
bly speak about race relations and ethnic identity 
when they speak about the use of Indian nick-
names and images in sports. And although many 
pro sports teams have been removing racist names 
and imagery, some steadfastly refuse. In addition, 
according to Mukherjee (2020), sports teams at 
about 900 high schools in the US use the names 
Indians, Warriors, Braves, Chiefs, Redskins, or 
Blackhawks.
An impressive literature has emerged discussing 
the racial politics of Native American mascots (see 
Connolly, 2000; King, 2016; King & Springwood, 2001; 
Spindel, 2000). It directs our attention to the ways indi-
viduals understand and construct race: identity, or how 
they imagine themselves; imagination, or how they per-
ceive others; and representation, or how they give life 
to social categories (such as bravery, physicality, and 
masculinity) through cultural difference. Scholars and 
activists have contended that the creation and more 
recent contentiousness of mascots illuminates the ste-
reotypical images central to Whites’ interpretations of 
Native Americans, the centrality of Indianness to the 
formulation of whiteness in the United States, and 
the changing place of Native Americans in American 
society.
In what follows, after a brief overview of some of 
the common stereotypes, I propose making sense of 
mascots by listening to the unfolding dialogues about 
these sports symbols in an effort to grasp the place 
of race in their popular interpretations. Moreover, to 
hear the positions advanced in these debates most 
clearly, I avoid rehearsed defenses, press releases, and 
official accounts orchestrated by institutions; instead, 
I concentrate on the ways in which citizens, consum-
ers, and fans interpret Native American nicknames 
and symbols. Throughout, I make sense of how media 
consumers talk about Indian images in sports and 
the arguments they advance to defend and criticize 
mascots.
The author claims that arguments about Native 
American mascots are actually arguments about 
race and hence a barometer of race relations in our 
society. Before reading this essay, see the first It’s 
Y our Turn activity.
3
AUDIENCE STUDIES
DOI: 10.4324/9781003193708-4

Audience Studies 55
Although els
ewhere I have openly criticized 
mascots (King & Springwood, 2001), here, I want to 
step back and analyze the positions of supporters and 
opponents. I focus my attention on one representative 
case, an electronic forum hosted by USA Weekend in 
1997. First, I briefly review the historical uses of Indian 
symbols and nicknames in American athletics.
Indian Symbols and Nicknames in 
Sports
For much of the past century, Indian symbols and 
nicknames have been a common, if increasingly 
contested, part of American sports. Euro-Americans 
have selected and supported Native American mas-
cots for a number of reasons. Some schools, such as 
Dartmouth College, have historically defined them-
selves through a specific relationship with American 
Indians. More often, especially at public universi-
ties, regional history and local pride have inspired 
students, coaches, and administrators to adopt 
Indian mascots. The University of Utah Running 
Utes provide a prominent example of this tradition. 
Elsewhere, historical accident, coincidence, or cir -
cumstance gave rise to mascots. For instance, St. 
John’s University was known as the Redmen initially 
because their uniforms were red; only later did fans 
and alumni create fuller traditions of playing Indian.
Whatever the specific origins of individual icons, 
Euro-Americans were able to fabricate Native Ameri-
cans as mascots precisely because of prevailing soci-
ohistorical conditions. That is, a set of social relations 
and cultural categories made it possible, pleasurable, 
and powerful for Euro-Americans to elaborate images 
of Indians in athletic contexts. First, Euro-Americans 
have always fashioned individual and collective iden-
tities for themselves by playing Indian. Native Amer-
ican mascots were an extension of this long tradition 
(Deloria, 1998). Second, the conquest of Native Amer-
ica simultaneously empowered Euro-Americans to 
appropriate, invent, and otherwise represent Native 
Americans and to long for aspects of indigenous cul-
tures destroyed by conquest. Third, with the rise of 
public culture, the production of Indianness in specta-
cles, exhibitions, and other sundry entertainments pro-
liferated, offering templates for elaborations in sporting 
contexts.
Given this history, it is not surprising that Native 
American mascots have relied on stereotypical images 
of Indians. Accentuating physical features (nose, skin 
color, or hair), material culture (buckskin, feathers, 
headdress), expressive forms (dance, face painting), or 
other attributes (stoicism or bravery) associated with 
the native nations of North America, they reduce past 
and present Native Americans to well-worn clichés 
derived from dime novels, wild west shows, movies, 
scouting, and advertising. More often than not, such 
renderings reflect Euro-American interpretations 
and preoccupations rather than indigenous cultures. 
Indian imagery in sport tends to be frozen in the past 
(romanticized representatives from a golden age), 
cluster around the peoples of Plains (the Lakota and 
other nomadic horse cultures principally), and allude 
to, if not emphasize, cultural conflicts between Euro- 
and Native Americans. In the process, generic Indians 
emerge, which cannot be faithful to native histories and 
traditions, precisely because their invention depends 
on decontextualization. These invented Indians that 
dance at half-time, mark the stationery of educational 
institutions, and appear on baseball caps and T-shirts, 
are of two types: the warrior and the clown, mirror-
ing the historic bifurcation of indigenous people into 
two types of savages—noble and ignoble. The warrior 
aspires to honor. Stressing bravery and bellicosity, the 
warrior exudes character traits Euro-Americans have 
long prized: individuality, perseverance, pride, fidel-
ity, and excellence. Numerous high schools, colleges, 
and professional teams have seized upon the warrior, 
real (Chief Osceola at Florida State University) and 
imagined (the former Chief Illiniwek at the Univer -
sity of Illinois). In contrast, the less common clown 
mocks, making Indians a joke, a sideshow burlesque. 
The Cleveland Indians’ Chief Wahoo was perhaps the 
most recognizable clown.
Despite, or perhaps because of, the imagery 
associated with them, Native American mascots 
have become increasingly contentious. More than 
three decades ago, amidst the civil rights movement 
and a cultural resurgence throughout Native Amer-
ica, Indians began questioning mascots, forcing both 
Dartmouth College and Stanford University to change 
theirs. More recently, although some institutions, 
including St. John’s University and the University of 
Miami (Ohio), have retired their mascots, a smaller 

56 Audiences
number, including, the University of Utah and Brad-
ley University, have revised their use of imagery. Other 
schools without Native American mascots, such as the 
University of Wisconsin and the University of Minne-
sota, have instituted policies prohibiting their athletic 
departments from scheduling games against institu-
tions with Indian mascots. At the same time, countless 
communities and boards of education have confronted 
the issue. Many have deemed such mascots discrimi-
natory, requiring (as did the Minnesota and New Y ork 
State Boards of Education and the Los Angeles and 
Dallas School Districts) that schools change them. 
In the wake of these events, numerous individuals 
and organizations have challenged the persistence of 
such icons. Nationally, numerous organizations, rang-
ing from the National Congress of American Indians 
and the National Education Association to the United 
Methodist Church and the National Association for 
the Advancement of Colored People, have taken 
positions against the continued use of Indian images 
in sports. Finally, the media have taken a leading role 
in modifying public perceptions of mascots, as when 
the Portland Oregonian changed its editorial policy and 
refused to print derogatory team names.
Arguments
In July 1997, the USA Weekend website asked its vis-
itors “What is your opinion about changing a sports 
team’s mascot because it offends Native Ameri-
cans?” Visitors could vote in support of changing or 
keeping such mascots and submit a reaction to the 
ongoing controversy. Of those who came to the site, 
2,419 participated in the quick poll with 42% voting 
to change and 58% voting to retain mascots. In turn, 
299 visitors (124 who opposed mascots and 175 who 
supported retaining mascots) offered a fuller opinion. 
These opinions form the basis of my analysis. The 
comments will be reproduced exactly as they were 
written, racial slurs, typos, and all, and people are  
identified here as they identified themselves online.
In Defense of Mascots
Supporters of mascots offer a number of inter -
connected arguments that collectively labor to 
make such images acceptable and to defuse the 
controversy. They stress respect, intention, fairness, 
and common-sense notions of symbols, play, and 
politics.
To many who support mascots, the use of Native 
American symbols and nicknames honors Indians. 
Michelle from College Station, Texas, gave clear voice 
to this perspective: “Team masots are adopted to 
reflect positively on a team, to symbolize an image of 
bravery, agility, tenacity, and strength. Native Ameri-
cans should view this as a compliment rather than an 
insult.” Likewise, A. McClung suggests, “The naming 
of teams…whether it be Braves, Warriors, Indians, 
Cherokees, etc. have been a thing of honor, prestige 
and recognition…[It] conjures up images that are in 
my opinion, positive and wholesome to our Native 
Americans.” Bob Dunwoody asserted that “Native 
Americans or American Indians whatever they wish 
to be known as today should be PROUD that they 
have been selected as a name because it their ances-
tors Pride, Honor, Bravery, and Physical Prowess and 
Endurance.” More hypothetically, Rick Bartholomew, 
a staunch Cleveland fan, remarks, “If I was an Indian, 
I would be as proud as pie to have a team named after 
my heritage.” Bee from Maine exclaims “YOU PEO-
PLE SHOULD LIGHTEN UP!!!!!!!!!!!!!! IT’S JUST THE 
NAME OF A BASEBALL TEAM. IT’S NOT EVEN 
MAKING FUN OF NATIVE AMERICANS. THEY 
SHOULD TAKE IT AS A COMPLIMENT.” Finally, 
Jimmy Conn overtly mixes insult and honor: “I feel 
that native americans should take it as a compliment 
and have better things to complain about like america 
being stolen from them, but i guess alcohol does bad 
things to your train of thought.”
Supporters often couple arguments about honor 
and respect with discussions of intentionality. Scott 
from Port Huron, Michigan succinctly presents this 
position: “I DON’T THINK THE NAMES WERE 
MEANT TO HURT ANYONE. THEY WERE PICKED 
OUT RESPECT IF ANYTHING.” Similarly, Hector 
Cadena notes: “If the team nicknames were meant to 
intentionally be derogatory, then I could understand 
someone taking umbridge with them. But in reality, 
the names are meant as a salute to the fierceness and 
bravery.” And according to Terri McDowell, “PEOPLE 
NEED TO FIND BETTER THINGS TO DO WITH 
THEIR TIME! THESE NAMES WEREN’T MEANT 
TO BE OBJECTIONABLE.”


Audience Studies 57
Ar
guments in support of mascots on occasion 
speak about race through analogies between Native 
Americans and other ethnic groups. Many, like Betty 
from Albert Lea, Minnesota, are proud to see “their 
heritage” displayed in an athletic context: “I am Nor-
wegian. I am happy to have the Vikings use this Scan-
dinavian heritage as their team name.” Jon from Apple 
Creek, Ohio wonders, “Why isn’t someone complain-
ing about Notre Dame?” Similarly, Jenni from South 
Dakota asks: “My husband’s family is of Norwegian 
heritage. Does this mean we should start a campaign 
to dump the Vikings?” Perhaps, she continues, those 
offended “should consider the advantages of the per-
petual mass marketing campaign that rides along with 
these mascots…It isn’t all bad!” Kim Stevens encour-
ages critics “to lighten up. Don’t take things so personal. 
Scandanvian people aren’t up in arms about Minnesota 
using the name ‘Vikings’ …Take it with a grain of salt.”
Many defenders of mascots, such as Terri 
McDowell and Bee from Maine, cannot grasp the 
importance of mascots and resort to dismissive com-
ments. They dub it “silliness” or “a waste of time” 
because other problems (usually unnamed) deserve 
attention. They encourage detractors to “lighten up,” 
“get over it,” “grow up,” “get a life,” “get a grip,” or “get 
real.” In part, this derives from a collective sense of 
sport as playful, frivolous diversion. As Ralph W. Sul-
livan asserts, “Sports is entertainment, anybody who 
takes it seriously enough to get upset over a name, a 
score, or whose on first needs help. How about putting 
first things first. There are other priorities.” Moreover, 
this refusal to take mascots seriously arises from a folk 
understanding of symbols. Richard from Salem, Ore-
gon argues against changing the nicknames because 
“After all it is just a name!” Brookie from Birmingham, 
Alabama does not understand “what the big deal 
is…A name is just a name, nothing else.”
Not all arguments in support of mascots lean 
on honor, intention, or analogy. In fact, some proudly 
flaunt their intolerance, overtly advancing racist claims. 
Rick from Las Vegas opined, “The native Americans 
are mostly peaceable. Some need to be reminded who 
won the wars.” Bill Smith from El Paso added:
I tend to think that all of this noise about mas-
cots offending certain groups of peoples is 
taking up valuable time and effort that could 
be directed at solving important issues. And 
besides the Indians lost the war and therefore 
it is our right to make fun of them (at least we 
give them welfare and a place to live).
Taken together, arguments in defense of mascots 
take five key positions. First, they refuse to engage 
or take seriously the concerns of living Native 
Americans in their defenses of “their” imagined 
Indians. Second, they exhibit a propensity to tell 
Native Americans how it is or how they should feel 
(namely respected and honored). Third, their argu-
ments question the grounding of critics, enjoining 
them to “get real” or “get a life,” precisely as they 
infantilize them through demands that opponents 
“grow up.” Fourth, supporters display an inability 
and unwillingness to see or talk about race. When 
race does enter into their discussions, moreover, 
they qualify and constrain it. On the one hand, they 
suggest that racism is meaningful only when it is 
intentional, guided by ill will, and truly significant 
(i.e., in the real world). On the other hand, many sup-
porters claim parity between their ethnic heritage 
and racial condition and that of Native Americans, 
arguing that Irishness, for instance, is equivalent to 
Indianness in terms of the privileges, possibilities, 
and histories.
In Opposition to Mascots
Opponents of mascots advance a set of overlapping 
arguments. Throughout, they foreground race, his-
tory, and power.
Not surprisingly, opponents of mascots devote 
great energy to challenging the arguments advanced 
in defense of such symbols and nicknames. In the USA 
Weekend forum, opponents frequently underscored 
the ignorance of supporters. In playful and pejora-
tive terms, they questioned supporters’ familiarity 
with Native American cultures and their knowledge 
of American history and the English language. With 
almost equal frequency, opponents dispute assertions 
that mascots honor Native Americans. Jay Rosenstein 
asks, “Why do people continue to insist these nick-
names honor American Indians when the people you 
claim to be honoring tell that it’s not? Y ou honor and 
respect someone by listening to them.” Jim Northrup, 

58 Audiences
an Anishinaabe, has never felt honored by mascots; 
and more, he continues, “Someone telling me I should 
feel honored does not feel the same as being honored.” 
As Arek Dreyer suggests, “It is pretty arrogant to dic-
tate what someone else should be honored by.”
Arguments against mascots pivot around race. 
Some note with sadness that Native Americans still 
lack parity with other ethnic groups. Elaine Flattery 
remarks, “Other races simply aren’t subjected to this 
sort of racial stereotype propaganda. Native American 
images and names should not be the ‘property’ of cor-
porate American exploit and merchandize.” Similarly, 
Beth from Alstead, New Hampshire, argues:
The fact that caricatures of American Indian 
people exist with the consent from white peo-
ple means that the race isn’t take seriously 
in this country and they are being “used” for 
the entertainment and contrived message 
that white people get from them. Y ou don’t 
see these kinds of mascots of other races…
Because American Indian Nations have been 
stuffed into third world roles for the past three 
centuries, they are being denied the voice to 
have white America listen to them.
Others question the racial content of names and 
symbols. Danielle N’Dhighe asserts:
Using Native Americans as mascots is racist 
and should be stopped immediately. After all 
we don’t see teams like the Washington Black-
skins…or the San Francisco Slant Eyes. Almost 
everyone would agree that such things would 
be racist and denigrating. Why then do we 
allow Redskins and Chief Wahoo?
And John Whalen asks “How can ‘redskins’ be 
interpreted as anything other than blatant racism? 
How can any ridiculous caricature such as Chief 
Wahoo be seen as anything other than demeaning?”
Opponents of mascots do not simply highlight 
racism, they also actively strive to make the racial 
content of mascots tangible, linking them to a more 
palpable and familiar version of race. For some, the 
historic tradition of blackface is a striking parallel. 
Nota Bell, for instance, finds mascots “no less dis-
tasteful than shuck & jive antics in blackface is to 
Black Americans.” More commonly, opponents offer 
racial analogies, comparing Native Americans with 
other racial groups. Frequently, they invent new and 
intentionally provocative team names. These include 
“New Y ork Niggers,” “Jersey Jewboys,” “Washington 
Wops,” “Mississippi Blackies,” “Atlanta Rednecks,” 
“Washington Palefaces,” “Los Angeles Spics,” “Chi-
cago Pollacks,” and “Cleveland Honkies.”
In contrast with supporters, opponents of mascots 
stress history and power, situating nicknames and sym-
bols in a broader context of oppression. Dolores Jones, 
for instance, suggests that “Native Americans have 
always been oppressed peoples…They DESERVE  
some RESPECT!!! What is being done by sports teams 
is mockery.” Eric Anderson, in turn, asserts:
This whole deal is a “controversy” only because 
non-Natives with power continue to show dis-
respect for Native peoples and cultures. Y ou 
might think that five hundred years of genocide 
has been enough, but corporate greed and the 
long-standing tradition of racism in America 
just won’t let go. If Native peoples are offended 
by these mascots—and they are—then the 
mascots should be changed. It is a matter of 
courtesy and respect.
Likewise, Bolaji from Pasadena, California laments 
“the past of the USA continues to haunt it.” Despite 
heartfelt claims to honor or respect indigenous peo-
ples through mascots, he continues, “the bloodiness 
and hate of the country’s history inevitably taints what-
ever good intentions there might be in [these] positive 
gestures.” A. T. Lang pushes this thinking even further:
The problem with this country now and in 
the past is they want to sweep “THE INDIAN 
ISSUE” UNDER THE RUG! Over 60 million 
Indians were slaughtered, raped, enslaved, and 
[had] their land stolen. The “Indian Ho locaust” 
was one of the cornerstones behind Hitler’s 
slaughter of 6 million Jews. It is long past due 
for this country to show respect for the rights 
of the FIRST AMERICANS. That includes not 
using them for “mascots” AND NOT sweeping 
Indian issues under the rug any longer!!!!
Undoing this history and respecting Native Ameri-
cans as equals, Andrew Jackson concludes, demands 
not only that mascots be retired but also that “THIS 


Audience Studies 59
CO
UNTRY HONOR THE TREATIES THAT WERE 
SIGNED WITH THE NATIVE PEOPLES.”
Arguments advanced against Native American 
mascots display four key features. First, they overtly 
engage with and challenge supporters’ knowledge 
and understanding. Second, they direct attention to 
race and its effects. Third, they actively racialize the 
debate over mascots, making analogies between the 
experience and condition of Native Americans and 
those of other racial groups, particularly African Amer-
icans. Fourth, they historicize the use of American 
Indian nicknames and symbols, connecting them with 
broader patterns of discrimination and oppression.
Interpretation of the Arguments
The arguments over the continued use of American 
Indian nicknames and symbols have much to teach 
us about race and the media. They remind us of the 
creativity and situated agency of media consumers. 
Texts, images, and performances do not have fixed 
meanings but rather audiences actively interpret 
them, negotiating and literally creating their signif-
icance. The critique and defense of mascots, along 
with the efforts (successful or not) to retire and retain 
them, underscore, moreover, that these processes 
are not singular. Rather, audiences struggle with one 
another, and often with social institutions, including 
the media, to give meaning to signs (mascots), their 
worlds of experience and collective heritage (identity), 
and their positions, perspectives, and possibilities.
Supporters and defenders of mascots clearly 
disagree about their significance. Whereas supporters 
insist that mascots foster respect and are meant to 
honor Native Americans, opponents assert that they 
denigrate Native Americans, perpetuating historical 
patterns of discrimination and dispossession. The dis-
tinct positions advanced in the unfolding debates point 
to deeper differences: supporters stress text (honor, 
intention); opponents emphasize context (history and 
racism). Supporters isolate; opponents make connec-
tions. Supporters argue for intent; opponents argue 
for effect. Supporters consider symbols and names 
flat and more or less unimportant; opponents think of 
symbols as powerful cultural forms that reflect social 
relations and reinforce historical inequalities. Support-
ers deflect and deny the import of race; opponents 
highlight the centrality of race.
In effect, supporters and opponents occupy what 
Prochaska (2001, p. 175) dubbed “mutually exclusive 
communicative communities” informed by distinct 
interpretive frameworks. To my mind, something fun-
damental is discernible in the arguments advanced and 
their “communities” of origin. That is, they advance 
competing visions of race. Supporters, who might be 
described as advocates of a more or less dominant, if 
not reactionary, notion, hold that “we are all more or 
less equal,” that the ill intentions of prejudiced individ-
uals produce racism, and that discussions of discrim-
ination should be confined to “real” and “important” 
social domains. In contrast, opponents advance an 
emergent, counter-hegemonic perspective—that is, 
an interpretation reading the social relations and cul-
tural categories against the grain, exposing the power 
and meaning embedded within accepted norms, ide-
ologies, and behaviors. Opponents argue that race 
and racism are central to the American experience, 
that the effects of racial hierarchy cannot be ignored, 
and that symbols such as mascots—far from being 
 fri
volous—are significant measures of race relations. 
In this light, the ongoing controversy over mascots is 
as much about conflicting interpretations of race as it 
is a series of arguments over the appropriateness of 
Native American images in popular culture.

names such as the Vikings or Fighting

3.2: FASHIONING THE UMMAH: A 
THOROUGHLY MODERN MUSLIM 
MOVEMENT
Sabah Firoz Uddin
Islamic dress in its various cultural iterations con-
tinues to provoke controversy, as Muslim actors 
weigh in on what dress for women is constitutive of 
Islam and representative of the ummah (the com-
munity as a whole). For many, focusing on aesthet-
ics (fashion and beauty) is an example of modern 
concepts polluting Muslim girls’ minds. Despite 
this, Islamic fashion aesthetics are increasingly 
evident on social media, where Muslim women 
use new technologies to produce blogs, Y ouTube 
makeup and fashion tutorials, and Instagram pho-
tographs and stories. These young Muslim women, 
clothed in hijab, a head covering worn by many 
Muslim women, keenly put themselves on display 
on social media platforms highlighting the trends 
in modest fashion. Ruba Zai’s Hijab Hills Insta-
gram account has 1.1 million followers, and self-
 
pr
ofessed “modest fashion know-it-all” Dina Tokio 
has 1.3 million followers. These and other Muslim 
fashionistas painstakingly document their daily 
sartorial journeys and memorialize their clothing 
choices through text and photographs. In so doing, 
they often overtly attempt to reconcile moder -
nity with faith and fashion within a global Muslim 
community.
Based on interviews with 15 women who blog 
on sites such as Haute Hijab, The Muslim Girl, Tales of 
a Muslim Fashionista, Modest Street Fashion, and Ya z  
the Spaz, and their social media content, I explore 
how social media operate as a forum for public dia-
logue without religious authority and contribute to the 
fashioning of a Muslim self through the performance 
of dress. I ask, What position do they hope to estab-
lish? How do they contribute to the debate on Islamic 
dress? To what extent and how do they cultivate an 
Islamic ummah consciousness and construct a mod-
ern religiously conscious identity independent from 
nation-state identity?
Islamic Fashion and Social Media
In the 1970s and 1980s, with the rise of Islamic 
revivalist movements in Egypt and Iran, dress 
became crucial to the construction of Islamic reli-
gious, cultural, and national identities. Whereas 
women sympathetic to secular leadership were 
uncovered and clothed in Western style of dress 
(short skirts, sleeveless tops), supporters of Islamic 
rule demonstrated their Islamic identity and public 
piety by advocating for a recognizable, purposely 
The author interviewed 15 modest fashion bloggers 
to understand how they offer an alternative reading 
of Muslim dress, and reconcile faith and fashion in 
a global Muslim community.
and ethnicity? What do they tell us about 
racial identity, privilege, and relations in 
the contemporary United States?
 3.
 W
hy are there no African American 
mascots? What does the prevalence of 
Indian symbols and nicknames paired 
with the absence of Black symbols and 
nicknames suggest about ethnic identity, 
racial stereotyping, and respect?


Audience Studies 61
unf
ashionable, uniform Islamic dress – full-length 
coat and hijab in muted colors.
Since the early 2000s, however, there has been a 
shift to a more individualized approach to religiously 
mandated attire. Today, women are challenging or 
resisting earlier edicts of dress and advocating the 
right to conform to religious rules of modesty and 
to negotiate their public bodies through dress on 
their own terms. Islamic fashion can be generally 
seen as a by-product of this approach – the fusion of  
stylistic clothing trends and theological principles of 
modesty.
Today, many Muslim women are responding to 
the emergence of hijab in public spaces in Muslim and 
non-Muslim countries by reconceptualizing Islamic 
dress and how best to express materially their 
 moder
n 
Muslim identity. Social media have facilitated an 
increasingly visible presence of Muslim women in the 
public sphere, many of whom are searching for ways to 
express themselves, to be socially acceptable to West-
ern eyes, and to distance themselves from lingering 
stereotypes surrounding Islamic dress.
Coded with a variegated set of meanings, the 
hijab remains salient as a visual trope. Reduced to 
a set of polarities: veiled/unveiled, religious/secu-
lar, traditional/modern, backward/progressive, and 
oppressed/liberated, the hijab, as part of religious 
dress, informs the Western narrative of the inferiority 
of the Muslim Other. In the post-9/11 era, the pur -
ported plight of the so-called “forcibly covered” Mus-
lim woman continues to serve Western ideological 
interests as it invites the moral justification for military 
intervention and austere policy measures for members 
of minoritized immigrant communities.
Muslim fashionistas, then, are confronting three 
distinct challenges. First, to resist internal fixed cultural 
notions about how Muslim women should look, dress, 
and behave, and to reconceptualize what constitutes 
an Islamic uniform for women. Second, to re-direct the 
Western gaze so that the hijab represents neither the 
truth of oppression nor women as insular, or as Reina 
Lewis (2013, p. 3) puts it, “representatives of essential-
ized, unchanging collective religious identities.” Third, 
to distance the narrative of the non-
 moder
n from 
women in Islamic dress and, instead, be seen and 
read in hijab as a modern subject. According to Salam 
Al-Mahadin,
The hijab is an instant problematization of 
the body. The hijab, that tiny piece of cloth-
ing, is often the main organizing principle of 
someone’s identity and subjectivity. Almost 
everything is anchored in it...The western 
gaze in particular is unsettled and unnerved 
by it, hence, the need to fetishize it by claim-
ing that the body behind the hijab is that of an 
oppressed and abused woman.
(2013, p. 5)
The inclination to associate hijab with the non-
 
moder
n encourages the edifice of social boundaries 
where shared values are rarely acknowledged and 
difference is highlighted.
My project began with the everyday task of 
searching the internet, looking for young women 
actively producing content about their Islamic fash-
ion choices. I utilized two methods of data acqui-
sition. First, once I identified popular social media 
personalities (based on number of followers), I 
reached out to them by email to be interviewed. All 
of my 15 participants are under the age of 30, and 
describe themselves in hyphenated identities. Their 
objectives, as stated on their social media platforms, 
share some commonalities: to express creativity; to 
promote personal style with modesty; to encourage 
diversity, representation, and inclusivity as Muslim 
women in the mainstream; and to provide an alter -
native space/platform for Muslim women to explore 
fashion. Most of these women post daily pictures of 
their outfits and makeup and unveil shopping hauls. 
Some post weekly photographic spreads displaying 
clothes outfitted for different occasions. The images 
are generally full body shots of the producer or 
models showcasing clothes and accessories (shoes, 
jewelry, handbags) accompanied by information 
about where to buy the items.
I asked my interviewees about their identity and 
the role dress plays in the construction of that iden-
tity and about their perspectives on religion and dress, 
including how they respond to criticisms that fashion is 
inherently incompatible with Islam. I also asked about 
the content on their social media sites, including how 
they determine what content is religiously permissible. 
I also analyzed my interviewees’ social media sites 
(including reader comments), without interpretation 
from the content producer. My goal was to stitch both 

62 Audiences
objective and subjective perspectives into what I see 
as a general pattern emerging about the role these 
women play in contributing to alternative narratives 
about Islam, women, and dress.
Mapping the Modesty Movement
For these content producers I interviewed, their faith 
is integral to their work. That is, Islam informs the 
spirit of the content. It reflects their Muslim identity 
and values and determines discursive boundaries. 
However, the women are cognizant of ensuring that 
there is never a singular focus on what dress is con-
sidered wholly “Islamic.” So although a post may 
include styling headscarves with jeans, dresses, and 
high-heeled footwear, the women do not suggest 
that all Muslim women cover or should cover. They 
want the reader to attach her own specific meaning 
to dress. For example, for Mariah Idrissi, the first 
hijabi model featured in a mainstream fashion cam-
paign for H&M, dress is a form of personal expres-
sion and spirituality connecting [her] to God and is 
solely done for [herself] and not for other people. 
Similarly, Iklas of The Muslim Girl Blog told me:
Muslim fashion is diverse. Depending on the 
region where Muslims live, the fashion is bound 
to be different. Everyone’s interpretation of 
modesty and Islamic fashion varies and so that 
leads to no one single idea or understanding of 
Muslim fashion.
When discussing the content on her blog, she 
explained,
It can be tough, as a hijabi, to keep myself 
in check and not cater only to hijabi fashion. 
Many girls don’t wear hijab, but also prefer to 
dress modestly, so that’s something I have to 
keep in mind as well.
Similarly, Asma, producer of The Haute Muslimah 
blog, includes a disclaimer on her site,
All the fashion and the looks that discussed 
are meant for people to take into consideration 
when dressing themselves, or thinking about 
what might work for them. I might have a look 
with a mini-dress. For some women, this may 
be how they dress out normally. For others, this 
can be worn with pants and something over 
it for more coverage. And yet for others, this 
dress may be worn only at women-only events, 
because they wear niqab, jilbab and are cov-
ered from head/hijab to toe otherwise.
She further makes the point,
I do try to choose modest pieces when writing 
about them. However, everyone has a different idea of 
what is modest and I leave it up to the reader to decide 
what is for them.
The bloggers, in general, seem to move away 
from the weight of naming their sartorial preference 
“Islamic.” Instead, all of the interviewees pointed to 
a renewed desire for modest dress and style – even 
though “modest” remains undefined. Sadiyya Ali from 
Tales of a Muslim Fashionista explains,
As a Muslim woman who dresses in the hijab 
I do feel the need to promote the idea that 
dressing modestly is part of my faith. As for 
a specific kind of dress, no, I don’t think it’s a 
religious obligation to promote only one kind 
of dress. Muslims come from different parts 
of the world and our way of dressing is influ-
enced by that. So having every Muslimah dress 
in one specific type of clothing is unrealistic 
and impractical. We all have different identi-
ties, experiences, and preferences that shape 
our way of dressing.
Additionally, Feexa Nicol of Hijab N The City told 
me,
I am not so quick to call anything as an Islamic 
Fashion as there will normally be people who 
will take advantage of the word “Islamic” and 
unnecessarily drive it to be out of context. I 
describe mine to be more of a modest 
 f
ashion – 
an exploration of creativity and individuality of 
fashion without losing sight of values and iden-
tities of a Muslim woman.
What I found is that for the bloggers and their fol-
lowers, clothing choices play a transformative role 
in the construction and (re)presentation of an alter-
native social self and in generating a new religious 


Audience Studies 63
f
orm of belonging based on an individual, creative 
self. The very naming of fashion “Islamic” might 
lead to an unintentional focus on religion. There-
fore, they distance themselves from a theological 
standpoint on dress and thus allow their readers  
to define piety for themselves. Although they take 
inspiration from Islam, their affect is instead a 
modern, organic expression of such identity, with-
out relying on dogmatic theological prescriptions. 
Angelini (2014, p. 3) described these new actors as 
“a new breed of Muslim hipsters called Mipsters” 
who self-identify as
Someone at the forefront of the latest music, 
fashion, art, critical thought, food, imagi-
nation, creativity and all forms of obscure 
everything...A Mipster has a social mind and a 
yearning for a more just order, a more inclusive 
community unbounded by stale categories.
I simply read it as a modesty movement.
The modesty movement, as I term it, transforms 
and normalizes the hijab – something often seen as for-
eign and a signal of not belonging. Playing with notions 
of visibility and invisibility, bloggers tend to normalize 
their sartorial practices by the complex and at times 
contradictory processes of mimicking images found 
in high-fashion magazines and reproducing the visual 
trope of Muslim women in hijab. However, although 
Muslim women’s dress code is seemingly uniform, 
the bloggers I spoke to shape new boundaries. Albeit 
rooted in a social expression of modesty, their lan-
guage appears flexible – enabling a new meaning of 
piety and modesty, resulting in new representations of 
the Muslim body.
The traditional function of the hijab is to veil, 
both physically and metaphorically, and “has been 
associated with a need to ‘hide’ the female body, an 
act of concealment of an object that could create 
desire, a symbolic erasure and a quest for invisibility” 
(Al-
 Mahadin, 2013, p
. 11). However, Muslim fashion 
bloggers are attempting to re-direct the gaze so that 
in many ways, the Muslim woman in hijab, previously 
perceived as inaccessible, has entered the public imag-
ination, her bodily performance in pictures (what she 
wears, eats, where she shops, travels, her life philos-
ophy) exposed. Whereas hijab is usually visual short-
hand for the invisibility and effacement of Muslim 
women in the public space, these women are reviving 
and reframing modest dress as a means to increase 
visibility of Muslim women. These bloggers define and 
contest the boundary markers for religious or cultural 
integrity and adopt what they perceive as correct reli-
gious attire, yet still ensure their legitimacy as Muslim.
What do these women hope to accomplish with 
their social media accounts? I believe that although 
they want to be active participants in the public dis-
course about Muslim dress, their goals are not overly 
ambitious. They do not debate religious issues and do 
not attempt to ascribe a global uniform of Islamic dress. 
In fact, they are acutely aware their bodily performance 
in virtual public space continues to be a profound site 
of contestation. The comment sections in their social 
media sites reveal some readers’ negative preoccupa-
tion with their dress, makeup, high heels, and so forth, 
in some cases deeming it un-Islamic. For example, 
one comment found in Saufeeya Goodson’s Instagram 
account read, “Y ou already show half your hair. What 
is the point of being hijabi in this case? Y ou represent 
us in a wrong way!” Although most of my interview-
ees do not respond to trolls, Saufeeya addressed the 
issue in a lengthy letter posted to her 325,000 Insta-
gram followers. In it, she wrote, “do not confine me to 
your labels and expectations. I’m not here to impose 
my beliefs on anybody, nor am I here to stand as a  
complete embodiment and representation of all Mus-
lim women.” She further addressed the troll specifically,
Y our definition and interpretation of mod-
esty will not be the same as everyone else. 
So, whether I choose to wear hijab or not, my 
choice of dress doesn’t diminish my worth or 
value. This is not a space for you to place your 
judgment and expectation on modesty and 
the hijab isn’t a meter to dictate a good person 
from a bad person, it is a personal choice.
Saufeeya and my other interviewees seek a more 
utopian endeavor and to transcend borders to con-
struct a global imagined Muslim community, exem-
plified in difference. Their musings express life at a 
local level in a national context but are rooted in the 
desire to build a sense of community, to reinforce 
solidarity with those who share their sacred identity, 
and to reorganize modern Muslim consciousness in 
public space.

64 Audiences
Transforming Islamic Dress
The constitutive effect of these social media sites 
is more far-reaching than a reader of fashion blogs 
or an Instagram follower might think. In a time 
when negative semiotic preoccupation with Islamic 
dress continues to endure both within and outside 
the Muslim community, these women boldly pro-
vide what I see as an alternative feminist identity. 
They resist ideological constructions of femininity 
as defined by others. Here I offer the following par-
allel to Charles Blow’s (2015) thinking about race 
and space. Blow discussed how, historically, Black 
bodies have been a battlefield, and how “black folks 
try to calibrate their bodies to avoid injury” (2015, 
p. A23). He then argued that “Y oung black folks are 
refusing alteration or the mollification of conform-
ity” (p. A23). I think this is analogous to how the 
Muslim women bloggers I spoke with occupy virtual 
space. In a self-conscious negotiation with religion 
and culture, they too, like those young Blacks, are 
active agents in reclaiming the narrative. By demon-
strating through the fashioning of the self in faith-
 
f
ocused dress, these blogs are a protest against both 
the chastisement and discipline of Muslim women’s 
bodies and the metanarrative of a conforming sin-
gular Muslim female subject. They continue to com-
plicate our understanding of what it means to be a 
Muslim woman in the modern world.
My interviewees no longer operate within the 
conventional modern/traditional dichotomy. Instead 
they are transforming Islamic dress behavior to reflect 
their modern selves. Their goal is to contest two simul-
taneously occurring assertions, both of which place 
limits on clothing practices: fashion is superficial and 
belongs to the West, and Islamic dress does not sit 
easy with fashion. The inevitable conclusion is that 
religiously conspicuous hijab is categorically not fash-
ion and thus does not belong in Western space. These 
women hope to dislocate the geographical and phil-
osophical borders associated with Islamic dress and 
to develop a system of dress reflecting both religion 
and elements of Western fashion (scarves, long skirts, 
jeans, long tunics). As Alexandru Balasescu noted, 
“There are modern ways of looking at tradition and 
modern uses of traditional clothes” (2007, p. 302). I see 
the re-fashioning of Islamic dress codes as an appeal 
to the multiple possibilities of expressing modernity. 
Hijab can be hip; modesty and modernity can reside 
comfortably alongside each other. The women I inter-
viewed are forging their own cultural spaces where 
Islamic fashion co-exists with the local system of fash-
ion. Emerging from their own personal challenges in 
finding clothing to fit both their desire for contempo-
rary Western fashion and their religious modesty, these 
women have found a way to express their belonging to 
faith and Western popular culture.
The changes in dress mirror the larger picture 
where Muslim women are no longer content in the 
margins and are visibly positioning themselves as 
active modern citizens in the public space. In this 
restaging of religion with fashion, we see the result of 
successful contestation and negotiation with multiple 
narratives. Never belonging to one singular space, 
these social media content producers are able to repo-
sition both traditional religion and modern secularism 
to complicate the relationship between the seemingly 
competing dress systems of mainstream fashion and 
Islamic dress. The space in which these women inte-
grate modesty with fashion provides a useful example 
of how modern Muslim women authorize not only 
Western discursive language and cultural tools in ser-
vice of innovating style but also new sites of belonging 
in a public space. Versed in ideas of multiculturalism, 
pluralism, and individualism, these women draw on a 
range of sources, negotiating and improvising tradi-
tional and modern cultural forms, to reveal the multi-
ple possibilities of modern Muslim identity and bodily 
practices in public. Although they frame their bodies as 
Muslim, they attempt to be seen as inclusive in the sec-
ular body politic. In the interstices, these women can 
be visible and concealing at the same time. By con-
signing traditions to their mothers, they resist serving 
as symbols of home and, instead, construct alterna-
tive femininities in the context of a secular space that 
includes sacred Islam. By offering an alternative read-
ing of Islamic dress, the women I interviewed re-work 
the ideological construction of hijab and Islamic dress 
so that it blurs contesting spatial and social codes and 
is no longer a currency of oppression or sidelined to a 
discourse of exclusion. The resolve to let their fashion 
define their hybrid identity and relationship with the 
mainstream secular public speaks to transformative 
potential of sartorial practices.


Audience Studies 65
Ref
erences
