hip hijabistas: Y oung Muslim women are debunking the 
stereotypical image of Islam by making a symbol of 
modesty look cool. The Sunday Times, p. 3.
Balasescu, A. (2007). Haute couture in Tehran: Two faces 
of an emerging fashion scene. Fashion Theory, 11(2–3), 
302.
Blow, C. (2015, November 16). Race, college and safe space. 
The New Y ork Times, p. A23.

3.3: THE (CLIMATE) REVOLUTION WILL 
NOT BE COLONIZED
Carolyn M. Cunningham
The past few years have seen the rise of climate girl 
activists who are demanding that policymakers and 
corporate leaders take immediate action to curb 
the rise in carbon emissions, which threatens future 
life on the planet. Perhaps the most famous climate 
girl is Greta Thunberg, who rose to fame in 2018 at 
age 16 when she started the movement “Skolstrejk 
för klimatet” (School Strike for Climate). A photo of 
Thunberg sitting alone outside the Swedish Parlia-
ment, dressed in her yellow raincoat, long blonde 
braids, and holding a hand-painted sign, went viral, 
quickly leading to a global school strike movement, 
Fridays for Future. Many have critiqued mainstream 
media for propping Thunberg up as the face of the 
youth climate justice movement, especially because 
she is White. Y et, many girls of color are taking an 
intersectional approach to climate activism, insist-
ing that to address climate change, we must also 
address structural inequalities.
One prominent climate girl leader is Jamie Mar-
golin, who identifies as queer, Latinx, and Jewish. She 
became involved in climate activism when she started 
high school. In 2016, at age 15, she started the non-
profit Zero Hour, whose aim is to train youth activists 
on grassroots organizing. Zero Hour is notable because 
it is led primarily by girls of color.
In this case study, I provide background on Mar-
golin’s story of climate activism, which is rooted in her 
experience growing up with anxiety about the environ-
ment, as well as her increased awareness about her 
own racial and sexual identity. I situate her work within 
girls’ studies, whose aim is to better understand girls on 
their terms. I show how Margolin’s activism demands 
structural change and capitalizes on digital networks 
to communicate and organize. Despite Margolin’s rad-
ical message and approach to climate change, main-
stream media tend to focus narrowly on her age and 
her exceptionalism.
Spectacular Climate Girls and Girls’ 
Studies
Why are girl activists suddenly on the cover of 
magazines, winning prestigious awards, and invited 
to speak on the global stage when it comes to the 
climate crisis? According to Taft (2020), some girl 
activists have risen to fame because they seem to 
be singlehandedly solving some of the most press-
ing global problems, such as access to education for 
girls (Malala Y ousafzai), gun violence (X González), 
and climate change (Greta Thunberg). Although 
A new wave of activism includes girls of color who 
take an intersectional approach to the climate cri-
sis. They frame their messages through creating 
their own media, as is demonstrated through a 
case study of Jamie Margolin, founder of the youth 
advocacy organization Zero Hour .
It’s Your Turn: What Do You Think? What 
Will You Find?
 1.
 Anal
yze a modest fashion social media 
account. In what ways do the images 
and posts reinforce or challenge your 
perceptions of Muslim women?
 2.
 Anal
yze your favorite social media 
account through a narrow lens. Explore 
what the carefully curated images are 
trying to say about racial and gendered 
identities in today’s society.

66 Audiences
these girls have mainstream media attention, Taft 
warns that their messages of social change are 
often downplayed because the girls are seen as 
spectacular or exceptional. Media frame them as 
lone girls fighting an unjust system, ignoring the 
larger networks within which they work, which 
“gives the impression that sociocultural and politi-
cal change happens as soon as one exceptional girl 
puts her mind to it” (Bent, 2020, p. 800). The icon 
of the spectacular girl activist is reinforced by sto-
ries emphasizing what the girls are wearing, what 
shows they are streaming, what they are eating, and 
how they manage to launch school strikes from their 
bedrooms while still making good grades.
This study draws on girls’ studies scholarship, 
which emerged in the 1990s as a response to femi-
nist scholarship that privileged adult women without 
considering the context of girls’ lives (Kearney, 2009). 
Girlhood was seen as a developmental stage that girls 
passed through before becoming adult women. How-
ever, scholars draw attention to the unique perspec-
tives girls have and to the pressures they face given 
interlocking identities including socioeconomic status, 
race, ethnicity, sexuality, and ability.
Girls engage in many forms of activism that chal-
lenge hegemonic norms of gender, age, and power, but 
face barriers, especially because mainstream media 
make them into spectacles while downplaying the 
seriousness of their messages. As girl activists capti-
vate the public, they become open to criticism. For 
example, Greta Thunberg has been the object of vitriol 
for adult White male politicians who have launched 
attacks on her on their social media, such as Donald 
Trump, who said she had an anger management prob-
lem and Boris Johnson who called her a “Bunny Hug-
ger” (Olesen, 2020).
Jamie’s Story
Within this context, Jamie Margolin has risen to 
fame. Born in Seattle, Jamie speaks about how the 
climate crisis has always been a part of her reality 
leading to anxiety and fear that she would not have 
a future:
My life, and that of my entire generation, is full 
of “ifs.” If climate change hasn’t completely 
destroyed society as we know it. If that part of 
the world isn’t uninhabitable by the time I’m an 
adult. If the coral reefs are still there.
(Margolin, 2019b)
In an interview, she said, “there is a recent United 
Nations [climate change] report that said we have 
12 years left to save the world. My life is just going to 
begin when the world ends” (Keating, 2018).
Anxiety fueled her climate activism, which 
includes giving climate action presentations to students 
and lobbying politicians. Climate activism also helped 
raise Jamie’s consciousness about how race, class, and 
sexuality influenced her own identity. She started vol-
unteering with the local Democratic campaign office; 
because she speaks Spanish, she could advocate for 
Spanish speakers’ concerns. She recounted how this 
experience made her aware of her own privilege: “out 
of my fear of how the world would react to me, and 
how big the issue was, I had assimilated into the white, 
heteronormative, climate-denying business as usual 
society” (Margolin, 2019b).
Jamie emphasizes how intersectionality allowed 
her to better understand her own identity as well as 
how it impacts climate change. First coined by legal 
scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw (1989), intersectionality is 
a framework for understanding interlocking systems of 
oppression. For example, Black women face oppres-
sion based on their gender and on their race. Intersec-
tionality is the framework that guides Jamie’s activism.
Zero Hour
Margolin started Zero Hour along with several other 
girls of color, including Nadia Nazar, who started 
following Margolin after who reading her editorial 
“An open letter to climate deniers” in Teen Ink. Mar-
golin’s Instagram exhortation to take “bold” action 
inspired Nazar to join the movement. One of Zero 
Hour’s biggest actions was a 2018 Y outh Climate 
March in Washington, D.C. It inspired 25 sister 
marches around the world; Greta Thunberg identi-
fied the march as sparking the idea for her school 
strikes.
Zero Hour uses online networks to organize, a 
form of activism Bennett and Segerberg (2012) call 
connective action, in which people organize outside 


Audience Studies 67
of
 traditional politics. The climate march was planned 
online and many of the organizers first met in person 
at the march itself.
Zero Hour’s intersectional platform recognizes 
that capitalism, racism, sexism, and colonialism all 
contribute to climate change. According to its website, 
“the mission of Zero Hour is to center the voices of 
diverse youth in the conversation about climate and 
environmental justice” (Zero Hour, n.d.). Zero Hour 
supports the Green New Deal and calls for a just tran-
sition to an environmentally sustainable economy that 
includes an infrastructure that relies on clean, renew-
able energy sources. This platform is coalitional, con-
necting social justice with environmental justice. Zero 
Hour calls for moving away from the school-to-prison 
pipeline and respecting the Treaty Rights of Indige-
nous Nations. Other principles include being peaceful 
and nonviolent, being humble and learning from each 
other, and extending the hand of friendship. Members 
of Zero Hour are creating the kinds of organizations 
that they themselves want to join.
As Margolin (2019b) said: “I am especially proud 
of building a movement that is run by women of color. 
It provides a safe place for girls like me to lead.”
Media Framing of Margolin
Framing refers to how media practitioners select 
information to highlight in their stories, influencing 
how we think about contemporary issues (Entman, 
1993). In my analysis of media framing of Margolin, 
I examined articles in popular culture texts, includ-
ing Teen Vogue and People, as well as traditional 
news outlets, such as the New Y ork Times, between 
2018 and early 2022. My analysis revealed that the 
mainstream media narrative contains three main 
frames: Margolin as spectacular, Margolin as just a 
teenager, and Margolin’s struggle as a girl activist.
The first frame is that Margolin is spectacular. 
This can be seen in the many awards that are bestowed 
upon her by popular culture texts, such as Teen Vogue 
(one of the top 21 changemakers under 21 years old), 
People (one of the 25 women changing the world), 
and Seventeen (one of 11 young voices changing the 
world). Articles in these texts frame her as spectacu-
lar, spotlighting how she seems to be single-handedly 
addressing the climate crisis by taking politicians and 
corporations to task.
The second frame focuses on Margolin’s age. For 
example, one article is titled “How to build a climate 
movement before your 17th birthday” (Penner, 2018). 
Margolin is featured in a New Y ork Times article titled 
“Teenagers at the end of the world” (Jarvis, 2020). As 
part of this focus on her age, articles often highlight 
how she balances both school and activism and her 
desire to be a normal teenager. Twersky (2019) wrote, 
“in between SAT prep and college applications, Mar-
golin travels the world promoting Zero Hour’s cause, 
and informing the public of the need to act now.” Jarvis 
(2020) observed, 
she had 345 unread emails, a Slack that was 
bursting with messages, a conference call with 
the Zero Hour leadership that afternoon and 
a growing backlog of homework. I watched 
as the array of organizers seamlessly pivoted 
between teenagehood and big-stakes action.
At the same time, mainstream stories allow her to 
speak about her experiences with misogyny, racism, 
and homophobia. In Teen Vogue, she stated, “If I got 
money every time I was laughed at, interrupted, 
blatantly told that what I said was ‘false,’ and just 
overall mansplained in a professional environment, 
I think I could pay for college” (Maloney, 2018). 
After a lobbying event in Olympia, Washington, she 
confronted one of the older White male fossil fuel 
executives about the industry’s climate denialism. 
He interrupted her, squeezed her shoulder, and 
said, “Sweetie, don’t worry yourself so much about 
this ‘environment’ thing, because we corporations 
are actually the ones who do the most for the envi-
ronment. We got it covered. Just focus on school” 
(Maloney, 2018). After winning the MTV Genera-
tion Change award in 2019, she spoke about how 
people tell her to not focus on LGBTQ advocacy 
because it detracts from her message about climate 
(Romero, 2019).
Margolin on Her Own Terms
Although mainstream media tend to spectacular -
ize Margolin and emphasize her age, she uses her 

68 Audiences
age strategically. Margolin frames her age in a way 
that enacts a form of citizenship that allows her 
to engage in the public sphere. She states that she 
doesn’t want to be doing the work of adults, but 
she has to because she is fighting for her future. She 
speaks out for all children who are anxious about 
climate change and fear the end of the world: “If 
adults want youth to be studious and pay attention 
in school to prepare for our futures, then they need 
to do their jobs to make sure that a future exists for 
us” (Margolin, 2019d). In her book Y outh to Power, 
Margolin wrote that “as a chronically exhausted 
high school student with too much homework who’s 
running an international movement, I don’t have 
time to sugarcoat” (2020b, p. xvii).
Because few articles mention her approach to 
activism, Margolin uses a variety of media—editorials 
in mainstream and alternative news outlets, TED talks, 
books, and social media—to counter-frame the domi-
nant media narrative of her as spectacular and tell her 
climate justice story on her own terms. For example, 
she explained why she organized school strikes in both 
the New Y ork Times: “I am striking because it is point-
less to study for a future that does not exist” (Margolin, 
2019d), and the Washington Post: “My generation is 
giving up our youth — our schooling, our fun and our 
freedom — so that you can see next year” (Margolin, 
2020a).
Using her own words, she highlights how racism 
and capitalism fuel the climate crisis. For example, 
in the Guardian, she wrote about the disproportion-
ate impact of the climate crisis on “people of color, 
women, poor people, disabled people, queer people, 
homeless people” (Margolin, 2019c). She also empha-
sizes the role of colonization in the climate crisis. In 
her New Y ork Times editorial, she challenged the idea 
that the Industrial Revolution started the climate crisis 
and instead argues colonization threatened biodiver-
sity and promoted the ideology that the Earth was a 
commodity to be bought and sold (Margolin, 2019d).
Besides editorials, Margolin delivered a TED talk 
titled “Patriarchy, Racism, and Colonialism Caused the 
Climate Crisis” in which she calls on the audience to 
“to call out these systems of oppression, and demand 
the livable earth that we all deserve” (2019a). Truth To 
Power: Y our Voice and How to Use I is her guidebook for 
youth activists. It includes tips for how to write an edi-
torial, creating art for activism, and self-care. Her book 
is dedicated “to the queer kids. We are unstoppable.”
Climate Girl Activists in the Spotlight
What is it like to be a girl activist publicly docu-
menting your work? As Bent (2020) noted, the way 
girl activists are scrutinized works to constrain their 
radical activism. Through her high-profile public 
presence, Margolin is the target for online trolls who 
tell her that she should worry more about getting a 
boyfriend than politics, call her dumb, and critique 
her for not smiling enough.
Being in the spotlight can be difficult, especially 
as girl activists express different parts of their identity. 
As of this writing, Margolin is studying film at New 
Y ork University and is sharing her new interests. On 
Twitter, she posts about her creative projects in school 
as well as her purpose for being a storyteller. And she 
continues to post about the different climate-related 
activism that she is involved in.
Margolin’s climate girl story shows a queer girl 
of color navigating the hostile space of public media. 
Perhaps what Bent told us was true: that we are just 
waiting for these girls’ downfalls because they dared to 
move outside the confines of girlhood. Despite these 
challenges and the backlash she has received, Margo-
lin says she has no choice but to remain hopeful (Keat-
ing, 2018).

Will You Find?

70 Audiences
3.4: A CASE STUDY OF RACE AND 
TWITTER ACTIVISM: #BAMASITS IN 
RESPONSE TO COLIN KAEPERNICK
George L. Daniels
When San Francisco 49ers Quarterback Colin 
Kaepernick dropped to his knee as the national 
anthem was played during a September 1, 2016 
NFL preseason game in San Diego, no one guessed 
his protest against police brutality would spark a 
national debate about race and patriotism in Amer-
ica (for more on Kaepernick’s protest and how it 
was framed in the media, see Brown, Reading 4.7).
As the discussion unfolded, the use of Twitter as 
a protest tool sparked my interest. I study mass media 
diversity and teach at a university that in 1963 was 
the last flagship institution to admit African American 
students. When in October 2016 an African American 
student’s life was threatened in an online discussion 
about football fans choosing to sit during the national 
anthem, I saw this as an unfortunate opportunity to 
look closer at the concept of Twitter activism in a 
local context and assess its real value in increasing our 
understanding of Twitter activism and the racial divide 
on a college campus.
Every day millions of tweets are sent using hun-
dreds of different hashtags. I restricted my study to 
tweets in a particular locality and campus. Just as 
Bosch (2017) did in her study of the #RhodesMust-
Fall hashtag protest in Cape Town, South Africa, my 
study of Twitter activism localizes the larger discussion 
about Black Lives Matter (BLM) inspired by athletes 
led by Colin Kaepernick.
Kaepernick’s Movement and Black Lives 
Matter
Colin Kaepernick’s decision to take a knee during 
the national anthem began a movement that spread 
to 
 Sa
turday college football, Friday night high school 
games, and youth athletics. That movement was 
addressed in a TIME magazine cover story, “The 
 P
erilous Fight,” that examined the debate about privi-
lege, pride, and patriotism (Gregory, 2016). The author 
noted that the mostly African American professional 
sports players who were prompted by the death of 
Trayvon Martin and the fatal shootings of unarmed 
African Americans such as Michael Brown to speak 
out, in some ways, mirrored the activist athletes of an 
earlier generation.
The first step these athletes took was a tweet of 
solidarity with BLM: a photo of players wearing hood-
ies similar to that worn by Trayvon Martin when he 
was killed. As the debate over equality, opportunity, 
and treatment of minorities in America grew, stronger 
stances were taken and bolder gestures were made 
(Gregory, 2016). In his book on athletes and activism, 
former NBA player Etan Thomas (2018) interviewed 
prominent sports sociologist Harry Edwards, who 
believes Colin Kaepernick should be in the Smithso-
nian’s National Museum of African American History 
and Culture because of his activism. Edwards likened 
Kaepernick to the late heavyweight boxer Muham-
mad Ali, who in the 1960s as a conscientious objector 
to the Vietnam War was stripped of his boxing titles. 
Kaepernick’s action while still an active player sparked 
a movement for athletes in the era of BLM.
Organized in 2013, Black Lives Matter came to 
national attention during its 2014 street protests fol-
lowing the murder of Michael Brown in Ferguson, 
Missouri. BLM is a civil rights movement that counters 
institutional racism, racial injustice, and police brutal-
ity. It is not against the flag, or the military, as it has at 
times been presented by critics, nor is it anti-American. 
This politically active movement carries a broad mes-
sage that there can be no economic equality without 
racial justice. Ultimately, BLM seeks criminal justice 
reform and moves by federal and local governments 
to alleviate systemic racism.
A distinguishing factor in the BLM movement is 
its access to social media. In a purely tactical sense, 
the movement’s use of technology to mobilize hun-
dreds of thousands of people through social media is 
light years away from the labor required in the 1960s 
and even just a few years ago (Harris, 2015). Today 
social media—particularly Twitter—can reach indi-
viduals in milliseconds, slashing the time it takes to 
organize protests.
The author analyzed Twitter activity that used the 
hashtag #BamaSits as part of a protest against 
racial injustice at a college football game in Ala-
bama. The dialogue was primarily localized, and 
did not expand the discussion about the racial 
divide in the United States.


Audience Studies 71
T
witter Activism and #BamaSits
This study of Twitter activism and race connects 
with recent scholarship in an emerging area known 
as intersectional critical race technology studies. 
Such studies take an epistemological approach to 
researching gendered and racialized identities in 
digital and information studies (Noble & Tynes, 
2016). For example, by studying the images asso-
ciated with tweets during the 2011 Egyptian rev-
olution, Kharroub and Bas (2016) understood the 
potential of both emotional and efficacy-related 
visual content for motivating activism. Research has 
shown that emotionally arousing images get more 
attention and improve our comprehension more 
than non-emotional images do. Efficacy, or the per-
ception that one will be able to make a difference, 
is related to movement size and identification with 
the movement. Kharroub and Bas’ analysis showed 
more efficacy-eliciting (pictures of crowds, protest 
activities, national, and religious symbols) than 
emotionally arousing (violent) content.
As exemplified in a study of #ConcernedStu-
dent1950, the Twitter hashtag used by University of 
Missouri football players in their protests of racial-
ized practices at their school, Twitter functions as 
a central locus in organizing protests from breaking 
news to building public networks (Yan, Pegoraro, & 
Watanabe, 2018). Bonilla and Rosa (2015) showed 
how and why social media platforms have become 
powerful sites for documenting and challenging 
episodes of police brutality and misrepresentation 
of racialized bodies in mainstream media. Using 
the digital protests that occurred as demonstrators 
took to the streets of Ferguson, Bonilla and Rosa 
explained that hashtags allow users to not simply 
file their comments, but to performatively frame 
these comments. The hashtag #Ferguson created a 
shared temporality during the protests and confron-
tations with police, with Twitter users feeling like 
they were participating as they tweeted in real time 
about the unfolding events.
#BamaSits
Colin Kaepernick’s activist stance in 2016 was imi-
tated on college football Saturdays—including a 
homecoming game at The University of Alabama 
where then-defending National Champion Alabama 
Crimson Tide faced SEC East rival the Wildcats of 
the University of Kentucky. But Alabama’s 34–6 win 
over Kentucky was not what made the headlines. 
What made headlines was the University of Ala-
bama students who sat during the national anthem 
in a symbolic act of protest over the treatment of 
people of color and recent shootings of Black men 
by police. The protest continued at subsequent foot-
ball games with students announcing their plans in 
advance, using the hashtag #BamaSits to organize 
and explain their views. The Twitter activism spread 
to other social media platforms, such as Facebook, 
where a White student wrote to a Black student “I’ll 
kill you n---, don’t speak to me wrong.” Another 
message said “I’ll kick your black -ss.”
To allow a focus on a local issue, I consider as a 
case study a single hashtag, #BamaSits. To understand 
how the hashtag was used, I analyzed all of the tweets 
using the hashtag. Using Twitter’s native search engine, 
I searched for all tweets using the hashtag #Bama-
Sits between October 1 and October 18, 2016, when 
activity seemed to naturally cease. Screen captures 
were taken, yielding pages of tweets with all attributes 
attached. These were coded for date sent, sender’s 
Twitter handle, number of replies, presence of pictures, 
originality or retweet marks, and number of retweets.
Additionally, the tweets were categorized for 
their support or non-support of #BamaSits. Support-
ive tweets explicitly mentioned agreement with those 
who chose to sit during the national anthem. Non-
 
suppor
tive tweets were explicitly critical of those who 
chose to sit during the national anthem. All but three 
tweets could be coded as one of these two values.
Beyond this frequency analysis of the tweets, I 
also reviewed the tweets for words used, manner in 
which the Twitter user characterized BLM and other 
issues related to race, and the exchanges between 
Twitter users. In this qualitative phase of the analy-
sis, I also paid closer attention to the types of images 
used (i.e., emotionally arousing or efficacy-inducting). 
All examples are quoted verbatim unless indicated by 
[brackets].
Lessons from the Tweets
A total of 155 tweets used the #BamaSits hashtag. 
It first appeared on October 1, 2016, the day of the 
first student demonstration at the homecoming 

72 Audiences
game against Kentucky. Five tweets using the hash-
tag were sent that day; activity peaked the next day 
at 55 tweets. Between October 3 and 14, 2016, only 
a single tweet per day used the hashtag; it appears 
to have run its course and appeared only four more 
times during the next year. Of the 155 tweets, 53 
received replies; 32 were retweeted once, and 28 
were retweeted two or three times; 24 of the tweets 
included pictures.
Most of the tweets (136 of 155) using #Bama-
Sits supported the goals of the student protest. They 
supported Colin Kaepernick and other activist athletes 
kneeling during the national anthem. In one example 
of support of the goals of the protest, a Twitter user 
wrote, “#BamaSits because we have a responsibility 
as students with the privilege of education to organize 
and fight injustice. Y ou should too.” Another supportive 
tweet read, “I sit because my Father died for the right 
for you to sit.” Only 16 were negative or against the 
demonstration. One example of a negative tweet was 
“I stand because my Father died for the right for you 
to sit.”
Going a step beyond whether the tweet was sup-
portive or non-supportive of the students who staged a 
protest by sitting, the online exchanges reflected differ-
ent ideas about race and patriotism. In one exchange, 
a Twitter user simply wrote the hashtag #BamaSits 
to which another user responded, “So disrespectful 
yuck.” Another more emotional exchange featured 
one user who wrote in multiple consecutive tweets:
If I witness you sitting I will personally make you 
stand. Y ou think I’m joking I will literally f**king 
pick you up and put you on my shoulder and 
hold you like a f**king child since you want to 
act like one. Go back to f**king New Y ork. Why 
did you come to a school in the south?
Responding to the extended post, another user 
direct messaged University of Alabama administra-
tors: “Is this student upholding the values of the cap-
stone creed? A threat in response to #BamaSits.”
In many of the exchanges between those post-
ing, retweeting, and replying, the matter of patriotism, 
constitutional rights, and race surfaced multiple times. 
For example, one Twitter user and student involved 
in the protest retweeted the following message: “Pro-
test is as American as America itself—but the history 
of American protest has been whitewashed @deray 
at #ydsleadership @YaleDivSchool,” and then in the 
retweet added: “I sit because it is our constitutionally 
protected right to protest injustice #BamaSits #Black-
LivesMatter.” The @deray reference is to DeRay 
McKesson, a former school administrator known via 
Twitter for his support of BLM and involvement in 
protests against police brutality in Ferguson, Baltimore, 
and Baton Rouge.
Reflecting the broader narrative beyond just Colin 
Kaepernick or BLM, those students staging the protest 
tweeted “#BamaSits with Kaepernick, Charlotte, UNC, 
Black Lives Matter, Standing Rock & Uniontown,” to 
which a person retweeting added, “Proud of my home 
state! #BamaSits is HUGE news and counters the UA 
(and general southern) stereotype.” In a tweet that was 
retweeted several times, one Twitter user wrote: “Stu-
dents at my school, University of Alabama, decided 
to sit in solidarity w/Charlotte, Kaepernick, UNC, & 
BLM #BamaSits #BlackLivesMatter.” Another user 
responded: “Color me shocked! I never thought I’d see 
the day #ThanksBama #BamaSits to do this in the 
#DeepSouth is very brave!” These examples speak 
to the value of the localized discussions reflecting the 
regional nature of discussions about race. In other 
words, the fact that the student protest was happening 
in the Deep South was part of what made the protest 
worthy of note on Twitter.
Among the most frequent Tweeters using the 
#BamaSits hashtag were three of the student protest-
ers. One of those protesters, who posted 14 tweets 
during the period that was monitored, wrote, “I sit bc 
UA is an institution that protected and supported KKK, 
slavery, convict leasing 7 segregation #BamaSits,” and 
“I sit bc football directly profits off of black labor yet 
fans are incapable of supporting the people they sup-
posedly cheer for #BamaSits.” Another protester in 
three consecutive tweets wrote “I sit for all of those 
who have been discriminated against, shot, killed, mur-
dered in cold blood. For no reason #BamaSits,” “I sit 
because after 400 years, our skin is still seen as lesser 
#BamaSits,” and “But most of all, I sit for all, I sit for 
hope, Hope that one day, the country I love, will one 
day love me back #BamaSits.”


Audience Studies 73
Onl
y about two dozen of the 155 tweets included 
pictures. A closer examination of those photos revealed 
few examples of what Kharroub and Bas (2016) called 
efficacy-eliciting or emotionally arousing images. One 
of the most retweeted images was a collage of three 
pictures of student protesters at the game, who were 
dressed in black. In one picture, two of the students 
are White, one wearing a BLM T-shirt, and in the back-
ground is an African American woman in red standing 
with her hand over her chest. Another photo showed 
African American male and female students in black 
T-shirts. The third was of a White student dressed in 
black who was also sitting. This collage exemplified 
the efficacy-eliciting impact of a tweeted photo. So did 
an image bearing the #BamaSits hashtag featured a 
flier promoting #TakeActionTuesday at The Univer-
sity of Alabama. The flier directly referenced police 
brutality and encouraged change in Tuscaloosa, home 
of The University of Alabama, and the adjacent City 
of Northport.
As much as this case study of Twitter activism 
sought to provide information about the racial divide 
on a college campus, the most significant outcome 
may be understanding that unlike a widely adopted 
hashtag such as #BlackLivesMatter used thousands 
of times, single hashtags generating from local efforts 
may be limited in their ability to expand our under -
standing of race. Despite the fact that the online dis-
cussion about the #BamaSits demonstration resulted 
in the threat on the life of an African American student 
by a White student, the dialogue online was actually 
fairly limited, localized, and lacking in specificity about 
many of the national discussions on race. In other 
words, it didn’t expand the discussion about the racial 
divide in this country or race issues related to the BLM 
movement. Tweets using #BamaSits were probably 
too few to engage anyone not connected to the Univer-
sity of Alabama. However, the use of 
 effic
acy-eliciting 
images, although limited, may have helped accomplish 
the goals of protest organizers, who, as the most fre-
quent authors of the tweets using the #BamaSits hash-
tag, were calling attention to their efforts.
What the tweets did contain were statements 
about race and its connection to those at the Uni-
versity of Alabama. The tweets provided evidence of 
the counterview of those protesting police brutality 
during the national anthem, which says staging such 
demonstrations is unpatriotic. The images depicted 
both Black and White students who were involved in 
the demonstration and showed that those willing to 
engage in dialogue about the issue of race are not just 
those from racial minority groups.
So, from this analysis, I learned three lessons. 
Lesson 1: the power of Twitter to at least get a con-
versation started about race and patriotism. Calling 
attention to racial injustice clashes with beliefs about 
the importance of supporting our American soldiers 
or troops, especially in areas such as the Deep South. 
Lesson 2: the virtual absence of emotionally arousing 
pictures may be linked to a limited expansion of social 
media exchanges about a demonstration on race. 
In other words, one may need emotional images to 
attract attention and engagement in the online/social 
media arena. And, finally, Lesson 3: research on Twit-
ter protests or Twitter activism may be most useful in 
expanding our knowledge of issues of diversity, equity, 
and inclusion when multiple hashtags or multiple pro-
test sites are included.

3.5: HOW TV NEWS MAKES ARABS AND 
MUSLIMS FEEL ABOUT THEMSELVES
Dina Ibrahim and Aymen Abdel Halim
Arabs and Muslims in America often find them-
selves in the awkward position of defending their 
faith and culture, in part due to news coverage and 
how it is interpreted by the audience. This reading 
focuses not on whether news stories contain stere-
otypes and negative images of Arabs and Muslims, 
but on Arabs’ and Muslims’ personal interpretations 
of news content, and the impact of those interpre-
tations on self-conception and public displays of 
identity. We use cultivation theory to elucidate the 
cultural framework in which religious identity and 
self-conception develop.
The central principle of cultivation theory is that 
people learn much of what they know from television. 
The internet and social networking apps also provide 
information we use to shape our social realities. Even 
with the dominance of the internet as a news source, 
TV news still reaches a significant segment of Amer-
icans. Gerbner, Gross, Morgan, and Signorielli (1980) 
argued that the cultivation process is one in which 
electronic media play a major role in how audiences 
achieve a common understanding of issues. Television 
in particular shapes how people from non-dominant 
ethnic backgrounds are portrayed and perceived. 
Media scholars have argued that by simply watching 
television, an act that seems inherently passive as we 
stare at the screen, we are in fact actively creating and 
interpreting meaning from the stories we see and hear 
This reading investigates how young Arab Ameri-
cans and Muslims think and feel about media rep-
resentation of their culture and faith. Focus group 
participants discussed how news programming 
makes them feel about themselves and its impact on 
their sense of identity.
from a different racial background) what 
they think when someone refuses to 
stand during the national anthem. Share 
the results with the group: how are the 
responses similar and how are they dif-
ferent? Have the class as a whole discuss 
this exercise. What does this tell you 
about race, and varied emotions and 
views surrounding singing our national 
anthem?
 4.
 Identif
y a recent political cause or mat-
ter of protest on your campus. Ask those 
on your campus what role social media 
plays in that cause. Now, to what extent 
are opposing views considered in the 
social media aspect of the cause or pro-
test? To what extent should social media 
platforms factor into the planning of a 
media campaign around that cause or 
protest for change? What hashtags were 
used and how frequently were those 
hashtags used in this cause or matter of 
protest? Did the involvement (i.e., use of 
the hashtag) appear to include those out-
side the geographic area of your school?


Audience Studies 75
(Mor
ley, 1986). The impressions we have about peo-
ple and places are often constructed using informa-
tion we get from television. Although reporters create 
the narratives, they don’t actually control what those 
stories mean to the audience. Viewers actively create 
meaning, and interpretations can vary widely depend-
ing on individual backgrounds.
Researchers studying how television affects view-
ers’ values and attitudes find that exposure to televi-
sion messages affects audiences’ perceptions of reality 
(Greenwald, 1968; Hawkins & Pingree, 1980). Kinch’s 
theory of the self-concept (1972) also helps us under-
stand how television audiences feel about themselves. 
Self-concept, or how people perceive themselves, is 
the result of how other people perceive them, and their 
opinion and evaluation of those external appraisals.
To see how media coverage of Muslims and 
Arabs makes them feel about themselves and their 
sense of identity, we conducted a focus group in San 
Francisco with 13 Muslim American men and women 
of varied ethnicities, between the ages of 18 and 32. 
Nine were Arab, three were Pakistani American, and 
one was Vietnamese American. They described feel-
ings evoked by media, where they get their news and 
information, and what they think of the content. We 
also asked them to offer recommendations for improv-
ing news coverage of Arabs and Islam. We identify 
participants by speaker number, gender, and age: for 
example (#3, M, 29).
Anger and Frustration
Most of the Muslims we spoke to expressed disap-
pointment with how mainstream news in the United 
States perpetuates images that lead to feelings of frus-
tration, anger, and disgust. Part of the frustration for 
these young Muslims is because they often feel help-
less to respond to criticism of their faith in electronic 
news discourse, particularly cable news stations such 
as CNN and FOX News, which rely heavily on the talk 
show format and often hire commentators they deem 
experts on Islam. The Muslims in our focus group did 
not consider the guests or commentators credible.
(#3, M, 29) It makes me feel mad, and pissed 
off. They’re on a TV station like CNN, these 
people they’re supposedly experts and they 
have no clue about what they’re talking about. 
It makes me sick turning on the TV , flipping 
through channels and finding these people on 
TV talking. It makes me feel like what can we 
do or how can we counteract that?
One young man was particularly annoyed with 
the way that cable news conducts interviews and 
discussions when it comes to issues in the Middle 
East. He noticed a systematic pattern of demean-
ing the Arab viewpoint that is manifested by inter -
rupting or abruptly ending a conversation. He finds 
this technique particularly disturbing to watch and 
also expresses feeling powerless to participate and 
engage in the public dialogue of cable television 
news channels.
(#2, M, 21) I can’t stand to watch certain sta-
tions like FOX News. And if you turn it off, 
you’re just going to be mad, and you want to 
see how it ends out. It always ends out bad. I get  
so pissed off, so angry, I start talking to the TV .
These feelings of anger and frustration were articu-
lated by more males than females in the group. One 
woman said she channels her anger at the news into 
being a better person and ambassador for her faith. 
Other participants, who felt it was counterproduc-
tive to get upset with people who misunderstand 
their faith and culture, said that ignoring society’s 
negative attitude toward Islam was their preferred 
coping mechanism.
(#1, F, 20) It’s frustrating but a lot of the time I 
just brush it off. I want people to not consider 
me for my race first. So, I try to be more edu-
cated. I read more, I try to excel in school bet-
ter, so I kind of have to prove to the world that 
you’re not the negative, and you’re not what-
ever the news tries to say you are.
(#2, M, 21) I can’t be bad, I can’t be like 
other kids and misbehave because I feel like if 
I do that people will be like “oh, he’s that way 
because he’s an Arab” or “he’s just that way 
because he’s a Muslim,” “he’s just an angry 
Arab like we see in the news.”

76 Audiences
The participants described how their feelings and 
self-conception evolved over time. A few said that 
even before they followed the news, as children in 
middle and high school, the influence of the news 
images on their peers had a much stronger impact 
than now, in their 20s. The male participants said 
they had been more physically and verbally aggres-
sive in middle and high school, but now they have 
a better grip on handling the fear of being different, 
and that fear has developed into pride in their faith 
and culture.
(#4, F, 19) Y ou’re afraid, but it makes you 
more powerful in a way, because during 9/11 
everybody used to say racist things to you, but 
it makes you want to defend yourself more, it 
makes you stand up, and be proud that you’re 
a Muslim.
Because these Muslims know the difference 
between news images of their faith and how Islam is 
practiced and taught within their families and com-
munities, it is frustrating for them to watch the news 
and hear from people who support Quran burning 
or oppose building Islamic community centers or 
mosques around the country. Many Muslims may 
feel rejected by American society, but those we 
spoke to felt it was important to strive for a better, 
more inclusive image of Islam that would be slowly 
constructed through their social interactions.
Islamophobia
The young Muslims in this group had many stories 
to tell when we asked how others’ perceptions of 
them, acquired through the news, affected their 
lives. Descriptions of harassment and abuse came 
pouring out. As these stories illustrate, their anger 
and frustration were not only directed at electronic 
news sources but also at the messages being sent to 
mainstream audiences.
(#12, M, 21) My sister wears the hijab, we 
used to go to the same high school, and people 
wouldn’t stop talking. People were calling her 
names, saying “go back to your country.” She 
used to go home crying every day. She had to 
drop out of school and move [back to Y emen]. 
She was a 4.0 student. I think the news just puts 
Muslims in the worst picture ever. Like, espe-
cially FOX News, they have no limit. They’ll 
just go all out.
(#8, F, 19) People would come up to me and 
be like “are you Iraqi? Are you Afghan?” They 
always said those two races. I’m from Vietnam. 
A lot of people were really ignorant. They really 
didn’t know anything about the whole religion, 
even the basics. Then a few years ago, some-
one tried to burn the masjid [mosque] out there 
[in Antioch, California].
Burning mosques and various other incidences of 
hate crimes against Muslims are well documented 
and have escalated since 2015 (Council on Ameri-
can Islamic Relations, 2017; Kishi, 2017). Our focus 
group participants regarded such verbal and phys-
ical attacks on Muslims as a by-product of news 
images and stories that fuel hatred and suspicion of 
Islam.
Sources of News
Most participants reported frequently augmenting 
television news content with social media to stay 
updated on current events. They had strong praise 
for online content, because they perceived that it 
promoted diversity of opinion more effectively than 
television did. The group had divergent views on the 
value of news consumption, and a few of them sim-
ply tuned out American news.
(#9, M, 20) Recently, I kind of barely watch 
the news now, American news. I’m usually just 
watching Al Jazeera. That’s where I get most of 
my news from.
Some of the group did not watch much televi-
sion news, preferring to access their news online, 
where they have the freedom to pursue their own 
research and reference multiple sources to arrive at 
an informed conclusion. Others praised the control 
that the internet gives them, a stark contrast with 
the helplessness they feel when they watch cable 
television news. The internet provides them with 


Audience Studies 77
a w
ay to personally navigate and have a stronger 
sense of dominating the news discourse.
(#11, F, 21) We don’t have time to sit there 
and watch TV , so a lot of us, including myself, 
watch things online. So the time that we have, 
we’re gonna sit there and watch what we like to 
watch, rather than whatever’s on.
Participants who rely on Facebook as a news source 
recognized the limitations of doing so. There was 
a strong sense of independence when it came to 
seeking electronic news sources. One of the partic-
ipants, a 19-year-old veiled and outspoken female, 
felt it was imperative to pursue diverse news per -
spectives and used Twitter to stay informed.
(#4, F, 19) A lot of people get their information 
on Facebook. I’m obsessed with Twitter. I don’t 
just follow Muslim bloggers, I follow Christian 
bloggers and Jewish bloggers. When they have 
blog posts, they tweet about it, and you can 
read it right then and there. Twitter has trend-
ing topics, the key words that are being said at 
a certain time. I was really happy because on 
Eid, “Eid Mubarak” was a trending topic. One 
day, I logged on to Twitter, and it said “Quran 
burning,” and I was like “Hold up. What is this?” 
and I had to click on it, and it’s cool because 
you get to see a live stream of what people are 
saying, and how they’re using that key word at 
the same time. I follow Anderson Cooper on 
Twitter and different journalists, but I try to 
follow independent media on there as well, 
because independent media tends to be more 
active on Twitter.
Impact of News Images on Identity
The group expressed the significance of having 
an Arabic or Muslim name as an expression of 
self-identification. Participants were proud of their 
names and believed the names were of central 
importance not only to their identities as Arabs and 
Muslims but also as tools to challenge negative ste-
reotypes and perceptions. Many Muslims named 
Osama or Jihad reported being constantly made fun 
of, but in this group, there was strong disapproval for 
people who change their names to more Western- 
sounding ones. They believe that in the context of 
negative news coverage relating to Arabs or Mus-
lims, it is important to take pride in their Arab and 
Muslim names.
(#2, M, 21) My dad is very proud of who he 
is because of the way he named me and my 
siblings after Quranic verses, great names, but 
with a lot of my uncles, a select few don’t like 
their name. They’d be called Sam, instead of 
like Samir, or Mike instead of Mahmoud.
The Muslim men in this group expressed that they 
had a much easier time than Muslim women did 
in evading the negative effects of news coverage 
regarding Muslims. Due to the negative attention 
Muslims receive, they considered Muslim women 
exceptionally courageous for wearing the hijab and 
admirably respect their decision to do so.
(#12, M, 21) It’s easier for a guy to dress a 
certain way. Usually on Eid or on Ramadan 
holiday, I wear traditional Arab clothing. And 
you know walking in the street, going to the 
mosque, I see those weird stares that you get 
from people, walking down the street, but not 
every day like Muslim women.
(#2, M, 21) It’s much harder for Muslim 
women. When a woman is wearing the hijab, 
she could be any culture, any race, wearing 
hijab, you’re considered an Arab, you’re con-
sidered a Muslim, based on what they’ve seen 
in the media. I can wash my face and put the 
flag in my room, and walk out and I’m just like 
everybody else. But they have to deal with it 
on a daily basis. They have to deal with the 
constant harassment everywhere they go. I 
definitely give the respect due to them because 
they can handle it.
The women in the group said they had become 
immune to non-Muslims staring at their head-
scarves and willingly explained that they choose to 
wear it as an expression of modesty. They admitted 
the challenges of being so easily identified as a Mus-
lim but they were proud of their faith and said being 
different made them feel stronger. They noted that 

78 Audiences
news images tended to portray Muslim women as 
weak and oppressed, but to them that was a mis-
conception. The veiled women in our group had 
vibrant career aspirations and were assertive about 
changing the way the news depicts them.
Part of the Solution: Recommendations
What do these young men and women intend to do 
about what they perceive as misperceptions and ste-
reotypes of Islam and Arabs in the news? One might 
expect them to disengage with the news and simply 
tune out. However, the participants want to remain 
informed with the latest news to engage others in an 
ongoing dialogue and debate of perspectives.
(#13, F, 22) I don’t want to tune it [the news] 
out because as Muslims living here, and wear -
ing the hijab, you stand out, so people are going 
to ask me about those issues. I try to make 
myself prepared and actually know about the 
issue beforehand.
One participant recommended examining alternative 
news sources, particularly international news websites, 
to better understand Muslim and Arab perspectives.
(#2, M, 21) Al Jazeera has an English page. I 
tell them “Y ou want to know what’s going on? 
Uncensored?” And people will go on there and 
be like “Oh my God, wow, they show dead 
bodies?”
The participants agree that the news industry needs 
to change its tone of coverage and treat people of 
all faiths with respect and dignity. Descriptors such 
as “terrorist” need to be universally applied, not just 
to people of their faith and culture. They said that 
when terrorism is in the news, the default assump-
tion is that an Arab or Muslim is responsible. They 
cited the story of a Caucasian man who crashed a 
plane into an IRS building in Texas. News organiza-
tions did not refer to him as a terrorist.
(#2, M, 21) “Terrorist” is now the derogatory 
term for Arab or Muslim, it’s not used for any 
other purpose. Right now, you can’t call a White 
man a terrorist. It’s against the rules and con-
fusing your viewers. They called him an “angry 
tax agent.” He’s terrorizing people, right? And 
he’s not called a terrorist, that word is reserved 
for Arabs.
Despite their harsh criticism of television and elec-
tronic news sources, some participants expressed 
a desire to work in media. Their objective is to 
change the industry from within; with a wider range 
of diversity in newsrooms that includes more Arabs 
and Muslims, the hope for these participants is that 
they can improve the quality of news stories.
(#4, F, 19) It really makes me sad because I 
know they’re working hard to be good jour -
nalists, and it sucks that these big-name cor -
porations that I’d one day like to work for, like 
CNN seem lazy in my eyes that they couldn’t 
go out and find a better person to interview. Or 
they couldn’t go out and properly research their 
story.
(#11, F, 21) It makes me feel outraged, but 
when I step outside, and when I talk to Amer -
icans, normal people, just as ourselves, I feel 
better. I’m changing one step at a time with the 
people that are fed this biased news.
Through sharing their opinions on news images 
and stories about Arabs and Muslims, the group 
agreed that TV news programming cultivates nar -
row and limited perceptions of their people. These 
young men and women believe that this cultivated 
imagery is directly responsible for how other peo-
ple perceive them, and consequently, how they feel 
about themselves.
Ultimately, they believed that these news images 
and stories contributed to their desire to educate soci-
ety and become positive, articulate role models who 
would eventually change social perceptions of their 
faith and culture. The participants expressed hope 
that they could change social perceptions of their 
faith and culture by augmenting news reports with 
their own interactions with their fellow Americans. 
Staying informed by continuing to consume the news 
with which they don’t necessarily agree is important 


Audience Studies 79
t
o these young Muslims and Arabs, but so is reaching 
out to people, answering their questions patiently, and 
excelling academically and professionally in order to 
counteract the news images.

3.6: THE INDIVIDUALIZATION OF 
VIOLENCE: AUDIENCE READINGS OF 
DIRECT , STRUCTURAL, AND CULTURAL 
GENDER VIOLENCE IN CASI DIVAS
Rebeca Maseda García, Dayna Jean DeFeo, and 
Zeynep Kılıç
In the US, the dominant ideology of meritocracy 
perceives success as a reward for individual ability 
and effort, and is presumed blind to considerations 
of attributes such as gender, race, or ability. The 
expansion of feminism seems to be a sign of our 
times, exemplified by the rise of (a mostly but not 
exclusively White) celebrity feminism (e.g., Emma 
Watson, Miley Cyrus, Beyoncé), making it hip, attrac-
tive, and fashionable. Meanwhile, as popular culture 
and the media echo long-held issues from feminist 
agendas, some assert that we live in a postfeminist 
world—a society that has risen above gender-based 
inequality and violence (Gill, 2007; Tasker & Negra, 
2007; McRobbie, 2009). However, despite this cel-
ebratory enthusiasm about meritocratic ideals, ine-
quality, discrimination, and 
 g
ender-based violence 
are still prevalent. We then may wonder why that is, 
if we are equal participants in a world of undiscrim-
inating opportunity?
The authors showed the Mexican film Casi Divas 
to viewers to determine perceptions of direct, 
structural, and cultural violences, and perceptions 
of how victims could respond to these injustices. 
Participants’ understanding of gender violence 
reflected current neoliberal frameworks of personal 
responsibility, empowerment, and resilience.
1
It’s Your Turn: What Do You Think? What 
Will You Find?
 1.
 Look a
t news in legacy media outlets, 
and online. Do you see some of the same 
things our participants discussed? Why 
do you think the coverage is as it is?
 2.
 If
 you are not Muslim, talk to Muslim 
friends and ask them about their inter -
pretations of and opinions about cover -
age of Islam in the media. To what extent 
do they think the news contributes to 
Islamophobia? If you are Muslim, talk 
with friends who are members of other 
marginalized groups and ask the same 
sorts of questions. Then, talk to White 
friends about the same issues. What dif-
ferences do you see, and why?
 3.
 Ima
gine you’re a reporter and want to 
be as neutral as possible on these issues. 
What would you do, when covering sto-
ries about Islam?

80 Audiences
Media and digital technologies have tremendous 
influence on our beliefs, social norms, and behavior. 
Although increasing visibility of BIPOC, disabled, 
queer, and trans people in popular culture is encour-
aging and coincides with the new feminist impetus, 
it coexists with the redeployment of misogynistic 
(Banet-Weiser, 2018), transphobic, and racist attitudes 
which can result in violence against minoritized 
groups. The persistence of neoliberal agendas, even in 
seemingly progressive media channels, impedes a real 
critique of the structural conditions that create and sus-
tain that violence, and hence help us understand why 
perceptions of gender violence remain problematic.
After all, if society has evolved, acts of violence 
must happen at the individual level, between a specific 
perpetrator and target. In such a framework, women 
are empowered to be more independent, resilient, 
confident, and competitive in the workforce. Known as 
neoliberal feminism (Rottenberg, 2014), this subjectiv-
ity centers entrepreneurship, self-reliance, and individ-
ualism within capitalist framework of the free market, 
and therein absolves the system from social or political 
responsibility.
In this essay, we study the audience reception 
of a popular Mexican comedy Casi Divas to examine 
contradicting discourses of female free will, empow-
erment, and body positivity in response to direct, 
structural, and cultural violences. The movie utilizes a 
beauty pageant narrative and telenovela template to 
reveal latent misogyny, sexism, racism, ageism, and 
sizeism through intertwining stories of five female char-
acters. Below we explore how the audience interprets 
gender violence in Casi Divas. When we watch movies, 
mostly to entertain ourselves, do we critically identify 
and differentiate these violences, and what responses 
do we provide for them?
Interpreting Violence in Casi Divas
Casi Divas is a film about a televised competition for 
a new telenovela star. Thousands of women audi-
tion from across Mexico, and the movie (in Spanish 
with English subtitles) centers on five characters 
who provide commentary on distinct social issues: 
Eva depicts ageism as the 35-year-old star fighting 
to keep her job because she is no longer considered 
young and thus not attractive enough to play a lead 
role. Ximena, who is rich and White, experiences 
sizeism as a person who struggles with bulimia and 
who was bullied relentlessly as an overweight child. 
Francisca is a Zapotec Indigenous woman repre-
senting racism, classism, and educational inequity. 
Y esenia, an inner-city character, showcases familial 
dysfunction and urban inequality as she conceals 
her transgender identity to qualify for the compe-
tition. Catalina’s story features misogyny, femicide, 
and classism in Ciudad Juárez where women are 
regularly harassed, kidnapped, raped, and murdered.
As each woman strives for fame as a means to 
reach her personal objectives, the competition shows 
the telenovela genre’s problematic reproduction of 
gender stereotypes and inequality through depicting 
female submissiveness, representing the body as a sex-
ual object with its value embedded in physical appear-
ance. As each character experiences different types of 
violence at the intersections of her identities, the film 
challenges the postfeminist notion that women are 
empowered to overcome the limitations that previ-
ously held them back.
To understand audience perceptions of violence 
in Casi Divas, we held three screenings, followed by 
facilitated focus group discussions with 15 univer -
sity students. We transcribed those discussions and 
coded participants’ perceptions of the forms of violence 
(physical, verbal, discrimination, and body image) and 
responses to the target of the violence (accepting the 
violence, fighting it, or blaming the victim).
What Is Violence?
What do we mean when we talk about violence? 
Johan Galtung (1969) differentiated between three 
types of violence: Direct violence is exercised in a 
visible physical or verbal manner. Structural violence 
is enmeshed with a society’s social, economic, and 
political structures, resulting from the unequal distri-
bution of power and resources. Cultural violence is 
articulated through the symbolic realm of language 
and culture that legitimizes direct and/or structural 
violence, most commonly by justifying injustice, 
violence, or inequality by assigning responsibil-
ity to the target or victim. These distinctions are 
important, especially when considering the experi-
ences of marginalized groups. As Galtung argued, 


Audience Studies 81
ho
wever, “in a static society personal violence will 
be registered, whereas structural violence may be 
seen as about as natural as the air around us” (1969, 
p. 173). We chose Casi Divas because it opens up 
many opportunities for discussion by presenting 
all three of Galtung’s forms of violence. However, 
our participants defined violence quite narrowly, as 
when one said, “violence is more like when some-
one does something to you, forces you into some-
thing, acts against you, usually in a physical manner 
that is against your will,” indicating that violence is 
limited to actions resulting in physical harm.
Through this lens, Ximena’s bulimia was, for 
instance, not considered the result of violence, 
although Galtung’s typology would consider it as such. 
While recognizing other forms of self-harm as vio-
lence, our participants excluded eating disorders from 
categorizations of violence because they were more 
psychological than physical:
When I think of violence, it’s either an act towards 
somebody else or towards oneself. It normally has 
to do … with a physical act, an actual act being 
done. And I see [bulimia] more as some sort of 
psychological disorder. Not really …violence. …  
Maybe it’s a hurtful act, but not violence.
Similarly, our participants contended that social 
injustices—including prejudice, racism, and 
 tr
ansphobia—are problematic and could be the 
underlying source of a violent act, but these were 
not themselves inherently violent. For example, 
one participant said, “I don’t see the thought of 
being racist as something violent because that’s a 
personal choice. But once it comes out of you in a 
certain way, then that’s something violent.”
The film provided numerous instances of both 
structural and cultural violences which audiences 
noted them as problematic but did not identify as vio-
lence. For example, the conception that Indigenous 
people are inferior physically, emotionally, and intel-
lectually (cultural) impedes Francisca’s equal access to 
a working position (structural). Similarly, the competi-
tion’s subtext that a woman’s best attribute is her figure 
and her compliant disposition (cultural) is used to jus-
tify her subjugated and narrow role (structural). In both 
examples, the cultural and structural violences serve 
to justify the direct violence that is perpetrated against 
those groups, but our participants conceptualized vio-
lence only at the physical level, when individuals exert 
direct violence on others.
We contend there is an important distinction 
between calling violence by its name (thus explicitly 
acknowledging it as harmful) and passively noting it 
as a contributing factor to “real” or direct violence 
when there is an absence of physical harm, especially 
in the context of social change. If we identify violence 
only in direct physical acts—especially in a world that 
we regard as just—the violence is reduced to specific 
perpetrators and becomes an individualized prob-
lem. When we regard violence this way, what kinds of 
resources do we set aside to combat it? And whose 
responsibility is it to change?
What Should Be Done About Violence?
After learning that audiences regard only some of 
these concerns as violence, and noting the individ-
ualization of violence at the perpetrator level, we 
wondered: does that also mean that they would 
expect a different response from victims? We cate-
gorized violences in the film within Galtung’s frame-
work to see how the audiences regarded the victims, 
the visible human beings in the film who were indi-
vidually experiencing different forms of violence. 
When identifying victim roles and responsibilities, 
our participants generated three types of responses 
depending on the specific form of violence: fight it, 
accept it, or suggest that the victim was to blame.
With regard to direct violence, participants sug-
gested that victims should fight it. Comments about 
fighting against bodily violence were made about 
sexual violence, rape, kidnapping, and generalized vio-
lence against women’s bodies. For instance, one par-
ticipant, said admirably,
[Violence against women] was portrayed as 
very nonchalant in its occurrence, but the 
response to the violence was nothing resem-
bling nonchalant at all. Like the women actu-
ally fought back for themselves.
This sentiment reflects an attitude that mirrors the 
advocacy of girl-power and against victimhood 

82 Audiences
(which depicts women as inherently vulnerable and 
in need of protection). In contemporary rhetoric, the 
power of enacting free will is a neoliberal sentiment; 
when women are told that “the power is in your 
hands,” it is their responsibility to be confident and 
to create effective ways of resisting.
Accepting violence was the most common 
response suggested when audiences discussed struc-
tural and cultural violence. We see this exemplified in 
comments around ageism, which audiences regarded 
not as violence, but rather a reality which aging individ-
uals should just accept. For example, a participant said
I’m just like…can you accept the fact that 
you’re just a little older and the role … is look-
ing for a particular character? … I’m like, wow, 
this is like a reality life. … She … kind of just 
refused to accept that. I was like, wow, just 
accept that. Go do something else.
Thus, in response to ageism and other forms of struc-
tural and cultural violence, audiences suggested that 
individuals should develop resilience to the violence 
and accept it by leaning in, playing along, or complying.
The exception to the suggestion that victims 
accept cultural and structural violence was in the realm 
of sizeism. When presented with structural violence of 
sizeism and cultural violence around body image, the 
most prominent audience response was to blame the 
victim, which participants suggested more than twice 
as frequently as they said a victim should fight or accept 
it. For example, one participant said,
I don’t think body image is necessarily just 
a negative thing and I don’t think it was  
portrayed only as a negative thing in this film 
either though. It was very clear that for each 
woman, … she each had her own perspective 
of what body image was, what a body image 
should be, how it is. But at no point did anyone 
blatantly say like, ‘Y our body’s your body and 
that makes it bad.’ Like, nobody ever said that.
We found this interesting, because the suggested 
response was not only distinct from responses to 
other forms of structural and cultural violence but 
also that audiences honed in on Ximena’s charac-
ter and eating disorder more than any other issue 
depicted in the film. Blaming Ximena for her eating 
disorder shifts responsibility entirely to her, targeting 
the individual as the party responsible for solving 
the problem. This reading of the character fits within 
neoliberalism where women take on the pain of 
existing inequalities but can only speak of suffering 
in purely individualized terms without any expecta-
tion for societal transformation (Gill & Kanai, 2018).
What Makes Sizeism Different from Other 
Forms of Structural and Cultural Violence?
The hyper-attention our participants paid to Xime-
na’s body size, although only one of five stories told, 
requires us to ponder how the neoliberal ideology 
and postfeminism treat the body through beauty 
discourses. On the topic of discrimination, why 
would we expect women to react differently when 
confronted with racism than when they are con-
fronted with sizeism?
On all the occasions where participants blamed 
the victim for body image issues, their reference point 
was Ximena. Although participants sometimes noted 
that bulimia is a psychological disorder where her 
brain was working against her body, they more fre-
quently identified her as the problem by framing her 
actions as her choice, as a way to better herself, or her 
failure to resist the societal constructs.
Only once was fighting suggested in response to 
sizeism, and even then, the reference was not about 
eating disorders, but a generalized beauty stand-
ard that pervades women’s lives. We find Ximena’s 
absence here significant, because, although our study 
participants challenged other forms of violence, fight-
ing against a system of body oppression did not seem 
to occupy our participants’ thoughts at all. Rather, they 
echoed neoliberal notions of resiliency and achieving 
success through leaning in, playing along, and accept-
ing these beauty standards through frameworks of per-
sonal choice and willpower.
The Importance of Perceiving Multiple 
Forms of Violence
Our study underscores the importance of defining 
and identifying violence correctly and in all its forms, 
beyond physical aggression. Our findings suggest 


Audience Studies 83
tha
t failing to consider anything non-physical as vio-
lence makes it easier to individualize experiences of 
both victimization and resilience. We problematize 
this conception of violence, noting how it detracts 
from broader structural, cultural, and systemic 
hegemonic forces within which these individual-
ized acts occur. It therefore perpetuates neoliberal 
positions around women’s roles and rights. Thus, we 
invite readers to develop emancipatory discourses 
through a more critical and engaged consumption 
of film and other media.
Our participants described the role of the victim 
through empowerment, resilience, and perseverance 
despite adversity by moving along (or accepting the 
violence as “the way things are”), or shouldering some 
of the responsibility for the violence itself (blaming the 
victim). The most interesting finding, however, was the 
frequency and vitriol devoted to body image and eat-
ing disorders. Participants blamed the victim accord-
ing to a neoliberal ethos of individual responsibility 
and self-surveillance. Van Amsterdam called this the 
“big fat inequality” where “processes of exclusion and 
marginalization based on body size categorizations are 
similar to racist, ableist and misogynist logics and prac-
tices” (2013, p. 155).
The notion of resilience is prominent in public 
policy and popular culture (Bull & Allen, 2018; Bracke, 
2016). It emphasizes bouncing back from adversity 
and echoes the neoliberal construction of the survivor, 
where the emphasis is intentionally on the individual’s 
emergence from suffering rather than the cause of her 
pain (Orgad, 2009). The resilient subject is expected 
to adapt and recover via a combination of intensive 
self-management strategies and positive mental atti-
tude, embracing a mindset in which negative expe-
riences are reframed in upbeat terms (Gill & Orgad, 
2015), individualizing both the responsibility for injuries 
and injustices and the action required to resolve them. 
Our participants’ responses draw a cultural landscape 
that embraces certain notions of feminism “and pull 
them into a less disconcerting agenda for change” 
(McRobbie, 2020, p. 43), thus, diffusing feminism as a 
threat.
Our study posits that audiences—even college 
students who are well positioned to identify and 
address gender violence—represent the neoliberal 
contemporary subjects who expect the individual 
to self-actualize, survive, and thrive despite struc-
tural oppressions. Their attention to direct or 
physical forms of violence at the expense of other 
violences, and the suggested victim responses, con-
firms their alignment with the larger cultural and 
media discourses. This pattern demonstrates the 
complex negotiation between what they perceive 
as absolute achievements for women and their per-
ceptions of the prevalence of gendered violence. 
They vacillate between ambivalent postfeminist 
notions about limitless possibilities for women 
and their recognition of the unfairness of gender 
violence. In the process, they reproduce some ste-
reotypes and propose no strategies for structural 
change.
We end with a call to action to critically evalu-
ate gender violence discourses through an increased 
attention to deconstructing our reading of popular 
media, and decolonizing our own subject position 
within the neoliberal system of cultural production and 
consumption.

a young Latino presented the tenuous balance of 
wanting to enact change in a tense political climate.
Y ounger generations in the United States 
are marked by characteristics including political
