Audience Studies 85
eng
agement, digital and social media use, and ethnic 
and racial diversity. Latinx millennials and generation 
Z (about one quarter of all US Latinx people) are likely 
to be US born and English proficient. Many use English 
for both media use and interpersonal communication. 
They are also more likely to use mobile and internet 
technologies than older Latinx generations are.
Translating language, social, and cultural norms 
has traditionally been an important role for Latinx 
youth in the US, especially for those whose fami-
lies have recently immigrated. With the increase of 
US-born Latinx people, has this role changed? Given 
their language skills and digital media proficiency, 
research has found that Latinx youth have a social 
and informational advantage, keeping family members 
tuned in to important political events (McDevitt & 
Butler, 2011). In this study, we contextualize the famil-
ial role of Latinx young people’s political opinion lead-
ership in the current polarized political climate.
Due to increased voter registration, and growing 
populations in states with vigorous competition among 
the dominant parties, Latinx people are receiving 
increased attention in the political arena. The current 
political climate, with a rise in a nationalist movement 
that includes a strong anti-immigrant rhetoric, may be 
hindering efforts to increase Latinx people’s political 
efficacy, or “the feeling that political and social change 
is possible, and that the individual citizen can play a 
part in bringing about this change” (Strokes-Brown, 
2009, p. 1283). Feeling like one can make a difference 
is an important component of political engagement 
and political participation.
We know Latinx people use social media at sim-
ilar or higher rates than non-Latinx people in the US 
(Lopez, Gonzalez-Barrera, & Patten, 2013), so under-
standing their social and digital media use is relevant 
when trying to understand political engagement. We 
therefore pose the following research questions:
RQ1: How do young Latinx people engage with social 
network sites (SNS) and digital news media?
RQ2: To what extent and how do young Latinx peo-
ple utilize social and digital media to engage 
politically?
RQ3: How do young Latinx people perceive their 
role in sharing political information and initiat-
ing political debates within their family circle?
RQ4: Is young Latinx people’s social media network 
and digital news media use nationally or inter -
nationally oriented?
To answer these questions, we received approval 
for this study and conducted three focus group 
interviews with 21 young Latinx people in Octo-
ber 2017. Each session lasted about one hour, and 
was assisted by two bilingual moderators, although 
the discussions occurred mainly in English. Our 
focus groups were conducted in Central Texas, an 
area with traditional ties to the Latinx community. 
There is great diversity within the Latinx commu-
nity, even in Central Texas, in the immigrant expe-
rience, background, country of origin, and more. 
Our participants were young (18–35 years old) who 
identify as Latinx. Two described themselves as 
first-
 g
eneration (born in a Latin American country 
or Spain), 11 as second-generation (their parents 
had immigrated), and eight as third-generation (their 
grandparents had immigrated).
Social Media Use Among Young Latinx 
People
Studies show that Latinx people use social media 
often (Pew Research Center, 2017). Our first research 
question looked into what SNS and digital news 
media young Latinx people use. Participants primar-
ily used Twitter, Facebook, Snapchat, and Instagram 
to keep in touch with friends and family. Interacting 
with family was an important part of their social 
media use, especially those living far from their family 
circle. When it comes to news and information, most 
participants said they rely on Twitter, Facebook, and 
Snapchat as their main news source. Although some 
participants mentioned news organizations by name, 
most mentioned using apps, without further elabo-
ration of the news source. Only one participant pre-
ferred traditional news sources, such as BBC, CNN, 
FOX News, and NPR, stating that they present more 
sides of an issue. Twitter was especially relevant for 
this group, for its instant news and connectivity. “I like 
how fast Twitter can go viral; it is a good thing and a 
bad thing depending on whether it is positive or neg-
ative,” according to a third-generation Latina. Partic-
ipants mentioned recent school shootings and being 

86 Audiences
able to get first-hand news account from friends 
who were near the scene. Thus, their news does not 
always come from news organizations.
Our participants also noted drawbacks of using 
Twitter as a news source, mentioning the distribution 
of fake news, biased information, and an overly hostile 
environment in which people feel empowered to be 
aggressive. As one participant said, “With Twitter, the 
positive thing is with news you are always connected. 
The very negative thing is that now everything turns 
very political really fast, and it is a really harsh environ-
ment, especially if you are a minority.” To combat the 
problem of fake news and biased information, some 
participants say that if they see a news story on Twitter 
they will then go to what they consider more reputable 
news sources.
Although many of our young Latinx participants 
look for news in their SNS, they indicated different 
preferences for interactivity. Most wanted to see how 
others are responding to news stories, whereas oth-
ers liked a clear separation from original content and 
responses:
With Twitter you can actually go along and 
read what others are saying through the com-
ments but with Snapchat if you get the news 
from there or even on the iPhone news app you 
are not seeing what other people are saying 
about it. All you are doing is reading about the 
content they are offering.
Participants primarily used social media outlets and 
mobile applications to get informed on political 
issues. Twitter, Facebook, and Snapchat were the 
most used. Other sources included Google search, 
Y ouTube, and News mobile applications. A few par-
ticipants occasionally watched CNN on television, 
for live coverage and visuals that differ from news 
shared on social media. Additionally, watching news 
on television did not spark backlash and discussion 
as found on social media.
Political Engagement in Hostile Times
One’s belief in political efficacy often stems from 
governmental responses to citizen demands. Social 
media can be a tool to increase political efficacy and 
participation, but that does not seem to be the case 
for our Latinx participants. Our second research 
question looked into the use of SNS and digital 
media for political engagement. Our participants 
were hesitant to engage politically through either 
social media or digital media, citing a hostile envi-
ronment. They seem to like the engagement that the 
digital environment provides and seeing others par-
ticipate in political conversations surrounding news, 
but they hesitate to participate themselves. As one 
said, 
I feel like there are already so many people 
attacking each other on the issue that I don’t 
want to be another voice adding. I get that I 
should at some point be standing on whatever 
side I stand on.
This partly contradicts prior research showing that 
young people no longer want to passively receive 
the news but rather engage in the conversation 
as a participant (Benkler, 2006). It is possible that 
with the tense political climate, actively partici-
pating in the conversation poses a threat to these 
young Latinx people; still, they believe that passive 
participation is possible and desired. Some of this 
tension experienced in social media is related to a 
broader political context. One focus group partici-
pant explained this tension by giving the example of 
then-President Donald Trump’s Twitter use, specifi-
cally in the aftermath of a hurricane that devastated 
Puerto Rico. She said, “It saddens me to see that 
people are that ignorant or people are arguing on 
Facebook through the comments about these situ-
ations and they don’t even know how to go about it 
and they are just saying racial slurs.”
When asked about political engagement 
online and offline, most participants believed they 
were ill informed about politics, and therefore not 
as engaged as they wished. Participants said they 
try to be informed, but the news is aggravating, and 
the climate is tense. Only a few believed they were  
actively engaged. These politically engaged partic-
ipants said that college classes related to politics, 
policy, and issues played a major role in their engage-
ment, reinforcing that information is essential for 
participation.


Audience Studies 87
T
he fear of backlash on social media, coupled 
with reliance on social media for news, has deeply 
affected these young Latinx people’s sense of political 
efficacy and has disengaged them from the political 
issues that matter most to them. This can lead to fewer 
participatory behaviors designed to enact change, 
including voting. One of our participants described the 
toxic climate for political engagement on social media:
It’s easier not to voice your opinion on social 
media because it doesn’t matter, somebody is 
going to call you out on your profile picture or 
someone can call you out on the way you type 
or call you out on something, even if you have 
a valid point—they are going to call you out on 
it. So, I would rather not voice at all because 
somebody is bound to call you out on...“oh you 
Mexican looking whatever” and comment on 
your picture even though it has little to no rel-
evance on what is being discussed and people 
are just going to find things to get at you.
A common theme for participants was that they 
wanted to be more engaged, involved, and motivated 
to enact political change, but they did not know what 
to do, or even how to do it, and what would actu-
ally have an impact. Although participants believed 
that voicing opinions on social media is important 
to enacting change, many resisted doing so.
Participatory behaviors for our focus group par-
ticipants seemed inspired by feeling that they could 
help friends and family, when being informed became 
a way to help others. For example, one participant had 
friends affected by the 2017 decision to phase out the 
Deferred Action of Childhood Arrivals (DACA) pro-
gram, and signed an online petition. Another felt the 
need to learn about this issue to help friends who may 
not know what to do if they could not renew their 
DACA applications. Overall, it seemed that becoming 
informed was the extent of the actions participants 
took toward enacting change.
Information Leaders?
Previous research suggests that young Latinos play 
the role of information leaders by sharing informa-
tion found on media with their families. As McDe-
vitt and Sindorf (2014) described it, the role of 
information leader may include acquiring, shaping, 
and relaying information about politics and candi-
dates to educate family members on relevant issues 
(regardless of voting status). Our third research 
question looked into how Latinx youth see their role 
in sharing political information and initiating politi-
cal debates within their family circle.
We found that many of our focus group partic-
ipants actively avoided political conversation, often 
because of the tense political climate. One partici-
pant said, “When it comes to my grandparents, we 
can’t touch certain topics and can’t talk about any-
thing because my grandparents are from Mexico. 
They freak out and they don’t want to know.” They 
expressed similar issues with parents, either because 
they seem to disagree politically, or it would make 
their parents too anxious. Participants who did dis-
cuss political issues with their families usually did 
so with family members who were deemed “open-
minded,” often the mothers. However, in these 
conversations, our participants often followed the 
information lead of older family members. In these 
cases, it was the parents who gathered and verified 
the information, usually from mainstream media, and 
transmitted it to them. The Latinx youth in our focus 
groups did not act as political information leaders. 
They either avoided such conversations altogether or 
followed their parents’ information lead.
Transcending Borders
Our fourth research question asked whether young 
Latinx people’s SNS and digital news media use 
reflected a national or international orientation. Our 
participants’ international family ties promoted a 
transnational social media use experience. Partici-
pants had family in Mexico, Nicaragua, El Salvador, 
Spain, and Puerto Rico, and used social media to 
maintain ties to their extended family and friends. A 
respondent with family in Mexico said that seeing 
their activities brought flair to his social media: “If I 
didn’t have those people my social media would be 
more boring.”
Most of our participants said they post in English, 
except when the intended audience is their family. Our 
first- or second-generation focus group participants 
were more likely to say they used Spanish on social 

88 Audiences
media, although most participants said they used at 
least some Spanish on social media. Using Spanish 
was in some cases a choice to narrow the audience of 
social media communication.
When it came to news, most of our respondents 
follow it in English. They search for news in English, 
and mainly on social media (Snapchat and Twitter 
usually). Some mentioned receiving notifications 
from the BBC, as a transnational news organization 
in English. Spanish-language news, whether from US 
or transnational sources, is accessed based on recom-
mendations or targeted information on our respond-
ents’ news feeds.
Latinx Young People and Social Media: a 
Paradox in Participation
Our focus group participants are heavy users of 
social media. They use SNS to maintain social rela-
tions with family and friends and form new social 
relations. However, when it comes to politics or 
political issues, they hesitate to participate in a con-
versation in social media.
“Discouraged” and “scared” are some of the 
words our participants used to describe how they 
feel about engaging in a political discussion on social 
media. The current political climate and the prolifera-
tion of extreme perspectives are deterrents to actively 
engaging political issues on social media. Although 
these Latinx young people do not actively participate 
in political discussions, they still follow the news, espe-
cially on issues they care deeply about.
Our participants say they understand the impor-
tance of being politically engaged, knowledgeable of 
the current events and policies that will affect them or 
their community, and sharing and deliberating about 
this information online and offline. But they seem 
not to know how they can make a difference. When 
they see the direct consequence of their action, such 
as informing a friend in need, they are more likely to 
engage politically.
Latinx youth are more likely to have the tools to 
be politically engaged and active than previous gener-
ations. They are likely to be English proficient and eli-
gible to vote, and have access to political information. 
But our focus group participants indicated that the 
sociopolitical climate is a barrier to engagement and 
that they don’t know how to enact change. As young 
adults, many of our focus group participants are just 
now learning what they can do, and how to go about it.
Our focus group participants are not leading or 
bridging the information divide in their families. Quite 
the contrary, they seem comfortable in relying on older 
family members to verify information or to bring them 
relevant information. Because parents and grandpar-
ents relied mainly on TV for news, using both 
 English-
 
and Spanish-language news, and some accessed news 
originating in Spain and Mexico, it is fair to say that 
Latinx-oriented media and transnational media in 
Spanish are making their way into young Latinx peo-
ple’s information cabinet as a two-step flow: from 
media, to information leader (parents), and then to 
our participants. Perhaps the uncertainty of the cur-
rent political climate, or the volatility of news found on 
social media, encourages Latinx youth to follow rather 
than lead when it comes to political information.
Our young Latinx participants are, however, ful-
filling other important social roles. Our focus group 
participants, some stating they were the first in their 
families to go to college, and all with a vast network 
of social connections, are observant and paying atten-
tion to what is happening around them. They monitor 
what is happening, and the discussion of these events, 
on social media. They have the social and linguistic 
capital to negotiate information from various connec-
tions: friends, relatives, and news organization from the 
US and beyond, in English and in Spanish. They are 
learning how they can enact change, academically and 
socially. They hesitate to participate, but they are mon-
itoring closely. Latinx youth are learning that the soci-
opolitical environment is toxic, and they are choosing 
not to engage, unless they know exactly how they can 
bring about the changes they want.
Our focus group participants indicated the 
importance of learning about the political process, 
and although they reported doing so in high school 
and college classes, they seemed not to have learned 
enough about civic engagement. General curricula 
should focus more on civics and the process of political 
engagement. The current climate in the US, reflected in 
social media, affects both political conversations and 
people of color. This too should be addressed in media 


Audience Studies 89
educ
ation. SNS can be an important tool for delibera-
tion but requires a respectful, civil environment before 
it will encourage more diverse participation.

PART II
CONTENT
When most people think about the media, they 
think about media content—a favorite film, book, 
song, video game, and so forth. But what do these 
and other mediated messages say about our 
social world? Some people may quickly respond  
“nothing!”—but that’s not so. The media content we 
use says a great deal about our world.
What that media content says about our world 
matters. If we don’t have firsthand experience with 
certain aspects of our world, and if we don’t know 
certain types of people, then what we know about 
that part of the world and those types of people 
comes from the media. Sometimes the media actively 
try to teach us, as when the Count on Sesame Street  
starts to…well…count, or when a show features a 
story line about bullying or mental health. It’s easy to 
see that audiences can indeed learn from the media. 
But we learn even when the media don’t intention-
ally try to teach us—media content consistently 
(if implicitly) demonstrates who matters and who 
doesn’t, who is taken seriously and who isn’t, who is 
feared and who is trusted, and who is best suited to 
perform certain roles or functions in our society. If 
you have any doubts as to whether we’re affected by 
media content, turn to Chapter 2, especially the first 
few readings.
The readings in this Content section critically 
examine the texts presented by the mass media—
everything from Disney films to menstruation imagery 
and beyond. The 33 readings are divided into three 
chapters. The alternative tables of contents provide 
other options for organizing these readings.
Chapter 4 covers Journalism and Advertis-
ing. Some of its 12 readings use content analysis, a 
method rooted in the social sciences that involves 
counting each occurrence of whatever is being stud-
ied. Other readings use qualitative methods such as 
textual analysis or rhetorical analysis to highlight and 
interpret the dominant themes found in media con-
tent. Reading 4.1 by Dwight E. Brooks analyzes a 
long-form documentary about James Baldwin’s ideas 
about race and media in the US: I Am Not Y our Negro. 
Christopher S. Josey and Andrea Figueroa-Caballero  
(Reading 4.2) test how positively Latinx people are rep-
resented on identity focused news sites. Diem-My Bui 
undertakes a critical discourse analysis of anti-Asian 
sentiment in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic 
(Reading 4.3).
The chapter includes multiple framing analyses. 
In reading 4.4, Emily Riewestahl, Emilee Baker, Sriv-
idya Ramasubramanian, and Laura Joy “Anangokwe” 
Merchant study how Indigenous and mainstream local 
newspapers frame a specific pipeline project. Newly 
Paul (Reading 4.5) looks at the framing of transgender 
politicians. Reading 4.6, by Rebecca Ann Lind and 
Colleen Salo Aravena, studies the framing of feminism. 
Patti Brown (Reading 4.7) discusses how media frame 
the immigration story. Jean Marie Brown (Reading 4.8) 
analyzes how Colin Kaepernick was framed before 
and after the killing of George Floyd.
Moving to advertising, Jean Kilbourne (Read-
ing 4.9) addresses the representation of women in 
advertising. In Reading 4.10, Greg Niedt and Julia C. 
Richmond look at gender-bending advertisements by

CoverGirl and War Paint. Mary Douglas Vavrus stud-
ies the political campaigns of women veterans, noting 
a reliance upon a weaponized gaze, and a novel way of 
highlighting both their military service and domestic/
maternal expertise (Reading 4.11). Finally, in Reading 
4.12, Seonah Kim & jas l moultrie analyze Run Out-
side the Lines, a lululemon ad that appears to celebrate 
Blackness and social justice but reinforces a postracial 
neoliberal ideology.
Chapter 5, Film and Television, contains 12 read-
ings, focusing on entertainment media. It starts with 
Jonathan Rossing’s analysis of how even well-
 meaning
 
attempts to address social justice and inequality in 
comedy can instead reinforce exclusionary practices 
(Reading 5.1). Natalie Jolly (Reading 5.2) looks at how 
menstruation is represented in popular culture, mak-
ing us realize how differently we respond to menstrual 
blood than to blood resulting from violence. Reading 
5.3, by Leslie A. Grinner, applies the SCWAMP tool—
which can help identify whether media content rein-
forces dominant ideologies by favoring certain social 
groups—to The Twilight Saga. Naomi Rockler-Gladen 
(Reading 5.4) looks at how The Lion King encourages 
and justifies racial separatism and hierarchy. In Read-
ing 5.5, Sarah E. Fryett examines Disney heroines who 
transgress previous gender and racial representations. 
Lea M. Popielinski (Reading 5.6) argues that The Devil 
Wears Prada and The Nanny Diaries represent the 
evolution of a familiar fairy tale: a maiden overcomes 
subjugation by a powerful older woman (the wicked 
stepmother) to gain freedom and happiness. Reading 
5.7 by Jennifer S. Kramer looks at how The Bachelor 
perpetuates an image of catty women who will go to 
great lengths to beat other women to win their man.
Madison Barnes-Nelson studies the centrality of 
women’s friendship, and how Brooklyn Nine-Nine exem-
plifies intersectional allyship (Reading 5.8). In Reading 
5.9, Kyra Heatly shows how the rom-com Long Shot 
seems to challenge hegemonic gender norms and the 
representation of women in politics, but ultimately does 
little to challenge the status quo. Sarah E. Fryett shows 
how I Love Y ou, Man and Get Hard reinforce dominant 
masculine ideals of aggression, sexual conquest, and 
avoiding emotion and other qualities often considered 
feminine (Reading 5.10). Anthony R. Ramirez looks at 
the Latinidad of male Latinx characters in superhero 
and comic book films (Reading 5.11). Finally, Robert 
Alan Brookey and Maria Williams-Hawkins study 
the first season of Pose, finding overlap between the 
AIDS crisis in the late 1980s and the recent COVID-19

Chapter 6 presents nine readings addressing 
Music and New Media. Christopher P. Campbell’s piece 
(Reading 6.1) broadly considers media created by or 
for the Millennial generation, considering (among other 
things) Beyonce’s “Formation” video and Amy Schum-

and Michael Huertas, studies the White authenticat-
ing strategies of rapper Jack Harlow and argues that 
Harlow represents the commodification of hip hop 
music by a White-dominated structure. Rachel Alicia 
Griffin and Joshua D. Phillips (Reading 6.3) argue that 
Eminem’s “Love the Way Y ou Lie” strengthens cultural 
myths about domestic violence and normalizes men’s 
violence against women. Kiana Cox (Reading 6.4) 
explores sexualized imagery in current rap music, with 
special attention to Nicki Minaj.
In Reading 6.5, Cynthia A. Cooper discusses the

social media to address and advance issues of social 
justice. In Reading 6.8, Gust A. Y ep and Ryan M. Les-
cure use the emerging field of Cute Studies to analyze 
the Instagram posts of Maru (a Japanese Shiba Inu), 
connecting to ideologies of gender and race/ethnicity 
and arguing that cute images are not apolitical. Finally, 
Reading 6.9 by Joseph Hoffswell is an analysis of the

4.1: I AM NOT YOUR NEGRO: JAMES 
BALDWIN’S CHALLENGE TO AMERICA 
AND ITS MEDIA
Dwight E. Brooks
This reading utilizes Critical Race Theories (CRTs) 
to analyze Raoul Peck’s critically acclaimed docu-
mentary of James Baldwin to show the relevance 
of Baldwin’s ideas about race and media in the 
United States 35 years after his death.
Prior to the 2016 release of Raoul Peck’s documen-
tary I Am Not Y our Negro (IANYN), many college 
students may not have been familiar with James 
Baldwin, a prominent African American writer 
and social critic. Baldwin’s novels, plays, speeches, 
and television appearances in the 1950s, 1960s, and 
1970s provided pointed critiques of 
 Americ
an 
society. Today, more students and scholars are 
acquainted with Baldwin—to quote him has become 
trendy. Filmmaker Raoul Peck, like so many others, 
has turned to Baldwin to help understand and con-
front the latest iterations of the American dream 
turned nightmare. Since the mid-1970s, the critical 
race theory movement has also sought to study and 
transform White supremacy in America. This essay 
draws from critical race theories to illustrate some 
of the ways IANYN projects Baldwin’s penetrating 
analyses of American media culture into the cur -
rent moment to provide a powerful reckoning with 
America’s failure to confront the untruths it tells 
about race.
I Am Not Your Negro
IANYN resurrects James Baldwin’s words and ideas 
with the same intensity as their initial expressions. 
Baldwin wrote and spoke extensively about many of 
the same issues that fuel so much of today’s social 
discord, making his analyses applicable 35 years 
after his death. IANYN is inspired by Baldwin’s 
unfinished book project, Remember This House, his 
story of America through the interconnected lives 
of his three friends and slain civil rights leaders—
Medgar Evers, Malcolm X, and Martin Luther King, 
Jr. Peck uses Baldwin’s manuscript notes alongside 
speeches, television appearances, and writings—
especially those about film—to provide a powerful 
cinematic projection of what the book might have 
embodied today.
IANYN captures Baldwin’s intellect, pugnacity, 
and wit to promulgate the writer’s contention that 
what is really at stake in racial matters is America’s 
soul. Peck spent nearly a decade on the film, shares 
screenwriting credit with Baldwin, and functions as 
Baldwin’s messenger. Baldwin’s words are heard on 
the soundtrack, either spoken by Baldwin himself or 
delivered by narrator Samuel L. Jackson. Jackson’s 
narrations are accompanied by music, on-screen text, 
natural sound, vintage photos, scenes from Hollywood 
cinema and television, and contemporary news foot-
age such as the protests in Ferguson, Missouri over the 
4.
JOURNALISM AND ADVERTISING
DOI: 10.4324/9781003193708-6

94 Content
shooting death of Michael Brown, which helped ignite 
the Black Lives Matter movement. The film’s loose 
structure and montages of spoken word, songs, pho-
tographs, and video overlap—sometimes seamlessly, 
oftentimes jarring, but always engaging.
IANYN deploys multiple cinematic techniques 
to trace the startling threads of analogy between 
America’s past and present. The film’s alluring editing 
and stimulating use of color create sizzling tableaux. 
IANYN includes clips from classic films such as King 
Kong, Stagecoach, and Imitation of Life to illustrate Hol-
lywood’s use of tropes of Black menace and subservi-
ence as foils for White purity and innocence. Baldwin 
was fascinated with American film and devoted an 
entire book—The Devil Finds Work (1976)—to his 
intimate and complex relationships with Hollywood. 
Peck uses Baldwin’s personal reflections on media 
stories in a penetrating assessment of American racial 
politics. The film functions as Baldwin’s warning about 
how the media’s obsession with racial stereotypes and 
misrepresentations dangerously perpetuates the myth 
of America as a bastion of freedom, democracy, and 
good life. IANYN’s images of Baldwin are fitting given 
the acclaimed writer was among a handful of African 
Americans with a sustained presence on national 
television.
IANYN opens with a 1968 scene from The Dick 
Cavett Show where the host asks Baldwin, “Why aren’t 
Negroes more optimistic? It’s getting so much bet-
ter.” Baldwin was well-known for his poignant social 
critiques laced with optimism. Civil disorder followed 
the 1968 assassinations of Dr. King and Robert Ken-
nedy. Protests of the Vietnam War generated milita-
rized policing on college campuses and cities with 
large Black populations. Calls for “law and order” led 
to the century’s largest mass incarceration of people 
of color and widespread state-sanctioned repression 
against Black Americans. Viewers are treated to a clas-
sic Baldwin response to Cavett: “It’s not a question of 
what happens to the Negro, the real question is what is 
going to happen to this country.”
Baldwin’s contention that America’s soul is at 
stake in racial matters is the thesis of IANYN. In sup-
porting this proposition, the film reveals Baldwin’s 
proclivity to identify as an American and challenge 
other Americans to use their power to save the nation. 
IANYN also uncovers Baldwin’s internal struggle with 
optimism: How is optimism possible in a country that 
betrays its citizens and terrorizes its children? IANYN 
questions American progress and compels audiences 
to rethink racial justice, a position consistent with the 
critical race theory (CRT) movement, which emerged 
during the final decade of Baldwin’s life.
Critical Race Theories
Most students have heard of CRT through media 
reports of attacks by politicians, soccer moms, and 
the religious right. Unfortunately, news accounts of 
CRT focus on slavery, anti-White sentiment, and 
K-12 education, but ignore what CRT actually rep-
resents and its intellectual foundations. Politicians 
and commentators have condemned an imagined 
version of CRT that does not exist and is not taught. 
CRT is a movement comprised of an assortment of 
scholars who deploy various theoretical approaches 
to study and transform the relationships between 
race, racism, and power. CRT evolved from critical 
legal studies that challenged the objectivity of the 
law with respect to race. CRT applies critical theo-
ries to question the effectiveness of post-civil rights 
legal policies through analyses of culture and soci-
ety by focusing on the intersections of race, law, and 
cultural power. Given recent discourses on CRT, I 
invite students reading this essay to accept or reject 
CRT’s premises and/or challenge its analytical suit-
ability for IANYN. But IANYN demonstrates that 
systemic racism in the U.S. cannot be denied.
CRTs are not anti-White and do not claim that all 
Whites are oppressors. These theories simply purport 
the reality of America’s history of racial subordination 
that requires acknowledgment and study. CRTs work 
from the premise that racism is ordinary, not aberrant—
the way American society does business and the com-
mon, everyday experiences of most people of color. 
CRTs have activist dimensions and encourage story-
tellers to chronicle their racial experiences (Delgado &  
Stefanic, 2001).
IANYN presents Baldwin’s understanding of race 
in America by deconstructing some of the myths and 
lies that support the everyday order of American life. In 
the section titled “Witness,” Baldwin sees himself in a 
distinct role compared to activists such as Dr. King and 
Malcolm X. He admits to not being a Black Muslim, a 


Journalism and Advertising 95
member of the NAACP, or any Christian congregation. 
He adds that he never joined the Black Panthers and 
“did not believe that all white people were devils.” Part 
of his responsibility as a witness “was to write the story, 
and to get it out.” IANYN adheres to the tenet of CRT 
that promote the legitimacy of experiential knowledge of 
subjugated people.
Another principle of CRT, social construction, 
holds that race and races are products of social 
thought and relations. Although IANYN never explic-
itly rejects race as an objective, fixed, biological, or 
genetic reality, Baldwin was keenly aware that race 
was a constructed category that determines social 
outcomes. He also understood that identities—racial, 
gender, or 
 other
wise—are invented. He wrote often 
how human categories prevent us from the complexi-
ties of the world and within ourselves. IANYN features 
a segment from the 1963 PBS program, The Negro and 
The American Promise, which mixes interviews and 
documentary footage of Martin Luther King, Jr., Mal-
colm X, and Baldwin offering differing perspectives on 
the Civil Rights movement. After rejecting the idea of 
a “Negro problem” as something made up by White 
Americans, Baldwin asserts that the “American peo-
ple are unable to face the fact that I am flesh of their 
flesh, bone of their bone, created by them.” The film’s 
final section, “I Am Not a Nigger” begins with histori-
cal photographs of African Americans as the narrator 
reveals: “White is a metaphor for power.”
IANYN also acknowledges the CRT theme of 
intersectionality—that no person has a single, easily 
stated, uniform identity. The section titled “Purity” 
begins with Jackson’s narration accompanied by pho-
tos of Black and White slaves from New Orleans:
I know very well that my ancestors had no 
desire to come to this place. But neither did 
the ancestors of the people who became white 
and who require of my captivity a song. They 
require a song of me less to celebrate my cap-
tivity than to justify their own.
Similar to the theme of intersectionality, anti-
 
essentialism
 in CRT acknowledges that everyone has 
potentially conflicting, overlapping identities, loy-
alties, and allegiances. IANYN contains a Baldwin 
speech lamenting the problem of essentialism in the 
country: “…what is really happening is that brother 
has murdered brother knowing it was his brother. 
White men have lynched Negroes knowing them 
to be their sons. White women have had Negroes 
burned knowing them to be their lovers.”
The concept of white privilege emerged from crit-
ical White studies and examinations of whiteness—
constructions of the White race. White privilege refers 
to the variety of social advantages and benefits that 
derive from membership in the dominant White race. 
Baldwin’s awareness of white privilege is expressed 
near the end of IANYN when he declares: “I attest to 
this: the world is not white; it never was white, cannot 
be white.” Baldwin sought to make White people aware 
of their whiteness and accountable for their white priv-
ilege. For Baldwin, whiteness was not a description of 
a race of people, but a subject position or identity in a 
power relationship, which is formulated in opposition 
of non-White people.
CRTs feature storytelling/counter-storytelling and 
often use media narratives to illuminate and explore 
experiences of racial oppression. Storytelling gives 
voice to the substance of racial experiences while per-
sonal, often first-person accounts provide alternative 
visions of social reality. Abraham Lincoln’s masterful 
use of storytelling amplified the power, impact, and 
persuasiveness of his arguments. Storytelling disarms 
people, whereas facts and statistics can threaten them. 
Baldwin is a true storyteller, and his narratives and 
counter-narratives are the centerpieces of IANYN.
One example of Baldwin’s narrative deconstruc-
tion of whiteness is his strategic use of the term “nig-
ger” in expressing his optimism for the country and its 
Black citizens. Despite the film’s title—I Am Not Y our 
Negro—Baldwin at times intentionally used the term 
“nigger.” In IANYN’s concluding interview footage, 
Baldwin tells the interviewer that White people had 
yet to ask themselves a crucial question:
… try and find out in their own hearts why it 
was necessary to have a “nigger” in the first 
place, because I’m not a nigger, I’m a man. 
But if you think I’m a nigger, it means you 
need him… If I’m not the nigger here and you 
invented him, you the white people, invented 
him—then you’ve got to find out why. And the 
future of the country depends on that….

96 Content
IANYN expresses Baldwin’s warning to America  
through his media narratives (television, radio, 
books, magazines, etc.). Similar to Dr. King, Bald-
win sought media to give him access to Whites who 
would not normally hear his ideas. Although Bald-
win was criticized by some Black leaders for seeking 
out and using White media for his own glory, he rec-
ognized that television and film both entertain and 
shape consciousness.
Baldwin’s Analysis of Media and Race
Baldwin wrote extensively about film and its role in 
shaping our culture and ideologies. Peck features 
Baldwin’s ideas on race, Hollywood, and the mythol-
ogy of White innocence and purity. For example, 
IANYN presents a scene of Joan Crawford dancing, 
from the 1931 film Dance, Fools, Dance. Narrator 
Jackson voices Baldwin’s thoughts: 
I am fascinated by the movement on and off  
the screen….I was aware that Joan Crawford 
was a white lady. Y et I remember … a colored 
woman, who, to me, looked exactly like Joan 
Crawford…. She was incredibly beautiful… 
She looked down at me with so beautiful a 
smile that I was not even embarrassed. Which 
was rare for me.
Although like so many media consumers the young 
Baldwin was often seduced by the power of Hol-
lywood’s construction of (White) beauty and inno-
cence, the older Baldwin understood the racial 
fantasies and racist stereotypes that dominated 
media representations and were reproduced glob-
ally. To Baldwin, White purity is but one of the racial 
fantasies used to safeguard whiteness—even though 
it was actually destroying people and the country. 
IANYN contains Baldwin’s analysis of the 1958 film 
The Defiant Ones, in which two escaped convicts, 
one White and one Black, are chained together and 
learn to get along to elude capture. Baldwin rejects 
the premise of the story because it is based on the 
“profound misunderstanding” of the nature of the 
hatred between Black and White people. Although 
Baldwin concedes hatred on both sides, the dif-
ference is that the root of the White’s hatred is a 
“bottomless and nameless terror,” which lives only 
in the mind of Whites. The root of Blacks’ hatred is 
rage; although they do not really hate Whites, they 
just want Whites out of their way.
Baldwin discusses the scene that depicts the 
Black man (Cullen, played by Sidney Poitier) unable 
to pull the White man (“Joker” played by Tony Cur-
tis) onto a moving train. Cullen jumps from the train 
and joins Joker to avoid abandoning him. Baldwin 
claims Black audiences resented this part of the film 
and yelled, “Get back on the train you fool.” He argues 
Cullen jumps off the train to reassure White people 
they are not hated. He adds that liberal White audi-
ences applauded Cullen’s actions out of relief and joy. 
For Baldwin, the myth of White innocence extends to 
White audiences. Baldwin articulates the long-held 
grievances that Black actors such as Sidney Poitier and 
Harry Belafonte were forced to suppress on-screen in 
order not to offend White audiences’ sense of inno-
cence. Although both were “sex symbols,” nobody 
dared admit it, nor would they ever be presented in the 
same way as White “Hollywood he-men.”
Baldwin detests the characters portrayed by Black 
actors such as Stepin Fetchit, Willie Best, and Mantan 
Moreland, who were known for their minstrel-type 
buffoonery. They “lied about the world I knew, and 
debased it, and I certainly did not know anybody like 
them.” The title character in the 1927 film Uncle Tom’s 
Cabin, played by James B. Lowe, also earned Baldwin’s 
scorn because he refused to take vengeance into his 
own hands.
Baldwin despised and feared White Holly-
wood heroes such as John Wayne and Gary Cooper 
because they did take vengeance into their own hands. 
The young Baldwin watched many of these Westerns 
before realizing he was an American Negro and thus 
one with the Indians—whom the cowboys were busy 
killing: “I understood that: my countrymen were my 
enemy. I suspect that all these stories are designed to 
reassure us that no crime was committed. We’ve made 
a legend out of a massacre.”
Despite its plethora of historical images, IANYN 
is about today. Peck juxtaposes history with images 
from contemporary events such as the Black Lives 
Matter movement; the murders by law enforcers of 
young African Americans such as Trayvon Martin, 


Journalism and Advertising 97
Tamir Rice, and Amir Brooks; and mass shootings on 
college campuses and schools: “The American way of 
life has failed—to make people happier or make them 
better… To look around the United States today is 
enough to make prophets and angels weep. This is not 
the land of the free…” These words are followed by 
a scene from Elephant (2003), chronicling the events 
surrounding a fictional high school shooting. Another 
Baldwin warning to America comes in a speech that 
echoes CRTs’ challenges to the law with respect to 
race and a commitment to social change:
Don’t write any voting acts. We had that—it’s 
called the fifteenth amendment—during the 
Civil Rights Bill of 1964. What you have to do is 
look at what is happening in the country… It is 
not a racial problem. It is a problem of whether 
or not you’re willing to look at your life and be 
responsible for it, and then begin to change it.
Instead of talking about the struggle for Black rights 
or civil rights, Baldwin talked about human rights. 
Baldwin believed that Americans must work with 
each other to make a better world: “It is a terrible, 
an inexorable law that one cannot deny the human-
ity of another without diminishing one’s own.” 
Although the term White supremacy is not invoked 
in the film, Baldwin alludes to it repeatedly in his 
discussions of whiteness. Baldwin would not restrict 
White supremacists to self-avowed members of 
hate groups. Baldwin, like CRT, connects whiteness 
to White supremacy. In a 1980 essay published in 
Esquire magazine, Baldwin wrote: “To be white 
was to be forced to digest a delusion called white 
supremacy” (p. 45).
Baldwin criticized a media environment designed 
to “reassure,” not “trouble.” IANYN’s critique of Amer-
ican consumer culture included a 1954 short promo-
tional film from the US Department of Commerce, 
The Secret Selling of the Negro. The film shows African 
American families shopping, consuming, and watching 
television as the announcer touts the increasing spend-
ing power of the Black consumer market. Baldwin 
says he was told (presumably by a media executive) 
that “people in general cannot bear very much real-
ity.” Baldwin’s interpretation was that people “prefer 
fantasy to a truthful re-creation of their experience.” 
Moments later, we see clips from The Gong Show  
(1976) while Baldwin offers his strongest indictment of 
commercial media culture: “The industry is compelled 
given the way it is built, to present the American people 
a self-perpetuating fantasy of American life. Their con-
cept of entertainment is difficult to distinguish from the 
use of narcotics.” Viewers then see clips from shows 
such as Jerry Springer (1991), Deal or No Deal (2005), 
The Price is Right (1972), and Let’s Make a Deal (2009) 
as Baldwin declares: “To watch the TV screen for any 
length of time is to learn some really frightening things 
about the American sense of reality.” He thought tele-
vision weakened the ability to deal honestly with the 
world and humanely with its people.
Before IANYN ends with Baldwin’s “I am not a 
nigger” passage, it presents a sense of Baldwin’s opti-
mism for the country: “I can’t be a pessimist because 
I’m alive… I’m forced to believe that we can survive 
whatever we must survive.” Baldwin believed that the 
future of African Americans in this country is “as bright 
or as dark as the future of the United States,” saying: “It 
is entirely up to the American people.”
It’s Your Turn: What Do You Think? What 
Will You Find?
 1.
 IANYN
 presents Baldwin’s prophetic 
warning to White America of the costs to 
the country if it continued to propagate the 
myths of America. Can you identify any 
of these myths and their consequences? 
Why do you think the country continues 
to promote or defend false ideals?
 2.
 One component of
 CRT is intersec-
tionality, or the importance of individ-
uals’ multiple identities. IANYN briefly 
includes an FBI memorandum on James 
Baldwin that refers to his homosexuality. 
Although Baldwin was one of the first 
American writers to write openly about 
homosexuality, the film ignores this 
aspect of his life and work. Why do you 
think the film omits Baldwin’s homosex-
uality? Would you have included this in 
the film? Why/why not?

4.2: SEARCHING FOR A SAFE SPACE: 
REPRESENTATIONS OF THE LATINX 
COMMUNITY ON IDENTITY-FOCUSED 
NEWS SITES
Christopher S. Josey and Andrea 
Figueroa-Caballero
In this study, the authors perform a content anal-
ysis of news sites that cater to primarily Latinx 
and other minoritized communities. Through this 
analysis, the authors seek to discover whether iden-
tity-focused news paints a positive picture of mar-
ginalized groups.
To say that the media in general do a poor job of rep-
resenting the largest racial and ethnic group in the 
United States would be an understatement (Dixon & 
Josey, 2013). Although Latinx individuals comprise 
more than 16% of the US population (depending on 
the exact collapsing of census categories), media 
outlets fail to pay sufficient attention to them. Media 
not only underrepresent Latinx people but also 
present them in highly problematic manners (Josey 
et al., 2010, Mastro, Figueroa-Caballero & Sink, 
2017). In general, when characters of color are cast 
in prominent roles, they are often sidelined to the 
least watched networks in shows largely featuring 
other actors of the same race (Tynes & Ward, 2009).
In print news, Turk et al. (1989) found that  
Latinx people appear more frequently in soft news 
sections (e.g., entertainment) and are nearly absent in 
hard news sections (e.g., business). In television news, 
Dixon and Linz (2000) found that Latinx people are 
portrayed as perpetrators of crime more than crime 
data would indicate is the case. In online news – the 
primary source of news for most people today – Josey 
et al. (2010) found that Latinx individuals are extremely 
underrepresented when compared to US census data 
and are associated with socially problematic issues 
such as poverty.
Searching for a Safe Space in News
The news people seek today differs from that 
of the past. People are more likely to look for 
news that maps closely with their social identity 
(Knobloch-Westerwick, Appiah, & Alter, 2008; 
Melican & Dixon, 2008) on sites that serve as safe 
spaces. In the context of seeking news and informa-
tion, a safe space is one that meets three criteria: 
any marginalized group is clearly visible in coverage, 
the site situates portrayals of a group in stories that 
are uplifting, and the site balances stereotypic con-
firming portrayals with stereotype-disconfirming 
or -neutral portrayals. Newspapers geared toward 
the Latinx community have traditionally been safe 
spaces for Latinx people; several important online 
news sites have emerged as safe spaces for Latinx 
people. Although we focus on news media, we note 
that the concept of safe media spaces extends into 
entertainment content, with shows produced by or 
featuring people of color serving as a safe space 
and providing many benefits for their audiences  
(Tynes & Ward, 2009; Ward, 2004).
Analyses of media content are important 
because problematic representations such as those 
mentioned earlier can profoundly affect both people 
of color (Ward, 2004) and Whites (Casas & Dixon, 
2003). Therefore, our goal is to analyze the content of 
important US-based Latinx-oriented news sites. In our 
study, we examine the sites that feature stories about 
Latinos that are the most consumed by readers. This 
includes a variety of news sources, such as traditional 
news outlets with Latinx-focused sections and online 
news magazines presenting in-depth profiles and short 
 3.  Ha ve your views on critical race theo-
ries changed after reading this chapter? 
Despite claims to the contrary, critical 
race theory (CRT) is not taught in K-12. 
Do you think CRT should be taught 
in schools? Should students have the 
opportunity to accept or reject CRT?


Journalism and Advertising 99
form news stories. We study the race/ethnicity of the 
characters represented in the news stories, the tone of 
the stories, whether the stories confirm or disconfirm 
stereotypes, and investigate whether a set of specific 
traits is associated with the characters.
Analyzing US Latinx News Sites
After performing an exhaustive search for US-based 
Latinx-focused news sites, we consulted multiple 
website ranking lists to determine which to include 
in our study. We focused on sites presenting con-
tent in the English language, given the primarily 
English-speaking research team, but we note that 
many US Latinx-focused news sites have bilingual 
presentations of material or separate Spanish and 
English sections. Ultimately, we selected four sites 
to analyze based upon the frequency of unique daily 
visits: News Taco (newstaco.com), Latina (latina.
com/), Latino Voices (huffpost.com/voices/
 
latino-
voices), and Al Dia (aldianews.com). We con-
structed our dataset from these four outlets using 
an equal probability sampling method (Dixon & 
Linz, 2000; Josey et al., 2010). Our analysis covered 
April 1, 2018, through March 30, 2019. This was 
the first year of an ongoing longitudinal analysis of 
 identity-f
ocused news sites that serve as safe spaces 
for marginalized groups. We chose to present year 
1 findings for one of the marginalized groups under 
analysis in our larger study (i.e., Latinx news). Owing 
to coverage of the COVID-19 pandemic, we felt this 
was the most typical year currently in our longitudi-
nal analysis. We created a composite month for each 
site, randomly choosing 30 days from the 12-month 
time frame. For example, each month’s first day was 
assigned a number from 1 to 12, and one of those 
dates were selected to represent the first day of a 
month for that site. We did this for all 30 days for 
each site in our composite month. On each date, we 
randomly chose five news stories for analysis. This 
yielded 150 news stories from each site and a total 
sample of 600. We downloaded all materials from 
the Wayback Machine, a website which preserves 
internet pages.
We analyzed each story according to the cod-
ing system described below. Stories were coded by a 
research team; coders were extensively trained so that 
they would interpret news stories in a similar manner 
and reached an acceptable level of intercoder reliabil-
ity on all variables.
We analyzed each story in our sample on multiple 
levels. First, global analyses were conducted based on 
each story and its headline. This allows us to meas-
ure stereotyping, or a lack thereof, in each story. The 
overall tone of the story (Josey et al., 2010) was judged 
using a 5-pt Likert-type scale ranging from extremely 
positive (value = 1) to extremely negative (value = 5).  
Coders determined tone from the words used in the 
headline or story (e.g., “rose above” is positive, whereas 
“failed” is negative).
Coders then moved to the character level of anal-
ysis, allowing us to tease out a nuanced presentation 
of stereotyping. The four most prominent charac-
ters were coded along multiple variables. Race was 
assessed using US census category classifications. 
Coders assessed whether characters were presented in 
ways that were stereotype-confirming, 
 -dis
confirming, 
or -neutral. Finally, coders assessed whether 33 indi-
vidual stereotype-confirming and -disconfirming 
traits were associated with each character using sev-
en-point semantic differential scales such as quiet/
loud, hardworking/lazy, unintelligent/intelligent, wel-
fare recipient/successfully employed, and unathletic/
athletic. The ends of these scales reflect clear stereo-
type-disconfirming or -confirming traits, whereas cen-
tral positions are neutral. The more the stories exhibit 
stereotype-disconfirming traits, the less stereotypical 
the coverage is and the more likely that the news site 
functions as a safe space for people of color.
Representing the Latinx Community
Recall that coders analyzed the four most prominent 
characters in 600 stories across four Latinx-focused 
news sites. Some stories had fewer than four char -
acters, and because we relied on conservative rules 
when coding race (not making any determination 
if were unsure), our sample ultimately included 763 
characters. This is a robust number that allows us 
to conduct meaningful qualitative and quantitative 
analyses. We present our findings first in terms of 
numerical representation before turning to the holis-
tic analysis (story tone), stereotype confirmation or 
disconfirmation, and analysis of character traits.

100 Content
We expected that Latinx news sites would feature 
markedly more Latinx individuals than observed in 
prior analyses of mainstream news sites. One way to 
test this is to examine the raw numbers of Latinx char-
acters as compared to other character races (e.g., an 
intergroup comparison). Considering the 763 charac-
ters whose race could be coded, the sample was quite 
diverse: 7.6% Black, 35% White, 2% Asian, 1.3% Arab, 
0.3% Native, and 54% Latinx. With more than half of 
the characters coded as Latinx, the sites we analyzed 
feature more Latinx people than all other races com-
bined. Making a qualitative comparison with prior 
analyses of mainstream news (Josey et al., 2010), we 
see that Latinx individuals are present at nearly 
 triple
 
the occurrence in our sample when compared to 
mainstream news sites.
Another way to examine numerical representa-
tion of groups is to perform an inter-reality comparison 
(Dixon & Linz, 2000; Josey et al., 2010). We do this 
with a z-test of independent proportions, a statistical 
test comparing the proportion of Latinx characters we 
observed in our sample to the proportion of Latinx 
individuals in the United States. The z-test provides 
further support that Latinx news features significantly 
more representation than we would expect based on 
US census data (Z = 28.78, p < 0.01). Importantly, this 
inter-reality test demonstrates that Latinx news sites 
feature significantly more Latinx characters propor-
tionally than are present in the US population. Further, 
our findings demonstrate that Latinx-focused news 
sites feature nearly triple the number of Latinx individ-
uals when compared to the findings of prior studies of 
mainstream news sites (Josey et al., 2010). Research 
on marginalized communities finds that representa-
tion is a cornerstone of any safe space (Tynes & Ward, 
2009). Taken together, it is evident that Latinx news 
does a much better job of showing Latinx individuals 
than prior analyses have found for mainstream news.
As important as the sheer volume of representa-
tion is for the Latinx community, equally so is the 
nature of these representations. As noted previously, 
Latinx representation on mainstream outlets has been 
problematic; we expected things to be better in our 
sample of Latinx news sites. One important indicator 
of problematic portrayals within news is the global tone 
of a story. As part of our conception of a safe space, we 
wanted to see if Latinx sites would feature stories that 
were more positive in tone when Latinx people were 
included. To test this, we performed an analysis of vari-
ance (ANOV A) comparing the tone of stories featuring 
Latinx individuals prominently (e.g., as top characters 
by count) to stories featuring other racial groups. An 
ANOV A is a statistical means for scholars to compare 
differences in average values (e.g., ratings of story tone) 
between two or more categories of measurement (e.g., 
racial groups). This test allows us to compare the aver-
age story tone where Latinx characters are prominent 
to stories where other racial groups are prominent. For 
all analyses below, we focus on stories featuring Black, 
Latinx, and White characters. We omitted other groups 
because so few stories featured them prominently. We 
performed a one-way ANOV A, which revealed signif-
icant differences in news coverage based upon char-
acter race (F [2, 1644] =78.82, p < 0.01). Follow-up 
tests revealed that stories featuring Latinx (M = 2.8, 
SD = 0.84) and Black (M = 3.0, SD = 1.1) characters 
prominently were significantly more positive in tone 
than stories featuring White (M = 3.59, SD = 0.85) 
characters prominently. There were no significant dif-
ferences in story tone between stories prominently fea-
turing Latinx and Black characters. Results support the 
expectation associated with our second criterion of a 
safe space (sites present a group in a positive/uplift-
ing manner). Even more, it appears as though Latinx- 
focused sites are a safe space of representation for 
both Latinx and Black people.
Now that our global analysis of the stories has 
shown that the stories help establish these Latinx 
news sites as safe spaces for Latinx readers, we turn 
to analysis of the characters. First, we approach Lat-
inx characters holistically as a group apart from other 
races to see whether they are shown in a stereotype-
 
confir
ming, -disconfirming, or -neutral manner. Doing 
this allows us to see the ratio of neutral-to-
 confir
ming-
to-disconfirming portrayals, an important means of 
assessing whether sites are a safe space for Latinx 
readers. The Latinx news sites presented Latinx char-
acters far more frequently in stereotype-
 dis
confirming 
ways (e.g., choosing to have fewer children for envi-
ronmental reasons; 110, 26%) than in stereotype-  
confirming ways (e.g., associated with gang activity; 32, 
7%). Interestingly, most portrayals were neutral (e.g., a 
librarian starting a book club; 288, 67%). This supports 
our expectation that Latinx sites would feature Latinx 


Journalism and Advertising 101
individuals in a far less stereotypical fashion than prior 
studies have shown mainstream sites do.
Finally, we move to an analysis of the traits 
associated with the individual characters analyzed. 
We expected that Latinx news sites would associate 
positive traits with Latinx characters. Looking at this 
allows us to take a more detailed look at individual 
character portrayals more deeply than simply asking 
if a character was associated with stereotypes. In a 
similar manner to that described above, we focused 
on Latinx, Black, and White characters featured 
in stories. For each ANOV A, we examined stereo-
typing of characters by placing semantically oppo-
site traits on each end of a scale. For example, the 
 st
ereotype-confirming trait “lazy” was on one end 
of the scale, and the stereotype-disconfirming trait 
“hardworking” was on the other end. Below we focus 
on three stereotypical traits known to be associated 
with Latinx individuals in mainstream news sites. 
These are lazy, violence-criminal, and loudness; their 
disconfirming opposites are hardworking, peaceful 
law abider, and soft-spoken. Our analysis showed 
that Latinx characters were portrayed as more hard-
working than the other races (F  [2,1484] =45.56,  
p < 0.01. Further, Latinx characters were the least 
associated with violent crime: (F  [2,1638] = 4.43, 
p < 0.05). Finally, Latinx characters were the least 
likely to be portrayed as loud (F  [2,1532] = 5.60, p 
< 0.01). For each of these analyses, no differences 
emerged between White and Black characters. Taken 
together, these findings support our expectation that 
Latinx-
 f
ocused news sites meet our third criterion of 
a safe space: balancing stereotypic portrayals with 
 st
ereotype-disconfirming portrayals.
What Can These Spaces Do for the 
Latinx Community?
We began our analysis with the belief that Latinx-
 
f
ocused news sites could serve as a safe space 
for Latinx people seeking news. Our study found 
that US Latinx news sites certainly do create a 
safe space for Latinx individuals seeking news. 
The Latinx sites we analyzed visibly feature Lat-
inx and Black characters in ways that are uplifting. 
Further, Latinx characters are portrayed in largely 
stereotype-
 dis
confirming manners. This is a stark 
departure from how mainstream news features Lat-
inx people. These spaces serve as a respite from the 
lack of visibility and deluge of negativity shown in 
mainstream news. This, in turn, could have powerful 
positive effects on a number of individual psycho-
logical outcomes for Latinx people, such as higher 
racial/ethnic and self-esteem. Mainstream news 
outlets could take an important cue from these sites 
and feature a greater number and diversity of Lat-
inx people than they currently do. Most importantly, 
mainstream news could balance stories incorpo-
rating stereotypic portrayals (e.g., undocumented 
immigrant) with stories that disconfirm stereotypes 
(e.g., city councilmember). This will take deliberate 
editorial intent, but as our analysis demonstrates, 
there are significant payoffs for that deliberate effort.

4.3: A CRITICAL DISCOURSE ANALYSIS 
ON ANTI-ASIAN SENTIMENT AND THE 
PANDEMIC
Diem-My T . Bui
The author uses critical discourse analysis to con-
nect historical claims that people of Asian descent 
are threats and cannot be assimilated into Amer-
ican society to contemporary discourse about 
Asians during the coronavirus pandemic.
In mid-March 2021, a mass shooting in Atlanta-area 
spas resulted in eight people dead. Although the gun-
man has not admitted to choosing the spas because 
of race or gender bias (Fausset, 2021), six victims 
were Asian American women. Fears increased across 
the nation about a wave of anti-Asian violence.
The shooting happened after a year of rhetoric 
blaming China for both the origin and spread of the 
coronavirus. During that year, there were multiple 
indictors of increased racism and hate: 58% of Asian 
adults said it was more common for people to express 
racist or racially insensitive views about Asians than 
before the COVID-19 outbreak (Ruiz, Horowitz, & 
Tamir, 2020), and anti-Asian hate crimes increased 
by 73% from 2019 to 2020 (Federal Bureau of Inves-
tigation, 2020). Media increasingly reported on ran-
dom violent attacks on Asians in public spaces with 
each person (e.g., business owner, pro-
fessor, undocumented immigrant, crime 
suspect). Did you find similar patterns to 
our study? Were there differences in the 
types of portrayals you observed? What 
impact might these portrayals have on 
the people reading these stories, and 
might the stories affect some groups dif-
ferently than others?
 3.
 Time t
