Journalism and Advertising 103
assailants blaming Asians for the pandemic or other-
wise expressing hostility toward Asians. For example, 
an Asian American couple was assaulted on a Seattle 
street by a man who proclaimed, “It’s all your fault” 
(Takahama, 2020).
In documenting anti-Asian violence, Ancheta 
(2006) argued that anti-Asian discourse is both racial-
ized and nativistic, which encourages hostility toward 
Asians. The racialization of Asian Americans means 
that all Asians are lumped into one category, despite 
ethnic and cultural differences. Nativism reflects a 
position of being opposed to people of color based on 
the assumption that they are foreign or un-American.
The Perpetual Foreigner in the 
COVID-19 Pandemic
Since labor migration of Asians in the 1800s, White 
Americans have characterized Asians as unassim-
ilable and unworthy of US citizenship. Indeed, the 
Chinese were subject to the only US law prohibit-
ing a specified national or racial-ethnic group from 
entering and settling in the US: the 1882 Chinese 
Exclusion Act (Okihiro, 2010). After the Act passed, 
countless Chinese who had come to the US to work 
the mines and build railroads were driven from their 
homes and killed by mobs or individuals supporting 
White American nationalism and racial exclusivity 
(Lee, 1999).
In the mid-nineteenth century, “yellow peril” dis-
course characterized Chinese and other Asians as infe-
rior and uncivilized people who needed to be expelled 
from the US (Ono & Pham, 2009). Newspaper edito-
rials, songs, fictional stories, and later, films, television, 
and comics constructed images of Asians as threats 
to Americans, American jobs, and American morals.
Asian Americans are still often seen as foreign, 
fueling a sense that Asians are perpetual foreigners – 
the same as Asians in Asia, even for those whose fam-
ilies have lived in the US for generations (Nakayama, 
1988; Tuan, 1998). As Darling-Hammond et al. (2020) 
found, during the COVID-19 pandemic, conservative 
media outlets and political figures used stigmatizing 
language for Asians; this language led to increased 
beliefs about Asian Americans as perpetual foreigners. 
It is important to examine this language in the con-
text of the history of discourse on Asian Americans 
as perpetual foreigners because the increase in hate 
crimes against Asians in the US may signal a link 
between such discourse and anti-Asian violence.
In this essay, I use critical discourse analysis to 
trace the perpetual foreigner belief and show how it 
contributes both to media discourse around Asian 
Americans as unworthy of American citizenship and 
to the increased anti-Asian violence during the pan-
demic. Media discourse plays a significant role in dis-
seminating ideas to audiences (Darling-Hammond  
et al., 2020). News media such as television news and 
newspapers often provide valuable information for 
audiences to use in making decisions about their lives. 
Social media, on the other hand, can easily circulate 
and amplify discourse about Asians that has no basis 
in fact or reality. Critical discourse analysis (CDA) can 
help us understand how media discourse can create 
representations and meanings that can become the 
impetus for action.
The study of discourse at its most basic is the 
study of language use (Tannen, Hamilton, & Schif-
frin, 2018). Scholars using CDA extend that to include 
both “linguistic and non-linguistic social practices 
and ideological assumptions that together construct 
or reinforce power or racism” (2018, p. 1). I use CDA 
to examine pandemic media discourse about Asians 
because it makes visible not only the structures of 
power and control in language but also language’s 
impact on how people perceive Asians during the pan-
demic. I couple this with a historical approach placing 
pandemic era discourse within a history of discourse 
defining Asians in the US as threats and as foreigners 
undeserving of American citizenship and rights. One 
of the most important contributions of CDA is that it 
can show how social power is manifested, distributed, 
and maintained throughout society over time. In the 
case of pandemic discourse about Asians, the racial 
order of subordinating Asian Americans through rhet-
oric manifests in harassment and violence. We can 
study this discourse in visual or verbal texts. I focus 
on media texts, where meaning is produced and circu-
lated to mass audiences.
Researchers can use multiple discursive strategies 
or plans of practice as tools in a historical CDA. Here 
I apply three discursive strategies identified by Reisigl 
and Wodak (2016): nomination, predication, and argu-
mentation. Reisigl and Wodak effectively used these 

104 Content
strategies to analyze climate change discourse, and I 
adapt them to study pandemic and perpetual foreigner 
discourses. Nomination strategies name and refer to 
how people, objects, phenomena, events, processes, 
and actions are related to a phenomenon, in this case, 
the COVID-19 pandemic. Predication strategies express 
negative and positive characteristics, qualities, and 
features attributed to social actors, objects, phenom-
ena/events, and processes. Argumentation strategies 
are the arguments, such as claims of truth, employed 
in these discourses and used to justify negative and 
positive attributes. An ideal historical CDA includes a 
large-scale collection of data and context. My analysis 
is on a smaller scale to show how discursive strate-
gies are deployed in discourse to create meaning 
that is consumed and interpreted by audiences. Like  
Darling-Hammond et al. (2020), I focus on conserv-
ative politicians and media outlets because of the 
increasing stigmatizing language since the start of the 
pandemic toward Asian Americans that is amplified 
in conservative media. As Darling-Hammond et al. 
found, when conservative media engaged in these 
discursive strategies of discourse, it contributed to the 
perception that Asian Americans are less American, 
or perpetual foreigners.
Nomination Strategies: The “Chinese Virus” 
and “Kung Flu”
Nomination strategies occur when the phenome-
non of interest is named, labeled, or linguistically 
identified. At the start of 2020, a novel coronavirus 
was identified as spreading rapidly and hospitaliz-
ing and killing a significant number of Chinese. The 
virus spread globally with the first case reported in 
the US on January 18. Media reports often included 
stigmatizing language connecting the virus to China, 
and the World Health Organization (WHO) soon 
explicitly recommended that people call the virus 
“COVID-19,” not the “Wuhan Virus,” “Chinese  
Virus,” or “Asian Virus” (WHO, 2020, p. 2). The 
WHO’s statement advocated non-stigmatizing lan-
guage because terms such as the ones it listed can 
perpetuate stereotypes and create assumptions 
about the disease.
Despite this directive, on March 8, 2020, Repub-
lican Representative Paul A. Gosar (Arizona) tweeted 
that he had contracted the “Wuhan Virus.” Two days 
later, prominent conservative activist Charlie Kirk 
tweeted a call to build a border wall to stop the spread 
of the “China Virus.” On March 16, President Don-
ald Trump tweeted a statement including the phrase 
“Chinese Virus.” Following this tweet, the #chinesev-
irus hashtag took off on Twitter. A flood of tweets 
used the hashtag, and as Hwsen et al. (2021) found, 
tweets with #chinesevirus were more likely to express 
anti-Asian sentiment than tweets with the neutral 
#covid19. Tweets with such sentiment often included 
other racist hashtags, such as #bateatingchinese,  
#yellowmanfever, #chopstickchins, and #chinkflu, as 
well as anti-immigrant sentiment and conspiracy the-
ories (e.g., #wuhancoverup). Hwsen et al. concluded 
that Trump’s tweet marked the turning point for anti-
Asian sentiment. Meanwhile, in public, Trump contin-
ued to refer to the virus as “Chinese Virus” and “Kung 
flu,” a play on kung fu, a Chinese martial art.
This nomination strategy of naming persons 
and phenomena parallels how early American media 
accused Chinese and other Asian immigrants of bring-
ing disease and immorality to the US. Publisher William 
Randolph Hearst often used the term “yellow peril” to 
refer to Asians in his newspapers. In the early 1900s, 
newspapers complained of “Hindu Hordes” in the US 
who were “dirty, diseased” and “not fit to become a 
citizen” (Lee, 2002, p. 45). Just as contemporary tweets 
used hashtags to racialize various Asian ethnicities into 
a generalized racial category, American newspapers 
and political figures after the 1882 Chinese Exclusion 
Act warned of an “Oriental invasion” from China, 
Japan, and India that would bring prostitution and 
disease (Lee, 2002). These immigrants were consid-
ered racially unassimilable and could never become 
Americans. This belief was codified in the 1922 Ozawa 
v. the United States case. Takao Ozawa, a Japanese man 
raised and educated in the US, requested citizenship 
and was denied. Although the Naturalization Act of 
1790 allowed “free white persons” to become natural-
ized citizens, the Supreme Court ruled that it did not 
apply to Ozawa because even though he was light-
skinned, he was not a White person; he wasn’t Cauca-
sian. These and other events show that Asians in the 
US have long been constructed as the perpetual for-
eigners who do not deserve US citizenship. By identi-
fying how political influencers name Asian Americans 


Journalism and Advertising 105
and phenomena such as the COVID-19 virus, we can 
see how names shape public attitudes and opinions 
about Asians and Asian Americans – in this case, 
fomenting anti-Asian sentiment.
Predication Strategies: “Dishonesty” and 
“Corruption”
The predication strategy attributes negative and 
positive traits to social actors, objects, phenomena/
events, and processes. In an interview with Sean 
Hannity on Fox News on March 12, 2020, Sena-
tor Tom Cotton (Arkansas) said that “China has 
unleashed this plague on the entire world through 
their dishonesty and their lack of transparency and 
corruption” (Cotton, 2020). He later repeated the 
claim on his Twitter account. Sean Hannity also 
stated later that month, “Their months-long cov-
erup is now causing death and destruction and car-
nage all over the world… People all over the world 
suffering and dying as a result of these lies” (Chiu, 
2020). From the beginning of the pandemic, political 
influencers negatively characterized China’s role in 
the spread of the virus.
Applying the predication strategy, the social 
actors named in these quotes are China and people all 
over the world. The qualities that Cotton attributed to 
China were dishonesty, lack of transparency, and cor-
ruption. Hannity described people all over the world 
as suffering and dying. The discursive qualifications by 
Cotton and Hannity las the foundation for their justi-
fication about China’s involvement. They used logic 
that connected discourse about China to discourse 
about death. When these negative traits are attrib-
uted to China, China is then deemed dangerous and 
untrustworthy.
Again, the US has a long history of discourse 
describing Asians as foreign, unworthy of citizenship, 
and unassimilable. Besides the 1882 Chinese Exclu-
sion Act, the 1875 Page Law which banned prostitutes 
was primarily used to prevent Chinese women immi-
grants from settling in the US. Lee (2002) described 
how, during this time, political leaders and newspapers 
attributed negative characteristics to Chinese and Jap-
anese as “unwelcome invasions,” “undesirables,” and 
“diseased” (p. 41). Predication strategies that charac-
terize Asian Americans as immoral and job stealers 
contribute to discourse of them as non-American. As 
perpetual foreigners, despite many having deep multi- 
generational roots in the US, Asian Americans have 
been viewed as the same as Asians. The man who 
beat the Seattle Asian American couple and claimed 
that it (presumably the virus) was their fault connected 
the discourse about China and the pandemic with the 
discourse about Asian Americans as perpetual for -
eigners. “Words matter,” said community advocate 
John C. Yang (PBS NewsHour, 2021), commenting on 
the increase of anti-Asian violence since the start of 
the pandemic.
Argumentation Strategies: “Enormous  
Evidence”
Argumentation strategies use arguments, such as 
claims of truth, in discourses and are used to jus-
tify negative and positive attributes. As Secretary of 
State in the Trump administration, Mike Pompeo 
had one of the highest appointments in the cabinet. 
His role was to advise the president and carry out 
the president’s foreign affair policies. Thus, when 
Pompeo spoke, his message came from a place 
of authority. A few months into the pandemic, he 
stated in a television interview:
there’s enormous evidence that that’s where 
this began. We have said from the beginning 
that this was a virus that originated in Wuhan, 
China…Remember, China has a history of 
infecting the world, and they have a history of 
running sub-standard laboratories. These are 
not the first times that we have had the world 
exposed to viruses as a result of failures in a 
Chinese lab.
(Basu, 2020)
In his argument, Pompeo claimed that laboratories in  
China infected the world. The conclusion rule in 
argumentation strategy says that if an authority 
figure says X, then X is a claim of truth. Therefore, 
Pompeo as an authority figure presents as truth the 
claim that China infected the world. Pompeo draws 
on his credibility. His claim leaves no other possi-
bility for the virus’ origins. In a historical context, 
Pompeo’s argument of China infecting the world 

106 Content
reinforces prior claims that Asian immigrants were 
diseased and a yellow peril.
Arguments that are not based in sound logic 
should not be trusted and certainly should not be used 
to guide policy. However, in some cases they have 
been, at times with devastating effects. For example, 
after the bombing of Pearl Harbor during World War 
II, the leader of the Western Defense Command sub-
mitted a report that argued for the incarceration of all 
Japanese Americans. This report by Lt. General John 
L. DeWitt claimed, without evidence, that thousands 
of Japanese Americans along the West Coast were 
indoctrinated by and loyal to the Japanese emperor. 
President Franklin D. Roosevelt used the argument to 
justify the internment of 120,000 Japanese Americans 
under Executive Order 9066. Think back to the previ-
ously mentioned claims by Senator Cotton and Sean 
Hannity about China being dishonest and involved in 
a coverup. At the time, Cotton and Hannity offered 
no evidence. They used their positions of authority 
to establish credibility and support their statements 
that China lied and spread the deadly virus – much 
like DeWitt’s report painted all Japanese Americans as 
disloyal, dangerous, and in need of removal to intern-
ment camps. Such arguments, relying on stereotypes 
rather than evidence, can produce harmful real-life 
consequences.
Engaging in and Challenging Discourses
During the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic, 
political influencers and leaders participated in 
discourse about the virus. This discourse named 
the disease “Chinese virus,” “Kung flu,” and other 
racially derogatory terms. It was then qualified with 
predications such as “dishonesty,” “corruption,” 
“lack of transparency,” “destruction,” “suffering,” 
and “carnage.” These nominations and predications 
became part of the argumentation structure of the 
leadership and supporting party of the most pow-
erful country in the world, and the discourse was 
further circulated and amplified in news media and 
social media. Simultaneously, anti-Asian sentiment 
and violence increased; Asian Americans were 
scapegoated for causing and spreading the virus. 
This discourse and resulting sentiment add to the 
long history characterizing Asians as perpetual 
foreigners and un-American, and subjecting Asians 
to violence and exclusions.
By conducting critical discourse analysis with 
a historical approach, we can see the power media 
discourse has had in shaping racial experience in 
the US. But we can change racist discourse. One 
way to do so is to support and amplify alternative 
voices. Several Asian American political leaders 
who have spoken out in the media against anti-
Asian hate include Vice President Kamala Harris; 
Representatives Ro Khanna, Ted Lieu, and Mark 
Takano; Senator Tammy Duckworth; and many oth-
ers. Social media allows us to exchange and discuss 
ideas. We can challenge fallacies about the virus 
and about Asians. We can support Asian American 
media organizations as alternatives to dominant 
mainstream media. Finally, we can recognize that 
words matter and have consequences.

4.4: FRAMING THE ENBRIDGE OIL 
PIPELINE #3 PROJECT IN INDIGENOUS 
AND MAINSTREAM LOCAL 
NEWSPAPERS
Emily Riewestahl, Emilee Baker, Srividya 
Ramasubramanian, and Laura Joy “ Anangokwe” 
Merchant
1
This essay examines media framing of the Enbridge 
Line #3 Pipeline Project in Indigenous newspapers 
and mainstream local newspapers. It highlights 
the importance of including and honoring Indige-
nous perspectives, which are often overlooked and 
underrepresented in mainstream news media.
Mainstream media and public discourse rarely dis-
cuss issues facing Indigenous communities, and if 
so, issues are often framed through a colonial lens 
(Walker & Walter, 2018). Although Indigenous com-
munities are often major stakeholders in issues of 
pipeline construction, media and scholarship rarely 
explore how Indigenous communities frame pipe-
line construction and environmental protection  
(Estes & Dhillon, 2019). Failing to cover issues fac-
ing Indigenous communities, such as pipeline devel-
opment projects, signifies that the “professional 
news industry did not believe this struggle merited 

108 Content
coverage” (Moore, 2019, p. 26). Such absence and 
underrepresentation of important issues in the pub-
lic sphere conveys powerful messages that Indige-
nous people and perspectives are not respected or 
valued.
This essay looks at media coverage of one key 
issue affecting Indigenous communities in Minnesota 
and Wisconsin: the Enbridge Line #3 pipeline pro-
ject. Although rarely covered by national news media, 
local news media covered the project from its 2014 
announcement. The pipeline is approximately 1,000 
miles long and transports 760,000 barrels of oil per 
day. It directly affects numerous local Indigenous com-
munities and has been the site of ongoing resistance by 
communities against its construction.
The Indigenous population in the surrounding 
area of Line #3 primarily consists of Anishinaabe or 
Ojibwe people. They are often referred to by the gov-
ernment as Lake Superior Bands of Chippewa Indi-
ans or Lake Superior Chippewa Bands.
2 Anishinaabe 
people have been residing on both ceded territory and 
tribal lands since the first treaties of this region were 
signed in the 1800s, ceding the lands to the US gov-
ernment. These land cessions were both a tragedy and 
blessing for the Anishinaabe. They lost the land from 
a non-Indigenous perspective but retained their inher-
ent rights to the land through guaranteed treaty rights, 
which allow the Anishinaabe to hunt, fish, and gather 
on ceded territory even off-reservation (a right many 
Indigenous people in the United States did not retain 
after colonization). Since long before land cessions, 
treaties, and creation of reservations, Anishinaabe 
people and other Indigenous peoples have referred to 
their homelands as Turtle Island, a term which reflects 
a complex system of beliefs passed down through oral 
tradition. The Anishinaabe call their oral tradition adi-
zookan (Child, 2012).
Indigenous Newspapers versus 
Mainstream Newspapers
We selected seven newspapers within the vicinity of 
the pipeline route, including four local Anishinaabe 
newspapers: Nahgahchiwanong Dibahjimowinan 
(Fond Du Lac Band), Inaajimowin (Mille Lacs Band), 
DeBahJiMon (Leech Lake Band), and Anishinaabe 
Today (White Earth Band) and three mainstream 
local Minnesotan newspapers: Duluth News Tribune, 
Crookston Daily Times, and Grand Rapids Herald-
 
R
eview. We analyzed news articles, opinion pieces, 
notices, and letters to the editors. The mainstream 
local newspapers were accessed via the News-
Bank database, and the Indigenous newspapers 
were accessed through archives on the papers’ 
websites. We selected articles containing the words 
“Enbridge” and “Line 3” from March 2014 to March 
2021. This resulted in 621 articles from mainstream 
newspapers (published daily) and 95 articles from 
Indigenous newspapers (published monthly).
Our qualitative approach involved conducting a 
close reading of each article to identify the key frames 
evident in coverage of Line #3. Media frames refer to 
the ways that certain aspects of our perceived reality 
are packaged into media messages that encourage 
certain interpretations over others (Entman, 1993). 
These frames direct readers’ attention toward cer -
tain costs, benefits, stakeholders, outcomes, and 
judgments and away from others. For example, Ernt 
(2020) found that environmental, political, and eco-
nomic frames dominated mainstream media framing 
of Line #3. Although we also observed these frames in 
our sample, our inclusion of Anishinaabe perspectives 
revealed that competing media frames stemmed from 
key differences in ways of knowing among local non-
 
Indig
enous and Indigenous communities. We focus on 
three competing frames: environment (kin vs. com-
modity), security (future vs. present), and resistance 
(protectors vs. disruptors).
Environment: Kin vs. Commodity
Environmental protection is the dominant media 
frame in Anishinaabe newspapers. This frame 
reflects Indigenous worldviews about the spiritual 
role of nature in community, where land, animals, 
and other natural resources are considered kin, 
rather than a commodity. Environmental concerns 
primarily focused on the potential for oil spills and 
lack of removal of the old pipeline, which could 
cause irreversible damage to ceded territories and 
reservation land. These concerns are not only 
about protecting life-sustaining natural resources 
such as water and wild rice but also about spiritual 
connection to the region. Unlike mainstream local 


Journalism and Advertising 109
newspapers, Anishinaabe newspapers often wrote 
in-depth on Indigenous perspectives about connec-
tions and kinship with nature. Boyd wrote,
The Anishinaabe connection to land is inter -
woven with spiritual beliefs and the under -
standing that the land, landscape, plants, and 
animals are all alive and have their own spirits. 
The Anishinaabe people have recognized these 
manidoo for as long as they have lived in this 
region, and though these things are intangible 
and unquantifiable, they are an imperative truth 
to Anishinaabe people. The people must care 
for the manidoo who, in turn, care for them, and 
it must be ensured that the ecosystem around 
these beings not be diminished. 
(2018, p. 6)
Perspectives of kinship in Anishinaabe newspapers 
support the concepts of commitment and care 
across past, present, and future generations. Anish-
inaabe newspapers often elaborated on concepts 
that were rare, or even absent, from local main-
stream news reporting on Line #3.
Anishinaabe newspapers discussed topics such 
as the cultural significance of Manoomin (wild rice), 
Traditional Ecological Knowledge, land-based knowl-
edge systems, and the concept of other than human 
animate beings. Rather than seeing nature and non- 
living things as “objects,” Anishinaabemowin (the lan-
guage of the Anishinaabe) sees them as animate and 
sentient beings with important roles both spiritually 
and within ecological systems. Anishinaabemowin and 
Anishinaabe beliefs also often consider many animals 
to have familial ties to humans; they are sometimes 
considered relatives or kin. From this perspective, it 
becomes clear why Anishinaabe communities take on 
the role of protectors of the environment: their value 
systems prioritize kinship over economic profits.
One article described Indigenous communities: 
“We Anishinaabe are a people of the water; we have 
traveled by it and lived by its gifts for as long as we 
can remember” (Boyd, 2017a, p. 12). This example 
illustrates kinship across generations past, present, 
and future; including water as kin further supporting 
environmental protection as the dominant frame. This 
explains why, even though Indigenous communities 
face high rates of poverty and unemployment (Office 
of Minority Health, 2021), many – but not all – 
 Indig
enous leaders refuse to exchange land or natu-
ral resources for economic gain. To put it simply “Y ou 
do not sell your relative” (Estes & Dhillon, 2019, p. 3). 
Some leaders have shifted their perspectives on kin-
ship due to colonialism and support the economic 
growth brought by pipeline developments to their 
communities. Overall, Anishinaabe news articles pro-
vided much more in-depth details and context about 
Anishinaabe worldviews or “ways of knowing” than 
mainstream news stories, which guide their relation-
ship with the environment.
Mainstream newspapers primarily discussed the 
pipeline project as an economic opportunity, fram-
ing the land as a valuable resource to be exploited 
and extracted to sustain human life. Economic secu-
rity was emphasized through references to “family-  
supporting jobs” and “boosting local economies.” 
Mainstream conceptualization of kinship generally 
includes immediate and extended family but not often 
include the environment. Although some mainstream 
articles mentioned that environmental and Indigenous 
groups resisted the pipeline, citing that the pipeline was 
an environmental risk and would breach treaty rights, 
they rarely discussed these issues in-depth or in rela-
tion to Anishinaabe values of kinship and care. These 
divergent perspectives on kinship played an important 
role in framing pipeline projects in terms of environ-
mental protection versus commodification.
Security: Future vs Present
In both types of newspapers, most local stakehold-
ers such as businesses, wildlife groups, non-profits, 
community members, and climate change activists 
advocated for the outcome they thought would best 
secure their future. There was a comparable sense 
of commitment to security in both types of news-
papers, whether through environmental protection 
or economic security. However, the future was dis-
cussed differently in mainstream and Indigenous 
newspapers. Mainstream newspapers generally 
were more present-focused, focusing on economic 
opportunities of the present or the near future to 
help sustain the next generation. Anishinaabe news-
papers were more future-focused, showing how 

110 Content
the pipeline could affect the environment for many 
future generations.
Mainstream present-oriented coverage framed 
the pipeline as an “economic lifeline” securing Min-
nesota’s future in economic development through 
the short-term process of “replacing” Line #3. 
Some articles mentioned the lack of economic 
opportunities in the region, expressing excitement 
that large projects such as Line #3 could bring 
money back into a region that has faced economic 
hardship. Mainstream news stories often empha-
sized economic security through an immediate 
increase in local jobs, local spending, infrastructure 
development, connection to local elections (as a 
political platform), and economic safety through 
environmental safety (i.e., integrity digs). Main-
stream newspapers framed Line #3 as constructing 
technological advancement, future security through 
economic development, and job security for the 
present. Job security and energy delivery were dis-
cussed as necessary outcomes, establishing security 
for the present generation (Slater, 2021). Economic 
security was mentioned in Anishinaabe as well, but 
significantly less and generally focused on increased 
jobs for all local communities. Mainstream newspa-
pers discussed security within the present moment 
for “all people” but rarely made connections to spe-
cific time periods or communities.
Anishinaabe newspapers discussed security and 
futurity through very different discourse than main-
stream newspapers did. Some writers in Anishinaabe 
newspapers recognized the commitment to jobs and 
local economy stimulation but urged community 
members and governmental agencies to acknowledge 
life beyond the present generation and include holis-
tic well-being for all people (i.e., our collective legacy). 
LaDuke wrote, “We understand your commitment to 
labor and jobs, and respectfully request that you look 
beyond a dirty pipeline during a pandemic, and make, 
instead a legacy of hope, courage and well-being for all 
of our people” (2020, p. 5).
In Anishinaabe newspapers, future generations 
were discussed frequently, for example, referring to 
“children,” “grandchildren,” and “future generations.” 
The Seventh Generation prophecy and the Anish-
inaabe concept of the Seventh Generation Earth 
Ethics dictates that thought should be given to seven 
generations ahead. This creates an expanded context 
for decision-making, especially for environmental pol-
icy (Loew, 2014). Boyd discussed the Anishinaabe 
Cumulative Impact Assessment (ACIA): “The ACIA 
takes a long view, historically and seven generations 
ahead, and gives honor to our Nibi, our water, and 
those as a first medicine” (2017b, p. 6). The idea of 
Seventh Generation Earth Ethics creates a long-term 
view into securing a future for all kin, including the 
land, water, and environment, and acknowledges his-
torical perspectives and future impacts.
Resistance: Protectors vs Disruptors
A common theme throughout Anishinaabe news-
papers was resistance, which framed pipeline resis-
tors as protectors, rather than as disruptors. Some 
community members resisted the pipeline and 
pointed out the lack of respect for Indigenous per -
spectives in the regulatory process. Anishinaabe 
newspaper articles referred to the “failings of the 
State regulatory process,” noting when regulatory 
bodies did not adequately include Anishinaabe 
people and worldviews in the regulatory pro-
cesses. As Kemper, an Assistant Mille Lacs Tribal 
Historic Preservation Officer said, “Our voices, our 
spirituality, our connection to these things doesn’t 
fit into their rules and guidelines” (Tribal Cultural 
Surveys, 2017). From this perspective, the checks 
and balances set in place by regulatory bodies 
were seen as lacking the sense of utmost care and 
respect for the environment and Indigenous per -
spectives on the relationship between humans and 
the natural world.
The ACIA is built around the understanding 
that Indigenous communities have fundamen-
tally different values than those of the domi-
nant corporate culture. Anishinaabe people are 
connected to the land in ways that the Minne-
sota state government doesn’t understand and 
can’t quantify. 
(Boyd, 2018, p. 6)
Given the lack of acknowledgement and integra-
tion of Indigenous worldviews into the regulatory 
processes, Anishinaabe communities often feel 


Journalism and Advertising 111
misunderstood or disrespected. Rather than simply 
complying with regulatory processes, they protect 
the environment by resisting both pipeline devel-
opment and regulatory processes. This resistance 
is through both grassroots protest and the legal 
system. “The role of a tribal government is to fight 
these matters through the courts and administra-
tive processes, on a government-to-government 
basis, which is ultimately where these matters are 
won and lost” (“Band Continues,” 2021). Ultimately, 
what many Anishinaabe community members and 
leaders are asking for is respect for their tribal sover-
eignty, their inherent right to assert legal jurisdiction 
that affects its people and land,
We respect the Minnesota government and 
hope they share the sentiment and respect 
our Tribal Sovereignty when we say loud and 
clear the position of the Leech Lake Band of 
Ojibwe: we want pipelines to end and we will 
not allow another oil pipeline to be laid in our 
Reservation. 
(Jackson, 2018, p. 2)
In mainstream news, regulatory processes were 
often perceived as robust; therefore, people who did 
not comply with or trust in the process were framed 
as disruptors. Some community members thought 
that the process was too time-consuming and repet-
itive, often mentioning how drawn out the regula-
tory process can be. Therefore, appeals brought by 
Indigenous communities were framed as a waste 
of time, essentially delaying the inevitable. In such 
articles, it appeared that pipeline supporters, includ-
ing Enbridge, wanted Indigenous communities and 
others resisting the process to simply comply with 
the regulatory bodies. For example, one reader of 
the Duluth News Tribune queried, “I’m sure all these 
protesters need these things also. Why in the world 
would they fight against things we all need? How 
do they think roads get built?” (2019). Notably, in 
mainstream newspapers, especially pieces writ-
ten by Enbridge representatives, relationships with 
local Indigenous communities were often framed 
positively, using terms such as “working with,” “col-
laborating,” and “consulting with.” However, when 
Indigenous communities were not complying or 
were actively resisting, they were framed as “disrup-
tors” through warnings that those involved in illegal 
activities will be “prosecuted to the fullest extent of 
the law.”
Building a Path Forward
Our research points to the importance of incor -
porating Indigenous perspectives in journalism, 
media education, and regulatory processes. The 
mainstream news media we studied often omitted 
or oversimplified Indigenous perspectives. They 
often did not explain the reasons why Indigenous 
communities are committed to defending the earth 
or acknowledge pipeline development processes 
as an extension of colonization. Minimizing Indig-
enous perspectives as solely environmental gener -
ates a gap in both public awareness of Indigenous 
perspectives and people’s understanding of what is 
at stake for the future.
Journalists and media storytellers from all 
backgrounds must respect multiple worldviews, 
including those approaching the environment with 
a sense of kinship, reciprocity, and care, ultimately 
recognizing all are related. Journalists should ele-
vate, support, and highlight Indigenous journalists 
and news organizations, to inform the public of 
the variety of Indigenous perspectives. Audiences 
should diversify their news media diet by reading 
Indigenous news sources such as indiancountry-
today.com and thecirclenews.org to gain a deeper 
understanding of Indigenous perspectives. Scholars 
should support collaborations that address issues 
faced by Indigenous and marginalized communities, 
which are often understudied, misrepresented, or 
even absent from scholarship. Understanding and 
respecting Indigenous perspectives, in news report-
ing and beyond, is a precondition for collaborative 
dialogue and action that could lead to solutions to 
protect everyone’s kin.
NOTES
 1.  W e express gratitude to Ashley Sierra of the Minnesota 
Historical Society and Gary Padrta of the White Earth 
Reservation, who assisted in our archival research 
for newspapers. We also thank Maleeha Bhadki and 
Maitreyee Shilpa Kishor for proofreading and providing 
feedback on early versions of this essay.

Superior Bands of Chippewa Indians and “Indige-
nous” when we are speaking about First Nation Peo-
ples of the United States and across the globe. The 
term “Chippewa” was a settler mispronunciation of 
the Anishinaabemowin word “Ojibwe” and is still used 
by the federal government today, as reflected in legal 
documents, treaties, and tribal names. Although there is 
no universally agreed-upon way of labeling Indigenous 
people, it is often best to refer to specific communities 
by name, when possible, to recognize the unique culture 
and practices of each community (Y ounging, 2018).

It’s Your Turn: What Do You Think? What 
Will You Find?
 1.
 T
hink of a community you are aware 
of but is unfamiliar to you. Write down 
your beliefs, perceptions, feelings, and 
attitudes toward them. Now locate a few 
community media sources such as web-
sites, newspapers, social media groups, 
and community events. Analyze what is 
being shared in these outlets and how it is 
being shared. Keep detailed notes about

4.5: EXPLORING MEDIA FRAMING OF 
TRANSGENDER POLITICIANS IN THE US
Newly Paul
The author explores how media have framed trans-
gender politicians. The analysis focuses on three 
groundbreaking trans politicians: Danica Roem, 
Stephanie Byers, and Sarah McBride.
Although LGBTQ rights have gained increased 
attention and prominence in the US since the 2000s, 
the election of LGBTQ political candidates at vari-
ous local, state, and national level offices has been a 
relatively slower process (Everitt & Tremblay, 2020). 
As of June 2021, there were 986 known out LGBTQ 
elected officials in the country, who made up 0.19% 
of the total number of elected officials in the US 
(Out for America, 2021). Although that percentage 
is miniscule, there was an overall increase of 17% 
from 2020. There are more trans women in office 
than trans men. As of 2021, 36 trans women hold 
elected office, up from four in 2017. In comparison, 
a total of two trans men held political office in 2017, 
and in 2021, this number rose to five (Out for Amer-
ica, 2021).
The slow but visible increase in representation of 
the LGBTQ community in politics is a result of factors 
such as improved media coverage, laws granting equal 
rights to LGBTQ community members, and a shift in 
public attitudes. For example, in 2021, 70% of Ameri-
cans agreed that same-sex marriages should be legal, 
up from 27% in 1996 (Gallup, n.d.). Despite the overall 
progress in LGBTQ rights, members of this commu-
nity continue to face challenges when seeking political 
office. These include stereotypical media coverage, 
negative public perceptions about their electability, 
and a lack of campaign funds.
News media are one of the main ways of inform-
ing people about the world, but at times (as other 
readings in this book have shown) this information 
is stereotypical. For example, political news tends to 
associate Latinx people with immigration (Gershon, 
2012) and Black candidates with racialized issues 
(McIlwain, 2011). Women candidates are portrayed 
as empathetic and as experts in dealing with childcare 
and women’s issues, whereas men are portrayed as 
tough and as experts in handling foreign policy and 
trade issues (Swers, 2007). As a result of these stereo-
typical portrayals, voters associate women and minor-
itized candidates with a certain narrow set of issues 
and characteristics, which affects voter choice (Bauer, 
2020). In the same way, journalistic narratives could 
determine what it means to be a transgender political 
candidate. If media coverage associates trans candi-
dates with a limited set of issues and characteristics, 
voters’ perceptions could be influenced.
Media framing of people or issues involves high-
lighting certain aspects of “perceived reality” (Entman, 
1993, p. 52) and thus focusing on particular points 
of view. Journalistic frames arise out of journalistic 
norms and routines, including what makes a story 
newsworthy and societal beliefs—the ideas that are 
most prevalent in public opinion and institutions such 
as law and religious organizations.

114 Content
Recent research on media coverage of the 
LGBTQ community has found that, overall, news 
coverage has improved from the 2000s onward. 
There are fewer instances of news articles framing 
trans people as deceptive, using pronouns incor -
rectly, and sensationalizing gender reassignment 
surgeries (Capuzza, 2016). Y et, news stories still 
tend to focus on trans people’s gender as their most 
newsworthy and defining characteristic. Stories on 
trans people tend to focus on a handful of issues 
such as the so-called bathroom bill (which deter -
mines access to gender-segregated public bath-
rooms based on the sex assigned to a person at 
birth). When media coverage focuses on LGBTQ 
candidates’ past political activism related to LGBTQ 
issues, it further portrays them as having a partisan 
agenda, which can lead voters to make assumptions 
about their issue positions.
The common themes that underlie media cov-
erage of LGBTQ candidates since the 2000s include 
portraying them as a threat to the norm, as scandalous 
and devious, as history-making candidates because 
they are openly gay politicians, and as representa-
tives of LGBTQ communities and interests (Everitt & 
Camp, 2009). When LGBTQ politicians are in relation-
ships and have children or families, they are framed 
as respectable, and the non-heteronormative nature of 
their relationship is considered unproblematic. How-
ever, when they are single or their relationship status is 
unknown, there could be speculation and scandalous 
coverage (Capuzza & Spencer, 2015).
Framing Roem, Byers, and McBride
Keeping this background in mind, I analyzed how 
the media framed three recent trans political 
 c
andidates—Danica Roem, Stephanie Byers, and 
Sarah McBride—during their campaigns. Roem 
(Democrat) is a member of the Virginia House of 
Delegates and in 2017 became the first openly trans 
person to be elected to a state legislature. In 2020, 
Democrat candidate Byers became the first trans 
person to be elected to the Kansas Legislature and 
is the first trans Native American elected to office 
in the US. McBride, a Democrat representing Del-
aware, was elected in 2021 as the first trans state 
senator in the US.
My analysis is based on a sample generated 
by searching Newsbank (a database that archives 
information from a variety of media sources) for 
all stories containing the terms “Danica Roem,” 
“Stephanie Byers,” and “Sarah McBride,” published 
from January to December of the year they got 
elected. I adopted an inductive approach, exam-
ining the coverage for recurring themes and key-
words. The three main frames I found are: unique 
candidate, competent candidate, and candidate 
with mass appeal.
Unique Candidates
Research has shown that when news coverage 
frames candidates as unique because of their phys-
ical characteristics, life experiences, or background, 
voters tend to think of them as outsiders to pol-
itics (Banducci, Gidengil & Everitt, 2012). Despite 
changing social norms, homosexuality is still con-
sidered a unique element with a strong news value 
and is often the subject of tabloidization. The nov-
elty of homosexuality can be attributed to same-sex 
relationships being illegal and taboo until not very 
long ago, and the legal age of consent changing 
over the years (Smith, 2012). Framing candidates 
as unique on account of their gender or sexuality 
inadvertently pushes the idea of the male, hetero-
sexual candidate as the norm (Gidengil & Everitt, 
2003). Mentions of an LGBTQ candidate as unique 
and the candidacy as historic bring sexuality to the 
forefront and prime people to think about the candi-
date primarily through the gender lens (Lalancette &  
Tremblay, 2019).
Prior research indicates that media coverage of 
LGBTQ candidates tends to focus on specific aspects 
of their lives such as their experiences in coming out 
or transitioning. Although explicit homophobia is 
uncommon, media coverage stereotypes gay men as 
feminine and as aligned only with LGBTQ issues. Cov-
erage tends to promote heteronormativity by focusing 
on the candidate’s family or highlighting elements of 
their lifestyle that are different from that of average 
voters. Gay men who are out or in stable relationships 
are not framed as threatening compared to others who 
are in secret relationships (Smith, 2012). The latter are 
framed as scandalous or threatening.


Journalism and Advertising 115
My analysis revealed much of the same. All 
three candidates were framed as unique, primarily on 
account of their sexuality. Danica Roem was described 
using phrases such as “the first transgender lawmaker,” 
“the only openly transgender person in a state legis-
lature anywhere in America,” “one of very few in the 
nation,” as having “made history,” and as “a trailblazer.” 
The body of the stories, as well as the headlines, high-
lighted her trans identity rather than her accomplish-
ments. A New Y ork Times’ opinion column expressed 
surprise and admiration that when a CNN interviewer 
asked Roem to reflect on her historic win, she chose 
to talk about her attempts to ease traffic congestion in 
her constituency, rather than her transgender identity, 
thus (as the columnist argued) denying the interviewer 
the “juicier” part of her life story.
The two other candidates were also framed as 
unique for being trans. Reports about Sarah McBride’s 
victory mentioned that she was the first out transgen-
der woman to work in the White House and the first 
transgender person to speak at a national party con-
vention. Stephanie Byers was described as “the first 
ever trans Native American woman” and “the first 
transgender lawmaker in the entire Midwest.”
In addition to priming gender identity by framing 
the candidates as unique, the articles used a number 
of implicit techniques which drew attention to gender. 
For example, in stories that discussed broader issues 
such as the rise of diverse candidates in American 
politics, the candidates were featured as examples of 
gender diversity. In one such story, Roem was featured 
with a Black trans politician, a Sikh candidate, a Latina, 
a Vietnamese trans woman, and a refugee who was 
running for political office. By highlighting religion, 
ethnicity, and sexuality as unique characteristics, the 
story implicitly reinforced the White, Christian, male 
politician as the norm.
Similarly, stories mentioning the candidates’ 
background and past experiences always included 
information about their sexual identities. Although 
reports mentioned the candidates’ former jobs—
Roem worked as a reporter and was a singer in a 
heavy metal band; Byers was a teacher; and McBride 
was a political activist—their sexuality was featured 
more prominently. Another technique foreground-
ing gender identity was the use of LGBTQ sources 
in articles about the candidates. In-depth features 
on all three candidates tended to feature quotes 
from other LGBTQ people, which further high-
lighted the frame that the candidates were unique 
trans politicians.
Competent Candidates
The media coverage I analyzed framed the three 
trans candidates as acceptable and competent 
candidates based on their service-oriented back-
ground, their honesty, and their ability to connect 
with a larger audience. McBride was described as a 
strong candidate and her election was described as 
a “landmark moment” because she won more than 
90% of the vote. She was portrayed as empathetic 
and caring because she was her husband’s primary 
caregiver when he was fighting cancer. Coverage 
of Roem’s campaign framed her as an ethical and 
hard-working candidate who, unlike other politi-
cians, had avoided negative campaign tactics. She 
was described as an authentic person because she 
advised other politicians to be themselves instead 
of changing their issue positions depending on the 
outcomes they wanted.
On the campaign trail, reporters described Roem 
as an energetic candidate who was competitive, as 
evidenced from her easy win in the primaries and her 
ability to fundraise. Journalists called Roem honest 
and even-tempered. They praised her for not reacting 
angrily when her opponent adopted negative tactics 
toward her such as not calling to concede the elec-
tion, not congratulating her on her victory, repeatedly 
misgendering her, and refusing to debate with her. 
Although her opponent made a big issue of her gen-
der identity, Roem was said to “let his cruelties roll 
off her.” Coverage highlighted her consensus-building 
approach; her background as a reporter was cited as 
the reason for her empathetic and helpful nature as 
well as her extensive knowledge about the area and 
the constituents’ needs.
Roem was framed as an astute and competent 
candidate based on her campaign tactics. In addition 
to her impressive ground game where she and her 
campaign representatives knocked on tens of thou-
sands of doors, news reports mentioned her strategic 
messaging where she avoided using vocabulary such 
as “gender binary” and “fluidity” but used more words 

116 Content
such as “stepmom” which helped her build a connec-
tion with voters.
Coverage for McBride and Byers also highlighted 
their fitness and competitiveness as candidates. 
McBride’s long-standing ties to President Joe Biden’s  
family were mentioned. She had worked on the pres-
ident’s late son Beau Biden’s campaigns for state 
attorney general, and the president himself had writ-
ten the foreword to her memoir. Her background as a 
transgender rights activist and her role in the fight for 
LGBTQ discrimination protections in Delaware were 
also emphasized. Byers’ background as a communi-
cations director for a local LGBTQ organization was 
mentioned, as well as her extensive volunteer work 
with local nonprofits.
Candidates with Mass Appeal
Framing a candidate as aligned with one issue or 
aligned mostly with issues of interest to the LGBTQ 
community can portray the candidate as threat-
ening to heteronormativity and unsuitable in rep-
resenting the general population. Although my 
analysis of media coverage of the three candidates 
established them as strong allies of LGBTQ causes, 
the coverage also implied that the candidates were 
acceptable to a broad cross section of voters. The 
coverage placed the candidates’ wins in a larger 
social context by attributing their success to stra-
tegic issue-based campaigning and changing social 
norms.
Media coverage of Roem praised her for her 
refreshing tactic of focusing on everyday issues in 
her campaign, as compared to other politicians who 
created divisions among voters by picking hot-button 
social issues. Although her opponent’s appeals were 
described as narrow and based solely on gender iden-
tity, Roem’s campaign messages were described as 
“broadly public.” Although her opponent tried to frame 
Roem as a one-issue candidate, media coverage indi-
cated that her platform included issues such as fixing 
traffic congestion that were of interest to the broader 
public. Coverage also praised Roem for running on an 
inclusive platform, instead of sticking to identity issues. 
In contrast, Roem’s opponent was painted as having a 
narrow agenda because he attacked her on her iden-
tity, not on issues.
Media coverage discussed Roem’s support for 
anti-discrimination legislation, her desire to provide 
clean drinking water, and her promises to create a pub-
lic records ombudsman and implement a shield law 
for protecting reporters. Similarly, coverage mentioned 
that McBride’s campaign was focused on issues such 
as health care, education, criminal justice reform, and 
well-paying jobs with good benefits—issues that affect 
all voters.
References to changes in public opinion and the 
growing acceptability of trans candidates also demon-
strated each candidate’s mass appeal. One story men-
tioned that Roem’s victory shows that people trust 
community leaders such as Roem to help them solve 
the issues that affect their day-to-day lives. Impor -
tantly, and atypically, the columnist referred to Roem 
simply as a “community leader,” instead of pointing 
out her uniqueness as a trans person. Some articles 
noted that voters were alienated by the negativity in 
campaigns and wanted to see change. Reporters also 
mentioned changing demographics, the rising number 
of millennials and immigrants, and the changing ideol-
ogy of the voters, indicating that the trans candidates’ 
victories signaled a larger shift in public opinion and an 
acceptability of LGBTQ candidates.
Rethinking Trans Candidates’ Media 
Portrayal
It is important for LGBTQ candidates to be well rep-
resented in politics. The themes I found in this study, 
framing the trans candidates as unique because of 
their transgender status, competent, and having 
mass appeal, indicate that journalists use mostly 
positive frames in covering trans politicians. Over -
all, media reports portrayed the trans candidates 
as competent politicians who worked on building 
consensus by highlighting common ground, com-
mon beliefs, and common life experiences with 
non-LGBTQ voters. Research indicates that LGBTQ 
candidates who have already established their rep-
utation for community service before the media or 
the voting public discovered their sexual orientation 
are more likely to win elections (Everitt & Camp, 
2014). My finding that media coverage of the candi-
dates highlighted their public service background is 
consistent with this. When reporters referenced the 


Journalism and Advertising 117
candidates’ families, their professional backgrounds, 
and their campaigning abilities, they implicitly 
framed the candidates as competent and accept-
able for mainstream audiences in contrast to other 
politicians who were portrayed as being behind the 
times and failing to meet constituents’ needs.
However, not all the themes I found are positive in 
the context of transgender political candidates. When 
candidates’ uniqueness is mostly due to their transgen-
der status, voters are less likely to know about their 
issue platform. My findings indicate that trans people 
still tend to receive trait-based coverage that focuses 
on their gender. Sustained focus on gender can dimin-
ish these candidates’ broad appeal and affect their 
chances of getting elected.
The frames journalists use to discuss disen-
franchised communities can change public opinion. 
Using a gendered lens in news coverage is not always 
limiting, because it can highlight the uniqueness and 
advantages of a candidate. However, we must remem-
ber that sexuality can be used as a tool for oppression. 
When heteronormative standards are projected as the 
norm in politics, representation can appear one-sided. 
Journalists should continue to educate and inform 
themselves to ensure that their coverage does not 
propagate unfair stereotypes.
References

4.6: FRAMING FEMINISM 1
Rebecca Ann Lind and Colleen Salo Aravena
An analysis of news and public affairs content 
reveals that women and feminists are portrayed in 
very different ways. The authors argue that, ulti-
mately, feminists are presented as out of the ordi-
nary, as not quite normal.
To frame something is to make sense of it. Accord-
ing to Gamson (1989, p. 157), “facts have no intrin-
sic meaning. They take on their meaning by being 
embedded in a frame or story line that organizes 
them and gives them coherence, selecting certain 
ones to emphasize while ignoring others.” News sto-
ries include factual elements, but as Gitlin’s analysis 
revealed:
the media were far from mirrors passively 
reflecting facts found in the real world. The 
facts reported were out there in the real world, 
true: out there among others. The media reflec-
tion was more the active, patterned remaking 
performed by mirrors in a fun house.
(1980, p. 29)
Roeh further argued the very process of select-
ing the words to describe an event is value-laden: 
“no author or speaker is free of the necessity to 
choose words, syntax, and order of presentation. 
It does make a difference if ‘friction’ and not ‘dis-
pute’ is chosen” (1981, p. 78). Such differences 
are important because research has shown that 
people’s attitudes and judgments can be affected 
by the media’s framing of issues, especially when 
people lack firsthand knowledge of an issue (Git-
lin, 1980).
So, what about feminism? How do the media 
frame feminism? Do the media even pay attention to 
feminism?
WordLink is a form of computerized network 
analysis (Danowski, 1993), which maps the relation-
ships among words within messages. Because Word-
Link can compute the frequency with which certain 
words, terms, concepts, attitudes, and values are 
associated with feminists, it helps identify the frames 
used to represent feminists. By also looking at how 
often those same words are associated with women 
in general, we can more fully understand the framing 
of feminism and feminists.
Our unit of analysis is the word pair. Because “you 
shall know the meaning of a word by the company it 
keeps,” we can infer the meanings of particular words 
(e.g., “feminism” and “feminists”) by investigating their 
surrounding word context. Using WordLink, we sifted 
through the text and found all words appearing within 
seven words before or after our target words “femi-
nism,” “feminist,” “feminists,” “women,” and “woman.” 
WordLink recorded and counted all of the word pairs, 
which we then compared with the media frames being 
investigated in this study.


Journalism and Advertising 119
The body of text we studied was two and a half 
years’ worth of transcripts of news and public affairs 
programs aired from May 1993 through January 1996 
on ABC, CNN, National Public Radio (NPR), and PBS.
2 
We analyzed every word in every story on every news 
and public affairs program, or just under 136 million 
words.
Our investigation of prior research helped us 
create a set of six frames that guided our analysis. 
We searched the text for evidence of demoniza-
tion, in which feminism and feminists are framed 
as deviant. The personalization and trivialization  
frame focuses on appearance, style, or personal 
qualities. The goals frame reflects attention to civil 
rights, reproductive rights, workplace rights, and 
the goals for equality generally held by feminists. 
The victimization frame reveals feminists as weak 
and vulnerable whereas the agency frame repre-
sents feminists as strong and capable. The site of 
struggle is the final frame, reflecting the variety 
of locations (home, school, religion, work, etc.) of 
feminist activities.
The Frames Revealed
Before addressing the framing of feminists and 
women, we first consider the relatively common 
complaint that women and women’s issues in gen-
eral are neglected in the mass media. We analyzed 
135,759,087 words. The target words “woman” and 
“women” appeared 1,158,756 times, or 0.85% of all 
words. The target words “feminist,” “feminists,” and 
“feminism” appeared 25,139 times, or 0.02% of all 
words. Clearly, feminism continues to receive rela-
tively little attention in the media.
The Demonization Frame. Critics claim femi-
nists are demonized when portrayed in the media as 
crazy, ill-tempered, ugly, man-hating, family-wrecking, 
hairy-legged, bra-burning, radical lesbians. We looked 
through the text for the co-occurrence of such words 
with our target words. Women/woman co-occurred 
with demonizing words 3,287 times, meaning that 
0.28% of all references to women/an appeared in a 
demonizing frame. (Table 4.3.1 presents an overview 
of the results for the first five frames.) Some of the 
most common co-occurrences were women—bad 
(202 appearances), women/an—lesbian/s (184), 
women/an—jerk/s (89), and women/an—bitch/y/
es (87). Feminist/s/ism co-occurred with demonizing 
words 507 times, or 2.02% of all references. The most 
common co-occurrence was feminist/s/ism—radical 
(57 times), followed by militant (13), lesbian/s (12), 
amuck/amok (12), raging (6), and masculine (6). Thus, 
feminists are demonized more often in the media than 
are women.
The Personalization and Trivialization Frame. 
This frame includes attention to personal 
 a
ttributes—appearance, marital status, personal 
habits, or personal style. A focus on style over sub-
stance trivializes people and their positions. Rhode 
(1997) argued that a focus on feminists’ appearance 
is particularly troublesome because feminists who 
reject traditional standards of femininity are ridi-
culed, whereas those who do not are deemed vain 
and perhaps even hypocritical.
Our analysis revealed 40,148 co-occurrences 
between women/an and personalizing words 
(3.46% of all women/an references), which seemed 
to emphasize romance and marital status, clothing 
and appearance, motherhood, sex, and body parts. 
The media paid a great deal of attention to women’s 
romance and marital status. For example, the word 
pair women/an—married appeared 1,217 times, 
whereas women/an—divorce appeared 98 times.

The Victimization Frame. Women and feminists 
are portrayed in a victimization frame when their rep-
resentation refers to weakness, vulnerability, mental 
illness, crime, fear, dysfunctionality, and so forth. Our 
target words women and woman co-occurred with 
victimization words 13,756 times, representing 1.19% 
of all women/an references. The most commonly 
occurring victimization word pairs were associated 
with crime: women/an and variations of abuse (1,078), 
rape (773), victim (477), and fear (456). Women/an—
vulnerable co-occurred 80 times, and women/an—
wounded co-occurred 65 times.
Feminists were presented in a victimization frame 
in 1.00% of references to feminist/s/ism, for a total of 
252 times. The leading word pairs were feminist/s—
violence (32), feminist/s with lexical variants of rape 
(10), and feminist/s/ism with victim (8). Although crit-
ics have decried the media’s tendency to portray femi-
nists as victims, we found that women are portrayed as 
victims more than feminists are.
The Agency Frame. This frame reflects an active 
individual having strength, capability, voice, leadership, 
power, etc. The words women and woman appeared 
in an agency frame 6,920 times, or in 0.59% of all ref-
erences. The most common word pairs were women/
an and lexical variants of power (861), strong (822), 
respect (274), leader (266), advocate (132), and activist 
(118). Feminist words co-occurred with agency words 
295 times, or 1.17% of all feminist references. The 
most common word pairs were feminist/s/ism and 
variants of activist (38), leader (34), power (28), voices 
(10), advocate (8), victory (6), and won (6). Thus, 
although neither group is strongly framed as having 
agency, feminists appear within an agency frame more 
than women do.
The Site of Struggle Frame. Our work with the text 
led us to wonder, “where are feminist ideas and actions 
located?” We identified ten sites, each of which will be 
discussed briefly: home, geographic location, health, 
media and the arts, workplace, court/law, education, 
politics, sports and leisure, and religion. Table 4.3.2 
presents more detail.
Home words orient the subject to the family, 
home, house, marriage, furniture, guests, kitchen, 
patio, apartment, and so forth. Our target women 
words co-occurred with home words in 1.73% of all 
references, whereas our target feminist words co-
 
oc
curred with home words in 0.88% of references. 
Thus, women were significantly more likely to be 
linked with home than feminists were. Geographic 
location words link our target words to some actual 
city, state, or country. Women/an co-occurred with 
geographic location words in 1.53% of references; 
feminists in 1.16%. Women were significantly more 
likely to be oriented to a specific location than fem-
inists were. Health words reflect states of illness 
and wellness (e.g., disease, health, cancer, doctor). 
Such words co-occurred with women/an in 1.45% 
of references, and with feminist/s/ism in 0.51%. 
Although issues of health and reproductive care 
may be feminist concerns, they’re more closely 
associated with women.

Media and the arts words include audience, 
theater, television, book, magazine, author, radio,

women/an, 1.23% were media and the arts words, 
as were 1.71% of all references to feminist/s/ism. 
Feminists are more likely to be framed in terms 
of media than women are. Workplace references 
include jobs, working, management, labor, and 
careers. Women/an co-occurred with workplace 
words 1.06% of the time, whereas feminist/s/
ism did so in 0.55% of all cases. Although work 
issues are part of the feminist agenda, women are 
more likely to be framed in terms of work than 
are feminists. Court/law words include all refer -
ences to the legal system, such as judge, jury, law-
yer, attorney, lawsuit, police, crime, and trial. Of 
all references to women/an, 1.01% co-occurred 
with court/law words, whereas 0.66% of refer -
ences to feminist/s/ism did so. Thus, women are 
more likely to be framed in terms of the legal sys-
tem than feminists are. Education words address 
concerns of teaching, learning, studying, school, 
colleges, universities, etc. They were applied 
about equally to the two groups—0.87% of refer -
ences to women/an, and 0.81% of references to 
feminist/s/ism.
Politics words deal with the political system 
and include government, congress, senate, senator, 
elections, voters, politicians, and so forth. Politics 
words occurred in 0.64% of woman/en references, 
and in 1.60% of feminist/s/ism references. Our 
target feminist words were more likely to co-occur 
with politics words than our target women words 
were. Sports and leisure words include recreational 
activities of all types, such as play, sports, base-
ball, team, exercise, aerobics, and jogging. They 
appeared in 0.43% of all references to women/
an, and in 0.14% of all references to feminist/s/
ism. Women were more likely to be associated 
with sports and leisure than were feminists. Reli-
gion words address religious beliefs of all types: 
god, catholic, muslim, bible, religious, etc. They 
appeared in 0.34% of all references to women/an, 
and in 0.62% of all references to feminist/s/ism; 
feminists were more likely to be associated with 
religion than women were.
What Do the Frames Reveal?
We found that feminists are portrayed in a remark-
ably different fashion than seemingly “regular” 
women are, but that isn’t necessarily bad. Although 
many people have argued that feminists are por -
trayed negatively, we found feminists are in many 
ways portrayed more positively than women are. 
Feminists are less often framed in a personalized 
and trivialized fashion than women are. Feminists 
are less often framed as victims, and more often as 
having agency, than women are. The goals of the 
women’s movement are more closely associated 
with feminists than with women.
However, the picture of feminism and femi-
nists in the media isn’t all good, either. As Tuchman 
(1978) argued, symbolic annihilation occurs when 
social groups (such as feminists) are absent from, 
condemned by, or trivialized in, the media. Our 
research shows that feminists are not subjected to 
trivialization to the same extent as women in gen-
eral, but feminists are personalized and trivialized 
in a substantial proportion of all references—the 
media clearly consider information such as a fem-
inists’ appearance and marital status important.
In terms of presence, feminists are relatively 
absent from the media content we analyzed for this 
study. “Woman” or “women” appear more than 40 
times as often as the words “feminist/s/ism,” indi-
cating that feminism is still routinely ignored by the 
media. We argue that by failing to attend to feminists 
and feminism, the media frame feminism as unim-
portant. After all, if feminism were of value, it would 
receive media attention. (Wouldn’t it?)
Feminists are also condemned in the media; we 
found feminists and feminism are significantly more 
likely to be demonized than women are. Feminists are 
nearly ten times as likely to be associated with words 
such as jerks, bitches, radical, or bad than women are. 
Of all the frames, demonization is the third most com-
mon for feminists, which becomes even more striking 
in light of the fact that demonization is the frame least 
commonly applied to women.
In analyzing the site of the struggle, we found 
feminists less likely to appear in the context of 
a home or in any specific geographic location, 
less likely to participate in the legal system, or the 


Journalism and Advertising 123
workplace, less likely to be engaged in issues of 
health and well-being, or sports or leisure activities, 
than “regular” women are. The sites where feminists 
appear more often than women include media and 
the arts, politics, and religion.
The media’s presentation of the domain in which 
feminism and feminists operate is important for several 
reasons. First, it implicitly informs the audience as to 
the appropriateness of feminist concerns—and hence 
a feminist perspective—in these domains. The media 
present a vision of a social world in which feminism 
doesn’t really belong in the home, or the workplace, 
or the legal system. Feminism doesn’t seem, at least 
according to the media, to function within the private 
sphere—it is more often found in the public sphere 
(media and the arts, politics, religion). This may rein-
force the perception that feminism is neither relevant 
nor particularly applicable to the bulk of daily life for 
the majority of citizens.
The pattern of mediated representation of the 
site of feminist struggles also implies that feminists are 
not quite normal, not quite regular. Regular women 
have homes, live in real places, and engage in regular 
day-to-day work and leisure activities. Regular women 
do the types of things we (audience members) do—
but feminists are much less likely to be portrayed in 
such situations than women are. Instead, feminists 
are involved with the types of things many regular 
women are not—politics, and media and the arts. To 
the extent that feminists don’t do the same things as 
regular women, audiences could easily assume that 
feminism and its concerns are not relevant to regular 
people, and perhaps, are actually abnormal.
