4.7: FRAMING THE IMMIGRATION 
STORY
Patti Brown
This reading explores how media have framed 
the immigration story and, in the process, how 
the media have shaped both the story and public 
opinion.
Immigration is one of today’s most important media 
stories. It is a story about millions of people who 
pick up their lives and move from one country to 
another. It is a story about national borders, laws, 
politics, war, persecution, economic hardships, and 
the promise of opportunities. It is at once a global 
story and as close as the people who live next door.
In the United States, there are two pressing immi-
gration stories. One deals with people who enter the 
country through official channels seeking lawful per-
manent residence (LPR) status. In 2019, 1.03 million 
people were granted LPR status, bringing the esti-
mated total of people with so-called “green cards” to 
more than 13.6 million, many of whom are eligible to 
apply for citizenship.
The other story concerns those who have entered 
the US without permission or who remain here after 
their entry visa has expired. This is a more difficult 
number to determine. The Department of Homeland 
Security estimates there were 11.4 million people liv-
ing in the United States in 2019 whose immigration 
status was unauthorized. All told, more than 45 mil-
lion immigrants from all over the world live in the US, 
accounting for 14% of the total population.
Media stories of authorized and unauthorized 
immigration are highly charged and politically polarizing 
for a variety of reasons. New arrivals compete for jobs 
alongside native born and naturalized citizens. They can 
place demands on communities to provide schooling, 
health care, and social services. Some communities 
call themselves “sanctuary cities” and offer to shield 
those with unauthorized status from federal authorities. 
Many people brought to the US without authorization 
as children know no other home and seek stability to 
plan their futures as Congress talks about immigration 
reform yet can’t agree on what that means.
Why does this matter? Because there is a strong 
correlation between the amount of coverage media 
give to stories such as immigration and the salience 
the public ascribes to those issues (McCombs & 
Shaw, 1972). Television, movies, online, print, and 
social media tell us not just what to think about (called 
agenda setting), but they can also influence how we 
think about these issues (known as priming). By lead-
ing a broadcast with a story about immigration or plac-
ing an immigration story on a newspaper’s front page, 
the media tell us that immigration is important. The 
way the media report on immigration—from the fre-
quency, quantity, and angle of coverage to the sources 
quoted—influences how we think about and judge the 
issue.
The Power of Words
The words we use to describe someone or some-
thing frame the situation in a positive, negative, 
or neutral light, and say as much about us as they 
do about the person or thing being described. The 
media face challenges in describing individuals who 
have entered the United States without permission 
(called improper entrance) or who have stayed in 
the country after their visas have expired (unlawful 
presence). Word choices—such as “illegal aliens” 
or “undocumented migrants”—are frames. Entman 
(1991, p. 7) described frames as central organizing 
themes in telling stories that are “constructed from 
and embodied in the keywords, metaphors, con-
cepts, symbols, and visual images emphasized in 
the news narrative.” Frames present a certain view 
of a story just as a picture frame or window frame 
limits what we see.
Media struggle to choose unbiased and accurate 
words when covering immigration. Although the US 
government has used the term “alien” since the 1798 
Alien and Sedition Acts to refer to anyone in the coun-
try who is not a US citizen or national, this is a dehu-
manizing descriptor of a human being. In 2013, the 
Associated Press (AP) revised its stylebook to avoid 
labeling people as “illegal” or “undocumented” unless 
those terms are part of a direct quote essential to the 
story. The AP’s current practice is to describe the 
activity being covered, such as “illegal immigration” or 
“unlawful entry.”


Journalism and Advertising 125
Language is organic and evolves over time. Y ears 
from now, people will look back at how the keywords, 
metaphors, concepts, symbols, and visual images used 
today shaped how audiences viewed the policies and 
the people at the center of the debate, and how the 
words themselves shaped the very tenor of public dis-
course. What will those future people find?
Framing Immigration
Although media coverage of immigration includes 
other frames (such as crime, sanctuary cities, immi-
gration reform legislation, education, and health 
care), this essay focuses on three dominant frames: 
homeland security and border control, the DREAM 
Act and Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals 
(DACA), and human rights and refugees.
Homeland Security and Border Control 
Frames
The Homeland Security frame deals with government 
efforts to protect the US from foreign and domestic 
threats. Since the September 11, 2001, terror attacks, 
homeland security has been a frequent theme par -
ticularly as it relates to who crosses the US border 
and how. The border control frame stems from the 
fact that all of the 9/11 terrorists were foreign nation-
als who professed a jihadist ideology against the US.
Just as we lock our doors to prevent others from 
entering our homes without permission, nations con-
trol who enters and how long they stay. More than 
one million people—citizens, immigrants, and non-  
immigrant temporary visa holders—enter and leave 
the United States every day. They come and go through 
one of 328 ports of entry operated by US Customs and 
Border Protection to conduct business, to work, to visit 
family, to study, and for vacation. An unknown number 
also cross the border without authorization.
The public relies on the media as a conduit of 
information. Unfortunately, media coverage can be 
sensationalized and can overemphasize the size and 
scope of legal and unauthorized immigration and their 
relationship to national security. As with any number of 
politically charged issues, each media outlet employs 
frames constructed to fit its biases in reporting the 
story.
When Donald Trump ran for president in 2016, 
border security was a signature issue of his campaign 
by promising to build a wall along the entire US south-
ern border. Photojournalists recorded images of his 
supporters wearing red “Make America Great Again” 
hats chanting “build that wall” at his rallies.
Support for the wall was divided along partisan 
lines and among members of the media, as evidenced 
by the choice of words and the quotes selected to 
frame the story. Some media outlets framed Trump 
and his supporters as patriots; others framed them as 
xenophobic White nationalists.
When Joe Biden ran for president in 2020, he 
promised to halt construction of the wall. Three 
months before the November general election, 
Biden was interviewed by a panel of journalists from 
the National Association of Black Journalists and 
National Association of Hispanic Journalists. He said 
that although he would not tear down the existing bor-
der wall, “There will not be another foot of wall con-
structed on my administration…I’m going to make 
sure we have border protection, but it’s going to be 
based on making sure that we use high-tech…at the 
ports of entry” (Sprunt, 2020).
Biden made his campaign promise in front of this 
particular audience of journalists knowing they would 
frame his policy intentions to appeal to voters who 
want progressive immigration reform.
As the future of the wall hangs in political limbo, 
the media continue to follow the story of its status, 
shifting the frame from national security to the wall’s 
environmental impact on the desert ecosystem. As 
Simonelli (2021) reported, the wall “is little more than 
a political prop that has failed to secure the border with 
Mexico but has damaged landscapes and habitat in 
southern Arizona.”
The DREAMers Frame
On August 1, 2001, a bipartisan immigration bill—
the Development, Relief and Education for Alien 
Minors Act or DREAM Act—was introduced in 
Congress. The bill’s first hearing was scheduled on 
September 11. However, due to the terrorist attacks 
that day, the bill languished. For more than a decade, 
attempts were made to move the measure forward, 
but the DREAM Act could not get enough support.

126 Content
Frustrated with Congress’ failure to act, President 
Barack Obama signed an executive order in 2012 
creating the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals 
(DACA), which gave temporary legal protection to chil-
dren and young adults—known as “DREAMers”—
who were brought into the country illegally as minors, 
or who had overstayed their visa. Although DACA did 
not offer legal status or a path to citizenship, it provided 
a deferment from deportation and allowed qualified 
applicants to work.
Supporters framed DACA sympathetically as pro-
tecting the DREAMers from the consequences of their 
parents’ actions. In a front-page article in the New Y ork 
Times, Preston and Cushman (2012) quoted Lorella 
Praeli, a leader of the United We Dream Network, the 
largest coalition of undocumented students, “People 
are just breaking down and crying for joy when they 
found out what the president did.”
Others framed the president’s executive action as 
creating an incentive for children to enter the US ille-
gally, and being unconstitutional because it surpassed 
Congress’ Constitutional prerogative to act on matters 
of immigration. Preston and Cushman also quoted 
Iowa Senator Chuck Grassley who said, “The presi-
dent’s action is an affront to the process of representa-
tive government by circumventing Congress and with 
a directive he may not have the authority to execute…
It seems the president has put election-year politics 
above responsible policies.”
In September 2017, nine months after becoming 
president, Trump said he would phase out DACA and 
gave Congress until March 2018 to pass the DREAM 
Act or some other protection legislation for those 
who qualified for DACA. When Congress failed to 
do so, Trump issued an executive order halting the 
program. The order was challenged and was heard 
by the Supreme Court which vacated the execu-
tive order. The Supreme Court did not rule on the 
merits or legality of DACA but on the “arbitrary and 
capricious” way the executive order had violated the 
Administrative Procedure Act, the statute which gov-
erns how federal agencies establish their operating 
rules.
Under the headline “Supreme Court Thwarts 
Trump’s Effort to Kill DACA” the Intelligencer, a news 
website within New Y ork magazine, reported that the 
SCOTUS “repudiated” Trump’s efforts to “kill Barack 
Obama’s Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals 
(DACA) initiative” (Kilgore, 2020).
In contrast, the right-leaning FOX News Network 
reported on the decision under the headline “Supreme 
Court rules against Trump administration bid to end 
DACA program” (Blitzer & Mears, 2020). We normally 
think of the media as framing issues, but individuals 
and organizations also frame issues by their choice 
of words, and social media platforms allow people 
to directly comment on the issues of the day. Some-
times other media pick up what individuals post on 
social media. Blitzer and Mears quoted two of Trump’s 
Tweets about the decision. In one, the president wrote, 
“These horrible & politically charged decisions com-
ing out of the Supreme Court are shotgun blasts into 
the face of people that are proud to call themselves 
Republicans or Conservatives.” In the other, Trump 
turned the focus on himself, “Do you get the impres-
sion that the Supreme Court doesn’t like me?”
Fox News shifted its framing to quote a Tweet by 
President Obama who wrote, 
Eight years ago this week, we protected young 
people who were raised as part of our Ameri-
can family from deportation. Today, I’m happy 
for them, their families, and all of us. We may 
look different and come from everywhere, 
but what makes us American are our shared 
ideals…
The Refugee and Human Rights Frames
Refugees are people who have been displaced 
from their home due to war, political conflicts, 
economic situations, or natural disasters. The 
United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees 
estimated that at the end of 2020 there were more 
than 82.4 million refugees around the world, the 
highest levels of displacement on record. Although 
millions of refugees are displaced within their own 
countries, others have fled across borders and find 
themselves in makeshift camps, often for years, not 
knowing whether they will ever be able to return 
home or allowed to immigrate to a new country 
and begin a new life.
The refugee frame is woven into the human 
rights frame, which concerns the fundamental rights 


Journalism and Advertising 127
of every human being to dignity, freedom, justice, and 
peace. Until refugees know what their path forward 
is, they live in limbo without the economic resources, 
political capital, or personal agency necessary for 
self-determination.
The United States has historically received and 
resettled more refugees than any other nation. In 1980, 
more than 207,000 refugees were resettled in the 
United States. During the 1990s, the US resettled on 
average a little more than 100,000 refugees a year. Fol-
lowing the September 11 terrorist attacks, the number 
fell to only 27,000 refugees admitted in 2002; by 2016, 
the number had risen to nearly 85,000.
Using the homeland security frame to justify cur-
tailing refugee admissions, Trump signed a series of 
executive orders beginning in 2017. One was titled 
“Protecting the Nation from Foreign Terrorist Entry 
into the United States.” Total immigration was capped 
at under 50,000 that year and refugee resettlement 
was put on hold; by 2020, immigration was capped at 
less than 12,000.
Media were swift to frame the policies as discrim-
inatory against Muslims because Islam is the predom-
inant religion in most of the countries named in the 
travel and refugee bans and in the immigration caps. 
Joe Biden promised to lift the “Muslim bans” upon 
becoming president. On his first day in office, Biden 
signed a proclamation reversing his predecessor’s 
executive orders. The title of Biden’s proclamation 
framed the difference between the two administra-
tions, “Proclamation on Ending Discriminatory Bans 
on Entry to The United States.”
As America’s immigration policies have fluctu-
ated depending on who is in the Oval Office and which 
political party controls each chamber of Congress, tens 
of thousands of people from Central and Latin Amer-
ica have risked their lives to get to the US–Mexican 
border. Although thousands have crossed successfully, 
thousands of others have been apprehended by border 
agents. Some individuals are detained, sometimes for 
months, others are released, and some are returned 
across the border. Many people have even sent their 
unaccompanied minor children to the border in the 
hopes that the children will be able to cross into the 
US and be granted some form of legal protection. 
The number of people at the Mexican–US border has 
created a logistical crisis for the Customs and Border 
Patrol agency to feed, clothe, and house all those who 
were detained.
In telling this story, media have focused on the 
plight of migrants fleeing poverty and violence. Pho-
tos of people behind chain link fencing at overcrowded 
detention facilities have been published across the 
world. An Associated Press article detailing the expe-
riences of detained migrants explained that they refer 
to Border Patrol stations “as ‘hieleras,’ or iceboxes, 
because they are cold, and to processing facilities as 
‘perreras,’ or dog cages, because of the fences” (Gal-
van, 2019).
Despite the risks, increasing numbers of people 
attempt to cross into the US. The BBC (2021) reported 
that although Joe Biden campaigned for a “more 
humane immigration agenda,” the situation remains 
rife with problems. Calling the conditions a “humani-
tarian crisis,” the report contained a photo of children 
wrapped in mylar blankets and crowded together on 
the floor of a detention facility. Another showed a man 
in the process of being detained wearing a t-shirt that 
read in bold letters “BIDEN PLEASE LET US IN.” The 
report quoted Vice President Kamala Harris telling 
migrants headed for the border “Do not come.”
Reframing, Refocusing, and Reporting
How media select, report, and edit stories is driven 
by factors attributed to dominant class biases inher-
ent within both the media and society. Mainstream 
media outlets are owned by corporate conglom-
erates and run almost exclusively by educated, 
upper income White elites. The dominant class is 
invested in maintaining the status quo to ensure its 
position of hegemonic power. Research shows that 
the media often perpetuate racial stereotypes and 
increase racial conflict which serves to reinforce the 
status quo—even though journalists, as individu-
als, are more likely to support progressive political 
causes that may serve to advance the agenda of 
immigration reform.
However, especially in recent years, changes are 
afoot. Alternative media platforms are chipping away 
at the dominance of traditional media, allowing new 
voices to challenge the status quo and to report com-
plex and controversial stories such as the contempo-
rary immigration story.

4.8: THE FRAMING OF COLIN 
KAEPERNICK BEFORE AND AFTER THE 
KILLING OF GEORGE FLOYD
Jean Marie Brown
This reading examines the framing of Colin Kaeper-
nick’s 2016 protest against police brutality and how 
it changed after George Floyd was killed by the 
police in 2020.
On August 26, 2016, the San Francisco 49ers hosted 
the Green Bay Packers in the third week of NFL 
preseason play. Quarterback Colin Kaepernick had 
taken the 49ers to the Super Bowl in 2013, but now 
he was struggling to remain on the roster. At the end 
of the season, he opted free agency after the 49ers 
said they planned to cut him because he no longer 
fit their style of play. No team picked him up. But 
Kaepernick’s career didn’t end solely because of on 
field play. That season, Kaepernick became a pariah 
for protesting during the national anthem. During 
the Green Bay game, he remained seated when the 
Star-Spangled Banner was played. When asked to 
explain, he said: 
I am not going to stand up to show pride in 
a flag for a country that oppresses black peo-
ple and people of color. To me, this is bigger 
than football and it would be selfish on my part 
to look the other way. There are bodies in the 
street and people getting paid leave and getting 
away with murder.
(Wyche, 2016)
In subsequent games, he knelt—took a knee—on 
the sideline. When the season opened on Septem-
ber 11, 2016, players across the league knelt in 
solidarity. Kaepernick’s protest attracted national 
and international media coverage, but the domi-
nant narrative was Kaepernick, not his motive for 
protesting.
In this essay, I examine how one story—  
Kaepernick’s protest—was framed at two points in 
time: 2016 and 2020 following the death of George 
Floyd. After Floyd, a Black man, was murdered by a 
White Minneapolis police officer in 2020, I noticed 
that Kaepernick’s name had resurfaced. I wondered 
how coverage of Kaepernick’s protest differed.
In journalism, how a story is framed is almost as 
important as the topic. The choices journalists make 
while reporting and creating news reports shape story 
frames. These choices include who is interviewed as 
well as who isn’t, how quotes are used, and the words 
used to describe events. Framing is one of the most 
powerful tools of storytelling. It can shape public per-
ception about events and actors, spark outrage or joy, 
or create villains and heroes. It can certainly influence 
how people interpret information and how they view 
an event.
To understand how media framed Kaeper -
nick’s protest, I conducted a qualitative analysis of 
the coverage from both periods, using the NexisUni 
database to retrieve articles and transcripts. This 
database includes content from print, broadcast, 
and cable news media, at the local, national, and 
international levels. The first sample consisted of 
articles and transcripts from August 27 to Septem-
ber 5, 2016, the earliest days of the story. A search 
for “Colin Kaepernick protest” in the NexisUni 
database yielded more than 1,000 articles and tran-
scripts. After sorting for relevance and duplication, 
498 articles were analyzed. The second sample 
used the same search term, “Colin Kaepernick pro-
test,” to collect transcripts and articles from May 26 
to June 14, 2020, the earliest days of coverage after 
Floyd’s death on May 25, 2020. This search returned 
666 articles. Once they were sorted for relevance 
and duplication, 136 articles were analyzed.
I read the articles and transcripts, for major recur-
ring themes or frames. As noted below, Colin Kaeper-
nick’s protest was framed very differently in 2016 and 
2020; media coverage shifted from focusing on the act 
of protest itself to acknowledging the reason for the 
protest: police brutality.

130 Content
2016: The Athlete Behavior Frame
Kaepernick had used his position as a public figure 
to protest police brutality by not standing during the 
national anthem. Although some media outlets men-
tioned the reasons for his protest, most emphasized 
his actions. From the outset, this story was framed 
around Kaepernick’s behavior, not his rationale. The 
earliest stories counterbalance his explanation with 
reactions from the NFL and San Francisco 49ers, 
in particular head coach Chip Kelly. They were pre-
sented as authorities who could answer, “Can he do 
this?” or “Why are you allowing him to do this?” Of 
course, the 49ers coach Chip Kelly was interviewed: 
“We recognize his right to do that,” Kelly said in a 
media conference call Saturday. “It’s not my right 
to tell him not to do something. That’s his right as a 
citizen” (Inman, 2016). The Marin Independent Jour-
nal in Marin County, California, cast Kaepernick as 
an outlier in the framing of an interview with Raid-
ers coach Jack Del Rio. “It’s never come to a point 
where I’ve had to address it, it’s always been under-
stood,” Del Rio said. “Y ou stand attention. Y ou pay 
respect to our flag, our country.” (Durkin, 2016)
Rather than turn to primary source reporting 
and investigate Kaepernick’s claims about police 
brutality, The New Y ork Times reviewed his Twitter 
account for mentions of high-profile events (Hauser, 
2016). Other journalists also turned to social media 
for public reaction. They tended to present reactions 
focusing on the behavior rather than the reasons for 
the protest. For example, Kaepernick’s statement 
that he’s “not going to stand up to show pride in a 
flag for a country that oppresses black people and 
people of color” was juxtaposed with a tweet from 
a disabled veteran that includes the silhouette of a 
soldier saluting from a wheelchair (Millward, 2016). 
Media outlets also included tweets urging sponsors 
to drop Kaepernick and calling his behavior foolish. 
For example, at least one paper reprinted New Y ork 
Giants lineman Justin Pugh’s tweet condemning 
Kaepernick’s method and suggesting that he disre-
spected the military (“Report: NFL team executives,” 
2016), and some coverage referenced social media 
reports that angry fans are burning Kaepernick’s 
jersey. This became an oft-repeated anecdote that 
demonized Kaepernick (Whitfield, 2016).
Although coverage was rarely framed around the 
underlying issues that Kaepernick was addressing, 
media did consider the reaction of law enforcement. 
Law enforcement officials represented authority 
in these instances. Interviews with members of law 
enforcement frame the protest as disrespectful. In an 
interview, the president of the Dallas Fallen Officer 
Foundation criticized the NFL for not sanctioning 
Kaepernick and questioned the validity of Kaeper -
nick’s argument: “I think the NFL, I mean, they are 
sending the wrong message here. Y es, we do want our 
NFL players to be advocates for social justice. But 
they’re taking on the wrong causes” (Giampia, 2016). 
The coverage even shifted to socks—emblazoned 
with cartoon pigs wearing police hats—that Kaeper-
nick had worn to practice in August. Coverage wasn’t 
framed to explain that Kaepernick said he was wear-
ing them to call attention to the dangers that some 
“rogue cops” pose to other officers. Instead, this was 
another episode of Kaepernick’s disrespect for law 
enforcement. An official with the National Associa-
tion of Police Organizations was quoted criticizing the 
NFL for being “silent when Kaepernick is dishonoring 
police officers with what he’s wearing on the field” 
(“Colin Kaepernick: My pig police socks,” 2016).
The language or imagery of the stories is also 
important. The words journalists used cast Kaeper-
nick in a harsh light and marginalized him. This 
description framed his actions as disrespectful and 
rebellious: “Kaepernick plopped himself on the bench 
and would not join his teammates for the anthem…” 
(Sanchez & Short, 2016). Headlines emphasized that 
Kaepernick didn’t stand during the national anthem 
(what he was doing), rather than the reason (why 
he was doing this). Journalists also stressed that 
Kaepernick “refused to stand,” rather than saying “he 
didn’t stand.” There is a nuance here, in that “refus-
ing” suggests defiance. There was also skepticism 
about his rationale, which even when acknowledged 
was rarely investigated: “San Francisco 49ers quar-
terback Colin Kaepernick is refusing to stand for the 
national anthem before games because he believes 
the United States oppresses African Americans and 
other minorities” (“Colin Kaepernick sits,” 2016).
Days later when then-President Barack Obama 
addressed the protest during a press conference, his 
remarks were framed to suggest that Kaepernick was 


Journalism and Advertising 131
under attack. Multiple outlets characterized Obama as 
“defending” Kaepernick. One outlet framed Kaeper-
nick as lonely and rejected—even by his birth mother 
(with whom Kaepernick has had little interaction):
Heidi Russo, the birth mother of the 49ers quar-
terback who has been refusing to stand for the 
national anthem, told Kaepernick—publicly, on 
Twitter—he is bringing shame to the family and 
the country
(Sanchez, 2016)
Coverage also focused on the national anthem, 
reinforcing the frame on Kaepernick’s actions—not 
standing for the “Star-Spangled Banner.” The inter -
section of sports and the national anthem was cov-
ered in multiple outlets (e.g., Barbash & Andrews, 
2016; Borden & Wagner, 2016) with some noting that 
some people view the anthem’s third verse as racist 
because it celebrates the deaths of freed men who 
fought on the side of the British (Willingham, 2016).
There were articles written and segments done 
in defense of Kaepernick’s right to protest, but Kaeper-
nick wasn’t trying to provoke a conversation about the 
First Amendment. He was addressing systemic racism 
and its role in policing. Starting with the death of Eric 
Garner in New Y ork on July 17, 2014, through July 
6, 2016, there were nine high profile deaths of Black 
people during encounters with police. This contextual 
information should have been pertinent to reports on 
Kaepernick’s protest, particularly since he cited police 
shootings in his earliest remarks telling NFL.com: 
“There are bodies in the street and people getting paid 
leave and getting away with murder.”
Of the nearly 500 articles in the sample, one  
article—from Aljazeera.com—took an in-depth look 
into police treatment of Black people and other peo-
ple of color in the U.S. This report stood out from oth-
ers because it examined whether there were facts to 
support Kaepernick’s rationale. Independent sources 
with knowledge of the subject matter were sought 
out. Ghani (2016) interviewed representatives of 
Black Lives Matter and included information about 
Black people killed by police that summer. He pro-
vided evidence of the increased likelihood of Black 
people being searched by police and of young Black 
men dying from police violence compared to other 
Americans. He also included perspective about the 
history of activism in professional sports.
Kaepernick played his last game in the NFL 
on January 1, 2017—the 49ers lost to the Seattle 
Seahawks.
2020: From Pariah to Social Justice 
Warrior
Three and a half years after Kaepernick’s last game, 
the world was stunned by a video of a White Min-
neapolis police officer kneeling on the neck of 
a Black man until he died. George Floyd’s death 
sparked worldwide outrage and prompted conversa-
tions about police brutality. It also changed the way 
Kaepernick’s 2016 protest was framed. The 136 sto-
ries I analyzed from 2020 revealed stark differences in 
the words, images, and sources used when discussing 
Kaepernick in 2016. Kaepernick’s redemption was 
swift. In five days’ time, he went from being framed 
as a pariah to a social justice warrior. His protest was 
no longer questioned or scrutinized. His method of 
protest—kneeling peacefully—
 consider
ed disre-
spectful in 2016 was juxtaposed with the actions of 
then-officer Derek Chauvin, subsequently convicted 
of murdering Floyd, and the people who rioted in the 
days following Floyd’s death.
Although not an integral part of the 2016 cover-
age, race and its role in policing were key elements of 
the coverage of Floyd’s death. Kaepernick’s protest 
became a “told you so” moment, as media quickly 
connected the meaning behind the protest to Floyd’s 
death—the frequency of Black people dying dur -
ing encounters with police. In 2016, media made 
little effort to find examples of police shootings that 
illustrated Kaepernick’s point. Floyd’s death changed 
that. Floyd’s murder was used to illustrate the point of 
Kaepernick’s protest.
Rather than questioning his rationale, moral 
authority, or patriotism, Kaepernick’s protest was now 
cited as a harbinger. On May 27, two days after Floyd’s 
death, CNN anchors discussed systemic racism 
(Lemon, 2020) and referenced a Tweet from Bernice 
King, daughter of slain civil rights leader, Dr. Martin 
Luther King, that juxtaposed a photograph of Chauvin 
kneeling on Floyd’s neck and Kaepernick kneeling on 
the sidelines. Journalists also noticed when NBA star 

132 Content
LeBron James tweeted the juxtaposed photograph 
with the caption “This … Is Why” (“LeBron James, 
Colin Kaepernick,” 2020). Coverage in 2016 had ques-
tioned Kaepernick’s right to protest, noting that he was 
a wealthy, bi-racial athlete who had been raised by 
a White family. But with Floyd’s murder, Kaepernick 
gained the moral authority to level charges of racism in 
policing. Media cited the “gruesome video” of Floyd’s 
death before noting “calls for justice” from Kaeper -
nick, James and other prominent athletes (Beer, 2020). 
Kaepernick was characterized as “a leading figure in 
the movement against systemic racial injustice” (“The 
cries for peace,” 2020); as one journalist declared, 
“Everything that Colin Kaepernick took a knee for has 
been on display in Minneapolis the last several days” 
(Smith, 2020).
In 2016, journalists had sought reaction from 
NFL owners, coaches, and players. But in the days 
following Floyd’s death, Kaepernick emerged as the 
hero, with celebrities and social justice advocates dis-
cussing the issue of race and policing and Kaepernick’s 
attempt to call attention to this. Journalists don’t reflect 
much on the role they played in Kaepernick becom-
ing an outcast, but they do take on the NFL. The 
league became the villain. NFL owners were accused 
of being hypocritical and of choosing “the knee on 
the neck” over “the knee of protest” (Jenkins, 2020). 
Jenkins called Kaepernick “a reformer, in the great  
American tradition.”
The Power of the Frame
The abrupt shift in the framing of Kaepernick’s 
protest underscores the power that journalists can 
wield. Although journalists were quick to blame 
NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell and NFL own-
ers for Kaepernick’s banishment, media coverage 
stoked the criticism and fueled the outrage that ulti-
mately led to that outcome. By focusing coverage 
on Kaepernick’s actions in 2016, rather than trying 
to explore the reason behind the protest, media 
gave the public the impression that Kaepernick had 
no legitimate reason to protest. It’s important for 
journalists to understand that their work influences 
public opinion. Everything from who is interviewed, 
to word choices and points of emphasis matter. 
George Floyd’s death in 2020 gave media a chance 
to reconsider the meaning and purpose of Colin 
Kaepernick’s actions in 2016, but they should have 
gotten it right the first time.

4.9: “THE MORE YOU SUBTRACT , THE 
MORE YOU ADD”: CUTTING GIRLS 
DOWN TO SIZE IN ADVERTISING1
Jean Kilbourne
The author discusses how girls and women are 
portrayed in advertising. She argues that we are 
relentlessly exposed to unattainable ideals of physi-
cal perfection and that women are portrayed as less 
powerful than men. She also considers the ramifica-
tions of such representations.
“The more you subtract, the more you add,” says an 
ad that ran in several women’s and teen magazines 
in 1997. Surprisingly, it is an ad for clothing, not for a 

134 Content
diet product. Perhaps it is overtly a statement about 
minimalism in fashion. However, the fact that the 
girl in the ad is very young and very thin reinforces 
another message, a message that an adolescent girl 
constantly gets from advertising and throughout 
popular culture, the message that she should dimin-
ish herself, she should be less than she is.
On the most obvious and familiar level, this 
refers to her body. However, the loss, the subtrac-
tion, and the cutting down to size also refer to 
her sense of her self, her sexuality, her need for 
authentic connection, and her longing for power 
and freedom. I certainly don’t think that the crea-
tors of this particular ad had all this in mind. And 
it wouldn’t be important at all were there not so 
many other ads that reinforce this message and did 
it not coincide with the current cultural crisis for 
adolescent girls.
When a girl enters adolescence, she faces a 
series of losses—loss of self-confidence, loss of 
a sense of efficacy and ambition, and the loss of 
her “voice,” the sense of being a unique and pow-
erful self that she had in childhood. Girls who were 
active, confident, feisty at the ages of 8 and 9 and 
10 often become hesitant, insecure, self-doubting at 
11. Their self-esteem plummets. As Carol Gilligan, 
Mary Pipher, and other social critics have pointed 
out in recent years, adolescent girls in America are 
afflicted with a range of problems, including low 
self-esteem, eating disorders, binge drinking, date 
rape and other dating violence, teen pregnancy, and 
a rise in cigarette smoking. Teenage women today 
are engaging in far riskier health behaviors and in 
greater numbers than any prior generation.
It is important to understand that these problems 
go way beyond individual psychological development. 
Even girls who are raised in loving homes by support-
ive parents grow up in a culture—both reflected and 
reinforced by advertising—that urges girls to adopt a 
false self, to become “feminine,” which means to be 
nice and kind and sweet, to compete with other girls 
for the attention of boys, and to value romantic rela-
tionships with boys above all else. Girls are put into 
a terrible double bind. They are supposed to repress 
their power, their anger, their exuberance, and be sim-
ply “nice,” although they also eventually must com-
pete with men in the business world and be successful. 
They must be overtly sexy and attractive but essen-
tially passive and virginal. How can we resist these 
destructive messages and images? The first step, as 
always, is to become as conscious of them as possible, 
to deconstruct them.
Regardless of the intent of the advertisers, what 
messages are girls getting? What are they told? Pri-
marily girls are told by advertisers that what is most 
important about them is their perfume, their cloth-
ing, their bodies, their beauty. Their “essence” is their 
underwear. “He says the first thing he noticed about 
you is your great personality,” says an ad featuring a 
very young woman in tight jeans. The copy continues, 
“He lies.” “If this is your idea of a great catch,” says an 
ad for a cosmetic kit from a teen magazine featuring 
a cute boy, “this is your tackle box.” Even very little 
girls are offered makeup and toys like Special Night 
Barbie, which shows them how to dress up for a night 
out. Girls of all ages get the message that they must 
be flawlessly beautiful and, above all these days, they 
must be thin.
Adolescent girls are especially vulnerable to the 
obsession with thinness, for many reasons. One is the 
ominous peer pressure on young people. Adolescence 
is a time of self-consciousness and terror of shame and 
humiliation. Boys are shamed for being too small, too 
weak, too soft, too sensitive. And girls are shamed for 
being too sexual, too loud, too boisterous, too big (in 
any sense of the word), having too hearty an appetite. 
Many young women have told me that their boyfriends 
wanted them to lose weight. One said that her boy-
friend had threatened to leave her if she didn’t lose 
five pounds. “Why don’t you leave him,” I asked, “and 
lose 160?”
The situation is very different for men. The dou-
ble standard is reflected in an ad for a low-fat pizza: 
“He eats a brownie... you eat a rice cake. He eats a 
juicy burger... you eat a low-fat entree. He eats pizza... 
you eat pizza. Finally, life is fair.” Although some men 
develop eating problems, the predominant cultural 
message remains that a hearty appetite and a large 
size are desirable in a man, but not so in a woman.
The obsession starts early. Today, at least one-
third of 12- to 13-year-old girls are actively trying to 
lose weight, by dieting, vomiting, and/or taking pills. 
Some studies have found that nearly 80% of fourth-
grade girls are dieting. And a survey in Massachusetts 


Journalism and Advertising 135
found that the single largest group of high school stu-
dents considering or attempting suicide is girls who feel 
they are overweight. Imagine. Girls made to feel so ter-
rible about themselves that they would rather be dead  
than fat.
No wonder it is hard to find a woman, especially 
a young woman, in America today who has a truly 
healthy attitude toward her body and toward food. 
Bulimia and anorexia are the extreme results of an 
obsession with eating and weight control that grips 
many young women with serious and potentially very 
dangerous results. Although eating problems are often 
thought to result from vanity, the truth is that they, like 
other addictions and compulsive behavior, usually 
have deeper roots.
Advertising doesn’t cause eating problems, of 
course. However, these images certainly contribute 
to the body-hatred so many young women feel and 
to some of the resulting eating problems, which range 
from bulimia to compulsive overeating to simply being 
obsessed with controlling one’s appetite. Advertising 
does promote abusive and abnormal attitudes about 
eating, drinking, and thinness.
Being obsessed about one’s weight is made to 
seem normal and even appealing in ads for unrelated 
products, such as the British watch ad featuring an 
extremely thin young woman and proclaiming “Put 
some weight on.” The additional weight is the watch. 
The woman is so thin she can wear the watch on her 
upper arm.
The magazines and the ads deliberately create and 
intensify anxiety about weight because it is so profit-
able. On a deeper level, however, they reflect cultural 
concerns and conflicts about women’s power. Real 
freedom for women would change the very basis of 
our male-dominated society. It is not surprising that 
many men (and women) fear this.
“We cut Judy down to size,” says an ad for a 
health club. “Soon, you’ll both be taking up less space,” 
says an ad for a collapsible treadmill, referring both 
to the product and the young woman exercising on 
it. The obsession with thinness is most deeply about cut-
ting girls and women down to size. Some argue that it is 
men’s awareness of just how powerful women can be 
that has created the attempts to keep women small. 
Indeed, thinness as an ideal has always accompanied 
periods of greater freedom for women—as soon as we 
got the vote, boyish flapper bodies came into vogue. 
No wonder there is such pressure on young women 
today to be thin, to shrink, to be like little girls, not to 
take up too much space, literally or figuratively.
At the same time as there is relentless pressure on 
women to be small, there is also pressure on us to suc-
ceed, to achieve, to “have it all.” We can be successful 
as long as we stay “feminine” (i.e., powerless enough 
not to be truly threatening). One way to do this is to 
present an image of fragility, to look like a waif. This 
demonstrates that one is both in control and still very 
“feminine.”
The changing roles and greater opportunities 
for women promised by the women’s movement are 
trivialized, reduced to the private search for the slim-
mest body. In one commercial, three skinny young 
women dance and sing about the “taste of freedom.” 
They are feeling free because they can now eat bread, 
thanks to a low-calorie version. A commercial for a 
fast-food chain features a very slim young woman who 
announces, “I have a license to eat.” The salad bar and 
lighter fare have given her freedom to eat (as if eating 
for women were a privilege rather than a need).
Most of us know by now about the damage 
done to girls by the tyranny of the ideal image and the 
obsession with thinness. But girls get other messages 
too that “cut them down to size” more subtly. In ad 
after ad girls are urged to be “barely there”—beautiful 
but silent.
“Make a statement without saying a word,” says 
an ad for perfume. And indeed, this is one of the pri-
mary messages of the culture to adolescent girls. “The 
silence of a look can reveal more than words,” says 
another perfume ad. “More than words can say,” says 
another. A lipstick ad says, “Watch your mouth, young 
lady,” while one for nail polish says, “Let your fingers 
do the talking,” and one for hairspray promises “hair 
that speaks volumes.”
An Italian ad features a very thin young woman 
in an elegant coat sitting on a window seat. The copy 
says, “This woman is silent. This coat talks.” Girls, 
seeing these images of women, are encouraged to be 
silent, mysterious, not to talk too much or too loudly. 
In so many different ways, they are told “the more you 
subtract, the more you add.”
It is impossible to know how much of this mes-
sage is intended by the advertisers. Is it harmless 

136 Content
wordplay, or is it a sophisticated and clever market-
ing ploy based on research about the silencing of girls, 
deliberately designed to attract them with the prom-
ise of at least some form of self-expression? I don’t 
know. Advertisers certainly spend a lot of money on 
psychological research and focus groups. They usually 
know what they are doing. But sometimes, they are 
just reflecting common cultural beliefs and concerns. 
It doesn’t matter whether it is intended or not. What 
matters is the effect. And I contend that the cumulative 
effect of these images and words urging girls to express 
themselves through their bodies and through products 
is serious and harmful.
As Erving Goffman (1978) pointed out in Gender 
Advertisements, we learn a great deal about the dispa-
rate power of males and females simply through the 
body language and poses of advertising. Women, 
especially young women, are generally subservient to 
men in ads, both through size and position. Sometimes 
it is as blatant as a woman serving as a footrest in an 
ad for Think Skateboards.
Other times, it is more subtle but quite striking 
(once one becomes aware of it). A double-paged 
spread for Calvin Klein’s clothing for kids conveys a 
world of information about the relative power of boys 
and girls. One of the boys seems to be in the act of 
speaking, expressing himself, while the girl has her 
hand over her mouth.
Girls are often shown as playful clowns in these 
ads, perpetuating the attitude that girls and women are 
childish and cannot be taken seriously, whereas even 
very young men are generally portrayed as secure, 
powerful, and serious. People in control of their lives 
stand upright, alert, and ready to meet the world. In 
contrast, females often appear off-balance, insecure, 
and weak. Often our body parts are bent, conveying 
unpreparedness, submissiveness, and appeasement.
We cover our faces with our hair or our hands, 
conveying shame or embarrassment. And, no matter 
what happens, we keep on smiling. “Just smiling the 
bothers away,” as one ad says.
An ad for vodka features a woman in the water 
and the copy, “In a past life I was a mermaid who fell in 
love with an ancient mariner. I pulled him into the sea 
to be my husband. I didn’t know he couldn’t breathe 
underwater.” Of course, she can’t breathe underwater 
either.
Breathe underwater. As girls come of age sexu-
ally, the culture gives them impossibly contradictory 
messages. Advertising slogans such as “because inno-
cence is sexier than you think” and “nothing so sensual 
was ever so innocent” place them in a double bind. 
“Only something so pure could inspire such unspeak-
able passion,” declares an ad for Jovan musk. And a 
very sexy ad features a couple making love while the 
woman is wearing a bra called “Pure.” Somehow girls 
are supposed to be both innocent and seductive, vir-
ginal and experienced, all at the same time. As they 
quickly learn, this is tricky.
Females have long been divided into virgins and 
whores, of course. What is new is that girls are now 
supposed to embody both within themselves.
This is symbolic of the central contradiction of the 
culture—we must work hard and produce and achieve 
success and yet, at the same time, we are encour -
aged to live impulsively, spend a lot of money, and be 
constantly and immediately gratified. This tension is 
reflected in our attitudes toward many things, includ-
ing sex and eating. Girls are promised fulfillment both 
through being thin and through eating rich foods, just  
as they are promised fulfillment through being inno-
cent and virginal and through wild and impulsive sex.
Advertisers are aware of their role and do not 
hesitate to take advantage of the insecurities and anx-
ieties of young people, usually in the guise of offering 
solutions. A cigarette provides a symbol of independ-
ence. A pair of designer jeans or sneakers conveys sta-
tus. The right perfume or beer resolves doubts about 
femininity or masculinity. Because so many anxieties 
have to do with sexuality and intimacy and because 
advertising so often offers products as the answers and 
uses sex to sell, it is perhaps the concept of sexuality 
that is most deeply affected.
“Y ou can learn more about anatomy after school,” 
says an ad for jeans, which manages to trivialize sex, 
relationships, and education all in one sentence. Mag-
azines targeting girls and young women are filled with 
ads and articles on how to be beautiful and sexy and 
appealing to boys—all in service of the advertisers, 
of course, who sell their wares on almost every page. 
“How Smart Girls Flirt,” “Sex to Write Home About,” 
“15 Ways Sex Makes Y ou Prettier,” and “Are Y ou Good 
in Bed?” are some of the recent cover stories for Jane 
magazine.


Journalism and Advertising 137
The emphasis for girls and women is always on 
being desirable, not on experiencing desire. Girls who 
want to be sexually active instead of simply being the 
objects of male desire are given only one model to 
follow, that of exploitive male sexuality. It seems that 
advertisers can’t conceive of a kind of power that isn’t 
manipulative and exploitive or a way that women can 
be actively sexual without being like traditional men.
Women who are powerful in advertising are 
uncommitted. They treat men like sex objects: “If I 
want a man to see my bra, I take him home,” says an 
androgynous young woman. They are elusive and dis-
tant: “She’s the first woman who refused to take your 
phone calls,” says one ad. As if it were a good thing to 
be rude and inconsiderate.
Mostly though, girls are not supposed to have 
sexual agency. They are supposed to be passive, swept 
away, overpowered. “See where it takes you,” says a 
perfume ad featuring a couple passionately embrac-
ing. “Unleash your fantasies,” says another. “A force of 
nature.” This contributes to the strange and damaging 
concept of the “good girl” as the one who is swept 
away, unprepared for sex, versus the “bad girl” as the 
one who plans for sex, uses contraception, and is gen-
erally responsible. A young woman can manage to 
have sex and yet in some sense maintain her virginity 
by being “out of control,” drunk, and/or deep in denial 
about the entire experience.
In adolescence, girls are told that they have to give 
up so much of what they know about relationships and 
intimacy if they want to attract men. Most tragically, 
they are told they have to give up each other. The truth 
is that one of the most powerful antidotes to destruc-
tive cultural messages is close and supportive female 
friendships. But girls are often encouraged by the cul-
ture to sacrifice their relationships with each other and 
to enter into hostile competition for the attention of 
boys and men. “What the bitch who’s about to steal 
your man wears,” says one ad.
Of course, some girls do resist and rebel. Some 
are encouraged (by someone—a loving parent, a 
supportive teacher) to see the cultural contradictions 
clearly and to break free in a healthy and positive way. 
Others rebel in ways that damage themselves. A young 
woman seems to have only two choices: she can bury 
her sexual self, be a “good girl,” give in to what Carol 
Gilligan (Brown & Gilligan, 1992, p. 53) terms “the 
tyranny of kind and nice” (and numb the pain by over-
eating or starving or cutting herself or drinking her -
self into a stupor). Or she can become a rebel—flout 
her sexuality, seduce inappropriate partners, seduce 
everyone, smoke, drink flamboyantly, use other drugs. 
Both of these responses are self-destructive, but they 
begin as an attempt to survive, not to self-destruct.
Many girls become women who split themselves 
in two and do both—have a double life, a secret life—a 
good girl in public, out of control in private. A feminist 
in public, involved in an abusive relationship or lost in 
sadomasochistic fantasies in private. A lawyer by day, 
a barfly by night. Raiding the refrigerator or drinking 
themselves into a stupor alone in their kitchens at 
night, after the children are in bed, the laundry done. 
Doing well in school, but smoking in order to have a 
sexier, cooler image. Being sexual only when drunk.
There are few healthy alternatives for girls who 
want to truly rebel against restrictive gender roles and 
stereotypes. What they are offered by popular culture 
is a superficial toughness, an “attitude,” exemplified 
by smoking, drinking, and engaging in casual sex—all 
harmful behaviors. In 1990, Virginia Slims offered girls 
a T-shirt that said, “Sugar and spice and everything 
nice? Get real.”
In 1997, Winston used the same theme in an ad 
featuring a tough young woman shooting pool and 
saying, “I’m not all sugar & spice. And neither are my 
smokes.” As if the alternative to the feminine stereo-
type was sarcasm and toughness, and as if smoking 
was somehow an expression of one’s authentic self 
(“get real”).
Of course, the readers and viewers of these ads 
don’t take them literally. But we do take them in—each 
is another grain of sand in a slowly accumulating and 
vast sand pile. If we entirely enter the world of ads, 
imagine them to be real for a moment, we find that 
the sandpile has entirely closed us in, and there’s only 
one escape route—buy something. “Get the power,” 
says an ad featuring a woman showing off her bicep. 
“The power to clean anything,” the ad continues. “Hey 
girls, you’ve got the power of control,” says an ad for... 
hairspray. “Y ou never had this much control when you 
were on your own” (hair gel). “Exceptional character” 
(a watch). “An enlightening experience” (face powder). 
“Inner strength” (vitamins). “Stronger longer” (sham-
poo). Of course, the empowerment, the enlightenment, 

138 Content
is as impossible to get through products as is anything 
else—love, security, romance, passion. On one level, 
we know this. On another, we keep buying and hoping.
Other ads go further and offer products as a way 
to rebel, to be a real individual. “Live outside the lines,” 
says a clothing ad featuring a young woman walking 
out of a men’s room. This kind of rebellion isn’t going 
to rock the world. And, no surprise, the young woman 
is very thin and conventionally pretty.
“Think for yourself,” says yet another hollow-  
cheeked young woman, demonstrating her individ-
uality via an expensive and fashionable sweater. “Be 
amazing” (cosmetics). “If you’re going to create elec-
tricity, use it” (watches).
“Break the rules,” says a perfume ad. It goes 
on to give the confusing advice, “Stand apart, keep 
your head, go with your heart.” The thin and pretty 
young woman featured with her boyfriend is a perfect 
example of conventional “femininity.” As is the young 
woman in the Halston perfume ad that says, “And 
when she was bad she wore Halston.” What kind of 
“bad” is this?
“Nude with attitude” features a Black woman in a 
powerful pose, completely undercut by the brevity of 
her dress and the focus on her long legs. Her “attitude” 
is nothing to fear—she’s just another sex object. Good 
thing, because a lot of people are especially scared of 
powerful Black women.
The British ad “For girls with plenty of balls” is 
insulting in ways too numerous to count, beginning 
with the equation of strength and courage and fiery 
passion with testicles. What the ad offers these girls is 
body lotion.
Some ads do feature women who seem really 
angry and rebellious, but the final message always is 
the same. “Today, I indulge my dark side,” says an ad 
featuring a fierce young woman tearing at what seems 
to be a net. “Got a problem with that?” The slogan is 
“be extraordinary not ordinary.” The product which 
promises to free this girl from the net that imprisons 
her? Black nail polish.
Nail polish. Such a trivial solution to such an enor-
mous dilemma. But such triviality and superficiality is 
common in advertising. How could it be otherwise? 
The solution to any problem always has to be a prod-
uct. Change, transformation, is thus inevitably shallow 
and moronic, rather than meaningful and transcendent. 
These days, self-improvement seems to have more to 
do with calories than with character, with abdomens 
rather than absolutes, with nail polish than with ethics.
This relentless trivialization of her hopes and 
dreams, her expectations for herself, cuts to the quick 
of a young girl’s soul. Just as she is entering woman-
hood, eager to spread her wings, to become more 
sexual, more empowered, more independent—the 
culture moves in to cut her down to size.
Black nail polish isn’t going to help. But it prob-
ably won’t hurt either. What hurts are some of the 
other products offered to girls as a way to rebel and 
to cope—especially our deadliest drugs: alcohol and 
nicotine. These drugs are cynically and deliberately 
offered by advertisers to girls as a way to numb the 
pain of disconnection, to maintain the illusion of some 
kind of relationship, to be more appealing to men, to 
be both “liberated” and “feminine,” and, perhaps most 
tragically, to subvert their rebellious spirits, the very 
spark within that could, if not coopted, empower them 
to change their lives.

It’s Your Turn: What Do You Think? What 
Will You Find?
 1.
 Look thr
ough the advertisements in a 
magazine catering to a diverse range of 
female readers (Cosmopolitan; Ladies’ 
Home Journal; O, The Oprah Magazine; 
Marie Claire; etc.). To what extent do the 
ads reflect the types of images discussed 
here? Do the different magazines repre-
sent women and girls differently? How?
 2.
 W
ork together in small groups to con-
ceptualize a magazine ad for a new line 
called “Vocal” jeans. Be sure the copy 
and artwork make the product appealing 


Journalism and Advertising 139
References
Brown, L. M. & Gilligan, C. (1992). Meeting at the Crossroads:

4.10: SEX SELLS—BUT GENDER BRANDS
Greg Niedt and Julia C. Richmond
This essay considers gender-bending branding 
by CoverGirl and War Paint as components of a 
discursive Conversation, which encourages us to 
think about heteronormativity, queerness, and 
consumerism.
Brands appealing to mainstream consumers have 
always catered to changing trends in consumption, 
both material and aesthetic. Fashion and beauty 
brands, in particular, are positioned to act as agents to 
challenge or reinforce accepted habits, which inform 
identity expression. The very work of branding con-
tains social and political aspects and codifies cultural 
norms and values—including those associated with 
gender (Goffman, 1979). Because gender is socially 
constructed, it can evolve. Brands have begun to 
accommodate changing, non-heteronormative 
expressions of identity and challenge the traditional 
understanding of how individuals are meant to look 
and behave. Gender and consumerism have become 
two of the constants that guide nearly all social 
practice, mediating our experiences not just of one 
another but also ourselves (Bristor & Fischer, 1993).
Although incorporating queerness into fashion 
marketing is nothing new, having been discussed by 
multiple theorists (Hennessy, 1995; West, 2000), the 
type of queerness displayed has evolved in tandem 
with the public’s developing understanding of gender. 
Historically, fashion challenged the idea of fixed mas-
culine/feminine beauty ideals; now, it is challenging 
the gender binary itself. Androgynous, transgender, 
and other gender non-conforming people and prac-
tices have become increasingly visible.
Our analysis unpacks examples from branded 
content that challenges gender norms by two beauty 
companies: CoverGirl and War Paint. These brands 
have recently positioned themselves as makeup pro-
viders for men and, in doing so, have become partly 
defined in relation to a practice that has historically 
been seen as queer. Through discourse and visual 
semiotic analysis, we contextualize the landscape of 
gender identity through the lens of corporate branding 
and marketing.
Market Blending and Gender Bending
Branding and marketing rely on product innovation, 
differentiation from competitors, and determination 
of target audiences by sorting them along various 
lines—with gender as a primary categorization 
(Auster & Mansbach, 2012; Kim, Lehto, & Morrison, 
2007). But this process relies on the signification of 
gender, and viewers’ understanding of how gender is 
supposed to work in accordance with social norms. 
Theorists from Butler (1990) onward have argued 
that gender is something we perform and construct 
through practices, rather than being an unchanging 
quality we possess. Codes of masculinity and fem-
ininity become solidified into standardized cultural 
practice; they are presented and recirculated so 
regularly that they are often only noticeable when 
they are disobeyed. We apply the label “fashion,” 
for example, to objects and practices whose default 
to consumers, but take care not to “cut 
girls down to size.”
 3.
 If
 you were the producer of a teen-ori-
ented TV program and an advertiser 
submitted a commercial demeaning 
overweight girls (and threatening their 
already fragile self-esteem), would you 
air it? Why or why not? Whose respon-
sibility is it to make sure that ads are 
appropriate for the audiences?
 4.
 Although the r
epresentation of men was 
mentioned, the focus of this reading is 
on women. Look through popular mag-
azines to see how men are represented 
in advertising. What do these images tell 
us about what it means to be a man in 
today’s society?

140 Content
subject is presumed to be feminine—otherwise we 
add a qualifier, as in “men’s fashion.” Such coding 
reinforces both a gender binary and its associated 
gender norms, and although LGBTQ+ representa-
tions have increased since 2009, most mainstream 
advertisements continue to reinforce heteronorma-
tivity (Nölke, 2018).
A trend in the last few decades of increasing 
queer visibility in mainstream media is driven in part 
by consumerism and media technology as compa-
nies realize they can approach an untapped market 
through different permutations of gender. By featuring 
alternative gender identities and de-contextualizing 
items such as clothing and makeup from the masculine 
or the feminine, they normalize queerness, instead of 
queering the normal. This matters because it implies 
that queerness is not simply other, but (still) deviant  
and atypical, in need of normalization to be accept-
able. Few advertisers engage in this practice, so gender 
bending is noticeable when it takes place. Essentially, 
gender bending serves as a mark of distinction that 
allows companies to position themselves as queer-
friendly, modernizing their brands and appealing to a 
queer audience.
The manipulation of codes to attract and intrigue 
audiences takes place within what Gee (2014) calls a 
discursive Conversation, with a capital C: a dialogue 
in the public sphere that takes place through medi-
ated texts. But how do gender-bending images relate 
to tensions currently surrounding concepts such as 
heteronormativity and queerness, and how do these 
representations show their creators taking a stance in 
that Conversation? Do the representations in adver-
tisements shed some light on the relationship between 
those stances and (a Conversation about) branding? 
The average viewer who comes into the space occu-
pied by an ad will have a firm idea of gender and its 
aspects; challenging the viewer’s expectations is one 
of the most immediate ways to call attention to those 
biases.
Visual Analysis of Gender-Bending Ads
To unpack what is going on in each of our cases, we 
draw upon the discipline of visual semiotics, which 
focuses on how meanings—intended or unintended—
are constructed and interpreted in images. Bell and 
Milic (2002) pointed out that analyzing the content 
of an image can be enriched by looking for the con-
crete relationships between what is shown and what is 
therefore implied from outside the image. For this kind 
of analysis, they specify three dimensions of mean-
ing-making in visual semiotics: representation, inter-
action, and layout. Here, we will restrict our analysis to 
representation, which is divided into narrative (what is 
happening in the image?) and conceptual (what ideas 
does the image highlight?) processes, and a very basic 
idea of interaction, which Bell and Milic condense into 
three levels of distance (personal, social, and public). 
In this case, the interaction is between viewers of the 
advertisement or brand materials and the people rep-
resented therein.
CoverGirl
In October 2016, CoverGirl introduced a new 
model, selected in part because of his massive 
makeup-related following on Instagram. Unlike tra-
ditional makeup models, then-17-year-old James 
Charles of New Y ork was a cisgendered male. 
Charles claimed not to represent drag performers, 
a familiar subculture in America, but rather “boys in 
makeup” (Safronova, 2016). This was a new market 
for CoverGirl: males who want to wear makeup in 
everyday life. As a model, Charles offered a fresh 
face which unapologetically critiqued and blurred 
the boundaries of gender and performance.
CoverGirl’s hiring of Charles is noteworthy for two 
reasons. First, unlike other companies that introduced 
male models as their spokespeople around the same 
time—L’Oréal, Maybelline, MAC—the word Girl is 
part of the brand name. For the company to so overtly 
state the gender of its consumers, and then seemingly 
contradict (or at least redefine) it, speaks to a change in 
how the company discursively situates itself in relation 
to gender, and how gender is constructed in Western 
society. This stance reinforces the fluidity of identity 
in Charles’ own tutorial videos: despite identifying 
as male, he refers to himself as “sister” and his audi-
ence as “girls” (Komulainen & Hjort, 2017). Further, 
CoverGirl’s market is young people following trends 
in makeup. Contrary to elite or high fashion brands, 
which have the cultural capital to exercise more flex-
ibility in creativity and presentation, CoverGirl must 


Journalism and Advertising 141
appeal to a broad audience, which suggests that the 
company expected a positive response to their use of 
a male model.
The first ad to feature Charles shows him wear-
ing his trademark backward baseball cap and a white 
T-shirt with suspenders: typical masculine attire, 
despite “CoverGirl” written in large purple capitals 
across the top of the image. It is immediately clear that 
his face is made up, most prominently his eyebrows 
and lips. His face is turned in three-quarter profile 
with his gaze looking outward at us, a common pose 
for modeling shots. But the construction of the scene 
is less important than the concept of a boy wearing 
makeup, which breaches traditional gender expecta-
tions and conveys CoverGirl’s stance in the Conver-
sation about traditional meaning-making. This was 
further articulated in the press release issued when hir-
ing Charles: “All of our CoverGirls are role models and 
boundary-breakers, fearlessly expressing themselves, 
standing up for what they believe, and redefining what 
it means to be beautiful.”
An image of a boy wearing makeup shows that 
gender is not a defining trait of CoverGirl’s custom-
ers; the close-up of Charles’ face creates a level of 
personal interaction with the viewer. His direct gaze 
challenges us to support this expanded idea of who is 
allowed to wear makeup, or perhaps to feel comforta-
ble trying it ourselves. Ultimately, the company’s goal 
is to sell products, so it has a vested interest in creating 
a personal connection to draw viewers into the ad. But 
ads such as this can also be agents of positive social 
awareness when they showcase people and practices 
that had not been well-represented before. Although 
the intervening years have seen Charles embroiled in 
a number of scandals and lawsuits, resulting in a dra-
matic fall in his popularity (Safronova, 2019), his ini-
tial professional appearance remains a milestone in 
brands breaking gender boundaries.
War Paint
In July 2021, the makeup brand War Paint opened 
a brick-and-mortar shop in London, hailed as the 
“first store in the world dedicated to selling makeup 
tailored specifically to the male market” (Cobham, 
2021). Media reports highlighted not only its similar-
ities to the outlets of existing beauty brands but also 
the obvious difference in intended audience, calling 
attention to the modernist aesthetic of the store and 
brand. Its location in the fashion hotspot of Carnaby 
Street further presented the brand as a player in the 
scene.
The company brands itself by centering the gen-
dering of makeup as a product and the practices sur-
rounding it, as well as the discourses that permeate 
both. Even the aggressive name choice, “War Paint” (in 
full form: War Paint for Men) highlights the gender par-
adox. It’s makeup for men – but because it’s for men, 
it can’t be “makeup.” War Paint’s web site emphasizes 
that the products are “made for men’s skin” because 
“makeup has never been made with us in mind.” Once 
again the male use of artistic products related to pres-
entation of self is differentiated.
Regardless of whether the makeup has ever been 
formulated based on secondary sex characteristics, 
men throughout history have indeed used makeup. 
What the company really means here is that a single 
brand has never been created and marketed solely for 
men, to this scale. Importantly, the masculinity visually 
coded on the web site is a fairly traditional, hetero-
sexual one, for example, models with facial hair and 
suits accompanied by attentive women, against starkly 
colored backgrounds. In videos, founder Danny Gray 
remarks on the importance of presenting the prod-
ucts using “a man’s language” to highlight how men 
too might derive self-esteem and body positivity from 
makeup, as he did.
This ongoing transformation of the market to 
overtly target heterosexual men in makeup advertise-
ments can be seen as a positive step in de-stigmatizing 
the queer crossing of gender lines. Fluidity is becom-
ing more recognized and accepted, male-identifying 
celebrities such as Alex Rodriguez are launching their 
own men’s cosmetic lines, and international markets 
(especially Japan and South Korea) demonstrate how 
this branding can be successful (Benissan, 2021; Hills, 
2021). From a social standpoint, the perception of 
men’s makeup, formerly directed by Y ouTube influ-
encers rather than corporations (Komulainen & Hjort, 
2017), has begun entering the mainstream, and many 
male-identified individuals report increased willingness 
to use these products and even improved self-esteem 
(Park & Kwon, 2017). Y et while the cultural meanings 
of makeup-related practice evolve, identities become 

142 Content
more solidified. For example, some of War Paint’s 
visual media use the hashtag #GivingMenAChoice, 
implying that despite their privilege, men haven’t had 
one before.
On the surface, all of these elements construct 
a narrative that gives contemporary cisgendered, 
straight men the freedom to engage with a cultural 
practice they have hitherto avoided. But given that 
they have already appropriated so many cultural 
practices in the past, are they queering themselves or 
de-queering makeup? The question of how this latest 
move might impact the concept of gender and its per-
formance, and the ongoing prejudices that result from 
it remains unanswered.
Reflections
So why does all of this matter? By engaging with 
queerness and embarking on a Conversation about 
gender, these brands have at least partially defined 
themselves by updating their relationship to gender. 
We have focused on makeup in these two cases, 
but other fashion and beauty industries are mov-
ing toward a re-imagining of gender as well. For 
example, with clothing, the high fashion brand Louis 
Vuitton released an ad campaign in 2016 featuring 
Jaden Smith as a cisgender male wearing clothing 
designed for women (Friedman, 2016). Although 
some may dismiss fashion advertisements featuring 
celebrity models as too removed from the average 
customer’s world to have much impact, this side-
steps the point of advertising: to get customers to 
relate to the ads and want the product. CoverGirl, 
War Paint, Louis Vuitton, and other companies are 
becoming comfortable showing consumers that 
not everyone fits into traditional ideas of gender. 
Gender non-conforming individuals are being rep-
resented and recognized, lending validation to how 
they want to present themselves. Through media, 
we see and understand ourselves and our places 
within the broader discourse of culture; therefore, 
the evolution of these representations, and the 
debates surrounding them, function as a shorthand 
for the ongoing evolution of queer identity politics.
As gender-focused branding changes, so does 
the dynamic media environment. Although traditional 
distribution patterns for editorial content endure in the 
market (such as live runway events and high fashion 
magazine spreads), newer media create emerging 
landscapes for brands to infiltrate and exploit (Find-
lay, 2019). Social media platforms such as TikTok and 
Y ouTube allow brands to distribute content affordably, 
directly, and subtly to targeted markets constructed 
through consumer engagement, both passive (e.g., 
watching content) and active (e.g., liking, sharing, com-
menting). These interactions are facilitated through 
advanced, often invisible, algorithms (Beer, 2013). Fur-
thermore, consumers are capable of uploading their 
own rich content, enabling makeup brands to better 
understand their own products’ practices, dupes, and 
flaws, as well as consumer needs. Brands can tailor 
content, including the gendering of their products, 
through data-driven analytics afforded by social media 
platforms, which influence the actual buying behavior 
of consumers (Darmatama & Erdiansyah, 2021).
The fashion industry is one of the best-positioned 
to act as an agent of social progress in this regard 
because the trend-centered businesses in this industry 
simultaneously create and serve consumer tastes. An 
increasingly open view of gender goes hand in hand 
with typical industry practices: highlighting the semi-
otics of gender norms and then immediately upend-
ing them in unexpected ways. This contribution to the 
gender Conversation helps create fashion’s air of nov-
elty; brands and producers that do it well accrue social 
currency, bit by bit, in the consumer consciousness 
(MacKinney-Valentin, 2013; Mears, 2011).
But is all of this simply an attempt to commod-
ify and hence profit from a new paradigm of gender? 
It is the nature of capitalism to co-opt social or tech-
nological changes, especially those outside the main-
stream, for the sake of profit. We have to wonder what 
CoverGirl and War Paint’s motivations are: capturing 
the youth zeitgeist, attempting to be distinctive as a 
brand, or embracing social responsibility? These are 
not mutually exclusive, and regardless of the compa-
nies’ goals, what stands out is their willingness to take 
risks in order to expand the customer base and engage 
with customers in ways that would have been unheard 
of only a decade ago. If this shift in fashion market-
ing reflects a deeper one in public consciousness with 
regards to the Conversation around gender identity, it 
is worth investigating how these companies choose 
to engage it, and how the public responds. Given the 


Journalism and Advertising 143
constant visibility of gender in clothing, makeup, and 
so on, we wonder whether—and hope that—it won’t 
be long before brands lead us by example from the 
acceptance of wear what you like to be who you are.
