4.11: PANNING FROM WAR TO 
LOVE: “GOOD OPTICS” AND THE 
WEAPONIZING GAZE OF MILITARY 
WOMEN’S POLITICAL CAMPAIGNS
Mary Douglas Vavrus
This essay investigates how women military veter-
ans running for political office have campaigned 
in a novel way that highlights both their military 
service and their maternal and domestic expertise. 
These appeals often employ a weaponized gaze 
and can shape civic consciousness about connec-
tions between war, military service, and public 
service.
Discussing the women military veterans running for 
elected office in 2018, The Politics Show from NPR 
co-host Scott Detrow confidently asserted, “That 
Top Gun graphic is good optics” (2018). Detrow 
was referring specifically to retired Marine Lieuten-
ant Colonel Amy McGrath’s campaign video Told 
Me.
1 In the video, McGrath, a Democrat who was 
then vying to represent Kentucky’s 6th Congres-
sional District, appears in images reinforcing her 
experience as a fighter pilot. These clearly could 
evoke an association with the megahit film, Top Gun 
(1986), about hotshot naval aviators. A number of 
other women veterans running for office since 2018 
have also centered similar visual narratives in their 
campaign materials: that their military careers qual-
ify them to be legislators and that they can move 
smoothly from combat to public service, all while 
making care and love – for family, for country, and 
for their constituents – their new mission.
In this essay, I dispute Detrow’s assertion that Top 
Gun or any other martial images make for good optics, 
particularly for women political candidates in this con-
text at this historical moment. My research shows that 
in creating their campaign videos, these candidates 
have drawn from the proliferation of media discourses 
about U.S. military women that glorify them for their 
service in the wars on Afghanistan and Iraq. In the pro-
cess, they have naturalized and normalized the incor-
poration of martial symbols and rationales for warfare 
into discourses about compassionate public service, 
rendering invisible the realities of combat and of war. 
At the very least, they encourage viewers to accept a 
seamless transition from war to love.
The Weaponizing Gaze of Military 
Women’s Campaigns
In my analysis, I employ Stahl’s (2018) theory of 
the “weaponized gaze,” a concept that explains 
how video footage of contemporary warfare posi-
tions viewers to be behind the crosshairs of various 
weapon cams, such as those on drones and so-called 
smart bombs, as they zero in on their targets. A gaze 
becomes weaponized when the camera affixed to 
these weapons generates images used by their oper-
ators to aim and fire them, which are also used by 
civilian media outlets; viewers of such footage from 
TV news or war films, for example, assume a position 
from behind the camera as they do when viewing 
any camera image. Stahl contends that such views 
of war now dominate Western media representa-
tions of war, particularly in the United States. Fur -
ther, because the public now views “war though this 
aperture, this gaze has become a powerful means 
through which the military-industrial-media com-
plex apprehends civic consciousness,” Stahl explains  
(p. 3). Stahl’s concerns (and mine) are about how 
these images position their viewers to be sympa-
thetic to the weapons and actions behind the cross-
hairs, and not to the humans who are their targets.
I have certainly found this in my analysis of cam-
paign videos for women military veterans. Because 
size limits for this reading preclude me from detailing 
all the campaign videos in this collection, I concen-
trate on the two most generative: Battle Up, a Marine 
recruiting video released in 2017 whose narrative 
weaves together themes of fighting spirit, compas-
sion, and military service; and Amy McGrath’s first 
campaign video, Told Me. I can only touch on cam-
paign videos of five other candidates for federal office 
(besides McGrath’s) that since 2017 employ the “good 


Journalism and Advertising 145
optics” that so enthralled Scott Detrow. These can-
didates are for House of Representatives, Kim Olson 
(Texas 24th) and Mikie Sherrill (New Jersey 11th); for 
House of Representatives and then Senate, MJ Hegar 
(Texas) and Amy McGrath (Kentucky); for Senate, 
Martha McSally (Arizona); and for President, Tulsi 
Gabbard.
Of course, generations of male military veterans 
have campaigned on their military service (e.g., Sena-
tors John Kerry and John McCain); similarly, women 
have campaigned on maternal and domestic expertise 
to make the case that these life experiences qualified 
them to be responsible and caring enough to hold 
public office (e.g., Senator Patty Murray and Speaker 
of the House Nancy Pelosi). But the way women can-
didates have knit together these two appeals in cam-
paign materials is novel. I focus on them here because  
I believe they are significant in how they may guide 
and shape civic consciousness about connections 
between war, military service, and public service. In 
these campaign videos, the weaponized gaze aligns 
viewers with an ostensibly feminist military appara-
tus – one that legitimates the military as a site where 
combat and compassion co-exist and, in some cases, 
where the former is a prerequisite for the latter.
In what follows, I identify and describe the visual 
and verbal tropes in the Battle Up and Told Me videos, 
connecting them to the concept of the weaponized 
gaze. Then, I discuss possible implications of these 
candidates’ invitation to warcare as it were – a narra-
tive that naturalizes war, erases the violence of com-
bat, and legitimates military service as a prerequisite 
for loving, caring, selfless public service.
First to Fight: The Marine Corps’ Battle 
Up
Battle Up (2017) was the first Marine Corps recruit-
ing video to feature a woman protagonist; she 
appears in multiple settings displaying both Marine 
mettle and care for suffering people. Battle Up’s 60 
second sequence, in which one scene breaks apart 
and fades to the next, begins with the young White 
protagonist intervening in a school hallway fight 
to protect a small girl being bullied by two older, 
taller girls. This scene breaks to the protagonist as a 
young adult playing fiercely in a game of nighttime 
rugby during a saturating rainstorm, when she’s 
tackled while diving for a goal. The scene breaks 
and she’s in a harsh, underwater training course dur-
ing boot camp, which she successfully traverses and 
then runs from through a dark and misty swamp, 
strewn with trees and stumps behind three other 
rain-soaked rifle-bearing Marines. As she looks over 
her shoulder, the scene breaks to a battle in what 
looks like a Middle Eastern country. Behind sand-
bags, she shoots a rifle, and the scene breaks to its 
coda: a setting where, dressed in civilian clothes, she 
delivers blankets to a homeless man in an under -
pass encampment. Over these scenes, a deep male 
voice slowly and solemnly intones,
No one knows where it comes from. Why some 
have it and some don’t. It’s the fighting spirit 
and it needs to be fed. It consumes fear, self 
doubt, and weakness. It stands ready to protect 
those in danger, and to fight whatever shape 
the battle takes. Because as long as there are 
battles, there will always be Marines.
Onscreen text below the video reads, “The fighting 
spirit lives within us. It conquers fear, doubt, and 
weakness. It drives us to serve our country and our 
communities. It makes us who we are: Marines.”
Outraged comments over featuring a woman 
to represent the Marines followed Battle Up’s release, 
which prompted the Marine Corps to issue a written 
response that accompanied the video (it has since 
been removed): “Fans, this is not ‘Social Justice War-
rior’ stuff - just warrior stuff.” After noting that the video 
depicts an actual Marine Captain, the response contin-
ues by confirming her authenticity and explaining that
she’s portrayed reacting under fire like all 
Marines are trained to do, which she’s done in 
real life, in a real firefight. Her story, service and 
dedication to our country is no less than any 
of yours because she happens to be a woman.
(BBC News, 2017)
This video’s visual sequence and the Marines’ 
defense of it provide insights into the mindset of at 
least one branch of the U.S. military, and it previews 
two important themes: the importance of serving in 

146 Content
one’s community and the seamlessness of the flow 
from being tough warriors to compassionate human 
beings.
Battle Up is one among a trove of books, videos, 
documentary films, and other media featuring mili-
tary women appearing in the U.S. since September 
11, 2001 – a media niche that I’ve labeled “Warrior 
Women” (Vavrus, 2016). This niche comprises con-
structions of women as competent martial subjects 
serving in a patriarchal institution that their presence 
has only improved, albeit not without struggles for 
them. As I’ll show in the next section, campaign videos 
signal that the candidates will bring this same martial 
competence to electoral politics.
Locked and Loaded: Told Me and Other 
Campaign Videos
In Told Me, Amy McGrath appears first in a leather 
bomber jacket striding around the nose of a fighter 
jet parked on a runway as she explains how, since 
she was 12 years old, she had wanted to fly fighter 
jets and land on aircraft carriers “because that’s 
the toughest flying you can do.” McGrath details 
her struggles to be allowed into combat roles as 
she matured, finally being permitted to fly once 
she was enrolled in the Naval Academy. “I’m Amy 
McGrath and I love our country,” she explains. A 
montage of shots with McGrath in uniform fades 
into a sequence of two different smart bomb target 
crosshairs as her voiceover enumerates her suc-
cesses: “I spent 20 years as a U.S. Marine, flew 89 
combat missions bombing al Qaeda and the Tal-
iban.” She continues with, “I was the first woman 
Marine to fly in an F-18 in combat and I got to land 
on aircraft carriers,” a statement accompanied by 
a photo of McGrath standing leg up on a ladder 
ascending into the cockpit. The camera shifts back 
to candidate McGrath on a landing strip in front of 
a bomber as she stares into the camera to explain, 
“Now I’m running for Congress against Andy Barr 
in my home state of Kentucky.” McGrath’s challenge 
was, she said, due to Barr voting “enthusiastically to 
take health care away from over a quarter million 
Kentuckians,” and his treatment of “the people of 
Kentucky like they’re disposable.” From there, the 
scene shifts to McGrath and her husband, holding 
hands as they stroll through a grassy field, two 
young children running ahead of them; McGrath’s 
husband holds a third child on his right hip as they 
all traverse the field, a line of leafy trees as backdrop. 
McGrath’s video garnered news coverage that was 
as much about this video content as it was about 
her candidacy.
Campaign videos for McGrath, Martha McSally, 
Kim Olson, and Mikie Sherrill all use some variation 
of the martial movement sequence – some while strid-
ing purposefully – through various scenes of their mil-
itary service, which shifts at various moments to more 
bucolic scenes of their family or political life, as each 
candidate narrates some version of how her military 
service grounds her love-infused desire to hold elected 
office. And although only McGrath’s video contains 
actual weapon cam images, I argue that the gaze that 
bathes these candidates in martial glory is weaponized 
because it both cleanses their combat service of the 
results of violence (as Stahl argues that the weap-
onized gaze does) and it encourages viewers to follow 
– and therefore accept – a sequence of images whose 
visual claim is that moving from combat to com-
passion is a smooth, straightforward, and righteous 
process. Verbally, this sequence is reflected in Mikie 
Sherrill’s description of herself as “a former Navy hel-
icopter fighter pilot, former federal prosecutor, and 
mother of four. I have spent my entire life serving our 
country.” Visually, the camera follows Sherrill wearing 
a combat pilot uniform, moving from a fighter helicop-
ter to a family room where she wears civilian clothing. 
Martha McSally’s first Senate campaign video begins 
with an image of McSally in her Air Force flight uni-
form, helmet hugged to her left side, standing in front 
of a fighter jet. A male voiceover intones, “26 years in 
uniform, she has taken the fight to the enemy…and the 
establishment.” McSally appears again, this time in a 
hangar wearing a flight jumpsuit, to explain that she is 
“now deployed to DC, fighting for Arizona, supporting 
our troops” as a series of martial images of troops and 
fighter jets moves across the screen (McSally was then 
a member of the House of Representatives).
This composition strategy is likely an attempt to 
counteract stereotypical news coverage of women 
political candidates. As Ross noted of such cover -
age: “The kinds of frames which routinely describe 
women politicians and candidates include political 


Journalism and Advertising 147
incompetence, political naïveté, insufficient political 
experience, lack of leadership skills, excessive emo-
tionality, and, most importantly, being not men” (2017, 
p. 59). Campaign videos refute several of these frames 
when they cast a candidate as a pathbreaking military 
leader who has sternly challenged the male-dominated  
military and has been a successful warrior. And 
although the videos are unusual in constructing women 
as competent warriors, they also make a second, more 
traditional, articulation of women – as involved in care 
work, domesticity, and motherhood.
I want to point out that my interest is not in 
whether this was a winning campaign strategy – all 
but one of these candidates, Mikie Sherrill, lost their 
elections; instead, I focus on the social and cultural 
implications of this strategy, the similarities in their 
visual and verbal components and sequences – and, 
importantly, their connections to the Marines recruit-
ing video – no matter who the candidate was. In other 
words, regardless of outcome, the fact that the candi-
dates and their respective teams believed that this was 
a winning strategy is significant. Composed of clips 
generated by the weaponized gaze, these campaign 
videos have inspired viral circulation, which pushes the 
candidates and their stories further into public view.
And even if these videos did not secure victories 
for most of the candidates, they did secure publicity 
in online and legacy media, which boosted their cam-
paigns’ messages. MJ Hegar’s videos from both her 
campaigns, for example, were circulated widely; her 
Senate campaign video, (Re)Introduction, includes clips 
from various cable TV news programs that reference 
her first campaign video Doors. Among other aspects 
of her biography, Doors tells the story of this “Air Force 
combat veteran and mom” witnessing her father 
throwing her mother through a door when Hegar was 
a child. van Zoonen suggests that reconfiguring gen-
der and using conventions of popular culture such as 
“personalization and dramatization” as these videos 
do with their warrior credentialing and dramatic life 
stories (such as those in Hegar’s and McGrath’s) may 
“offer a way into politics for people otherwise excluded 
or bored” (2005, p. 150). Following van Zoonen, these 
videos might be expected to pique the interests of 
disaffected voters. Both Hegar (2017) and McGrath 
(2021) also wrote campaign-accompanying memoirs 
that amplified dramatic parts of their life stories. And 
regardless of whether this video content garnered any 
votes, it suggests that militarization has a place in lov-
ing public service – a feature of militainment that is 
also linked to a recruitment mandate.
The Weaponizing Gaze, Militainment, 
and Militarization
Beyond whether this collection of videos proved 
to be electorally successful, the implications of this 
trend are numerous. First, these videos in themselves 
represent a form of militainment. Singer defined 
militainment as “the fascinating, but also worri-
some, burring of the line between entertainment 
and war” (2010, p. 92). Stahl goes further to observe 
that militainment translates “state violence into an 
object of pleasurable consumption” (2010, p. 6).  
Such content means that the videos’ drama and 
personalization work not only to pump up the can-
didates in the eyes of voters but also to glorify mili-
tary service and weaponry, which occupy a central 
place in all the candidates’ appeals. In this context, 
Scott Detrow’s reference to Top Gun is worth revisit-
ing. Robb made two relevant points about this film: 
That when it was released “Top Gun [was] the most 
successful collaboration between Hollywood and 
the military of all time…and [that] a flood of young 
men…joined the navy after seeing it” (2004, p. 154). 
Navy recruiters set up recruitment booths inside 
movie theaters showing the film, and “recruitment of 
young men wanting to become naval aviators went 
up 500 percent after the film was released” (p. 182).  
Now as then, one condition that film and TV pro-
ducers who wish for support from the Department 
of Defense are required to meet is that they “aid in 
the recruiting and retention of personnel” (p. 26). 
And although campaign videos I analyzed may not 
have such recruitment as their explicit goal, as Top 
Gun apparently did, they drew liberally from the 
Marines’ video, which was  for recruitment. If the 
campaign videos’ glorification of combat service 
resulted in viewers enlisting, that may have been a 
fringe benefit.
A second significant implication of these videos 
resides in their seamlessness of the pan from war 
to love, a treatment that obscures how fundamen-
tally incompatible these two realms are – both in the 

148 Content
practices and affects associated with each. The gaze 
that weaponizes women’s combat service by making 
it a prerequisite for compassionate public service is 
rooted in militarism. Militarism, as Enloe reminded us, 
is produced by a process of militarization. As “militari-
zation transforms an individual or a society, the more 
that individual or society comes to imagine military 
needs and militaristic presumptions to be not only val-
uable but also normal” (2000, p. 3). This is what Stahl 
warned about the weaponized gaze: it has the potential 
to influence civic consciousness by repeatedly placing 
viewers behind – not on the receiving end of – the 
crosshairs, thereby adopting the perspective of those 
imposing violence.
In the case of the candidates’ videos, this is a point 
of pride. Y et the social and health problems the candi-
dates claim to want to solve if elected are those for 
which martial solutions are inappropriate; they divert 
funds from human services budgets to military budg-
ets, from the care economy to the war economy. This 
sequence of images and claims in the videos moves 
the subject, and therefore the viewers, between dia-
metrically opposed affective realms – fear/terror and 
love/compassion – which smooths and naturalizes 
perceived ease of movement between them. When 
the U.S. military budget has eclipsed the federal budget 
for social services and agencies such as the Centers 
for Disease Control (National Priorities Project, 2021), 
this pan from war to love is alarming. If there is any 
hope for bringing these realms into balance, then view-
ers and voters must decline the invitation of the weap-
onized gaze and, most importantly, to warcare.

4.12: LULULEMON IS FOR EVERYONE! 
ISN’T IT?: POST-RACIAL POLITICS IN 
RUN OUTSIDE THE LINES
Seonah Kim and jas l moultrie
The authors use the frames of post-racism and 
neoliberal multiculturalism to examine a lululemon 
advertisement’s visual and textual components. 
They demonstrate how the ad commodifies Black-
ness, rather than challenging neoliberal capitalism.
The Canadian company lululemon athletica, better 
known as lululemon, is a top athletic apparel brand. 
Strategic brand initiatives and expanded product 
offerings have contributed to its growth since its 
1998 launch. lululemon is typically seen as the go-to 
brand for White upper middle class women (Taylor 
& Janelle, 2017), but the brand is trying to shift this 
narrative and positions itself as an inclusive brand 
that celebrates diversity and body positivity, even 
pointing to its “global community” as the place to 
find its “soul.”
lululemon is just one of the thousands of brands 
employing inclusion strategies to reach diverse audi-
ences. Marginalized communities are increasingly rep-
resented across media as models and spokespeople 
in advertising, lead actors in mainstream films, and 
influencers on social media. But is this inclusion a sign 
of progress?
This reading looks at whether the increased visi-
bility of marginalized communities in advertising indi-
cates ideological progress in social justice, especially 
racial justice in the US. Using the lens of neoliberal 
multiculturalism, we analyze lululemon’s Run Outside 
the Lines ad, a racial justice-oriented ad published on 
Y ouTube in August 2020 in conjunction with the com-
pany’s annual SeaWheeze Marathon. After introducing 
neoliberal multiculturalism and post-racial politics, we 
will turn to the ad and our analysis.
Neoliberal Multiculturalism and Post-
racial Politics
Neoliberalism is a political, economic, cultural, 
and cultural ideology that influences and shapes 
individuals’ minds, behavior, and lifestyles. Specifi-
cally, it considers every aspect of human life as a 
biopolitical resource to govern social relations and 
maintain social hierarchies. As a form of economic 
policy, neoliberalism supports deregulated markets, 
privatization, and consumerism. Ideologically, it 
does so much more. Just as the neoliberal economy 
emphasizes individual efforts, neoliberal cultures 
value individuals who endeavor to optimize them-
selves and take full responsibility for all aspects of 
their lives and well-being (Gill & Kanai, 2019). Neo-
liberalism proposes that each of us can accumulate 
more wealth, gain access to healthcare, and obtain 
adequate housing if we work hard. This stress on 
individualism and meritocracy means that failure 
to succeed is our own fault: we didn’t work hard 
enough. This narrative overshadows collective and 
communal possibilities and excludes the realities 
of systemic inequality and how it affects racialized, 
gendered, sexualized, and disabled people.
Interestingly, neoliberalism leaves space for the 
marginalized through its attachment to multicultural-
ism, a national doctrine that considers racial and eth-
nic diversity pivotal to a unified, democratic society. 
Neoliberal multiculturalism commodifies difference by 
affirming marginalized identities and cultures as long 
as they are marketable, non-threatening, and not too 
different. This means that increased representations of 
racialized communities in mainstream media may not 
indicate progress. Instead, the White-good/Black-bad 
dichotomy has been reformulated as valued/devalued 
(Hong, 2015), where some (e.g., Black entertainers) 
are valued but others (e.g., Black people experiencing 

150 Content
homelessness) are not. When multicultural representa-
tions are highlighted as examples of individual achieve-
ment, and when a focus on identity politics produces a 
mere reflection of equity and racial justice, we are left 
with a superficial wokeness, and exploitation stands in 
for progress.
This strategy of commodified inclusion is most 
readily apparent in advertisements in which calls for 
diversity and equity exploit historically marginal-
ized identities to sell products. Kanai and Gill (2020) 
found that advertising, a capitalist institution that has 
been dominated by highly paid White men, advo-
cates for feminism, anti-racism, LGBTQ rights, and 
eco-friendly consumption as a way to promote a 
corporation’s socially conscious brand image. This 
is called affirmative advertising. For example, in one 
Pepsi ad, a crowd of young and attractive people is 
featured, cheering each other and exchanging high 
fives while holding placards with apolitical mes-
sages such as “join the conversation.” In the follow-
ing scene, Kendall Jenner appears to hand a can 
of Pepsi to a police officer. This ad was accused of 
trivializing the Black Lives Matter movement when 
the seriousness of racism and police brutality is rep-
resented in a celebratory and joyful way to make  
it promotable and consumable (Kanai & Gill, 2020).
In addition, corporations often recast and recon-
figure marginalized groups (e.g., people of color, 
overweight people, Muslims, and queer people) in 
advertising, using them as a visually valuable resource. 
By rendering their bodies as a visual proof that justi-
fies and ensures corporations’ devotion to diversity 
and inclusivity, corporations commodify marginalized 
groups as a visual spectacle and persuade consumers 
to purchase their products to be part of this “good” pro-
ject. This strategic inclusivity of marginalized groups in 
advertising can function to maintain – not challenge – 
neoliberal capitalism. Visibility via representation does 
not bring an end to the disproportionate suffering that 
capitalism and racism create. Instead, it offers the illu-
sion of a post-racial society: a colorblind society that 
has overcome and moved past race and racism.
Commodified inclusion also resonates with 
Nishime’s (2014) argument that racial politics of being 
able to see and be seen is about more than who or 
how many people are represented. Instead, it is 
important to examine whether racial others are appro-
priated and commodified when they are represented 
in media, and if they are, how so. Importantly, appro-
priation manifests visually and textually in advertising. 
For example, following a widespread protest against 
anti-Black racism, brands (e.g., Nike) incorporated 
social justice language such as “Black Lives Matter” in 
their advertising, presumably to appeal to increasingly 
conscious consumers.
Additionally, in 2018, Nike launched an adver-
tising campaign with the American football star 
Colin Kaepernick who was dropped by the National 
Football League after kneeling during the national 
anthem as a bodily gesture to protest police brutality 
in the U.S. Despite its explicit support and endorse-
ment for Kaepernick, Nike was also criticized for its 
lack of diversity. The company has less than 10% 
Black vice presidents worldwide (Duarte, 2020). 
Nike strategically appropriated and commodified 
a Black athlete but does not have Black people in 
corporate leadership positions.
Effectively, these ads reinforce neoliberal mul-
ticulturalism – they co-opt social justice movements 
and promote an individualized, performance-like, and 
consumerist approach to activism (e.g., you can be the 
change you want to see by buying this #BLM Nike 
shirt).
Audiences need to understand how mainstream 
narratives deploy the overt visibility of people of color 
to reinforce post-racism and neoliberal multicultural-
ism. We need to identify and challenge inaccurate and 
stereotypical representations of marginalized commu-
nities. With that in mind, we conducted a close analysis 
of the visual and textual (voiceover) elements of lulu-
lemon’s Run Outside The Lines ad. After describing the 
ad, we show how it employs ambiguity (textually) and 
hypervisibility of Blackness (visually) to reinforce and 
perpetuate a post-racial neoliberal ideology.
Run Outside the Lines
Run Outside the Lines is a racial justice-oriented ad 
published to Y ouTube in August 2020. It follows a 
group of nine runners through the streets and parks 
of New Y ork City. The runners are Black, athletic, and 
on the go. Of nine runners, two are women. In the first 


Journalism and Advertising 151
scene, a mixed-racial family is featured: a White wife, 
a Black husband, and two light-skinned mixed-race 
kids. The husband, the lead actor, texts his running 
group. In the following scenes, we see the individual 
runners on sidewalks and crosswalks, running through 
parks, tree-lined paths, and across state buildings and 
monuments as hip-hop-infused instrumentals play in 
the background. We also see them stretch, stop for 
breaks, visit Black-owned businesses, and wave to 
the owners. As runners are introduced, we learn what 
running means for some of them. Through captioned 
voiceover, running is described as an “escape,” a 
“break from the norms of regular life,” and something 
that “belongs to everyone.” The voiceover calls for 
“having people recognize the injustices” Black people 
face and more “dialogue about these issues.” Near 
the end of the ad, we see close-ups of each runner’s 
face, and in the final scene, the lead stops for a break, 
catches his breath, and resumes his run.
Visual Strategy: Hypervisibility of 
Blackness
Black people with their Black skin, wearing black 
clothing and black masks, waving at Black business 
owners as they run past Black Lives Matter signs 
and Black cultural symbols (e.g., Frederick Doug-
lass statue) contribute to a hypervisible presence 
of Blackness in the ad. This all-black-everything 
approach also signals a particular scripting of 
Blackness within urban spaces. Here, running while 
Black is devoid of historical context – Blackness 
as criminal, as fugitive, as a victim of police brutal-
ity – rendering a Blackness that is everywhere and 
nowhere. Also, despite seemingly affirmative, here 
Blackness is visualized through the distinctly White 
gaze of what hooks (1992) called “eating the other,” 
where non-White peoples are commodified for the 
viewing pleasures of Whites. This is most visible as 
the ad hypersexualizes Black masculinity.
Most people in the ad run casually, but 49 sec-
onds into the ad, we see a different kind of runner – a 
shirtless man with a distinctly muscular body wearing 
closer-fitting shorts.
Unlike the others, he also does more. He is the 
only one who engages in push-ups and agility exercises 
prior to running; he runs faster than the others, disrupt-
ing the script of leisure running woven throughout; 
and his depiction embodies the trope of hypersexu-
alized Black masculinity: a dehumanizing narrative 
that narrowly defines Black masculinity as excessively 
promiscuous, aggressive, and uncontrollable. His near 
nakedness and the way the camera films him signify 
sex and produce a dominant White gaze of him as a 
sexualized object to consume, rather than a human 
being engaging in a daily running routine. Just as he 
takes off running, the camera cuts to a shot of him at 
crotch level. Although it does not last long, this shot 
demands that the viewer gaze at this part of his body, 
rendering him an object. Also, twice he is filmed run-
ning toward the camera.
The first time, he is captured up close, running 
so quickly that his body almost fills the entire frame. 
Later, he is shot from a distance, running through 
the park, surrounded by trees, again coming toward 
us. In this ad for lululemon, he is represented as a 
dark body in an urban jungle. Here, his humanity is 
appropriated to convey the trope of the black body 
in motion: as animalistic, tied to nature, and lacking 
rationality. This specific appropriation is overrep-
resented in advertising, both historically and con-
temporarily, via depictions of the fugitive slave and 
professional athlete (Johnson, 2003). Depictions of 
the Black masculine body running in nature cannot 
be divorced from the connotations it produces. lulu-
lemon, while appearing to affirm Blackness, rein-
scribes it to the margins.
The superficial centering of racial justice nar -
ratives, as we explain in detail below, appropriates 
systemic racism as an issue to be overcome in the 
market: by an individual’s purchase of or affinity for 
lululemon. As viewers of this ad, we are expected 
to think through, ignore, support, and/or resist the 
narratives presented to us. This popular, polarizing 
strategy is a cooptation of consciousness where 
ongoing demands for equity and inclusion are inte-
grated to sell products. It is problematic because it 
detracts from ongoing efforts to dismantle systemic 
racism. It is illusory in that it mediates the work 
while overshadowing the actual work of confronting 
and dismantling. Representation matters, but it is an 
increasingly unviable solution for racial equity. And 

152 Content
as an ad, this form of representation is inevitably 
colored by capitalism and the company’s desire for 
profit.
Textual Strategy: Ambiguous Rhetoric of 
Racism
The ad’s textual components reflected ambigu-
ity, implying certain messages rather than stating 
them directly. Ambiguity is a useful rhetorical tool. 
In Run Outside The Lines, ambiguity is employed 
as a post-racial rhetorical strategy (Joseph, 2016). 
Although race/ethnicity and “Black people” are 
mentioned, the issue of racism is referenced using 
unclear words such as “these issues,” “difficult con-
versations,” “what’s going on in the world,” or sim-
ply “injustices.” Never explicitly mentioning racism, 
by employing the voices of Black people to narrate 
(and appear in) its ad, we are encouraged to assume 
that lululemon as a corporation pursues racial 
justice.
The voiceovers and the text of the wall painted 
with Black Lives Matter suggest that these “difficult 
conversations” are about racial injustice. But that is 
never verbally expressed. Instead, it’s coded into the 
neutral or apolitical language of “what’s going on in 
the world” narrated in the following scene. We argue 
that this ambiguous language is deployed as a post-ra-
cial rhetorical strategy. Although the visualized text of 
Black Lives Matter, which people can easily ignore or 
need extra attention to recognize, appears in the ad, 
it is never explicitly narrated as a racial injustice. Con-
trasting the visuals with narration, this ad adopts and 
encodes the post-racial idea that people talk about 
racism as long as the talk does not make them uncom-
fortable. This post-racial rhetorical strategy operates 
to blur and minimize systemic discrimination by mar-
ginalizing and commercializing politically progressive 
attitudes.
The lululemon ad strategically utilizes Black 
bodies and voices to showcase the corporation’s 
consideration of social justice efforts. However, 
it never explicitly addresses or challenges sys-
temic racism. It avoids or neglects words such 
as racism, systemic discrimination, or institution-
alization of racism, the foundational conditions 
reproducing and perpetuating anti-Black racism 
in the US. The use of neutral and vague language 
implying without calling out racism is a rhetori-
cal strategy to frame racism as just one of many 
social issues.
The ad also implies that the social issue of rac-
ism can be overcome by individuals’ efforts, in this 
case, by running. Along with the ambiguous language 
implicitly referencing racial injustice, the ad articu-
lates the meaning of running as a social action that 
can liberate all types of people from social inequity 
and injustice. By representing running as an escape 
from social norms or constraints, the ad turns the 
physical act of running into social, political, and cul-
tural practice. The first runner says, “Running for me 
is a sport but, just a way to escape…just like a break 
from the norms of regular life,” and the second run-
ner continues, “It is a way to get away from what’s 
going on in the world.”
These statements imply that running is not sim-
ply an individual’s choice to participate in a sport or 
enhance one’s physical body but is instead a way 
to express individual frustrations and escape from 
social problems. Running is represented as creating 
an imagined community where racial discrimination 
and injustice no longer persist. Running becomes 
inoculated from institutionalized racism and mar -
ginalization. Anyone is welcome to join running to 
make our society a better place, and they can do 
this by purchasing lululemon.
This ad embeds a politically progressive idea 
or stance into its representation of running. Inter -
twined with implicit progressive ideas, the message 
is that consuming lululemon athletic gear and going 
for a run is a valid way to participate in social move-
ments or activism. Consumers are invited to identify 
as racially conscious individuals when they buy and 
wear clothes from lululemon.
Through close engagement with the visuals 
and voiceovers, we have discussed how an ad 
like this emerges during widespread social move-
ments to affirm Black humanity. Our analysis, 
conducted through the lens of neoliberal multicul-
turalism, reveals an unsettling truth: Visual rep-
resentation of the marginalized can be itself a form 
of marginalization.


Journalism and Advertising 153

 1.
 V

hat are the advantages and disadvan-

 2.
 Media t
exts can be read or interpreted 
differently by different people. Our anal-
ysis uses the lens of post-racism and 
neoliberal multiculturalism. Watch the ad 
(youtube.com/watch?v=Mp7t31KfprA).  
How do you respond to and understand 
it? How do you make sense of lulu-
lemon’s representation of Blackness? 
How do you make sense of the agency 
of the runners?

ch for another ad that is generally

What are your initial reactions to the

5.1: HOW (NOT) TO INTERRUPT THE 
INTRACTABLE WHITENESS OF LATE-
NIGHT COMEDY
Jonathan P . Rossing
Even well-meaning attempts to address social jus-
tice and inequality in comedy can instead reinforce 
exclusionary practices. This essay compares how 
diversity is addressed in comedy on Late Night 
with Seth Meyers and Last Week Tonight with 
John Oliver.
Late-night TV comedy has traditionally been the 
territory of White, straight, and male comedians. 
Shows such as The Tonight Show, The Late Show, and 
Late Night feature a long line of White male hosts 
from Johnny Carson to Stephen Colbert. Although 
comedians such as Trevor Noah (originally from 
South Africa) and Samantha Bee (a White woman) 
have found success with late-night comedy shows, 
they remain exceptions. Numerous underrepre-
sented comedians have made forays into late-night 
comedy (mostly on streaming platforms) only to 
have their shows cancelled in short order.
As social movements such as Black Lives Mat-
ter and #MeToo shape public conversations, some 
White and male comedians are trying to find their way 
into the conversation. Some are eager to showcase 
their commitments to diversity, equity, and justice—
with varying degrees of success. Stephen Colbert’s 
race-centered comedy that critically engages racial 
injustice and White privilege has not always been well 
received or recognized as progressive (Rossing, 2019). 
White feminist comedians such as Tina Fey and Amy 
Schumer have also received well-warranted scrutiny 
for attempts to address racism that ultimately perpetu-
ate dominant racist ideologies (Colpean & Tully, 2019; 
Oh, 2020).
In this essay, I explore the role and responsibility 
of White male comedians in confronting inequity and 
injustice, and consider how some efforts to advance 
diversity and equity ultimately perpetuate oppressive 
cultural norms. I perform a critical textual analysis 
of two acclaimed White male comedy hosts’ efforts 
in this regard: Seth Meyers and his recurring segment 
“Jokes Seth Can’t Tell” on Late Night with Seth Meyers, 
and John Oliver and several featured segments from 
Last Week Tonight with John Oliver.
The Exclusive Domain of Late-Night 
Comedy: Why Study Two White Men?
Late-night comedy has traditionally been a fairly 
non-political experience with material designed to 
appeal to a broad audience without taking a posi-
tion on the most serious of social debates (Peterson, 
2008). However, in the last 10–15 years, White male 
hosts appear willing (even eager) to confront serious 
social issues and injustices such as sexual harass-
ment and sexual violence or the persistent racist 
injustice of police violence against Black commu-
nities. Given the overall lack of diversity in the writ-
ers’ rooms plus the dominant identity positions of 
most late-night hosts, it is important to interrogate 
5.
FILM AND TELEVISION
DOI: 10.4324/9781003193708-7

Film and Television 155
ho
w White male comedians navigate their social 
responsibility around issues such as feminism, racial 
justice, and anti-racism from their privileged identity 
positions and platforms.
Focusing on White male comedians runs the risk 
of continuing to decenter and marginalize comedi-
ans of color and female-identified comedians whose 
voices and comedic perspectives need to be ampli-
fied. I do not wish to displace such perspectives and 
voices. Rather, I believe that conversations about 
social 
 justice—be it anti-r
acism, feminism, queer jus-
tice, disability rights, and so on—demand participa-
tion from everyone, especially people who occupy 
dominant identity positions who can serve as allies 
and accomplices. That said, we must interrogate how 
comedians who hold dominant identities participate in 
these conversations—to call attention to well-meaning 
attempts that reinforce exclusionary practices, to raise 
the bar for participation in the conversation, and to 
invite White audiences to take seriously their responsi-
bility for engaging the conversation about racial justice.
Whiteness remains a powerful and malleable 
social construct and ideology that readily adapts to 
appear less oppressive than it is. Carefully analyzing 
how White male comedians tackle topics of diversity, 
equity, and justice helps us identify ways that whiteness 
persists as a dominant ideology. Like any social iden-
tity, whiteness intersects with multiple subjectivities 
and influences everyone in complex ways. I approach 
whiteness as a “necessary shorthand for a colossally 
powerful social entanglement” (López, 1997, p. 11). 
Whiteness refers to the structures, practices, dis-
courses, worldviews, and cultural norms that produce 
and sustain white privilege and systemic racism and 
exclusions. Rhetorical scholars of race and whiteness 
argue that discourses of whiteness are strategic; that is, 
they carefully adapt to protect privilege and to escape 
detection. Further, whiteness typically is “only invisible 
to those who inhabit it” (Ahmed, 2004); for many peo-
ple of color, whiteness and the systems of privilege and 
oppression it maintains are visible everywhere.
Bits Seth Shouldn’t Perform
A recent trend across the White male saturated late-
night comedy landscape is to feature occasional 
writers and comedians from underrepresented 
identities in short segments. For example, The Daily 
Show with Jon Stewart regularly featured comedians 
such as Larry Wilmore, Jessica Williams, and Wyatt 
Cenac as “Senior Black Correspondents” and Kris-
ten Schaal and Samantha Bee as “Senior Female 
Correspondents.” These artists frequently engaged 
the host in a comedic dialogue about a news story 
where hearing only a White male perspective would 
seem tone deaf at best. “Jokes Seth Can’t Tell,” a 
popular, recurring segment on Late Night with Seth 
Meyers, extends this trend. The premise is simple: 
Meyers explains that the Late Night writers’ room 
features a diverse team of comedy writers which 
pens many jokes that Meyers—a straight, White, 
cisgender male—cannot tell. Meyers says that his 
identity shouldn’t stop the audience from enjoying 
these jokes, so he brings out two writers/comedi-
ans to help deliver the punchlines: Amber Ruffin, 
a Black female, and Jenny Hagle, a White-passing 
lesbian with Puerto Rican roots. The set-up prom-
isingly calls attention to the lack of diversity in the 
comedy business while simultaneously celebrating 
the importance of a pluralistic team of writers and 
providing a spotlight for Ruffin and Hagle as they 
disrupt the whiteness of late night. Moreover, it calls 
attention to Seth’s whiteness and appears to estab-
lish appropriate boundaries and responsibilities for 
how he jokes about race. On the surface, this seg-
ment foregrounds and recognizes the contributions 
of underrepresented writers and comedians while 
seeming to disrupt the strategic silence of whiteness.
Pushing deeper, however, reveals the segment’s 
failure to upend whiteness; on the contrary, it subtly 
upholds ideologies of whiteness and secures the White 
racial frame (Feagin, 2013), an overarching worldview 
that normalizes whiteness and provides a basic set of 
racial ideas, meanings, and ideologies that many White 
people and some people of color use to understand 
and navigate social settings. The segment’s title, “Jokes 
Seth Can’t Tell,” positions Meyers as key character. It 
neither foregrounds the writers of color nor cedes the 
spotlight to Ruffin or Hagel; it directs the audience’s 
attention to the restrictions placed on the White male 
host. Consider some alternatives and how they might 
change the segment’s vibe: “Jokes from Amber and 
Jenny”; or “Jokes Y ou Need to Hear (but Usually 
Don’t)” . The title alone could direct focus away from 

156 Content
Meyers (his name is already embedded in the show) 
and toward Ruffin, Hagel, or his “diverse team of writ-
ers”; instead, it keeps Seth—and his straight, White, 
maleness—front and center.
The audiovisual elements also reinforce the 
centrality of whiteness. The opening and closing ani-
mation features a smiling caricature of Meyers as 
the title flies into the frame. This positions Seth and 
his whiteness and masculinity as the focal points, an 
emphasis underscored by musical jingle which is remi-
niscent of a 1950s television sitcom and evokes a type 
of White nostalgia. The animation concludes with the 
sound of peeling tape as Seth’s caricature is visually 
silenced by a piece of tape covering his mouth. Rather 
than emphasizing the amplification of underrepre-
sented voices or bringing forward historically excluded 
voices, the tape highlights Seth’s muzzling. The staging 
and pacing further this framework: in every iteration, 
Meyers remains in his host seat with Hagel and Ruf-
fin flanking him. Visually centered, Meyers delivers 
the set-up, whereas Hagel and Ruffin only deliver the 
punchlines. He remains the ringmaster, so to speak, 
who dictates the flow of the sequence; Hagel and Ruf-
fin remain visually marginal.
The content also reinforces a White male frame 
far more often than it offers humanizing attitudes 
toward people of color or queer folks. The jokes fre-
quently rely on hackneyed stereotypes with punch-
lines that mostly punch down—that is, they target 
people who are already minoritized—but for the 
supposed authorized identity of the joke teller. Many 
jokes denigrate and dehumanize people of color and 
queer people, reinforcing rigid and fixed identity stere-
otypes. The stereotype-laden jokes become especially 
visible when Hagel tells the occasional joke targeting 
the Latinx community. In these moments, she adds a 
caveat such as “I can tell this one because I’m Puerto 
Rican,” as if acknowledging the problematic nature 
of the joke (particularly from the mouth of some-
one people may presume to be White) but justifying 
it through identity membership. Ultimately, the seg-
ment characterizes a type of “plastic representation,” 
that is, identity representation which appears to be 
meaningful, but is ultimately “hollow and cannot sur-
vive close scrutiny” (Warner, 2017, p. 35). Promising 
to showcase the important perspectives of a diverse 
team of writers, the segment fails to challenge identity 
privilege or counter dominant ideologies and assump-
tions about minoritized identities. On the contrary, it 
ultimately repeats stereotypical and often demeaning 
jokes, thereby reinforcing oppressive cultural norms 
that maintain oppressive systems.
Each segment ends with Ruffin and Hagel inviting 
Meyers to tell one of their jokes. After some over-
 the-
t
op protest from Seth and mock pressure from Ruffin 
and Hagel, he agrees. As he delivers the punchline, Ruf-
fin and Hagel feign outrage and horror that Seth would 
be so boldly inappropriate. Meyers incredulously 
pleads that they told him it would be okay, attempt-
ing to fend off their umbrage before declaring: “Black 
women and lesbians are liars!” This ending recreates a 
familiar White racial frame by presenting Meyers as the 
racial victim. It dramatizes contemporary White fears 
such as the belief that “discrimination against Whites 
has become as big a problem as discrimination against 
Blacks and other minorities” (Jones et al., 2015, 38). In 
sum, the segment tells a story where Meyers gallantly 
opens up his desk to traditionally marginalized voices 
only to have them trick him and besiege the supposed 
hero who welcomed them. Thus, despite the surface 
appearance that “Jokes Seth Can’t Tell” disrupts white-
ness and celebrates inclusion, the systems and ideolo-
gies of whiteness remain strong.
Can a White Comedian Ever Responsibly 
Joke about Race?
Before concluding that straight White male come-
dians can’t broach subjects of race or queerness, 
let’s compare “Jokes Seth Can’t Tell” to a model 
for White comedians to emulate: John Oliver and 
his HBO series Last Week Tonight. In contrast to 
Meyer’s performative allyship, scrutiny of Oliver’s 
approach suggests at least the possibility of agitating 
and rewriting the norms and ideologies of whiteness. 
First, the content and format reveal stark differences. 
Oliver’s weekly news satire is well known for his 
extended segments – a type of comedic investigative 
 r
eporting – that bring attention and awareness to a 
complicated social issue and typically advocate for 
change. Where “Jokes Seth Can’t Tell” showcases 
diversity through formulaic, often stereotypical, 


Film and Television 157
identity-based set-ups and punchlines that happen 
to be penned by his “diverse team of writers,” Oliver 
commonly tackles identity-based social justice issues 
where the jokes punch up at powerful systems, insti-
tutions, and social actors or mock the absurdity of 
systems of oppression. He has addressed issues such 
as racism and incarceration, income inequality, police 
militarization and violence against communities of 
color, transgender rights, voter ID laws and voter sup-
pression, and other issues that require complex inter-
sectional thinking. Dedicating roughly 20–25 minutes 
to each segment topic, Oliver weaves together inves-
tigative interviews, news reports, and expert voices 
from social identities most affected by the issues. He 
retains the roles of joker and anchor, but the show’s 
attention to privileging underrepresented voices and 
lived experiences offers a stark contrast to the hollow 
representational practices of having a Black female 
and a (to many) White-passing lesbian tell questiona-
ble jokes on the grounds that they happen to occupy 
the social identities as the center of their jokes.
Consider a 2019 episode on racial and gender 
disparities in health care. Immediately Oliver highlights 
the broader social injustice: “If you are a woman and/
or a person of color in the U.S. you may well have a 
very different relationship to the health care system 
than a White man.” In the next beat, he also flags his 
whiteness and mocks the fact that he is the person sat-
irizing this bias: “So frankly, who better to talk at you for 
20 minutes about this than me – the whitest of white 
men.” Oliver alliteratively amplifies his whiteness by 
emphasizing and extending the exhale on the “wh” of 
White. He casually mocks the practice of whitesplain-
ing as he positions the segment as “talking at” the 
audience. This opening setup draws attention to Oliver 
as the expected and normative White comedy host, a 
position he carefully works to dismantle as the segment 
unfolds. As Oliver discusses sexist and racist diagnosis 
and treatment practices, he consistently provides evi-
dence with interviews and news segments that feature 
the voices of White women and women of color tes-
tifying to the disparate treatment and encounters with 
bias. As is typical of the news satire genre, Oliver offers 
comic barbs and quips following these segments that 
provide comic relief even as they sharpen the critique 
and target systems and structures of racism without 
undermining or demeaning the traditionally marginal-
ized voices the segment showcased.
Notably, Oliver turns over part of his segment to 
feature a bit by Wanda Sykes from her special Wanda 
Sykes: Not Normal. Oliver leans on Sykes, a Black les-
bian, to supplement his argument, introducing her 
comedy bit with the acknowledgment that “Wanda 
Sykes summed this [racial bias in medicine] up best.” 
In her special Sykes comments that doctors hand out 
opioids to White patients “like they’re tic-tacs,” but not 
to Black patients. She cites her treatment plan follow-
ing her double mastectomy: “Y ou know what they sent 
my Black ass home with?! Ibu-f**king-profen.” Fea-
turing an extended bit from Sykes’ stand-up special 
isn’t the end of Oliver’s disruption. Near the end of his 
critique, Oliver again acknowledges that his whiteness 
necessarily limits his authority on this topic: “I know 
that I am just not the best vehicle for this message. 
What we really need is someone who can speak with 
authority from real experience.” Once again, he turns 
to Wanda Sykes—by welcoming her to the stage. Sykes  
stands beside Oliver, who remains seated while they 
briefly banter. However, Sykes quickly asks, “Am I just 
gonna have to stand here?” Oliver quickly vacates his 
seat as Sykes settles in. Initially, he crouches beside 
her, but she soon shoos him away and out of the frame 
entirely.
Juxtaposed with the “Jokes Seth Can’t Tell” seg-
ment, Last Week Tonight’s intentional disruption of 
the White racial frame becomes even more signifi-
cant. Where “Jokes Seth Can’t Tell” presents a story 
in which diversity threatens White men, Last Week 
Tonight with John Oliver celebrates gender and racial 
representation through direct amplification of minor-
itized voices most affected by persistent structural 
inequities and bias. Additionally, Oliver and Sykes don’t 
simply share the stage, while Oliver continues to host 
the show. Sykes physically replaces Oliver, unseating 
him from the host’s desk, while she assuredly contin-
ues the segment. Through topic selection, the ampli-
fication of underrepresented voices and experiences, 
and other symbolic cues including giving up the host’s 
seat, Last Week Tonight provides model strategies by 
which White male comedians might use their privilege 
to disrupt established racial hierarchies and expose 
oppressive systems of whiteness.

158 Content
Seeking and Screening Models Worth 
Repeating
Although writers’ rooms (too) slowly move toward 
mirroring societal demographics and although 
some comedians of color have found opportunities 
in late-night comedy, straight White male comedi-
ans retain a strong hold on opportunities across the 
industry.
Although some comedians with dominant social 
identity positions seem eager to use their comedic 
insights to broach significant social justice issues, it’s 
vital to interrogate how comedians – and really any 
content producers – who occupy dominant identity 
positions might responsibly, ethically, and thoughtfully 
address social concerns that don’t necessarily reso-
nate with their own lived experiences. We should also 
study how comedians with underrepresented social 
identities give voice to their experiences with systems 
of oppression. For instance, how does Amber Ruffin 
address racial injustice on The Amber Ruffin Show? Or 
how does Hannah Gadsby address intersections of 
gender, sexuality, and neurodivergence in her Netflix 
specials Nanette and Douglas?
Careful consideration is required of comedy and 
other media texts that appear equity-oriented and 
 justice-minded t
o ensure that those texts don’t per -
petuate the systems of power and social hierarchies 
that they purport to dismantle. In the case of “Jokes 
Seth Can’t Tell,” the narrative and symbolic elements 
actually reinforce the identity privileges and power 
structures that the segment applauds itself for resist-
ing. In contrast, although no perfection without flaws, 
Jon Oliver’s ability to thoughtfully educate audiences 
from his dominant identity position makes Last Week 
Tonight a model for comedy writers and other content 
producers who wish to responsibly engage the press-
ing issues of the times.

5.2: A BLOODY MESS: MENSTRUATION 
IMAGERY IN THE MEDIA
Natalie Jolly
Before you read this, be honest with yourself. Does 
the idea of discussing menstrual blood seem in any 
way different than the idea of seeing blood in any 
typical horror, slasher, or otherwise violent film?
When Beth Harmon felt a twinge of pain in her 
abdomen during the second episode of Netflix’s 
2020 hit drama The Queen’s Gambit, her trip to the 
rest room revealed more than just a streak of blood 
down her leg. That scene demonstrated how rare 
it was to see menstrual blood onscreen and made 
visible our cultural squeamishness over women’s 
periods. It’s hard to even imagine a movie or show 
where fighting, stabbing, or shooting doesn’t result 
in blood being spilled and often in an extraordinarily 
graphic manner. Why are we culturally comfortable 
with the latter but remain so squeamish about the 
former?
Despite nearly half of the population bleeding on 
a regular basis, media depictions of the routine experi-
ences of menstruation are rare. We do not see women 
experiencing low-key freak-outs over a breakthrough 
leak or the existential dread of realizing they’ve run out 
of pads. We never learn about the side-splitting humor 
of trying to fish out a menstrual cup for the first time 
or the brilliant messiness of period sex. Instead, we 
watch padBe hennis skirts, neither of which do much 
to honestly convey the daily reality of women’s men-
strual lives. In this essay, I consider the history of the 
menstrual taboo and how those historical roots shape 
today’s queasiness about women’s periods, and by 
extension, women’s bodies. In doing so, I explore how 
social norms get codified in media representations 
and discuss how menstrual invisibility in the media 
reinforces a menstrual taboo. Not seeing periods 
depicted onscreen has broader implications for how 
women and girls relate to their bodies, and I discuss 
some of the public health concerns that impact girls 
and women. I conclude by introducing new media 
imagery that has begun to challenge this menstrual 
taboo and discuss how these more recent depictions 
may shed light on a topic that has long remained in 
the shadows.
Taking the Plunge: The History and 
Durability of the Menstrual Taboo
Hollywood certainly cannot be credited for invent-
ing the taboo on menstruation, and skepticism 
about women’s flow can be traced back to ancient 
times. We can begin with Aristotle, who posited 
that menstruation made women closer to animals. 
According to Mazokopakis and Samonis (2018), 
Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, all prohibit sex dur-
ing menstruation. In studying the menstrual taboo 
in the Judeo-Christian tradition, Phipps noted that 
in medieval Judaism, the Talmud referred to the 
uterus as a “place of rot” (1980, p. 300). The fear 
stemmed from the idea that any baby conceived 
during period sex would have leprosy. The assumed 
connection between leprosy and menstruation was 
strong during those times, and women who died 
while menstruating were often buried with lepers 
because of their implied contamination (Phipps, 
1980). Multiple faith traditions have also limited 
women’s participation in religious rituals during 
menstruation. For example, early Christian leaders 
prohibited women from taking communion (Huf-
nagel, 2012), and traditionally, female Muslim pil-
grims who were menstruating could not perform 
the hajj ṭawāf because they were seen as being in 
a condition of major ritual impurity (al-ḥadath al-
 
ak
bar) (Nurgat, 2020). Menstruation has also been 
used as a reason to prevent women from attaining 
certain leadership roles in many faith traditions. And 
despite Americans increasingly describing them-
selves as having no religious affiliation, the taboo, 
with its deep socio-religious roots, remains.
Multiple cultures have found similar ways to hide 
women’s monthly lady business from view, and girls 
and women regularly miss out on social, domestic, 

160 Content
and educational activities because of a lack of access 
to menstrual products caused by a broader menstrual 
taboo. In India, Vashisht et al. (2018, p. 167) found 
that nearly 65% of girls in their study reported miss-
ing their classes “as a result of pain, anxiety, shame, 
anxiety about (menstrual) leakage, and staining of 
their uniform” and concluded that mothers play an 
important role in addressing menstrual taboos that 
prevent clear communication about periods. Similarly, 
in Kenya, more than one million girls miss up to six 
weeks of school each year because of taboos that cast 
menstruation as dirty and shameful (Ssewanyana & 
Bitanihirwe, 2019). Nepalese women practice chhau-
padi, temporarily moving to small huts or sheds so 
as not to pollute broader society while they are men-
struating (Thapa & Aro, 2021). To the extent that such 
practices represent social exclusion rather than cele-
bration, they can make the so-called impurity of men-
struation seem normal and further substantiate and 
bolster a taboo that prevents menstruating women 
from participating and being seen as equal members 
of society. Interestingly, a primary tactic of European 
settlers and Christian missionaries was to denigrate the 
Native American practice of celebrating menses and 
cast indigenous menstrual traditions as shameful and 
primitive. Doing so shifted the indigenous menstrual 
narrative from one of menstrual celebration to one of 
menstrual taboo and became a strategy for indigenous 
community destabilization and eventual land con-
quest (Baldy, 2018).
The Curse: A Cursed Topic in Media 
Today
Although the menstrual taboo presents itself 
slightly differently in US dominant culture today, 
it is no less pervasive in shaping our cultural 
understanding of women’s bodies. Menstruation 
has largely been invisible in our popular culture, 
and when it has bled through, the depictions have 
not always been positive. In 1976, Stephen King 
brought us Carrie, and in the first scene introduced 
us to Carrie White, crouched naked in the gym 
showers. While blood dripped onto the drain tiles, 
her peers hurled tampons and pads at her, chant-
ing “Plug it up!” Carrie used menstruation to mark 
the character’s shift from awkward teenage girl 
to terrifying, vengeful monster and – rather than 
remove the stigma of menstruation – cemented 
it both in cinematic history and in our collec-
tive imagination. It was a welcome shift (albeit a 
rare one) in 1990 to see The Cosby Show offer a 
touching scene where Clare Huxtable reassures 
her daughter Ruby about the arrival of Aunt Flo, 
saying “People should be very happy when women 
get visits from their aunts, because if they didn’t, 
there’d be no uncles.” It wasn’t until 2002 that we 
see another mention of periods in a non-stigma-
tized context, on NBC’s hit show Friends. And 
although the Friends scene is quick and clinical, it 
nonetheless marked a small shift in how periods 
were discussed in popular culture. Despite Friends  
and The Cosby Show trying to move the needle on 
menstrual representation, these two episodes were 
exceptions to the rule of period omission. These 
rare moments of period positivity were not enough 
to challenge the media silence around menstrua-
tion, and the taboo has endured in part because of 
menstruation’s invisibility on screen.
Even questionable depictions of menstruation 
are better than the silence that has characterized the 
American media landscape. Movies such as The Blue 
Lagoon (1980) may have used period blood to increase 
dramatic tension, but in doing so, they also challenged 
the cultural reticence to depict menstruation. Mov-
ies such as Superbad (2007) have used period blood 
as a punchline, but also have created an opportunity 
for viewers to engage with and reflect on periods as a 
central component of women’s (and men’s) lives. The 
“joke” in Superbad involves a group of lads laughing 
and retching as their buddy finds his pants stained with 
blood after grinding on the dance floor with a menstru-
ating woman. The humor was, dare I say, superbad, 
but did bring an actual depiction of menstrual blood 
to the silver screen. It also reminded us why the hor-
ror of a surprise leak may be such a pervasive fear for 
girls and women, and why period shame and secrecy 
have become normalized. These fleeting glimpses of 
period blood notwithstanding, menstruation has been 
largely invisible in our media environment, with con-
sequences of invisibility extending well beyond the big 
screen.


Film and Television 161
Bleeding T
hrough: The Unmentionable 
Nature of Menstruation
Today, the invisibility of menstruation in the media 
continues to normalize the unmentionable nature 
of periods for a new generation of young people. 
Without periods being a normal part of our media 
landscape, it is difficult to see them as an appropri-
ate subject to discuss in our daily lives. As a result, 
young people continue to grow up thinking that 
menstruation happens on the margins and that peri-
ods are somehow shameful or embarrassing.
Girls learn early that menstruation is unmention-
able (Rubinsky, Gunning, & Cooke-Jackson, 2020). 
Research has shown that until puberty, girls are hardier 
than boys, with higher rates of physical and mental health 
and more competence in social relations. Once puberty 
and menstruation arrive, however, that advantage evap-
orates and the likelihood that a girl experiences body-
 
r
elated clinical depression increases drastically (Rodgers 
et al., 2010). “By age thirteen, 53% of American girls 
are unhappy with their bodies; by age seventeen, 78% 
are dissatisfied” (Brumberg, 1997, p. xxiv). We know 
that body dissatisfaction is the top risk factor for many 
unhealthy behaviors, including eating disorders and 
chronic dieting, both of which increase dramatically at 
the onset of menses (Abraham et al., 2009). It is impor-
tant to understand how menstruation and body dissatis-
faction are deeply intertwined if we hope to address the 
negative health outcomes that girls face during puberty 
(Mills et al., 2017).
But even beyond menstruation, when girls and 
women fail to see the realities of their daily lives 
reflected in their media world, it becomes difficult for 
them to connect positively to those issues. The media 
imagery we consume serves as an instruction manual 
of sorts and teaches us what society expects from us. 
It is hard to feel even remotely proud of the Red Badge 
of Courage when periods remain so shrouded in 
shame and embarrassment. Indeed, Fahs (2020) found 
that women could not identify a single positive anec-
dote about menstruation in their lives. In many ways, 
women’s experience of the invisibility and implied 
indignity of their periods mirror women’s broader bod-
ily relationship, one often characterized by disgust and 
resentment (Roberts & Waters, 2004). These negative 
sentiments can lead to a form of self-consciousness 
characterized by a woman’s preoccupation with the 
how her body looks rather than what it can do (its 
health or functioning) (Jolly, 2018), and has been sug-
gested as a contributing factor in the higher level of 
depression that girls face during adolescence (Seque-
ira et al., 2017). Apprehensiveness toward menstrual 
blood is a touchstone of a society’s attitude toward 
women, for, as Simone de Beauvoir observed, “men-
strual blood is peculiar, it represents the essence of 
femininity” (1952, p. 168). We don’t often consider 
how this silence around periods is just the beginning 
of erasing women’s reproductive experience onscreen, 
spanning first period (menarche) through the last 
(menopause) (Sveinsdóttir, 2017).
Society shapes us, mind and body. Social norms 
influence how we experience and relate to our bodies 
in real and consequential ways, and how others relate 
to us. Media imagery serves as one of those normative 
messengers; a clear and readable set of instructions 
from our culture regarding how to properly perform 
gender and conform to society’s gender norms. Media 
imagery and the social norms it telegraphs justify how 
we relate to one another and what we expect of our-
selves and of others. For instance, research has shown 
that men who suspect a woman is menstruating are 
more likely to see her as incompetent (Stubbs, 2008), 
and menstruation continues to be a justification for 
excluding women from leadership roles and military 
duties unless women agree to suppress their menstru-
ation (Fahs & Swank, 2021). Because menstruation 
remains culturally invisible, we continue to see this 
taboo affect and undermine women, keeping women 
from being full and equal members of society. Period 
invisibility in our media imagery is really cramping 
women’s equality in the real world.
Periods Are Bloody Important: Changing 
the Landscape of Menstrual Imagery
Norms can and do change over time, and media are 
both the vehicle for that change and the location 
within which those changes can be seen. Recent 
media depictions of menstruation have begun 
to show the graphic, mundane, messy nature of 
women experiencing their periods. In 2016, Jenji 
Kohan brought us blood aplenty, depicting the perils 

162 Content
of having a period in prison during a pad and tam-
pon shortage in Season 4 of Netflix’s Orange Is the 
New Black. Similarly, Chris Kraus reminded us about 
the wrong kind of vaginal wetness when Dick mur -
murs, “Y ou’re so wet” only to realize that his hand 
is covered with period blood in the final episode of 
Amazon’s 2017 show I Love Dick. HBO’s Girls and 
G.L.O.W . also waded into the fray, depicting period 
sex in innovative ways. But none with such reality 
as Michaela Coel in HBO’s I Will Destroy Y ou (2020), 
who showcased not only a male sexual partner 
calmly removing a bloody tampon before sex but 
also a matter-of-fact discussion of a clot that also dis-
charged with the tampon. What do all these shows 
have in common, besides a commitment to explic-
itly depicting menstrual blood? All were written by 
women. And adults aren’t the only ones starting to 
see red onscreen; youth entertainment is similarly 
tackling the tricky conversation of periods. Pixar’s 
first feature length animation written, directed, and 
produced by women (Turning Red, 2022) showcased 
– you guessed it – a cringy but funny portrayal of 
teenage menstruation. Media content, especially 
when written by women, is beginning to challenge 
and disrupt the long-held invisibility of menstrua-
tion onscreen.
Screen media are not the only places these 
changes are beginning to happen. NPR declared 2015 
the “Y ear of the Period” to try to change the cultural 
climate around periods. And athletes have also taken 
a stand, with Chinese swimmer Fu Yuanhui disclos-
ing that she was on her period when she won bronze 
in the 2016 Olympics, and Israeli marathoner Lonah 
Chemtai Salpeter posting about running with period 
cramps after unexpectedly adding 30 minutes to 
her time in the 2021 Tokyo Olympics. Kiran Gandhi 
brought the term “free bleed” into popular conver -
sation when she ran the London marathon in 2016 
despite not having menstrual supplies on hand. Simi-
larly, poet Rupi Kaur created a sensation in 2015 when 
Instagram censored a picture of her in pants stained 
with period blood. Instagram later apologized for 
removing the picture, but not before spurring a lively 
conversation about censorship, indecency, and the 
menstrual taboo.
The media imagery we consume has the power 
to challenge deeply held myths about women’s 
menstruation that have long cramped their quest for 
equality. Media imagery matters, and the invisibility of 
menstruation in popular media has left us ill-equipped 
to talk about puberty, periods, and women’s reproduc-
tive cycles. Moreover, it has obscured the very real 
ways that current public health concerns facing girls 
and women (including depression and eating disor-
ders) may be connected to the invisibility of girls’ and 
women’s bodily experiences onscreen. Norms do 
change, and a new and more authentic depiction of 
menstruation may be on the horizon. Let’s hope so 
because it is high time for women’s time-of-the-month 
to take the spotlight.
