5.3: BELLA’S CHOICE: 
DECONSTRUCTING IDEOLOGY AND 
POWER IN THE TWILIGHT SAGA
Leslie A. Grinner
The author presents a framework—applicable 
to any text—that can help determine the extent to 
which media content perpetuates dominant ideol-
ogies. Using the SCWAMP framework, the author 
concludes that The Twilight Saga film series rein-
forces dominant ideologies.
The cinematic version of The Twilight Saga consists 
of five films: Twilight (2008); The Twilight Saga: New 
Moon (2009); The Twilight Saga: Eclipse (2010); The 
bodies, etc.) that exists in current media 
representations of society today. What 
broader social norm is being reinforced 
when this topic is not visible in media? 
How might media depictions of this topic 
change how people understand their social 
world?

164 Content
Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn, Part I (2011); and The 
Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn, Part II (2012). Based 
on a popular book series by Stephenie Meyer, the 
five films released thus far have garnered nearly two 
billion dollars in revenue globally. The three lead 
actors—Kristen Stewart, Robert Pattinson, and Tay-
lor Lautner—have provided major star power and 
sex appeal. Given the popularity of the franchise 
and its actors, it is easy to overlook some of the ide-
ological messages the films contain.
The Twilight Saga introduces us to Bella Swan, a 
17-year-old, middle-class White girl who moves from 
Phoenix to Forks, Washington, to live with her father 
Charlie after her mother remarries. Through Charlie, 
Bella becomes reacquainted with Charlie’s best friend 
Billy Black and his son Jacob, who are Quileute Indi-
ans. Although Bella is introverted and awkward, she is 
easily accepted by her high school peers; she quickly 
becomes the romantic interest of Eric, Mike, and Tyler 
while being embraced as a confidante and counselor 
to Angela and Jessica. But Bella is most attracted to the 
odd and aloof Cullen siblings: Edward, Alice, Jasper, 
Rosalie, and Emmett. The cultural stories of forbidden 
love, teen angst, vampires vs. werewolves, idyllic mar-
riage and family, and good vs. evil are told with all of 
the drama, action, suspense, and intrigue one would 
expect from a Hollywood blockbuster series.
It may seem that I’m overanalyzing these films 
that they are less influential than I make them out to 
be. Certainly, The Twilight Saga follows the same for-
mula as many teen romance films, using rites of pas-
sage such as prom and graduation to maintain the 
focus on youth culture. Furthermore, the pervasive cul-
tural story of forbidden love stands as the foundation 
for these films. But there’s something else—an invisible 
set of ideals that guides this film and others. We need 
to make these ideals or ideologies visible, and in doing 
so, we can become a more media-literate population.
Ideology can be defined as a set of beliefs that 
guide a culture—the most commonly known and 
understood values and mores. However, the role of 
ideology is much more complex than this. Ideology 
tells us who or what is most valued in our culture (and 
by extension, who or what is least valued). It’s so per-
vasive that it lies at the very foundation of our soci-
ety. Media can reinforce or resist ideology. In order to 
analyze how The Twilight Saga reinforces our dominant 
ideologies, we must first identify what they are. I’ve 
developed a framework to help assess the dominant 
ideological positions at work in media/popular culture 
texts and to explore what the material consequences 
of these may be. I call this tool SCWAMP.
SCWAMP, which stands for Straight/Cisgender, 
Christian, White, Able-Bodied, Male, and Property 
Holding, is an intersectional framework. Intersec-
tional analysis explains that ideological positions are 
interconnected and relational. These relationships are 
shaped and impacted by the society in which they’re 
embedded. Being able to identify the dominant ide-
ologies present in media and how we buy into those 
ideologies provides us with a way to either consciously 
conform to or actively resist them. We can become 
more media-literate and thereby more educated and 
informed consumers of media.
I’ll use The Twilight Saga to demonstrate how 
the SCWAMP framework operates. The series is well-
suited for this type of analysis because it reinforces 
dominant ideologies yet obscures this by placing them 
within a discourse of teen romance. Once you learn 
to use SCWAMP, you can apply it to any media text.
Applying the SCWAMP Framework
How can we discern whether the components of 
SCWAMP are at work in The Twilight Saga, and in 
society at large? The components can be easily 
tested by investigating the privileges and benefits 
connected to them, the ways in which they consti-
tute societal norms, and the consequences associ-
ated with deviance from those norms.
Straight and Cisgender
The first component of the SCWAMP framework 
considers both the normative sexual orientation (to 
whom one is sexually attracted; e.g., heterosexual-
ity) and gender identity (how one experiences gen-
der; e.g., if one is cisgender, one’s gender identity 
matches the sex assigned at birth). How do we 
know that straightness/heterosexuality and being 
cisgender are most valued in our culture? Evidence 
of this can be found in the treatment that lesbian, 


Film and Television 165
g
ay, bisexual, and transgender people encounter on 
a daily basis, such as gay-bashing and other forms of 
discrimination. In contrast, heterosexuality is taken 
for granted as a normal, natural part of human-
ity. Adrienne Rich (1994) calls this compulsory 
heterosexuality. When we meet people, we often 
assume that they are heterosexual and treat them 
accordingly.
Heterosexuality is the hegemonic norm in The 
Twilight Saga (as it is in so many films), with the pri-
mary relational focus on the forbidden love between 
Bella and Edward. But these films also convey com-
pulsory heterosexuality by having every primary char-
acter either involved with, pursuing, or avenging the 
death of a heterosexual partner. Although vampires 
have long been conceptualized as having bisexual 
identities, a non-heterosexual identity does not exist 
among the vampires in these films. The Cullen fam-
ily is a nuclear unit with a mother, a father, and five 
kids; four of the kids are involved in heterosexual cou-
plings with one another—Emmett with Rosalie, and 
Jasper with Alice. The audience is asked to overlook 
the incestuous nature of these relationships because 
all of the Cullen children are adopted. Bella’s new 
peers are also preoccupied with heterosexual desire. 
In fact, when Bella realizes that every male in her peer 
group is romantically interested in her, she becomes 
a matchmaker, setting up partnerships between Mike 
and Jessica as well as Eric and Angela. Bella chooses 
to live with her father so that her mother can focus on 
her new marriage; in Eclipse, Bella questions her father 
about his status as a single man. Jacob pursues Bella 
and explains the concept of “imprinting”—an invol-
untary mechanism by which shape shifters find their 
soulmates—which can obviously transcend species 
but not sexual orientation. And the vampire Victoria is 
obsessed with avenging the death of her heterosexual 
partner, James.
As noted above, a cisgender person is one whose 
gender identity matches the sex they were assigned 
at birth. For example, I am cisgender because I was 
assigned female at birth and the gender identity 
“woman” is one that feels natural for me. A transgen-
der person is one whose gender identity does not 
match the sex they were assigned at birth, and a non-
binary person is one whose gender identity falls across 
or outside of the woman/man gender binary. Trans-
phobia is an ideology that highly values the cisgender 
identity and posits that people who are transgender or 
nonbinary are deluded, disturbed, unnatural, and even 
dangerous.
There is no evidence anywhere in The Twilight 
Saga that any character is transgender or nonbinary. In 
most media outlets, and especially in film and televi-
sion, transgender characters are marginal members of 
the cast and are most often played by cisgender actors, 
although there are many transgender and nonbinary 
actors available. In The Twilight Saga, everyone is both 
cisgender and heterosexual.
Christianity
In a society founded in part on the premise of reli-
gious freedom, how can Christianity be considered 
a dominant ideology? Certainly numerous ideolog-
ical positions are rooted in non-Christian religious 
beliefs. However, we continue to conduct life in 
the United States according to the Christian calen-
dar, where even in public schools and government 
institutions, breaks correspond to Christmas and 
Easter. Christian-based discourse—phrases such 
as “sacrificial lamb” and “prodigal son”—pervades 
our language. In film, Christian-based morality 
tales underpin almost every narrative. The conse-
quences for not conforming to a Christian ideology 
can include living with a poor reputation because 
of sexual practices or other choices of individual 
morality. In most Hollywood films, people who 
don’t prescribe to the dominant Christian ethos are 
often punished in some way, such as experiencing 
illness, financial hardship, or unhappiness.
In The Twilight Saga, the Christian ethos is 
best embodied by Edward Cullen. This is ironic 
because vampires are soulless—and, by Edward’s 
own 
 admission—damned cr
eatures. Strangely, this 
damned creature provides a moral compass for Bella, 
especially regarding issues of sexuality. Eclipse begins 
with Edward asking Bella to marry him and her refusal. 
Later, after she talks with her father and confirms her 
status as a virgin, Bella tells Edward that she desires 
to have sex with him. When he rejects her advances, 
saying he fears he might hurt her, she bargains with 

166 Content
him: she appeals to his class status by saying she will 
allow him to pay for an expensive college or car, and 
that she will marry him. Edward finally admits that his 
rejection of her advances is rooted in his concern for 
her soul. Although he’s agreed to transform her into 
a vampire—which would render her soulless—he will 
not engage in sex with her before they marry. Thus, her 
status as a virgin is held in higher moral regard than her 
status as a human being. Bella stands in direct contrast 
to Edward; she has no concern whatsoever for her 
own soul and is represented as largely non-spiritual. 
It is the men in her life, both human and non-human, 
who keep her morally sound.
Whiteness
Numerous examples demonstrate that whiteness is 
most valued in our culture. Most positions of politi-
cal and financial power are held by White men. Spe-
cific racial and ethnic groups continue to be racially 
profiled and are often prohibited from obtaining 
employment, housing, and other resources. Like all 
components of SCWAMP, whiteness is an attribute 
that is taken for granted such that it is almost invis-
ible. In media, we refer to certain television shows, 
types of music, and films as “Black”; we almost 
never hear that a film is “White”—even though 
many are written, directed, and produced by White 
people and contain an entirely White cast. There 
are myriad images of whiteness in media and very 
few depictions of other racial and ethnic groups.
Although it contains a somewhat diverse cast, 
The Twilight Saga also reinforces whiteness as a stand-
ard of superiority. Twilight introduces us to Bella’s peer 
group: an Asian male and female, a White male and 
female, and a Black male. This peer group appears 
throughout the films; the exception is Tyler, a Black 
male who loses control of his van and almost kills 
Bella, who is saved by Edward (Twilight). Tyler appears 
briefly in New Moon, but not in Eclipse. Bella is literally 
the whitest human being in this film. She’s as pale as 
the vampires in the area, and she is desired by boys 
from every racial group. The vampires in this series 
are almost entirely White, except for Laurent (who 
is Black) and several nameless, lineless members of 
Victoria’s newborn army. Although all of the films’ 
other vampires located in the US are represented as 
American, Laurent’s accent distinguishes him as a for-
eigner. He is also represented as a trickster throughout 
the series. He first warns the Cullens about James and 
Victoria (Twilight), then tries to kill Bella when he real-
izes that the Cullens have left Forks (New Moon), and 
is finally referenced as having told Victoria about the 
special abilities that the Cullens possess so that she 
may defeat them (Eclipse). The Volturi—or vampire 
royalty, the most powerful vampires in the world—
reside in Italy and are all White.
Native Americans, on the other hand, are repre-
sented in stereotypical ways: they are closer to nature, 
and some are even animals. Jacob’s explanation of 
the treaty between the Quileute People and the Cul-
len ancestors invokes the history of broken treaties 
between Indigenous and White people in the United 
States. In Eclipse, Bella becomes the first outsider at 
a Quileute Council meeting; her status as a paleface 
is overlooked, even though it is well known that she is 
dating the natural enemy of the Quileutes—a vampire. 
When given a choice between a boy of color who is 
at least half-human and completely alive and a White 
boy who is both inhuman and dead, Bella chooses the 
White boy.
Able-Bodiedness
To be blind, deaf, to read/write/comprehend differ-
ently, to have autism or a developmental disability, 
to be in a wheelchair or to walk differently—in short 
to be disabled—in our culture is to be devalued. 
Disabled people continue to struggle against debil-
itating stereotypes and must fight to maintain basic 
rights to access, agency, and resources. Mainstream 
culture continues to covertly add more attributes to 
the disabled list; people who are overweight, don’t 
speak English, or don’t fit into the dominant beauty 
standard of our culture are often treated as if they 
are disabled. In media, disabled people are often 
portrayed as villains or comic relief. They are often 
placed in media to be pitied, laughed at, or despised.
We are able to discern that physical ability is highly 
valued in a film dedicated (at least in part) to showcas-
ing creatures with superpowers. In Eclipse, when Jacob 
and the werewolves decide to unite with the Cullen 


Film and Television 167
f
amily in an effort to save Bella from Victoria and her 
newborn vampire army, Bella expresses concern that 
the wolves will not be fast or strong enough to fight 
this army. She has these doubts despite the fact that 
in New Moon, she learned that werewolves are faster 
than vampires and have it as their destiny to kill them. 
The one physically disabled character in the films—
Jacob’s father Billy Black, who uses a wheelchair—is 
also a man of color. Edward emerges as the most able-
 
bodied of
 the Saga; he saves Bella by killing both Vic-
toria and her protégé, whereas Jacob is left injured after 
he is overcome by a member of the newborn vampire 
army. In this way, Bella’s choice of Edward over Jacob 
as a mate is justified in part by physical ability.
Male
Examples of men being valued more than women 
and nonbinary people abound in everything from 
language to economics. When people perform a 
courageous act, it is often said that they “have balls.” 
This always refers to testicles; people never say that 
someone “has ovaries” when they’ve taken a risk or 
shown bravery. The common belief in US culture is 
that anything associated with the feminine is weak, 
whereas masculine traits are deemed stronger and 
more valuable to society. A material consequence 
of this belief is that women are paid less than men 
for performing the same work, and work perceived 
as feminine—parenting, nursing, teaching, and the 
like—remains undervalued in our culture.
Gender is written on The Twilight Saga in a variety 
of ways, including the policing of Bella’s sexuality by 
males, as well as her choice to forsake everything 
and everyone she knows and loves to become a 
vampire and be with Edward for eternity. During 
a conversation about the new boy in her life, Bel-
la’s mother expresses an assumption that Bella is 
already sexually active by telling her to “Be safe” 
(Eclipse). Conversely, three men—Bella’s father, 
Jacob, and Edward—place themselves as the keep-
ers and protectors of her sexuality by insisting that 
she not indulge her desire to engage in sexual inter-
course with Edward. Unlike Shakespeare’s Romeo 
and Juliet, where both characters end their lives 
rather than live without the other, Bella is the only 
partner who must give up everything in order to be 
in a relationship. Edward can remain in his nuclear 
family unit and is not required to sacrifice fam-
ily, lifestyle, or his very soul. In New Moon, we are 
introduced to Emily, a Quileute woman who is the 
mate of Sam, leader of the wolf pack. Emily’s face 
is disfigured; Bella learns that in a fit of anger, Sam 
became a wolf and mauled her. Like Bella, Emily is 
willing to overlook and endure the inner beast of 
her male partner and place herself in harm’s way to 
be with him.
Property Holding
The term property holding as I use it here refers not 
only to land as property, but to capital in its many 
forms: economic, intellectual, and cultural. Eco-
nomic capital includes cash, credit, and other mate-
rial possessions. Intellectual capital consists of a 
level of education deemed most valuable by society. 
Cultural capital often includes both economic and 
intellectual capital but can also include athletics and 
other accepted forms of coolness or street credibil-
ity. In media, material wealth and social status are 
presented repeatedly, which reinforce their desir -
ability. Lower class or unpopular people are often 
presented as despicable characters, and the empha-
sis is often on either their transformation into more 
socially acceptable human beings or their demise.
The Twilight Saga is heavily inscribed with issues 
of class. Although her father is working class, Bella 
is most drawn to the wealthy Cullen family. Carlisle, 
the Cullen patriarch, claimed the top spot in Forbes  
magazine’s 2009 Fictional 15 list of the wealthiest fic-
tional characters. The Cullen children exhibit obvious  
wealth: all possess expensive cars and clothing, live in 
a luxurious home, and are lavishly groomed. Edward 
exhibits his elite status by listening to the music of 
Debussy. In contrast, Jacob Black lives on the dingy 
and dilapidated Quileute reservation. His mother is 
never mentioned, and he exhibits his inferior social 
position by working with his hands. Although Bella 
insists throughout the series that she is not materialis-
tic, she is clearly impressed by the trappings of wealth 
enjoyed by the Cullens. Thus, she chooses a damned 
but wealthy creature over one who is mortal but work-
ing class.

168 Content
Media Literacy: A Strategy to End 
Oppression
With SCWAMP as a framework, we can begin to 
understand the multiple and sometimes hidden 
messages that exist in media. They may not other -
wise be obvious to us, for good reason. The more 
comfortable we are with our media experiences, the 
less we question them; we dutifully support existing 
structures that are oppressive to ourselves and oth-
ers. We don’t often think about ideology because it 
has been normalized and naturalized to the point 
that it’s no longer visible to us. It is the air we breathe 
and the food we eat. Identifying ideology is the first 
step in becoming a media-literate society. We must 
take this step in order to work on ending oppression 
in our culture.
Reference
Rich, A. (1994). Compulsory heterosexuality and Lesbian 
existence. In A. Rich (Ed.), Blood, Bread, and Poetry: 
Selected Prose (pp. 23–75). Norton Paperback.
5.4: RACE, HIERARCHY , AND 
HYENAPHOBIA IN THE LION KING
Naomi Rockler-Gladen
The author argues that Disney’s The Lion King  
reinforces the concept of a hierarchical society in 
which it seems only natural that one social group 
(in this case, the hyenas, whose portrayal echoes 
stereotypes of African Americans) is outcast and 
doesn’t receive adequate resources.
If you’re like many of my students, you might be 
puzzled by the title of this reading. Race and hier -
archy in The Lion King
1? Why would anyone think 
about a children’s movie in such a manner? After 
all, if you’re like my students, you love The Lion King. 
In my public speaking classes, I ask my students to 
give an introductory speech about three objects that 
represent their past, present, and future. One semes-
ter, three different students brought in a copy of The 
Lion King as the object to represent their past. Peo-
ple love this film. The Lion King is a hugely popular, 
Academy Award-winning film. It spawned a land-
mark, Tony Award-winning stage show. Disney even 
remade the film using new animation techniques. 
So why take such a lovable, popular film and think 
about what it has to say about race?
Many people are reticent to analyze Disney films 
critically, as Bell, Haas, and Sells found:
Even our own students, occupying a halfway 
house between film critic and mass audience, 
are extremely resistant to the critique of Disney 
film…[O]ur students commonly complained, 
“Y ou’re reading too much into this film!” and 
“Y ou can’t say that about Walt Disney!” These 
students consistently cite four easy pardons for 
their pleasurable participation in Disney films 
and its apolitical agendas: it’s only for children, 
it’s only fantasy, it’s only a cartoon, and it’s 
just good business. These four naturalizations 
create a Disney text exempt from material, 
historical, and political influences…Our stu-
dents’ attitudes suggest that Disney success-
fully invites mass audiences to set aside critical 
faculties.
(Bell, Haas, & Sells, 1995, p. 4)
It’s Your Turn: What Do You Think? What 
Will You Find?
 1.
 Choo
se several different texts and apply 
SCWAMP to each of them. If any of the 
SCWAMP elements don’t apply, explain 
why.
 2.
 W
e all buy into the dominant ideolo-
gies of our culture (SCWAMP) at some 
level, even if we don’t fit into one or all 
of the SCWAMP elements. With a part-
ner, list some of the ways your beliefs 
and actions might reflect the dominant 
ideology.
 3.
 Identif
y some popular culture texts that 
have helped you buy into SCWAMP 
and some that have helped you resist 
it. Explain how the texts support each 
position.
 4.
 If
 you were going to retell The Twilight 
Saga in such a way that the SCWAMP 
elements wouldn’t apply, what would 
you change?


Film and Television 169
Y
ou may feel the same way, or perhaps you’ve never 
given much thought to what the “messages” of a 
Disney film might be. I invite you to put your skep-
ticism on hold for a few pages and think critically 
with me about The Lion King. Here, I argue that The 
Lion King makes the concept of societal hierarchies 
seem natural and desirable, especially in relation-
ship to race.
This is a textual analysis of The Lion King. As with 
any textual analysis, I’m not looking for hidden or sub-
liminal meanings in The Lion King, nor am I arguing 
that I am telling you the correct meaning of the film. 
Rather, I offer my interpretation of what I think this 
film says about race and hierarchy. I doubt very much 
that Disney intended the film to be interpreted in this 
way, and I doubt your average four-year-old viewer 
even knows what a racial hierarchy is. Textual crit-
ics assume that films implicitly teach members of a 
culture about the rules, norms, and power structures 
of their culture. In other words, the media are one of 
the places where people learn about their culture’s 
 ideolo
gy—just as we also learn about a culture’s ide-
ological rules, norms, and power structures from our 
parents, peers, teachers, and clergy.
The Lion King is one of many places where a child 
might learn implicitly about how race and hierarchy 
function in his/her culture, and it’s important for us to 
think critically about what we’re watching.
Hierarchy and The Lion King
A hierarchy is a system in which some members of 
a culture have more privilege, economic resources, 
status, or other form of power than other members 
do. Y our classroom is a hierarchy. The instructor has 
more power than the students. They decide what 
you will do in class every day and have the power to 
assign you a grade. Hierarchies usually are shaped 
like triangles whereas few people have power and 
many people do not. Students outnumber instruc-
tors, yet instructors have all the power. There are 
even fewer deans and administrators, who have 
power over instructors.
Most important, hierarchies are naturalized. That 
is, they seem normal and typical to many or most 
members of the hierarchy, even to the people without 
the power. Y ou have spent many years of your life in a 
classroom, and it seems normal to you that the instruc-
tor has more power. Y ou’ve probably never questioned 
this. Because hierarchies often remain unchallenged, 
the powerful people stay in power.
There are many hierarchies within societies. In 
US culture, for example, we have a gender hierarchy. 
Although there are many individual exceptions to this 
statement, in general, men have more power than 
women. Similarly, although there are many individ-
ual exceptions, we also have a racial hierarchy in the 
US. As Lipsitz (1998) argued, people of color in the 
United States disproportionately live in toxically pol-
luted environments, are more likely to receive longer 
prison terms than White people for the same crimes, 
and receive inferior health care. Unlike many people of 
color in the US, most White people have never been 
pulled over unfairly by police, followed around a store, 
or otherwise experienced racial profiling. Unlike peo-
ple of color, White people can turn on a television set 
and see many people who look like them.
The Lion King is about a lion cub named Simba 
who is heir to the throne of the Pridelands, a fictitious 
animal jungle society. Scar, the brother of King Mufasa, 
longs to become king himself. He enlists the help of 
the hyenas, a group of outcast animals who live out-
side the Pridelands, to help him kill the king and usurp 
the throne. After murdering Mufasa, Scar persuades 
Simba that he’s to blame for his father’s death. Simba 
goes into exile, and Scar assumes the throne, telling 
the other lions that Simba is dead. In exile, Simba is 
befriended by a warthog and meerkat who teach him 
to live the carefree life of hakuna matata. Meanwhile, 
the Pridelands fall apart under Scar’s rule, largely 
because the hyenas have been allowed to move in 
and have depleted all the resources. Simba’s child-
hood friend Nala finds Simba, now grown, and urges 
him to dispense with his hakuna matata lifestyle and 
claim the throne. After seeing an image of his father 
from the heavens, Simba goes home, defeats Scar, and 
becomes the rightful king. Order and beauty is restored 
to the Pridelands.
The Lion King contains a society in which power is 
in the hands of a few, and in which this hierarchy is nat-
uralized and deemed desirable to all. In the Pridelands, 
the lions are the most powerful members of society, 
with all other animals hierarchically inferior. This is 
demonstrated visibly at the beginning of the film, when 

170 Content
the newborn cub Simba is presented to the Pridelands 
as the future king. All of the kingdom’s animals gather 
around Pride Rock, the lions’ den which, physically, is 
high above them, to watch Simba’s presentation. As 
Rafiki, a monkey and spiritual figure, presents the cub 
to the Pridelands, a beam of light illuminates the cub, 
a Christian allusion suggesting divine sanction of the 
cub’s predestination to power. As Simba is presented, 
the other animals in the kingdom bow and applaud 
wildly.
In an early scene, King Mufasa justifies the hier-
archical society to young Simba, referring to the hier-
archy as the “circle of life,” which he claims must not 
be violated for fear of chaos. However, the circle of life 
operates in the interests of the lions, who thrive at the 
top of the hierarchy as the dominant elite. Mufasa jus-
tifies the inequality by arguing that it’s beneficial to all. 
None of the other animals in the Pridelands question 
their inferior status, despite the fact that sometimes 
the lions eat them. No revolutionary antelope group 
is shown plotting to demand more equitable condi-
tions. Even Zazu, a dodo who is the king’s servant, 
doesn’t question the hierarchy, although he is humil-
iated repeatedly by Simba and by Mufasa. The only 
resident of the Pridelands who questions the societal 
hierarchy is Scar, the film’s villain. Thus, the hierarchy 
is naturalized; it’s made to look normal, desirable, and 
necessary for the good of all.
Race and Hyenaphobia in The Lion King
The Lion King contains a number of hierarchies. For 
example, The Lion King naturalizes a gender hier -
archy. The lions clearly have more power than the 
lionesses. Although Nala is shown to be physically 
stronger than Simba, it is Simba who is predestined 
to be the leader. Power is passed in the kingdom 
from male to male, even though in the case of Scar, 
the kingdom falls apart under male leadership, and 
the Pridelands would have been better off with a 
female leader such as Nala. But here, I’ll focus spe-
cifically on the topic of race, and what I believe The 
Lion King says about race and hierarchy.
Historically, racial hierarchies often involve seg-
regation of hierarchically “inferior” groups, who are 
separated from the rest of society and forced to live 
with inadequate resources and few opportunities. 
In Nazi-occupied Poland, for example, Jews were 
removed from society and forced to live in desolate 
ghettos, where they eventually were murdered. In 
South Africa, through the system of apartheid, the 
indigenous African population was segregated from 
the more affluent White population and forced into 
inadequate living conditions with inadequate school-
ing. Similarly, in the Southern US until the 1960s, Jim 
Crow laws legally separated African Americans from 
Whites and forced them into inadequate housing, 
schools, and economic situations. In the United States 
today, de facto segregation and White flight make 
segregation a continuing reality, we have angry public 
sentiment about immigration, and Native Americans 
for years have lived on reservations where they suffer 
some of the country’s highest poverty rates.
In The Lion King, the segregated group is the hye-
nas. The hyenas don’t necessarily represent any par-
ticular group (although as I argue below, their portrayal 
especially in the original version echoes derogatory 
stereotypes of African Americans), but rather might 
represent any hated group of outsiders throughout 
history—Native Americans, Mexican Americans, 
immigrants, and so forth. They represent the concept of 
the feared and hated outsider whom the mainstream 
culture fights to keep out. The order of the circle of life 
depends on the hyenas staying outside the lush Pride-
lands. When hyenas are integrated into the Pridelands, 
the Pridelands disintegrate.
Similar to other segregated groups throughout 
history, the hyenas live in a poverty-stricken land. 
Unlike the lush Pridelands, the hyenas’ land is barren. 
They don’t have enough food. Unlike beautiful Pride 
Rock, where the lions live, the hyenas live in caves and 
among elephant skeletons that are the Lion King hous-
ing equivalent of dilapidated projects in the inner cities. 
Although they’re wealthy, the lions feel no obligation 
to help the hyenas overcome their poverty. In fact, 
when the hungry hyenas venture into the Pridelands in 
search of food, Mufasa chases them out.
At no time in The Lion King do we learn that seg-
regation is not a good thing and that lions ought to 
learn to overcome their “hyenaphobia” and create a 
more multicultural society. Quite the opposite is true. 
Hyenaphobia is never proven irrational. When King 
Scar invites the hyenas to move into the Pridelands, 
all of the lions’ worst fears are realized. Eventually, 


Film and Television 171
the Pridelands ar
e as barren as the hyena lands, and 
the food supply runs out. In response to the decay of 
the Pridelands, the lionesses encourage Scar to desert 
the Pridelands and move on. It is the story of White 
America’s flight to the suburbs. As the old unspoken 
fear goes, if people of color are integrated into main-
stream culture, everything will fall apart. The Lion King 
creates a situation where these fears are justified and 
naturalized. Some creatures, The Lion King tells us, 
really do deserve to live in poverty and be segregated.
The Lion King does contain some positive nods 
to African Americans. Well-known actors of African 
descent provide the voices of prominent characters: 
James Earl Jones as Mufasa in both versions, Whoopi 
Goldberg as a hyena in the original, and Beyonce 
Knowles-Carter, Donald Glover, Chiwetel Ejiofor, 
Alfre Woodard, and many others in the remake. Many 
people of African descent were involved in the pro-
duction of both versions, and the films contain a good 
deal of African music (both of these are even more 
pronounced in the theatrical version of The Lion King). 
However, although these inclusions shouldn’t be dis-
missed, they don’t mask the negative stereotypes of 
African Americans that surface.
The hyenas signify the stereotypical caricature 
of the African American welfare recipient. Popular-
ized in the 1980s, the legendary welfare queen, who 
poached the taxpayers’ money by having babies out of 
wedlock, became the scapegoat for the nation’s eco-
nomic problems. Like the welfare queen, the hyenas 
are the villains in this individualistic tale, because they 
are scavengers taking resources they haven’t earned. 
They aren’t self-sufficient; they sneak into the Pride-
lands and poach food. No explanation is ever given as 
to why the hyenas aren’t entitled to share the resources 
of the Pridelands, just as no clear explanation is given 
as to why the Pridelands disintegrate when the hyenas 
are integrated. The needy hyenas simply are assumed 
to be unworthy scavengers.
Physically, in the original version, the hyenas 
resemble the post-slavery Black Sambo stereotype 
that was prevalent in US popular culture for many 
years, including in the popular radio and television 
series Amos ’n Andy. This stereotype emerged from 
the traditional minstrel show, in which African Ameri-
can or White men would mock African Americans by 
covering their faces with unnaturally dark blackface, 
exaggerating common African American physical 
features, and acting comically inarticulate and insipid. 
The hyenas resemble this stereotype. They have bulg-
ing eyes, protruding lips, and as Scar describes them, 
“vacant expressions.” They laugh hysterically and 
loudly all the time. Two of the main character hye-
nas show some intelligence, but the hyena Ed is the 
ultimate Sambo. He never speaks; he just laughs and 
laughs, and wags his protruding tongue like a rabid dog.
The hyenas represent an odd, contradictory mix 
of racial phobias. They are violent, and the lions’ ste-
reotypes of the violent hyenas are justified throughout 
the hyenas’ actions. At the same time, they are help-
lessly buffoon-like—especially Ed. They are at the bot-
tom of the food chain and scarcely can find enough 
food to stay alive. When Scar instructs the hyenas to 
kill young Simba, they fail miserably, falling into a pile 
of thorns as they run after the cub. In accordance with 
their dishonest nature, they lie to Scar and claim they 
have killed Simba. This is similar to stereotypes of 
minoritized groups throughout history, including Afri-
can Americans, who contradictorily are considered by 
many to be ignorant, yet somehow frighteningly vio-
lent. In addition, the hyenas roam together like gang 
members, representing stereotypical fears of gangs of 
minoritized people.
Scar’s use of the hyenas to usurp the throne 
reflects the fear that people of color might be mobi-
lized to overthrow the powers that be, reminiscent of 
Birth of a Nation (Griffin, 1915), the epic Ku Klux Klan 
propaganda film in which Northern outsiders mobi-
lize evil, stereotypical former slaves to wreak havoc 
upon the South. In addition, the original version of “Be 
Prepared,” the musical sequence in which Scar invites 
the hyenas to support his coup, alludes visually to Hit-
ler’s propaganda film Triumph of the Will (Riefenstahl, 
1935). The hyenas march in perfect procession, their 
forms emphasized by tall, looming shadows, a scene 
that echoes the high-stepping, redundant marching 
scenes from Triumph of the Will. Scar, through this 
analogy, is like Hitler. “Stick with me and you’ll never 
go hungry again!” he roars throughout the canyon, 
a promise similar to Hitler’s promise in the skeletal 
remains of post-World War I Germany. The analogy 
between the hyenas and the Nazis is evidence of the 
film’s justification of the race hierarchy. The Nazis, 
after all, are widely understood as racial oppressors, 

172 Content
not as victims of an unjust racial hierarchy; by com-
paring the hyenas to Nazis, the film shows no sympa-
thy for the hyenas’ plight.
The hyenas, as it turns out, fight miserably in the 
final race battle between the lions and the hyenas. The 
race hierarchy is restored at the conclusion of The Lion 
King. The surviving hyenas presumably are sent back 
to the shadowy place, and the Pridelands are once 
again idyllic. The circle of life is restored—and part of 
that circle of life includes the exclusion of the outsider 
hyenas.
Reconsidering the Circle of Life
We live in an unjust, hierarchical world. A relatively 
small number of people have access to wealth, priv-
ilege, and opportunity, while millions and even bil-
lions of others live in poverty and have little access 
to resources. In the United States, we live in a nation 
where equality and justice are valued highly, and yet 
our nation is filled with economic, gender, and racial 
hierarchies.
One might say that this is just the way the world 
works. Some people will always have more money, sta-
tus, freedom, and resources than other people. How-
ever, the fact that hierarchies do seem like “the way 
the world works” is evidence that they have become 
naturalized. It seems natural, normal, and perhaps 
even desirable that some people are more powerful 
than others.
But it’s just a children’s film, you might say. How 
can a children’s film have such impact? It is precisely 
because The Lion King is seen as just entertainment 
and just a children’s film that it does have impact. 
Viewers don’t take it seriously. People assume that as a 
popular, lovable Disney film, its message must be pos-
itive. The film’s larger ideological implications remain 
unchallenged.
The Lion King is by no means the only example of 
media content that teaches us about concepts such as 
race, segregation, and hierarchy. As you read this book, 
you’ll find other discussions of media texts that rein-
force similar lessons. As I noted earlier, an assumption 
of textual media analysis is that through the media, 
members of a culture learn implicitly what the rules, 
norms, and power structure of their culture ought to 
be—the ideology of their culture. Certainly, The Lion 
King does not turn children into racists. However, 
when members of a culture view many messages such 
as The Lion King, the ways in which we as a culture 
view ideological concepts such as race, segregation, 
and hierarchy are shaped.
NOTE
 1.  T he arguments made in this reading apply equally 
to the original, traditionally animated 1994 version 
and the photorealistic computer animated 2019 ver -
sion. It is worth noting that the fundamentally different 
approach to the animation in the remake precludes 
some of the artistic liberties taken in the original.

5.5: MOANA AND RAYA TO THE 
RESCUE: NEW REPRESENTATIONS OF 
DISNEY HEROINES
Sarah E. Fryett
This analysis of Moana and Raya and the Last 
Dragon argues that Moana and Raya represent 
new types of Disney heroines: young women who 
transgress previous gender and racial representa-
tions steeped in the norms of patriarchy and white 
privilege.
In a scene peppered with humor from Raya and 
the Last Dragon, Raya observes: “Only a monster 
would choose to wear this outfit on the regular,” 
a reflection on her constricting and uncomforta-
ble clothing. This comment introduces viewers to 
a new type of Disney heroine – one that refuses 
traditional tight-fitting, revealing clothing. Raya’s 
image as a new type of Disney heroine does not 
stop at that, but encompasses progressive traits 
including emotional and physical strength, belief in 
herself and self-sufficiency, and determination to 
rescue her community from the Druun, a sickness 
conceived from human conflict. Moana, from the 
Disney film Moana, offers viewers a similar image. 
Both heroines are people of color: Moana is Poly-
nesian, and Raya is Southeast Asian. Unlike Dis-
ney’s traditional female protagonists (Cinderella, 
Sleeping Beauty, Ariel, and Jasmine), Moana and 
Raya demonstrate an individual agency that allows 
them to work to alleviate their communities’ suf-
fering. Moana and Raya are Disney heroines who 
transgress previous gender and racial representa-
tions steeped in the norms of patriarchy and White 
privilege.
This essay, through a textual analysis of Moana 
and Raya, examines how and in what way that trans-
gression occurs. I begin with a brief look at why it 
is necessary to examine Disney representations 
and their effects. Then, I look to scholarship on 
specific Disney films in order to substantiate a con-
versation about the representation of gender and 
race. Subsequently, I offer an overview of the two 
films discussed. I then argue that Moana and Raya, 
although not perfect, offer a new vision of a Disney 
heroine in two unique ways: the films emphasize the 
importance and necessity of strong female friend-
ships, and Moana and Raya demonstrate a fierce 
emotional and physical strength. Together these 
elements allow our heroines to embark on their 
successful quests and restore peace and prosperity 
to their suffering communities. In other words, they 
become the rescuers.
Studying Disney Princesses and 
Heroines
It is important to examine this vision of a Disney 
heroine, because Disney representations affect all 
our children in many ways in relation to normative 
gender roles and racial privileging. In an extensive

other on the topic. Afterward, discuss the 
exercise and the film. Has your perspec-
tive on The Lion King changed after this 
activity? Do you agree with me that The 
Lion King promotes segregation?
 4.

gine you wanted to create a film like 
The Lion King but one that didn’t promote 
segregation. Could you tell the same 
story in a different (more inclusive) way? 
How? Using the same characters, what 
other stories could you tell that would be 
compelling but not exclusionary?

174 Content
study of young girls, Golden and Jacoby (2018) 
found that four themes surround young girls’ prin-
cess play regardless of race or ethnicity: emphasis 
on physical appearance, objectification of female 
bodies, embrace of traditionally feminine behavior 
through body movements, and exclusion of males. 
By analyzing the princess play of these young 
girls, Golden and Jacoby located a disturbing 
trend in the performance of normative femininity 
and its inherent restrictions and objectifications, 
at least in part, a result of Disney films and its 
surrounding industry. A similar conclusion was 
reached by Coyne, who found “that engagement 
with Disney Princesses can be limiting, as young 
girls especially are more likely to embrace tradi-
tional female stereotypes” (2016, p. 1923) – not 
only at the time of viewing, but also for the long 
term. Although the studies are not exhaustive, 
they show that Disney tales cannot be dismissed 
as “just a story” because their effects are evident 
and demonstrate the perpetuation of normative 
femininity.
The influence of Disney representations 
extends into elements of White supremacy and priv-
ilege. Hurley (2005) examined the effects of classic 
and modern Disney versions of fairy tales on chil-
dren of color and found: “The problem of perva-
sive, internalized privileging of Whiteness has been 
intensified by the Disney representation of fairy tale 
princesses which consistently reinforces an ideology 
of White supremacy” (p. 223). She added: “The Dis-
ney film versions … reveal indisputable evidence of 
White privileging and a binary color symbolism that 
associates White with goodness and black with evil” 
(p. 224). The lack of people of color in traditional 
Disney films, coupled with occasional representa-
tions which connote evil, leads to marginalization 
and discrimination, which affects how children view 
themselves and others. Since the 1990s, however, 
Disney has presented some female protagonists of 
color: Pocahontas, Mulan, Jasmine (Aladdin), Tiana 
(The Princess and the Frog), Moana, and Raya. A 
total of six! I cannot discuss all these protagonists 
of color, but before moving to my main analysis of 
Moana and Raya, I pause to examine Mulan – the 
first Asian (Chinese) character.
Mulan, Disney’s First Asian Heroine
Mulan’s relationship to the newer vision of Asian her-
oines must be contextualized. Scholarship on Mulan 
traverses the gamut. One sector examines globaliza-
tion and hybridization in relation to the different nar-
rative versions. Another contingent argues that Mulan 
is a feminist hero, challenging gender norms; others 
argue Mulan reaffirms hegemonic femininity. Xu and 
Tian, cataloguing the adaptations, reformulations, and 
as they say “deformations,” of the story of Mulan, con-
tended that the Disney version alters the narrative in 
order to appeal to American audiences in what they 
term Disneyfication: “the products of other cultures 
are Americanised according to American values, ide-
ologies and expectations, in line with Disney’s organi-
zational imperative and formulaic approaches” (2013, 
p. 205). Simply put, the 2,400-year-old story of Mulan 
has been appropriated. Dong adds that the Disney ver-
sion of the “Ballad of Mulan” exoticizes Chinese cul-
ture and that “Disney attempted to authenticate Mulan 
as the Oriental ‘other’ that, ironically, represents the 
values of the American ‘self’ in order to appeal to an 
American and international audience” (2006, p. 229). 
Such contentions showcase the complicated and con-
troversial process of adaptation.
Another avenue of critique for Mulan focuses 
on Mulan herself – What does it mean that she dons 
men’s garb to fight in the army in place of her father? Is 
she a heroine? Does her return to the domestic sphere 
after completing her quest complicate her character-
ization as a heroine? Dundes and Streiff’s analysis of 
Tiana (The Princess and the Frog) and Mulan concluded 
that protagonists of color are not entitled to the same 
life of opulence as White princesses are, and that 
Mulan, although seemingly a feminist icon, continues 
a traditional feminine role as a devoted daughter and 
family member (2016, p. 4). They argued that Mulan 
joins the army “to fulfill her traditional domestic role 
that has been portrayed as full of sexist prescriptions 
like beauty norms” (p. 4) and returns willingly and hap-
pily to that feminine sphere at the film’s end. Concerns 
abound in relation to Mulan – from Orientalist appro-
priation to continued sexism. However, we must note 
that Mulan, even with her drawbacks, is a far cry from 
Snow White or Sleeping Beauty in her ability to briefly 
act of her own volition and not rely on a male savior.


Film and Television 175
Moana and R
aya
Prior to discussing Moana and Raya as characters, 
I’ll provide a brief overview of each film. Moana 
(2016) is set on an island that is slowly wasting away 
due to environmental disease caused by the theft 
of the goddess Te Fiti’s heart. In order to combat 
the disease, Moana must travel the seas to find and 
return the heart. Along the way, she must convince 
the demigod thief, Maui, to help restore it.
Raya and the Last Dragon (2021) begins similarly 
with a plague, known as the Druun that is destroying 
the land and turning everything into stone. This back-
ground story concludes with several dragons creat-
ing a gem that eliminated the Druun. The film then 
fast-forwards 500 years to the tribe of heart, including 
Raya and her father Chief Benja, who are the guardi-
ans of the gem. During a clash of the different tribes, 
the gem is shattered, and the Druun return. Raya’s goal 
is to reunite the pieces and rid the lands of the Druun.
Both Moana and Raya traverse long distances 
and dangerous territories to restore their communities. 
Neither is a princess per se, but both are daughters of 
tribe chiefs and thus embody similar roles. Although 
these representations of Polynesian and Southeast 
Asian characters are not perfect, Moana and Raya 
ultimately challenge traditional Disney images of nor-
mative femininity and White privilege and supremacy, 
by maintaining strong female friendships among peo-
ple of color and exemplifying emotional and physical 
strength. These interrelated themes foster a transfor-
mation of the normative Disney narrative: our hero-
ines, instead of requiring a rescuer, become the rescuer 
of their communities.
Strong Female Friendship among Women of  
Color
Genuine female friendship is rare in Disney films 
(and media in general); however, Moana and Raya – 
to slightly different degrees – offer visions of just that. 
Both films depict strong female friendships devoid 
of competition and pettiness. Moana’s relationship 
with Grandma Tala and Raya’s relationship with 
her friend Sisu (who takes both dragon and human 
forms) offer positive and productive images of 
women’s solidarity. Grandma Tala, an at-times-batty 
but ultimately funny and kind older woman, offers 
Moana guidance and love throughout the film, 
even through afterlife spirit visits. She encourages 
Moana’s appreciation for the ocean (a love that is 
discouraged by Chief Tui, Grandma Tala’s son and 
Moana’s father) and suggests that she pursues that 
passion. Their bond also takes a co-conspiratorial 
turn when Grandma Tala finds Moana playing by 
the ocean after Chief Tui expressively told her not 
to do so. Moana worries that he may find out, but 
her Grandma responds: “I’m his Mom; I don’t have 
to tell him anything,” clearly demonstrating that she 
is on Moana’s side.
Throughout the first part of the film, before Moa-
na’s quest, Grandma Tala offers wisdom, inspiring 
Moana to recognize her own strength and the need 
to travel beyond the reef to save her community. Her 
last word to Moana, as she is passing, is “Go” – a final 
note of encouragement and support. Even though 
Grandma Tala dies, her spirit returns, first as a ray and 
then in human form. When Moana doubts her ability 
to complete the quest, Grandma Tala’s spirit visits her 
boat and observes: “Y ou’re a long ways past the reef.” 
Moana laments: “I tried, Grandma… I couldn’t do it. I 
am not the right person. Y ou have to choose someone 
else.” Grandma Tala responds: “I never should’ve put 
so much on your shoulder.” Those words recognizing 
Moana’s fear foster a realization: She will complete 
the task of restoring Te Fiti’s heart. Grandma Tala, at 
every step of the way, remains a beacon of guidance 
and love; her friendship empowers Moana’s quest to 
rescue the village community.
In Raya and the Last Dragon, Raya’s relationship 
with the dragon (and occasional human) Sisu also 
offers an image of female solidarity. At a low point 
in her quest to reunite the broken gem pieces, Raya 
sits by the river, recites a short prayer, and lights some 
incense. As her tears drop, Sisu emerges. Sisu plays 
what I see as an older sister role, offering support and 
encouragement (and humor: “I’m not like the best 
dragon.”) Without hesitation, Sisu offers to help Raya 
restore the gems. Sisu often lends her expertise to aid 
Raya. For example, Sisu uses her dragon tail as a motor 
to help everyone escape Raya’s nemesis, Namaari. 
Similarly, when Raya is unable to defeat Namaari in the 
land of Spine, Sisu uses her powers of fire-breathing to 

176 Content
create chaos so Raya and her friends can escape. Such 
moments occur throughout the film and demonstrate 
how Sisu encourages Raya and her goals.
One of the most important aspects of Sisu’s 
friendship, though, is inspiring Raya to work on trust. 
Conversations about trust pervade the film, and Sisu 
offers many variations on the following general sen-
timent: “Maybe the world’s broken because you don’t 
trust anyone.” Although Raya is initially unreceptive, 
Sisu persists in encouraging her to embrace trust as 
an avenue. After Sisu’s accidental death, Raya and 
Namaari fight. Raya hears Sisu’s words in her mind 
and realizes Sisu was correct: “It’s about trust,” and 
she begins to trust. She hands Namaari her gem pieces 
and observes: “I’m doing the one thing Sisu wanted 
us to do.” Namaari reunites the pieces, and the Druun 
are destroyed. Sisu’s advice and Raya’s belief in that 
advice brought the clans together and made the land 
whole again.
The affirming friendship offered by Grandma 
Tala to Moana and Sisu to Raya engendered confi-
dence and resolve in our heroines, enabling them to 
fulfill their commitments to the tribes. Although their 
relationships appear different on the surface, they each 
embody a positive and productive female friendship – 
of people of color – that sustains the significance of 
women’s solidarity and community.
Exemplifying Emotional and Physical Strength
Moana and Raya, unlike other Disney heroines 
or princesses, demonstrate emotional and physi-
cal strength throughout the films. Just think about 
heroines of other Disney films. Although Jasmine 
and Mulan have significantly more agency than, 
say, Sleeping Beauty does, Moana and Raya por -
tray people of color having a holistic agency. From 
the very first time we meet Moana, she embodies 
a daring spirit that, despite her youth, showcases 
her strength. When the spirit of the sea calls her 
to extract the heart of Te Fiti, she is unafraid. That 
unswerving fearlessness grows and deepens as she 
matures. At one point, during her first venture off  
the island in a boat, she capsizes. As she struggles 
to right the boat, fear overwhelms, but she wran-
gles the boat upright and proceeds home. Although 
this moment of fear affects her deeply, she puts it 
aside to embark on her quest to save her village. 
Moana’s physical strength is evident throughout 
her journey: saving the demigod Maui, steering her  
boat through storms and rough weather, and ulti-
mately returning Te Fiti’s heart. Her physical agility 
allows her to escape when Maui locks her in a cave, 
and to fight, with brawn, a bunch of creepy pirate 
coconuts.
Along with these demonstrations of physical 
courage, Moana shows emotional strength. Her father 
says: “Y ou are the future of our people, Moana,” and 
she understands and accepts that responsibility. She 
helps her people: When the diseased fish and coconut 
trees are discovered, she suggests practical solutions. 
Once they realize that those measures are insuffi-
cient, she vows to leave the island to save her peo-
ple, thus demonstrating emotional resolve. The film 
contains many more examples of her emotional and 
mental strength, which are also linked to her physical 
strength. For example, when she encounters Maui, she 
emphatically states: “I am Moana of Motuni, you will 
board my boat.” Her ability to stand up, as a mortal, 
to a demigod and ask for what she needs to save her 
village emphasizes her unique mental strength. She 
uses her intellect to distract Tamatoa, the large crab 
obsessed with things that glitter, from hurting Maui. 
Maui appears grateful, and slowly, through Moana’s 
encouragement, recognizes that he should work with 
her, saying “I want to help.” She uses her emotional 
strength not only to combat villains and ensure her 
people’s sustenance, but also to support her new-
found friend. As her journey continues, she gains 
confidence in herself; she determines to restore Te  
Fiti’s heart: “I will restore the heart of Te Fiti.” Moana 
and Maui descend on the island where Te Ka – the evil 
version of Te Fiti – resides, and Maui begins a battle 
while Moana secretively ascends the cliff to return the 
heart. Te Ka subsides, and Te Fiti returns – as a flower-
ing goddess. Moana has eliminated the diseased fruit 
and fish. Her physical and emotional strength, sup-
porting her dedication and determination to save the 
village, establish Moana as a heroine who is a positive 
role model for young girls’ play through her demon-
strated agency.
Raya similarly exhibits physical and emotional 
strength, offering a positive role model. The first 
moment viewers meet her she is stealthily moving 


Film and Television 177
thr
ough a narrow passage, working to gain entrance 
to a cave. Upon her arrival, she meets and fearlessly 
fights her father. The altercation – all in good fun – 
exhibits her precise, conscientious swordplay skill. 
Shortly thereafter, Raya’s emotional courage is dis-
played when her father is one of the earliest casualties 
of the Druun’s return. She refuses to allow her grief and 
anger to overwhelm her, and she resolves to unite the 
scattered gem pieces to defeat the Druun and return 
the tribes to peace.
Raya’s fearlessness as she sets out on this difficult 
task is reminiscent of Moana’s. Raya’s skills regarding 
physical and emotional strength shine through many 
attempts to locate the gem pieces: when she quickly 
sidesteps several booby traps, creates a daring escape 
through water to avoid extra-large cats, and tricks a 
super smart baby. A bit later, she encounters the last 
member of clan Spine, Tong. Tong captures Raya, but 
she breaks free and convinces him to join her. As her 
crew is leaving, Namaari descends, and Raya con-
fronts her, telling herself: “Note to self, don’t die.” Not 
only is she brave in the face of adversity, but she is also 
aware of not taking herself too seriously. She fights 
Namaari single-handedly, so that the folks in her small 
crew can escape.
In the final land of Fang, Namaari’s land, Raya 
simultaneously employs physical and emotional 
strength to rescue not just her tribe but all the tribes 
from the Druun. She confronts Namaari for another 
battle – a battle of incredible physical fighting where 
both are locked in a duel of swords. Interestingly, dur-
ing this moment, Raya pauses and realizes that all the 
people of Fang are slowly being turned to stone by the 
Druun. She immediately stops the fight to rescue them, 
remembers that uniting the gem pieces is the goal, and 
sacrifices herself – momentarily – to hand Namaari all 
the pieces. Namaari unites them, and as noted above, 
the Druun are repelled. Once the plague vanishes, the 
lands of the tribes become fertile and the fighting 
ceases. Raya is the catalyst; she is a heroine of strength 
and courage and commitment to her community.
Rescuing the Disney Heroine
Moana and Raya – as new representations of Dis-
ney heroines – rescue their respective communities. 
These two characters, Polynesian and Southeast 
Asian, though clearly couched in some traditional 
Disney components (e.g., idealized thin bodies), 
are a significant improvement from previous char -
acterizations. For one, there is a lack of any type 
of romantic attachment or return to the domestic 
sphere, which place these films above the minimal 
agency visible in Mulan. As non-White characters, 
Moana and Raya offer a vision of female bodies and 
of female agency that embraces diversity, eschews 
White privilege, and transforms traditional gen-
der norms. Their physical and emotional strength, 
demonstrated throughout many feats, crystalizes this 
vision. Moreover, the representations of Grandma 
Tala and Sisu maintain the importance of female 
friendship and community. These representations, 
although not without flaws, offer positive role mod-
els for all children – regardless of gender, race, or 
ethnicity. Moana and Raya have rescued the Disney 
image of a heroine.
It’s Your Turn: What Do You Think? What 
Will You Find?
 1.
 P
ositive images of heroines exist in 
other realms outside of Disney films. 
Pick a children’s television series, novel, 
or magazine, and examine the charac-
teristics of those heroines. Identify the 
positive and negative aspects of these 
characters’ portrayal.
 2.
 T
he essay mentions that although the 
characterizations of Moana and Raya 
are largely positive, they are in some 
ways flawed. What flaws do you see? 
How could the film or story be changed 
to remove these flaws?
 3.
 T
his essay focuses on young heroines. 
What characteristics of heroines do you 
see in adult films or television series? 
How are they similar to or different from 
Moana and Raya?
 4.

e Moana and Raya to any one of
