5.6: WICKED STEPMOTHERS WEAR DIOR: 
HOLLYWOOD’S MODERN FAIRY TALES
Lea M. Popielinski
The author argues that The Devil Wears Prada 
and The Nanny Diaries represent the evolution of 
a familiar type of fairy tale: a maiden overcomes 
subjugation by a more powerful older woman to 
gain freedom and happiness.
A young woman gazes up from the foot of a Man-
hattan skyscraper, awed by its power to dwarf her 
and excited by the challenge it represents. She’s just 
finished college and is about to enter a world prom-
ising to transform her and deliver her into the profes-
sional life of her dreams. She’s no Rapunzel, waiting 
inside a tower for a dashing hero to whisk her away, 
but an adventurer in her own right, prepared to scale 
the tower herself. With an ambitiousness as inspired 
as it is naïve, our young woman is about to become 
the heroine of the modern-day fairy tale.
The films The Devil Wears Prada (2006) and The 
Nanny Diaries (2007) follow protagonists much like this 
young lady as they begin jobs, they consider transi-
tional but necessary trials toward their ultimate aspi-
rations. The only obstacles confronting Devil’s Andrea 
“Andy” Sachs and Diaries’ Annie Braddock in attaining 
their career goals, ironically, are their employers. This 
essay discusses the evolution of a familiar subset of 
fairy tales: the story of a maiden overcoming subju-
gation by a more powerful older woman to gain free-
dom and happiness. Once upon a time, this antagonist 
was often a witch or a wicked stepmother motivated 
by jealousy, greed, or fear of being dethroned; but in 
contemporary films targeting an adult audience, she 
appears as a wealthy woman whose status allows her 
to make the rules. Andy and Annie are hardly Snow 
White and Cinderella, but the spirit of the charac-
ter type is maintained in a form relatable to young 
21st-century women.
Archetypes are classic models of a person or 
concept that take a consistent form by appearing 
repeatedly within a cultural genre. The wicked step-
mother and the innocent, persecuted heroine are 
major fairy-tale archetypes. Psychoanalysts have inter-
preted the use of archetypes in storytelling as sym-
bolic of the beliefs of a culture’s collective unconscious 
(Franz, 1973); other authors look at how archetypes 
reflect their cultures (Zipes, 1993). I use a combina-
tion of the two methods, in using Devil and Diaries  
to explore how the two archetypes have changed in 
some ways but are still recognizable in others, in rela-
tion to women’s changing roles and concerns. I suggest 
that North American culture is conflicted about how 
contemporary women’s roles diverge from fairy-tale 
ideals: proud of the independence and ambition of 
young women with no real influence yet ambivalent 
about women who are aged and/or successful enough 
to wield social and economic power, and that the race, 
sexuality, and class status of the women in these films 
are significant to the reproduction of these archetypes.
The Movies
In Devil, Andy Sachs has moved to New Y ork seek-
ing work in her dream profession of journalism. She 
procures a position that “a million girls would kill 
for,” as junior assistant to Runway fashion magazine’s 
notoriously patronizing editor in chief, Miranda 
Priestly. Although her frumpy style indicates to 
Miranda a lack of credibility, Andy is determined 
to persevere because the experience will open 
all the doors in Manhattan’s journalistic offices to 


Film and Television 179
her
. Eventually, with help from coworker Nigel, she 
adapts to her circumstances and the workplace’s 
standards of appearance while developing the busi-
ness contacts and self-confidence that boost her job 
performance and Miranda’s approval. As she grows 
devoted to her job, however, she loses touch with 
her boyfriend and friends. When she becomes party 
to politics and back-stabbing, she finally wants out, 
unwilling to sacrifice her ethics. As the movie ends, 
Andy’s boyfriend is moving away, and she goes to 
work at a more modestly run newspaper, on Miran-
da’s favorable recommendation.
Meanwhile, Annie Braddock is less certain about 
her ambitions. After failing a job interview, she saves 
a child named Grayer from an accident and is invited 
by his wealthy mother, Mrs. X, to become his nanny. 
Believing that the work will be a good source of 
income while she figures out her life, Annie accepts. 
She finds herself performing all the parental duties for 
a socialite mother and philandering father. She finds 
support from her friends and from a studly neighbor 
in the Xs’ building she calls “Harvard Hottie.” Annie’s 
affection for Grayer balances her growing frustration 
until Mr. X makes an unwanted pass at her, which Mrs. 
X uses as an excuse to fire her. She vents her anger on 
a teddy bear outfitted with a nannycam; the resulting 
video, in which Annie pleads that the Xs become more 
active parents, shames Mrs. X in front of a seminar, 
although she later learns that Mrs. X has taken her 
advice. Meanwhile, she applies to graduate programs 
in anthropology, and her romance with Harvard Hottie 
appears to be underway.
The Innocent Persecuted Heroine
I have used the phrase “innocent persecuted her -
oine” several times already because it is a stand-
ard way of describing this character type among 
fairy-tale theorists (see Western Folklore, vol. 52, no. 
1, 1993). It should be immediately apparent that in 
the present-day fairy tale, this figure has undergone 
dramatic transformations, not least of which is the 
fact that Andy and Annie are not persecuted in 
any traditional sense, having freely accepted their 
jobs. Although surface details differ, the changes 
are consistent with the innocent persecuted hero-
ine’s (IPH’s) history as an archetype and the core 
elements to the narrative structure and positioning 
of the IPH tale. Andy and Annie are not actual IPHs, 
but their films belong to a related subgenre.
It’s essential to see the development of arche-
types within their historical contexts. Many European 
fairy tales began as products of oral folklore before 
being published (Franz, 1973; Tatar, 2002), often exist-
ing in multiple forms in different periods and locales. 
Publication and distribution, however, caused particu-
lar versions, such as the Grimm brothers’ adaptations, 
to become more widely accepted. These privileged 
versions obscure the diversity of the previous contexts 
in which the stories appeared.
Even within the IPH subgenre, the heroines were 
not always innocent and persecuted but often became 
so when their stories were adapted for wide appeal. 
Little Red Riding Hood is a fascinating example:
[in] an oral version of the tale recorded in 
France at the end of the nineteenth century, 
Little Red Riding Hood performs a striptease 
before the wolf, then ends the litany of ques-
tions about the wolf’s body parts by asking if 
she can go outside to relieve herself.
(Tatar, 2002, p. 17)
Thus, she outwits the wolf and escapes, rather than 
being saved by a hunter. Other heroines are inno-
cent throughout the story but allow brutal violence 
to occur once they’ve attained higher status: the 
Grimms’ Cinderella invites her stepsisters to her 
wedding, where birds peck out their eyes, and Snow 
White allows her stepmother to be placed in red-hot 
iron shoes that cause her to dance herself to death. 
The idealistically innocent heroine did appear in 
earlier eras, but she was not as monolithic as she 
gradually became.
Since the 1930s, probably the most influential 
transcriber of fairy tales has been Disney, whose ani-
mated feature film versions of IPH tales are so iconic 
that many in recent generations regard them as the 
gold standard and may not be familiar with earlier 
versions. It may be worth considering why the IPH 
archetype proliferated at this time. The construction of 
morality and femininity in 20th-century North Amer-
ica may have demanded less ambiguity than Europe-
ans of earlier periods were comfortable with.

180 Content
Things became more complicated with the emer-
gence of the women’s movement, beginning in the 
1960s. The first feminist engagements with fairy tales 
appeared in the early 1970s (Lieberman, 1972; Lurie, 
1970; Rowe, 1979), and even non-feminists in the 
present day recognize feminist objections to the arche-
types. Some latter-day Disney films feature noticea-
bly more active or intelligent heroines, and parodies 
such as Shrek defy the archetype altogether. Likely 
because of feminist influence and the sense that the 
archetype has become cliché, it has become difficult 
to produce straightforward IPHs. A fairy tale meant to 
be relevant to contemporary women must be more 
complex. Thus, the fact that the goals and concerns 
of the heroines of Devil and Diaries diverge dramati-
cally from those of Disney’s mid-century prototypes 
does not necessarily exclude them from being kin to 
the IPH subgenre. In some ways, the stories and their 
protagonists conform to the conventions of standard 
IPH narratives, such as in the heroines’ solitude and in 
their search for identity.
Mendelson (1997) observed that whereas male 
heroes and wicked women in Grimms’ Fairy Tales  
occasionally collaborate with one another, young, 
virtuous women seldom do so. Although Andy and 
Annie have friends and boyfriends outside of their 
workplaces, their social lives conflict with their jobs. 
Annie has no peer coworkers at all. Andy begins her 
job as an outcast among her colleagues. The nearest 
that women in the Grimms’ tales come to a collabora-
tive relationship, Mendelson suggested, is when a fairy 
godmother or similar figure arrives to offer temporary 
assistance to a heroine. Andy has a helper of this sort 
in Nigel; the scene in which he brings her to Runway’s 
closet and dresses her, Cinderella-like, in designer gar-
ments, marks a turning point, after which she becomes 
a model employee and eventually impresses Miranda.
Mendelson also focused on “the coming into self-
hood” and how “[i]n this singular process of psycho-
logical individuation, the solitary figure takes center 
stage” (1997, p. 120). Andy has chosen her future 
identity, and her time at Runway is her journey toward 
self-realization. In Diaries, this process is even more 
transparent. In an early scene, a job interviewer asks 
our heroine, “Who is Annie Braddock?” Annie’s ina-
bility to answer this question leads her to take the job 
she believes will help her find herself. That she expects 
to find self-discovery through nannying makes most 
sense with respect to her relationship with Mrs. X: hav-
ing one’s very own wicked stepmother becomes a rite 
of passage toward adulthood.
The Wicked Stepmother
The stepmother is so important to the Western 
coming-of-age story that now that she is no longer 
a domestic terrorist infiltrating the heroine’s home; 
the young women must seek her out on her own 
territory. Andy would not have the credentials, the 
recommendation, or the first-rate experience to 
compete for her dream job, and Annie might still 
be taking ill-fated interviews at business offices, had 
they not first passed through gauntlets conceived 
by Miranda and Mrs. X. Besides the familial quality 
of the workplaces, both films include the motif of 
parental replacement. In Devil, Andy’s father visits, 
but she is continually interrupted by telephone calls 
from Miranda and her impossibly urgent demands. 
The evening grows increasingly frustrating, peaking 
when the distracted Andy shuts a taxi door on her 
father, literally and painfully. In Diaries, the mother 
substitution is more overt. Annie has been raised by 
a single mother and nurse, whom she doesn’t want 
to disappoint. When she takes the nanny job, she lies 
to her mother and says she was offered a financial 
position. The ruse falls apart in a tense confronta-
tion between Mrs. X and Mrs. Braddock, in which 
the former seems surprised to learn that Annie has 
a mother.
Compared to Andy and Annie as IPHs, Miranda 
and Mrs. X retain more traditional characteristics 
relating to the wicked stepmother, most visibly in 
their dictatorial styles. Jones (1993, p. 28) regards 
the “jealous stepmother who favors her own daugh-
ter and forces the heroine to perform disagreea-
ble, dangerous, or impossible chores” as a staple of 
the IPH genre. Miranda reduces Andy to running  
errands and performing menial tasks, culminating in 
an ultimatum for Andy to find an unpublished Harry 
Potter manuscript; Mrs. X’s to-do list for Annie is less 
demanding but more degrading and emphasizes their 
difference in status. Although danger is not a theme 
in either movie, disagreeable and impossible chores 
certainly are.


Film and Television 181
In a Land N
ot So Far Away
The release of two very similar films that reinvent 
these archetypes in familiar guises suggests that 
there’s a social need or desire for such images to be 
reproduced in this way. The critical questions are 
“What do Devil and Diaries say about their social 
context?” and “Why are the symbols packaged the 
way they are?”
We must view these symbols in terms of how we 
understand race, gender, class, and sexuality in our 
cultural context. In some respects, the archetypes are 
still strongly bound to the correct combination of these 
four dimensions. Marginal archetypes, such as the fairy 
godmother, may be flexible. Others, such as Prince 
Charming, are optional. The heroine and the step-
mother, however, might not be recognizable as such 
were they not both White, heterosexual women of the 
economic classes appropriate to their character types.
Archetypes must appear to represent the broadest 
range of subjectivity possible. The cultural separation 
of social categories into One and Other, in which One 
is not merely the dominant of the two but the standard, 
neutral, and default category, casts Othered categories 
as marked identities, seen in terms of their difference 
from the “norm.” Using the example of sex/gender, 
Simone de Beauvoir (1989 [1949], p. xxi) wrote, “Man 
represents both the positive and the neutral, as is indi-
cated by the common use of man to designate human 
beings in general; whereas woman represents only the 
negative, defined by limiting criteria, without reciproc-
ity.” Applying the concept to race, then, a Black hero-
ine would be able to stand as an archetype for all Black 
women, but only a White heroine is constructed to 
stand for all women; Whiteness, unlike other(ed) races, 
does not need to be articulated. Only Whiteness, in de 
Beauvoir’s terms, is neutral.
Similarly, a version of Devil with Andy as a lesbian 
would probably not allow her to “just happen to be” 
a lesbian. Rather, her inevitable tomboyishness might 
be used comically as she fumbles with feminine cloth-
ing, or she might grapple with homophobic parents. 
There’s nothing wrong with producing a film about a 
straight, White woman, but we can’t assume that her 
race and sexuality are any less important to her char-
acter development than for those with more marked 
identities. Whiteness and heterosexuality are just as 
central to constructing these characters as class and 
gender.
The centrality of Andy and Annie’s Whiteness is 
actively reinforced by the fact that each one’s closest 
female friend is Black. Annie’s friend Lynnette directly 
emphasizes that Annie’s choice to enter domestic ser-
vitude is made from a position of racial privilege when 
she points out that generations of women in her own 
family have worked hard not to perform that labor 
again. Annie can only submit herself to it knowing that 
her racial privilege grants her other options. She herself 
acknowledges that her race, citizenship, and English 
language fluency make her “the Chanel bag of nan-
nies.” Andy and her best friend Lily never talk about 
race as overtly, but the absence of other White women 
in Andy’s social circle highlights her dyadic relationship 
with the older White mother-substitute.
Andy and Annie’s heterosexuality is also rein-
forced by those around them; Lynnette’s roommate 
Calvin is openly gay, and Nigel uses stereotypically 
gay mannerisms. The deflection of homosexuality 
away from the main characters renders gayness as 
a marked identity, so that any character not read as 
gay will appear to a heterosexist audience as straight. 
The heroines’ heterosexuality is not incidental: it’s 
necessary to maintain the characters as archetypes, 
not only because of heterosexuality’s default status 
but also because it leaves open the possibility of a 
Prince Charming, necessary for the fairy-tale frame-
work, even if that possibility does not come to fruition. 
Straight womanhood must be opposed to straight 
manhood, without all of the complicated ambiguities 
that lesbian and bisexual identities and nonconformist 
gender expressions introduce.
Class advancement has always been a central 
theme of fairy tales, especially IPH tales (Panttaja, 
1993). Andy and Annie frame their ambitions as paths 
to careers rather than wealth, but the economic dispar-
ity between the heroines and their employers under-
lines a direct correlation between money and power. 
Reading the films side by side illustrates that the dif-
ferences between women who marry into money, 
such as Mrs. X, and women who earn it themselves, 
like Miranda, are not necessarily significant to arche-
typal readings. Andy and Annie’s seemingly humble 
approach to money is necessary to further contribute 
to their neo-IPH profile to the extent that standard 

182 Content
IPHs are often rewarded specifically for not seeking a 
reward. The connections among power, money, and a 
lack of ethics demonstrate why the wicked stepmother 
archetype has been revived in this form at this time: 
contemporary North American culture feels very dif-
ferently about young women who work hard to achieve 
all the hallmarks of middle-class female success than 
it feels about older women who have actually attained 
positions of power.
Women’s liberation of the 1970s gave way to girl 
power by the 1990s. Girls now are often taught they 
can do anything. North American culture is proud of 
young women earning college degrees and entering 
the job market because it exemplifies cultural progress 
and open-mindedness. Critically, this pride only lasts 
while these women have little social power. Our cul-
ture feels much more ambivalent toward successful 
older women: workplace advancement grows increas-
ingly more difficult for women than for men (and more 
difficult for Black men than for White men) over the 
course of their careers (Maume, 2004). The face of 
new employees is diverse in many fields, but our cul-
ture is still most comfortable with White men in the 
most elite positions. Although many claim to support 
the advancement of women and people of color to 
powerful positions, there may still be an unconscious 
cultural anxiety about this ideal’s realization. Because 
it is inappropriate to admit this anxiety, it emerges in 
our cultural products through the use of archetypes 
embedded in the collective unconscious.
For example, Miranda acts as both Andy’s chal-
lenger and her mentor. She considers Andy, on some 
level, a successor. But Miranda is not depicted as a 
strong executive who takes employees under her wing 
to groom them, a character type more strongly asso-
ciated with men; she’s depicted in a gendered man-
ner, insofar as terms such as “shrew,” “ice queen,” 
and “dragon lady” exist only at the intersection of 
femaleness and class power. Movies about this type of 
powerful woman give voice to otherwise suppressed 
cultural fears about giving women too much power. 
Andy’s refusal to be seduced into this role is crucial to 
the archetype she continues to embody.
What’s more, these fears are not restricted to the 
office setting. Mrs. X obtained her power by marrying 
a rich man. The differences and similarities to Miranda 
are notable. On the one hand, her power is much more 
limited, lacking a career to provide upward mobility. 
She restricts her nannies from dating out of concern 
that the nanny will be less devoted to her work; but 
when she learns of Annie’s relationship with a young 
man in their own building, the offense is doubly threat-
ening for the transgression of class boundaries. Mrs. X 
thus exhibits more of the classic wicked stepmother’s 
characteristics of jealousy and fear of losing her privi-
lege. The gulf between her and Annie is much smaller 
than the gulf between Miranda and Andy. The former 
is a question of whose wedding band lands on one’s 
finger; the latter is a matter of years of experience and 
ladder-climbing.
On the other hand, all of the emblematic terms 
I listed above—shrew and so forth—are similarly 
applicable to Mrs. X. Bestowing economic power on 
a woman, according to these narratives, transforms 
her from naïf to harpy. Both films give their stepmoth-
ers a personal edge but do so through tumult in their 
marriages. The only person who has the power to hurt 
each of these women is her husband. The circum-
stances under which the divorces loom and the impact 
they have on the two women are very different, but it 
is intriguing how the same device is used in both to 
create chinks in the stepmothers’ armor.
Happily Ever After?
This discussion of Devil and Diaries suggests that 
contemporary North American culture strongly 
values progressive gender politics to the extent that 
it results in young, educated, unmarried women 
joining the workforce with great ambition but mod-
est goals. It also suggests that this same culture is 
simultaneously ambivalent about women gaining 
a surplus of power within the same context. I call 
this “ambivalence” because there is less an outright 
objection to women holding positions of power than 
a sense that women who hold these positions fit a 
certain—and not always complimentary—
 c
ategory 
of womanhood. On this note, it is important to end 
by observing that neither film completely demonizes 
its wicked stepmother. In the transition from fairy-
tale archetype to contemporary social construc-
tion, this character type has grown more complex, 
appropriately so, for her relevance in an increasingly 
complex society.


Film and Television 183
Ref
erences

5.7: IT’S OKAY THAT WE BACK-STAB 
EACH OTHER: CULTURAL MYTHS THAT 
FUEL THE BATTLING FEMALE IN THE 
BACHELOR
Jennifer S. Kramer
The Bachelor has been a fixture on ABC since 
2001, and in each season, eligible bachelors sift 
through a harem of 25 women. The Cinderella  
format is common in many reality shows, but 
what is largely ignored—and what this reading 
addresses—is how The Bachelor perpetuates an 
image of catty women who will go to great lengths 
to beat other women to win their man.
When I was in high school, my ex-boyfriend’s sister 
and I were interested in the same boy. We battled 
for him. I won. It was not pretty. She and I sparred, 
and eventually, I broke up with the guy to get back 
together with my ex-boyfriend. She dated the object 
of our once joint affection for years, eventually mar-
rying someone else, as did I. I often thought about 
how much I was in the wrong for hating her so much 
for having the same good taste in boys. Why did I do 
this? I’d never fought over a guy before, or since. The 
It’s Your Turn: What Do You Think? What 
Will You Find?
 1.
 W
ith a partner, choose a different film 
genre—e.g., action, romance, science 
fiction—and discuss the types of female 
characters it presents. What patterns can 
you recognize in their depiction? What 
cultural beliefs about womanhood or 
femininity seem to be illustrated in these 
character types? How do race, sexual-
ity, age, and dis/ability (even if they are 
unmarked) contribute to creating these 
character types?
 2.
 Find a book cont
aining fairy tales you’ve 
never read or heard before, perhaps from 
a non-European culture. Choose one and 
imagine what would change or remain the 
same if it were made into a movie. Which 
themes or characters seem to fit easily 
into contemporary scripts, and which 
don’t? Thinking about elements such as 
violence, morals, and characters’ objec-
tives, what aspects of 21st-century cul-
ture, possibly aspects we take for granted, 
make an adaptation of the story difficult?
 3.
 Look 
for articles in news magazines about 
women and men in powerful positions, 
such as politicians and business leaders. 
Compare the way the authors describe 
their subjects. To what extent do they 
discuss their subjects’ family lives, career 
histories, appearance, and professional 
success? How positive or negative do they 
sound? What similarities and differences 
are there in the articles and any accompa-
nying photography? If you can, find news 
magazines from 10, 20, and 30 years ago to 
see if, and how, profiles of female and male 
professionals have changed.

184 Content
foundation to fight for my man was set in motion 
long before my interlude with the claws. Fighting for 
your man is seen as necessary for many women, 
particularly in order to earn that brass (diamond) 
ring. It’s one of the few scenarios in which women 
are required to be aggressive. Just watch The Bach-
elor, you’ll see. The story of women desperate 
to find a man in The Bachelor for their Cinderella 
happily-ever-afters includes mythic battles between 
women to win the man.
Entwined within the story of Cinderella are 
American cultural myths that perpetuate the normalcy 
of women fighting each other. Those myths include 
“the possibility of success,” “the value of a challenge,” 
and being a “woman’s woman” (Larson, 2004, pp. 222, 
229). These myths can be found in Cinderella imita-
tors such as The Bachelor and serve as powerful per-
suasive forces because they are valued by the culture. 
This reading examines the myths that fuel the success 
of The Bachelor, not only in its popularity but more 
importantly for the lack of critical analysis that sheds 
light on the weekly battles among the gaggle of women 
vying for the bachelor. This battleground is a uniquely 
feminine one where the women’s aggressive style is 
acceptable because their stake as desirable women is 
challenged.
1
Cinderella Myth in The Bachelor
The Cinderella fairy tale as told today depicts a 
beautiful young woman forced to be a slave for her 
stepfamily after her father dies. The local prince 
searches for a wife by hosting a ball, which Cin-
derella attends through the magic of her fairy god-
mother. However, the magic disappears at midnight, 
causing Cinderella to lose a glass slipper which 
eventually leads the prince to her. He delivers her 
from slavery into a happily-ever-after. Tannenbaum 
(2002) sums up the message from Cinderella as “To 
get the prince, a woman must (a) be beautiful and (b) 
compete with the evil Other Women” (p. 140). The 
Bachelor lives up to this simplistic Cinderella plot 
quite nicely and is regularly touted as a Cinderella 
story. The premise of the show is that one desirable 
eligible man has multiple available women and can 
choose one for the happily-ever-after. The series 
rarely creates a lasting relationship, although there 
have been a few exceptions. The draw of the Cin-
derella myth is so powerful that the show’s ratings 
remain strong, despite the format’s repetitiveness.
Each season proceeds with the bachelor progres-
sively whittling down his choices by offering roses to 
women he’d like to continue dating. The progression 
moves from the bachelor meeting 25–30 model-thin 
and perfectly coiffed, dressed, and stilleto’d women 
over much alcohol to a rose ceremony where 5–10 
women are dismissed. Subsequent episodes see the 
bachelor winnowing his choices, typically by a third to 
a half after a few fantasy one-on-one dates, and a vari-
ety of group dates, which typically show the women 
openly competing through challenges derived by pro-
ducers. Once the bachelor has his harem down to four, 
he visits the women’s families, followed by another 
cut. The bachelor then spends more significant over-
night time with the remaining three women in exotic 
locales, makes a cut, and in the next episode, the final 
two women meet the bachelor’s family. After another 
date at the bachelor’s mansion, the bachelor chooses 
his princess in a dramatic rose ceremony where the 
one left standing receives not only the final rose but 
also a large diamond ring and, ostensibly, the bache-
lor’s heart.
The women claim the opportunity to meet the 
bachelor is like being in a fairy tale and that they really 
do believe their foray into reality dating television is a 
viable way to find the perfect husband. For example, 
in the first episodes, the women refer to the bachelor 
as Prince Charming and themselves as Cinderella. In 
season 9, ABC tried to make the fairy tale even more 
real and procured an Italian prince as the bachelor. 
The stakes were clearly higher in this season because 
the women no longer were just fighting for their man 
but for the position of real princess.
Why the Myths Work So Well
We need to take a more critical gaze at the dating 
reality television genre because as Kavka claimed, 
it “works at the level of feeling rather than cognitive 
content” (2008, p. x), and viewers are enthralled by 
watching the performance of love; love is too diffi-
cult to describe. Viewers suspend disbelief watching 


Film and Television 185
thes
e shows because they feel a sense of intimacy 
with the contestants. The intimacy is heightened 
by contestants’ true confessions into the cam-
era (Aslama & Pantti, 2006). The result is as if the 
contestant’s confession is not about the “we” of 
television talking to the “us” of viewers, but rather 
“individuals addressing individuals” (p. 179) in the 
privacy of one’s home. The hook of feeling inti-
macy sneaks in cultural messages because reality 
television
…circulates informal “guidelines for living” that 
we are all (at times) called upon to learn from 
and follow. These are not abstract ideologies 
imposed from above, but…practical techniques 
for reflecting on, managing, and improving…
our personal lives with the resources available 
to us.
(Ouellette & Hay, 2008, p. 2)
Reality television reinforces many taken-for-granted 
ideological discourses of popular cultural myths, 
such as Cinderella. Fiske (1987, as cited in Ouellette, 
2003) explained that ideological discourse stems 
from those who are in power who work to natu-
ralize meanings “about an important topic area…
[to the point that the meanings seem like] common 
sense” (Ouelette, 2003, p. 117). The ideological dis-
course for women is based upon economic social 
power relationships which work to keep women in 
submissive roles (Cupaiuolo, 2004); therefore, dating 
reality television “drive[s] home the notion that no 
emotional, professional or political accomplishment 
can be possibly compared with the twin vocations 
of beauty and marriage” (Pozner, 2004).
Tannenbaum explained that the socialized role 
of being feminine forces women into a double bind 
because women need to demonstrate independence, 
yet they still need a man to be complete. Mingling the 
myth of Cinderella with its supporting myths has thus 
created an ideological discourse: “Being competitive, 
catty, and cunning are part of the stereotype of fem-
ininity” (2002, p. 27). We have come to expect and 
desire such depictions of women who back-stab each 
other in their quest to win the bachelor’s love. Larson 
(2004) argued that the power of such myths is rooted 
in their ability to become shorthand for persuasion 
because those who believe in them are emotionally 
attached to the myths. These myths work to support 
the belief in a happily-ever-after derived from a man 
whisking a woman off into the fairy tale while the 
remaining women fight one another.
Possibility of Success (through) Valuing 
Challenges
The possibility of success myth explains that 
“through hard work, ethics, and future orientation, 
[one] will succeed and succeed very well” (Larson, 
2004, pp. 220–221). We sympathize with Cinderella 
because her situation will not allow her to rise above 
her servitude through hard work. The myth of valu-
ing challenges saves Cinderella because she perse-
veres. The valuing challenges myth says that those 
who struggle will earn great rewards, almost as if it is 
a “rite of passage or initiation” (Larson, 2004, p. 222). 
Wisdom comes from surviving the challenge, and 
the survivor has “a sense of something good coming 
out of the suffering” (Larson, 2004, p. 223).
These myths are intertwined in The Bachelor . The 
future orientation of the challenge to win the bache-
lor’s heart is stressed repeatedly by the contestants. 
Throughout the first few episodes of each season, the 
women confess to the camera how ready they are 
for this challenge and what they bring to the compe-
tition to overcome the other women. For example, 
the women claim their competitive prowess, as when 
Kristin (fighting for season 25 bachelor Matt’s affec-
tion) tells the camera if one has to fight to get one’s 
man, she’s going to fight. Likewise, Corinne (season 
20) is clearly proud of the fact that she is fighting for 
the possibility of winning the bachelor, such as when 
she bit the rose she was given, proclaiming “I love the 
taste of victory!” Even after the competition is over, 
the valuing challenge myth is reinforced, as when the 
runner-up for season 10 Andy’s heart, Beavin (bawling 
in the back seat of the limo taking her away from her 
love), states that this will not destroy her, but rather will 
make her more resilient.
Valuing the challenge of winning results in the 
women directing their competitiveness toward one 
another through aggression, which even they describe 

186 Content
as catfights. The producers play up the catfight spec-
tacle through promos before commercial breaks such 
as in the first episode of season 20; Lace is shown sev-
eral times saying, “I’m gonna go call someone out to 
their face. I’m gonna punch her in the face. Seriously.” 
Likewise, in season 21, Corinne is shown repeatedly 
claiming she was going to punch Taylor. In season 
20, the preview for episode 2 describes another vil-
lain, Olivia, as fighting the entire house of women. In 
season 13, Molly and Jillian tell one another they will 
kick one another’s ass over Jason, and later, a verbal 
group catfight breaks out about the most malicious of 
the women, Megan. The catfight is broken up when 
Shannon leaves the rose ceremony formation for the 
bathroom. Her microphone picks up the sound of 
vomiting, and the camera cuts to Megan demean-
ing Shannon with a storm of epithets because Shan-
non simply is not strong enough. Likewise in season 
25, Sarah starts to faint during a rose ceremony and 
needs help from paramedics. Season baddy Victoria 
responded telling the camera, “Sarah’s such a calcu-
lating little bitch. Sarah doesn’t need Matt, she needs 
a Xanax” because to Victoria, Sarah was clearly doing 
this to win Matt’s sympathy. Sarah left the competition 
in the next episode. The stress was too much, and her 
father was close to death from ALS. Nevertheless, 
when Sarah left, Victoria exclaimed that “The trash 
took itself out!”
Woman’s Woman Myth
Larson described the woman’s woman as “soft spo-
ken, kind, and nurturing. She may work, but she is 
also the perfect wife and mother, and is immaculately 
groomed. However she is also vain, rarely has mean-
ingful thoughts, and never wastes time on serious 
things” (2004, p. 229). By depicting women solely 
as physical objects, we rarely see them as powerful. 
Women have often seen each other as competition 
and so have become adept at quickly sizing up their 
female competition (Russ, 2008; Tannenbaum, 2002). 
In season 21, Corinne is the center of the women’s 
fury due to her flaunting her sexuality with bach-
elor Nick, including taking topless photos with him 
and straddling him in a drawn out sexual maneu-
ver in a bouncy house on the lawn. The women’s 
nurturer capabilities are also up for evaluation as 
the women regularly tell the bachelor they are there 
for him and understand how difficult this process is 
for him. Raven emphasized this trait in the “After the 
Rose Ceremony” episode (a cast reunion and season 
recap) when she and Nick discussed their break-up. 
Raven proclaimed she just wants Nick to be happy 
and that is all she ever wanted for him.
The Bachelor women’s stake in being seen as 
desirable, acceptable women is constantly in question 
throughout the show, fostering whirlwinds of insults. 
Comments made behind each other’s backs criticize 
one another’s adequacy for the bachelor, decency 
as a woman, and even their human decency. Some-
times these criticisms are shared with the bachelor. 
In season 20, many of the women say to the camera 
that Nick needs to be told how awful Corinne is, but 
only Vanessa is shown taking Nick aside to tell him 
how displeased she was with Corinne’s actions in the 
bouncy house and Nick’s apparent receptive response. 
In a later episode, Corinne reciprocated by telling Nick 
about a conversation in which she claimed Taylor bul-
lied her. Subsequently, in the middle of this date, Nick 
sent Taylor home. However, Taylor crashed Corinne 
and Nick’s date that evening, saying she cares about 
Nick as a person and that he needs to know how much 
Corinne has been lying to him. While Nick is off talking 
to Taylor, Corinne is heard saying that Taylor is “an 
evil, annoying, lying, bitch.”
Any woman who is assertive when seeking the 
bachelor’s attention is criticized by the others for 
not demonstrating woman’s woman characteristics. 
Although women are just as aggressive as men, they 
are more likely to express this in a passive aggres-
sive, or indirect, manner (Richardson, 2005). As the 
prior examples demonstrate, The Bachelor highlights 
the plight of women in the woman’s woman double 
bind. They are supposed to allow the bachelor to 
make his choice, but the cultural myth of the wom-
an’s woman forces them to compete. They need to 
hide their aggression so as to still be seen as femi-
nine and because of “fear of physical, economic, or 
emotional retaliation if they openly expressed overt 
opposition to someone more physically or socially 
powerful” (Tannenbaum, 2002, p. 63). Women’s fear 
of negative consequences is confirmed through The 


Film and Television 187
B
achelor when Taylor is cut by Nick after calling out 
Corinne as a liar. Similarly, Stephanie and Kate are 
cut by season 10 bachelor Andy following their criti-
cisms of other women. Initially in season 25, bache-
lor Matt believes Victoria’s complaint that Marylynn 
was bullying her (although no such depiction aired), 
but by episode seven, Victoria was sent packing as 
one of the real culprits of back-stabbing the women 
in the house.
Pozner pointed out that in reality television 
romance, “Only the prettiest, most passive girls 
without agency or voice, without ambition or indi-
viduality were rewarded with love, financial success, 
and the ultimate prize: being picked by the prince” 
(2009, p. 58). There are rare exceptions to this rule 
such as in season 21 when Vanessa—who called 
out Corinne’s and Nick’s bouncy house behavior—
earned the final rose and Nick’s heart. Season 16 
bachelor Jake went so far as to choose the aggres-
sive woman, Vienna, despite the other women 
regaling him with tales of her bitchiness. However, 
within mere months both couples split.
And the Back-Stabbing Continues…
It’s easier to resort to following cultural plotlines in 
our lives when faced with difficult situations such as 
looking for love. And The Bachelor serves them up 
for us on a silver platter laden with a rose. Perpetu-
ating the cultural myths of Cinderella, the possibility 
of success, valuing challenges, and being a woman’s 
woman has helped put women in a double bind, as 
women:
…can be successful [only] as long as [they] 
stay “feminine” (i.e., powerless enough not to 
be truly threatening)….Powerful women are 
seen by many people (women as well as men) 
as inherently destructive and dangerous. Some 
argue that it is men’s awareness of just how 
powerful women can be that has created the 
attempts to keep women small.
(Kilbourne, 1999, pp. 137, 262)
Because the women are all dating the same man, 
they spend more time with one another than with 
the bachelor. The way out of this situation requires 
one to be partnered because this means a woman 
“has attained a measure of power” (Tannenbaum, 
2002, p. 169). So the women fight in the manner in 
which they’ve been socialized—by stabbing one 
another in the back.
In American society, the richest, most powerful 
people are still White men (Fixmer-Oraiz & Wood, 
2019). As a result, it makes sense that shows such 
as The Bachelor are desirable to the predominantly 
male television executives—these shows preserve 
the cultural plotlines that have kept them in power. 
In addition, if enough women watch the show, they 
perpetuate the myths that keep women back-stab-
bing each other instead of challenging the man who is 
cheating on them and the double bind that continues 
to limit their power.
NOTE
 1.  Ev en if you haven’t watched the show, you may have 
assumed the cast members are White. Although you 
would largely be correct, such assumptions reflect 
the implicit bias of whiteness. However, race came 
to the fore in season 25 of The Bachelor. Y ou may find 
the author’s analysis of race on season 25 at https://
tinyurl.com/RGCMKramer. The representation of 
race in that season isn’t explained by recreated myths 
but clearly highlights the issues of racial power in  
the US.

Will You Find?

ou are part of the casting team for The 
Bachelor. What socioeconomic back-

contestants? Compare your list to the

of The Bachelor, or through online biog-
raphies. Determine what class or cultural 
myths related to gender are communi-
cated through The Bachelor.
 2.
 In 
small groups, produce a proposal for 
a romance reality television show that 
would not rely on the cultural myths 
presented here, or other cultural myths 
that position men or women as superior

5.8 FEMALE FRIENDSHIP AND 
INTERSECTIONAL ALLYSHIP ON 
BROOKLYN NINE-NINE
Madison Barnes-Nelson
This reading explores how the central women’s 
friendship on the television sitcom Brooklyn Nine-
Nine exemplifies intersectional allyship and pro-
vides commentary on how women of color friends 
on TV negotiate contemporary social issues in 
interpersonal and professional spheres.
In the final moments of the Brooklyn Nine-Nine sea-
son six episode “Four Movements,” Gina Linetti, 
Rosa Diaz, and Amy Santiago share an emotional 
goodbye regarding Gina’s departure from the police 
precinct. Over the course of nearly six years, the 
women have cultivated a supportive friendship in 
their workplace. As the three embrace, Gina says 
through her tears: 
Amy, the lesson I wanted to leave you with is 
to just be yourself. If you want to cry like an 
idiot for hours on end, just do it. Y ou want to 
make a big old ugly book full of all my brilliant 
thoughts, do it. Do you! 
Emotional exchanges such as this permeate the 
series. These women have individual qualities that 
deconstruct familiar tropes of female sitcom char -
acters, and their interplay throughout the series 
demonstrates an intersectional female friendship 
narrative built on allyship.
Women characters on television have often been 
relegated to one-dimensional stereotypes without con-
sideration of their identities, career goals, or interper-
sonal relationships. Popular television programs such 
as Friends or Sex and the City have historically tended 
to center whiteness, heterosexuality, domestic life, and 
affluence in adult female friend groups. The absence 
of women of color and queer women of color in these 
texts demonstrates whose experiences are most often 
invisible in television narratives.
Brooklyn Nine-Nine (2013–2021) challenges the 
mostly White and heteronormative representations 
of women friends. It has been hailed by many critics 
to the other. How likely is your show to 
succeed, and why?

atch the credits (or check online) to

 4.

amine the communication of your

Film and Television 189
f
or its nuanced representations of racial profiling, gun 
control, and sexual harassment. The three female pro-
tagonists include two Latina detectives: Amy 
 Santia
go, 
who is type A with dreams of becoming captain; 
Rosa Diaz who comes out at bisexual in season 5 and 
shows emotional sensitivity despite her cold exterior; 
and civilian administrator Gina Linetti, a sarcastic and 
egomaniacal Italian American who becomes a mother 
in season 4. These three women differ in their charac-
ter traits but rely on each other in work and at home 
throughout the series.
In my analysis, I highlight the show’s unique 
 por
trayal of a female friend group aware of the inter-
secting oppressive social hierarchies of race, gender, 
and sexuality in the structural domains of work and 
family life. Intersectionality recognizes how interlock-
ing systems of power across multiple axes of social 
identity (such as race, gender, and sexuality) affect 
one’s opportunities and disadvantages (Crenshaw, 
1989). Seeing representations of female friendships 
that deal with issues of intersectionality on television 
is crucial for constructing more inclusive, woman-of-
color centric televisual representations and centering 
women’s solidarity against oppression and support in 
the wake of hardships across different parts of life. The 
police precinct as a setting allows Nine-Nine to reflect 
current social discourses of women, in particular 
women of color, in White male dominated workplace 
cultures that Scharrer (2012) characterized as hyper-
masculine, racist, and misogynistic.
Television programs with female protagonists 
have tackled friend dynamics that reinforce behavio-
ral and stereotypical clichés, including HBO’s Sex and 
the City (Stillion Southard, 2008), which upheld ideals 
of heteronormativity and material desire. NBC’s The 
Office (Birthisel & Martin, 2013) relied on gender hier-
archies of masculinity and the stereotypes of female 
professionals as either bossy and domineering or shy 
and powerless when interacting with each other. HBO’s 
Girls (Silverman & Hagelin, 2018) focused on aimless, 
antiaspirational White women friends who struggle in 
their careers and intimate lives, feeling simultaneously 
liberated and constrained by contemporary feminist 
politics. In reality TV , Dubrofsky (2006) found that 
ABC’s The Bachelor franchise continues to construct 
women singularly based on stereotypical behavioral 
traits and women of color as lesser romantic partners 
compared to White women, and Kramer (this 
 v
olume) 
presents the catfights between women on the fran-
chise as entrenched in cultural myths surrounding 
female competition over male partners.
Brooklyn Nine-Nine presents an alternative to 
these programs by depicting characters who are not 
wholly representative of their womanhood, sexual-
ity, race, or life experiences. They navigate the social, 
patriarchal hierarchies of their workplace and interper-
sonal lives together in a supportive manner that is not 
without conflict. My analysis will illuminate Brooklyn 
Nine-Nine’s commitment to intersectional storytelling 
and allyship.
Intersectionality and Allyship
Although many television shows depict back-
 
st
abbing behavior among women (Glascock, 2008; 
Kramer, this volume; Lauzen et al., 2008), the 
Nine-Nine friends disrupt this trope by engaging in 
intersectional allyship. Allies are members of dom-
inant groups who build relationship with and take 
stands against the oppression of members of non-
 
dominant g
roups. The female allies here are espe-
cially useful to consider in a context containing few 
women, let alone women with identities other than 
White or heterosexual. These allies affirm each oth-
er’s queer and/or woman of color identities. When 
they do appear in plotlines involving a date setup, 
women of color and queer characters have tended 
to be sidelined as the best friend; Brooklyn Nine-Nine 
challenges that trope by centering Rosa’s bisexuality.
In season 5, Gina attempts to set Rosa up on a 
date, and says, “Men are difficult, because they’re all 
secretly monsters, and now that I know you’re bi, that 
changes everything. I know so many great women!” 
In a previous episode, Rosa’s family was shown as not 
supportive and as confused about her bisexual iden-
tity. She thus struggled to come out to her friends at 
work. Gina’s outspoken allyship as a female friend in 
this moment is significant, because she does not posi-
tion her heterosexuality as a superior identity. She also 
does not ask Rosa to pick a side of her bisexuality, 
instead offering her support as a reliable wing-woman 
in finding Rosa a female partner. Rosa’s romantic life as 
the central narrative also takes an oppositional stance 
to discourses about “women of color, who work only 

190 Content
to frame the narrative about white people forming a 
romantic union” (Dubrofsky, 2006, p. 40). Gina’s sup-
port as a female friend demonstrates more broadly 
the informed action that White, heterosexual allies can 
take to demonstrate a personal commitment to their 
queer female friends of color.
The second way Nine-Nine demonstrates inter-
sectional allyship is an acknowledgement of the strug-
gles over normative feminine behaviors and workplace 
behavior as they intersect with Latina identity. In this 
example, the Latina characters contend with familiar 
female friendship discourses in the contexts of bach-
elorette parties and weddings. They also deconstruct 
the identity balance among women of color who may 
struggle to embrace their work ethic and simultane-
ously conceal desires for traditional feminine cultural 
norms deemed as weak. While shopping for her wed-
ding dress with Rosa, Amy attempts to conceal her 
desire for the feminized, heterosexual norms of wed-
ding culture and married life. Amy’s wedding dress 
try-on is interrupted by a street chase, ending with 
Amy handcuffing the criminal with a wedding sash. 
Amy tries to dismiss her emotional state about her 
upcoming nuptials, but Rosa tells her, 
No, we’re going to talk about it, because while 
wearing a wedding dress you leapt over a 
couch, sprinted down an alley, and jumped off  
of a car to subdue the crap out of a perp like 
you were Wonder Woman!
Rosa and Amy’s conversation is representative of 
how women of color’s allies negotiate identity in the 
interpersonal domain of power identified by Col-
lins (2000), which involves the everyday practices 
of how people treat each other, subordinate each 
other, or in this case, support each other. As Amy 
struggles to negotiate her performance of feminin-
ity, as a product of a culture that tells women to 
self-surveil their gender performance and stance 
on feminism, Rosa’s support makes visible “the 
smaller connections in intimate conversations that 
have become direct products of the macro and have 
become tactics of both oppression and survival” 
(Ghabra & Calafell, 2018, p. 46) for women of color. 
The two characters have a small, but significant 
interaction that exemplifies allyship among Latina 
women through their creation of a support network 
that doesn’t negatively frame any of Amy’s struggles 
with femininity.
Addressing Social Inequalities Through 
Intersectional Women’s Allyship
Brooklyn Nine-Nine continues to exemplify an 
intersectional feminist narrative by incorporating 
a conversation about Latina female support in a 
workplace dominated by men and sexism. Conver-
sations about support between two Latina detec-
tives demonstrates how Brooklyn Nine-Nine utilizes 
awareness of the oppressive nature of the police pre-
cinct for a moment of allyship. It exemplifies Collins’ 
(2000, p. 282) notion of “working the cracks,” which 
involves “changing her workplace by persistent use 
of her insider knowledge concerning its pressure 
points…find[ing] innovative ways to work the sys-
tem so that it will be more fair.” During the first sea-
son, Rosa is asked to be captain at a smaller nearby 
precinct. Amy, who aims to become a captain of an 
NYPD precinct, is frustrated by Rosa’s success. Rosa 
utilizes an intersectional framework to confront 
Amy’s anger. When Amy stated, “I’m competitive. I 
have seven brothers and I was the only girl. I always 
had to fight for a place at the table,” Rosa replied, 
“Well you’re not the only girl anymore. We work at a 
police force full of dudes, we gotta have each other’s 
backs, OK?” Amy responded, “Are you saying you 
have my back?” , with Rosa telling her she has her 
back. This conversation offers a reflection of issues 
that women of color face to transform institutions 
to be more equitable. The characters recognize the 
problems associated with competing against and 
putting down other women at work, illustrating the 
harmful, neoliberal feminist mindset hinging on the 
myth that because of the limited number of seats 
at the table, women must push other women aside 
in order to achieve success. Acknowledging that 
they have each other’s back, Rosa and Amy culti-
vate female Latina solidarity, showcasing the poten-
tial for vocal, outspoken woman-of-color support 
among colleagues.
A final example of intersectional allyship among 
women friends includes a plotline about workplace 
sexual misconduct. Previous studies of crime dramas 


Film and Television 191
suc
h as Law and Order have indicated problematic 
narratives related to vilification and objectification of 
female sexual assault victims, with women of color 
notably erased from these storylines (Cuklanz & 
Moorti, 2006). In response to current sociopolitical 
conversations about harassment and inclusion, epi-
sodes of television programs (Ryan, 2016; Strause, 
2019) are including conversations about workplace 
sexual misconduct.
Brooklyn Nine-Nine offers an intersectional narra-
tive for women addressing workplace sexual miscon-
duct. In the sixth season episode “He Said, She Said,” 
Amy helps a White woman named Keri who reports 
that her boss sexually assaulted her, and is apprehen-
sive of making her claims public for fear and cynicism 
of not being believed. Amy feels compelled to help this 
woman, having been sexually harassed by an older 
male captain as a young officer years earlier. Amy 
and Rosa disagree on whether to press charges—Amy 
pushes for immediate justice, and Rosa explains the 
social backlash, career setbacks, and red tape that Keri 
will face when the charges are made public, when the 
press “drag[s] her name through the mud,” making her 
life even more difficult.
Ultimately, Keri presses charges against the boss 
so she can begin living her life again, but loses money 
and quits her job. What seems like a loss to Amy, typ-
ically an idealist in terms of feminism and justice, is 
seen by Rosa as progress toward justice. She gestures 
to a Black woman co-worker of Keri’s who comes 
into the precinct to report sexual assault at the same 
workplace. Rosa, pointing to the pervasiveness of sex-
ual abuse as a larger, societal problem, explains: “Two 
steps forward, one step back, is still one step forward.” 
The disagreement between Rosa and Amy over jus-
tice for Keri offers a nuanced depiction of women’s 
experiences witnessing other women’s abuse while 
simultaneously grappling with their own experiences 
of workplace sexual misconduct. The narrative also 
recognizes that there are complicated opinions on 
how to stop sexual harassment in Rosa’s acknowl-
edgement of the bureaucratic complexities and inter-
personal turmoil of seeking justice for female sexual 
assault victims.
The end of the episode, when a Black woman 
comes to Amy and Rosa for help on another sexual 
assault case, demonstrates why intersectional allyship 
is necessary for finding and establishing support net-
works. Without Amy and Rosa’s empathy and support, 
Keri would have never been able to feel safe report-
ing her assault, and would have likely not told other 
women that Amy and Rosa were trusted sources. In 
this way, Brooklyn Nine-Nine identifies workplace sex-
ual misconduct as part of broader, structural patterns 
of abuse. The show presents allyship between women 
of differing races, jobs, sexualities, and other identities 
as a way forward, even though such allyship cannot 
guarantee ideal circumstances for women. Intersec-
tionally, the conversations in this episode demonstrate 
that reporting workplace sexual misconduct involves 
recognizing the unequal power relations across identi-
ties and structures that hinder women from reporting.
The disagreement between Rosa and Amy over 
how they seek justice for Keri shows that allyship with 
other women cannot always be easily achieved, but it 
is ultimately necessary in order to build collectives of 
women allies who are willing to take down systems 
that perpetuate their inequality. This episode shows 
that the complexities of reporting to authorities and 
grappling with the potentially negative repercussions to 
a woman’s career must be considered, because it is not 
so easy to accuse those in power without pushback. 
Rosa’s reassurance to Amy that what they did, even 
if it wasn’t what they wanted, for Keri was a way for 
her to live again, is important. It reinforces why seeking 
justice alongside other women who are allies and can 
provide alternative perspectives is necessary to dis-
mantle systems of oppression and seek support in the 
wake of trauma. Disagreement, exemplified by Rosa 
and Amy’s differing perspectives on the case, and the 
implicit message that their perspectives are informed 
by their experiences as Latina women, is bound to 
occur in social movements such as #MeToo where 
people of many identities must collectivize their voices 
to upend destructive systems of power. Their iden-
tities as Latina women navigating power in a police 
precinct—and for Amy, grappling with her assault—
adds an intersectional perspective to #MeToo. Such 
intersectionality is needed to be inclusive of the range 
of women’s social locations and experiences in rela-
tion to power, and to address the depth of inequality 
related to workplace sexual misconduct.

192 Content
The Value of Intersectionality and 
Allyship in Entertainment
Rosa, Amy, and Gina recognize each other’s races, 
sexualities, and experiences as allies for one another. 
They support each other interpersonally and profes-
sionally and do not shy away from disagreement or 
criticism of each other’s perspectives. Amy and Rosa’s 
layered discussions of their oppression as Latina 
police officers shows an “intra-cultural conversation 
and confrontation in order to build an unyielding 
platform of equity among [women of color]” (Mor -
aga, 2015, p. xxii). By addressing the inequalities they 
face as women of color police officers and for Rosa 
as a Latina queer woman navigating interpersonal 
oppression, the characters engage in productive 
discourse on how they can build networks of inter -
sectional feminist solidarity. By upending television 
stereotypes of female friend dynamics, amplifying 
each other’s sexuality, and verbally acknowledging 
the oppressive social hierarchies of workplace cul-
ture for women and specifically Latina women, the 
central friendship of Brooklyn Nine-Nine is an insight-
ful portrayal of the social truths of women of many 
backgrounds’ experiences and is valuable for depict-
ing women’s allyship with each other.

5.9: HEGEMONY IN ROMANTIC 
COMEDIES: THE POLITICAL WOMAN IN 
LONG SHOT
Kyra Heatly
This analysis of the rom-com Long Shot reveals 
that the film frames women in politics as successful 
if they follow hegemonic gender norms. As a result, 
the film does little to challenge the current status quo 
of representations of women in politics.
Narratives are part of our everyday life. News, social 
media posts, films, and television shows present sto-
ries that influence how we understand the social world 
around us. When evaluating media narratives about 
women in politics, Sheeler (2010) and Sheeler and 
Anderson (2013) found that mediated representations 
of political women served to limit their credibility and 
created barriers to success. According to Anderson, 
focusing on candidates’ appearance and domestic 
life “undercut[s] women’s agency by reducing their 
power to sex appeal and rewarding their attractiveness 
with heterosexual male approval rather than respect” 
(2011, pp. 338–339). When media focus on women’s 
domestic lives and bodies rather than their credentials, 
they portray women as less credible than their male 
counterparts.
Representation of political women in fictional 
narratives also plays an important role in construct-
ing discourses about women in politics. Through a 
feminist analysis of the romantic comedy Long Shot, 
I demonstrate that although the film challenges some 
aspects of hegemonic ideology, it ultimately reaffirms 
ideological constraints that limit political (and other) 
women.
Narratives are a major pillar of human expe-
rience. Carr (1986) contended that a community’s 
actions and experiences do not differ much from the 
stories told about it. The stories and narratives we 
consume reflect our own understanding of the world 
around us. By analyzing these stories, we can reveal 
the ideology embedded in our culture.
Ideology is a complex construct that encourages 
us to understand our social world in a particular way. 
Dominant ideologies are powerful because they may 
lead people to unconsciously accept interpretations 
without critical thought (Anderson, 2021). They often 
function hegemonically – meaning that some groups 
are able to maintain dominance over others through 
at times subtle ideological and political means (Clark, 
2002).
Ideologies exist on a spectrum, from reaffirming 
to challenging culturally accepted assumptions about 
how the world works (Jasinski, 2001). Using a femi-
nist approach, we can deconstruct a text’s narrative 
to reveal how it reinforces and subverts dominant 
oppressive hegemonic ideology about women (Dow, 
1990), in this case, women in politics.
Dow defined hegemony and hegemonic pro-
cesses as strategies that function to maintain the status 
quo, in this case that allow men to continue to hold 
more power than women do. People whose behaviors 
and beliefs are consistent with traditional gender ide-
ology can reproduce gender norms in such a way that 
they end up reinforcing an ideology of inequality even 
when it oppresses them. Even when we encounter 
narratives that seem to reflect or advocate for social 
change, real change is difficult to achieve. Hegemony 
protects dominant ideology by “absorbing it into forms 
compatible with the core ideological structure” (Gitlin, 
1982, p. 450). In other words, ideology might be pro-
tected and reinforced in a film even when it appears to 
be challenged. I extend Dow’s (1990) critical feminist 

194 Content
work on sitcoms to highlight how films that appear 
progressive can actually contradict social progress and 
reinforce the dominant ideology. I identify some ways 
different gender norms work to undercut the potential 
for social progress in Long Shot.
Exposing Gender Norms in Long Shot
According to Negra (2008), modern romantic com-
edies often feature successful women who present 
hyper-feminine, nonthreatening personae and are 
too busy climbing the corporate ladder to pursue 
romantic interests. Despite their success, these 
women are unsatisfied with their lives and willing 
to sacrifice their professional goals for romance. 
Typically, rom-coms portray women through a 
male-centered gaze that reinforces conventional 
gender norms and traditional female roles at wom-
en’s expense; such a gaze limits the revolutionary 
or subversive potential of the narrative (Cafarelli, 
1996). These narratives utilize traditional gender 
norms to portray the contemporary idea of a pro-
gressive woman, but then these norms are used to 
try to fix the problems. By doing so, the narrative 
contradicts the portrayal of the progressive woman 
because the gender norms themselves contribute to 
the discrimination (Negra, 2008).
Long Shot (2019) tells the story of presiden-
tial hopeful and current Secretary of State Charlotte 
Field (Charlise Theron) and speechwriter Fred Flar-
sky (Seth Rogen). After an unexpected reconnection, 
Field learned that Flarsky was a journalist and hired 
him as her speech writer, despite her chief of staff’s 
horrified reaction and attempts to dissuade Field from 
doing so. While traveling around the world, Flarsky 
writes speeches that help Field become more likable 
to voters. Even though they are diametrically opposed, 
sparks fly between them. Their relationship is threat-
ened as circumstances force Field to choose between 
Flarsky and her presidential ambitions.
In what follows, I argue that although Long Shot 
seems to challenge the dominant ideology and present 
as inappropriate the sexist challenges that women in 
politics experience, it ultimately functions hegemoni-
cally. Charlotte Field is largely presented as competent, 
and references some of the barriers faced by women 
politicians, but along the way she works within rather 
than dismantling those barriers and subverting gender 
norms. Although other gender norms are present, my 
analysis will focus on three: the importance of appear-
ance, a focus on women’s emotional expressions, and 
choosing between love and a career. Overall, the nar-
rative reinforces the idea that women in politics must 
conform to these hegemonic gender norms in order to 
be successful.
The Importance of Appearance
Appearance gender norms require women to fol-
low strict standards of beauty. Dominant ideology 
describes an ideal woman as thin, graceful, with 
youthful skin, professionally dressed, and in full 
makeup, all of which Field epitomizes. Her dedica-
tion to her physical appearance is further reflected by 
showing her working out and pressing cold spoons 
to her eyes so she does not look tired from working 
late nights. Her appearance and her actions to main-
tain it reinforce dominant standards of beauty. She 
takes this further by practicing how she waves when 
acknowledging others because her political consult-
ant told her that the public reacts negatively to her 
natural wave. The steps Field takes to appear the 
perfect candidate reinforce the idea that appearance 
– not qualifications – is the key to success.
Importantly, Long Shot at times uses the appear-
ance gender norm to challenge its validity. By incor-
porating news reports about Field’s appearance 
throughout, the film calls attention to the fact that 
reporters are more likely to cover women politicians’ 
appearance than their policy stances. For example, 
when a male news anchor justifies commenting on 
Field’s attractiveness by claiming that “when we talk 
about women in this way it’s because we respect 
them so much, and that starts with their body,” the 
film reflects the reality that too often, attractiveness is 
related to perceived competency. In reality, if the focus 
is on looks, political women’s qualifications are at best 
minimized and ignored.
Presenting the focus on political women’s appear-
ance as foolish helps challenge hegemonic gender 
norms. However, the film fails to reflect actual change; 
the character does not subvert the norm. For exam-
ple, during an interview about democracy in Eastern 
Europe, Field challenged a reporter’s question by 


Film and Television 195
r
etorting “Would you be asking a male cabinet mem-
ber what products they use in their hair?” The film 
again problematizes media focus on women’s physi-
cal features instead of their policies and qualifications. 
But the protest was withdrawn: Field quickly added, 
“I’m just kidding. No, it’s olive oil and mayonnaise.  
So cheap, and so much shine!” She undermined the 
power of her initial response. Although she began to 
challenge the dominant ideology, she instead rein-
forced it.
The way Long Shot highlights the norm that a 
woman’s appearance is one of her most important 
attributes even extends to how women eat. Stereotyp-
ically, women are expected to eat politely, in a ladylike 
fashion, taking small bites. After a long day, Field, rav-
enous, attends a party. But all of the food is skewered. 
How can she eat this food elegantly? Her advisors form 
a wall and she crouches down behind them and takes 
a huge bite of chicken off a skewer – at which point the 
Prime Minister of Canada approaches. She rises, quickly 
spitting the chicken into a napkin, and eats nothing else. 
The visual absurdity of this scene echoes the absurdity 
of the gender norm. It shows that for women in the pub-
lic eye, preserving appearances is more important than 
the need for basic nutrition. Field knows that how she 
eats her food could affect her likeability as a presiden-
tial candidate. The film shows us that this norm only 
applies to women; the high-profile men at the party eat 
with abandon. Y et even as the film ridicules the hegem-
onic norm, Field adheres to it and stops eating despite 
her hunger. In the process, she reinforces that political 
women must function within the hegemonic norms, 
including maintaining socially defined standards of 
attractiveness, in order to be successful.
Focus on Political Women’s Emotional  
Expression
Stereotypically, women are seen as emotionally 
driven, irrational, and hysterical, all of which describe 
women as too weak to lead. Y et, women must show 
some level of emotion in order to succeed. Thus, 
women must be careful when displaying their emo-
tions. This means working within other gendered 
expectations about women such as elegance and 
lightheartedness, and using emotions strategically 
to appear competent and compassionate.
One way Long Shot highlights the stereotype that 
women are overly emotional is through Field’s recog-
nition that people interpret women’s actions differently 
than they do men’s. She doesn’t want her anger and 
emotion to be associated with an inability to lead, just 
as she doesn’t want to be seen as cold and passionless 
if she is not warm and personable. During a conflict 
with Flarsky over some inappropriate humor he’d 
included in a speech draft, Field articulated how wom-
en’s emotions are often perceived: “yeah, listen Fred, if 
I’m angry, I’m hysterical. If I’m emotional, I’m weak. If 
I so much as raise my voice, I’m a bitch.” Field under-
stands the nuances of being a woman in politics. She 
cannot be assertive or angry. She also knows she must 
appear humorous and lighthearted. However, recogni-
tion is only the first step toward challenging this stere-
otype, and the film only takes that first step. Ultimately, 
she and Flarsky add some lighthearted humor about 
her personal life to the speech. As a result, Long Shot 
again shows Field functioning within – and reinforcing –  
expectations of appropriate behavior for women. No 
alternative is proposed.
In addition, Long Shot shows us the double stand-
ard of femininity that women in leadership positions 
experience, which as Sheeler and Anderson (2013) 
said increases the difficulty of creating a positive 
image of a woman in power. Field reinforces hegem-
onic ideology by adhering to other positively perceived 
gender norms, which are portrayed as character traits. 
For example, Field’s consultant (Lisa Kudrow) pre-
sents opinion research measuring Field on traits such 
as charisma, elegance, passion, and humor. Field isn’t 
convinced that these are the most important variables: 
“I am really interested in knowing how people feel 
about my accomplishments,” The consultant replies, 
“We don’t drill down on specific policy, and that’s 
because people don’t seem to care.” This exchange 
challenges the norm by foregrounding the traits Field 
must display in order to appear composed and not 
overemotional. Field’s desire to list her accomplish-
ments and the consultant’s direct response to that idea 
poke fun at the belief that voters don’t measure women 
by their accomplishments but by their character traits 
and strategic expressions of emotions. Although this 
points out the gendered expectations, the narrative 
fails to disrupt it. Field continues to reference the trait 
scores and adjust her behavior to try to increase them. 

196 Content
In doing so, Long Shot reinforces the fact that women 
must adhere to positive aspects of femininity to remain 
likeable and avoid being labeled too emotional or not 
feminine enough in order to succeed. The focus on 
personal attributes rather than political accomplish-
ments limits the public’s perception of political women, 
which undermines their credibility and attempts to run 
for office (Sheeler & Anderson, 2013).
However, the film fully challenges and subverts 
gendered expectation that women lack mental and 
emotional strength. Typically, women are seen as not 
mentally tough enough to endure the stress of war 
or violence. The film directly disrupts this norm by 
placing Field and Flarsky in a war zone. When their 
building is bombed, Field and Flarsky take cover in a 
cellar. Flarsky is on the verge of a panic attack and 
questions why Field is not panicking. Field explains 
that she stays calm using a Navy SEAL breathing tech-
nique. The contrast between Flarsky and Field is strik-
ing, with the woman remaining strong while the man 
collapses. Field’s explanation demonstrates that emo-
tional strength can be learned and shows that women 
can be emotionally tough. In so doing, Long Shot dis-
rupts the norm and communicates that women have 
the emotional and mental tenacity to withstand even 
the toughest situations in politics.
Choosing Between Love and Career
Negotiating a successful career and a fulfilling roman-
tic relationship is a site of tension for many women. 
Women are often told they cannot have it all and 
are often expected to sacrifice their career for love. 
Assuming a heterosexual relationship (the norm in 
rom-coms), this could mean quitting work altogether, 
or changing jobs to either allow the man to further his 
career or allow the woman more time to take care of 
the man, the family, and the household duties. The 
gendered power dynamic is that the man is dominant 
and the woman is subordinate. Long Shot challenges 
this power dynamic by presenting Flarsky as overe-
motional, uncontained, unaccomplished, and unpro-
fessional. He is professionally subordinate to Field; 
he is a member of her staff. By framing Flarsky in this 
manner, the narrative shows that women need not be 
subservient to a man. This is in some ways progres-
sive because its challenges the gendered hierarchy of 
heterosexual romantic relationships. However, it is a 
weak challenge at best. Because Flarsky is so clearly 
incompetent on so many levels – at least based on 
the application of men’s gender norms – it is no 
stretch to imagine many women being more capable 
and powerful than he is.
Still, as previously mentioned, rom-coms often 
feature successful women who willingly sacrifice their 
career for romance, and Long Shot also addresses the 
expectation that women must choose between their 
career and love. The film presents an obstacle affect-
ing both the potential Field presidential candidacy 
and the Field–Flarsky relationship when a sexually 
revealing video of Flarsky surfaces. President Cham-
bers and another high-profile man use the video to 
blackmail Field: they will pull their endorsement if 
she doesn’t scale down her environmental initiative. 
Field must choose between declaring her presidential 
candidacy and a robust initiative that she believes in 
strongly. She decides to sacrifice the initiative so she 
can keep the political endorsement. Having made 
that decision, she must now determine whether she 
can run for president while maintaining a relationship 
with Flarsky (still seen as an inappropriate partner 
for a president, especially in light of the video). In an 
attempt to have both love and success, she tries to 
convince Flarsky to change his image, or if not to 
drop out of sight and become her secret lover. He 
refuses both options. Field’s attempt to challenge the 
norm and have both love and a career fails. With just 
minutes left in the film, it seems she will be left with 
only her career, reinforcing the norm.
However, Field takes control. In her announce-
ment that she is running for president, she discloses 
the blackmail attempt and declares she loves Flar -
sky. Shortly thereafter we see Field being inaugu-
rated as president with Flarsky by her side. The 
norm is challenged and subverted. She can have it 
all. Reading this scene as a subverting the gender 
norm creates an idealized vision of disrupting politi-
cal culture because it happens at the film’s end, with 
no development between the announcement and 
the inauguration. Nevertheless, presenting a woman 
in the highest position of power in the United States 
in a happy and loving relationship does challenge 
the norm that women must choose between their 
career and love.


Film and Television 197
W
orking Within the System
The purpose of my critique is to expose how gender 
norms function hegemonically, despite the inclusion 
of narratives that appear to reflect social change. Long 
Shot effectively highlights a number of problematic 
norms and stereotypes and, in the process, acknowl-
edges that women are held back by these reflections 
of the dominant ideology. However, the narrative 
does little to subvert or undermine the norms or ste-
reotypes that function to hold women back. Charlotte 
Field is a strong, intelligent, ambitious woman who 
overcomes barriers and does succeed. But along 
the way she navigates around obstacles; she doesn’t 
strike them down. Working within the system in this 
way reproduces the norms and the sexism within the 
political sphere. Rather than demonstrate how we 
can improve and rebuild politics to be a more inclu-
sive environment, Long Shot reinforces the idea that 
women must figure out how to win while playing by – 
not changing – the rules. Success requires adherence 
to hegemonic norms.
References

5.10: HONING HEGEMONIC 
MASCULINITY: A LOOK AT I LOVE YOU, 
MAN AND GET HARD
Sarah E. Fryett
The author explores how the hit comedies I Love 
Y ou, Man and Get Hard reinforce dominant mas-
culine ideals of aggression, sexual conquest, and 
avoiding emotion and other qualities often consid-
ered feminine.
What does the phrase “men in Hollywood” bring 
to mind? The strength and aggressiveness of John 
Wayne, the emotionless anti-hero of Al Pacino, or the 
sexual conquests of James Bond? Or, does the phrase 
bring to mind allegations of sexual harassment and 
It’s Your Turn: What Do You Think? What 
Will You Find?
 1.
 Pic
k a romantic comedy with female 
lead character. What gender norms do 
you see, and how might these might limit 
the character’s ability to succeed?
 2.
 Sear
ch news sites for articles about 
high-profile female politicians. To what 
extent do the stories present content 
that reflects the gender norms discussed 
in this reading? What norms present

resented in fictional media to what you

 3.

roups of 3–5, write a short script that 
incorporates a gender norm but chal-

challenged. As a class, discuss various
