198 Content
the #metoo movement? Could there be a  connection  
between our favorite film heroes and the very real 
displays of toxic masculinity in the 21st century? The 
answer, quite simply, is yes. Chung (2007) argued: 
“Exposure to popular media may be the dominant 
means by which children, as well as most adults, learn 
about others and acquire and internalize social norms, 
values, and beliefs as manifest in the expressions and 
presentations of the media” (p. 99). The time, then, is 
ripe to critically examine our Hollywood men. Although 
the representation of masculinity shifts somewhat over 
time, some disturbing patterns and traits remain firmly 
entrenched. In this essay, I demonstrate how Holly-
wood’s representation of masculinity in several popu-
lar bromances offers a clear way to be a man.
The bromance film centers on the intimate 
friendship of two male protagonists. I analyze the hit 
comedies I Love Y ou, Man and Get Hard, both of which 
focus on a protagonist who learns, through a friend’s 
tutelage, to be more appropriately masculine. I explore 
how these films present an acceptable, dominant mas-
culinity, or hegemonic masculinity. The films follow 
the same trajectory: laughing at the unacceptable per-
ceived feminine traits, recognizing and then learning 
to overcome the traits, and finally embracing hegem-
onic masculinity. The films subtly construct a narrow 
conventional definition of masculinity that sidelines 
women while adamantly sustaining the systems of 
patriarchy and heteronormativity.
Hegemonic Masculinity and the 
Bromance
The concept of hegemonic masculinity (Connell, 
1983) was first used to examine the patriarchal 
system of gender relations. Since then, feminist 
theorists, sociologists, and cultural studies scholars 
have employed the concept for multiple purposes; 
I use the definition provided by Ricciardelli, Clow, 
and White (2010): hegemonic masculinity is the 
“culturally normative ideals of masculinity within a 
structure of social relations” (p. 64). In other words, 
hegemonic masculinity is a set of characteristics—
for example, aggressiveness, risk-taking behaviors, 
misogyny—that create the dominant masculinity. 
Thompson and Whearty (2004, p. 6) argued that 
even though “hegemonic masculinity may not be 
the lived form of masculinity at all…it remains a 
powerful, perhaps dominant script against which 
self and others are evaluated across the life course.” 
Thus, even when men do not achieve this ideal, the 
script remains a conditioning component (Connell & 
Messerschmidt, 2005) and allows “a way of talking 
about overarching ideologies at the level of every-
day, taken-for-granted ideas and practice” (Hearn, 
2004, p. 53). Such taken-for-granted ideas and prac-
tices are subtly reinforced throughout the bromance.
The bromance traces its roots to the buddy films 
of the 1970s—a set of films that adamantly perpetu-
ated hegemonic masculinity. Wood’s seminal work on 
Hollywood explored the rise of the buddy film, which 
he situated with Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid, 
Easy Rider, and Midnight Cowboy. Wood argued that 
the popularity of the buddy films of the 1970s “testifies 
to the contemporary ‘heterosexual’ male audience’s 
need to denigrate and marginalize women, but…also 
to validate love relationships between men” (2003,  
p. 205).
The bromance has retained many characteristics 
of the buddy film, but has a slightly altered vision of 
hegemonic masculinity. As DeAngelis (2014) noted:
The buddy film and the bromance are certainly 
similar in that both feature a homosocially 
grounded “male love story,” but in bromance 
this designation of “love story” is always brack-
eted by scare quotes, signaling a romance that is 
never actually or intentionally romantic but that 
gains cultural currency by adopting the pretext.
(p. 11)
The bromance, then, centers on a male love story—
or strong male friendship in the case of the films dis-
cussed here—while firmly eschewing the possibility 
of any actual homosexual romance. Bromances 
also negate—through laughter—any characteris-
tics such as effeminate mannerisms that might be 
seen as stereotypically gay. DeAngelis also argued 
that whereas “women in the buddy film were vir -
tually absent, women in the bromance narrative 
are often represented misogynistically as loving yet 
controlling” (2014, p. 12). A final element of the bro-
mance, according to DeAngelis, is the construction 
of “intermale closeness as healthy, especially in the 


Film and Television 199
s
ense that it can foster or renew manliness” (p. 16).  
This renewal of manliness does not—as Alberti 
(2013) and others posit—offer a plurality of mascu-
linities; instead, the bromances examined here paint 
a singular clear image of what it means to be a man.
The bromances I analyze maintain the tradition 
of hegemonic masculinity, although the plots differ 
drastically. I Love you, Man revolves around Peter 
Klaven (Paul Rudd) who, after getting engaged to 
Zooey (Rashida Jones), realizes that he has no one to 
ask to be the best man. This prompts Peter to begin 
searching for male friends. The first few tries fail, but 
he eventually finds Sydney Fife (Jason Segel). They 
become fast friends and spend a lot of time together 
much to the chagrin of Zooey. Get Hard, on the other 
hand, begins with James (Will Ferrell)—a hedge fund 
 mana
ger—being wrongly convicted of fraud and 
embezzlement. The judge, wanting to make an exam-
ple, sentences him to San Quentin. James realizes that 
he is ill-equipped (i.e., not masculine enough) to with-
stand prison, so he employs Darnell (Kevin Hart)—his 
car detailer—to toughen him up. The traditional three 
stages of the bromance described above are evident 
in these films, although for different underlying rea-
sons. The outcome is the same: the maintenance of 
hegemonic masculinity in support of patriarchy and 
heteronormativity.
Masculinity in Jeopardy
At the outset of each film, the protagonist’s mascu-
linity is presented as deficient. The deficiencies dif-
fer, but the message is the same: something is wrong 
with your masculinity, and thus, the viewer should 
laugh at you. Peter is painted as a “too thought-
ful” man, both in his relationship with Zooey and 
his career as a real estate agent. For example, after 
his proposal, Zooey starts calling around to tell her 
friends the news and asks Peter if he wants to call 
his friends. His puzzled look and “Huh?” make for 
a comedic moment, one of the first signals that 
something is wanting. Shortly thereafter Peter’s 
mother sighs and observes: “He’s always connected 
with the girls more.” The film suggests that if a guy 
does not have any close male friends, his mascu-
linity is defective. This scene is followed by Peter 
serving drinks and snacks at a girls’ night, and  
Zooey’s friends playfully making fun of him. These 
three scenes introduce the viewer to Peter, making it 
clear he fails to adhere to the ideal masculine script; 
something must be done.
Recognizing his failure, he observes: “I got to get 
some f**king friends,” and thus begins his journey to a 
more acceptable masculinity. The first few individuals 
he tries to befriend, however, also present unaccept-
able versions of masculinity. One candidate (Zooey’s 
friend’s husband) disappoints because he is a beer 
swilling, swearing poker player who mainly grunts and 
yells—too masculine. In another failed attempt, Peter 
is set up on a man-date with someone who dresses 
well and takes Peter out for an expensive meal and 
good wine. The man mistakes Peter for being gay, and 
when the man tries to kiss him, Peter vomits. Because 
of Peter’s failure to practice or at least attempt to 
practice hegemonic masculinity, his sexuality is con-
structed as in jeopardy. The remainder of the film is 
spent remedying this uncertainty in order to reestab-
lish the systems of patriarchy and heteronormativity.
James’ masculinity, like Peter’s, is subtly ques-
tioned throughout the opening of Get Hard. The very 
first shot of the film—which lasts a few seconds—
shows James crying hysterically: large tears, hiccough-
ing, and wails. The close-up forces the viewer into this 
overwrought moment. It takes only seconds for us to 
recognize this unusual behavior—out of the normative 
ideal—which makes us laugh. In the next shot, the film 
flashes back one month to James waking and doing 
naked yoga-like exercises. The viewer is encouraged to 
laugh at this behavior because it also contradicts tradi-
tional masculinity. The subsequent scene furthers this 
perspective when James’ fiancée Alissa (Alison Brie) 
says: “Y ou are a great man, James,” as though he needs 
constant encouragement. She throws him into bed 
and initiates sex, but the blueprints of their new home 
strewn across the bed distract him. He cautiously asks: 
“Y ou don’t think it’s too much house, do you?” She bul-
lies him into saying: “This house is a shithole.” These 
first images of James portray him as weak, unable to 
stand up for himself, and controlled by his fiancée—
similar in many ways to the initial images of Peter.
Although James is revered in the corridors of his 
office building, he is painted as uncharacteristically 
feminine in an exchange with his boss and soon to be 
father-in-law, Martin (Craig T. Nelson). After a personal 

200 Content
conversation, Martin says: “Call me Dad,” and then 
James, sniffling, responds: “My real father never had 
time for me,” and starts to cry. A worker at the firm 
mouths: “What the f**k?” The viewer embodies the 
place of the worker and is thus encouraged to recog-
nize the exchange as an unacceptable display of emo-
tion. These displays continue during the 30 days he has 
to get his affairs in order. Many hysterical sobs occur: 
he cries while performing martial arts, eating breakfast, 
and drinking wine, and when Alissa says she is leaving 
him. For the first 25 minutes of the film, James weeps. 
His lack of emotional control and inability to be domi-
nant with Alissa render his masculinity in jeopardy.
Masculinity in Progress
The male friendships at the center of the films occur 
for vastly different reasons, but each provides the 
catalyst for moving the protagonist from a fragile 
masculinity to a hegemonic masculinity. In order 
to accomplish this transition, hyper-masculine role 
models (the friends) are needed. It should be noted 
that whereas Sydney fully embraces his hyper-
 
mas
culinity, Darnell’s is artificial; it is a mask worn to 
make money. Peter meets Sydney at an open house 
where Sydney is looking for female divorcees. This 
is our first sign of Sydney’s misogyny, which fosters 
various moments of comedic release devoid of eth-
ical repercussions. One of their first conversations 
revolves around the sexual conquest of women, and 
Sydney’s mantra is: “No lag between the vag,” which 
translates to an unceasing stream of sexual partners. 
Sydney justifies this: “I’m a man, Peter...We are ani-
mals.” Men, according to Sydney, have uncontrollable 
desires that should be satisfied at any cost. Moments 
later he states: “There’s...this nurse there that I want 
to f**k so badly.” Women are sex objects and good 
for little else in this dynamic. Although Peter does 
not fully embrace Sydney’s mantra, this remains 
an educational moment in how to be a man within 
the system of patriarchy. Sydney’s demonstration of 
hyper-masculinity encourages Peter to distance him-
self from his earlier perceived feminine characteris-
tics, thereby reestablishing heteronormativity.
Peter’s second lesson, similar to James’ first, is to 
learn aggressiveness—a characteristic of hegemonic 
masculinity. Sydney curses a lot, makes rude gestures, 
and refuses to pick up his dog’s feces. On a walk, a 
passerby yells at Sydney and Peter because he stepped 
in the feces. Sydney yells right back and intimates phys-
ical violence. Violence is condoned through the humor 
of the situation, which further legitimates aggressive-
ness. Peter becomes flustered, which prompts Sydney 
to teach him how to yell. Peter’s initial yell is quiet and 
weak, which fosters yet another comic moment. After 
practice and encouragement from Sydney, he finally 
roars. In this moment, he taps into what the film sug-
gests is a primal masculinity, which has remained hid-
den. His facial expressions show a seemingly unknown 
pleasure: he is starting to embrace normative mascu-
linity. Sydney also teaches him through various other 
activities—playing the drums, drinking, and doing 
risky stunts on the scooter. Peter’s engagement with 
the hyper-masculine Sydney fosters a re-forming of 
his masculinity that condones the objectification of 
women and admires aggressive actions.
James’ journey in Get Hard is unlike Peter’s 
because he wants to practice a hegemonic mascu-
linity in order to survive prison; however, the actual 
journey and lessons taught parallel those in I Love 
Y ou, Man. James approaches Darnell pleading “Help 
me to not be someone’s bitch. Y ou can be Athena to 
my Odysseus.” Darnell agrees—for $30,000—and 
thus begins James’ toughening up. Darnell arrives at 
James’ house and sprays him with mace, admonish-
ing “Always be on your guard,” and “Y ou’re going to 
have to work harder than you’ve ever worked before.” 
James finds it difficult to embrace a normative mas-
culinity, and these moments cause significant laugh-
ter. For example, Darnell encourages him to make a 
“mad dog face”—a scrunched up look designed to 
evoke fear. James fails miserably, and instead starts 
crying, again, moaning: “I miss her so much,” and “I’m 
extremely sad.” Darnell mocks him as a punishment 
for the emotional outburst. The training continues 
when Darnell takes James to the park and tells him to 
get into a fight. James repeatedly fails at this task and 
is violently assaulted each time. These assaults are, I 
suggest, attempts to correct James’ inability to adhere 
to normative masculinity.
Because James cannot work past these feminine 
characteristics, Darnell takes a different tactic, one 
that ultimately leads to James deciding to get hard—
embrace hegemonic masculinity. This disturbing scene 
is reminiscent of when Peter is mistaken for being gay. 
Darnell says: “I don’t feel like you’re giving me 100%,” 


Film and Television 201
and ther
efore, “Y ou’re going to learn how to suck dick.” 
They go to a brunch restaurant frequented by gay men. 
James goes to the bathroom and tries to psych him-
self into performing fellatio: “I’m going to put it in my 
mouth,” and “Down the hatch.” He repeatedly tries, 
but is overcome with disgust. He leaves the restroom 
emphatically stating: “Y ou have to train me. I’m ready 
to get hard.” This experience is the catalyst for James 
to inaugurate his transformation. His adamant rejec-
tion of homosexuality helps him reject his feminine 
characteristics. He begins training, working on his trash 
talk, and fighting, and when Darnell pretends to stab 
him, James deflects the knife—showcasing his arrival 
at a new masculinity. As with Peter, James’ hegemonic 
masculinity manifests through the excoriation of per-
ceived femininity and homosexuality.
Masculinity in Its Ideal
The hyper-masculine personas of Sydney and 
Darnell differ, yet allow Peter and James to truly 
embrace and subsequently practice hegemonic mas-
culinity. The denouements of these films reveal how 
the protagonists reached the normative ideal. Peter 
has learned the right kind of masculinity because he 
vehemently slaps a difficult coworker; this moment 
cements his new and acceptable hegemonic mas-
culinity. The hegemonic ideal is subsequently priv-
ileged when the male friendship threatens to take 
precedence over Peter’s wedding. Peter tells Sydney: 
“I think we should spend some time apart” because 
Sydney’s hyper-masculinity is a bit excessive. How-
ever, they reconcile at the wedding where they 
profess their love: Peter: “I love you, man.” Sydney: 
“I love you, too, bud.” The male friendship bond 
is re-solidified in the middle of Peter’s marriage to 
Zooey, and then the film abruptly ends. This ending 
privileges male friendship even over a marriage bond 
typically presented as lasting “till death do us part.”
Just as Peter learns to be more aggressive, James 
becomes mentally and physically aggressive through 
Darnell’s coaching. By the end of the film, James’ ref-
erences to Balzac and Shakespeare are replaced with 
rampant cursing and the erasure of emotion. James 
fights a gang, and his new appreciation for violence 
and aggression culminates at the film’s end when he 
confronts his former boss, Martin, who had orches-
trated the arrest in order to cover up his own illegal 
doings. James shouts, “I’ve been pushed around for 
too long!” A violent fight ensues; they bring down Mar-
tin’s henchmen and obtain the information needed to 
exonerate James. At this point, James repeatedly tells 
Darnell “Y ou got me so hard. Y ou got me so hard.” 
This phrase translates to “Y ou helped me to learn the 
appropriate way to be masculine.” James’ masculinity 
is reformed; he has learned to take risks, be violent, 
and eradicate emotionality.
I Love Y ou, Man and Get Hard present a very 
clear image of what it takes to be a man. According 
to these films, it is unacceptable for a man to be too 
emotional, too sensitive, or possibly gay. These films 
demonstrate that nonhegemonic masculinity is intol-
erable. Through the hyper-masculinity of Sydney and 
the pretend hyper-masculinity of Darnell, Peter and 
James are reformed: they learn to erase any char -
acteristic that could be construed as feminine. They 
learn to act tough; they learn that violence is the solu-
tion. Hegemonic masculinity sustains the systems of 
patriarchy and heteronormativity, and these systems 
perpetuate toxic masculinity, rape culture, sexism, and 
homophobia. It is time to call for representations that 
offer diverse images of how to be a man and to advo-
cate for change on and off the screen.
It’s Your Turn: What Do You Think? What 
Will You Find?
 1.
 T
o what extent do other genres focused 
on male friendships (Westerns, crime, 
detective, and so forth) perpetuate or 
challenge hegemonic masculinity? Look 
for an example of a film that challenges 
this rigid vision of masculinity.
 2.
 T
here is a variety of female buddy films 
such as Bridesmaids, The Heat, and Thelma 
and Louise. In what ways do these films 
maintain or challenge a hegemonic femi-
ninity reflecting traditional feminine ideals?
 3.
 Heg
emonic masculinity can be found in 
other forms of popular culture. Select a 
TV series, a musical genre, a type of mag-
azine, or a novel. To what extent does this 
material challenge or perpetuate hegem-
onic masculinity?

202 Content
References
Alberti, J. (2013). “I love you, man”: Bromances, the construc-
tion of masculinity, and the continuing evolution of the 
romantic comedy. Quarterly Review of Film and Video, 
30, 159–172.
Chung, S. K. (2007). Media literacy art education: Decon-
structing lesbian and gay stereotypes in the media. Inter-
national Journal of Art & Design Education, 26, 98–107.
Connell, R. W. (1983). Which Way Is Up? Essays on Sex, Class 
and Culture. Allen and Unwin.
Connell, R.W. & Messerschmidt, J. (2005). Hegemonic mas-
culinity: Rethinking the concept. Gender and Society, 
19(6), 829–859.
DeAngelis, M. (2014). Reading the Bromance: Homosocial Rela-
tionships in Film and Television. Wayne State University 
Press.
Hearn, J. (2004). From hegemonic masculinity to the hegem-
ony of men. Feminist Theory, 5(1), 49–72.
Ricciardelli, R., Clow, K., & White, P. (2010). Investigating 
hegemonic masculinity: Portrayals of masculinity in

5.11: BATMAN IN THE BARRIO: A 
CRITICAL LOOK AT THE LATINIDAD 
OF MALE LATINX CHARACTERS IN 
SUICIDE SQUAD, EL CHICANO, AND 
SPIDER-MAN: INTO THE SPIDER-VERSE
Anthony R. Ramirez
The author uses Latina/o critical communication 
theory to analyze the Latinidad of three charac-
ters in superhero and comic book films: El Diablo 
from Suicide Squad (2016), Miles Morales from 
Spider-man: Into the Spider-verse, and Diego 
Hernandez from El Chicano (2019).
Comic book films are extremely popular but are 
largely White with few Latinx characters. This study 
will investigate the Latinidad of three comic book/
superhero Latinx characters.
I use Latina/o Critical Communication Theory 
(Anguiano & Castaneda, 2014) to guide my analysis. 
This perspective addresses “the material, verbal, visual, 
and discursive experiences of Latinos” (p. 107). This 
theory bridges Critical Race Theory, Latina/o Critical 
Race Theory, and Latina/o Communication Studies, 
to centralize the Latinx experience within communi-
cation and media.
Molina-Guzmán (2013) defined Latinidad 
as “the material conditions of Latinas/os and the 
semiotic process of being, performing, and com-
modifying US Latina/o identity” (p. 212). Latinidad 
is an umbrella term including the qualities, markers, 
and characteristics of what it means to be Latinx. 
Latinidad can be applied with different foci such as 
race, color, legal status, class, nation, language, pol-
itics of location, and more. As Molina-Guzmán and 
Valdivia (2004) stated, the construction of Latinidad 
has been primarily through mainstream popular cul-
ture. Thus, my essay helps provide an understanding 
of the construction and representation of Latinidad 
in comic book films.
The three characters analyzed are El Diablo 
(Suicide Squad), Miles Morales (Spider-Man: 
Into the Spider-verse), and Diego Hernandez (El 
Chicano).
Suicide Squad (2016) is a major studio release 
about a group of dangerous, incarcerated, and 
expendable supervillains, “Task Force X,” which is 
sent on a top-secret mission. The Latinx character 
Chato Santana a.k.a. El Diablo (Jay Hernandez) is 
only on screen for about five minutes but has a piv-
otal role. He is a pyro-powered supervillain who 
helps save his team by sacrificing himself during 
battle. Spider-Man: Into the Spider-verse (2018) is a 
major studio release about a Brooklyn Afro-Latino 
teenager, Miles Morales (Shameik Moore), who 
is bitten by a radioactive spider. Morales meets 
various spider characters from the multiverse 
and works with them as he transforms into the 
 Spider
-Man of his universe to stop the evil Kingpin. 
El Chicano (2018) is an independent film about a 
Los Angeles police officer, Diego Hernandez (Raul 
Castillo), who slowly becomes the vigilante El Chi-
cano or as (Ehrlich, 2019) put it, the “Batman in 
the barrio” as he tries to unravel the mystery of his 
twin brother’s death.


Film and Television 203
T
he Latinidad of El Diablo, Miles 
Morales, and Diego Hernandez
My analysis of these characters in relation to the 
process of being, performing, and commodifying 
their Latinidad is revealed in five main themes: 
appearance, language, espirtualismo, machismo, 
and familismo. Each will be discussed in a term.
Appearance
Character appearance was a major signifier of 
Latinidad in all three films. One obvious form of 
Latinidad is the cholo culture, especially in Suicide 
Squad and El Chicano. The cholo is a heavily used 
stereotype in both mainstream and Latinx media 
to represent hypermasculine and threatening fig-
ures. The cholo is a descendant of another Latinx 
stereotype: the Mexican Bandido (Mora, 2011; 
Ramirez-Berg, 2002). Cholos are Mexican gang 
bangers, usually seen wearing white tank tops, 
Dickies’ shorts, Nike Cortez shoes, and Ray-Ban 
sunglasses. Occasionally, cholos have tattoos that 
represent religion, culture, family, and other mark-
ers of Latinidad.
The primary signifier of El Diablo’s Latinidad 
in Suicide Squad is his appearance, which heavily 
reflects cholo and Mexican gang member stereo-
types. El Diablo is the only one of the three char -
acters analyzed to have tattoos. He is tattooed all 
over his body, including his face and head, with 
various gang or cholo-inspired symbols. His facial 
tattoos give him the appearance of a skull with dark 
eyes, skull teeth above his upper lip, and the word 
“Diablo” right above his chin. Other tattoos feature 
skulls in a variety of fashions, including an Aztec 
warrior skull. In Mexican culture, the skull can be 
connected to the calavera from Dia de Muertos (Day 
of the Dead) or to Aztec culture; skulls are symbols 
of the existence of humanity, life, and regeneration 
(Wade, 2018).
El Diablo wears a white tank top undershirt, 
which is a stereotypical look for gang members and 
cholos. At times, he is also seen wearing a blue let-
terman jacket with “Diablo” stitched in the front and 
a large white patch with a skull wearing a fedora. This 
imagery of the fedora or pachuco hat is very similar to 
that of the zoot suit culture and low rider culture. The 
patch has the words “Thee Hillsiders” and “East Los 
Angeles” with the year 1922, signifying his Los Angeles 
and gang member roots.
Diego from El Chicano (when taking his El Chi-
cano alter-ego) features many cholo-esque signifiers as 
well. His look and style are a combination of Batman 
mixed with cholo and biker culture. El Chicano wears a 
long leather trench coat with a hoodie and mask. Many 
cholos wear hoodies that are either all black or have 
some imagery such as a sports team’s logo, or regional, 
religious, or cultural symbolism. El Chicano’s hoodie 
and costume are all black, with cultural symbolism 
appearing on his mask. The leather mask covers his 
mouth to hide Diego’s identity and is reminiscent of 
cholo-esque tattoos and Aztec culture. The mask fea-
tures a skeleton-like scorpion with Aztec-style motifs. 
The mask also reflects cholo culture’s use of a ban-
dana to cover the mouth like a mask. Ironically, wear-
ing a bandana in this way is usually associated with a 
gangbanger stereotype whereas El Chicano is a hero/
vigilante. In contrast to what he wears while assum-
ing the El Chicano persona, Diego in his everyday 
life does not present cholo stereotypes. He is a police 
officer and wears his uniform or other non-cholo-  
related clothing.
Miles Morales did not include cholo signifiers in 
his appearance. Although Miles does have a hoodie 
similar to that worn by El Chicano, the aesthetic is very 
different. Miles’ hoodie represents a youthful, urban, 
and street-centered style in comparison to that of El 
Chicano’s cholo style.
Language
Language was another important marker of Latini-
dad in the three films. Spanish was used in all three 
of the films, but it was clear that Suicide Squad and 
Spider-Man: Into the Spider-verse were produced for 
general (White) audiences. Although El Chicano 
was also produced for a general audience, it is also 
aimed toward a Latinx audience.
In Suicide Squad, El Diablo uses some Spanish 
although he primarily speaks English. He uses Spanish 
in his final pivotal scenes as he battles the villain. “Let 

204 Content
me show you who I really am,” as he transforms into 
an Aztec skeletal figure that is on fire. His final words 
are, “Ahora si, cabron,” (“it’s on, bitch”) and “ya te chin-
gastes, guey,” (“now you are screwed”) as he sacrifices 
himself. By using Spanish, he had the chance to show-
case his authentic self as well as a more confident and 
assertive version of himself. The film uses English sub-
titles when Spanish is spoken, which further demon-
strates that the primary market is English speakers.
Throughout El Chicano, Diego mainly uses Eng-
lish. Early in the film, he is with his brother as a child 
and he uses Spanish slang terms such as “vatos” 
and “el cucuy,” but as an adult, Diego rarely speaks 
Spanish. Throughout the film, Diego code-switches 
languages from English to Spanish and continues to 
use Spanish slang. He also uses Spanglish, a mix-
ture of English and Spanish. When speaking with his 
mom about the murder of his brother, Diego starts in 
English, but code-switches to Spanish. “Y ou dishonor 
me, and the hard work that I put in to not be dead 
before my thirtieth birthday.” His mother responds, 
“Are you really going to find out who killed my son?” 
Diego responds, “Y our son? Who are you speaking 
to right now? La jura? The police? Y ou never made 
me feel bad about being a cop, Susanna. Don’t start 
now.” Later in the film, when Diego is in his El Chi-
cano persona, he tells one of the villains, “Venieste 
aqui a buscar venganza, and here I am.” This con-
tinues the idea of Diego using Spanglish to commu-
nicate and perform Latinidad. This was common in 
the film. However, Diego and other characters per-
formatively used Spanish words and phrases, which 
at times seemed over the top and forced, even a 
commodification of Latinidad. Overall, El Chicano  
seems to oversell its Latinidad, feeling disingenuous.
Into the Spider-verse uses Spanish briefly. In an 
early scene, Miles’ mother, who is Puerto Rican, 
speaks to Miles in Spanish. This scene includes signifi-
ers of being and performing Latinidad as Miles briefly 
replies to his mother saying, “hasta luego.” This phrase, 
widely understood by English speakers, is the only 
time that Miles uses Spanish.
Although all three films do use Spanish in some 
capacity, they never fully take advantage of what using 
the Spanish language could contribute to a robust 
depiction of Latinidad. This is probably because the 
films are meant for general audiences who speak  
English. The producers might have feared that exten-
sive use of Spanish would reduce these films’ profita-
bility. Still, the inclusion of some Spanish adds some 
diversity and inclusion of Latinx folks and Latinidad, 
and at least acknowledges the bicultural identity of 
these Latinx characters.
Espirtualismo
Espirtualismo is a Latinx religious cultural signifier 
that showcases a sense of spirituality. This cultural 
value emphasizes achieving spiritual goals even if 
at the cost of material satisfaction (Calvillo & Bailey, 
2015). El Diablo’s tattoos of a rosary and an angel 
visually signify espirtualismo, but other tattoos and 
some of his statements reflect a conflicted stance 
on religion and spirituality. He sports a tattoo of a 
praying hand with the middle finger extended. He 
says, “God didn’t give me this [power], why should he 
take it away?” and that he was “born with the Devil’s 
gift.” He reflects on how his wife had prayed for him 
to leave the life of crime behind—and that he had 
killed his wife and kids by using his “Devil’s gift.” He 
knows he did wrong and believes that he does not 
deserve God’s forgiveness or to be redeemed. Over-
all, although El Diablo does have a sense of faith or 
spirituality, it is not straightforward or traditional.
El Chicano visually depicts espirtualismo by 
showing various images reflecting spirituality, includ-
ing the Mexican patron saint, La Virgen de Guadalupe, 
and the saint commonly associated with the cartel, 
Santa Muerte.
Machismo
El Diablo exudes machista-like (male chauvinistic 
behaviors) aggression, as he admits, “When I get 
mad, I lose control. I don’t know what I do.” Latino 
male masculinity or machismo is a hypermasculine 
trait that includes aggression, dominance, and chau-
vinism, all traits Diablo shows in the film (Liberato 
et al., 2009). As noted, Diablo had killed his family 
due to his machismo and anger, although he tries his 
best moving forward to remain calm and not use his 
powers to hurt others.


Film and Television 205
In El Chic
ano, Diego Hernandez exudes and 
performs machismo both as himself and his super -
hero alter-ego El Chicano. Diego, when not wearing 
his superhero costume, is a police officer who enacts 
the tough or mean cop stereotype. Diego even tries to 
prove that he is more Latinx than his partner, going so 
far as to challenge his partner’s Mexicanidad. Diego’s 
Mexicanidad, and by extension his Latinidad, is also 
questioned in the film. This theme of not being Mexi-
can or Latinx enough, or not being American enough, 
is a common trope in Latinx films and represents a 
struggle many Latinx people face. Diego clearly feels 
divided, but as the film progresses, his actions as the 
vigilante El Chicano become much more vengeful 
after he realizes that his brother was killed by a gang 
and cartel members. Diego, both as himself and the 
vigilante El Chicano, reinforces the idea of machismo 
throughout the film as he displays aggressive and dom-
inating behaviors.
Of the three characters analyzed here, Miles 
Morales is the only one who does not display 
machismo. In contrast, Miles displays a sense of inclu-
sivity, familismo, which is discussed below.
Familismo
Familismo is a cultural signifier that drives the narra-
tive of all three characters. Cardoso and Thompson 
(2010) define familismo as a broad group of cultural 
characteristics, such as loyalty, respect, solidarity, 
and interdependence, that exists within nuclear and 
extended kin networks. Family played a big part in 
El Diablo’s origin story and in his quest for redemp-
tion as part of his new family, the Suicide Squad.
Early in El Chicano, familismo is displayed as 
we see a young Diego and his brother Pedro grow 
up together and were close until Pedro joined a gang. 
He eventually left the gang and wanted to turn his life 
around but was killed in a gang fight. The loss and 
memory of Pedro lead Diego to become a police 
officer, take on the identity of El Chicano, and go after 
the cartel.
Throughout Spider-Man, familismo is a featured 
theme and a major part of the narrative of the char-
acters. Both of Miles’ parents want the best for their 
son, including getting the best education possible. His 
father seems to have high expectations for him and 
demand too much from Miles. The overdemanding 
father figure is a common trope in Latinx films. At one 
point, Miles overhears his father saying how proud he 
is of his son. Miles had sought this fatherly pride and 
approval throughout his life, both from his father and 
from his superhero mentor, Peter Parker (Spider-Man). 
Receiving this fatherly approval is crucial to Miles as 
he becomes Spider-Man. He slowly gains confidence 
in all areas of his life and becomes the son his family is 
proud of—and the new Spider-Man. As did El Diablo 
(with the Suicide Squad), Miles Morales also found a 
secondary family (with the various spider characters). 
Overall, familismo seems to be the main cultural value 
of all three films; it carries the Latinx character’s narra-
tives and the direction of the films.
Signifying Latinidad
All three films, through various cultural values and 
signifiers, feature at least some representation of 
Latinidad. All three of the characters analyzed are 
completely different. They represent different sides 
of good and evil and different aspects of Latinx cul-
ture. In some cases, the representation of Latinidad 
was subtle; in other cases, it was shallow, and in still 
other cases, it was over the top. These are all action 
films centered around comic book superheroes, so 
of course, they are at times extreme. Y et, even so, I 
believe that filmmakers need to do more to tell stories 
that showcase Latinidad in an accurate and complex 
manner. They should not just rely on classic racialized 
stereotypes and tropes or representations of Latini-
dad designed to appeal to general (White) audiences. 
Filmmakers should highlight additional values of Lat-
inidad such as perseverance, hard work, and the like. 
They should expand their representation to include 
more cultural signifiers that represent Latinx folks in 
a positive manner. I believe these three films begin to 
highlight positive subjects such as family, spiritualism, 
and language, but as these Latinx comic book films 
continue to be made, filmmakers need to create com-
plex Latinx characters that reflect their cultures more 
richly. Filmmakers should depict Latinx culture more 
positively and at minimum rely less on drug dealers, 
cholos, and other negative stereotypes.

206 Content
References
Anguiano, C., & Castaneda, M. (2014). Forging a path: Past

and ethnic identity. Journal for the Scientific Study of Reli-

Molina-Guzmán, I. (2013). Commodifying Black Latinidad 
in US film and television. Popular Communication, 11(3), 
211–226.
Molina-Guzmán, I., & Valdivia, A. N. (2005). Gendering Lati-

tal. Science. https://www.science.org/content/article/ 
feeding-gods-hundreds-skulls-reveal-massive-scale-

acrifice-aztec-capital
5.12: CATEGORY IS PANDEMIC 
REALNESS: POSE AND THAT OLD 
PANDEMIC
Robert Alan Brookey and Maria 
Williams-Hawkins
The authors analyze the first season of Pose , a 
drama with groundbreaking representations of drag 
queens. They argue that the show’s depiction of the 
AIDS crisis in the late 1980s demonstrates distrust of 
doctors and scientists – a suspicion they argue also 
exists in the time of the COVID-19 pandemic.
On June 5, 1981, the CDC published an article 
about cases of Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia 
It’s Your Turn: What Do You Think? What 
Will You Find?
 1.
 W
atch a film or TV show featuring 
Latinx characters. What cultural signi-
fiers of Latinidad are included? What 
cultural values are portrayed? What do 
these cultural signifiers and values tell us 
about that culture and about diversity in 
media? How important is it to showcase 
specific cultural signifiers and values, 
and why?
 2.
 La
tinx culture is not monolithic; it 
includes many diverse people from 
many different countries on different 
continents. Working in pairs or small 
groups, watch 2–3 episodes of a TV 
show (assigned by your instructor) fea-
turing at least one Latinx character. Do 
the episodes you watched mention the 
Latinx characters’ heritage, or are they 
generally presented as Latinx or His-
panic? What cultural signifiers do you 
see? Then, as a class, discuss your obser-
vations. To what extent and how do the 
characters and cultural signifiers reflect 
the richness and diversity of what we 
broadly consider Latinx people? How do 
you think these representations would 
affect audiences’ understanding of Lat-
inx people?
 3.
 Ha
ve the class select one of the episodes 
from the activity above. Again, working 
in pairs or small groups, imagine you’re 
consulting with the sh  ow’s writers to 
present a more well-rounded depiction 
of the Latinx characters you analyzed. 
How would you represent these Lat-
inx characters? Besides including cul-
tural signifiers, what are some other 
forms of inclusion you could recom-
mend to create diverse and complex 
characters?


Film and Television 207
a
ppearing in otherwise healthy gay men (A Time-
line, 2021). It was the first official medical report 
on what would become the AIDS pandemic. Forty 
years later, we find ourselves in the COVID-19 pan-
demic, and those of us old enough to have lived 
through both pandemics see some distributing 
similarities. In an editorial for the scientific journal 
Nature, Dr. Anthony Fauci (2021), a prominent figure 
in the study of infectious diseases including AIDS, 
compared the two pandemics:
There are many similarities that sadden me: 
how hard some patient groups need to fight for 
recognition; how misinformation and denial-
ism can promote illness and death; how slowly 
interventions reach vulnerable populations; 
how easy it can be to overlook patient inputs 
when setting research priorities.
A similarity that Fauci omitted is the suspicion of 
scientific and medical institutions that emerged in 
both pandemics – an important omission – because 
the problems Fauci does identify are correlated to 
this suspicion. In other words, vulnerable popula-
tions who must fight for recognition and care (he 
uses the term intervention) and who feel they are 
being treated as subjects (not patients) come to 
distrust doctors and scientists. Such distrust may 
also produce misinformation and denialism, but the 
overarching problem, we maintain, is suspicion.
Watching the FX show Pose within the context 
of the current pandemic sparked our memories of the 
prior one. Although those memoirs are consistent with 
Fauci’s observations, we also recall how the victims of 
the early AIDS crisis often came to distrust the medi-
cal community. Through critical analysis, we use Pose 
to remind us of the suspicion that emerged in the AIDS 
crisis; although as we note, the suspicion of the AIDS 
and the COVID-19 pandemics reflect markedly differ-
ent political dynamics.
Strike a Pose
The FX network first aired Pose (2018–2021) on 
June 3, 2018. The show dramatically depicted New 
Y ork City’s drag ball culture scene in the 1980s 
and 1990s. This scene was made up primarily of 
African-Americans and Latinos and consisted of 
competitions in various drag categories focused on 
fashion and movement (posing). The participants 
were often part of houses, groups of competitors 
who have formed chosen families, headed by a 
drag mother (an experienced and successful drag 
competitor).
We analyze the first season of Pose, which fol-
lows the experiences of participants in the New 
Y ork drag ball scene in 1987 and 1988. The AIDS 
crisis figures prominently in the stories of some of 
the main characters. In fact, the series’ narrative arc 
arguably begins when Blanca Rodriguez-Evangelista 
(Michaela Jaé Rodriguez) discovers her HIV-positive 
status and forms her own house of drag ball com-
petitors. Our analysis is informed by an approach to 
media criticism focusing on the relationship between 
media and memory. Plate and Smelik (2013) observe 
that memory is inflected by social and cultural con-
text and we would add that these contexts are also 
often political. Garde-Hansen presents memory as a 
critical agency, one that can be used to “study how we 
individually and collectively make sense and order of 
our past through media” (2011, p. 8). We intend to do 
just that, but we also hope to make some sense of 
our present – specifically, that the current suspicions 
of the medical community often manifest in vaccine 
resistance.
In this way, this critical agency aligns with the 
reception practices theorized by Hall (1980) who 
argued that people’s interpretation of television mes-
sages is influenced by their social, cultural and polit-
ical contexts. Although memory can have agency in 
the creation of a work that captures the past, memory 
also can have agency in the act of critically engaging 
such a text. In other words, by experiencing mediated 
representations of past events, we can compare those 
experiences to our own memories of those events.
This is how we engage Pose. Although our identi-
ties are different (a gay White man and a straight Black 
woman), we are both old enough to have experienced 
the AIDS crisis as adults. We highlight this because 
we were both socially and politically conscious of the 

208 Content
impact of the AIDS crisis as it was happening, and 
we were aware of how the crisis was experienced by 
marginalized groups. We critique Pose as a text that 
remembers the AIDS crisis and we examine it in rela-
tion to our own memories and experiences. We focus 
on how characters in Pose reflect then-current suspi-
cions of medical systems; this reflection can give us 
perspective on our current pandemic crisis.
Death Sentences
Pose’s pilot episode presents Blanca Rodriguez, a 
member of the House of Abundance, led by cham-
pion house mother Elektra Abundance (Dominique 
Jackson). Early on Blanca voices her dissatisfac-
tion with the way Elektra runs the house, and more 
specifically how she takes credit for Blanca’s ideas. 
Blanca’s dissatisfaction is compounded when she 
learns she is HIV positive. Her doctor encourages 
her to undergo treatment and says, “This doesn’t 
have to be a death sentence.” Blanca responds, “Isn’t 
it, though?” Here Blanca challenges her diagnosis 
outright. She continues, “It must be hard telling peo-
ple they are going to die day after day.” Here Blanca 
voices her suspicion of what the doctor is telling her; 
in spite of the doctor’s claims, Blanca feels her diag-
nosis is a death sentence and implies that issuing 
these death sentences is all the doctor seems able 
to do. This suspicion is well founded because at the 
time, 1987, people diagnosed with HIV often went 
on to die of AIDS complications. Indeed, we both 
can recall many friends diagnosed during this period 
who would experience a drop in their T-cell count, 
followed by infections from their weakened immune 
systems that would then lead to their deaths.
The scene then shifts to Blanca having just dis-
closed her status to Pray Tell, an emcee at the drag 
balls and Blanca’s close friend. He voices his own sus-
picion of medical institutions when he tells her, “I do 
not understand for the life of me, why you would have 
gone and got that test. Y ou already knew the answer.” 
Implicit in Pray Tell’s statement is the understand-
ing that by being tested, Blanca has rendered herself 
a mere statistic in a health system that is not really 
interested in helping her. Indeed, one of us recalls how 
among White gay men during this time, testing was 
viewed as a form of tracking. This suspicion, voiced 
by two people of color in Pose, needs to be understood 
in relation to the way medicine has historically used 
people of color as objects of study (Understanding 
and ameliorating, 2021), with little regard for their 
well-being (the Tuskegee Study and Henrietta Lacks 
are just two cases in point). In other words, vulnera-
ble populations have had a historical struggle with 
doctors and scientists to be recognized and treated as 
patients and not research subjects. From this struggle, 
distrust and suspicion have often emerged.
In fact, this suspicion seems to inform Pray Tell’s 
advice to Blanca: “Keep living! Put on your tallest 
pumps and get back out into the world. Y ou ain’t dead 
yet.” One of us, in talking to White males who were 
“likely” to get AIDS, heard the same kind of attitude 
that Pray Tell espouses. In similar conversations with 
Black, educated, upscale men, the statements were 
similar but the attitude was one of resolution; “When 
time is up, it’s up.” Pray Tell’s statement mirrors Blan-
ca’s own suspicion of her doctor; Pray Tell also believes 
Blanca has been given a death sentence, and so she 
must make the most of her life. This advice inspires 
Blanca to leave The House of Abundance and form 
The House of Evangelista. Therefore, the narrative arc 
of the first season of Pose is driven by Blanca’s diag-
nosis but also by an underlying distrust in the medical 
systems that inspires her to do the most with the time 
she has left.
To form her new house, Blanca takes in a young 
homeless dancer, Damon Richards (Ryan Jamaal 
Swain). Damon is kicked out of his home when his 
parents discover he is gay. His own mother tells him, 
“God will punish you by giving you that disease.” In 
other words, she imagines that Damon’s sexuality is a 
death sentence; a scene that painfully parallels expe-
riences one of us encountered when coming out to 
his own parents. Another one of us was reminded 
of how AIDS was generally regarded in the religious 
right community, members of which taught that get-
ting AIDS was God’s punishment for being gay, a les-
son that was embraced by congregations across racial 
lines. She is also mindful of how the religious right has 
responded to the pandemic, with members of various 
racial congregations being both passively and actively 
resistant to masking guidelines and vaccine regimes. In 


Film and Television 209
s
ome cases, these churches taught that “True believ-
ers” would not die from COVID-19, and consequently, 
whole churches refused to mask up. It is interesting 
to note, too, how the members of the religious right 
offer up both pandemics as the “will of God,” imagin-
ing how they will be protected, whereas others will be 
punished.
It appears that his mother’s words are prophetic 
when Damon begins exhibiting the signs of HIV infec-
tion. Blanca is worried about Damon and shares her 
concerns with Pray Tell. Blanca claims as Damon’s 
house mother (or, at this point, only mother) it is her 
duty “to protect them from the one thing we know is 
coming for them.” She insists that the children in her 
house must be tested for their sake and the safety of 
others. Pray Tell admits that he stopped getting tested. 
He relates the experience of his boyfriend Costas 
(Johnny Sibilly), whose health significantly worsened 
with his AZT treatment, a drug introduced in the early 
days of the epidemic: “He’s not the first. I know of 
about five people where the drugs killed them faster 
than the virus did.” He then places his decision in a 
broader social and political context. “I know that 
[then-president} Ronald Reagan will not say the word 
AIDS. Health insurance will not cover any treatment. 
The world wants us dead.” Implicit in his argument is 
the belief that the government and the health industry 
have no real interest in people suffering from AIDS.
Blanca pushes back by claiming that Pray Tell is 
“just whistling past the graveyard” and that she does 
not share his pessimism. He counters that their knowl-
edge of their HIV status “will not change the fact that 
this shit is going to run us all down.” Although Blanca 
calls him pessimistic, he believes he is being realistic 
and admits that he is scared. Blanca observes, “What 
is scared to us? It’s like water to a fish… We are all 
going to get tested and we are all going to get through 
this together.” We should note that although Blanca 
does not share Pray Tell’s suspicions about testing, she 
imagines any support will come from the members of 
her house and not the medical institutions. In other 
words, because they both assume that their lives do 
not matter to doctors and scientists, the disregard and 
neglect they experience are intrinsic to their lives as 
LGBTQ+ people of color; therefore, they must depend 
on each other.
Blanca seems to have convinced Pray Tell, and 
he in turn convinces the children in her house that they 
should all get tested. The children test negative but not 
Pray Tell. He hides his status from them. Later, he con-
fesses to Blanca and shares his fear of wasting away in 
a hospital, neglected and ignored by the staff. Here too, 
we are reminded of the experiences of our friends with 
AIDS and how the neglect of one of our friends by a 
hospital nurse even became a local news story.
This neglect is also on display in the hospital ward 
where Costas is housed. Food trays are left in hallways, 
and bloody and soiled sheets are left on the hospital 
beds. When he complains to the nurse (Sandra Bern-
hard) asking, “Does it have to be so drab in here, so 
awful?” she responds,
So you want me to be a f***ing interior dec-
orator on top of keeping AIDS patients alive, 
Mary? We don’t have a budget for new bed 
sheets… I’m a nurse on a ward where no one 
gets better, you think I don’t want to do some-
thing to make these people more comfortable 
when they are on their way out? We are under-
staffed and over worked.
In other words, she verifies that the ward and its 
patients are not a priority for the larger medical 
institution. She challenges him to do something for 
the patients himself, “Aren’t you the entertainer?” 
He accepts the challenge and arranges and per -
forms a cabaret in the recreation room on the ward.
Bianca joins Costas to render a performance that 
acknowledges the despair in the room but responds 
to it with joy. The moment of joy is brief. Back in his 
hospital room, Costas tells Pray Tell, “I’m never leaving 
this place and you know that.” Although Pray Tell tries 
to tell him he can get better, Costas recognizes, “I’m 
going to die soon.” Costas asks Pray Tell to move on 
without him when he is gone and not to give into the 
fear that he will have the same fate. Pray Tell tearfully 
agrees. In the next scene, Pray Tell receives a call from 
Judy that Costas has passed.
Later, as Pray Tell and Bianca walk home after 
a ball, he tells her he plans to scatter Costas’ ashes 
along Fifth Avenue, “a little bit at a time because he 
loved to window shop.” He also intimates that he 

210 Content
promised Costas he would go on and live with joy, 
“but it’s hard… We are living in a world where all of 
us can truly be gone one day. Where our kind is just a 
memory, one the rest of the world would be happy to 
forget.” Y et, Pray Tell says he will keep his promise to 
Costas as an expression of his love. This scene is posi-
tive to the degree that it shows how Pray Tell responds 
to the neglect and disregard he has experienced with 
the support and commitment to his dead partner.
Indeed, to the degree that the AIDS crisis 
motivates the characters in Pose, that motivation is 
informed by the understanding that help will not come 
from the medical system, the politicians, or the world 
that “wants them dead.” Both Blanca and Pray Tell 
must depend on each other, and the community they 
have formed through the drag balls, to help them get 
through this pandemic. They cannot count on any 
other support. Although their suspicions of the med-
ical systems may be informed by their experiences as 
people of color, it is compounded by the fact that even 
within the communities of color, they cannot depend 
on support. As Damon’s biological mother indicated, 
people inside and outside both those systems and 
communities often shared the belief that AIDS was a 
just reward.
Lessons Not Learned
We started by noting that although Fauci (2021) 
identified similarities between the AIDS and COVID 
pandemics, he did not mention the suspicion of sci-
ence and medical institutions that emerged in both 
pandemics. As communication scholars, we should 
never forget that in Pose as in life, this suspicion 
could be related to a lack of effective communi-
cation. In Pose, we are reminded of how both the 
medical community and politicians failed to reach 
vulnerable populations in a way that said, “Y ou mat-
ter.” This created the suspicion that various charac-
ters expressed in the first season of the series.
What is remarkable in the current pandemic is 
how the political ground has shifted. Now, we find the 
political right espousing the same suspicions of the 
medical community, a shift that has been well noted 
by Louis Anslow (2021). Anslow, however, traces the 
suspicion back to GMO products, but Pose reminds us 
that the suspicion can also be traced to the AIDS crisis. 
Today, that suspicion has been manifested on the right, 
some conservative politicians work behind the scenes 
to pass along incorrect medical information, and some 
of those politicians work with religious groups. Some 
of these politicians have even bemoaned how the cur-
rent pandemic has become politicized, often ignoring 
how the inaction of a political leader they admired 
(Reagan) inspired the political action of the old pan-
demic, and the rise of ACT-UP, Queer Nation and the 
contemporary LGBTQ+ movement.
Therefore, the most important lesson that Pose 
offers is the reminder that both pandemics were polit-
icized and that politicization manifested suspicion. In 
the case of Pose, we see the suspicion begin to erode 
once the victims of AIDS began experiencing a sense 
of care. In fact, later in the series, Blanca takes on the 
role of a caregiver, becoming part of a medical institu-
tion that she once viewed with suspicion.
We do not pretend to have the answers to the 
current suspicions regarding the COVID-19 crisis or 
the attendant vaccine resistance. Indeed, although 
the political lines in this crisis seem clear, they are not 
immutable. There are people on the political left who 
also have chosen to forgo vaccination, and Donald 
Trump has been quite vocal about his vaccinations 
and has chided other politicians who have not been 
forthcoming about their own vaccination status. But 
Pose reminds us that people need to feel that institu-
tions (both medical and political) have their interests in 
mind and that they “matter” to these institutions.

6.1: “TRUST ME. I AM NOT A RACIST”: 
WHITENESS, MEDIA, AND MILLENNIALS
Christopher P . Campbell
The author argues that media created by or for the 
Millennial generation reflects postracial whiteness 
and hampers understanding of contemporary rac-
ism and its impact on our culture.
If nothing else, the election of Donald J. Trump as 
the 45th president of the United States made the 
irreverent skit-comedy program Saturday Night 
Live (SNL) relevant again. The show’s skewering of 
Trump during and after his election repopularized 
the 40-year-old program in an age when younger 
media audiences were turning away from traditional 
television programing and finding their TV content 
online and through streaming services.
The program’s new relevance is significant in 
the age of what is called the media “echo chamber,” 
a phenomenon cited as central to Trump’s surprising 
2016 election victory. As young audiences gravitated 
to social media and left- or right-leaning video stream-
ing services and cable news channels, they were much 
less likely to participate in the shared experience of 
previous generations of TV viewers who—despite 
demographic and political differences—had flocked 
to the broadcast networks for news and information.
But SNL’s resurgent popularity—especially when 
considering the significant number of replays of its 
skits on social media sites—may be approaching the 
impact of an earlier era; when SNL’s first program after 
Trump’s election featured the popular African Ameri-
can comic Dave Chappelle, it attracted its largest audi-
ence of the season. Following a monologue in which 
Chappelle intimated that White progressives had 
underestimated the appeal that Trump’s thinly veiled 
racism had for many White Americans, the show’s first 
sketch hammered home the point. Joined by another 
popular African American comedian, Chris Rock, the 
two attend an election-night party with a small group 
of White Millennials prepared to celebrate Democrat 
Hillary Clinton’s victory. As the night wears on, and 
as Trump’s election becomes apparent, Chappelle 
and Rock feign surprise as the other partygoers are 
shocked that somebody such as Trump could actually 
have won the election. “Oh my God,” one said, “I think 
America is racist.”
The skit’s keen insight into progressive White 
America’s failure to grasp the role that contempo-
rary racism played in the election was a more tell-
ing analysis than that undertaken by journalists and 
spoke to pop culture’s potential to address Ameri-
ca’s racial divide. But the skit’s important message 
was lost among the flood of Millennial media mes-
sages that continue to reflect the postracial mythol-
ogy of previous generations. In this essay, I discuss 
media created by and/or designed for the Millen-
nial generation (those born between 1985 and 2005) 
and argue that postracial whiteness will continue to 
haunt media texts and delay yet another generation 
of Americans from arriving at a more sophisticated 
understanding of contemporary racism and its 
impact on our culture.
6.
MUSIC AND DIGITAL MEDIA
DOI: 10.4324/9781003193708-8

Music and Digital Media 213
R
ace, Myth, and Contemporary Media
Much critical analysis of race and media begins 
with the work of Stuart Hall who challenged the 
“preferred reading” of media texts; he described 
the cultural power of analyzing those meanings 
as the “politics of signification” (1980, p. 138). For 
Hall, the analysis of media representations is key to 
unlocking the power of the dominant meanings—
meanings that indirectly serve the interests of the 
wealthiest and most powerful members of society.
Gray (1991, p. 304) identified the “twin representa-
tions” of African Americans in fictional and nonfic-
tional television, contrasting the upper 
 mid
dle-class 
life portrayed in the 1980s mega-hit The Cosby Show 
with the underclass Black life portrayed in a 1985 
PBS documentary titled The Vanishing Family: Crisis in 
Black America. Race on fictional television appealed 
to the American Dream, and, as Gray observed, “to 
the utopian desire in blacks and whites for racial one-
ness and equality while displacing the persistent reality 
of racism and racial inequality or the kinds of social 
struggles and cooperation required to eliminate them” 
(1991, p. 302).
My own examination of local TV news (Camp-
bell, 1995) revealed similar representations and their 
underlying myths. Reflecting the myth of marginality, 
people of color are ignored and therefore marginalized 
and less significant in news coverage. Second, the myth 
of difference is reflected when people of color are rou-
tinely represented differently than White people, rein-
forcing historical stereotypes, especially the negative 
stereotypes of people of color (mostly African Ameri-
can and Hispanic men) as violent criminals. Finally, the 
myth of assimilation (now referred to as postracialism) 
is a cherished newsroom myth that presents people 
of color, especially African Americans, as having over-
come racism and fully assimilated into the American 
mainstream, where equality has been achieved.
I have long expressed concern about news organ-
izations creating a mythical world in which racial har-
mony is the norm when seen in the broader context of 
newscasts that routinely include images of people of 
color as suspects in stories related to violent crime. In 
1995, I wrote that:
…if our society is the just and fair one that was 
portrayed [in the coverage of Dr. Martin Luther 
King Jr. Day], the constant barrage of menac-
ing images of minorities that more commonly 
appear on local TV news will undoubtedly fuel 
racist attitudes.
(p. 111)
In 2012 (Campbell, LeDuff, & Brown), we found few 
changes to these mythic notions; indeed, the mythic 
representations of race in journalism in the age of 
the Barack Obama presidency were even more 
problematic.
A useful tool in examining contemporary racism 
in the media is critical race theory (CRT), which posi-
tions the notion of whiteness (and white privilege) at the 
center of discussions about race. CRT argues that rac-
ism functions institutionally, and Mahoney explained 
that “part of white privilege is not seeing all we (white 
people) have and all we do, and not seeing how what 
we do appears to those defined as other” (1995, p. 306) 
and that:
This country is both highly segregated and 
based on the concept of whiteness as “nor -
mal.” It is therefore hard for white folks to see 
whiteness both when we interact with people 
who are not socially defined as white and when 
we interact with other white people, when race 
doesn’t seem to be involved.
(p. 306)
As LeDuff observed, “Today it seems that many 
of the old challenges that society faced in pre-civil 
rights America are coming back to haunt us with a 
new and different twist” (2016, p. 71). LeDuff argued 
that Millennial media, including social media, have 
yet to provide more insightful and accurate rep-
resentations in contemporary media: “This technol-
ogy, which was once touted as being almost utopian, 
has instead become one of the places where we can 
witness first hand the great divides among race and 
class in modern society” (2016, p. 72).
In looking at Millennial media in the Trump era, 
including Beyoncé’s video for “Formation” and come-
dian Amy Schumer’s odd recreation of it, I build on 
the work of Hall, Gray, and critical race theorists by 
examining racial meanings and myths in media prod-
ucts directed at young people in the era of Black Lives 
Matter.

214 Content
Race in the Age of Millennials
White Americans tend to embrace the notion 
of postracialism, the idea that the civil rights era 
generally ended discrimination against African 
Americans and fostered a new society marked by 
economic, social, and political equality. A few facts 
contradict the notion that Black opportunity has 
improved or flourished, even during the Barack 
Obama era. Over 38% of Black children lived in 
poverty, nearly four times the rate for White children 
(Tavernise, 2015). The median household income 
for Whites was $71,300 compared to $43,300 for 
Blacks (Vega, 2016). The unemployment rate for 
African Americans, 8.8%, was more than double the 
rate for Whites (Glinton, 2016). Twenty-one percent 
of White Americans were college graduates; 13% 
of Black Americans were graduates (Cook, 2015). 
Black Americans were incarcerated in state prisons 
at an average rate of 5.1 times that of White Ameri-
cans (Puglise, 2016).
Although the notion that America has overcome 
its racist legacy seems preposterous in the face of such 
statistics, it continues to reflect the attitude of more 
than half of White Americans who hold “explicit anti-
Black attitudes” (Edsall, 2013, p. 1). Remarkably, most 
Whites believe there is more anti-White than anti-
Black discrimination, which they believe has been “all 
but eliminated” (Fletcher, 2015). Although the Occupy 
Wall Street movement and the wide support of young 
people for avowed socialist Bernie Sanders’ 2016 
presidential campaign are regularly cited as evidence 
of a generational shift to more progressive political 
attitudes, White attitudes about race do not seem to 
be shifting.
The presidential election of 2016 provided evi-
dence that racial animosity among young Whites has 
not dramatically lessened; White Millennials leaned 
heavily toward Trump. Why? Smith (2015) argued that 
White Millennials cling to a worldview not that differ-
ent from previous generations: “They were taught by 
their elders, Baby Boomer and Gen-Xers…that racism 
is a matter of personal bigotry…not one of institutional 
discrimination and exploitation.” White Millennials’ 
support for Trump (like the earlier opposition of many 
Whites to Barack Obama) is couched not as racism 
but as an endorsement of political positions that just 
happen to be informed by layers of institutional and 
historic racism.
Millennials, Race, and Media
Although White supremacist ideology is easy to 
find in media targeting young adults, it is even more 
disturbing that White Millennials whose politics are 
otherwise progressive still seem tone-deaf when 
it comes to issues of race. Writer-director-actress 
Lena Dunham, whose hit HBO show Girls was 
widely praised for its offbeat form of third-wave 
feminism, has been bashed for the show’s near com-
plete lack of racial diversity. Keeping with the trend 
of previous generations’ hit shows about White New 
Y orkers living sheltered existences in the most multi-
cultural city on the planet (think Seinfeld, Friends, Sex 
and the City), Dunham’s edgy progressivism would 
seem a ripe platform on which to present a cultur -
ally diverse cast and to address race in a sophisti-
cated manner. As Daniels observed, “If ‘Girls’ were 
a show about four white women but it was at all 
thoughtful, reflexive or critical of their whiteness, 
I’d have a different take on the show.” However, he 
said, the show is “the opposite of being thoughtful 
and reflexive about whiteness” (2014).
Comedian-actress Amy Schumer, an avowed 
feminist and Hillary supporter, has faced even more 
scathing criticism for her blind spot regarding race. 
Like much of her work, her 2015 film Trainwreck was 
criticized for its failure to problematize the racist atti-
tudes of her character, and the movie’s racial jokes fell 
flat. She also has taken heat for jokes in her stand-up 
routine, including one from 2013 in which she framed 
Latinos as rapists: “I used to date Hispanic guys, but 
now I prefer consensual.” She apologized a few years 
later, offering this defense: “I used to do a lot of short 
dumb jokes like this. I played a dumb white girl onstage. 
I still do sometimes” (The Hollywood Reporter, 2015). 
In a widely viewed social media post, her defense 
continued:
Stick with me and trust I am joking. I go in and 
out of playing an irreverent idiot. That includes 
making dumb jokes involving race. I enjoy play-
ing the girl who time to time says the dumbest 
thing possible and playing with race is a thing 


Music and Digital Media 215
w
e are not supposed to do, which makes it so 
fun for comics. Y ou can call it a “blind spot for 
racism” or “lazy” but you are wrong…. I am 
a devout feminist and lover of all people. My 
fight is for all people to be treated equally.
(Quoted in Mallenbaum, 2015)
In the same post, she made a comment that sounds 
like it could have come from Donald Trump: “Trust 
me. I am not a racist.”
Two “Formations”
Schumer’s curious examination of race continued 
when she decided to produce a video parody of 
Beyoncé’s Grammy-winning video “Formation” 
in 2016. Beyoncé’s version, released on Tidal and 
Y ouTube the weekend before her performance at 
the 2016 Super Bowl halftime show, “sent shock-
waves of glee through social media” (Guo, 2016). 
The glory of the song “is in its sheer blackness,” as 
Guo observed: “There is a feeling that Beyoncé has 
written a song specifically for black ears, finally” 
(2016). She sings about embracing her Negro and 
Creole heritage, her nose, and her hair. The images 
in the video are politically pro-Black, described by 
The New Y ork Times as a “high-level, visually striking 
Black Lives Matter allegory” (Caramanica, Mor -
ris, & Wortham, 2016). Artistically shot by director 
Melina Masoukas, the video pays tribute to Julie 
Dash’s visually stunning 1991 film about Gullah cul-
ture, Daughters of the Dust; it references the horrify-
ing treatment of African Americans in New Orleans 
after Hurricane Katrina, and it pays direct tribute to 
the Black Lives Matter movement with “hands up, 
don’t shoot” gestures and posters with the words, 
“Stop shooting us.”
In accepting the 2017 Grammy for Best Urban 
Contemporary album, Beyoncé described the pro-
ject’s preferred reading:
My intention for the film and album was to cre-
ate a body of work that will give a voice to our 
pain, our struggles, our darkness and our his-
tory… It’s important for me to show images to 
my children that reflect their beauty.
(Quoted in Guo, 2016)
In Amy Schumer’s curious rendition of the video, she 
and White actress Goldie Hawn parody Beyoncé 
and her dancers, imitating the moves and mouthing 
lines about “my Negro nose” and having a Negro–
Creole heritage. The sight of Schumer and Hawn 
mimicking Beyoncé functions as a kind of post-
modern blackface; their whiteness allows them the 
privilege of ridiculing even the most popular African 
American performer of the day at the moment she 
most overtly embraces her blackness. The parody 
fails to acknowledge any interpretation of “Forma-
tion” as an important cultural moment; instead, like 
clueless White frat boys who inevitably choose to 
don minstrel-era blackface at Halloween, Schumer 
hides behind her ignorance, telling us that the video 
was a “tribute” with only good intentions.
After coming under attack from Beyoncé’s sub-
stantial social media fan base, Schumer (2016) pub-
lished an essay on medium.com, praising Beyoncé’s 
“Formation” and arguing that her video:
…is fun and the women in it are strong and 
want to help each other. That’s what it was 
about for me… My mission is to continue to 
work as hard as I can to empower women and 
make them laugh and feel better and I won’t let 
anything stop me.
This defensive response conflates Schumer’s sup-
port for feminism with her support for racial pro-
gress, a theme she seems to adopt each time she is 
criticized for her racist material.
That attitude—that because she is a politically 
aware feminist (and a comedian, so it’s just jokes) 
she gets a pass on her racially offensive material—is 
precisely the way that whiteness seems to function 
for many progressive Millennials. Crenshaw (1989) 
coined the term “intersectionality” to describe the 
importance of understanding how sexism and racism 
intersect. The term has also been used to describe the 
ways in which multiple forms of otherness overlap; 
for instance, cultural critic bell hooks frequently used 
the phrase “White Supremacist Capitalist Patriarchy” 
to describe how race, class, and gender function in 
unison to prop up hegemonic power (Jhally, 2002). 
Scholars who examine LGBT issues, disability rights, 
xenophobia, ageism, and other forms of discrimination 

216 Content
also cite the ways that multiple forms of discrimination 
intersect. Schumer and other White progressives—
including those who struggled to understand Trump’s 
victory over Hillary Clinton—seem not to grasp the 
notion that real progress requires overcoming the 
white privilege which allows them to embrace some 
social issues and ignore (or compound) others.
Sadly, White Millennials seem not to have learned 
from the lessons of previous generations who appro-
priated and commodified Black culture. Baby Boom-
ers embraced Elvis. Gen-Xers embraced Madonna. 
But neither adequately acknowledged their debt to 
the African American performers whose art and style 
they copied. They failed to grasp the privileged posi-
tion that their whiteness provided them. When Amy 
Schumer declares that she is not a racist while making 
unambiguously racist jokes and ignoring the privilege 
that comes with her whiteness, she is continuing a long 
tradition of mediated messages that inform racist atti-
tudes. She is also reinforcing such behavior for a new 
generation of Whites, many of whom consider them-
selves politically progressive and living in a postracial 
era.
The Historical Persistence of Racism
Perhaps we should not be surprised that whiteness— 
a kind of post-racial racism—persists in Millennial 
media. In examining racism in the South, Achara, 
Blackwell, and Sen (2016) advanced a theory of 
historical persistence to explain how racist attitudes 
are transmitted across generations. They argued 
that racial threat—irrational fears about African  
Americans and other minoritized groups—do not 
drive White racial attitudes. “Much work,” they 
explain, “focuses on contemporary respondent fac-
tors, such as income, age, gender, education, and so 
on, in trying to explain contemporary public opin-
ion” (2016, p. 639). But they say those factors over-
look historical and cultural explanations, and their 
findings “suggest that historical institutions like slav-
ery are significant in shaping American culture and 
politics, even if they no longer exist” (p. 639).
The notion of historical persistence, then, may 
explain why White Millennial media, including the 
work of the most politically progressive comics, may 
not be able to contribute to a more helpful dialogue 
about contemporary American racism. As Bouie 
(2014) explained:
Millennials have grown up in a world where we 
talk about race without racism—or don’t talk 
about it at all—and where “skin color” is the 
explanation for racial inequality, as if ghettos 
are ghettos because they are black, and not 
because they were created.
He noted the irony: “A generation that hates rac-
ism but chooses colorblindness is a generation that, 
through its neglect, comes to perpetuate it.”
At the conclusion of the Chappelle–Rock SNL  
skit about Trump’s election, one of the White par -
tygoers comments, “This is the most shameful thing 
America has ever done.” The two Black comedians 
laugh, sharing knowing smiles. This is not even close 
to America’s most shameful moment, especially if you 
consider the history of racism in America.

It’s Your Turn: What Do You Think? What 
Will You Find?
 1.
 V
iew Beyoncé’s “Formation” video on 
Y ouTube. Then view Amy Schumer’s 
version. What does each tell viewers 
about race and race relations?
