6.2: HIP HOP’S WHITE HOUSE GUEST: 
JACK HARLOW AND WHITE RAP 
AUTHENTICATING STRATEGIES
Melvin L. Williams and Michael I. Huertas
In this essay, the authors analyze Jack Harlow’s 
music for the presence of White rap authenticating 
strategies and discourses on racial injustice, white-
ness, and white privilege in society and rap culture.
“White rappers, …you are guests in the house 
of hip hop.” 
– Lord Jamar (Harling, 2013)
Despite having participated in rap for more than 
40 years, White rappers are often viewed as 

218 Content
problematic culture vultures or cultural appropriators, 
 manuf
actured by capitalist record labels to serve as 
White leaders for rap’s largest consumer base: White 
suburban kids (Morales, 2000). Although White rap-
pers have had commercial successes and remain vis-
ible in rap and Black popular culture, most of rap’s 
discourse reflects the thoughts, feelings, and ethos of 
Black men. Many argue that White involvement in its 
art forms is emblematic of continuous expropriations 
of Black cultural forms (Williams, 2017).
One White rapper currently visible in rap and 
Black popular culture is Jack Harlow, of Louisville, Ken-
tucky. Endorsed by acclaimed rap deejay and record 
executive, DJ Drama, Harlow was included in the rap 
publication XXL’s 2020 Freshman Class and achieved 
multiplatinum success and two number-one Billboard 
Hot 100 singles, “Industry Baby” with rapper Lil Nas X 
and “First Class,” which received multiple Black Enter-
tainment Television (BET) and Grammy Award nom-
inations. Harlow adopts recognizably Black aesthetics 
and sounds steeped in the rap genre, contrasting with 
his current White rap peers (e.g., G-Eazy, Machine Gun 
Kelly, Post Malone). He acknowledges his White priv-
ilege as a “dorky outsider” participant in Black culture 
and engages in political commentary and protests 
on behalf of Black Lives Matter, domestic violence, 
and the 2020 murder of fellow Kentuckian, Breonna  
Taylor (Verry, 2021). He claims, “I lead by example for 
all the White kids looking at me. This is what you do. 
Y ou don’t just enjoy Black culture. Y ou stand up next to 
Black people in a time of need” (Mano, 2021).
There are many questions about the authentic-
ity of Jack Harlow’s background and rap persona. He 
refers to himself as “the hometown hero” of Louisville, 
yet grew up on a suburban house farm in Shelbyville 
before moving to an affluent Louisville neighborhood. 
Rap fans also accuse Jack Harlow of being an industry 
plant created by music executives to appropriate a fal-
sified rap persona, pander to Black audiences (namely 
Black women), and achieve more commercial success 
than Black rappers due to his White privilege (Cruz, 
2022). Rapper David Banner noted White privilege’s 
role in Jack Harlow’s and other White rappers’ suc-
cesses: “White people’s privilege is a benefit to them 
anywhere in the world. If White people run the struc-
ture [whiteness] is going to benefit. I think he [Harlow] 
would tell you that” (TMZ Hip Hop, 2022). Lil Uzi 
Vert defended Harlow, proclaiming, “Nah, he doesn’t 
have White privilege…he’s signed to Black people”  
(Martinez, 2022). Harlow addressed the industry plant 
rumors, declaring:
My career had very humble beginnings. That’s 
why anytime I see my name associated with 
anything like ‘industry plant,’ it makes me so 
proud to really be able to say that I’m like, out 
of everyone in the game right now, one of the 
furthest from it.
(Cardenas, 2022)
These discourses are significant when situ-
ated within the music industry’s history of White  
American mainstream rappers. Rap’s crossover 
appeal represents a form of cultural tourism for 
young White American suburban men who gravitate 
to hip hop to vicariously experience the resilience of 
ghetto youth through the pleasures of consumption 
rather than actual contact, lived experiences, and 
social location (Watkins, 2005). Also, hip hop fans 
and industry insiders speculate about the growing 
influence of outside forces (i.e., media corporations, 
record label executives, social media algorithms, 
and streaming bots) on the genre, as White-owned 
music executives and record labels control corpo-
rate hip hop and strategically implant White rappers 
to entice White consumers. Further, Jack Harlow’s 
signing to DJ Drama’s record label is reminiscent 
of Dr. Dre’s signing of Eminem; other Black music 
executives (Diddy, DJ Drama, Eazy E, Jay-Z, T.I., 
and others) also recognized the opportunity to 
carry rap’s Black musical style to White consum-
ers, signing White rappers and profiting from their 
music careers. As Queen Latifah declared, “All of 
us Black label owners know we’d sign [a White kid] 
because White kids want their own hero more than 
they want ours” (White, 1999, p. 198). Thus, Jack 
Harlow’s desire to be an example and hometown 
hero for rap’s White kids is “merely the latest chap-
ter in a recurring American dream, in which a good-
 
looking 
White kid borrows a Black sound and style 
and walks off with the prize” (Brown, 1991, p. N11).
Jack Harlow offers a fruitful case study in rap’s 
relationship with whiteness and the authenticating 
strategies of a commercially successful White rapper 


Music and Digital Media 219
in a m
usical genre hard-coded to the racial injustices 
of Black Americans. We analyzed Harlow’s music for 
the presence of White rap authenticating strategies 
and discourses on racial injustice, whiteness, and white 
privilege in society and rap culture.
Critical Whiteness Studies and White 
Authenticity in Rap Culture
Hip hop remains a space where whiteness and 
White rappers are interrogated, and the authenticity 
of their rap identities in relation to White privilege 
is openly questioned. In response, White rappers 
cultivated authenticating strategies (Hess, 2005) to 
negotiate and rearticulate whiteness as they strived 
for authenticity and cultural inclusion by Black rap 
peers and fans.
As Fraley (2009) noted, hip hop’s interrogation of 
White rappers encourages mass publics to “explore 
the intersections of rap music, race, Whiteness, and 
the politics of representation” (p. 39). We must also 
acknowledge the historic relationship between music 
genres and racial boundary work, which habitually 
associates artists of color with rap and rhythm and 
blues (Schaap, Waal, & Koster, 2021). Such indus-
try politics perceive White rappers as authenticity 
mismatches between minoritized racial groups and 
rap audiences. Given this history’s relevance to Jack  
Harlow’s positioning as a White rapper, we drew on 
Critical Whiteness Studies (CWS) and Armstrong’s 
(2004) and Hess’s (2005) conceptualizations of White 
rap authenticating strategies.
Critical Whiteness Studies and Hip Hop Culture
Whiteness studies as an academic field confronts 
White privilege on various levels. With roots in 
critical race theory, CWS critiques and destabilizes 
the hegemonic conceptualization of whiteness by 
“[looking] behind the privilege that Whiteness pro-
vides” (Hurtado & Stewart, 2004, p. 297). By inves-
tigating racial division and racial hierarchy through 
the lens of the dominant racial group, whiteness 
is systematically dissected rather than taken for 
granted and left unexamined.
Research on whiteness focuses on the omnipres-
ence yet invisibility of whiteness, White privilege, and 
the social construction of whiteness. According to 
Frankenberg, “White stands for the position of racial 
‘neutrality,’ or the racially unmarked category” (1993, 
p. 55). With other races often stereotyped as con-
verses, whiteness remains the generic, assumed con-
dition. The invisibility of whiteness gives it tremendous 
power. Through this invisibility, whiteness secures and 
perpetuates white privilege. (Wildman & Davis, 2008).
Hip hop is one of the few cultural spaces where 
whiteness is regarded as “Other” and considered sub-
ordinate to Blackness. Whiteness is not invisible in 
rap. The relations of power and privileges that make 
whiteness powerful in society at large make the racial 
category powerless for White artists in hip hop culture 
due in part to rising fears of cultural appropriation and 
imitation.
Authenticity in Hip Hop and Rap
Authenticity claims pervade hip hop music commu-
nities as artists and fans struggle to maintain their 
identity by “draw[ing] clearly demarcated bounda-
ries around their culture” (McLeod, 1999, p. 136). 
In popular music studies, authenticity considers the 
performance’s proximity to an original culture that 
once existed outside of the record industry (Hess, 
2005). In the United States, authenticity is particu-
larly complex, given the legacy of stolen labor, capi-
talism, and the commodification of Black art forms.
Hip hop remains reluctant to accept White art-
ists due to its history as a resistance culture. Given the 
racial tensions underpinning hip hop’s reluctance to 
render White hip hop artists as authentic, White rap-
pers’ performances of authenticity are their greatest 
assets in the genre’s hypermasculine and consumerist 
world.
Contemporary rap labels are increasingly stra-
tegic about how artists’ identities are created, per -
formed, and distributed to mass audiences, especially 
in the case of White rappers. Despite rap’s push for an 
authentic self, White cultural production in rap is often 
anything but genuine. White rappers historically pre-
sented multilayered identities constructed by record 
labels to appeal to contemporary and historic rap 
trends, acknowledge and reject white privilege, and 
advance a narrative of hip hop authenticity to fore-
ground a presumably original and authentic self (Hess, 

220 Content
2005). Recently, modes of White rap are changing as 
some White rappers (e.g., G-Eazy, Machine Gun Kelly, 
and Post Malone) conveniently alter their sounds and 
engage in genre-roaming with rock and roll and pop at 
a time when conversations around systemic racism are 
louder than ever. A.D. Carson declared that the current 
state of White rap has “a lot more to do with capitalism 
than it does White rappers reading the room” and sug-
gested their labels could be steering them away from a 
Black hip hop sound to avoid criticism (Hobbs, 2020).
Exploring rap’s racial politics and its implications 
for White rappers, Armstrong (2004) identified three 
authenticating strategies of White rapper Eminem: 
(1) being true to oneself or keeping it real; (2) claim-
ing local allegiances and territorial identities; and (3) 
establishing a connection to an original source of rap 
through locale, style, or links to an established artist.
Hess (2005) extended Armstrong’s work, detailing 
three authenticating strategies historically employed 
by White hip hop artists. These are (1) cultural immer-
sion, in which White artists assert their immersion in 
hip hop culture without imitating a model of Black 
authenticity; (2) imitation, in which White artists imi-
tate explicit models of the Black aesthetics (e.g., lan-
guage, oral culture, musical traditions, and political 
location); and (3) the inversion of the rags-to-riches 
success stories of Black rap stars, in which White art-
ists frame their whiteness as a disadvantage in a form 
that remains dominated by Black artists.
Harlow’s Authenticating Strategies and 
Discourses on Race, Rap, and White 
Privilege
We conducted a textual analysis of Jack Harlow’s 
two studio albums, That’s What They All Say (2020) 
and Come Home the Kids Miss Y ou (2022) to investi-
gate the use of White rap authenticating strategies 
(Armstrong, 2005; Hess, 2005). We also examined 
Harlow’s potential social criticisms of racial injus-
tice, whiteness, and white privilege in rap and society. 
Textual analysis is a qualitative research methodol-
ogy used to critique media culture and determine 
the meaning of language. Textual analysts focus on 
meanings by reading for detail and emphasis; inter-
preting narrative elements, keywords, and themes; 
and evaluating how these meanings act as examples 
of larger stories or broader social systems.
We downloaded the verified lyrics of all 34 songs 
on the two albums from Genius.com and conducted 
a close reading of the lyrics. We noted each time the 
lyrics presented discourse aligning with the White rap 
authenticating strategies of Armstrong (2004) and 
Hess (2005). We also investigated whether the lyrics 
advanced any cultural commentary or criticisms of 
racial injustice, whiteness, or white privilege in rap and 
society.
Jack Harlow’s Complicated White Rap 
Realness
Jack Harlow incorporated all six of Armstrong and 
Hess’s rap authenticating strategies in his attempts 
to validate himself as a White rapper. Throughout 
both albums, Harlow claimed to be an A-lister and 
hometown hero who was automatic with his rap 
penmanship, the face of his city, the hottest [rapper] 
out, the one to be trusted, and a White boy with a 
little Habanero, among other self-descriptions. Har-
low emphasized authenticity, claimed local territo-
rial allegiance to Louisville, and acknowledged his 
whiteness, yet did not discuss any issues of racial 
injustice. Instead, he advanced familiar rags-to-
riches narratives chronicling his humble beginnings 
in the industry, strong work ethic, and challenges 
as a White rap artist. He communicated hardships 
related to industry pressures and record label con-
cerns about his whiteness and ability to stand next 
to Black rappers in “Churchill Hills” and chastised 
White geeks and Internet critics for questioning his 
rap persona in “Tyler Herro.”
To Harlow, his greatest adversaries were White 
people who discredited his talent with online music 
criticisms and think pieces. However, his commentary 
on intracultural audiences represented an interesting 
spin on Hess’s “inversion of the rags-to-riches suc-
cess stories of Black rap stars” for two reasons. First,  
Harlow identified White audiences—not reluctant 
Black audiences or social class challenges—as poten-
tial detriments to his success. In doing so, he reflected 
a strategy used by Eminem to combat critics who 
doubted the authenticity of his lyrics (Hess, 2005). 


Music and Digital Media 221
Second, Har
low’s discourse revealed noteworthy intr-
aracial tensions that placed critical intracultural lenses 
on his rap authenticity.
As a White rapper, Harlow heavily leaned on 
influential Black rappers and industry gatekeepers 
who endorsed his rap ascension, cultural immersion, 
and genre inclusion. He also advanced a Louisville ter-
ritorial identity rife with contrasting narratives that bor-
dered on imitation. Harlow most frequently employed 
Armstrong’s strategies of “establishing a connection to 
an original source of rap through links to established 
Black rap artists” and “claiming territorial identities.” 
He prominently featured Black producers and rappers 
and openly touted his various cosigns by Black indus-
try gatekeepers and rappers such as Big Sean, Diddy, 
Drake, Lil Baby, Lil Wayne, and Snoop Dogg. Of the 34 
songs, 27 involved Black producers, 10 featured Black 
rap artists, and 9 included Black song samples.
Harlow’s content was rife with lyrical references 
to Black cultural figures, music executives, producers, 
rappers, and singers. For example, in “Rendezvous,” 
Harlow cited the impact of Wacka Flocka Flame’s 
2009 hit single “O Let’s Do It” on his middle school 
rap career. ”Rendezvous” also referenced the indus-
try gatekeepers who bolstered his career, made him 
a millionaire at 22 years old, and granted access to 
popular rappers for collaborations. This theme con-
tinued as Harlow bragged about receiving an industry 
cosign from Diddy (“Face of the City”), having access 
to women and any rapper he wanted on his album due 
to industry connections (“21C/Delta”), and receiving 
an approval stamp from Drake (“Churchill Downs”). 
Overall, Harlow’s lyrics supported rather than rebuked 
prior industry plant accusations.
Harlow also featured White artists (e.g., Adam 
Levine, Fergie, and Justin Timberlake) who, like Har-
low, gained popularity with Black audiences through 
collaborations with Black rappers. Their presence 
added dimensions of credibility and nostalgia to his 
rap image. However, Harlow othered himself from 
White artists and rappers such as Beastie Boys, the 
Dixie Chicks, and Vanilla Ice in “Route 66” and “Y oung 
Harleezy,” making it clear that he should not be com-
pared to their musical legacies and social locations.  
Harlow extricated his rap identity from 
 Souther
n- 
centric bluegrass genres commonly affiliated with 
Kentucky and Texas while presenting himself as an 
authentic, wealthy rap superstar whose dedication to 
the craft allowed him to reach a mainstream audience.
Armstrong’s (2004) rap authenticating strategy 
of White rap artists “claiming local allegiances and 
territorial identities” pervaded Harlow’s music and 
revealed several inaccuracies about his biography, rap 
authenticity, and whiteness. Harlow designated him-
self the face and hometown hero of Louisville with 
brothers who would ride for him, cited prominent cul-
tural sites (i.e., Morris Deli), and declared he was from 
the city where residents might shoot you in the head. 
His lyrics painted a rough image of the city, which he 
leveraged to reinforce his rap masculinity, toughness, 
and ties to Black urban culture.
Still, there were noteworthy incongruities in Har-
low’s local allegiance assertions. Although situating 
himself within Louisville’s urban ecosystem, Harlow 
infamously changed his story on “Route 66,” a collab-
oration with Black rapper and Louisville native EST 
Gee. In the song, Harlow admitted he was from the 
White side of Louisville and raised in an affluent neigh-
borhood. This admission, made in a song featuring a 
Black artist from the same city, also raised questions 
of cultural imitation. How can Harlow claim author-
ity over Louisville’s street culture when he resides in a 
White suburban community?
Harlow’s contradictory discourses resurfaced 
in “Parent Trap,” a collaboration with Justin Timber-
lake. Harlow rapped about the challenges of being a 
successful rapper and wanting to move to the sub-
urbs where the “Karens” (demanding, often racist, 
White women) live for peace. The lyrics supported 
Y ousman’s (2003, p. 166) argument that White subur-
ban youth identification with rap music often evokes 
“Blackophilia (manifested by White consumption of 
Black popular culture)” and “Blackophobia (fear and 
dread of African Americans).” The White rapper val-
ued proximity to Black culture for rap fame and wealth 
but covertly wanted off-work access to familiar safety, 
social class upbringing, and white privilege. Of equal 
importance, Harlow exhibited how White artists can 
appropriate, benefit, and detach from Black culture 
when convenient due to white privilege.
Ultimately, Jack Harlow’s rap authenticating 
strategies embodied white privilege at its finest and 

222 Content
the genre’s complex relationship with White rappers. 
To be clear, Harlow is not a reflection of authentic hip 
hop culture. He represents the commodification of hip 
hop music by an industry produced under a White-  
dominated structure that habitually advances nega-
tive stereotypes of Blacks and propels White artists 
forward as gatekeepers of the genre. Based on these 
industry politics, Jack Harlow is simply the contem-
porary manifestation of a commodified recording 
industry, the historic profitability of White rappers, 
and White suburban fascination with Black music for 
 quasi-tr
ansformative purposes.

supremacy. Communication Theory, 13(4), 366–391.
6.3: EMINEM’S “LOVE THE WAY YOU 
LIE” AND THE NORMALIZATION OF 
MEN’S VIOLENCE AGAINST WOMEN
Rachel Alicia Griffin and Joshua D. Phillips
The authors analyze Eminem’s Love the Way Y ou 
Lie from a rhetorical feminist perspective and illumi-
nate how the song strengthens cultural myths about 
domestic violence and subsequently normalizes 
men’s violence against women. Before continuing, 
we urge you to go online and read the lyrics and 
watch the music video.
Eminem’s “Love the Way Y ou Lie” featuring pop/
R&B singer Rihanna was number one on the Bill-
board Hot 100 Chart for 11 weeks in 2010 and 
remains popular. Neither of these artists is com-
pletely naïve about intimate partner violence (often 
called domestic violence). Eminem has rapped 
about his violent behavior toward women, and 
Rihanna is publicly recognized as a survivor of inti-
mate partner violence. How does this song reflect 
the issue?
We argue that the song’s lyrics and video imagery 
reproduce cultural myths about domestic violence 
including notions that (1) men and women are equally 
responsible for perpetuating violence in relationships, 
(2) women ask to be abused, and (3) violence is a 
means to ignite sexual arousal.
Highlighting the prevalence of violence against 
women, Alhabib, Nur, and Jones (2010) assert 
“Worldwide, domestic violence is as serious a cause 
of death and incapacity among women aged 15–49 
years as cancer, and a greater cause of ill health than 
traffic accidents and malaria combined” (p. 370). 
The National Intimate Partner and Sexual Violence 
Survey (Smith et al., 2018, p. 2) found that “43.6% of 
women (nearly 52.2 million) experienced some form 
of contact sexual violence in their lifetime.” Although 
males are abused by female partners, women are far 
more likely to experience domestic violence than men. 
Therefore, through a feminist lens, we position intimate 
partner violence as a cultural epidemic that renders 
females systemically vulnerable to male aggression.
To critique “Love the Way Y ou Lie,” we use a rhe-
torical feminist perspective (Hart & Daughton, 2005) 
to deconstruct the lived experiences the artists repre-
sent and the gendered implications of the song. A fem-
inist critique promotes critical consumption of popular 
culture (Sellnow, 2010), which necessitates mindful-
ness toward the covert ways that sexism and patriar-
chy infiltrate our everyday lives. According to Johnson 
(2004), a society is patriarchal when it is dominated 
by males, identified according to masculine norms, 
and centered on male interests. A feminist perspective 
also recognizes popular culture as far more than just 
entertainment; rather, popular culture is positioned as 
pedagogical (Brummett, 2011; Sellnow, 2010), which 
highlights the ways that audiences learn from what 
they see and hear via popular culture (Sandlin, 2007). 
Therefore, it is important to critique popular culture 
because mediated messages are capable of furthering 
the dehumanization and commodification of women 
(hooks, 1996; Kirk & Okazawa-Rey, 2010).
The Normalization of Men’s Violence 
against Women
Our analysis revealed three main themes by which 
“Love the Way Y ou Lie” functions to normalize 
men’s violence against women.
Men and Women Are Equally Responsible
As noted earlier, although females can be violent 
toward male partners, the opposite (men attack-
ing women) is the norm. Representations negating 
this reality rigorously reduce perceptions of male 
accountability. Consider Eminem’s lyrics that con-
tinuously bring attention to the violent behavior of 
both partners. For example, during an abusive scene 
in the music video between Megan Fox
1 (the female 
partner) and Dominic Monaghan (the male partner), 
Eminem raps about how both Fox and Monaghan 

224 Content
are enraged and links their behaviors to their state of 
mind. He indicates that neither partner has a handle 
on their emotions, and therefore, the collective and 
impersonal “rage” of the situation is at fault.
Later Eminem indicates that the two people have 
equally bad tempers. He compares one to a tornado 
and the other to a volcano. Referencing the partners as 
equally fierce natural disasters leads the audience to 
understand that men’s and women’s tempers in a vio-
lent relationship are comparable. This interpretation is 
problematic because it does not account for the cul-
tural systems that privilege men who oppress women. 
To symbolically depict men and women as equally 
sharing the blame in a violent relationship grossly 
undermines the social reality that men are more 
likely to be the cause of the violence. If a female does 
engage in violence toward her male partner, she most 
likely does so to protect herself and/or her children  
(Campbell, Rose, Kub, & Nedd, 1998).
Because Fox and Monaghan are depicted as 
equally violent toward each other, it also becomes 
easy to dismiss their violence at the micro level with-
out noting the epidemic prevalence of violence in 
heterosexual partnerships at the macro level. Rep-
resenting both partners as violent excuses society’s 
culpability because the issue is presented without the 
contextual consideration of the systemic legacies of 
hegemonic masculinity and female oppression. The 
audience, especially males, can identify with Eminem’s 
lyrics and the video’s visual narrative which voice 
their frustrations with women and subsequently mark 
them as helpless men who become violent only when 
pushed over the edge by women. This interpretation, 
in accordance with dominant patriarchal ideologies, 
exonerates abusive males from responsibility for their 
choices and positions them as victims rather than 
frightening mirrors of society.
Women Ask to Be Abused
The second cultural myth, that women ask to be 
abused, beaten, and raped, is rooted in our patriar -
chal culture as a means to hold women responsible 
for the acts of violence perpetrated against them. 
This myth justifies men hurting women as an accept-
able means to discipline and punish those who are 
not in alignment with patriarchal expectations of 
femininity. Despite the efforts of anti-
 g
ender-based 
violence activists to uproot this myth, it remains 
highly visible in cultural texts such as “Love the Way 
Y ou Lie.”
A specific point of concern is Monaghan’s char-
acter who is lyrically and visually represented as being 
driven to batter Fox’s character. This idea surfaces dur-
ing the music video when Monaghan violently slams 
Fox onto their bed after she slaps him on the chest. 
The audience witnesses Fox “enticing” him to beat 
her even to the point of engaging in violence herself.
2 
Because Fox is depicted as the partner who gets phys-
ical first, the audience is given the perception that the 
woman is responsible for starting the violence. In this 
vein, it becomes possible to read the bruises on her 
face as justifiable. With that, the song reinforces the 
dominant ideological tendency to blame the victim 
which positions women at fault for the choices that 
their male counterparts make to hurt them (Kirk & 
Okazawa-Rey, 2010).
After this fight scene, Fox attempts to leave 
the house and presumably the relationship. As she 
approaches the front door, Monaghan grabs her 
shoulder bag causing her to spin around and the 
couple’s fighting resumes. The imagery and lyr -
ics offer two conclusions. First, if Fox had not hit 
Monaghan, he would not have been forced to use 
physical violence against her. Second, if Fox had 
not tried to leave, Monaghan would not have been 
forced to physically stop her. In both instances, we 
are beckoned to view Fox as the instigator and con-
sequently view Monaghan’s behavior as a reaction 
to that behavior.
The culmination of Fox’s attempt to leave the 
relationship is summarized in Eminem’s final lyrics of 
the song. The last three lines of the third verse present 
a musical narrative of what domestic violence looks 
like—corroborating the notion that the violence men 
inflict on women is only in response to the actions of 
women. Therefore, we can assume that if Fox would 
have “acted right” (e.g., in accordance with patriarchy), 
she would not have been physically abused, verbally 
abused, and eventually threatened with being burned 
alive. This logic not only assumes that men cannot 
control their anger but also reinforces the idea that 


Music and Digital Media 225
w
omen, not men, need to change their behavior if they 
wish to end the cycle of domestic violence.
Violence Ignites Sexual Arousal
The third myth involves blurring the distinctions 
between violence and sex. We see this each time 
Rihanna sings the chorus. She repeatedly presents 
a horrific image (being burned) as something that is 
not only acceptable but also delectable.
Domestic violence is thus described as a passion-
ate exchange between two lovers. By alluding to the 
idea that being burned is enjoyable because the pain is 
desirable, Rihanna encourages the audience to believe 
that women not only ask to be abused but that they 
also take pleasure in being abused. Each time Rihanna 
mentions being hurt, her lips curl, she licks her fingers, 
and the audience is invited to extract sexualized mean-
ings that directly correlate pain and pleasure. We read 
the lyrics coupled with Rihanna’s lip curl as an enticing 
moment of audience appeal. Every close-up of Rihan-
na’s voluptuous red lips becomes a sexualized symbol 
of how violence may be transformed into enticing 
lust. She appears to crave sexual contact overlapping 
with gratifying pain, which in accordance with cultural 
myths about sex and love allows violence to be misin-
terpreted as unbridled passion.
Coupled with Rihanna’s lyrics are the images of 
Fox and Monaghan’s characters living out the cycle of 
domestic violence. Throughout the video, the audience 
is bombarded with quick-cutting scenes illustrating 
their relationship as violent one moment and passion-
ate the next. For example, after Fox has attempted to 
leave the house, Monaghan throws her against a wall 
and ferociously punches his hand through the drywall 
next to her head. After a quick cut to a remorseful 
Monaghan regretfully bowing his head, the two lov-
ers instantaneously engage in hot passionate kissing, 
standing upright against the damaged wall.
The hypersexualized pushing, shoving, and 
punching between Fox and Monaghan is accom-
panied by Eminem’s lyrics delivered with a tangible 
intensity. The second verse frighteningly describes 
how feelings of love become quite the opposite. It 
details specific violent actions taken against one’s 
partner—including clawing, biting, hitting, scratching, 
knocking down, and more. The aggressive video 
imagery coupled with the lyrics discursively invites 
the audience to blur the lines between romantic inti-
macy and domestic violence.
The repetitive cycles oscillating between violence 
and sex provide the foundational narrative for Fox and 
Monaghan’s relationship throughout the music video. 
This oscillation subjects the audience to Monaghan 
and Fox’s reconciliation represented as kissing, sex, 
and other forms of intimacy only to be thrown back 
into acts of physical and verbal abuse. Alarmingly, 
when the conflation of sex, passion, and violence in 
“Love the Way Y ou Lie” is read from a feminist rhetor-
ical standpoint, we bear witness to the ways that men’s 
violence against women can be misinterpreted as sex-
ual rather than criminal. At the end of the music video, 
the audience leaves these two intimate partners where 
we first encountered them: peacefully asleep in their 
bed, limbs harmoniously entangled.
The Power of Popular Culture
The greatest danger of this song is the subtlety 
of the dominant messages imparted to casual 
 list
eners—so subtle that perhaps even Rihanna and 
Eminem genuinely believe that the song serves as 
a warning of the dangers of intimate partner vio-
lence. Y et, we must recognize that even if the song 
is intended and/or interpreted as a warning about 
the cycle of domestic violence, it serves as a warn-
ing to the women who are beaten rather than the 
men who choose to beat them. Therefore, violence 
against women is discursively positioned as a wom-
en’s issue despite the overwhelming research and 
advocacy that positions violence against women as 
an issue caused by males (at the micro level) and 
patriarchy (at the macro level) (Kirk & 
 Ok
azawa- 
Rey, 2010).
Incredibly indicative of the recentering of male 
privilege despite the song’s depiction of the cycle of 
domestic violence is Eminem’s placement at the core 
of the song not only as the main artist but also as the 
perpetrator who sings about being an abuser. In this 
context, Eminem’s real-life persona as a musician who 
has rapped about his abuse of women in such songs 
as “Kim” and “My Mom,” coupled with his role as the 

226 Content
primary artist, positions him at the center of attention. 
In contrast, Rihanna as the survivor (both in real life 
and in the song) is rendered to the periphery by way of 
singing the chorus and being the guest artist featured 
on Eminem’s album.
To be fair, it is also important to mark this rhetori-
cal text as a site of struggle. Borrowing from Brummett 
(2011), the song might be positioned as a “battlefield” 
of social and political forces where the line between 
healthy and unhealthy relationships is a struggle, the 
cycle of intimate partner violence is a struggle, and 
Fox and Monaghan literally struggle with each other. 
Likewise, the song lyrics and music video visibly posi-
tion domestic violence in mainstream culture and 
accurately mark the cyclic nature of intimate partner 
violence. For instance, near the end of the first verse, 
Eminem acknowledges the insanity of the situation, 
rapping about the tortured swings from the highest of 
highs (when things are going well, he’s Superman to 
her Lois Lane) to the lowest of lows.
In addition, Fox is shown in the video attempting 
to leave the violent relationship three times but is emo-
tionally drawn (Monaghan offers her a teddy bear) and 
physically dragged (Monaghan grabs her shoulder bag) 
back in despite her desire to break free. This specific 
representation mirrors the reality that most battered 
women attempt to leave several times before they 
leave for good or are murdered (Jenkins & Davidson, 
2001). The final verse unequivocally marks the omni-
presence of danger in violent intimate relationships. 
Thus, as Eminem indicates, false promises of changed 
behavior will not protect women.
“Love the Way Y ou Lie” should be understood 
as a pedagogical rhetorical text that illustrates and 
reproduces cultural myths about domestic violence. 
Shockingly, “[m]ost women…experience a certain 
amount of what could be defined as sexual violence as 
part of daily life” (Kirk & Okazawa-Rey, 2010, p. 257). 
Naming this reality, Jensen (2013) offers “sexual intru-
sion” meaning the everyday nature of patriarchy that 
degrades female intellect, invades female bodies with 
unsolicited commentary, and imposes an omnipresent 
sense of fear. Deconstructed from a rhetorical feminist 
standpoint, “Love the Way Y ou Lie” is exemplary of 
sexual intrusion as a pervasive popular culture text that 
perpetuates dangerous cultural myths about domestic 
violence and subsequently dehumanizes women as 
survivors and victims of gender violence. Although 
the intent of the artists may have been to shock their 
audience with images of burning homes and private 
moments, the results of their efforts clearly reproduce 
damaging messages concerning violence against 
women. Such reproductions unmistakably contribute 
to the normalization of men’s violence against women.
NOTES
 1.  F ox donated her appearance fee to a shelter for 
abused women (Dinh, 2010). Although this gesture 
was noteworthy and admirable, it did not receive 
nearly as much coverage as did her role in the video.
 2.
 Our ar
gument here is not to excuse or minimize the 
ways that Fox engages in violent behavior but rather 
to contextualize the differences between this rep-
resentation of domestic violence and the realities of 
most battered women.
It’s Your Turn: What Do You Think? What 
Will You Find?
 1.
 F
rom your perspective, does “Love the 
Way Y ou Lie” affirm and/or contest the 
normalization of men’s violence against 
women? Which aspects of the authors’ 
argument do you agree and/or disagree 
with?
 2.
 Other 
singers, including Ludacris and 
Mary J. Blige (“Runaway Love”) and 
the Dixie Chicks (“Goodbye Earl”), have 
released songs about violence against 
women and girls. After listening to these 
songs, how are the messages that Emi-
nem and Rihanna send in “Love the Way 
Y ou Lie” similar and/or different?
 3.
 U
sing clippings from magazines and 
newspapers, create a collage that resists 
the reproduction of cultural myths about 
intimate partner violence in “Love the 
Way Y ou Lie.” Be sure to include words 
and images that communicate the mes-
sages that you feel are missing from the 
lyrics and/or music video.

6.4: NOT JUST JEZEBEL: BLACK 
WOMEN, NICKI MINAJ, AND 
SEXUALIZED IMAGERY IN RAP MUSIC
Kiana Cox
The author explores sexualized imagery in current 
rap music through the lens of Black feminist theory, 
paying special attention to the work of Nicki Minaj.
What kind of knowledge is constructed about Black 
women in contemporary rap music? In this piece, 
I use Black feminist theory to explore sexualized 
imagery in rap. I pay special attention to Nicki Minaj, 
who in 2017 became the female artist with the most 
Hot 100 singles in Billboard history, surpassing Are-
tha Franklin (Stutz, 2017). She is ranked 10th overall, 
sitting ahead of such greats as Ray Charles, Elton 
John, and the Beatles (Trust, 2017).
Black Feminist Theory and Imagery
Black feminism is a scholar-activist tradition posit-
ing that intersectionality is the most effective way to 
analyze the lives of Black women. That is, we can 
best understand Black women’s experiences by 
looking at the ways that axes of inequality interlock 
and overlap (Crenshaw, 1989). One recurrent theme 
in Black feminist scholarship is analysis of how gen-
der ideologies apply to Black women. Collins (2004) 
put forth a theory of hegemonic femininity, which is 
a set of characteristics, behaviors, and interactions 
that represent the totality of so-called normal wom-
anhood. These are standards against which the femi-
ninity of all women is measured. They are hegemonic 
in that only particular women can achieve them, 
although most women tend to deem them normal 
and accurate. Hegemonic femininity specifically sets 
the boundaries for acceptable actions of the body, 
including how it is used sexually and how women 
should act in relation to men. Overall, a woman is 
more feminine if she is submissive and deferential 
to male authority. This also includes sex, where a 
truly feminine woman only allows heterosexual men 
access to her body, and only within the confines of 
marriage (Collins, 2004).
 4.  T hink about the lyrics and music video 
of your favorite song about relation-
ships. What messages does that song 
send about gender identities, love, and 
intimacy?
 5.
 Ho
w do popular media such as hashtags 
(e.g., #WhyIStayed, #HeForShe, and 
#MeToo) challenge “Love the Way Y ou 
Lie” and representations that similarly 
condone men’s violence against women?

228 Content
When it comes to Black women specifically, Col-
lins (2000) presented the controlling images typology 
as a way to analyze how Black women have been neg-
atively represented in US culture. The effectiveness 
of these representations (mammy, matriarch, Jezebel, 
and welfare mother) is bolstered by their reliance on 
this hegemonic notion of women’s submission (or lack 
thereof) to men. Both the mammy and welfare mother 
submit to actual or symbolic White male power as 
homeowners or the state. However, and most relevant 
for this study, the Jezebel and matriarch refuse to sub-
mit to male power and are denigrated for it. They are 
the direct opposite of the hegemonic ideal. Matriarchs 
are undesirable women who rule Black homes with 
an iron fist and emasculate Black men in the process. 
Jezebels are attractive but have too much control over 
their sexuality, refusing to submit it to male authority. It 
is these messages I consider when analyzing the songs 
and artists included in this study.
Hip-Hop Feminism
The issue of sexualization and the male gaze are 
points of contention between Black feminists who 
came of age in the 1960s and 1970s and those who 
grew up in the hip-hop generation (Peoples, 2008). 
For younger feminists, it is not enough to conclude 
that hip-hop portrays women negatively and to 
reject the music without considering the nuances 
of Black women’s position within it (Morgan, 
2015). Black feminists of the hip-hop generation 
discuss controlling images and their institutional 
implications, but argue that Collins’ typology falls 
short because it does not account for Black wom-
en’s agency or pleasure. As Morgan (1999, p. 59) 
famously put it, Black women who have come of 
age since the 1980s need a feminism “that f**ks 
with the grays.” Black feminists of this generation 
continually grapple with these grays: What it means 
to be both ratchet and respectable (Boylorn, 2015) 
and how they can enjoy hip-hop culture even while 
critiquing its misogyny. Hip-hop feminists teach us 
that analyses of the representations of women in 
rap music cannot simply see Nicki Minaj twerking in 
“Anaconda,” declare her a Jezebel, and stop there. 
Rather, we should look at both rap music’s empow-
ering and misogynistic tendencies—particularly as 
related to how women are portrayed sexually and 
how women use sexuality to disrupt hegemonic 
femininity. My study of Billboard’s Hot Rap Songs 
from 2010 to 2017 takes this approach.
Rap music is a dominant aspect of American pop-
ular culture. In 2017, it surpassed rock as the leading 
genre in the music industry (Hyman, 2017). Nielson’s 
2017 statistics bear this out: 25.1% of total consump-
tion and 30.3% of all on-demand audio streams are 
rap and rap-influenced R&B compared to 18.1% for 
rock (Hyman, 2017). This is largely due to the surge 
in popularity of music streaming services, where rap 
songs make up 65% of the 8.2 billon on-demand audio 
streams. The success of rap as a Black cultural form 
makes it a useful site to examine hegemonic ideologies 
about Black women. In order to pursue this, I used Bill-
board’s Y ear End: Hot Rap Songs charts for 2010–2017. 
Billboard constructs these charts based on music sales, 
radio airplay, and on-demand audio stream. Although 
not the only compiler of music charts, it is considered 
the fairest and least subjective (Lena, 2006). The Hot 
Rap Songs chart lists the top 50 rap songs for each 
year. Using only the top 10 and eliminating songs that 
charted more than once, I had a sample of 79 songs. 
I used Google Play lyrics and Genius lyrics to locate 
lyrics. I began my study with the 2010 chart, because 
that is the year Nicki Minaj first broke into the top 10 
on the charts as a lead artist with “Y our Love” (#9). I 
included all the Hot Rap Songs charts through 2017.
Not Just Jezebel
I conducted a close reading of the lyrics for the 
songs in my sample in two phases. First, I examined 
each song looking for references to women. I then 
conducted a close examination of lyrics referencing 
women based on the tenets of hegemonic feminin-
ity: How women’s bodies are described, whether 
these descriptions are sexual, and how women 
act in relation to men in the narrative of the song. 
I also applied Black feminist theory, specifically 
the perspective of hip-hop feminists, by looking at 
the extent to which Black women are subjects or 
objects in the song and the level of sexual agency 
they exhibit. In total, the sample featured men as 
lead artists in 88.6% (70 of 79) of the songs. Nicki 
Minaj’s music alone makes up five of the nine female 


Music and Digital Media 229
lead s
ongs. Most of the songs (74 of 79, or 94%) 
feature lead artists who were Black. Songs with sex-
ual references to women make up 53.1% (42 of 79) 
of the sample, and songs with non-sexual romantic 
representations of women make up 16.5% (13 of 
79). Overall, I found that women are still sexualized 
in rap music, but such imagery appears alongside 
songs presenting Black women as desirable rela-
tionship partners apart from their sexual availability 
to men. Furthermore, Nicki Minaj’s music serves 
as the kind of disruption in rap music imagery that 
younger Black feminists were looking for. She owns, 
controls, and in some cases, destroys male authority 
through her lyrics.
Sexual Imagery
The knowledge constructed about Black women 
in the 2010–2017 Hot Rap Songs charts proceeds 
primarily from Black men’s points of view, because 
their work comprises nearly 90% of the sample. 
Given the history of male dominance and misog-
yny in rap (Conrad, Dixon, & Zhang, 2009), it is no 
surprise that more than half of the songs (42 of 79) 
mention women solely as sex partners. However, 
the larger narrative of these songs demonstrates 
that these sexualized depictions of women are not 
primarily about their sexual submission, but pres-
ent such submission as one aspect of an actual or 
imagined successful life filled with money, partying, 
and recreational drugs. For example in “Miss Me” 
(#10, 2010), Drake compares his wealth to winning 
the lottery and his attitude to that of a World Series 
baseball champion. His reference to Black women 
occurs in the context of him explaining how his fun 
“champagne bottle” life involves hanging out with 
his friends, smoking weed, and going to the King of 
Diamonds strip club.
Rap group Migos tell a similar story in “Bad and 
Boujee” (#3, 2017). Group member Offset describes 
“taking” another man’s “thot” and having sex with her 
as one of several components of his “new money” life-
style, which also include smoking marijuana, driving a 
drop-top car, carrying a lot of cash, and dealing with 
haters. Both Drake’s and Migos’ lyrics exemplify the 
broader ideology in which the sexualization of women 
occurs: hegemonic masculinity. Sexually accessible 
women; visible wealth in the form of cash, champagne, 
and cars; and the use of these things as evidence of 
their superiority over other men are quintessential 
ways that hegemonically masculine men reaffirm their 
places in society (Connell & Messerschmidt, 2005).
Black Women as Desirable
The relatively flat representations of Black women 
as sexually available certainly are widespread within 
rap music content. However, it is incorrect to con-
clude that rap music is singularly about impersonal 
sex with “thots” and strippers. Throughout the his-
tory of rap, songs have discussed romantic rela-
tionships with Black women beyond their sexual 
availability. The Complex magazine list of 25 Best 
Hip-Hop Love Songs (Frederick, 2012) included 
such classics as L.L. Cool J’s “I Need Love,” A Tribe 
Called Quest’s “Bonita Applebum,” and Method 
Man and Mary J. Blige’s “All I Need/I’ll Be There 
For Y ou.” My sample is no exception, with 16.5% 
(13 of 79) of the songs falling into this category.
In “Nothin’ On Y ou” (#1, 2010), B.O.B. highlights 
the desirability of the woman he is involved with by 
calling her the “whole package” who outpaces the 
other women he could be pursuing. In contrast, in 
“Say Something” (#5, 2010), Timbaland laments how 
a good relationship could not endure the pressure of 
fame and contemplates fame’s value in the absence 
of the woman he loves. To be clear, this category is 
not without its hegemonic elements. Several of these 
songs still include prescriptions for women’s bodies 
and actions, such as Y oung Jeezy telling his girlfriend 
to keep her stomach, thighs, and legs in the condi-
tion he prefers in “Leave Y ou Alone” (#10, 2012) and 
Fetty Wap mentioning how his “Trap Queen” (#2, 
2015) works the pole. However, as in the sexualized 
representations noted above, these elements occur in 
the context of narratives describing relationships with 
women these rappers appear to care about in ways 
extending beyond their bedroom performance. This 
is important given the history of controlling images 
of Black women, where her relationships with Black 
men are ones in which she emasculates or neglects the 
men. For her to be desired by a man in the context of 
a loving relationship moves Black women from object 
to subject, albeit still from the male gaze.

230 Content
The Complexities of Nicki Minaj
Although the male gaze still dominates the rap 
music landscape, Nicki Minaj represents a complex 
challenge to that system. Minaj’s power and desire 
are centered visually, lyrically, and sexually in her 
music. She makes eight different appearances in 
this sample, five as lead artist and three as a guest 
rapper. She made history in 2017 by charting on 
the Billboard Hot 100 for the 83rd time. Fifteen of 
those entries were in the top 10, and 28 were as lead 
artist. All three of her albums (“Pink Friday,” “Pink 
Friday: Roman Reloaded,” and “The Pinkprint”) 
made the top 3 of Billboard’s Top 200 albums chart 
in the years they were released. Because Minaj is 
an industry heavyweight, specific attention should 
be paid to her work in any discussion of women’s 
representations in rap music.
Visually, Minaj disrupts hegemonic notions of 
White womanhood and male dominance through her 
use of Barbie doll imagery. In several of her videos, 
she invokes Barbie by wearing pink hair and outfits, 
but rebuts the wholesome image of White woman-
hood represented by the doll when she raps openly 
about her sexual pleasure and control. In “Anaconda” 
(#5, 2014), she wears a pink wig and a pink thong as 
she eats a phallic-shaped banana and twerks. In this 
song, Minaj denotes her sexual control by labeling 
Troy a “boy toy” with whom she has sex in her car. 
She pushes back even further against Barbie’s physi-
cal and sexual ideal by talking about her curvaceous 
body. At the end of the song, she doubles down with a 
callout to her fans who have a “fat ass,” disparaging the 
“skinny bitches.”
Lyrically, Minaj rejects sexual subordination and 
centers her own desire in “Only” (#10, 2015). In the 
song, she powerfully dispels rumors that her success is 
a result of submitting to the sexual demands of fellow 
Cash Money/Y oung Money crew members Lil Wayne 
and Drake. She emphatically swears “on my life, man” 
that it did not happen—and it would be on her own 
specific sexual terms if it did. This rejection of subor-
dination is personified in the video for “Only,” which 
features women (including Minaj) dressed as domina-
trixes. The men in the video occupy submissive sexual 
bondage positions, and even Drake and Lil Wayne are 
pictured looking up at Minaj as she towers over them 
in stiletto heels.
Although it did not make the top 10 on the Hot 
Rap Songs charts, perhaps the most visually stunning 
of Nicki Minaj’s counterhegemonic imagery occurs in 
the video “Looking Ass.” Topping out at #28 on the 
2014 Hot 100, “Looking Ass” features Minaj’s blazing 
critique of men who are entranced with her body but 
cannot live up to her sexual ideals and those who lie 
about being wealthy. As she raps, the video imagery 
alternates between her dancing seductively on a chair, 
a literal male gaze in the form of a widescreen shot of 
a Black man’s eyes with images of Minaj in his pupils, 
and her ultimate destruction of the gaze by firing a 
machine gun at it.
All of these examples from Minaj’s career under-
score the nuanced place that Black women’s sexual 
subjectivities occupy within the rap music landscape. 
It is overly simplistic to analyze Minaj’s music and label 
her a Jezebel simply because her music expresses sex-
ually explicit themes. As these examples demonstrate, 
sex in Nicki Minaj’s world occurs on her terms. This 
fact alone allows her music to differ significantly from 
the male-dominated industry she occupies, where 
lyrics often indicate that women’s sexual deference to 
men is expected. Minaj’s music and videos are openly 
sexual, but this in no way implies her availability or 
subordination.
Black feminist—and other—scholars of rap must 
take care not to overuse Collins’ (2000) typology by 
simply labeling as Jezebels or mammies this type of 
Black women’s representation. Rather, hip-hop fem-
inism requires us to ask questions about both the 
oppressive structures which constrain Black women’s 
lives and the agency they exercise within and against 
those structures. It calls us to ask deeper questions 
about the ways that Black women’s representations 
might be both the objectifications that we are familiar 
with and also the subjectivities we have not afforded 
them. Examining the work of Nicki Minaj in the cur-
rent rap landscape demands that we ask: What stories 
do Black women tell about themselves?

Will You Find?

VALUES AND HATE: THE RISE OF  
ANTI-GAY INTERNET HATE SPEECH
Cynthia A. Cooper
Log into Godhatesfags.com, and you’ll see vivid 
photos, videos, and sermons celebrating the death 
of service members, the rise in cancers, the death 
and destruction by natural disasters, all in-service 
to a God who punishes a nation for its acceptance 
of members of the LGBTQ+ community. Wel-
come to the world of cyber-hate: internet sites run 
by hate groups seeking to spread their ideology to 
the masses and to recruit like-minded people. This 
reading discusses the main themes of anti-gay hate 
speech on the Internet.
Godhatesfags.com is among the most extreme 
examples of anti-gay speech on the web, but it’s 
not alone. Sites advocating hate against gays, Jews, 
Blacks, and immigrants have grown so fast that it’s 
hard to count them. A recent Southern Poverty Law 
Center (SPLC) report shows that the number of

in the past 20 years, with a 25% increase in the past 
five years alone (Hankes & Janik, 2021). Much of 
the increase is attributed to recent racial strife as 
well as anti-immigration and anti-
 g
overnment rhet-
oric. The growth of hate groups also coincides with 
an increase in reported hate crimes. A recent report 
on crimes motivated by a bias against persons 
based on race, religion, sexual orientation, and eth-
nicity/national origin found that 20% of hate crimes 
(most commonly aggravated assault, intimida-
tion, and property destruction or vandalism) were 
linked to sexual orientation and gender-identity bias 
(Federal Bureau of Investigations, 2019). Although 
no explicit connection can be made between the 
increase in Internet hate-group sites and bias crimes 
against the LGBT+ community, it’s clear that both 
are on the rise.
Most hate-group sites offer information about 
the organization’s ideology; some sell merchandise 
such as books, T-shirts, and even music, or solicit 
memberships and donations. Access to traditional 
media (even newsletters and brochures) is expen-
sive, so the Internet is a powerful and economical 
tool in the hatemonger’s arsenal of communication 
platforms. The anonymous access, video and audio 
capabilities, and relative lack of regulation make it 
the perfect medium.
Anti-LGBTQ+ rhetoric is nothing new. Inter -
net hate speech directed at the queer community 
is simply an outgrowth of hate against other groups. 
For example, the Christian Identity Movement and 
Aryan Nation traditionally promote the belief that 
Whites are the Bible’s chosen people; their primary 
enemies are Jews—often dubbed the “Agents of 
Satan.” As mainstream media and legislative initi-
atives have given more exposure to the queer com-
munity, many groups have expanded their focus to 
include hate against gay, lesbian, and transgender 
people. Each occurrence of Pose, Euphoria, Schitt’s 
Creek or legislation protecting trans youth is met 
with an equally prominent anti-queer voice. Fox-
man and Wolf (2013) found that under the guise of 
promoting so-called family values, many organiza-
tions such as the Family Research Council (FRC), 
Americans for Truth about Homosexuality, and the 
American Family Association depict the LGBTQ+ 
community as subhuman. Although most extremist 
hate organizations were once dismissed as insu-
lated fringe groups preaching to small, geograph-
ically bound congregations, the active curation of 
websites, social media sites, and email campaigns 
provides a centralized information center that 
unites hate groups across economic and geographic 
boundaries.
I became interested in this increase in Inter -
net hate speech and began a series of studies 
accounting for much of what I discuss here. Over 
a 25-year period, I’ve studied websites of hate 
groups for form and content. By coding the content 
of these sites (content analysis) and exploring the 
texts and messages on these sites (textual analysis), 
I gained greater understanding of the meanings 
behind the messages and the motivations of anti-
gay groups. Although there are differences, most 
anti-gay websites share some basic characteristics. 
First, the major theme is to speak out against the 
so-called queer lifestyle, although in recent times, 
many groups are criticizing LGBTQ+ equal rights 
as “Special Rights” and advocating for protection 
of traditional family values. Second, most anti-gay 
organizations identify as Christian and rely heavily 
on scripture to justify their hate. As a report by the 
SPLC noted:
…anti-gay sentiment is exploited by Christian 
white supremacists to organize the bigoted. 
Neo-Nazis, Skinheads, Christian Identity fol-
lowers, white robed cross burners and talk 
show circuit “racialists” may be divided over 
tactics, but they agree on who their enemies 
are. And gays, like Blacks and Jews, are cate-
gorically hated.
(Berrill, 1992, p. 31)
Berrill’s words still hold true today.
A warning: Many sites discussed here track vis-
itors and post the comments and email addresses of 
anyone who criticizes their organizations. Y ou should 
consider this before deciding whether you want to 
view any Internet sites of hate groups, and perhaps 
visit groups fighting against hate speech instead.


Music and Digital Media 233
T
he Anatomy and Communication of 
Hate
Explaining why people hate others is a difficult task. 
It is hard to find any person completely without preju-
dice or dislike of some person or group. But, hate and 
justification of violence or oppression against those 
different from us is a different level of behavior alto-
gether. Most research on hate has focused on describ-
ing its behavioral and psychological underpinnings. 
Biologists often describe hate as a biological mech-
anism of adaptation, a natural outgrowth of the fight 
or flight reflex. Psychologists study manifestations of 
hate as societally created attitudes, especially in the 
form of prejudice against certain groups that are seen 
as threats to one’s own identity. As Eisenstein (2000, 
p. 93) succinctly stated, hate is a learned trait; it “seeks 
safety and self-protection on one hand, destruction, 
and annihilation on the next.” This involves not 
merely disliking others but supporting (through words 
or actions) attempts to cause them harm. Such atti-
tudes often result from complex interaction among 
societal, political, and religious institutions.
Politically, hate defines communities exclusively 
by race, religion, ethnicity, or sexual orientation. This 
isolates people and continues the cycle of prejudice, 
discrimination, and even violence. Socially, people 
who aren’t members of the targeted group are often 
willing to turn a blind eye to hate and discrimination. 
Although they may not participate themselves, their 
unwillingness to speak out against hateful speech and 
action allows the hate to flourish.
Hate also often has a religious component. Many 
anti-gay groups root their hate in the Bible, which they 
believe justifies their actions against others. The use 
of Christian ideology and dogma can be a powerful 
ally when trying to convince others of the validity of 
a viewpoint. Hate speech denounces whole groups of 
people solely because of their race, ethnicity, religion, or 
sexual orientation. It can be delivered through a variety 
of communication channels, whether printed in bro-
chures or newsletters, recorded on audio or videotape, 
or delivered to large audiences at rallies, revivals, and 
meetings. Although hate crimes are illegal, hate speech 
is not; it is generally protected by the First Amendment.
To understand anti-gay hate speech on the Inter-
net is to consider the union of basic human instincts 
with advancing technologies, the clash of protected 
rights with concerns for social responsibility, and the 
evolving distinctions between traditional and chang-
ing meanings of community. There is little doubt 
that the development of the Internet has changed 
how people communicate and form communities. 
Some have envisioned the Internet as the ultimate 
public sphere where individuals define themselves 
by choosing which communities to join. The poten-
tial for individual empowerment is deemed a major 
benefit of Internet communities. Indeed, LGBTQ+ 
advocates have long argued against Internet filter -
ing systems that block community health and edu-
cation sites, because this deprives users of essential 
resources. Linking to PFLAG (Parents and Friends of 
Lesbians and Gays), The Trevor Project, or the Gen-
ders and Sexualities Alliance Network (GSA) may be 
the only source of information and belonging for an 
isolated youth struggling with their sexual identity.
But the Internet’s empowering force can’t be 
harnessed only for so-called positive purposes. If the 
Internet has the potential to bring together people to 
enlighten, educate, and form communities, it may also 
be used by groups who intend to defame, misinform, 
or even harm others. This equal opportunity commu-
nication medium can’t make a distinction between 
good and bad communities. In fact, the special quali-
ties of the Internet make it a perfect meeting hall for 
hate groups whose beliefs are not readily given voice 
in traditional media. Likewise, the anonymity provided 
by the Internet can fuel more aggressive behavior 
than may be expressed in traditional social situations, 
especially if people are not immediately criticized for 
their beliefs. The disinhibiting effects of the Internet 
can easily turn aggression into cyber-violence, caus-
ing users to feel empowered to express anger and 
hatred they’d censor in more public, and accountable, 
settings. Megan Phelps-Roper (2019), a former mem-
ber of the Westboro Baptist Church, recounted in her 
memoir how “virtual picketing,” posting photos, videos, 
and messages via the Internet without actually trave-
ling to the site or event they were protesting became 
one of the church’s most successful and economical 
tactics. “There is nothing inherently dishonest about 
this 
 t
actic—injustice in one city often inspires public 
demonstrations in another—except, of course, that our 
intent was to deceive” (p. 139).

234 Content
Anti-LGBTQ+ Speech on the Internet
As stated before, many anti-gay websites share sim-
ilar themes and tactics. Specifically, one feature of 
many anti-LGBTQ websites is the focus on the sex-
ual behaviors of gay men almost to the exclusion of 
all other aspects of gay life. Westboro Baptist Church 
once equated gays as “Filthy sodomites [who] crave 
legitimacy as dogs eating their own vomit & sows wal-
lowing in their own feces crave unconditional love.”
The American Family Association character -
izes gay men’s lifestyle with anonymous sex, perver-
sion, and “As with smoking, homosexual behavior’s 
 ‘s
econd-hand’ effects threaten public health. … Thus, 
individuals who choose to engage in homosexual 
behavior threaten not only their own lives, but the lives 
of the general population.” This misrepresentation of 
gay men easily becomes a basis for hatred as well as 
implicit and explicit calls to action against gays.
In recent years, many groups have expanded their 
focus to include commentary on political and social 
issues involving the queer community. For instance, 
after the Boy Scouts of America’s historic vote to allow 
gay members and leaders, the Liberty Counsel’s Mat 
Staver remarked that 
Now [the group will] allow homosexual young 
boys in the Scouts and allow homosexual lead-
ers in the Scouts, and what are you going to 
have? Y ou are going to have all kinds of sex-
ual molestation. This is a playground for pedo-
philes to go and have all these boys as objects 
of their lust.
Ignoring government statistics proving otherwise, 
gays are shown to prey on young boys to recruit 
and perpetuate the “species.” When hate groups do 
address the political issue of queer equal rights, it 
too is typically reduced to terms of sexuality and 
disease. For instance, former conservative talk-
show host Bob Enyart labeled any AIDS advocate 
as someone who “does everything in his power to 
spread AIDS” and encourages citizens to fight for 
the re-criminalization of homosexual behavior. His 
long list of gay mass murders includes no proof 
that any of the convicted murderers is gay. Simi-
larly, the conservative Christian organization Fam-
ily Research Council posts that a goal of the queer 
rights movement is to “abolish all age of consent 
laws and to eventually recognize pedophiles as the 
“prophets” of a new sexual order.”
Most disturbing is the mainstreaming of an out-
reach ministry named Watchmen of the Wall whose 
website declares that they are particularly “focused 
against homosexuality because those who practice 
this self-destructive vice…are the chief enemies of the 
natural family.” Watchmen began as an anti-LGBTQ 
global coalition by Scott Lively, the author of a book 
titled The Pink Swastika which claims that Hitler was 
gay and that fascist gays were the masterminds behind 
Nazism and the systematic murder of millions of Jews, 
gays, and gypsies during the Holocaust. Lively himself 
was once ordered in civil court to compensate a les-
bian for assault, and Watchmen members are linked 
to assaults at gay pride events and gay rights rallies 
throughout the Western US. Several members were 
charged in the death of Satender Singh, a 26-year-
old man who was picnicking with friends when self-
 
identified c
hurch members attacked him because they 
thought he was gay. Singh was not gay and later died 
from his injuries. Today, Watchmen on the Wall is affil-
iated with the FRC as its official ministry to Christian 
pastors, mobilizing them to spread its agenda to “Pray, 
Vote, Stand.” Included is FRC’s communication that 
“the transgender movement is a cult. And it’s affecting 
families, science, medicine, education—you name it. 
America is now blindly embracing the trans cult and 
silencing those who won’t get on board.”
Although the representation of the queer com-
munity on these sites is disturbing, the techniques 
employed are commonplace. Reducing individuals 
to a singular undesirable trait lays the groundwork 
for hate against them. It follows that anti-gay groups 
paint queer life as one-dimensional, revolving around 
an insatiable need for “bizarre” sex. Representing indi-
viduals as single-dimensional beings, especially as 
“deviant” or “predatory,” begins the process of dehu-
manizing them and targeting them for acceptable ver-
bal or physical violence.
Another shared characteristic of anti-gay web-
sites is the encouragement of some call to action or 
advocacy. Although anti-LGBTQ sites are steeped 
in Christian dogma, some also encourage proactiv-
ity in the “fight” to stop gays, lesbians, and transgen-
der citizens. The Westboro Church, through its site 


Music and Digital Media 235
Godha
tesfags.com, pickets against community, busi-
ness, and civic leaders who support equal rights for 
the queer community. Westboro Church began its 
pickets at funerals of AIDS patients, but expanded 
its anti-LGBTQ protests at funerals of fallen service 
members. The group shows up at funerals with signs 
reading “God Hates America,” and “Thank God for 
Dead Soldiers” to support its belief that God is punish-
ing America for its acceptance of the queer commu-
nity by killing active-duty soldiers. The church’s efforts 
have resulted in a federal law and several state laws 
banning protests within certain distances of cemeter-
ies. Still, the group protests nearly every day and fea-
tures hundreds of photos on its website to memorialize 
its efforts. Its’ most recent protests have expanded in 
scope again, including sporting events, concerts, and 
middle schools in district that have adopted measures 
to protect transgender and queer students.
Other groups advocate much less confrontational 
action. The American Family Association site once 
advocated protests over Ellen DeGeneres’ appear -
ance on Sesame Street, claiming that PBS was push-
ing a homosexual agenda on unsuspecting children. 
Concerned citizens were encouraged to complain to 
their congressional leaders. In bolder terms, the Chris-
tian Gallery encouraged citizen’s arrest of all gays and 
lesbians, the FRC endorsed a “war” against so-called 
destructive homosexuals, and Westboro’s Baptist 
Church protest signs advocate for the death penalty for 
members of the LGBTQ+ community and their allies.
Most anti-gay websites also share common 
characteristics of prejudice rooted in biblical teach-
ings, and the use of American patriotism to promote 
hatred toward LGBTQ citizens. The use of the Bible as 
authority is a staple, reinforcing the divine justification 
for hatred and bigotry against the queer community. 
Absent any scientific, legal, or statistical evidence to 
support their claims, these religious groups rely on 
their interpretation and enforcement of God’s word as 
their sole authority. After all, there’s no need to defend 
one’s position when it has been ordained by God. 
Almost as prevalent as the appeal to God as author-
ity is the theme that hate is an American value. Sites 
include American flags, songs, and strong patriotic 
images such as the bald eagle to convey that support 
of the queer community is un-American, and that it 
is a citizen’s responsibility to combat homosexuality. 
FRC campaign materials in support of the Defense 
of Marriage Act featured a crumbling wedding cake 
with a FRC logo of the US Capitol surrounded by an 
unfurled American flag and the words “Defending 
Family, Faith, and Freedom.” A Truth In Action Minis-
tries fundraising letter featured Joe Rosenthal’s famous 
photo Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima as a watermark 
behind the appeal “Pledge of Support for America’s 
longstanding ban on homosexuals in the military.” 
Finally, one cartoon features Uncle Sam in his typical 
finger-pointing stance proclaiming “I WANT YOU—
TO HATE FAGS.”
Combating Anti-Gay Speech on the 
Internet
When the polarizing and disinhibiting effects of 
cyber-communities lead to the spread of hate, ques-
tions often arise as to whether these expressions 
are protected speech under the First Amendment. 
Throughout our nation’s history, the concept of 
free speech has been valued and is typically chal-
lenged only when it conflicts with other universally 
acknowledged values such as national security and 
public safety. Supreme Court rulings historically have 
extended constitutional protection to all speech unless 
such speech encourages imminent incitement to vio-
lence or serves as fighting words—words which by their 
very utterance inflict injury or tend to incite violence.
What’s to be done to combat the hatred and vio-
lence advocated on anti-gay internet sites? Until such 
speech crosses the line into advocacy of imminent 
criminal behavior against LGBTQ citizens, it’s pro-
tected by the very same laws that prohibit censorship 
of websites providing useful resources to queer youth.
The answer is more speech, not less. Undesirable 
(even bad) ideas are best countered not by censorship 
but by better, more enlightened speech. Although it 
may not be comforting to those who find themselves 
targets of hateful rhetoric, it is best when hate speech 
is out in the open. Without their protected right to 
expose themselves and their rhetoric, the messages 
of anti-gay groups would flourish in an underworld of 
hate. Indeed, anti-gay groups are often their own worst 
enemies when their messages are exposed as unsub-
stantiated claims and falsehoods that don’t represent 
the world in a truthful manner.

MFM adapts true crime storytelling for female 
listeners by incorporating elements of women’s 
media, including interpersonal talk among female 
friends, confessional and therapeutic discourse,

comedy podcast and hosted by two self-described 
feminists, MFM also brings a sense of humor and
