or Documenting Hate (www.document-
inghate.com). 
What group(s) does this organization identify as 
spreading hate on the Internet? How do they 
define hate speech and determine that a group 
should be identified as a hate group? Do you 
agree/disagree with these definitions? How 
does the organization combat hate speech on 
the Internet? What approach or strategy does 
it take to counter those who spread hate? What 
can you do?


Music and Digital Media 237
mess
ages of female empowerment to the mix. By 
repositioning true crime entertainment as explic-
itly feminine and feminist, MFM has achieved cul-
tural notoriety and commercial success, with over 
35 million listener downloads per month and a #2 
ranking on Forbes magazine’s highest earning pod-
cast list.
MFM presents true crime from a female per -
spective that avoids objectifying women and strongly 
empathizes with female victims of murder and sex-
ual assault. However, it centers White middle-class 
women, both in how it narrates murder and violent 
crime and in its prescriptions for female empowerment 
and justice. Drawing from critical studies of feminism, 
race, and the prison industrial complex, I show how 
MFM uses popular White feminism to package true 
crime as a gendered cultural commodity and chan-
nels anxieties about gendered violence into carceral 
(pro- imprisonment) solutions. MFM embraces popu-
lar feminist rhetoric but obscures intersectional expe-
riences of crime and punishment, including racialized 
police violence and mass incarceration in the United 
States.
True crime is an enduring and evolving staple 
of popular media culture. Stories of real-life murder 
and mayhem originated with 19th-century broad-
sheets and took modern shape in hardboiled mid-
century pulp magazines (Murley, 2008). Packaged 
for mass consumption and sensational appeal, the 
narratives hid the sociopolitical dimensions of crim-
inality with rousing tales of dangerous individuals, 
objectified victims, and heroic law enforcement 
officials. In recent decades, true crime has become 
more pervasive and culturally mainstream, and it 
now circulates across an endless array of television 
networks and cable channels, streaming platforms, 
websites, and podcasts. In The Rise of True Crime: 
20th Century Murder and American Culture, cultural 
historian Murley characterized contemporary true 
crime as a “multi-faceted and multi-genre aesthetic 
formation” that constitutes a “worldview, an out-
look, and a perspective on contemporary life, one 
that is suspicious and cynical, narrowly focused on 
the worst kinds of crimes, and preoccupied with 
safety, order, and justice” (2008, p. 2).
True crime geared for women emerged in the 
1970s with the ascendancy of female authors such 
as Ann Rule, a former police officer who developed 
a “female-centered strand of true crime” that placed 
a greater emphasis on the everyday lives of victims 
(Murley, 2008, p. 72) and “envisioned her writing 
as a way of preparing women ... for how to deal 
with potentially dangerous situations” and MFM 
updates this tradition (Horeck, 2019, p. 2). Women 
are now the presumed audiences of true crime 
content across all media and platforms (Horeck, 
2019; Monroe, 2019). Since its launch in 2016, 
MFM has encouraged female listeners to embrace 
the MFM brand of storytelling about murder, rape, 
and assault as a source of pleasure, knowledge, 
and empowerment. The podcast is differentiated 
in the sea of true crime podcasting by its intimate 
tone, influencer hosts, and parallel attention to the 
historically female domains—domesticity, lifestyle, 
consumer culture, self-work—where popular White 
feminism thrives. In this sense, MFM is more than 
a true crime podcast: MFM is a cultural brand that 
presents templates for living to an intimate public of 
female listeners and cultivates an extended commu-
nity of so-called murderinos who attend MFM live 
shows, submit hometown murders, purchase MFM-
branded merchandise, follow the hosts on social 
media, read the MFM book, and participate in the 
official “fan cult.”
On each episode, the White female creators 
of MFM (comedy writer Karen Kilgariff and for -
mer Food Network presenter Georgia Hardstock) 
take turns narrating true crimes, with information 
culled from newspapers, TV programs, other pod-
casts, and Wikipedia. They unabashedly admit their 
lack of journalistic skills and present the podcast 
as a forum for women’s true crime fandom. MFM 
claims to “wrest the narrative” away from mascu-
linist true crime by avoiding graphic violence and 
the sexualization of women’s bodies, empathizing 
with female victims, celebrating survival stories, and 
enabling women’s safety and self-reliance. The hosts 
also feminize true crime storytelling by sharing their 
opinions and feelings, revealing details about their 
mental health and relationships, offering lifestyle 
advice, and pitching consumer goods and services 
to women (home security systems, beauty and 
fashion products, therapy apps, meal delivery sub-
scriptions, home furnishings) as paid sponsorships. 

238 Content
Although MFM does not release the demographics 
of its listenership, Kilgariff and Hardstock function 
as proxies for an imagined female audience that is 
signified as White and middle class. Murderinos are 
expected to share (and learn from) the experiences 
and feminist sensibilities of the hosts. Because fem-
inism is not monolithic but diverse, it is important 
to pinpoint which expressions of feminism inform 
MFM as a feminized cultural commodity.
In The Trouble with White Women, Kyla Schuller 
characterized White feminism as an approach to 
feminism that works “to liberate privileged women” 
while ignoring barriers faced by women of color 
and poor women and “keeping other structures of 
injustice intact” (2021, p. 4; see also Hamad, 2020; 
Zakaria, 2021). MFM takes for granted the universal 
benefits of objectives such as gender equality, repro-
ductive freedom, and harsher punishments for rapists 
that slide into White feminism when they “discount 
entirely the gross disparities of capitalism, the barri-
ers of pregnancy and healthy child-rearing that poor 
women face, and the violence perpetuated by cops, 
courts, and prisons” (Schuller, 2021, p. 4). But MFM 
is ultimately less interested in feminist activism than 
in mining the popularity of feminism for ideas, slo-
gans, and affective sensibilities that enhance the MFM 
brand. This perpetuates White feminism in a different 
way. As Banet-Weiser argued, expressions of femi-
nism now permeate media culture—feminism has 
become a selling point. However, some understand-
ings of feminism are more welcome than others. What 
Banet-Weiser calls popular feminism “exists along a 
continuum where media friendly expressions such as 
celebrity feminism and corporate feminism achieve 
more visibility, and expressions that critique patriar-
chal structures and systems of racism and violence 
are more obscure” (2018, p. 4). The most popular 
expressions of feminism are often superficial endorse-
ments of female empowerment that “claim to include 
all women,” but conceive of gender in universal terms 
that signify “white, middle class, cis-gendered, and 
heterosexual identity” (2018, p. 14). MFM presents 
violent crime within the narrow parameters of White 
feminism while also conflating female empowerment 
with popular feminist slogans, attitudes, and regimens 
that universalize gender as the domain of privileged 
White women.
The debut episode of MFM creates a blueprint for 
the podcast. Setting the tone for future episodes, the 
hosts share details about their personal lives (e.g., both 
struggle with anxiety) and compare notes on The Stair-
case, the true crime TV program they are watching 
(both are certain the husband is the murderer). They 
tell each other about their all-time favorite murders in 
a conversational format, pausing to comment on the 
cases and make tangential remarks. The tone is chatty 
and filled with both giggles and audible gasps as they 
discuss the slaying of child beauty pageant contestant 
JonBenet Ramsey and the Golden Gate rapist and 
serial killer of the 1970s. Much time is spent speculat-
ing about why women enjoy true crime. Kilgariff and 
Hardstock trace their mutual fascination with “mur-
der and stuff you’re not supposed to talk about” to 
apprehension about becoming a victim. True crime, 
they suggest, offers a release valve and preventative 
knowledge: “the more you know about something 
the less likely it is to happen to you.” This echoes a 
smattering of scholarship proposing that female audi-
ences use true crime stories to work through anxie-
ties about violent crime and glean survival strategies 
(Browder, 2006). This explanation is too simplistic, 
however, because media also play a constitutive role 
in perceptions of criminality and risk. By overestimat-
ing the prevalence of murder and other violent crime, 
media—particularly true crime entertainment—
 cr
eate 
and perpetuate concerns about personal danger. The 
framing of the question (“Why do women enjoy true 
crime?”) is problematic as well; it presumes the social 
positioning of White middle class women, who are the 
major consumers of true crime and are disproportion-
ately featured as true crime victims. MFM’s discus-
sion of this matter does not acknowledge BIPOC and 
poor women with experiences of violence and abuse 
(including at the hands of police) that receive far less 
attention in the media (Williamson, 2021).
Kilgariff and Hardstock acknowledge their belief 
that the vast majority of criminalized activity is “bor-
ing.” They prefer—and emphasize—cases that satisfy 
a desire for intrigue and speculation on the motives 
and abnormalities of criminal masterminds and “mon-
sters,” epitomized for them by the “diabolical, intelli-
gent and handsome” serial killer Ted Bundy. The hosts 
are not interested in “gang murders,” husbands who 
kill their wives for mundane reasons such as “they are 


Music and Digital Media 239
c
heating on them,” or “crimes of desperation” car -
ried out by people “raised in shitty neighborhoods.” 
This focus is undoubtedly shaped by their admittedly 
vast consumption of true crime entertainment, which 
has long obscured the societal contexts of criminality 
and reified “dangerous individuals” as outsiders and 
psychiatric puzzles (Foucault, 1978). It also mirrors 
reality-based entertainment in general, which mines 
actuality to construct and sell dramatic stories. MFM 
mines real life in the service of dramatic narrative 
expectations and spectatorial pleasures, as understood 
by White female middle-class true crime aficionados. 
This hierarchy of entertainment value underwrites the 
premise of picking a “favorite” murder and seeps into 
the podcast’s expectations for criminal justice, as sug-
gested by Kilgariff and Hardstock’s closing remarks on 
the JonBenet Ramsey and Golden Gate serial killer 
cases, which had not yet been solved at the time of 
the recording. Collapsing any meaningful bounda-
ries between crime and true crime storytelling, they 
demand a “better” policing system to punish those 
responsible for these horrific acts, and simultaneously 
complain that unsolved murder cases deny true crime 
audiences the satisfaction of a resolution (“We want 
the answer to the riddle”). The gendering of MFM and 
its expression of feminism takes place within these 
parameters.
In episode six, the MFM hosts signed off with 
a slogan that has become their catchphrase and is 
incorporated into MFM’s marketing, merchandise, 
and fan forums: “Stay Sexy and Don’t Get Murdered.” 
The phrase defined the podcast, branding MFM as 
female-centric and contemporaneous within the 
cultural landscape of popular feminism. With some 
cheekiness, the call to “Stay Sexy and Don’t Get Mur-
dered” established MFM as a podcast for women who 
embrace conventional femininity, reject patriarchy, 
and take responsibility for their safety. The rejoinder 
suggests that women can have it all but places the 
onus on them to avoid violence and victimhood—in 
part by listening to and learning from the MFM pod-
cast. This displaces societal responsibility onto indi-
viduals and ignores intersecting systems of oppression 
that devalue the choices and undermine the safety of 
BIPOC, poor, gender fluid, and queer women. In 2019, 
Kilgariff and Hardstock published Stay Sexy and Don’t 
Get Murdered: A Definitive How-To Guide, a bestseller 
that recapitulated the popular feminist logic at the core 
of the MFM brand. The book provides a glossary of 
other catchphrases, mantras, and slogans popular -
ized on the podcast. Topping the list is “Fuck Polite-
ness,” which gives women permission to reject gender 
oppression without reference to structural changes or 
intersectional critique. “Fuck the way we’re socialized. 
Fuck the expectation that we put other people’s needs 
first. And while we’re at it, fuck the patriarchy!” , the 
authors wrote (p. 29). However affirmative this mantra 
may feel, it conflates power with attitude and assumes 
a universal understanding of woman, obscuring the 
intersection of gender, race, class, and other forms of 
oppression. Offered as a remedy to becoming a vic-
tim, “Fuck Politeness” calls on women differently posi-
tioned by structures of patriarchy, White supremacy, 
and capitalism to take responsibility for sense of dan-
ger MFM packages and sells. The barest form of this 
can be found on the “merch corner” of the MFM web-
site, where listeners can signify their empowerment by 
purchasing the slogan on a t-shirt or mug.
Stay Sexy and Don’t Get Murdered elaborates on 
the self-work promoted by MFM. Across the podcast 
episodes and in the book, the hosts reflect on their 
ongoing struggles with addiction, mental health, and 
body image. They also discuss their home décor, 
media consumption, fashion and style, careers, and 
personal relationships. MFM’s view of true crime is 
articulated in tandem with this inward focus and the 
therapeutic and self-fashioning frameworks upon 
which it depends. The point here is that popular White 
feminism flourishes when empowerment is conceived 
as the outcome of self-work, lifestyle choice, and con-
sumer culture rather than political action. This is espe-
cially the case when power dynamics and unequal 
resources among women are unacknowledged. “Y ou 
are responsible for your own quality of life,” Kilgariff  
and Hardstock tell their readers (2019, p. 69). Women 
signified as White and middle class are encouraged to 
get started immediately, ideally “with a licensed ther-
apist” (perhaps through a company advertised on the 
podcast). Women are also advised to prioritize self-
care, defined as the procurement of scented candles, 
pedicures, and “well-made shoes, purses, and jeans.” 
The authority of the hosts to dispense such advice is 
bolstered by the visibility of MFM in the media (the 
podcast was even spoofed on The Simpsons) and 

240 Content
Kilgariff and Hardstock’s influence on social media 
where they extend their celebrity and embody the pre-
scriptions for femininity and feminism circulated in the 
book and on the podcast.
MFM mediates crime for female consumers in 
particular ways, with tangible consequences. Although 
“innocent” female victims (characterized by the MFM 
slogan “sweet baby angels”) preyed upon by lone mon-
sters are treated with concern, innocence is imbued 
with whiteness and middle-class status. By churning 
out one-off crimes against innocent sweet baby angels 
each week, MFM can endorse a tough on crime stance 
without appearing racist or classist. However, “In the 
rush to punish bad apples, real and imagined, we tend 
to forget that the criminal justice system is culturally 
ordered, technocratic, and beholden to specific politi-
cal forces” (Gruber, 2020, p. 9). Abolition feminists have 
shown how liberal White feminist collusion with law-
and-order harms women of color, poor women, and 
particularly Black women, the fastest growing group of 
incarcerated people in the United States—the coun-
try with the highest rate of incarceration in the world 
(Alexander, 2010/2020; Davis, et al., 2022; Schuller, 
2021). Although MFM adopts a progressive tone, its 
approach to crime draws inspiration from carceral 
feminism, defined by Angela Davis, Gina Dent, Erica 
Meiners, and Beth Richie in Abolition. Feminism. Now. 
as an “overreliance on carceral approaches” (p. 107) to 
solve address the problem of gendered violence. As a 
strand of White feminism, carceral feminism assumes 
that “gender oppression is a common experience 
... and that the state should intervene by increasing 
policing, making legislative changes, creating new laws 
and arrest policies, prosecuting more people, expend-
ing imprisonment, and implementing other carceral 
strategies” (p. 107). For abolition feminists, who are 
committed to ending violence against women through 
alternative means, carceral reforms do not produce 
safety or justice as much as the “greater criminalization 
of marginalized groups” (p. 107).
MFM takes for granted that bigger and better 
policing, more punitive prison sentences, and the 
death penalty are warranted to manage the violent 
crimes, often against White women; it narrates these 
assumptions for entertainment purposes. In episode 
18, deemed a “listener favorite,” MFM conveys the 
1978 rape and attempted murder of Mary Vincent by 
Lawrence Singleton, who cut off her arms, threw her 
over a cliff and left her for dead. The hosts celebrate 
Vincent’s determined survival and lament that Single-
ton, who was convicted but eventually released from 
prison, murdered another woman and was reincarcer-
ated, where he “unfortunately died of cancer before 
he could be fried.” In the context of this horrific story, 
MFM’s advocacy of punishments such as execution by 
electrification may seem reasonable and warranted to 
some. However, the podcast does not consider here or 
elsewhere how “investment in the criminal justice sys-
tem” also leads to harm for marginalized groups (Davis 
et al., 2022, pp. 107–108).
Following the murder of George Floyd by White 
police officers and the racial unrest that ensued, MFM 
declared its commitment to Black Lives Matter and 
expanded its coverage of Black women and people 
of color. The podcast presented some stories about 
Black and indigenous victims of murder and violence 
and highlighted the work of Black female civil rights 
activists. However, adding a few women of color to 
the MFM formula has not fundamentally changed its 
popular White feminist priorities. As Schuller pointed 
out, “embracing inclusion as a brand, believing that if a 
Black woman like Sojourner Truth and other women 
of color are stirred into the mix … doesn’t eradicate 
white feminism—it merely extends its reach” (2021, 
p. 251). MFM is out of sync with efforts to stop racial-
ized police violence, reform police departments, and 
end mass incarceration. Until MFM focuses its lens 
on broader sociopolitical contexts and the work of 
abolition feminists, it will remain an instrument of 
White feminism and its popular cultural forms.

6.7: “THE ISSUES THAT ARE TAKING 
PLACE IN THE WORLD AFFECT US”: 
HOW THE MINNESOTA LYNX CRACKED 
THE CODE FOR PUTTING SOCIAL 
JUSTICE INTO SOCIAL MEDIA
Andrew C. Billings and Joshua R. Jackson
The authors investigate how the Minnesota Lynx 
WNBA team uses social media to address and 
advance issues of social justice. In the process, the 
Lynx and the WNBA demonstrated deeper engage-
ment with such issues than either the NBA or the 
NCAA.
Traditional media sources have consistently disap-
pointed fans, players, and coaches of women’s bas-
ketball. Decades ago, this meant televising only a 
handful of games or having print coverage relegated 
to a box score. The internet era brought slightly bet-
ter coverage. More games were televised, but they 
were on channels with relatively low brand recogni-
tion. More scores were shared, but usually only via 
scrolling tickers at the bottom of the screen while 
showing men’s sports.
Given the lack of attention by mainstream media, 
women’s basketball needed its own form of direct-to-
consumer communication, which it finally found in the 
rise of social media. Social media meant that women’s 
basketball didn’t need ESPN or any other gatekeeper 
to advance its brand and create its community. Wom-
en’s basketball fans could follow their favorite athletes, 
teams, and players without the filter of mainstream 
media. Leagues and players loved social media as well, 
believing that the platforms represented a “powerful 
tool for increasing fan-athlete interaction” (Pegoraro, 
2010, p. 501).
Athletes were finding their voices and increas-
ingly using them to advance social issues occurring 
well beyond the basketball court. When Phoenix 
Mercury forward Mistie Bass took a knee during the 
national anthem in 2016, her subsequent explanation 
implied that speaking out about social justice issues 
was a part of the league’s DNA. “We are a walking pro-
test at all times,” she said (Abrams & Weiner, 2020).

242 Content
The question became a pragmatic one: How could 
women’s basketball harness social media to advance 
the causes they cared about?
We analyze how the Women’s National Basketball 
Association (WNBA)—led by the Minnesota Lynx—
found ways to advance social justice causes on social 
media. We show that the Lynx incorporated local 
rhetoric about a galvanizing event in the team’s home 
state (George Floyd’s murder by a Minneapolis police 
officer) to secure international attention. We discuss 
how they did so before examining three ripple effects 
of their actions, showing how the Lynx’ efforts led to 
a league-wide expansion of racial justice initiatives, a 
league-wide campaign to #StopAsianHate, and a viral 
movement for improving gender equity issues within 
the NCAA (National Collegiate Athletic Association).
(Re)Setting the Tone: The Minnesota 
Lynx and Social Media-Based Athlete 
Activism
In May, 2020, the killing of George Floyd, a Black 
male, by a White male police officer in Minneapolis 
was the latest in a series of dark moments involving 
police brutality in America and resulted in protests 
both physically and digitally. With this incident hap-
pening in the home city of the WNBA ’s most vocal 
teams, the Minnesota Lynx would find themselves a 
critical part of the online conversation.
It wasn’t out of character for the Lynx to be 
involved in conversations around social justice 
and equality. Following multiple instances of Black 
deaths in police custody in 2016, WNBA players 
used their platforms to speak out. The Minnesota 
Lynx posted a news conference on its Facebook 
page hours before a game against the Dallas Wings. 
In that video, star players Maya Moore and Rebek-
kah Brunson said that the team hoped to promote 
change by wearing warm-up shirts calling for more 
accountability in police brutality cases. The shirts 
said “Black Lives Matter”; in addition, by including 
the names of Philando Castile and Alton Sterling, the 
shirts supported the efforts of the #SayHerName 
and allied movements working to bring visibility to 
and foster compassion for the victims in such cases.
In 2020, the Lynx, one of the most popular 
WNBA teams on social media platforms, helped 
lead the league in social activism during the peak of 
movements such as #BlackLivesMatter and #Say-
HerName. As more reports of police brutality made 
national headlines, other WNBA teams followed suit. 
Those digital stances of solidarity took physical form 
as players took a knee during the national anthem or 
even refused to play entire games. It took the NBA (the 
men’s league) months before players or teams joined 
in the protests; the WNBA remained the more activist 
of the two leagues. While engaging in their activism, 
Lynx players have emphasized that being an athlete 
does not function as their primary identity. Lynx center 
Kayla Alexander explained:
The issues that are taking place in the world 
affect us. Whether we’re athletes or not, at the 
end of the day we’re all human. And when I’m 
going out into the world, people don’t see ‘Kayla, 
the athlete,’ they just see ‘Kayla, a Black woman,’ 
(Dichter, 2020)
The organization used its platform and position to be 
proactive on social justice issues by partnering with 
the Minnesota Timberwolves NBA team on an online 
video series entitled Voices. In it, they addressed top-
ics such as racial injustice, voting rights, and gender 
equality. According to the Lynx’s press release, the 
series was an extension of the teams’ commitment 
to lead conversations about these issues. The Lynx’s 
website presented the ambitions of the joint project:
The goal of “Voices” is to bring awareness to 
these difficult topics that are impacting com-
munities across the world and focus on how we 
can all make positive changes by being present 
and making space for these discussions to be 
had in a productive and educational way.
(“Minnesota Timberwolves and Lynx,” 2020)
WNBA Hall of Famer and former Lynx star Maya 
Moore took an even further step in social justice 
efforts. The former league MVP left the game in 
2019 to work full time on criminal justice reform. 
She used her social media followings to raise visibil-
ity for an egregious case of the wrongful conviction 
of Jonathan Irons in 1997. Persistent and increased 
posting from Moore resulted in the overturning of 


Music and Digital Media 243
Ir
ons’ conviction in 2020. Moore’s decision served 
as another example of female athletes not only 
addressing present issues, but other race-based 
concerns that remain endemic in American society.
Ripple Effects: The Lynx Show the Way
Whether online or offline, the effectiveness of most 
protest movements can be judged—at least in 
part—by the ripple effects linked to the Lynx move-
ment. In this regard, three will be highlighted here: 
league-wide adoption of racial justice, expansion of 
racial justice to fight Asian hate, and broadening of 
justice initiatives to include gender inequity at the 
collegiate basketball level.
Ripple #1: The WNBA Embraces Racial 
Equality
Building upon the efforts of the Minnesota Lynx 
regarding social activism, the WNBA and the Wom-
en’s National Basketball Players’ Association ded-
icated the entire 2020 season to social justice. The 
league proclaimed the season “The Justice Move-
ment” and formed a Social Justice Council com-
prised of players and advisors whose goal was to 
continue critical conversations about race, gender 
and advocating for other minoritized groups. Presi-
dent of the WNBA players’ union Nneka Ogwumike 
hoped that women’s basketball would always be “at 
the forefront of initiatives” relating to equality and 
social justice (Feinberg, 2021). She further explained:
With 140-plus voices all together for the first 
time ever, we can be a powerful force con-
necting to our sisters across the country and in 
other parts of the world. And may we all rec-
ognize that the league’s stated commitment to 
us – in this season and beyond – offers a pivotal 
moment in sports history.
(“WNBA announces,” 2020)
During the year, teams promoted awareness online 
through hashtags such #BLM, #BlackLivesMat-
ter, and #SayHerName. Many would debate the 
effectiveness of such hashtags, yet the WNBA has 
noted that letting these issues pass without formal 
change is part of the overarching problem (Cooky & 
Antunovic, 2020). The teams and players continue 
to use social media and digital platforms to engage 
with fans and trolls alike in hopes of altering the sta-
tus quo surrounding such issues.
During the 2020 season, which was shortened 
due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the WNBA contin-
ued to use social media to direct people to stories the 
league, teams, and players cared about. For instance, 
the WNBA account tweeted on August 14, 2020: “On 
this day in 2014, Phoenix Police took the life of Michelle 
Cusseaux during a mental health call. #SayHerName 
lifts Michelle’s story and her family’s call for non-lethal 
responses in mental health encounters.” The Lynx’s 
effort to contribute to conversations involving social 
issues spread to other WNBA teams and created an 
obligation for the league itself to be a voice for change 
and awareness. The decision of one team to speak out 
became amplified by the organization, establishing a 
path for these women to be a continuous leading voice 
in these critical matters.
Ripple #2: The WNBA Expands Definitions of 
Racial Equality Via #StopAsianHate
Months before the WNBA ’s 2021 season began, the 
league and its players were once again at the fore-
front, taking a stand against discrimination and racial 
injustice. In the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic, 
racism against Asians and Asian Americans rose, due 
at least in part to media reports debating the virus’ 
origin (Levin, 2021). To wit, the number of reported 
hate crimes in America’s 16 largest cities increased 
164% between 2020 and 2021 (Levin, 2021). As vio-
lence rose, the WNBA ’s New Y ork Liberty turned 
to social media to call for action after a wave of 
attacks on Asian Americans in the New Y ork metro 
area. Partnering with non-profit Stop AAPI Hate, the 
Liberty utilized #StopAsianHate online to promote 
awareness of the issue. That statement said in part: 
 …the New Y ork Liberty organization stands 
vehemently against racism, xenophobia, hatred 
and violence against the Asian American and 
Pacific Islander community. We will not ignore 
this issue and will continue to use our platform 
in the fight for justice and equality for all people. 
(“NY Liberty’s #StopAsianHate,” 2021)

244 Content
The team went on to release multiple statements 
during the peak of the attacks, even offering support 
for some victims and bolstering fan engagement.
Like the Minnesota Lynx, individuals within the 
Liberty organization also addressed social issues 
affecting them personally. Joe Tsai and Clara Wu Tsai, 
owners of the New Y ork Liberty and the NBA ’s Brook-
lyn Nets, were highly critical of people who framed 
COVID-19 as the “kung flu” or “Chinese virus,” believ-
ing that escalated resentment toward Asian people. 
Liberty center Han Xu spoke out to encourage soli-
darity during a time of uncertainty. Xu, who also plays 
for the Chinese national team, noted that the efforts 
of the Lynx and support of her team’s owners made 
her more comfortable with speaking out in favor of 
#StopAsianHate.
According to The Institute for Diversity and Eth-
ics in Sport, the WNBA reported just two players who 
identify as Asian in 2021 (Lapchick, 2021). However, 
the league acknowledged the importance of stand-
ing up for the lives of Asian people as much as any 
other marginalized group, supporting the mission of 
#StopAsianHate through posts on social media as it 
had done earlier with #BlackLivesMatter. The Seattle 
Storm released a statement on Twitter condemning 
the violence toward Asian communities. Washington 
Mystics guard Natasha Cloud also tweeted in soli-
darity: “To the Asian community, I am so sorry. I see 
you, I hear you, I grieve with you, and I will fight for 
you. #StopAsianHate.” As was the case with #BLM, 
athletes from other sports would later follow with their 
own messages of support, but the early efforts of the 
New Y ork Liberty expanded the WNBA ’s branding as 
a racially inclusive community.
In March of 2021, the need to advance this mes-
sage became even more urgent, as a mass shooting 
occurred at three Asian spas in Atlanta. Of the eight 
people killed, six were Asian women. The shooter 
was not charged with a hate crime, but many char -
acterized the shooting as such, noting the rising anti-
Asian sentiment in America. The league partnered 
with Asian designer Jasper Wong, to create a hoodie 
athletes could wear and post on social media, urging 
fans to donate online with proceeds directed toward 
organizations working to prevent anti-Asian discrimi-
nation. Players such as Brianna Turner of the Phoenix  
Mercury posted images wearing #StopAsianHate 
apparel. As we write this in 2022, tweets continue to 
surface with the hashtag, reflecting initial statements 
from the New Y ork Liberty, its owners, and Han Xu. 
In doing so, the WNBA—and its stakeholders—
embraced being a voice for equality even outside of 
basketball. With social media as a primary platform, 
they continue to draw awareness to social issues that 
emphasize the mistreatment of marginalized groups.
Ripple #3: Equality Expands to the NCAA—
and to Gender Issues
Women’s collegiate sports are still more often dimin-
ished due to gender biases than are men’s sports. 
Having a smaller fan base has been used to advance 
many inequalities. For instance, men play in college 
basketball’s March Madness, whereas the women’s 
tournament is often referenced as Women’s March 
Madness. Even then, that label is controversial and, 
according to the NCAA, not to be used for women’s 
tournament games because of broadcast partner 
branding concerns. On the courts, the men’s logo 
says “March Madness” and the women’s logo says 
“NCAA Women’s Basketball.” Belittling language 
can sometimes yield belittling actions and policies 
as well. Never has there been a greater opportunity 
to visually highlight such egregious differences than 
on modern social media platforms.
During the March 2021 NCAA women’s tour -
nament, players and coaches used social media to 
highlight inequities. The most prominent of those 
involved a viral TikTok post from Oregon Ducks 
forward Sedona Prince. With over 18 million views 
by the end of the summer, Princes video’ highlighted 
the differences in weight rooms: a small single pyr -
amid of 10 free weights constituted the women’s 
weight room as opposed to a full array of options 
for the men. She also included the NCAA ’s response 
that it was a “space” issue, which she countered by 
panning around the single set of weights to reveal 
thousands of empty square feet surrounding it, con-
cluding that “if you aren’t upset about this problem, 
then you’re a part of it” (Marnin, 2021).
Social media responses of support for Prince’s 
position came from other athletes, both women 
(WNBA ’s A ’ja Wilson called it “beyond disrespectful”) 
and men (NBA star Steph Curry posted: “wow-come 


Music and Digital Media 245
on 
now! @marchmadness @NCAA yall trippin 
trippin”).
Other players joined in using social media to 
highlight other inequities. Players compared swag 
bags of gifts to one another in Instagram, concluding 
the women’s offerings were woeful when compared to 
the men’s. Prominent coaches weighed in as well. Leg-
endary Notre Dame coach Muffet McGraw offered an 
extended social media statement, which included:
the fact that there are inequities in facilities, 
food, fan attendance, and swag bags is not what 
bothers me. What bothers me is that no one 
on the NCAA ’s leadership team even noticed…
time’s up gentlemen. This generation of women 
expects more and we won’t stop until we get it. 
Red Smith Award columnist Christine Brennan 
offered strong a strong rebuke:
Y ou might say this is a little thing, just an over-
sight. It’s not. Not in 2021. It’s active, continu-
ing, omnipresent sexism … If everyone does 
nothing now, the NCAA might as well go ahead 
and slap a trademark on Spring Sexism.
(2021)
Ultimately, the NCAA promised to remedy the 
weight room situation, with NCAA Vice President 
for Women’s Basketball Lynn Holzman enacting 
remedies for the pair of 2022 March Madness tour-
naments (Clarke, 2022).
Synergy in Media for Justice
We bring these examples together is to highlight 
their interconnectivity—showing that women’s bas-
ketball, on a professional and collegiate level, used 
social media as a platform to address and advance 
conversations of social justice. The Minnesota Lynx 
served as the catalyst, using #BlackLivesMatter to 
bring national attention to a local issue in the mur -
der of George Floyd and the protests that followed. 
Once the Minnesota Lynx utilized social media to 
advance racial justice issues—and did not lose fol-
lowers or ratings in the aftermath—they became 
bolder in their objectives and the scope of what 
could be accomplished. After showing what could 
be accomplished when creating a platform them-
selves, the New Y ork Liberty used similar meth-
ods to address the violence targeted at Asians and 
Asian-Americans through #StopAsianHate. This 
ripple supported the notion that these athletes, and 
their efforts, were not isolated to bringing aware-
ness to only one issue, as well as displaying the 
strength that came with athletes of all backgrounds 
coming together online. Women’s college basket-
ball players would take note of both ripples, creat-
ing their own when facing gender discrimination by 
the NCAA during the most important time of their 
season. Digital spaces such as Instagram and Twit-
ter drew the attention needed to ensure male and 
female basketball players were treated more equally 
in terms of what resources were provided during  
March Madness. A rising tide arguably lifted all boats. 
Women’s basketball players at both the professional 
and collegiate level felt they were enacting positive 
change in society, while also raising the profile of the 
sport they loved. The end result was an empowered 
women’s basketball community, one that could feel 
and see change that it believed it had a hand in caus-
ing through harnessing their social media influence.
Social media has enough ills to fill many books, 
Y ouTube videos, and casual and formal discussions. 
However, we demonstrate that a highlights the pos-
itive impact can be forged when athletes produce 
media messages designed to draw attention to social 
justice concerns. The support of the WNBA—and, 
by extension, the NBA—could be characterized as a 
fairly sharp contrast with the less overt support from 
the NCAA, both professional and collegiate players 
made both overt and tacit inroads, highlighting those 
aims and achieved objectives 280 characters or one 
TikTok at a time.

6.8: MARU ON INSTAGRAM: CUTE 
STUDIES AND THE INTERSECTIONAL 
VECTORS OF DIFFERENCE
Gust A. Yep and Ryan M. Lescure
Using Cute Studies, the authors examine how such 
posts characterize vectors of difference, such as 
race/ethnicity, gender, and sexuality, and explore 
their implications for consuming these images.
With a perpetual smile, perfectly round face, 
golden coat, naturally curly tail, and fluffy pos-
terior, Marutaro, commonly known as Maru, is a 
Shiba Inu from Japan and an Instagram celebrity 
with 2.5 million followers.
1 Once a forgotten puppy 
increasingly visual, were these nonverbal 
approaches particularly timely, savvy, or 
effective?

atch Sedona Prince’s video highlighting

Music and Digital Media 247
a
t a pet store because of his round body—he is a 
big Shiba—Maru became popular when his owner 
Shinjiro Ono started posting photos of him on Ins-
tagram during a devastating 2011 earthquake in 
Japan to ease “people’s anxiety, even a little bit” 
(Tang, 2019). With the belief that photography can 
transcend barriers of race, gender, religion, phi-
losophy and politics, Ono continued posting three 
pictures of his beloved dog every day. Maru, the 
cute dog, became “an international language”—an 
ambassador of Japanese culture and a source of 
comfort, encouragement, and inspiration to people 
around the world (Swan, 2020; Tang, 2019). He has 
Y ouTube videos, memes, meetups, merchandise, 
and a store in Tokyo.
Our reading examines Maru’s Instagram posts 
through the lens of Cute Studies, a framework for 
examining cuteness in popular culture with a focus on 
vectors of difference. We analyze race/ethnicity, gen-
der, and sexuality, using an intersectional lens.
Contextualizing Cute Studies
Cute Studies is an emerging interdisciplinary field 
focusing on cuteness as a physical and affective 
response, a global popular cultural phenomenon, 
and an aesthetic category in legacy and new 
media (Dale, 2016). This theoretical approach 
examines the social construction of cuteness, 
including how cuteness relates to power. For 
example, the word “cute” has trivializing implica-
tions; cute things tend to be constructed as low 
status and insignificant (Dale, 2017). Even when 
viewers might have a positive emotional response 
to a cute picture of Maru, this response is a pater -
nalistic one that encourages viewers to perceive 
Maru as a helpless object that needs care and 
protection. This power dynamic is complicated, 
however, as “the intense appeal of cuteness can 
produce a sense that the subject [the person doing 
the viewing] is under the cute object’s control” 
(Arkenberg, 2017, p. 61).
Cute Studies contests constructions of cute-
ness as apolitical and detached from identity 
and its symbolic and material consequences 
(Schlesselman-Tarango, 2017). In fact, audiences 
sometimes assign more humanity to, feel greater 
sympathy for, and show more generosity to people 
with marginalized identities when those people are 
thought to have cute pets (Dale et al., 2017). Media 
featuring cute animals can be a form of escapism 
and relief for viewers, numbing them to the racism, 
brutality, inhumanity, and violence woven into the 
fabric of contemporary US culture (Dale et al., 2017; 
Page, 2017). Emotional responses such as anger are 
rational reactions to injustice and can often inspire 
activism. Cute images and videos can dull these 
emotional responses, making it easier for people to 
accept a climate of injustice (Page, 2017).
Analysis of Maru’s Instagram Posts
Providing his fans with a “daily dose of cuteness” 
(Page, 2017, p. 84), Maru’s posts showcase every-
day activities, including waking up, eating, explor -
ing nature and the city, playing, napping, and 
getting ready to sleep. Such images, according to 
 Sc
hlesselman-Tarango, suggest that “cuteness regis-
ters and is registered by race, gender, and sexuality” 
(2017, p. 13). Further, an intersectional approach 
maintains that these vectors of difference occur 
simultaneously (Y ep & Chivers, 2017). More specifi-
cally, the perception of a dog’s cuteness depends on 
how various forms of difference, such as size, breed, 
age, gender, and so on, are considered at the same 
time in the process of sensemaking. For example, 
a growl by a small long-haired female Chihuahua 
puppy and a large adult male Pitbull mix might be 
viewed differently—perhaps “cute” and “aggres-
sive,” respectively. Keeping intersectionality in 
mind, we discuss three vectors of difference—race/
ethnicity, gender, and sexuality—in Maru’s postings.
Maru and Race/Ethnicity
Although Maru’s Instagram account mainly features 
Maru by himself, multiple posts depict Maru with 
dogs of various sizes and breeds, stuffed animals, 
and other animals such as pigeons, cats, alpacas, 
and sheep. Although none of these posts say any-
thing literal about race, ethnicity, or racism, they 
encourage audiences to perceive Maru as coexist-
ing harmoniously with animals and things that are 
different from him and that humans should emu-
late this. Advocating for connectedness across dif-
ference without fully exploring the unequal power 

248 Content
dynamics of these connections symbolically resem-
bles colorblind approaches to race and ethnicity. 
Colorblind approaches are problematic because 
they advance the idealized notion that race and 
ethnicity should have nothing to do with how a per-
son is treated or perceived while simultaneously 
denying or ignoring that these identity categories 
significantly influence how people are treated and 
perceived (Burke, 2017).
We argue that some of Maru’s posts advance this 
idealized notion without exploring its power dynam-
ics. In other words, they advance a utopian notion of 
communication across difference that suggest “we 
should all just get along” without exploring how that 
goal might realistically and meaningfully be attained. 
Two of Maru’s posts depict him as a benevolent leader 
to a flock of pigeons who seem unbothered by—or 
perhaps disinterested in—Maru’s presence. Both vid-
eos depict Maru above the pigeons. The December 
15, 2020 post features the caption “everyone gather 
together. I have a story to tell.” The December 19, 2020 
post says, “Good morning, pigeon team. Today is the 
day of the interim report.” Both videos construct Maru 
as existing harmoniously with these pigeons, but the 
captions suggest that he is in a leadership role.
Additional posts construct Maru as friendly with 
animals that are bigger than him as well as with stuffed 
toys. A video from September 6, 2019 shows Maru 
walking alongside a sheep with the caption “walking 
with fluffy.” An image from October 23, 2019 depicts 
Maru next to a larger dog with the caption “you’re so 
tall. I’ve been greeting the big dog.” Some of Maru’s 
posts feature Maru with a congregation of stuffed ani-
mals that conjure up notions of familial togetherness. 
An image from July 4, 2020 depicts Maru with two 
stuffed toys with the caption “happy families. Please be 
safe, everyone who has a hard time due to heavy rain.”
Finally, some posts feature Maru meeting animals 
that seem defensive, unsure, or wary. Despite this, the 
captions construct Maru as friendly with the other 
animals. For example, a video on December 20, 2020 
shows Maru meeting another dog who seems unsure 
of him and slightly defensive with the caption “fine. I’m 
not scared.” A video from September 11, 2020 depicts 
Maru approaching another dog who is slowly backing 
away. The caption says, “Don’t be shy #come a little 
closer.” A post from March 19, 2019 depicts Maru 
approaching a cat hiding behind a tree in a park. The 
caption states, “Come over here. Let’s play with cats.” 
These captions seem to mask the possibility that these 
other animals are fearful of Maru. To connect symbol-
ically to race and ethnicity, this masking resembles the 
construction of whiteness as benign and nonthreat-
ening rather than as a source of terror (hooks, 1997). 
Additionally, denying potential perceptions of Maru 
as a source of fear is a strategic element of construct-
ing his cuteness. Noting that Maru’s presence might 
provoke fear or defensiveness would contradict con-
structions of his cuteness. It is not cute to understand 
something as scary, bad, or complicated. Describing a 
cute thing in these terms is also unlikely to be popular. 
This resembles the phenomenon where people are 
written off as “killjoys” because they have identified 
racist and sexist practices in everyday life that others 
would have preferred to ignore (Ahmed, 2010).
Maru and Gender
Like humans and robots, animals are gendered. A 
cute male dog, for example, might be viewed through 
traits attributed to boys and men. Several postings 
on Mother’s Day provide glimpses of how Maru is 
gendered. A post on May 9, 2015 shows a smiley 
Maru with squinty eyes, a basket of pink carnations 
and a card. The caption reads “Happy Mother’s Day!! 
I’ve grown up to be such an attractive big Shiba-boy, 
thank you, mother!” Several features associated 
with Maru’s gendering appear in the post. First, as a 
self-defined “Shiba-boy,” Maru takes on the qualities 
of a young human. As an adult dog—he was over 
seven years old at that time—he seems to main-
tain the qualities of a boy, not an adult. This boyish 
gendering through the simultaneous juxtaposition 
of the visual image and the written caption makes 
him particularly cute and endearing: He brings pink 
flowers to his mother on her special day; he thanks 
his mother for his chubby good looks; he is grateful 
that he exists because of her; he wishes her a happy 
day. Other Mother’s Day posts echo similar aesthet-
ics and sentiments. For example, a May 9, 2020 post 
shows a smiley Maru with his paws folded under his 
fluffy and chubby body, a bouquet of red, white and 
pink flowers, and a card. The caption says, “Happy 
Mother’s Day! Thank you for always being there for 


Music and Digital Media 249
me! Mom!” In r
eality, Maru’s mother has never been 
in his life—they were separated when he was a young 
puppy taken to a pet store to be sold in 2007 (Swan, 
2020). However, in the representations, Maru main-
tains the qualities of a grateful, dutiful, and innocent 
young son, or a dog with male childlike qualities, that 
make him cute (Cross, 2004).
Maru’s male childlike attributes are a form of boy-
ish gender performance, that is, the ongoing enactment 
and repetition of acts that congeal his gendered cute-
ness (Butler, 1990). These acts include Maru’s affinity 
for stuffed animals—hedgehogs, bears, rabbits, among 
others—and popular plush toys, such as Pokemon 
Pikachu and Kumamon Bear. As a “Shiba boy,” he is 
frequently shown posing with them (e.g., December 
23, 25, 26, and 27, 2019), sleeping with them (e.g., 
November 21, 22, and 27, 2021; December 3, 2021), or 
holding them on his head (e.g., August 19 and 26, 2020; 
November 6, 2020; February 25, 2021). Another act 
of gender performance is Maru’s attire, which includes 
hats and scarves typically worn by boys and men. In 
a posting on August 12, 2019, Maru is shown smiling 
and wearing a Trilby hat with the following caption: 
“Y ou should prepare for the heat before you go out. 
Wear a hat, and carry a bottle of water with you to 
stay hydrated.” The image and the caption give him 
qualities of a friendly and helpful young male.
Despite Maru’s presentation as gendered male, 
he also defies hegemonic gender. Two repeated acts 
of gender performance illustrate his subtle contesta-
tion of gender expectations: his love of flowers and his 
preference for wearing colorful headscarves on rainy 
days. Flowers are a major theme on his Instagram 
page. There are frequent posts of Maru with flowers—
standing next to them, commenting about them, and 
sniffing them. Although he appears to like different 
types of flowers, his favorite seems to be hydrangeas. 
In a video posted on June 25, 2019, we see a happy 
Maru walking by a line of hydrangea bushes with the 
caption “This blooming hydrangea looks so pretty,” 
which could be viewed as contesting the normative 
gendered behaviors of a “Shiba boy.” In addition, Maru 
frequently wears colorful towels as headscarves when 
he goes out for walks in the rain. A post on July 14, 
2019, for instance, features two pictures of Maru, both 
smiling, one with squinty eyes facing upward, and 
both wearing a white towel adorned with red apples 
and hearts on his head like a babushka. When it is not 
raining, we see Maru with colorful flowers on his head. 
Seemingly going against normative gender perfor -
mance, on August 18, 2018, for example, we see a post 
with two pictures of Maru wearing a sunflower crown 
captioned, “Does it look good on me?”
Maru and Sexuality
Cuteness, according to McIntyre (2017), involves 
sexuality and sexualization. In her work on animal 
stories for young readers, Flegel (2016) noted that 
dog sex and sexuality are not as public as those of 
cats, possibly due to differences in narratives. Cat 
narratives, argued Flegel, emphasize intraspecies 
relations, such as relationships (including sexual 
ones) between cats. Dog narratives, on the other 
hand, focus on interspecies relations, particularly 
ones of devotion between canines and humans. 
Despite these differences, cuteness shapes and is 
shaped by sexuality (Dale et al., 2017).
Although Maru’s sexuality is generally invisible 
on Instagram, a July 9, 2018 post generated reac-
tions about his sexual relationship status. The video 
shows Maru and Cocoa (a white, fluffy Spitz-type 
dog) interacting and waiting to receive treats from 
a woman. Perhaps because of the prospect of food, 
they did not appear particularly affectionate toward 
each other. The caption, however, states, “It’s been a 
while since I met my girl friend last time. Her name is 
Cocoa!” His fans reacted in multiple languages. The 
underlying assumption, based on the comments in 
English, is one of heterosexual coupling. One wrote 
“Even marutaro has gf” and another stated “Y ou two 
look so cute together.” Although Maru’s sexuality 
appears to be unclear, fans attributed heterosexuality 
to their favorite cute dog. In doing so, they projected 
and reified heteronormativity, that is, the normaliza-
tion of heterosexuality (Y ep, 2003) in animals, thus 
exemplifying the relationship between cuteness and 
sexuality.
Putting It All Together: Maru and the 
Vectors of Difference
By examining Maru’s postings through vectors 
of difference in Cute Studies, we can see how 

250 Content
cuteness constitutes and is constituted by race/
ethnicity, gender, and sexuality. Approaching these 
differences intersectionally suggests that we must 
attend to them together rather than considering a 
singular difference at a time (Y ep & Chivers, 2017). 
Maru’s images with stuffed animals on his head, for 
example, are interpreted as cute by simultaneously  
considering how he approaches others, his boyish 
gender performance, his round and fluffy body, and 
so on.
Cute Studies reminds us that images and rep-
resentations of cuteness, such as cute animals, are 
socially constructed. In other words, cuteness is a 
cultural invention infused with social meanings at par-
ticular moments in history—nothing is inherently cute 
by itself. Further, “cuteness engenders an intimacy 
between subject [e.g., the viewer] and object [e.g., a cute 
animal] that involves the cathexis of human qualities 
[e.g., race/ethnicity, gender, sexuality] onto an object 
of affection” (Gn, 2017, p. 178). In other words, cute-
ness creates and sustains an affective bond between 
a subject and an object that involves power. However, 
power in this relationship is not always straightforward. 
For example, Maru’s fans (the viewers) might have 
power over his worldwide popularity but Maru (the 
object) also has power over his fans through the quality 
and quantity of his postings.
To become a critical consumer of images of cute 
animals, we must remember that such images are nei-
ther innocent nor purely entertaining. Cute images are 
not apolitical. Indeed, they involve particular view-
points or ideologies that guide us to see and act in the 
world from those perspectives, such as colorblindness, 
normative gender performance, and heteronorma-
tivity. A critical consumer must pay attention to how 
these ideologies are circulating in the images and how 
power might operate in the affective bond between 
viewer and cute animal.

6.9: A GUILD OF STEREOTYPES: 
EXAMINING GENDER, RACE, AND NERD 
STEREOTYPES IN THE GUILD
Joseph Hoffswell
This content analysis of the award-winning web 
comedy series The Guild investigates the extent to 
which the series reinforced and challenged stereo-
types of gender, race, and nerd/gamer culture.
In the early days of independent web-based content 
creation, Felicia Day created a show about online 
gamers that touted a deliberately diverse cast and 
a goal of providing positive representation of nerds 
and gamer culture. The Guild (2007–2013) follows 
the exploits of a six-member online gaming guild 
called the Knights of Good in a massive-multiplayer 
online role-playing game (MMORPG) referred 
to simply as The Game. Although The Guild as a 
series has ended, it is still relevant to its fans. The 
actors continue to engage with fans online. Fans 
also maintain a wiki site devoted to the show and 
its characters (https://theguildshow.fandom.com/
wiki/The_Guild_Wiki).
Day’s show was ground-breaking. It was one of 
the first internet series produced by actors with the 
help of their fans. The Guild’s first season was written, 
directed, produced, and paid for by Day and fans who 
sent donations via PayPal. The second season was 
partially funded by DVD sales of season one, until 
Microsoft got wind of the success and offered Day 
a distribution deal (Brophy-Warren, 2009). The Guild 
demonstrated that dedication and a fan base cultivated 
through the internet could allow low-budget passion 
projects to turn into fully sponsored shows. Besides 
enjoying fan and sponsor support, the show was a crit-
ical success. It was a multiple winner at the inaugural 
Streamy awards (honoring online video) in 1999, tak-
ing home Best Web Series, Best Comedy Web Series, 
Audience Choice Award, and Outstanding Actress in 
a Web Series for Day. The Guild was nominated for 34 
awards during its run and won 14.
As noted, Day wanted the show to be diverse and 
to represent gamers and nerds positively—but how 

252 Content
well was she able to accomplish this goal? I examine 
the series to answer the question: To what extent do 
characters in The Guild challenge or reinforce stereo-
types related to gender, race, and gamer/nerd culture?
Content Analyzing The Guild
To answer my question, as part of a larger study, 
I conducted a quantitative content analysis of the 
web series The Guild. Of the show’s 70 episodes, 40 
met the inclusion criterion of featuring both primary 
and secondary characters. Four of these episodes 
were used to train coders (who achieved accept-
able levels of intercoder reliability), leaving a final 
sample of 36 episodes. Coders analyzed all primary 
and secondary characters every time they appeared 
in a scene interacting with others. Primary charac-
ters (n = 6) are characters who constitute the main 
cast of the show. Secondary characters (n = 20) 
are characters who appeared in-person outside of 
The Game, interacted in-person with the Knights of 
Good, appeared in at least five episodes, and were 
involved in at least one main storyline. Background 
characters, who did not reach the threshold for 
being considered a primary or secondary charac-
ter, were not coded. Characters who did not interact 
with others were not coded. Primary and secondary 
characters were coded as present or absent in each 
scene. This gives a total of interactions with others 
throughout the episodes analyzed, which can then 
be subject to statistical analysis. Here, I focus on 
variables related to gender, race, and nerd/gamer 
stereotypes.
Representation of Gender
Gender representations were explored through five 
variables with characters: character attractiveness, 
provocativeness of attire, appropriateness of attire, 
intelligence, and aggression. The Guild had equal 
gender representation for the primary characters 
(three men and three women) and screen appear -
ances of the primary characters. Of the 262 scenes 
analyzed, 142 featured male characters and 120 
featured female characters. To examine the pres-
ence of gender stereotypes, I conducted chi-square 
tests on the five variables to see whether men and 
women were depicted differently in the scenes. A 
chi-square test allows us to determine whether dif-
ferences across groups are statistically significant, 
that is, greater than would be expected by chance. 
The results showed that although some gender ste-
reotypes were reinforced, some were not.
Character attractiveness yielded a significant dif-
ference based on gender (X
2 [2, n = 262] = 32.608, 
p <.001), with women appearing as attractive more 
often than men characters. This conforms to gender 
stereotypes. Even when the women were depressed 
and had little concern for self-care, they were still 
significantly more attractive than the men. Besides 
reinforcing the importance of physical attractiveness 
in women, this finding may also reflect stereotypes 
of how male nerds/gamers are represented, which 
will be addressed below. However, it is interesting 
that although women were more attractive than men, 
women were significantly more likely than men to be 
obese (X
2 [1, n = 262] = 50.985, p <.001).
Other gender stereotypes were not upheld. For 
example, there was no statistically significant differ-
ence in levels of aggression between the male and 
female characters of The Guild. Stereotypically, men 
are the aggressors, but The Guild portrayed few aggres-
sive actions by either male or female characters. No 
significant gender-based differences emerged for either 
appropriateness of attire or provocativeness of attire; 
although the female characters were more attractive, 
they were not dressed in ways that reinforced gen-
der stereotypes. Women were not overtly sexualized 
by their wardrobe. The Guild resoundingly subverted 
gender stereotypes around intelligence of the char -
acters, which was measured by perceived education 
and problem-solving abilities. Stereotypical treatments 
present female characters as less intelligent than their 
male counterparts. A chi-square test revealed that the 
women of The Guild were significantly more intelligent 
than the men (X
2 [2, n = 262] = 32.981, p < 0.001). 
Although the women did at times behave foolishly 
this was much less often than the men, who were fre-
quently shown as genuinely inept and juvenile in their 
actions. Female characters were more competent than 
men; many storylines presented them as composed 
and effective problem solvers who got the Knights of 


Music and Digital Media 253
Good out of
 many tricky situations both within and 
outside of the online game. The Guild gave the female 
characters more power and more appealing portrayals 
when compared to the male characters. Codex (Day) 
often rallied her friends, organized and coordinated 
their raids, and was the player who won a pivotal duel 
against a rival guild during their adventures. Overall, 
The Guild seems to have been effective at avoiding 
many gender stereotypes, which is in line with Day’s 
goals.
Representation of Race/Ethnicity
Race and ethnicity were explored using seven var -
iables: attractiveness, weight, provocativeness of 
attire, intelligence, temperament, aggression, and 
accent. Of the 262 instances of characters interact-
ing, 185 featured White characters and 77 featured 
APIDA (Asian Pacific Islander Desi American) 
characters. Characters from other racial groups 
appeared briefly or in minor roles, but because 
they did not meet the secondary character criteria, 
they are not included in the sample. In this regard, 
although Day avoided using an all-White cast, and 
The Guild features people of color in multiple impor-
tant roles, the lack of characters of other racial or 
ethnic groups is noticeable.
My analysis compares White and APIDA charac-
ters. Stereotypes of people of APIDA descent include 
being an exotic other, having high intelligence, and 
being calm and good workers (Hsu, 2015). I found 
some statistically significant differences between 
White and APIDA characters, although as noted below 
the results should be approached with caution. APIDA 
characters were significantly more attractive than 
White characters (X
2 [2, n = 262 = 62.642, p < 0.001) 
and significantly more intelligent than White charac-
ters (X
2 [2, n = 262] = 15.545, p < 0.001). In addition, 
White characters were significantly more likely to be 
depicted as obese than APIDA characters X
2 [2, n = 
262] = 16.569, p < 0.001). These findings reinforce ste-
reotypes relating to the attractiveness and intelligence 
of APIDA people. However, it should be noted that 
the results are not entirely reliable. The chi-square test 
expects a certain number of observations across each 
condition; that expectation was not met. Thus, the 
differences in attractiveness, weight, and intelligence 
are best considered examples of stereotyping, rather 
than statistical proof that White and APIDA characters 
were presented differently.
There were no statistically significant differences 
between White and APIDA characters for provoca-
tiveness of attire, temperament, aggression or accent. 
Therefore, these components of the APIDA stereo-
type were not emphasized when representing APIDA 
characters, and in the process challenged stereotypes. 
Overall, Day seems to have partially met her goals for 
diversity on The Guild.
Representation of the Nerd/Gamer Stereotype
Attributes often associated with nerds/gamers 
include being male, intelligent, White or APIDA, 
obese, and lacking motivation beyond gaming. Kow-
ert et al. (2014) studied four specific stereotypes of 
nerds/gamers: unpopular, unattractive, lazy (coded 
as unmotivated in my analysis), and lack social skills 
(coded as socially awkward interactions). Because 
most of the show’s characters are gamers, my anal-
ysis does not compare gamers and nongamers. 
Instead, I explored nerd/gamer stereotypes by 
studying the frequencies of the following variables: 
character attractiveness, socially awkward interac-
tions, gender, and motivation. As seen with gender 
and race, The Guild both reinforced and challenged 
nerd/gamer stereotypes.
The Guild reinforced the stereotype that male 
gamers are unattractive when compared to the female 
characters. As noted above, the women were signifi-
cantly more attractive than the men, even though 
women were also more likely to be obese. A second 
stereotype, that nerds/gamers lack social skills, was 
strongly reinforced in The Guild. Lack of social skills 
was explored by having coders examine interactions 
between characters for social awkwardness (violat-
ing social norms or generating a feeling of vicarious 
unease). Chi-square tests revealed no race-based dif-
ferences on social awkwardness, but men were sig-
nificantly more likely than the women to be socially 
awkward (X
2 [2, n = 262] = 47.468, p < 0.001). This 
reinforces the commonly held stereotype that male 
nerds/gamers have poor social skills. For example, 

254 Content
during an early quest, Codex chatted with Zaboo, who 
interpreted it as flirting. Later Zaboo showed up at 
Codex’s apartment saying he is there to live with her. 
Examining the frequencies of socially awkward inter-
actions throughout The Guild reveals that 37% of inter-
actions were socially awkward. Even without making 
a comparison to other shows or to the general pop-
ulation in real life, this seems a very high proportion, 
and reinforces the stereotype that gamers have trouble 
understanding and recognizing social cues.
In contrast, several other stereotypes were chal-
lenged in The Guild. The most obvious challenge to the 
stereotype that gamers are men is the strong presence 
of women discussed above. The simple stereotype 
that gamers are male is unequivocally disrupted both 
in the show’s content and by having a female gamer as 
creator and main writer. In addition, as noted above, 
female gamers in The Guild were more responsible, 
intelligent, and skilled gamers than the male gamers. 
For example, Codex and Tinkerballa (both women) 
took down a rival guild and completed multiple diffi-
cult quests in The Game, clearly demonstrating their 
prowess as gamers. Further gender diversity was intro-
duced because although the main characters were 
straight, a variety of secondary and background char-
acters openly expressed their LGBTQ identities.
Further, The Guild subverted the stereotype that 
nerds/gamers lack motivation in life. Of the 262 char-
acter appearances coded, only 19 were coded as lazy. 
The Guild subverted the nerd stereotype because char-
acters showed motivation through their questions, jobs, 
and life goals. Codex’s story arc provides an excellent 
bookend to the series. The series begins with Codex 
discussing her plans and lamenting her lack of a job. 
She rotates through multiple jobs throughout the series 
to pay her bills, and finally lands a great job working 
with the creator and owner of The Game. In the series 
finale, she shares her plans for the future and happily 
exclaims that she loves her job. Although she is happy 
in her job, she was always motivated to succeed even 
when working in far less satisfying positions.
Progress Through a Careful Eye
A content analysis of the web series The Guild 
explored whether a series about gamers made by 
gamers could challenge stereotypes. Gender, race, 
and nerd/gamer stereotypes were confirmed, 
but the show juxtaposed stereotype-confirming 
representations with stereotype-disconfirming 
representations.
Creator Felicia Day wanted to challenge stere-
otypes. In the process, The Guild brought nuance to 
gamers. The show expanded media representations 
of gamers while at least partially challenging gamer 
stereotypes. It showed the characters’ growth over 
six seasons by depicting their daily lives and exploits 
outside of The Game. Codex eventually turned her 
game addiction into a job. Zaboo and Vork mined 
in-game gold and items to turn into real money to sup-
port themselves. Bladezz went viral as the spokesper-
son for a restaurant featured in the show. Tinkerballa 
learned that the male gamers thought she was mean, 
which caused her to reflect on her past behavior. Clara 
demonstrated that she was a caring and warm mother, 
after earlier episodes implied that she neglected her 
family due to The Game. Being gamers defines the 
characters in The Guild but also brings them happiness 
and life fulfillment.
In addition, The Guild brought awareness to gam-
ing addiction even before it officially became a diag-
nosable mental illness. Day said that she created The 
Guild to process her own personal gaming addiction 
to World of Warcraft (Cobb, 2016). Including this topic 
challenged the gaming industry and addressed some 
of the problems that may arise if players become too 
caught up in games. The Knights of Good even encour-
aged one of its members to take a break from The 
Game after seeing how it was affecting her behavior.
Overall, then, what do my findings reveal? How 
successful was Day at accomplishing her goal of cre-
ating a show that was diverse and represent gamers 
and nerds positively? Clearly, she was very success-
ful in creating a show that was embraced by fans and 
critics alike, lasted for six seasons, won many awards, 
and is still relevant to fans’ lives. That part of her goal 
was unequivocally met. She was also fairly successful 
at meeting the goals of having a diverse cast and pre-
senting nerds and gamers positively.
My analysis of diversity focused on gender, 
race, and nerds/gamers. Day seems to have come 
closest to achieving her goal of representing gender 


Music and Digital Media 255
in a nonst
ereotypical or stereotype-disconfirming 
fashion. The women in The Guild were more attrac-
tive than the men, but they were also significantly 
more intelligent and often demonstrated superior 
gaming skills. Day also seems to have had mixed 
success in achieving a goal of racial/ethnic diver -
sity. On the one hand, the cast features a significant 
number of non-White people. The strong presence 
of people of color in crucial roles, in a multiracial 
cast, is solid progress. On the other hand, the over -
reliance on APIDA characters reinforces the ste-
reotype that APIDA people are smart, good with 
math, science, engineering, computers, and gaming. 
No other racial or ethnic groups are represented as 
primary or secondary characters. Finally, Day was 
largely successful in challenging some nerd/gamer 
stereotypes. The Guild highlighted multiple aspects 
of the varied lives and identities of The Knights of 
Good outside of The Game, depicted the gamers as 
motivated, and even showed some ramifications 
of excessive gaming. However, The Guild resound-
ingly reinforced the stereotype of the socially inept 
gamer, relying on that trope for much of the show’s 
humor.
Ultimately, it seems that Day largely, but not 
fully, met her self-proclaimed goals. The Guild did 
follow some Hollywood traditions of relying upon 
stereotypes for character definition, but it also 
challenged stereotypes held about nerds/gamers 
and created a positive portrayal of gamers. The 
Guild brought more realistic depictions of nerd/
gamers to Hollywood and was one of the early 
integrations of nerd/gamer culture into the media. 
It clearly disrupted numerous stereotypes about 
women and avoided the worst pitfalls of having an 
all-White cast. Still, despite the show’s strengths, 
my analysis might indicate that it may be harder 
to avoid stereotypical representations than con-
tent creators may think. Perhaps the assimilation 
of stereotypes is so prevalent that they are used 
even in shows that actively try to counter those 
stereotypes and create positive depictions of 
groups of people who are discriminated against 
and marginalized.
References
