PART III
PRODUCTION
Films, TV shows, newspapers, and websites don’t 
appear out of thin air; they exist because people 
create them. Although that statement may appear 
so obvious that it borders on the absurd, the fact 
remains that we often forget about the constructed 
nature of all media messages. Who produces the 
content consumed by media audiences? What pres-
sures do they face?
Most mainstream media content is produced by/
for large corporations that focus on the bottom line. 
But digital media and the internet also allow regular 
people to produce and distribute our own mediated 
messages. Independent filmmakers still strive to real-
ize their dreams and visions. And it doesn’t mean that 
everything mainstream is profit-driven, nor that profit 
is attainable only at the sacrifice of social responsibility.
If you’ve ever been involved in media produc-
tion—even for TikTok—you’ve operated equipment 
(even if just your smart phone); you’ve thought about 
how to tell a story and how various elements of sight, 
sound, and motion can help you convey your mes-
sage. Y ou’ve probably also considered your target 
audience, so that your content will serve your own 
and the audience’s needs, desires, and interests. Even if 
you have not been involved in media production, you 
may understand that the process of content creation 
is often complex and always involves a wide range 
of activities spanning preproduction, production, and 
postproduction.
This section won’t address things such as whether 
female producers have a different working style than 
men do, or whether people of color employ various 
production aesthetics in an identifiable or unique 
style—although those are interesting topics. Instead, 
these readings look at a variety of situations in which 
people creating media content operate. Specifically, 
in this section, authors discuss race, gender, and  
class in media production by addressing the reality of 
what it’s like to create various types of content and by 
examining media professionals or media organizations 
to illuminate the environment in which these people 
work.
The eight readings in this section fall into one 
chapter: “Media Industries and Producing Media 
Content.” In Reading 7.1, Gina M. Chen and Parom-
ita Pain interview women journalists of color to learn 
more about the harassment they face in their online 
workspaces. Charisse L’Pree Corsbie-Massay and 
Kandice N. Green (Reading 7.2) report on interviews 
with Black content creators to understand how they 
approached fighting stereotypes and telling stories rep-
resenting a historically marginalized group. In Reading 
7.3, Melissa Greene-Blye examines challenges facing 
Native American journalists, connecting today’s chal-
lenges to those faced by early Native media. Rebecca 
Ann Lind (Reading 7.4) discovers that the intersection 
of race and gender has meant that women and people 
of color have followed different paths in their quest to 
gain access to the mass media. Barbara G. Friedman 
(Reading 7.5) analyzed interviews with the writers/
directors of modern rape-revenge films to identify 
four themes that were important to these artists when 
creating their films. Dear Aunaetitrakul, in Reading 
7.5, reviews multiple sources to shed light on Eddie 
DOI: 10.4324/9781003193708-9

258 Production
Huang’s short-lived involvement with the television 
show based on his memoir, Fresh Off the Boat.
The final two readings consider the relationship 
between race, gender, class, and the very technology 
that supports so much of our daily lives including 
our entertainment. Michael L. Austin, in Reading 7.6, 
encourages us to think about algorithmic bias and how 
potentially vulnerable groups are often affected the 
most. Eric Freedman (Reading 7.7) goes even deeper, 
asking whether tools such as the MetaHuman Creator 
are democratizing the field of digital content creation, 
fostering more diverse representations and narratives, 
and supporting the free play of identity in playable 
media.

7.1: “NEVER ABOUT MY WORK, 
NEVER ABOUT MY MOTIVATIONS”: 
EXPLORING ONLINE EXPERIENCES OF 
WOMEN JOURNALISTS OF COLOR
Gina M. Chen and Paromita Pain
The authors interviewed female journalists of color 
to understand their experiences with incivility in 
readers’ responses to their articles.
The female journalist—a Black television/web 
reporter with 18 months’ experience—braces for 
the onslaught of nasty comments when she does a 
story on a hot-button topic. “I really don’t respond 
because I believe that it won’t change anything,” 
she explains. “I get abused mostly online where 
people leave really nasty comments on certain sto-
ries, like those with political overtones, especially 
immigration.”
This journalist is hardly alone. Journalism has 
turned into a two-way street where engaging with 
audiences online via comments on news sites and on 
social media is the norm (Santana & Russial, 2013). 
This reciprocity between the journalists and the audi-
ence (Lewis, Holton, & Coddington, 2014) can make 
the internet a truly democratic and shared space, 
opening areas for rich citizen–professional collabora-
tions (Reese, 2016) and creating direct links between 
media organizations and the audiences whose infor-
mation needs they serve.
But the interactive digital space also offers a 
darker side. Online comments on news stories are 
rife with vitriol. Recent research shows that as many 
as one in five online comments are uncivil (Chen, 
2017). Journalists are particular targets for these 
attacks (Chen & Pain, 2017), and women journalists 
face the additional challenge of gendered harassment 
(Chen, Pain, Chen, Mekelburg, Springer, & Troger, 
2020). Gendered harassment is a “special kind of sex-
ualized and misogynist hate speech” (Edström, 2016, 
pp. 98–99) that targets women for attack based on their 
gender or sexuality. Interviews with female journalists 
from across the world (Chen et al., 2020), for example, 
found that women aren’t just criticized for their stories 
or attacked verbally as male reporters are—they are 
called “bitches” and threatened with rape.
In this reading, we explore the specific experi-
ences of women journalists of color as they navigate 
the digital space. Women journalists of color are at 
greater risk of attacks because the online space—like 
the offline world—is shaped by societal norms that 
value White males over others. Critical race theory 
explains this by asserting that racism is not an anom-
aly in our culture, but rather a means of reinforcing the 
power of the dominant group, White men (Delgado & 
Stefanic, 2012). The media—through news stories and 
even online comments—reinforce these viewpoints, 
creating an inaccurate view of race (Campbell, 1995). 
People of color in general are portrayed as other to 
the dominant White society (Liebler, 2010), decreas-
ing their value in what is called inferential racism (Hall, 
1992). This marginalization is amplified for women 
7.
MEDIA INDUSTRIES AND PRODUCING 
MEDIA CONTENT
DOI: 10.4324/9781003193708-10

260 Production
of color because they experience two intersecting 
 c
ategories—race and gender—by which they are the 
other (Crenshaw, 1991). In addition, the anonymous 
nature of the internet encourages people to say things 
they perhaps wouldn’t say offline (Li, 2008), such as 
racist or hateful comments.
To understand their experiences, we interviewed 
20 American female journalists of color. Our partici-
pants’ ages varied from 22 to 45 years, and their pro-
fessional experiences (television, online, and print) 
ranged from 2 to 30 years. All names and news organ-
izations are withheld to protect the women’s privacy. 
Interviews lasted about 30 minutes. We asked open-
ended questions about the kind of online comments 
their articles elicited, how audiences engaged with 
them on social media, and how they dealt with inci-
vility. We also asked whether their organizations had 
training programs or other help for women journalists, 
especially given the rising awareness that women are 
trolled more than men. We analyzed data from our 
interviews using a constant comparative method and 
by immersing ourselves in the subjects’ cultural and 
social norms to make meaning from their statements 
(McCracken, 1988). The dominant themes that arose 
were the nature of hate online, whether to engage, and 
organizational support.
Nature of Hate Online
Participants said that the nature of hate directed at 
them online was racist and misogynistic. The most 
bothersome part, some participants said, was the 
way comments referred “to some body part,” and 
were “always sexual.” These were clearly racist and 
often referenced the journalists’ color and gender. 
For example, some online commenters seemed to 
assume that journalists of color would take both a 
gender- and race-biased angle with stories, writing 
about their “sisters,” as one woman in our sample 
explained. Commenters felt that Black women jour-
nalists would not be objective in their reporting on 
issues facing Black communities.
One participant, from an outlet that focuses on 
race and social justice, said:
It’s especially hard because we are 
 pr
oducers 
for Black audiences and focus on Black issues. 
Color is important for us. But that also opens us 
up to people who openly are vitriolic. Sometimes 
I feel only racist people flock to our site.
Attacks singled out the women by their race or gen-
der, or both. The women said the barbs were more 
personal than those aimed at men or even White 
women. A man might be called “stupid” for choos-
ing certain sources in his story, but women jour -
nalists of color get attacked in a different way. For 
example, a Latina journalist reported being called a 
“needy Hispanic” and peppered with misogynistic 
statements when she wrote a story about a rape vic-
tim who spoke out against President Donald Trump. 
“I have faced extreme misogyny and harassment,” 
she explained. “I don’t feel scared…. I get trolled for 
my race and gender.”
Hate online was sexist, but race also came into 
play, particularly for certain topics such as politics or 
immigration. One participant explained: “I get trolled 
for my race and gender. Mostly for my gender. Race 
too plays back sometimes like when I was covering 
the Clinton campaign and what she was doing for 
Hispanics.” For example, one participant faced attacks 
when she wrote about the Black Lives Matter move-
ment, which arose in response to a rash of police 
shootings of African Americans. “When I wrote about 
the violence surrounding the Black Lives Matter 
Movement, the F bomb was hurled at me in a way 
that I have never experienced before. It was a frenzy,” 
she recalled.
Another journalist noted that the attacks make 
her feel as if the goal of her journalism—what she 
hopes to achieve in telling stories—didn’t matter. 
Nasty commenters see her only as her race and gen-
der: “They are misogynistic and aimed at my race and 
color. It is never about my work, never about my moti-
vations,” she explained. Women also reported visual 
attacks through pictures or memes that contain insults, 
such as bitch. Most often these came from anonymous 
accounts. As a Black TV journalist with two years’ 
experience asked: “What do you say to someone who 
is calling you ‘cunt’ with a profile picture of a cucum-
ber?” These attacks left the women perplexed and 
weighed heavily on their minds. The attacks also rein-
forced their marginalization as women, and as female 
journalists of color.


Media Industries and Producing Media Content 261
Deciding W
hether to Engage
A second theme that emerged in our interviews 
was whether the women journalists of color should 
engage with hateful comments online. Most in our 
sample choose not to. As one participant said: 
“They are misogynistic and aimed at my race and 
color. I am not about to school White privilege, so 
I don’t engage. I get the most vitriol on Facebook. 
That surprises me.” Other women echoed this 
experience of heightened attacks on Facebook, 
particularly on the women’s public pages that their 
employers required they maintain. The women 
weren’t sure why Facebook elicited more abuse 
but posited that it may be because that platform 
doesn’t limit the length of the posts. On Twitter, 
women found it easier to block trolls although the 
trolls often just created a new account and attacked 
again.
Many women in our sample said they try to read 
comments on their stories but are cautious about 
responding back. A Black newspaper journalist said 
she considers all reader input important, even if it is 
negative. But she feels no need to respond. “They all 
start a conversation and that’s what my job as a journal-
ist is. I am here to make people think,” she said. “Even 
if the comment is very vitriolic, it’s evoked a reaction 
and that’s good enough for me. But that doesn’t mean 
I will engage with negative commenters.” Y et some of 
the journalists we interviewed did choose to engage. 
They felt that opening a dialogue, showing trolls that 
they were conversing with an actual human being, and 
being firm, eased the situation. As one interviewee, 
with 10 years of television experience, said:
…directly engaging such people doesn’t 
help. They are doing it for a reaction any-
way. But once when I reacted [for a story on 
a transwoman], and it did shut them down. I 
responded saying everyone was human and 
had a place in the world.
A few women said that in spite of the hate, com-
ments sometimes provided valuable tips, access 
to sources, and constructive suggestions that often 
sparked different angles for stories. But because 
of incivility, many often avoided looking carefully 
at comments and may have lost out on useful 
information.
Online harassment did not deter them from 
doing their best in their jobs, the women said, but it did 
have negative effects on the way they worked. As one 
participant said: “I don’t feel scared. So that doesn’t 
affect the way I do my stories but personally they do 
affect me. I often overthink certain angles and [am] 
extra vigilant that all angles are covered.” Participants 
said that they often re-read stories ensuring that they 
had covered everything possible. They doubted their 
judgment and it took them longer to file their stories. 
Respondents were clear that although they “hated” 
receiving upsetting messages online, abuse against 
sources was even more galling. Journalists were pro-
tective of their interviewees for stories, especially those 
who are poor and powerless. As one participant said: 
“Rude comments can influence sources. I have to tell 
them that they are just mean people and have to be 
ignored. There’s always a sense that we may have 
betrayed the source in some way.”
Three participants who joined the profession 
before the rise of the internet said that they viewed 
online commenting as a sort of letter to the editor 
that happened faster and enabled them to react in real 
time. They often responded, even to the hate, because 
they believed that by not responding they would be 
excluded from the reciprocal social media experiences 
that are part of today’s evolving newsrooms.
Some of the journalists we interviewed said they 
often did not engage because they did not believe that 
people who used abusive words and terms to describe 
their stories wanted a real conversation. But some-
times they were torn, especially if their publication 
catered to niche audiences, such as Black audiences.
Lack of Organizational Support
Our final theme reflects respondents’ concern that 
although their organizations were aware of online 
harassment or even threats, they did very little to 
support the women when attacked. Our interview-
ees urged news organizations to implement policies 
to deter abusers and to help journalists. As one 
said: “The belief that targets of abuse have a social 
responsibility to protect themselves is not enough. 

262 Production
Our content gets them the page views that gets the 
advertisers and revenue. We need more checks 
and balances.” Although the women could speak 
to editors and supervisors, who often understood 
the issues, these conversations did little to stop the 
abuse or make the online space safer. Organizations 
are not equipped to handle incivility online. Some 
supervisors were aware of what the women faced 
and were sympathetic but did not know how to help. 
So, although they were open to conversations, little 
was done to ensure safer online experiences. For 
example, as one participant said:
I get a lot of sexist comments. Our readers are 
mostly men. I remember this one story; my 
boss wrote a funny headline for. Our readers 
thought I had written it. Since most of our read-
ers are men, they accused me of hating men 
and wanting them to get hurt. Finally, my boss 
had to step in and say, “I am a man and I wrote 
that headline.”
Our participants said that most supervisors are 
White men, to whom trolling about race and gender 
seemed alien. Although some supervisors did try to 
understand the problem, our participants felt that 
they needed more concrete reassurances. Few news 
organizations had programs to directly deal with this 
issue, or resources to moderate and monitor com-
ments on social media.
Although some sympathetic editors and supervi-
sors are open to talking about the issue, some employ-
ers just seemed to pay lip service to the problem. One 
interviewee said her employer asked her to conceal 
her identity online to prevent abuse. “I am young, and 
I work in a medium that’s visual. I can’t hide my color. 
Nor do I want to. But sometimes I get scared and wish 
people didn’t say these things,” she said. Many of our 
interviewees said their organizations provide some 
guidance for responding to abusive comments. “We 
have strict rules on how we enter such 
 con
versations. 
I identify myself and I try to clarify things. I am forth-
right and straightforward when I do enter such conver-
sations,” said one participant. But such clarity is often 
not rewarded. Trolls come back with redoubled vigor 
and find new reasons to be abusive. Rarely has inter-
vention from the journalist resolved issues; only one 
participant described a positive experience. A man, 
who had clearly identified himself, was abusing her for 
her religion (Islam) and gender. She told him she was 
just trying to do her job to the best of her ability. She got 
an apology, and they actually had a fruitful interaction.
Some journalists we interviewed could block 
nasty commenters, but the women felt pressured not 
to do this because their news organizations wanted 
them to have high numbers of followers on social 
media. They thought long and hard about blocking or 
deleting accounts in spite of the tension brought about 
by the incivility.
Combatting Dangers Online
If these interviews are anything to go by, comment-
ing and promoting stories on social media has not 
really helped make journalism more democratic, 
nor has it created precious channels of interaction 
and information exchange. The goal of true rec-
iprocity between the audience and the journalist 
(Lewis et al., 2014) is hampered by the hurtful and 
biting words hurled at women journalists of color. 
The sexism and racism permeating our society 
and our legacy media (Campbell, 1995; Hall, 1992) 
reign in the digital space as well. The online vitriol 
that all journalists face (Chen & Pain, 2017) and 
that particularly targets women (Chen et al., 2020) 
is heightened for female journalists of color. The 
reinforcing power of the dominant group, White 
men, casts female journalists of color as the other 
(Delgado & Stefanic, 2012) online, interrupting the 
ease with which they can do their jobs. The threat 
of racist and sexist barbs makes journalists look 
over their shoulders too often. Although journalists 
are encouraged to engage and grow new audiences 
(Lewis et al., 2014), media organizations appear to 
be doing little to deal with the fallout from the abuse. 
Some supervisors are sympathetic, but others are 
not. And even supervisors who appreciate the prob-
lem have few resources to combat it or to help the 
women recover. All too often, female journalists of 
color are left on their own to protect themselves as 
they try to do their jobs.
Y et what is a viable solution to the issue? Some 
media organizations have required that comment-
ers use a real name or register to prevent incivility 


Media Industries and Producing Media Content 263
(Ksiaz
ek, 2015), but that does little to prevent abuse on 
social media. And even with these measures uncivil 
attacks continue (Chen, 2017). We suggest that news 
organizations need to do more. They must train their 
employees to better understand how technology 
works and provide concrete guidance for counter -
ing attacks. They should also moderate and monitor 
their comment sections, take women’s complaints of 
abuse seriously, and take action against repeat offend-
ers. Engaging online is part of a journalist’s job today, 
and news organizations must make these spaces safer. 
It shouldn’t be up to the women journalists of color, 
themselves, to fix the problem.

264 Production
7.2: CONVERSATIONS ON RACE AND 
ENTERTAINMENT MEDIA: BETWEEN 
THEORY AND INDUSTRY
Charisse L’Pree Corsbie-Massay and Kandice N. 
Green
This essay describes the themes in extended con-
versations with prominent media professionals in 
television, film, and digital around issues of being 
Black and producing Blackness in the 21st century.
Entertainment media content has the power to 
inform audiences by implicitly or explicitly address-
ing topical, sensitive, and controversial issues. For the 
purposes of this reading, we define entertainment 
media as content that activates an emotional response 
in audiences. Although entertainment is often associ-
ated with positive responses (i.e., to be entertained), 
responses can be positive, negative, or both. Creators 
who champion diversity are aware of entertainment’s 
emotional potential and make conscious decisions 
about content that can drive social change.
Past iterations of mainstream entertainment in 
the United States featured dominant groups deploying 
marginalized racial or ethnic groups to elicit emotional 
responses (Corsbie-Massay, 2022). Comedy has elic-
ited laughter by mocking marginalized and minoritized 
groups as jokes for the amusement of dominant eth-
nic groups (e.g., blackface). In drama, people of color 
have historically been constructed as the antagonist or 
the villain; Black characters are more likely to be vio-
lent, Latino characters are framed as gang members 
or criminal masterminds, and Middle Eastern charac-
ters more likely to be terrorists (Mastro, 2017). These 
patterns continue in unscripted or reality television, 
because of institutionalized norms established over 
centuries that ensure that the voices and perspectives 
of some groups are valued and amplified over others 
(Orbe, 2008).
In 2020, one-quarter of writers and 28% of char-
acters in broadcast, cable, and digital series were 
people of color (POC), markedly below the 42.7% of 
Americans that qualify as POC (Hunt & Ramón, 2021). 
Furthermore, only about 10% of show creators during 
this time were categorized as POC, indicating a racial 
disparity in who controls the narrative despite greater 
numerical representation on screen. This is deeply 
problematic given the hunger that audiences have for 
diverse stories. Almost half (40%) of White Americans 
have no non-White friends (Dunsmuir, 2013), mean-
ing that media content informs their understanding of 
almost half the population. Furthermore, audiences 
show up for entertainment content that features non-
White casts (Hunt & Ramón, 2021), but non-White 
storytellers are systematically excluded (Dunn et al., 
2021). For students aspiring to work in the entertain-
ment industry, both from marginalized and nonmar-
ginalized backgrounds, understanding this process and 
how to succeed in this environment is invaluable.
In 2002, professor Richard Dubin launched 
the “Conversation on Race and Entertainment 
Media” series at the S. I. Newhouse School of Public 
Communications at Syracuse University. As a long-
standing figure in American television, Dubin invited 
his friends and connections from industry to have inti-
mate and friendly discussions about their experiences 
with race in the industry as students listened. Corsbie-
Massay (the first author) began hosting the conversa-
tions in 2014 and focused on defining diversity and 
historically shrouded practices that inhibit diversity 
as well as addressing effective strategies to make the 
entertainment industry more inclusive.
Over the next eight years, seven media pro-
fessionals who self-identified as Black shared their 
experiences, survival strategies, and wisdom. They 
were associated with content in legacy (e.g., ABC, 
BET, CNN, Lionsgate, Syfy) and digital outlets (e.g., 
Apple TV+, Netflix, Y ouTube). They were committed 
to making the entertainment industry more inclusive 
and welcoming during the concurrent rise of stream-
ing services, influencer culture, and the Black Lives 
Matter movement. This essay combines industry stud-
ies with academic theory, outlines recurring themes 
across these conversations, and encourages students 
to consider how they can catalyze change at both an 
individual and institutional level.
Entertainment Media Is a Form of 
Activism
Several interviewees said that their 
 in
volvement in 
the entertainment industry was driven by a desire to 
change the world. Media content is designed to 
be seamless, and the production process is largely 
obscured from audiences. Over time, 
 int
erviewees 


Media Industries and Producing Media Content 265
r
ecognized that the process of culture creation 
occurred behind closed doors and they needed to 
access these veiled spaces to create the change that 
they wanted to see.
I realized that, as an actor, I was participating 
in the creative conversation way too late for my 
taste… So I made a very conscious 
 decision 
t
o enter television… It was both a creative 
 decision and it w
as also a political decision.
In media production, minor decisions can have 
large impacts on society by affecting how audiences 
think about the individuals featured on screen. 
From seemingly small casting decisions to refusing 
B-roll shots, or changing one word in a script, every 
 int
erviewee shared a story of making a choice with 
the intention of affecting how certain groups were 
presented, both overtly and covertly.
Furthermore, the capacity to tell stories and 
make emotional connections through media—either 
by featuring people with whom the audience may be 
unfamiliar or by telling stories and showing charac-
ters in nuanced ways—was an opportunity to engage 
with the tropes of the past and demand change in the 
future. Watching people grow and change is an oppor-
tunity to see their humanity and telling more 
 st
ories 
about a wider variety of people helps audiences 
become accustomed to seeing the diversity of human-
ity. Interviewees tried to build empathy by presenting 
different perspectives.
As Black creators, interviewees also specifi-
cally sought to share stories of Black humanity and 
 centr
alize the Black experience. This was more than 
simply having a Black lead. They sought to share the 
experience of being Black in the United States. Several 
mentioned tropes such as the “White savior” or “Black 
best friend,” wherein Black characters supported or 
provided context for White characters. There was 
pervasive frustration with such sidelining
 , which fos-
ters the White perspective as dominant and ignores 
the fact that humanity is often embedded in everyday 
activities.
When we say Black Lives Matter, we, we mean 
Black Life Matters. Day to day life. Just day-
to-day life. Going to work as a Black person 
matters. Getting up in the morning and making 
breakfast for yourself or for your loved one. 
That matters.
Interviewees emphasized that regardless of one’s 
best intentions, working in this industry meant 
entering a system with “ideological underpinnings” 
that was not built for change. Simply staying in the 
industry and continuing to tell diverse stories was a 
form of activism given that they were working from 
a hegemonic deficit. One interviewee expressed 
frustration with the unquestioned assumption that 
“Black writers weren’t as good as White writers… 
and also by extension, Black shows weren’t as good 
as White shows” in response to Stuart Hall’s (2003) 
definition of inferential racism. Another decried per-
formative diversity that publicly demonstrated the 
efforts of—often White—stakeholders, while still 
maintaining the stereotypes, norms, and expecta-
tions of mainstream—read White—audiences.
We’re being sidelined… Many [Black execu-
tives] end up in a division of these networks 
and studios called “Diversity and Inclusion” … 
The studios can say, “We absolutely support 
diversity initiatives here. See, we have this 
whole division that is dedicated to it. Don’t you 
see? We’ve got people on staff, we pay them. 
We’re spending our money.” (whispering to 
audience) It’s a write-off.
Interview after interview, there were stories of 
“battle scars”; battles fought behind the scenes to 
make sure that the onscreen representation was 
robust and considerate. This activism takes its toll, 
but every interviewee said that they were excited 
and honored because working in the entertainment 
industry provided an opportunity to produce culture 
and create the lens through which we understand 
ourselves and each other.
Stories That Aren’t Being Told Are 
Important and Profitable
When asked about their creative process, multi-
ple interviewees said they considered what sto-
ries were not being told at the time. This included 
the traits of the main characters, narrative trajec-
tories, editing, and more. Innovation is essential 

266 Production
in the media industry and helps spark inspira-
tion,  maint
ain relevance, and ultimately promote 
diversity. Furthermore, interviewees cited recent 
blockbusters such as Black Panther (2018) and 
Crazy Rich Asians (2018) as well as past content 
such as In Living Color (1990–1994) to demon-
strate how diverse content can be profitable, a 
phenomenon quantified by Hunt and Ramón 
(2021). As one interviewee said “Everybody 
understands green.”
Interviewees often drew from their own lives 
and experiences as Black people in the United 
States, embracing the opportunity to tell stories of 
Black lives that were not told: love between darker 
skinned characters (i.e., “chocolatey sex”), gifted 
Black children, socioeconomic debates, serodiscord-
ant (mixed HIV status) couples, heroes and antihe-
roes, intersectional Blackness, and more. Working in 
television meant that they could acknowledge and 
reject stereotypes directly (“The way that we utilize 
tropes is normally we sort of hang a light on them 
for comedy”).
Interviewees touted the importance of listening 
to oneself and others. Although many entered the 
industry to tell stories they wanted to see or hear, they 
had to learn to listen to themselves before they could 
tell their own story. Then they had to listen to others 
to learn more stories that were not being told. They 
advocated for a greater awareness of stories happen-
ing worldwide, saying that it was not sufficient to sim-
ply tell the story you want to hear or the story you 
want to write.
There are a lot of different experiences…
There’s a lot of realities that are very distinct. 
And I don’t know I’m the best person to talk 
about those because those aren’t necessarily 
mine. But I’m willing to do the research on it. 
And so I have to be careful when I’m in a room 
to not presume that I’m the expert about a 
swath of people.
This commitment to amplifying previously untold 
stories was an overwhelming hurdle given insti-
tutional barriers. Being at the forefront of cultural 
change often meant that others were unaware of—
or outright resistant to—the stories that they wanted 
to tell and the discrimination that they wanted to 
portray (“Just being a Black man in America, with 
a lot of decisions being made about me, that I have 
no overt control over”). Being patient and willing to 
listen to oneself and to others was essential to get-
ting honesty from others and making change.
If you’re doing something that no one’s done, 
consider that a good thing, not a bad thing. ... Y ou 
might be leading the way instead of following the 
way. So don’t be afraid to lead into areas that peo-
ple haven’t been yet. It’s okay. If people don’t get 
your thing, maybe they just don’t get it yet.
Even at low points, interviewees expressed that 
they always believed in themselves, or choose to 
“greenlight” themselves, because they were secure 
in the story they wanted to tell and their ability 
to tell it effectively. Interviewees also relied on 
communities of Black people in the industry with 
whom they shared stories, commiserated, and 
recharged. This group served as a foundation from 
which they could go on fighting for themselves and 
their goals of visibility and representation.
Showing Up With Your Honest Self 
Inherently Enhances Diversity
Showing up with your honest self was one of the 
loudest themes throughout the conversations as 
interviewees expressed their hope for the next gen-
eration of creators. This involved telling stories that 
were not being told, as well as sharing their perspec-
tives, listening to the perspectives of others, and 
being a responsible audience member.
Interviewees were aware of the stereotypes 
applied to them by others. As one said, “Y ou have 
walked into a space that is defined by history and 
by contemporary practices that are entrenched.” 
Many interviewees said they had self-censored 
in the past to avoid appearing stereotypical or 
drawing the ire of their colleagues or employers 
(“I don’t want always be seen as the angry Black 
girl”). However, they came to appreciate what they 
brought to the room and understood that every 
person brought something unique to the conver -
sation and the culture creation, despite the added 


Media Industries and Producing Media Content 267
b
urden of being the only person speaking on behalf 
of these issues.
If something’s on the table to be contributed to 
the show that is problematic for me, I’ll speak 
up. There’s no point in being there and not 
speaking up. The problem [is that] what offends 
me doesn’t necessarily offend all Black people 
and vice versa. So if there’s only one person of 
color in the room, then I’m de facto the mouth-
piece for everybody. And we’re not a monolith, 
so that’s not a fair burden.
Showing up with one’s honest self also means lis-
tening to the honest selves and stories of others. 
Interviewees expressed how—in order to create 
disruptive and inclusive narratives—everyone 
needs to encourage and support people who are 
different from them throughout the production pro-
cess. When defining diversity, interviewees empha-
sized a multitude of perspectives, experiences, and 
voices, not just checking externally imposed race 
and gender boxes. They delighted in learning about 
the nuances within groups of which they were not 
members, including other ethnic groups, religious 
groups, and sexualities (“We call them ciphers. 
When we get off topic and we get in there and we 
start mixing it up”). In doing so, they learned more 
about themselves and their craft.
Listening to others also allowed them to be 
specific, which drives diversity. Multiple interview-
ees expressed frustration with the terms “diver -
sity” and “multiculturalism” because they are too 
generic to be effective (“I’m more specific. I would 
never use the word diversity at the network. I was 
like ‘No. Put Black people on’ .”). These terms also 
allow people to deflect the difficult and often pain-
ful history that accompanied the need for diversity 
efforts (“Culture has gotten very good at finding a 
multitude of ways to take the off ramp so that they 
do not have to talk about Black and Brown peo-
ple”). No single story can accomplish diversity, but 
a multitude of specific stories could showcase the 
diversity of humanity.
The more specific you are, the more universal 
those emotions are. If you try to do everything 
for everybody, it ends up being kind of boring 
and ridiculous. But if you tell a very specific 
story about this person’s idiosyncratic experi-
ence… you get a story that resounds in people 
rather than “Been there. Heard that.”
Interviewees also expressed the importance of 
being an attentive audience member. They felt 
responsibility as creators to produce ethical and 
inclusive content as well as to support content that 
moves larger cultural conversations forward and 
avoid content that does not (“Shut it down. Because 
you’re donating to the Nielsen ratings. Y ou are why 
these shows continue”). At the same time, inter -
viewees were driven by content they disliked to cre-
ate material that included their perspectives. One 
interviewee described how the intersection of frus-
tration and specificity led to a successful web series.
We wanted to see images of Black women and 
the complexities of those Black women in ways 
that we had not seen them before. And we 
wanted to share that with the world because we 
wanted people to know that we exist, and all 
Black women are not the same and we are not 
those same images that you see of us on real-
ity shows or on like silly sitcoms. We’re not all 
sassy. We’re not all loud. We’re all different. So 
we were very specific in terms of brainstorm-
ing what types of characters we wanted to be 
in the web series, and how they were different 
from one another.
Ultimately, Change Is Built
The opportunity to work with forward-thinking 
powerhouses also spawned frustration with industry 
leaders who had to be dragged into today’s diverse 
environment (“Lorne Michaels should’ve been hir -
ing Black people a long time ago…There’s some 
funny sisters out there!”) and well-meaning execu-
tives’ desire to fulfill diversity quotas while perpet-
uating problematic narratives (“This is a room full 
of good guys…and one of them said, ‘Where’s the 
sassy Latina chick? We should have a sassy Latina 
chick’”). Every progression in their career exposed 
the regressive attitudes of people in increasingly 

268 Production
powerful position, forcing them to adapt in order to 
advocate.
Interviewees consistently said that change does 
not come from a single show, episode, or character; it 
requires continued effort. They expressed gratitude for 
the foundations laid by the likes of Cicely Tyson, Oprah 
Winfrey, the Wayans Brothers, and Ava Duvernay. 
These ground-breaking figures had the vision and 
power to change the industry and their work facili-
tated future success and allowed the next generation 
to overcome barriers.
Shondaland is just a place where it is. It’s 
because [Shonda Rhimes’] experience and her 
view of the world sees what looks like this audi-
ence, that’s what it’s going to be reflected on 
television. Not because it’s magical or because 
she has a mandate to do it.
Interviewees were also committed to paying it 
forward. They recognized that their Blackness did 
not automatically equate to diversity; instead, they 
knew they must actively work to tell nuanced sto-
ries of historically marginalized and stereotyped 
groups and bring in voices not yet at the table. They 
applied their own experiences to better empathize 
with others who experienced similar but different 
forms of oppression and discrimination. In doing so, 
they seek to open doors so that others—and their 
 st
ories—reflect the world in which they live.
Y ou always have to go out of yourself and find 
other people… Bring them in… Stop talking 
about the difficulty of making a writer’s room 
diverse. Stop talking about how difficult it is to 
find actors of color that are up to the standard 
or “I don’t think the pool is large enough.” Shut 
up and just effing do it already.

7.3: A CAREFUL BALANCE: AN 
EXAMINATION OF CHALLENGES FACING 
NATIVE AMERICAN JOURNALISTS 
IN THEIR WORK AS ADVOCATES, 
EDUCATORS, AND STORYTELLERS
Melissa Greene-Blye
The author investigates both the value of and the 
challenges faced by contemporary Native media, 
connecting today’s challenges to those faced by 
early Native media. Whether contemporary or 
historical, these media outlets cover issues, events, 
and governmental affairs relevant to their own 
communities.
Native media outlets, in the form of newsletters, 
newspapers, magazines, radio and television pro-
gramming, and online publications, are an important 
way that Indigenous individuals and communities 
stay informed. Native media cover events, govern-
mental affairs, and news within their own commu-
nities as well as issues, events, and news across 
Indian Country (a term used to describe Native 
spaces/places within the borders of the now-
United States, including the self-governing sover -
eign tribal nations that occupy those spaces). It is 
a space where Indigenous people and communities 
can find authentic, accurate coverage of issues that 
affect their daily lives in tangible ways, coverage 
that is often missing from, or misrepresented in, 
non-
 N
ative media outlets. As a citizen of a sover -
eign Native nation (I am Miami Tribe of Oklahoma), 
who spent 20 years as a broadcast journalist, I have 
always noticed important differences in the way 
stories are covered in different media outlets; I did 
not fully realize the causes of those differences until 
I become a Native scholar, specializing in research 
about Native representation in news media.
According to the latest figures from the Native 
American Journalists Association (2020), there are 
approximately 400 Native media outlets in the United 
States and Canada. In this essay, I will focus on 
 outlets
 
operating within the United States. I’ll use the term 
“Native” when broadly referencing media outlets run 
by and for tribal communities, as well as media outlets 
targeting a broader audience across Indian Country. 
Otherwise, when possible (such as when outlets incor-
porate the term “Indigenous” or a specific tribal iden-
tity in their name), I will use the name chosen by the 
outlet to identify itself.
I will explain how the historical events surround-
ing the birth of Native media shaped it, as well as 
discuss how those events continue to inform the con-
tent, and challenge the practice of, Native journalism. 
I begin with a history of the Cherokee Phoenix, examin-
ing the ways in which it set the standard for the Native 
media that followed, and conclude with a discussion of 
ways to offer improved representation of Native issues, 
people, and identities in non-Native media outlets.
Native media have a rich history that is inextrica-
bly intertwined with the policies, events, and people 
that comprise the history of the now-United States 
and of the Indigenous peoples who lived, hunted, 
and farmed on this land long before Euro-American 
explorers and settlers found its shores. Storytelling 
has long been an important part of Native American 
culture, with stories handed down generation-to-
 
g
eneration, but it wasn’t until the early 19th century 
that journalism was introduced as a new form of sto-
rytelling. Journalism told stories advocating for Native 
American rights and resisting federal and state policies 
which threatened tribal sovereignty and often meant 
the loss of traditional homelands.
The Cherokee Phoenix
The Cherokee Phoenix, the first Native newspaper 
in North America, launched in New Echota, capi-
tal of the Cherokee nation (present-day Georgia) on 
February 21, 1828, as a tribally operated bilingual 
weekly printed in both the English and the Cherokee 
language. The Phoenix began publishing at a critical 
time for the Cherokee; Georgia lawmakers, anxious 
to please land-hungry farmers and miners (gold had 
been discovered on Cherokee land) passed new laws 
which sought to undermine Cherokee sovereignty 

270 Production
and advocacy. This included a law which outlawed 
meetings of the tribal council for any purpose 
other than ceding tribal land to the United States 
(González & Torres, 2012). Recognizing that the 
Cherokee were not alone in facing these challenges 
to tribal sovereignty, Editor Elias Boudinot changed 
the name of his publication to the Cherokee Phoenix 
and Indian Advocate to better reflect its purpose as 
an advocate for Native interests beyond just issues 
affecting the Cherokee (Murphy & Murphy, 1981).
Boudinot used the Phoenix to challenge each 
new restriction of Native rights. When his staff was 
harassed or attacked, he would report on these events 
as well. When Boudinot published an exposé in 1830 
revealing that the local postmaster had been illegally 
selling liquor to local tribes, the postmaster directed 
the post office to withhold delivery of the paper’s 
printing supplies and its access to exchange papers. 
Boudinot responded in the pages of his paper:
This ‘new era’ has not only wrested from us 
our rights and privileges as a people, but it has 
closed the channel through which we could 
formerly obtain our news. By this means the 
resources of the Phoenix are cut off.
(Boudinot, 1831, p. 2)
It is worth noting the postmaster would again employ 
such means to restrict and control abolitionist pub-
lications in the antebellum South. Still, the Phoenix 
was able to continue publishing with little disruption 
in its regular printing schedule; copies of the Phoenix 
reached subscribers in several states and as far away 
as Germany, Paris, and London via the same postal 
service that was attempting to block its production 
(Murphy & Murphy, 1981). Some Phoenix articles 
were occasionally reprinted in the evangelical press 
and a few influential Northern commercial newspa-
pers including Niles’ Weekly Register in Washington, 
DC (González & Torres, 2012).
Congress’ passage of the 1830 Indian Removal 
Act, authorizing the forcible removal of the Cherokee 
and other nations from their traditional eastern 
homelands to land west of the Mississippi, was also 
highlighted in the Phoenix. The paper mounted a cam-
paign of advocacy and resistance. However, differ -
ing opinions about removal— acquiescence versus 
resistance—led to sharp divisions within the Cherokee 
leadership. Boudinot eventually sided with a group 
agreeing to sign a removal treaty. Cherokee Chief 
John Ross ordered Boudinot not to report on those 
internal divisions, and Boudinot resigned rather than 
face censorship. This was the first, but certainly not the 
last, time that tribal leadership would seek to control 
 cont
ent in tribal media.
Elijah Hicks, Ross’ son-in-law, replaced Boudinot 
as editor of the Phoenix and would continue the 
 c
ampaign against removal. When some Cherokee 
leaders signed the 1835 New Echota Treaty agreeing 
to removal, Hicks and leaders opposed to removal 
planned to move the Phoenix to a more secure loca-
tion in Tennessee. Georgia state militia intercepted 
the wagon train carrying the newspaper’s equipment, 
seized the press at gunpoint, and dumped its lead type 
into a well (González & Torres, 2012).
That attack may have destroyed the Phoenix’s  
ability to continue publishing, but it did not destroy 
the paper’s legacy or deny its future. Nine years later, 
Chief Ross and the Cherokee Council established a 
new weekly bilingual tribal newspaper, the Cherokee 
Advocate. It would become the longest running Native 
American newspaper of the 19th century, in print until 
1906 (Danky & Hady, 1984). And, true to its name, 
the Phoenix rose from the ashes to publish again, 
currently operating as an online news source cover-
ing news, culture, health, financial and sports news 
of interest and import to the Cherokee Nation. The 
Phoenix also has an active presence on radio, social 
media, and Y ouTube (https://www.cherokeephoenix.
org/). Ultimately, the Phoenix created the blueprint for 
a Native press serving its community as information 
source, educator, and advocate, while also providing a 
counterpoint to anti-Native American narratives and 
misrepresentations in the non-Native press.
Challenges Facing Native Media: The 
Phoenix’s Legacy Today
The Phoenix’s story revealed an important tension 
surrounding the purpose of Native media: is it 
intended to be an instrument which represents the 
interests and policies of tribal government, or is it 
meant to be a watchdog, holding that government 
accountable? That tension is one of the challenges 


Media Industries and Producing Media Content 271
N
ative media, particularly tribal media, continue to 
grapple with (Trahant, 1995).
In addition to issues of censorship, Native media 
face economic challenges and pressures stemming 
from the need to balance respect for tradition and 
culture with the practice of journalism. In the sections 
below, I’ll address each of these challenges in turn. 
Although it is true that some of these challenges are 
felt by all media, they seem particularly germane for 
Native media because of its history, unique purpose, 
and target audience.
Economic Realities
Today’s Native media grapple with the same finan-
cial struggles facing the media industry at large. 
When asked to rank the greatest threat to Indigenous 
media, more than half of the respondents to NAJA ’s 
Red Press Initiative (a 2018 survey of Native media 
producers and consumers) identified budgetary 
constraints and a lack of financial resources as the 
top threat (Pollard, 2020). Although many outlets 
are owned and supported by tribal governments, 
those which are not rely on subscriptions, advertis-
ing, or donor support to stay afloat; it is not always 
a successful approach and many outlets have been 
forced out of business.
Jodi Rave of the Indigenous Media Freedom 
Alliance reported a drop in media sources serving 
Indian Country from about 700 in 1998 to about 200 
in 2018. These ranged “from tribally owned newspa-
pers to freelancers (Rave, 2018).” New media tech-
nologies and platforms have since allowed both new 
entrants and returning voices to serve Indian Country, 
bringing the number of outlets to the 400 mentioned 
earlier, still a notable decline since 1998. However, it 
has not been easy. According to Bryan Pollard, former 
associate director of the Native American Journalists 
Association, even Indian Country Today (ICT), an 
established and widely respected entity in the field 
of Native journalism has struggled to stay in business 
(Pollard, 2020).
ICT got its start as a newspaper serving the 
Oneida Indian Nation in New Y ork, eventually becom-
ing an online publication called Indian Country Today 
Media Network in 2011. Six years later, ICT went on 
hiatus and its publication assets were donated to the 
National Congress of American Indians (Donella, 
2017). ICT relaunched in 2018 as a mobile-based 
publication with a new business model which sought 
advertising and donations from foundations as well 
as individual readers. In 2019, ICT added a television 
broadcast and now offers content to other tribal and 
public television outlets (Pollard, 2020).
Ongoing challenges related to economic sustain-
ability help to explain why tribal governments continue 
to be the largest ownership group in Native media, 
controlling an estimated 72% of newspapers and radio 
stations (Rave, 2018).
Editorial Control and Issues of Censorship
Although tribal ownership provides economic 
security, it often comes with editorial expecta-
tions, meaning limits on press freedom or out-
right censorship for many Native media outlets. 
For example, in 2018, the National Council of 
the Muscogee (Creek) Nation voted to repeal 
the tribe’s Free Press Act and move its award-
 
winning inde
pendent media arm, Mvskoke Media, 
under the nation’s Department of Commerce. The 
repeal also dissolved the outlet’s three-member 
editorial board, and staff members were told to 
report to the tribe’s commerce secretary (NAJA, 
2018). What happened with Mvskoke Media is 
not unusual; according to the Native American 
Journalists Association Red Press Initiative sur -
vey, journalistic freedom remains a challenge 
and is inconsistent. Nearly a third of tribal media 
producers responded that the tribal government 
tries to control tribal media through their budget 
at least half the time (NAJA, 2020). Additionally, 
nearly a fourth of tribal media staff responded 
that stories about tribal affairs or officials went 
unreported due to censorship, or that public rela-
tions staff influenced published news all or most 
of the time. Lastly, nearly half of tribal media staff  
reported that they were subject to intimidation or 
harassment when covering tribal affairs (NAJA, 
2020). These challenges around tribal ownership 
often hinder Native media’s ability to serve as an 
advocate for its intended audience. The censure 
of Mvskoke Media highlighted the need for an 
independent press in Indian Country and spurred 

272 Production
other tribal nations to take action; 172 years after 
the first issue of the Cherokee Phoenix rolled off the 
press, the Cherokee Council passed the Cherokee 
Independent Free Press Act of 2000 aimed at pro-
viding coverage of tribal government affairs that 
was free from political influence (Rave, 2018). But 
there is still much work to be done when it comes 
to press freedom in Indian Country.
Blending Cultural Tradition with the Practice of 
Journalism
Another important area highlighted by the Red 
Press Initiative is the cultural labor that is an inte-
gral part of the work of tribal media specifically 
and Native media in general. The educational and 
 inf
ormation-sharing roles of the Cherokee Phoenix 
continue in the mission and content of today’s 
Native journalism. Connection to culture is a cor -
nerstone of Native media, and Native editors and 
reporters bring their cultural values to their work. 
More than half of Native media workers surveyed 
said that their outlet reinforced cultural values most 
of the time (NAJA, 2020).
Language is an important way Native media offer 
cultural connections to audience members through 
publishing or broadcasting in their traditional language. 
The Phoenix, printed in Cherokee and English, used 
its pages to educate its audience about Sequoyah’s 
syllabary, a written form of the Cherokee spoken lan-
guage, resulting in an increased literacy rate among the 
Cherokee. Today’s Native media outlets often act as 
agents of language preservation for the communities 
they serve.
For Native journalists, cultural values inform their 
work. LaPoe and LaPoe (2017) found three important 
ways the cultural ritual of storytelling informs report-
ing in Native media: privacy, detailed meaning, and 
descriptive language.
Tom Arviso, CEO and publisher of the Navajo 
Times explained it this way:
We are taught there are certain things that you 
don’t let the public know. Even our own cere-
monies…There are still things we hold sacred. 
And, it is because of our Navajo beliefs and cul-
ture. We stick with that.
(LaPoe & LaPoe, 2017, p. 54) 
This means that editorial decisions about coverage 
of funerals or issues within a family may not be cov-
ered out of respect for the wishes of those involved 
or affected and because the good of the collective 
community is valued above the need to report the 
story. However, if the story involves a public official, 
then it will be reported because that individual has 
chosen to represent the interests of the community 
(LaPoe & LaPoe, 2017).
Richer detail and longer form writing are another 
way cultural values inform and are reflected in report-
ing by Native media outlets. According to LaPoe and 
LaPoe, this allows an emotional style of storytell-
ing which serves to tell a story that represents and 
respects culture, while fulfilling the journalistic man-
date of informing the public; they use an example of 
a story about horses who are not being cared for from 
the perspective of Navajo journalists.
Details are important in stories, such as abuse, 
because these stories reflect a larger cultural story. 
For example, discussing roaming horses not receiving 
enough water is more than an investigative story in the 
newspaper. The abuse reflects how Navajo lives might 
be changed in the future because the land and animals 
are lacking essential survival resources… The tragedy 
surrounding horses may appear as a sad isolated story 
from a mainstream media perspective. However, the 
story is tied to violations of Native beliefs (LaPoe & 
LaPoe, 2017, p. 56).
Making room for this type of storytelling within 
the framework of journalism empowers Native view-
points and offers Native journalists a place (and the 
space) to report on topics that are important to their 
audience in a way that resonates with that audience: 
water and land rights, sovereignty, and issues of iden-
tity. These stories are often overlooked by non-Native 
media outlets because they are not seen as stories rel-
evant to their audience or because they do not have 
the necessary context to understand why the story 
matters. In contrast, when non-Native media do cover 
stories in Indian Country, they often default to tired 


Media Industries and Producing Media Content 273
nar
ratives which only serve to reinforce old stereo-
types (Greene-Blye, 2020).
What Can Be Done?
We can focus on efforts and initiatives that sup-
port Native media and improve mainstream media 
coverage of Native issues. As I have shown, Native 
media face multiple challenges, including economic 
pressures. We can help support Native journalism by 
subscribing to Native information sources, support-
ing programs that offer professional development 
opportunities for Native journalists, increasing col-
laboration between Native and non-Native media 
outlets for purposes of sharing content produced 
by Native journalists, offering financial support to 
Native media, and seeking out and supporting pro-
grams that educate the next generation of Native 
journalists. Tribal leadership involved in tribally 
owned media outlets can be encouraged to value 
freedom of the press and the vital role played by the 
Native media in reporting on tribal governments.
In addition to bolstering Native media, we can 
help mainstream journalists move past stereotypi-
cal coverage of Native American issues, communi-
ties, and identity. Building relationships is a strong 
first step. Make contact and connections in Native 
American communities and find out what matters to 
those communities. Too often non-Native journalists 
practice parachute journalism—only jumping into our 
communities during times of conflict or tragedy and 
not being present to cover events and happenings 
in other contexts. If you are a non-Native journalist 
seeking to cover Indian Country, educate yourself via 
the resources available through the Native American 
Journalists Association and make a Native media out-
let part of your regular news diet. Avoid using stereo-
typical imagery and wording in your content.
W. Richard West, founding director of the 
National Museum of the American Indian, said that 
“it is only when a people assume authority over their 
stereotypes that they can truly begin to dispel them” 
(2007, p. xiv). West went on to say that it is “Only by cit-
ing facts and stories from their own communities and 
tribal cultures can Native people hope to convey the 
breadth and richness of Native life in this hemisphere, 
both today and in the past” (p. xiv).
Native media, and the Native journalists working 
for those outlets, are doing the important and neces-
sary work that West described. The impetus to give 
those voices the power to effect change lies with all of 
us and our decision to act on the suggestions outlined 
above.
