7.4 THE HISTORICAL CONTEXTS OF 
WOMEN’S AND PEOPLE OF COLOR’S 
ACCESS TO BROADCASTING
1
Rebecca Ann Lind
This essay argues that, due in large part to the inter-
section of race and gender, women and people of 
color have tended to follow different paths in their 
quest to become broadcasters.
A career in broadcast media can be exciting and 
fulfilling, and is a goal of many young people. But 
it’s not easy to get one’s foot in the door; in my own 
career as on-air talent, promotion director, and pro-
gram director, I encountered resistance because 
of my gender. There are multiple gatekeepers con-
trolling whether we may approach the microphone 
or camera, and if so, what we can say (in whose 
voice we may speak). So how do we gain access? 
This essay expands Susan Carter’s (1996, 2004) 
framework for conceptualizing women’s access to 
radio, to include people of color.
Although the contemporary media environ-
ment is undergoing rapid change, traditional broad-
casting and legacy media remain critical players 
and cannot be ignored. Radio is of particular value 
to Spanish-language listeners, in part due to its low 
cost; it is their medium of choice (Casillas, 2014). 
Sauls (2011) noted two key attributes of broadcast 
media: they are free, and they are local. Most impor-
tantly, perhaps, Jones (2009) argued that contrary to 
many people’s assumptions, social media and the 
internet have increased the power of legacy media. 
And Vos (2015) said that user-generated content 
has not increased the coverage of certain key sto-
ries, especially if the information is complex or is 
being hidden.


Media Industries and Producing Media Content 275
T
hree Models of Access
In Carter’s first model of women’s access, only the 
gender of the broadcaster changes. Women (or peo-
ple of color) fill positions traditionally held by men, 
but the message is unchanged. Despite the change 
of presenter, the content reflects the status quo and 
perpetuates the dominant ideology. In the second 
model of access, women formed collectives to pro-
gram discrete slots on a broadcast schedule. As a 
result “the gender content of a small part of the 
radio station programming was changed” (Carter, 
1996, p. 1). Program collectives of minoritized 
people function similarly, and challenge normative 
whiteness. In the third model, “the entire radio sta-
tion is dedicated to women’s programming” (2004, 
p. 170). Expanded to people of color, this includes 
stations focusing exclusively on the needs and inter-
ests of the minoritized group.
Although Carter didn’t present the models as a 
tool of criticism, they lend themselves well to the crit-
ical stance I take when considering their hegemonic 
functioning. I argue that for the most part, due to the 
intersection of race and gender, combined with an 
evolving cultural, political, and regulatory environ-
ment, women and people of color have rooted their 
access to media in different models. Although there 
are variations, the predominant pattern of access is 
that women typically used model one and people 
of color used models two and three. My examples 
primarily illustrate African Americans’ access, but 
Casillas’ (2014) impressive study of Spanish-language 
radio—although not invoking Carter’s models—is 
consistent with my argument.
Access for Women: Model One
Even from the very earliest days of radio, women 
(usually White) have followed Carter’s first model 
of access: they stepped into the shoes of (usually 
White) men to present the same type of content. 
Especially in the days before the commercial poten-
tial of radio was realized, radio was fairly open to 
the women who expressed an interest. Later, Halper 
wrote, “as radio grew more popular, some station 
owners, responding to letters from female listeners, 
decided they should devote more time to the house-
wives in the audience” (2014, p. 16), and many wom-
en’s programs were launched. These shows provided 
what was, per the dominant ideology, a natural place 
for women in radio. Thus the content, though pre-
sented by a woman, was what Carter called “gender 
neutral”—which of course meant that it reinforced 
traditional gender roles and heteronormativity.
America’s overt culture of segregation dur -
ing radio’s early days meant that Black people were 
unlikely to gain access via this model. People of color 
rarely appeared on general market (i.e., White) stations; 
when they did—even though the roles held by the few 
Black people on the air in the early days lacked the 
stigma of the minstrelsy tradition—they were racially 
anonymous. They lacked authenticity and did not 
reflect a culturally Black voice. Thus the performer’s 
race had changed, but the message hadn’t. The broad-
casts continued to function hegemonically.
By not providing visual cues to the speaker’s race, 
radio allows for a phenomenon Barlow (1999) called 
racial ventriloquism. Hence, the first seemingly Black 
superstar characters of radio—Amos ’n Andy—were 
voiced by White actors, and the first announcers of 
African descent in the US sounded White. When Jack 
L. Cooper began on WCAP in Washington, DC in 
1924, he did numerous accents including Black dialect 
(Spaulding, 1974). Nobody knew he was Black, and 
“for all intents and purposes it appeared that blacks 
still did not talk on the air” (Newman, 1988, p. 56).
Broadcasting, like other industries, allowed 
women increased access during World War II, when 
women were needed in both technical and on-air 
roles. Still, the trade publication Broadcasting called 
female engineers “feminine invaders.” And although 
the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers 
(IBEW) decided that women could join the union 
during the war, their membership would be only tem-
porary; after the war ended, they must quit their jobs 
as technicians and withdraw from the union (Halper, 
2014). Apparently, the threat of allowing women to 
invade the Brotherhood was eclipsed by the threat of 
hiring nonunion workers.
As times changed, by the 1950s, a new on-air role 
for women emerged. Sounding sexy might have been 

276 Production
an alternative to the happy homemaker, but it still rein-
forced traditional gender roles. This role became even 
more important when album-oriented rock gained 
strength on FM, creating what Halper called “a new 
archetype for women” (2014, p. 214).
For the most part, women seeking access to 
commercial broadcasting needed to ignore their gen-
der, their ethnic background, and their own voices, and 
produce an assimilationist message acceptable to the 
status quo. This happened in radio’s early days, but it 
remains evident. Connie Chung, with a degree in jour-
nalism, took a job as newsroom secretary at WTTG 
in Washington, DC. Accepting this traditionally female 
role eventually opened the door to a successful career 
which broke many barriers. A Chinese-American 
woman, Chung says she experienced more sexism 
than racism in her career. This may be attributable 
in part to the so-called model minority stereotype in 
which Asian Americans are assumed to be submis-
sive and “diligent, hardworking, quiet, high achiever[s]” 
(Chao, Chiu, Chan, Mendoza-Denton, & Kwok, 2013, 
p. 85).
Generally, being allowed access meant highlight-
ing neither one’s gender nor one’s race—
 especiall
y if 
one were not a member of a model minority. Newkirk 
(2000) argued that African Americans on television 
have been required to mimic Whites in their behavior, 
attitudes, and appearance, including speech 
 pa
tterns. 
Even allowing one’s hair to appear in a natural state—
when one was of African descent—revoked access. 
For example, in 1971, Melba Tolliver was assigned 
by WABC-TV , New Y ork, to cover the White House 
wedding of Tricia Nixon. But Tolliver appeared 
with her hair styled naturally in an Afro, and was 
suspended (Newkirk, 2000). What was natural for 
African Americans was deemed unacceptable even 
for a station in the nation’s largest market. After a 
while, a moderate Afro became acceptable—but the 
conscious manipulation of hair into an Afro-centric 
style for purely aesthetic reasons was still too much: 
in 1981, Dorothy Reed was suspended by KGO-TV , 
San Francisco, for wearing her hair in cornrows 
(Newkirk, 2000). Bringing attention to one’s race by 
consciously celebrating one’s racial identity remained 
at odds with the conditions by which access had been 
granted.
Access for People of Color: Models Two 
and Three
As noted above, although a few Black people had 
gained access to the airwaves despite segregation, 
early access for people of color followed what 
Carter identified as the second and third models. 
Jack L. Cooper became frustrated with the racial 
ventriloquism that limited him on WCAP, and 
which required him to produce material conform-
ing to general market expectations, thus epitomizing 
Carter’s first model of access. Although successful, 
Cooper left WCAP for Chicago, where he began 
programming discrete slots on the schedule.
Model Two
In this model of access, discrete blocks of time are 
programmed by people outside of the dominant 
group, to serve people outside of the dominant 
group. This model (as does the third) provides space 
for counter-hegemonic messages. The first exam-
ples of true Black-appeal radio—messages pre-
sented by Black people for Black people—followed 
Carter’s second model of access. On November 3, 
1929, Jack Cooper bought some time on WSBC in 
Chicago and launched The All-Negro Hour, provid-
ing entertainment, religion, and service to a Black 
audience. By buying the airtime outright and sell-
ing advertising time on his own, Cooper was a 
time-
 br
oker. In time-brokering, the station makes 
its money up front, and it’s up to the producer to 
recoup the investment. Cooper went on to make 
radio history, becoming, as Newman put it, “the 
starting point of any analysis” of Black-appeal radio 
(1988, p. 52).
It wasn’t uncommon for weak radio stations in 
large cities to split their broadcast schedules and sell 
blocks of time to others wanting to reach a specific 
ethnic group. Thus, “the opening of the airwaves to 
Black-oriented radio programming can be directly 
attributable to the profit motive rather than any feel-
ings of brotherhood or altruism” (Spaulding, 1974, p. 
35). This second model of access can still be found 
in independent commercial stations with weak signals 
(including, as of this writing, WSBC), but it is rarely 
used by women to gain access to commercial stations. 


Media Industries and Producing Media Content 277
W
hen women seek blocks of time to program in a way 
that reflects their own voices—and they certainly have 
done so—it has typically been on noncommercial 
(public) stations.
Model Three
People of color have a rich tradition of follow-
ing Carter’s third model of access (programming 
an entire station to appeal to a particular non-
 
dominant 
social group). Although individual women 
routinely appeared on the air since radio’s inception, 
few stations have catered exclusively to women. 
Because this model by definition means presenting 
content that is at least partly counter-hegemonic (if 
not, it would represent Carter’s first model), I can 
only identify two true women-oriented radio sta-
tions: WOMN and WWMN. Model three does not 
mean simply having an all-female (or, for example, 
all-Black) air staff. For example, WHER’s all-female 
air staff did not challenge the dominant ideology. 
WHER (Memphis) was presented as a novelty 
“all-girl station” and positioned itself as “1000 
Beautiful Watts” (Ganzert, 2003, p. 83). The studio 
was called “The Doll’s Den” and the control room 
“The Playroom”; engineering was decorated “with 
a clothesline and women’s undergarments” (p. 86). 
Because WHER changed the speakers but not the 
messages, it represents the first model.
Launched on August 28, 1978, WOMN-AM 
in Hamden (New Haven), Connecticut was run by 
women, emphasized women’s music, and highlighted 
women’s issues in its public affairs programs (Halper, 
2014). The station’s launch was promising. But unable 
to maintain an advertising base, the station stopped 
programming for women in September 1979. The 
next women-oriented station didn’t appear for more 
than two years. WWMN-AM in Flint, Michigan, 
debuted January 1, 1982, but had an even shorter life 
than WOMN; lacking sufficient ad revenue, it “was a 
dedicated women’s station for only 7 months” (Carter, 
2004, p. 179).
In contrast, by the late 1970s, Black-appeal radio 
stations had established a firm, clear, long-lasting, and 
valued presence in the African American communities 
they served. According to Spaulding (1974, p. 5), Black 
radio played “a significant role in developing a Black 
cultural consciousness.” He argued that “as Black ori-
ented radio stations sold consumer goods, they also 
sold the concepts of equality, increased the Blacks’ 
cultural self image and helped develop social, religious 
and political institutions and organizations within the 
Black community” (1974, p. 5).
On October 25, 1948, WDIA, Memphis, became 
the first Black-oriented radio station in the country. 
Cantor (1992) described the station as a legendary 
powerhouse of information, entertainment, and public 
service. It was a spokesperson and a communication 
network for the community, performing direct service 
such as public appearances, fund-raising, and support-
ing community projects.
Shortly after changing to the Black-appeal for -
mat, the station started making money—something 
its White owners had not been able to do through-
out multiple format changes. The owners realized 
the value of the Black marketplace. Popular wisdom 
held that Blacks had little money, didn’t own or listen 
to radios, and would not seek out products aimed at 
them. Popular wisdom encouraged lowering ad rates 
with the format change, but the owners did just the 
opposite (Cantor, 1992). The strategy worked; the 
money started rolling in.
By 1954, only about six years after WDIA ’s 
transformation and still a quarter century before the 
debut of WOMN, there were some 400 Black-appeal 
stations in the US. According to Newman, “these 
stations blanketed the country with black-appeal 
programming that was similar in format but individ-
ually tailored to the needs of local audiences” (1988, 
p. xii). Whether owned by Blacks or Whites, whether 
motivated by altruism or profit, Black-appeal 
radio 
 st
ations across the country shared a sense of 
purpose.
Some of those pursuits were overtly political. In 
the early 1960s, WVON in Chicago may have been 
“the first Black-oriented station in the country where 
management openly endorsed Black attitudes and 
the Civil Rights movement” (Spaulding, 1974, p. 70). 
WVON’s activist stance was made clear by its call let-
ters, standing for “Voice of the Negro.” As with WDIA, 
the station was profitable, with ad rates higher than 
those at the general market competition.

278 Production
Hopes and Fears: LPFM and Media 
Consolidation
One way that more people may gain access to 
broadcast radio is through low power FM (LPFM) 
stations. Instead of covering an entire urban area, 
the LPFM signal covers a neighborhood or a 
 comm
unity—about 2–4 miles. LPFM’s relatively 
low construction and operating costs put broad-
casting within reach of varied religious organiza-
tions, schools, and other nonprofit or community 
groups. However, there are only about 800 LPFM 
stations across the US.
Even if LPFM does expand and reach its full 
potential—which it still might—it is not a panacea. The 
mainstream media are still the key, still the media that 
matter the most to most of the US—and most of the 
mainstream media are owned by just a few big corpo-
rations. Many scholars have considered the impact of 
media consolidation on the diversity of media content 
(Byerly, 2014; Craig, 2015; Negrón-Muntaner & Abbas, 
2016). Craig’s case study of Black Entertainment 
Television revealed that within a few years of its acqui-
sition by Viacom, it had been turned “into another 
generic media outlet” (2015, p. 88). Economic pres-
sures and consolidation have similarly constrained the 
diversity of Spanish-language radio, which Castaneda 
Paredes (2003) argued may be of greater concern than 
with English-language radio, given the smaller number 
of stations broadcasting in Spanish.
Ownership matters, and we must not forget that 
corporate leaders’ overarching responsibilities are 
to shareholders, not citizens. Although owners aren’t 
involved in the day-to-day decisions made by media 
outlets, they “have significant influence on the develop-
ment of corporate policy and practice, as well as in the 
hiring of the personnel who directly make decisions” 
(Craig, 2015, p. 5). Craig argued that “the absence of 
African Americans among media owners equates 
to silencing alternative voices” (p. 5). Byerly made a 
similar claim: “media conglomeration signals the con-
solidation of men’s economic and political power, and 
the further marginalization of women’s [power],” and 
presents “structural blocks to women’s voices in public 
discourse and the social and political participation that 
flows from that discourse” (2014, p. 323).
One of the most significant fears about media 
consolidation is that it will limit the flow of information 
on which citizens of a democracy rely. According to 
Grossman:
The number of news channels is certainly mul-
tiplying in this telecommunications era, but the 
number of news sources is shrinking…We are 
seeing a kind of reverse funnel effect, in which 
more and more channels are pumping out the 
same news headlines gathered from a single 
all-purpose source.
(1999, p. 21)
Indeed, Jones, stating that most of the news dis-
seminated via social media originates from legacy 
media, highlighted the irony that “the Web, which is 
usually touted for its power to diminish the power of 
established media, has effectively concentrated that 
power into even fewer institutions” (2009, p. 186).
Although the internet has changed many things 
in our world, it hasn’t significantly reduced the power 
of the media giants, who continue to rule the media 
landscape. We must continue to think about whether 
women and people of color are being granted access 
to the media.
Contextualizing Access at the 
Intersection of Race and Gender
Why did individual women approach the media so 
differently than individual people of color? Why did 
stations programming for women fare so differently 
than, for example, Black-appeal stations? Certainly 
segregation and discrimination help explain why 
people of color didn’t use the first model. But why 
didn’t women more fully embrace the second and 
third models? And why didn’t women’s stations 
thrive, as did Black-appeal stations? We should 
consider the intersection of race and gender, pub-
lic acceptance of the women’s movement at any 
particular point in time, and media policy and reg-
ulation. For example, WWMN and WOMN were 
launched “near the end of the modern women’s lib-
eration movement” when the “backlash against the 
women’s movement was gaining energy” (Carter, 


Media Industries and Producing Media Content 279
2004, p
. 181). Those stations unsuccessfully resisted 
being called “feminist” due to the term’s negative 
connotations; even today, the backlash to feminism 
has not abated.
Thus, especially in the early days of broadcasting, 
White women could access mainstream airwaves, but 
did not question the status quo. This is Carter’s first 
model of access. The messages were comfortable to 
society; the women presented themselves as happy 
homemakers or sexy companions. Later, women of 
color were at times granted access, but if they cele-
brated their ethnic or racial identity, their access was 
often revoked.
Early broadcasting did not welcome people rec-
ognized as non-White. Reflecting both the dominant 
ideology and the culture of overt segregation, the first 
seemingly Black voices on radio were presented by 
White actors. The first African Americans on the air 
sounded White. Station owners believed that their 
White audiences would not welcome Blacks into their 
homes. The only options were to carve out a few hours 
here and there (model two), or to appear on a Black-
appeal station (model three).
When blocks of time are programmed by women 
and people of color they frequently bring issues of 
race/ethnicity and gender to the foreground. They 
are more akin to what is generally called the minor-
ity press than to contemporary commercial broad-
casting, usually with a counter-hegemonic mission. 
However—especially after deregulation resulted in 
the removal of many requirements for news and public 
affairs programming (Carter, 2004)—because the sta-
tions making time available to these groups tend to be 
weak, the message will not reach the bulk of the pop-
ulation, and change will be that much harder to realize.
The third model of access, a station fully and 
robustly featuring the voices of women or people of 
color, presents both the greatest possibility and the 
greatest frustration. Members of subordinated groups 
can use their own voices to create their own messages 
in an environment welcoming them in all their cultural 
richness. Their authentic voices can be fully embraced 
and explored in attempts to entertain, enlighten, and 
educate not only members of their cultural group but 
also mainstream culture. Ironically, these messages are 
easy for members of the dominant group to ignore sim-
ply by not including the station among their favorites.
In 2004, Carter argued that only the first model of 
access has survived to any great extent. Extending her 
argument to include people of color:
the lesson of the three models of access for 
women [or people of color]…[is] a sober one: 
Women [or people of color] could speak if 
they kept the content “gender [or race] neu-
tral.” Messages that were gendered feminist [or 
advocated for racial equality or celebrated a 
racial/ethnic perspective] were either margin-
alized or silenced altogether.
(2004, p. 181)
Equal opportunities laws have removed the overt 
restrictions preventing people of color from using 
the first model of access, but this assimilationist 
model precludes drawing attention to one’s race 
or ethnicity. To the extent that the access route 
is paved with the ideologies of colorblindness or 
postracialism, the messages cannot but function 
hegemonically.
All in all, the history of women’s and people of 
color’s access to broadcasting, and the extent to 
which they were allowed to speak in their own voices, 
demonstrates that society continues to be less threat-
ened by women (at least not those labeled “feminist”) 
than by people of color. Simultaneously, in today’s 
deregulated and increasingly consolidated media 
environment, true alternative voices in mainstream 
broadcasting are becoming harder and harder to find. 
As citizens, we need alternative voices (with a nod to a 
banner splashed across WVON’s home page in 2016) 
“Now , more than ever!”

7.5: WHAT WAS SHE THINKING?: 
ENCODING MEANING IN THREE 
MODERN RAPE-REVENGE FILMS
Barbara G. Friedman
This analysis of writers’ and directors’ approaches 
to making rape-revenge films (films in which a per-
son who has experienced rape enacts vengeance 
on their rapist) discusses four themes important to 
the writers/directors: finding currency, confront-
ing rape culture, incorporating authenticity, and 
advancing the genre.
When Leah McKendrick began writing her film 
MFA in 2015, stories about campus sexual assault 
filled the news, including the alarming case of Brock 
Turner, a Stanford athlete given a lenient sentence 
following his conviction for sexually assaulting an 
unconscious woman. The same year, CNN reported 
a national survey that found 23% of college women 
had experienced sexual assault, and The Hunting 
Ground documentary showed how ill-equipped uni-
versities were to confront the issue (Wallace, 2015).
“I was sick of reading the same story over and 
over, and [of] administrations across the country doing 
nothing,” said McKendrick, whose experiences as a 
young actress included being groped and kissed with-
out consent at an audition (Roberts, 2017). Expressing 
fury and frustration in her art, McKendrick made 
MFA’s protagonist, Noelle, a rape survivor-turned vig-
ilante who orchestrates a killing spree against campus 
rapists who’ve gone unpunished. It was “my act of 
rebellion,” McKendrick said (Buder, 2017).
Rape-Revenge Films
“Rape—real, threatened or implied—has been a 
staple of American cinema more or less from the 
beginning,” wrote Clover (2015), but the “rape-
 
r
evenge story as drama…came into its own” in 
the late 1970s during the feminist rape reform 


Media Industries and Producing Media Content 281
mo
vement. In films of this period, “rape becomes 
a problem for women themselves to solve” (pp. 
137–138). This genre has resurfaced amid renewed 
antisexual violence activism, including the #MeToo 
movement calling powerful men and institutions to 
account for their abuses.
At its simplest, a rape-revenge film “is one 
whereby a rape central to the narrative is punished by 
an act of vengeance, either by the victim themselves 
or an agent (most commonly a partner or family mem-
ber)” (Heller-Nicholas, 2021, p. 19). Unlike narratives 
depicting a man taking revenge for the rape of a wife 
or daughter—which use sexual violence to justify a 
hyperviolent version of masculinity—rape-revenge 
narratives “offer an entire genre with the potential 
to articulate a feminist response to rape” (Projansky, 
2001, p. 60). They empower characters rather than 
increasing their experience of vulnerability. When 
revenge is taken by a woman who has experienced 
rape, Projansky argued, those films “can be under -
stood as feminist narratives in which women face rape, 
recognize that the law will neither protect nor avenge 
them, and then take the law into their own hands” (p. 
60). “What could be more empowering than watching 
a woman wreaking violent vengeance on her abusers,” 
asked one critic, calling rape-revenge films “a feminist 
weapon for the #MeToo generation” (Bilson, 2018).
Encoding Meaning in Rape-Revenge 
Films
More than simply reflections of external reality, 
media texts are encoded with meaning derived 
from cultural norms, industry structures, lived expe-
rience, and human decision-making. Thus, when 
filmmakers talk about their work, they are telling 
a story about encoding, a defining moment in the 
production process when ideas and influences are 
turned into communication.
Encoding begins early in the communication cir-
cuit, with a filmmaker’s worldview and influences—it 
is the “story [she] sees in her head.” As a film makes 
its way through development, production, and distri-
bution, those collaborative processes inevitably shape 
a film’s final version—as the expression goes, things 
get “left on the cutting-room floor.” Further, audiences 
might decode a media text in a way other than the 
message creator intended (Hall, 1980/2012).
I analyzed published interviews with filmmak-
ers (writers and directors) to understand how they 
encoded meaning in three rape-revenge films: MFA 
(2017), Black Christmas (2019), and Promising Y oung 
Woman (2020). These films were chosen for their 
focus on campus sexual assault, pervasive in the 
United States. In the thriller MFA (2017), written by 
Leah McKendrick and directed by Natalia Leite, the 
accidental death of an art student’s rapist sends her 
on a killing spree that simultaneously disinhibits her 
creativity. The slasher Black Christmas (2019), writ-
ten by April Wolfe and Sophia Takal, and directed 
by Takal, is the second remake of a 1974 classic, in 
which a group of female students stalked by a cam-
pus killer during their Christmas break decide to band 
together and fight back. A main character is a survivor 
of sexual assault. Promising Y oung Woman, hereafter 
PYW (2020), written and directed by Emerald Fennell, 
has been called a dark comedy, thriller, and romantic 
comedy combined. The film’s main character avenges 
the rape at a med-school party of her best friend Nina, 
who later died by suicide. In each of the three films, it 
is revealed that the rape victims reported their assaults, 
but no perpetrators were punished.
Interviews with filmmakers are a standard part of 
promotional tours and often a contractual obligation. 
They share a purpose with this study—to capture film-
makers’ understanding of their work and its relevance. 
The interviews I analyzed, conducted by mainstream 
and niche media, occurred near the time of each film’s 
theatrical release or award nomination. I undertook a 
close reading of the writers’ and directors’ own words 
describing their actions, experiences, and intentions. 
Four themes were identified: finding currency, con-
fronting rape culture, incorporating authenticity, and 
advancing the genre. Each theme, revealing an active 
process, is discussed in turn.
Finding Currency
Filmmakers encode their work with meaning by 
drawing “topics, treatments, ‘definitions of the sit-
uation’ …from the wider sociocultural and political 
structure” (Hall, 1980/2012, p. 138). McKendrick 

282 Production
reacted to cumulative reports about campus sexual 
assault, and Fennell said PYW  contributed to “this 
conversation we’re having about how we [as a soci-
ety] treat women and ask them to make the best of 
their trauma” (Seth, 2021).
As Takal weighed the offer to remake Black 
Christmas, she searched for “its connection to this 
moment in time” (Page, 2019), and found it in the 
televised confirmation hearings for then-Supreme 
Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh, who stood accused 
by three women of sexual misconduct—charges he 
denied in a fit of rage and tears (Hauser, 2018). Takal 
told The New Y ork Times she “was really struck by how 
emotional he was, how aggrieved he was”—behavior 
that proved familiar to many observers (Hart, 2018). 
Takal said Kavanaugh became a model for one of 
the film’s villains, described by the interviewer as “a 
priggish classics instructor who spends a lot of time 
with frat boys, laments the good ol’ days when men 
ran everything, and goes into a rage when he thinks 
women are trying to usurp his power” (Ito, 2019).
Confronting Rape Culture
Encoded in the three films was recognition of the 
normative and pervasive nature of rape culture, 
“this thing that we all grew up with,” said Fennell 
(Seth, 2021). “There’s something profoundly dis-
turbing about how completely endemic this idea 
is that if you got drunk at a party, whatever hap-
pened was…your problem” (Verhoeven, 2021). The 
premise of PYW reflects that encoding: Cassie trolls 
bars feigning drunkenness, then confronts the “nice 
guys” who, predictably, try to take advantage of her. 
Fennell deliberately cast likeable actors in the roles 
to “play with the idea that men who are perceived 
as ‘good guys’ are also capable of bad behavior” 
(Sandberg, 2021).
Rape culture is supported by rape myths: false 
beliefs about rape, rape victims, and rapists that create 
a climate hostile to rape victims. The women filmmak-
ers in this study encoded their work in ways that con-
front rape myths, including the belief that “real rape” 
is committed by strangers, that drunkenness equals 
consent for sexual activity, and that women lie about 
rape when they are embarrassed or disappointed with 
a sexual encounter, as Banet-Weiser (2018) noted in 
her study of feminism and misogyny. When PYW’s 
Cassie finally confronts Nina’s rapist, for example, he 
recites an all-too-familiar litany of excuses: Maybe 
she regretted it after. She was into it. We were drunk. 
I didn’t do anything! Both MFA and Black Christmas 
provide their protagonists with the opportunity to con-
front their rapists, who respond with similar incredulity. 
“What can be worse than gathering your strength to 
speak out against your rapist, and being told…it never 
happened,” asked McKendrick (Subissati, 2018).
Rape culture was encoded in the films’ rep-
resentation of male-dominated groups. Research on 
campus sexual assault has found that members of male 
athletic teams and fraternities are overrepresented 
among rape offenders; these groups tend to encourage 
and enforce a model of masculinity in which women 
are exploited for sex and status (Syrett, 2009). Riley’s 
rapist and the killers in Black Christmas are members of 
a fraternity who act in concert to destroy “disobedient 
women.” Wolfe encoded the group as an evil cult of 
“men who really want to keep a stranglehold on that 
[male-female] binary” (Lopez, 2019). Noelle’s targets 
in MFA are fraternity members and athletes who have 
gotten away with rape, and in PYW, Nina’s rapist is 
insulated from consequences by his fraternal group.
Incorporating Authenticity
Rape-revenge films are about fantasy-wish fulfill-
ment, but these filmmakers talked about encoding 
their work with authenticity. In a familiar gesture, 
a Black Christmas character walking alone at night 
weaves her keys between her fingers as a weapon 
of self-defense. It was a “little detail that felt real to 
[women’s] experiences of going through the world,” 
said Wolfe (FilmIsNow, 2019). PYW ’s Fennell said 
she wanted to engage “the deliciousness of the 
[revenge] genre” but show “the reality of what 
vengeance is and what grief is” (Sandberg, 2021). 
As a result, her original script avoided the “big, ‘f**k 
you’ cathartic ending” in which the protagonist 
“put[s] on a sexy outfit and she’s going to kill a ton 
of guys,” she said, and instead, Cassie is killed by 
Nina’s rapist. “I cannot imagine being in a room with 
a man and threatening him where it plays out in any 
different way—no matter how much we want it to 
be the case.” When funders balked, Fennell had her 


Media Industries and Producing Media Content 283
pr
otagonist devise a contingency plan that secured 
her killer’s arrest (Aurthur & Donnelly, 2021).
Advancing the Genre
Takal’s first script for the remake of Black Christmas 
was a “straight-ahead slasher movie with a little 
bit of campus sexual politics thrown in” (Erbland, 
2019). But “in 2019, I didn’t want to make a movie 
about a bunch of women getting slaughtered. It just 
gave me a pit in my stomach” (Collis, 2019). She 
asked Wolfe, a film critic and horror fan, for help 
with the script. “Women do die in slashers,” Wolfe 
said. “But we thought there might be a better way to 
tell a story” (FilmIsNow, 2019).
The two concentrated on the feelings that the 
original film evoked rather than its specific plot points. 
“I wanted to make something scary and horrific, but…
moving the genre forward in some way,” said Takal 
(Crucchiola, 2020). Among the changes she and Wolfe 
made were to add depth to the women characters, so 
they weren’t treated like “disposable bodies” (Erbland, 
2019), render the villain as a system (patriarchy) rather 
than a crazed stranger and have the women under 
assault engage in collaborative vengeance for collec-
tive gain. The latter strategy was a deliberate subver-
sion of the slasher genre’s “final girl,” a trope coined by 
film scholar Clover (2015) in which a smart, capable, 
virginal girl is the last character left alive to confront 
the killer. The final girl is a masculine conceit, said 
Wolfe, “individuality triumphing over everything as 
the ultimate success.” A feminist approach called for 
egalitarianism and was in keeping with the time, she 
said. “Y ou can’t win without multiple people pulling 
together” (Lopez, 2019).
The filmmakers were intentional about subvert-
ing the “male gaze,” referring to Mulvey’s (1975) theory 
of gendered subjectivity and visual pleasure. MFA ’s 
Leite said, “Most rape-revenge films fetishize the rape 
and the woman in it. It’s like they are trying to make 
it hot that she is seeking revenge” (Gallagher, 2017). 
MFA depicts Noelle’s rape, but Leite said to convey its 
seriousness, she put viewers in Noelle’s point of view. 
“I wanted to show it exactly how it might happen, not 
move the camera, just do a long take.…There’s no 
scary music leading up to this moment, it’s just hap-
pening and that’s how she would feel. She would be 
so surprised and shocked that all of a sudden this boy 
who was being sweet to her is pushing her down on 
the bed. I think that’s how a lot of women feel in those 
situations…you’re just so shocked you don’t have time 
to react because your reality has been turned upside 
down” (Peterson, 2017).
Encoding as a Way to Understand 
Change
This analysis of published interviews with the cre-
ators of three modern rape-revenge films helps 
us understand how they encoded their work with 
meaning at a complex cultural moment. Although 
the filmmakers at times tried to unlink their work 
from #MeToo—Fennell urged interviewers to 
pay attention to “the film itself,” not the context 
(Fleming, 2021)—the work is nevertheless bound to 
present-day calls to break the silence around sexual 
assault, just as the 1970s rape-revenge genre flour -
ished alongside the feminist rape reform movement. 
Studio decision-makers surely recognized the bene-
fits of supporting women-led films that “tapped into 
something…so of-the-moment” (Crucchiola, 2020).
The films in this study—MFA , Black Christmas, 
and Promising Y oung Woman—address campus sex-
ual assault, a current issue on the public agenda. A 
still wider range of rape-revenge-themed films and TV 
series uses similar encoding to explore sexual assault 
in different settings: Revenge, I May Destroy Y ou, The 
Handmaid’s Tale, to name a few. That the subgenre is 
being populated rapidly, and mostly by women crea-
tors is inarguably a statement on contemporary social 
relations and indicative of greater opportunities for 
women in the film industry.
Given the ways the filmmakers challenged genre 
boundaries, their impact could resonate for gener -
ations. In Black Christmas, Takal and Wolfe upended 
the slasher’s “final girl” conceit by fashioning a radical 
feminist sisterhood fighting against a harmful system, 
rather than a lone girl battling a deranged individual. 
Importantly, they insisted on writing characters with 
intersectional identities (Wolfe, 2020). MFA’s Leite and 
McKendrick resisted the fetishized male gaze common 
in rape-revenge films and instead centered the protag-
onist’s point of view as she channeled rage into retribu-
tion. Finally, PYW, by Fennell’s admission, embraced a 

284 Production
“see-saw” of genres, effectively destabilizing them all. 
In 2019, Wolfe anticipated “hybrid movies…a bit wild, 
a bit ‘kitchen sink’ ,” as a way the horror genre would be 
transformed (Reeves, 2019). Thus, transforming gen-
res requires encoding that recognizes and transcends 
them.
Whether audiences decoded MFA, Black 
Christmas, and PYW as their creators intended is 
beyond this study’s scope; yet a negotiated reading 
(Hall, 1980/2012) might recognize, for example, 
that sexual assault affects all demographic groups. 
Despite the films’ narrow focus on women, however, 
they were encoded in a way that connected with 
wider audiences, and as a result, won the filmmak-
ers awards and fresh opportunities (Rubin, 2021). 
Perhaps these successes will inspire new filmmak-
ers whose worldviews encode “a better way to tell 
a story.”

7.6: EDDIE HUANG: FRESH OFF THE BOAT
Dear Aunaetitrakul
The author studies Eddie Huang’s involvement with 
and response to the ABC television series based on 
his memoir Fresh Off the Boat. Dissatisfied with 
how the series reworked the material, and feeling 
like it did not accurately reflect his experiences, 
Huang left after the first season.
On February 4, 2015, ABC premiered Fresh Off the 
Boat, a sitcom based on the best-selling memoir of 
Taiwanese-Chinese American chef Eddie Huang. 
For many millennial Asian Americans, who finally 
get to see a show resembling their lived experiences 
in America, the show is a ground-breaking moment. 
Fresh Off the Boat is the first show with a dominant 
Asian American ensemble cast on television since 
Margaret Cho’s short-lived sitcom All-American Girl 
in 1994.
Fresh Off the Boat was a big deal, especially for 
millennials—finally, there was Asian American rep-
resentation on primetime television. When I worked 
at an Asian American cultural center at a California 
university, students talked about the show nonstop 
after the premiere. Asian American students from 
various ethnic identities bonded over the show. As a 
student affairs professional whose work is to support 
historically marginalized students, I noticed how the 
show brought students together and enabled them to 
share experiences in navigating their racial identity, 
specifically in a culture that promotes and maintains 
whiteness.
In general, the Asian American community wel-
comed the show with open arms. But despite jubila-
tion from the Asian American community and rave 
reviews, Fresh Off the Boat faced backlash from an 
unlikely source—Eddie Huang.

286 Production
Setting the Stage
Huang became a celebrity chef and household 
name after he opened his restaurant, BaoHaus, in 
2009. In 2013, he published Fresh Off the Boat: a 
Memoir. The book provides a glimpse into Huang’s 
struggle to reconcile his Asian American identity 
and his cultural affiliation with Black culture while 
growing up in a predominantly White neighbor -
hood in Orlando, Florida. Huang shared narratives 
of racism he encountered and his relationship with 
his parents. The success of the book led to a his-
toric moment in Asian American television history 
when ABC agreed to a pilot commitment based on 
Huang’s memoir in August 2013. Nahnatchka Khan, 
the show writer, served as the executive producer 
along with Jake Kasdan and Melvin Mar; Huang 
also joined the production team as a producer.
In January 2014, ABC ordered the production of 
the pilot. Constance Wu and Randal Park were cast 
as Huang’s parents, Jessica, a real estate agent, and 
Louis, owner of the Cattleman’s Ranch restaurant in 
Orlando; Hudson Yang was cast to play 12-year-old 
Huang. In May, Fresh Off the Boat was picked up as a 
series. Kourtney Kang joined the team as co-executive 
producer, and season one production took place from 
August to December.
The Pressure
Being the first Asian American sitcom on television 
in 20 years came with insurmountable pressure 
for the Asian American producers. “It freaks me 
out that if it doesn’t work for some reason, it’ll be 
another 20-year drought,” Mar said (Caramanica, 
2015). The show had a lot at stake, even apart from 
the financial pressures and risks associated with 
new TV programs. It was about time to make the 
Asian American community more visible on televi-
sion. Khan and Mar were interested in making the 
show because of their own immigrant experiences 
(Hibberd, 2015; Andreeva & Petski, 2017). Everyone 
involved knew they were part of history and wanted 
to make it right—so it was no surprise that Huang 
wanted a seat at the table. Typically, when a studio 
pays for the rights to a property the author is not 
involved with the production, but Mar revealed that 
Huang “insisted on being brought on as producer 
as a condition of the sale” (Yang, 2015). Huang said 
that he wanted to be a part of the show because he 
thought he could change the way media portrayed 
Asian Americans on television.
Despite a shared interest and similar family 
backgrounds, Huang, Khan, and Mar had different 
approaches on how to make Fresh Off the Boat come to 
fruition. There were problems and conflicts among the 
production team and with the network. These started 
before production began on the pilot and didn’t end 
until Huang called it quits at the end of season one 
production.
The first problem was the pilot’s working title: Far 
East Orlando. ABC did not explain the name change 
(Nguyen, 2014), but Huang did not like it. In March 
2014, he tweeted “ATTN ASIAN & ALL OTHER 
PEOPLE: Isn’t ‘Far East Orlando’ an archaic name? 
Let @ABCNetwork know you want it to be called 
FRESH OFF THE BOAT!” In response, a number of 
his followers expressed how the name Far East Orlando 
watered down the content of Huang’s memoir. When 
ABC ordered the production of the series in May 2014, 
the title had been restored (Boedeker, 2014).
Generally speaking, fresh off the boat, or FOB, is a 
phrase describing immigrants, particularly Asians, who 
are unfamiliar with American culture and traditions. 
The label is a byproduct of the perpetual foreigner 
stereotype which assumes that Asian Americans will 
always be seen as foreigners regardless of their citizen-
ship and social status. Huang said he called the book 
Fresh Off the Boat because “[he] identified more with 
my parent’s generation and our generation of overseas 
Chinese than anything else because we have no home. 
We are literally fresh off the boat” (Huang, 2015b). 
He intentionally used a derogatory phrase that has 
plagued Asian Americans for generations, to acknowl-
edge his pride as an immigrant and his family’s struggle 
to assimilate to the American culture. Khan agreed and 
joined Huang in advocating for the phrase as the sit-
com title (Chen & Jha, 2014).
To name the show Fresh Off the Boat suggested 
that the producers and the network were ready to 
tackle the term and Asian American stereotypes 
through the Huangs. With the name set, and the first 
major problem resolved, production began.


Media Industries and Producing Media Content 287
So did the s
econd major problem: represent-
ing the material in Huang’s memoir. As noted above, 
Huang was named a producer, a credit he received 
throughout the series, and was actively involved in 
the first season’s 13 episodes. He was often dissat-
isfied with how the show portrayed his life stories, 
and shared his concerns. For example, three weeks 
before the show’s premiere, Huang published an essay, 
Bamboo-Ceiling TV, which was republished on the night 
of the premiere (Huang, 2015a). In it, Huang provided 
a detailed narrative of what transpired behind the 
scenes and called out Khan and Mar for whitewash-
ing the show. Huang had multiple concerns about the 
show, including the voice-over narration, the scripting, 
and the reconceptualization of the characters and their 
experiences.
One of the key components of season one was 
Huang’s voice-over narration. This had not been part 
of the original concept, but was added after audience 
testing (Huang, 2015a). According to Huang, Mar 
thought the show needed to do more to appeal to 
White people, so he pitched the notion of a voice-over, 
mimicking the narration that had worked well in ABC’s 
sitcom The Wonder Y ears (1988–1993). Mar suggested 
Huang do the narration so that White audience mem-
bers could get a better understanding of Eddie as a 
character. Huang’s excitement about the creative pos-
sibility of the narrative technique was strong, yet tem-
pered by the knowledge that it was simply to comfort 
and entice White audiences.
Huang’s concerns grew stronger when he read 
the script. During production, Huang (2015a) attended 
meetings and “checked [the scripts] for authenticity.” At 
first, the writers seemed receptive to Huang’s feedback, 
but that changed. Huang (2015a) thought “the lines [for 
the voiceover] were more or less in some acceptable 
‘network Eddie’ compromise voice.” Huang wanted to 
keep the show true to his lived experience—to reflect 
his memoir as written—and he didn’t think the narra-
tion (or the scripts in general) did so.
Huang’s problems with the scripts culminated 
when the writers wanted his character to say “America 
is great” in the last scene of episode 8, in which Eddie 
and Walter (who had called Eddie a chink in the pilot) 
bonded. In this scene, Eddie saw Walter, a Black class-
mate with whom he’d had a strained relationship, wear-
ing the same Beastie Boys t-shirt as him. They learned 
that they’d both attended a Beastie Boys concert over 
the weekend and connected over their shared love of 
rap. The line seems to have been intended to acknowl-
edge the robustness of American diversity—two 
children of color bonding over White Jewish rappers. 
But using the Beastie Boys in this narrative troubled 
Huang, who was more connected with Black hip-hop 
artists. This was designed to be comfortable to the 
White audience: an “acceptable, unthreatening [gate-
way] to black culture” (Huang, 2015a). It can perhaps 
even be interpreted as an act of a White savior—White 
rappers can unite Blacks and Asians. Ultimately, to say 
“America is great” would have been to dismiss Huang’s 
complicated relationship with America and his experi-
ences with racism. Huang (2015a) refused to read the 
line. In November 2014, Huang (2015a) tweeted his 
frustration: “Producers of #FreshOffTheBoat want me 
to say ‘America is great’ or they’ll replace me. What’s 
a chink to do?” Eventually, the line was cut, but it had 
become clear to Huang that the TV version of Fresh 
Off the Boat didn’t reflect his memoir.
When reporters asked Mar and Khan to respond 
to Huang’s critiques, the producers said the show was 
loosely inspired by the memoir. It was not a direct 
translation of the source text or even the characters 
within that text:
[The show] is not a documentary or a bio-pic 
of [Eddie’s] life but it’s inspired by his story...Y ou 
start with the source materials, which inspires 
the show, then you build it up and make it 
something everyone is proud of. These are 
fictionalized characters that do and say things 
that Eddie’s family never said or did.
(Ann, 2015)
The writers had rewritten Huang’s story into some-
thing to which he could no longer relate. After epi-
sode 11 aired in April, 2015, Huang tweeted “I’m 
happy people of color are able to see a reflection 
of themselves through #FreshOffTheBoat on @
ABCNetwork but I don’t recognize it.” Fresh Off the 
Boat resonated with many immigrant stories, but 
not his. Huang (2015a) understood that the show 
could not represent everyone. But for those the 
show did represent, he wanted the representations 
to be accurate. Huang had said that the pilot was the 

288 Production
only episode to which he could relate—it even tack-
led the word “chink,” a racial slur against Asians. It 
showed the young Eddie’s attempt to fit in with his 
classmates: trying to gain acceptance from White 
students by eating Lunchables at school instead of 
the traditional Taiwanese food.
To Huang, the way the show re-conceptualized 
the characters meant mis-representing the stories 
Huang had articulated in the memoir. For example, 
Huang related to hip-hop and Black culture because 
of his struggle to fit in as an Asian American. Hip-
hop music expressed his pain with assimilation, and 
the pain he felt growing up in an emotionally abusive 
home and navigating his racial identity. But on the 
show, Eddie is just a rebellious teen who uses hip-hop 
to get on his mother’s nerves. Jessica is a stereotyp-
ical Asian tiger mom who wants to be in control of 
everything including the family’s business. Louis is a 
businessman, a laid-back father who believes in the 
American dream. Emery, Eddie’s younger brother, is 
a charismatic nerd. Evan, the youngest, is flamboyant 
and a mama’s boy. Jenny, Eddie’s grandmother, is often 
times treated as a wallflower. These characters mis-
represented the real-life Huangs. When the show failed 
to reflect Huang’s memoir accurately, he believed he 
had no choice but to leave.
Eddie Huang Peace Out
After 18 months of back and forth, I had 
crossed a threshold and become the audience. 
I wasn’t the auteur, the writer, the actor, or the 
source material. I was the viewer and I finally 
understood it. This show isn’t about me, nor is 
it about [Asian Americans]. The network won’t 
take that gamble right now.
(Huang, 2015a)
Huang was naïve about the network television busi-
ness, and struggled to accept the direction of Fresh 
Off the Boat (Huang, 2015a; Yang, 2015). Huang’s 
public vacillation between criticizing and praising 
the show conveyed that he was not ready to accept 
that the show differed from his memoir and that he 
had no control in the writing room. It could also be 
argued that he did not know how to navigate the 
dual pressures of unfamiliarity with the industry and 
of his story representing the first Asian American 
sitcom in two decades.
Prior to the premiere, Huang had been elated 
to see a Fresh Off the Boat promo during a televised 
football game (Huang, 2015a). He tweeted and posted 
Instagram pictures of Fresh Off the Boat billboards, and 
encouraged his followers to watch the show. At an 
industry conference a few days after his Bamboo-Ceiling 
TV essay appeared, Huang retracted his prior criticism 
of Khan: “I absolutely feel we should have more writ-
ers of Asian-American descent in the writers’ room but 
I don’t debate [Khan’s] ability at all to do the show” 
(Hibberd, 2015). Throughout season one, Huang cri-
tiqued the show as much as he praised it. In the end, 
he came to an uneasy acceptance that his memoir had 
to be repackaged for network TV so that it could bring 
visibility to the Asian American community and reach 
mass audiences including White Americans and Asian 
Americans who do not identify as Taiwanese or share 
the same immigrant experience as his (Huang, 2015a).
About two-thirds of the way through the first sea-
son, the show started focusing more on Jessica and 
Louis. It became evident that Eddie would no longer 
be the central character. Huang’s voice-over narration 
also began to dwindle, appearing mostly at the begin-
ning and end of the episodes. Huang left the show after 
season one, and the producers discontinued the nar-
ration. The show fully shifted its focus from Eddie to 
other family members, especially on Jessica and Louis’ 
parenting style, and pop culture in the late 1990s.
What Does All This Mean?
It is undeniable that the television and film indus-
try lacks diversity (Smith, Choueti, & Pieper, 2016). 
Fresh Off the Boat allowed the Asian American com-
munity to create and represent their own stories, and 
a sense of belonging in the United States (Lopez & 
Pham, 2017). The show represented a generation of 
Asian American millennials whose racial narratives 
were missing from the mainstream media. However, 
the reconceptualization of the memoir suggested 
that the producers and the network were not ready 
to discuss the real cost of assimilation: conformity 
to Whiteness, anti-Blackness, and erasure of immi-
grants’ cultural heritage.


Media Industries and Producing Media Content 289
Huang’
s memoir has a darker tone than the sit-
com, which the producers apparently did not want 
to incorporate into the comedy. Saying the show is 
inspired by the Fresh Off the Boat memoir allows pro-
ducers to tell a story that is accessible and attractive 
to audiences who do not necessarily know about the 
Asian American community. The show’s oversimpli-
fied version of Huang’s immigrant and assimilation 
experience suggests that the television industry views 
race from a Black and White binary. Asian Americans 
are often left out of the race conversation (Lopez & 
Pham, 2017).
Because of the fierce competition in network 
television, the producers felt the need to broaden the 
storyline and attract and maintain a larger audience. 
It was inevitable that Fresh Off the Boat was geared 
toward non-Asians. As Mar said: “Y ou have to remem-
ber we’re not making a show just for Asian-Americans, 
we’re making a show through the Asian-American 
point of view for everybody” (Caramanica, 2015). In 
essence, the show was not about the Asian American 
immigrant experience. Instead, it was a general immi-
grant story: move to a new country, learn the language, 
and be successful.
If the intent of the show had been to highlight 
an Asian American immigrant experience, the pro-
ducers would have needed to find a way to challenge 
the dominant narrative about the community and tell 
the truth, the real story. Huang (2015a) wanted to use 
humor to call out White people for their contributions 
to systemic racism and anti-immigrant rhetoric. From 
Huang’s perspective, if the show was based on his 
memoir, it should not be just to entertain the audience, 
but to educate them about the struggles of being an 
immigrant of color in the United States.
Despite all the challenges, Fresh Off the Boat  
(which ended in 2020) was a breakthrough moment in 
American television history. The show brought pride 
and visibility to the Asian American community. It 
provided a platform for Asian American actors such 
as Park, Wu, and Yang to showcase their talents on 
prime time television. Nevertheless, the show missed 
the opportunity to educate mass audiences about the 
Asian American community and the stereotypes the 
community grapples with, and fails to address White 
supremacy within the community. Deviation from 
Huang’s book is an indication that network television is 
not ready to talk about the realities of systemic oppres-
sion in the United States, specifically in the context of 
the Asian American identity. As Huang said:
The network’s approach was to tell a univer -
sal, ambiguous, cornstarch story about Asian 
Americans resembling moo goo gai pan written 
by a Persian American who cut her teeth on 
race relations writing for Seth MacFarlane. But 
who is that show written for?
(2015a)
Y ou decide.

one group taking the perspective of

iew an episode of other shows featur -
ing characters of color such as Superstore

7.7: IS SIRI A LITTLE BIT RACIST? 
RECOGNIZING AND CONFRONTING 
ALGORITHMIC BIAS IN EMERGING 
MEDIA
Michael L. Austin
This essay considers the power of algorithms in our 
lives, and how—even unintentionally—racial and 
other biases can be introduced into algorithms.
Y our morning routine: first, wake up. Second, turn 
off your alarm. Next, brush your teeth, shower, get 
dressed, eat breakfast, etc. Y ou may use a different 
routine on weekends: rearrange steps, take more 
time between steps, or skip some steps altogether. 
At the most basic level, an algorithm is a set of steps 
used to complete a particular task, and our lives are 
full of them. Y our morning routine is an algorithm. 
So are the recipe used to prepare a particular dish 
and the arithmetic you use to calculate the total 
price of your grocery purchases.
Algorithms and Algorithmic Bias
Algorithms are key in the software that our comput-
ers and smart devices use to solve problems, help 
us make choices, and work more efficiently. In com-
puter science, an algorithm is 
any well-defined computational procedure that 
takes some value, or set of values, as input and 
produces some value, or set of values, as output. 
An algorithm is thus a sequence of computational 
steps that transform the input into the output.
(Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, & Stein, 
2009, p. 5)
Algorithms help your computer sort your email 
by sender, date received, read status, and so forth. 
and Black-ish. To what extent and how 
can TV shows generate conversations 
about race in America without general-
izing, stereotyping, or dehumanizing the 
experiences and people of racial or eth-
nic minorities?


Media Industries and Producing Media Content 291
W
hen you use a map application, the software uses 
algorithms to calculate the quickest or most direct 
route. In a process called machine learning, data 
are regularly collected—often continuously and in 
real time—and are processed using algorithms to 
make more informed decisions about how the soft-
ware should operate. Algorithms help online search 
engines rank results based on relevance and popu-
larity by monitoring the activity of millions of users. 
Dating apps sort and present your potential mates 
depending on information gathered from each user’s 
profile and an algorithm’s estimation of what bits of 
information cause you to swipe right or left.
Algorithms increasingly influence our media 
landscape. They help Netflix suggest the next movie 
or TV show you should watch based on information 
gathered by tracking your viewing habits. Facebook 
uses algorithms to suggest friends, boost important 
posts in our news feed, and inconspicuously draw our 
attention to ads for products we are likely to purchase 
by monitoring our online activity on Facebook and 
other websites. Journalists use algorithms to monitor 
social media for important breaking news, to check 
facts, and to sniff out fake news posted online.
We assign positive values such as fairness and 
objectivity to computers and other devices controlled 
by algorithms because they seem to follow rules and 
avoid interference from human emotion, human error, 
or human bias. But because algorithms are created by 
humans, they are often programmed—both purpose-
fully and unintentionally—with intrinsic biases having 
considerable implications. Although some instances 
of algorithmic bias are innocuous, many are not. 
Algorithmic bias can introduce insidious and offensive 
racial profiling, cultural insensitivity, racism, sexism, 
homophobia, ageism, and ableism in technology we use 
every day. These biases can wreak havoc on members 
of minoritized communities, especially now that algo-
rithms are being used to help colleges process appli-
cations, companies choose who to interview for a job, 
banks decide whether to approve loans, law enforce-
ment assesses the probability that a person will commit 
a crime, or predicts an incarcerated person’s potential 
for recidivism (and thus influence his or her chance of 
parole), among myriad other issues related to voting, 
healthcare, employment, housing, education, and more.
In this essay, I address algorithmic bias in new 
and emerging media, examine its implications for 
potentially vulnerable groups, and discuss algorithmic 
accountability and ways to identify and rectify negative 
biases ensconced within the application software we 
use every day.
How Do Algorithms Learn to Be Biased?
Outside of dystopian science fiction novels and 
films, we generally hold a positive view of technol-
ogy. We have long seen technology as a progress, 
and a desirable and worthwhile augmentation of 
our human capabilities. In the first monograph on 
the philosophy of technology, Ernst Kapp (1877) 
saw technological artifacts as man-made imita-
tions of and improvements on human organs. In 
1966, Marshall McLuhan wrote that technology—
and media—has extended both human ability and 
human consciousness:
During the mechanical ages we had extended 
our bodies in space. Today, after more than 
a century of electric technology, we have 
extended our central nervous system itself in 
a global embrace, abolishing both space and 
time as far as our planet is concerned. Rapidly, 
we approach the final phase of the extensions 
of man – the technological simulation of con-
sciousness, when the creative process will be 
collectively and corporately extended to the 
whole of human society….
(McLuhan, 1966, p. 19)
Later, Rothenberg (1993, p. 16) called technology 
an extension of human faculties, such as our eyes, 
feet, or hands that are “appendable by a device,” 
although he argued that technology cannot extend 
into our ability to make ethical or moral decisions. 
But that was before the advent of social media and 
communication technologies allowing us to extend 
our sense of place from one specific geographic 
location to an almost limitless sense of telematic 
presence across the entire globe. Have we been able 
to prove Rothenberg wrong about the other impos-
sibilities of technology—to make ethical or moral 
decisions? So far, not really.

292 Production
For example, in 2011, Apple introduced its 
voice-controlled intelligent assistant, Siri, which allows 
users to control devices using voice commands. Soon 
after Siri’s launch, Apple’s online Support Communities 
were flooded with complaints from customers who 
were upset that Siri could not understand them. Many 
suspected that their accents were the cause. Although 
Siri uses voice-recognition algorithms to categorize 
users’ voices within Apple’s database of accents and 
regional dialects, users with thick accents, or those 
not closely matching Standard American English, 
often had—and as of this writing still have—difficulty 
using Siri. In a 2016 interview with Tom Dart for The 
Guardian, sociolinguist Lars Hinrichs recounted, “I’ve 
had a bunch of people from Australia and India say 
they only really get along with Siri if they fake an 
American accent” (Dart, 2016). It is hard to believe 
that the bias imbedded within these algorithms against 
people who speak nonstandard forms of American 
English (such as Chicano English, African American 
Vernacular English, etc.) and those with thick foreign 
accents is intentional. But should nonnative English 
speakers, users with speech disorders, or those who 
use various nonstandard dialects be expected to con-
form to clear, enunciated Standard American English 
just to be understood by their devices? With the emer-
gence of the Internet of Things (IoT), smartphones and 
voice-controlled virtual assistants such as Amazon’s 
Alexa and Google Home can operate household 
appliances, lighting, thermostats, door locks, and var-
ious media devices. As manual operation of each of 
these home gadgets becomes obsolete, addressing 
algorithmic bias becomes urgent. Accessibility is rap-
idly becoming a necessity for many users.
Does Siri’s inability to understand some people 
make her a little racist? Y es, I’m sure that to some users 
who speak English with an accent as a result of learn-
ing another language before English, or those who 
speak a variation of Standard American English, Siri 
probably seems a little racist. Racist or not, does this 
make Siri biased to the disadvantage of a wide range 
of people? Absolutely. So where does this bias come 
from?
Garbage In, Garbage Out
An algorithm is only as good as the data it uses to 
accomplish the task at hand, so bad data inevitably 
lead to bad results. And even with good data, an 
algorithm can only make great decisions or accom-
plish complex tasks if it is thoughtfully designed 
and trained to handle such complex situations. 
Technology’s inability to make ethical decisions 
was highlighted during Microsoft’s attempt to mimic 
social interactions through machine learning, using 
unfiltered training data taken directly from the pub-
lic. In March 2016, Microsoft introduced the world 
to an AI chatbot named Tay that was designed to 
chat like a teenage girl. The public was encouraged 
to teach Tay to talk by interacting with her using 
social media and messaging apps. This social exper-
iment quickly devolved into racism, anti-
 Semitism, 
and g
eneral chaos. Tay’s first tweet, at 8:30 pm, was 
“can I just say that im stoked to meet u? humans 
are super cool.” By 11:45 the next morning, Tay 
was saying unfathomably horrible things such as, 
“I f**king hate feminists and they should all die 
and burn in hell,” “Bush did 9/11 and Hitler would 
have done a better job than the monkey we have 
now. donald trump is the only hope we’ve got,” and 
“Repeat after me, Hitler did nothing wrong.”
Tay is an extreme example of a problem with 
algorithmic bias: “Garbage in, garbage out” (GIGO). 
Because algorithms draw information from data sets 
to complete their tasks, biases in the data sets will be 
incorporated into the end product. Tay performed 
exactly as designed—she learned and repeated 
phrases taught by users who interacted with her. And 
she became a deplorable simulation of humanity.
Siri has also been susceptible to GIGO, subject-
ing her to even more credible accusations of racism 
than her inability to comprehend users with accents. 
In the summer of 2017, users who asked, “Siri, what 
is an Indian?” received this response: “They are a lit-
tle brown and they smell like curry and they eat it.” 
Siri’s question-answering algorithm relies on informa-
tion gleaned from internet searches, and often prior-
itizes information from Wikipedia. Wikipedia’s article 
on “Indian” had been vandalized, and unsuspecting 
iPhone users were confronted with this racially charged 
and stereotype-laden rhetoric when it was parroted by 
Siri. Siri also provided insensitive answers in April 2015 
when Russians asked “Siri, gay clubs around me?” or 
“How to register a gay marriage in the UK,” replying “I 
would have turned red [blushed] if I could,” or “I will 
pretend I haven’t heard it.” Apple claimed the answers 


Media Industries and Producing Media Content 293
w
ere caused by a bug in an operating system update, 
but there is speculation that Apple acted out of an 
overabundance of caution after Russia passed a law 
prohibiting people under the age of 18 from receiv-
ing information about homosexuality. Either way, Siri 
received garbage as input and transmitted garbage as 
her output.
Most striking of all is the fact that Siri, Alexa, 
and others consider nonstandard forms of English 
and regional accents “garbage” to be avoided; in fact, 
Lawrence (2021) argued that virtual assistants even 
discipline nonnative English speakers and those with 
regional accents by forcing them to code-switch or 
otherwise alter their language patterns to facilitate a 
successful interaction. Koenecke et al. (2020) deter-
mined that averaging the performance of the top five 
commercially available virtual assistants, these auto-
mated speech recognition (ASR) systems had a word 
error rate of 19% for White speakers and 35% for Black 
speakers. The error rate rose to 41% for Black men.
Bias by Design
Sometimes bias is included in an algorithm by its 
creators. In late 2020, Zoom faced criticism when 
a White Ph.D. student went on Twitter to point out 
that any time his Black professor would try to use a 
virtual background, his head would be cropped out. 
Although Zoom did not purposefully exclude its 
users’ faces, it did program its algorithm to interpret 
darker areas as inconsequential information to be 
replaced by the background image. To make mat-
ters worse, Twitter’s own algorithm prioritized the 
White student’s face in the image preview (Dickey, 
2020).
Unfortunately, this was not the first time con-
spicuous racial bias was intentionally programmed 
into facial recognition applications. In April 2017, the 
makers of FaceApp were forced to apologize after 
they were confronted for creating a racially biased 
app. FaceApp allows users to dramatically alter selfies 
using various filters powered by artificial intelligence 
algorithms. In addition to imagining what users would 
look like as another gender, an older adult, or a baby, 
the app also featured the “hot” filter. This filter adjusted 
facial features into a more conventionally aesthetically 
pleasing form. People with black or brown skin were 
shocked when the app lightened their skin. Meitu faced 
similar criticism in 2017 for lightening the skin of users, 
and in 2016, Snapchat released a Bob Marley filter that 
essentially applied blackface to a user’s selfie.
Bias by Omission
Other times, bias comes from omission. One of the 
most well-known examples came to light in 2015, 
when Flickr and Google Photos’ autotagging systems 
mislabeled photos because the data set from which 
they learned was incomplete. As a result, Flickr 
labeled images of concentration camps as “jungle 
gyms,” and both Flickr and Google’s Photos app 
labeled images of Black people as apes or gorillas. 
This bias may become exponentially more prob-
lematic as facial recognition software becomes 
more ubiquitous. What if it does not recognize 
Black faces as human, or as we saw in late 2017 
with iPhone X’s Face ID, has trouble distinguishing 
between two different Asian faces? Likewise, an 
image search for “babies” on Bing in April of 2017 
returned only images of White babies. How do these 
types of biases affect availability of searchable infor-
mation for people of color? How do unintentional 
algorithmic biases affect the representational poli-
tics of social media, or media in general, or politics? 
Problems that aren’t seen are not fixed, and those 
of us who rely on social media for important infor -
mation such as news and politics are at the mercy 
of the biases imbedded within the social media 
applications.
Bias by Default
Through processes called surrogate objectives, soft-
ware employing artificial intelligence and machine 
learning uses algorithms to make predictions or to 
decide which blanks to fill in when information is 
missing. In social media apps, this type of algorith-
mic bias prioritizes the content in our news feeds 
and search results based on search trends, links to 
other sites, and other user-driven criteria—but not 
necessarily on relevance or trustworthiness. Ideally, 
algorithms could make choices based on value (as 
previously discussed) and populate your feed with 
the most important, fair, balanced, and unbiased 
information. But, machines are currently unable 
to do that. Instead, we’re offered fake news, trashy 

294 Production
stars, and cute cats because by default, the algo-
rithm values—and ironically, reinforces—their pop-
ularity. Further, groups with fewer members face 
the threat of what Taina Bucher (2012) called “algo-
rithmic invisibility,” or hiding certain information 
or forms of social interaction that are not valued 
highly by the medium’s algorithms. For example, 
friends who post less frequently on Facebook and 
with whom you communicate infrequently may 
be hidden from your timeline, giving preference to 
friends with whom you use Facebook’s chat feature, 
whose posts you like, and with whom you other -
wise regularly interact through Facebook. Likewise, 
topics trending on Black Twitter might not get the 
coverage they deserve in dominant news outlets or 
may not be adequately shared on other social media 
platforms simply because they are not among the 
top trending issues on Twitter overall.
Addressing Algorithmic Bias
How do we fight algorithmic bias and make our 
technology more fair? I argue that algorithms are 
already fair—they are mathematical equations, 
and as a result, they follow the laws of math to a 
T, free from favoritism, emotional manipulation, 
or self-interest. Instead, we should seek to make 
algorithms more just, taking things such as race, 
ethnicity, gender inequality, and affirmative action 
into consideration. All of the issues above boil 
down to representation—the representation of 
perspectives and ideas that are encoded within 
algorithms when they are programmed and when 
design decisions are being made—so the point of 
view of groups which can be affected negatively 
by biased algorithms should be considered and 
accounted for in all stages of an algorithm’s lifecycle, 
from conceptualization, to release, to various ver -
sions and updates, to its eventual replacement by 
more advanced technology. The following are just 
a few ways algorithmic bias can be accounted for, 
and perhaps prevented. Companies should explain 
to users how their algorithms work and what steps 
are being taken to avoid bias against protected (and 
unprotected) classes. They should also empower 
users to report instances of bias, make the report-
ing process easy, and address the reported issues 
expeditiously. Programmers should be trained to 
detect and limit bias in their algorithms; this can be 
accomplished by regular audits to identify explicit 
and implicit biases. Hiring people of various races, 
genders, sexual orientations, and dis/abilities will 
provide perspectives that may help identify a prob-
lem in an algorithm or its training data and prevent 
unintentional bias before it takes root. Further, pro-
grammers should avoid so-called “blind” program-
ming; for example, if a programmer insists that an 
algorithm is “colorblind,” that means the machine 
is left to construct race on its own terms based only 
on the data it has on hand. Without human inter -
vention, the machine’s ideas about race—without 
the benefit of empathy, the lessons learned from 
interracial interactions, history, human conscience 
and morals, and so forth—could be severely flawed 
and dangerous for minoritized communities. Finally, 
curricula in STEM fields (science, technology, engi-
neering, and math)—particularly in engineering, 
computer science, and other technological fields—
should include coursework in ethics and techno-
logical values. We all should re-evaluate the faith 
we place in the so-called “mathematical purity” of 
algorithms, recognizing that social justice is more 
important than mathematical fairness.
Bias is built into the world around us, and espe-
cially in the West, the default setting usually privileges 
whiteness. This fact is hard for me to ignore when I 
can easily find bandages matching my skin tone, digital 
cameras see me better than they do people of color, 
and Siri can understand my questions. As we strive 
for better representation in media for communities of 
color and other minoritized groups, we should work 
equally hard to raise awareness of the unseen, underly-
ing systems that produce, protect, and proliferate bias 
in these media—all the way down to the level of indi-
vidual lines of computer code.
