7.8: NONBINARY BINARIES AND 
UNREAL METAHUMANS
Eric Freedman
Rooted in software studies, which examines the 
role of software in everyday life, this analysis of 
Epic Game’s MetaHuman Creator explores how 
the tools of efficient real-time 3D visualization are 
powering our visual futures and shaping how we see 
and know the world.
Imagine you could create your own digital human; 
not a simple avatar, but a photorealistic 3D charac-
ter. Just open up your library, choose a few human 
variants, blend them together, and go. Although 3D 
character creation has long been a part of AAA 
(blockbuster) video game development, the indus-
trial processes of game design and development are 
becoming more open and accessible. What once 
required advanced 3D drawing and modeling skills 
and hours of labor is now possible in an instant, with 
simple drag-and-drop techniques.
Video games are built on game engines, code 
frameworks that define the field of play (the game envi-
ronment and its assets) and the executable functions 
of gameplay. Game engines are influencing a broad 
swath of visual culture—film, television, virtual reality, 
architecture, automotive design, fashion, and more. 
Many images we interact with are artfully crafted digi-
tal objects borne by advanced hardware, software, and 
programming; they are engineered media. Video game 
engines and their attendant data infrastructures are 
the building blocks of the emerging metaverse, where 
developers such as Unity Technologies and Epic 
Games are using their proprietary holdings and buying 
up complementary technology companies to move 
into new markets and create integrated world-building 
systems.
In this essay, I examine a fairly new tool offered 
by Epic Games: the MetaHuman Creator. Part of 
Epic’s proprietary Unreal Engine, the MetaHuman 
Creator was released in April 2021. The free web-
based application features an accessible user interface, 
allowing game developers and 3D content creators to 
quickly build high-fidelity digital humans that can be 
a different race or gender? How would 
your experience change if you were una-
ble to see, hear, or use your hands in a 
conventional way, for example? Can you 
find any implicit or explicit biases toward 
you or other people in this app?
 2.
 Do companies ha
ve an ethical respon-
sibility to make their software unbiased? 
What should companies consider in 
making their software unbiased? How 
might this affect a company’s bottom 
line?
 3.
 Can y
ou identify other ways to prevent 
algorithmic bias than those presented 
here? What suggestions do you have for 
programmers and media companies that 
produce software? What suggestions 
do you have for the educators of future 
programmers?

296 Production
animated within a variety of other programs. I  pose 
two 
 int
errelated questions. Are tools such as the 
MetaHuman Creator democratizing the field of digital 
content creation? And, are they fostering more diverse 
representations and narratives and supporting the free 
play of identity in playable media?
Game engines and their tool sets shape visual 
culture by translating it into a data set that can be 
manipulated by an algorithm; in a 3D rendered world, 
everything must be understood as data. Digital con-
tent developers can transform visual artifacts—
 
en
vironments, objects, and characters—in real time 
with simple drag-and-drop controls, variable sliders,  
and c
lickable attributes. These tools embody a way of 
seeing, knowing, and transforming the world.
Epic’s MetaHuman software framework draws 
from a library of scans of real people. It allows 3D 
content developers to quickly create unique photore-
alistic fully rigged digital humans by mixing together 
different parts of real people while changing each 
character’s facial textures and geometries and updat-
ing the underlying rig (a rig is the equivalent of a digital 
character’s skeleton that gives it functional and logical 
animation and movement). The MetaHuman library 
contains customizable prefabricated presets that rep-
resent the generalized contours of racial, ethnic, and 
gender diversity. Artists can rapidly and seamlessly 
manipulate facial features, adjust skin tone, and select 
from a range of body types (referenced as feminine 
or masculine) and styles. Finished characters can be 
exported, fully rigged and ready to animate in Epic’s 
Unreal Engine.
MetaHuman Creator advances the field of virtual 
production for games, immersive experiences, and 
other media. However, it also animates the cultural 
politics of the face-generating algorithm that were 
vividly illustrated on the cover of Time magazine on 
November 18, 1993. Time’s portrait of “The New Face 
of America” was created from a computer-generated 
mix of individuals across racial and ethnic groups. 
This synthesis, designed to illustrate how immigrants 
are shaping the United States into a multicultural soci-
ety, belies the work involved, the policy decisions, 
the socioeconomic divides, and the myriad forces 
of 
 dis
enfranchisement that impede such a vision of 
progress.
Because it depends on deeply multilayered 
 alg
orithmic manipulation, MetaHuman creation 
shares an awkward legacy with visual trickery and dis-
information, an unfortunate byproduct of generative 
adversarial networks (GANs). Generative modeling 
broadly refers to an unsupervised learning task, made 
possible through machine learning, which can auto-
matically discover and learn from the patterns of input 
data, such as a large warehouse of images, to gener-
ate new examples that plausibly represent the original 
data set. GANs are often associated with the produc-
tion of deep fakes that use artificial intelligence (AI) 
algorithms and big data sets to replicate real-world 
image patterns. GANs can also develop unique human 
faces that pass for real people.
These systems render visual culture from a per-
spective that, as it advances, is less and less deter -
mined by human intervention. The machine learning 
of GANs requires training two opposing but comple-
mentary algorithms: a generator learns to create plau-
sible data and a discriminator learns to discriminate 
between the generator’s fake data and real data. The 
two algorithms work in tandem to create a system that 
gets better over time at generating realistic synthetic 
media (images, voices, and videos).
In 2018, a team of NVIDIA technology research-
ers proposed StyleGAN, a style-based generator 
architecture tasked with analyzing and synthesizing 
existing facial image data to produce new photoreal-
istic images (Karras et al., 2019). In 2019, Phillip Wang 
used NVIDIA ’s open-source generator to create This 
Person Does Not Exist, a website that conjures its fake 
portraits from existing image data and produces new 
human faces with each page refresh. This data-driven 
image modeling is based on a degree of normalization, 
of training an algorithm on existing data sets to gener-
ate new and unique images that conform to common 
facial shapes and facial features. Although it is a fasci-
nating visual tool it carries with it stark undercurrents.
Modeling with Artificial Intelligence
Artificial intelligence tools are widely deployed, 
including within institutions historically marked 
by systemic discrimination—housing, the work-
place, the criminal justice system, and financial 


Media Industries and Producing Media Content 297
institutions
. Unfortunately, bias is baked into the 
outcomes, even as AI design methodologies are 
commonly conceived to support and not replace 
human-centered decision-making. The data used 
to train machine intelligence often underrepresent 
people of color, women, and other marginalized 
groups, which affects the design, development, 
implementation, and outcomes of AI across a 
broad range of tech and tech-dependent industries. 
Although the MetaHuman Creator does not rely on 
artificial intelligence per se—it focuses on the phys-
ical aspects of character creation—its assets are 
primed for intelligence uses as nonplayer characters 
driven by AI subsystems or as intelligent agents in a 
wide array of media environments.
The MetaHuman Creator carries the same cul-
tural weight as other simulation systems, intelligent 
or not, that approximate human subjects. Although 
designed with distinct content creation applications in 
mind, we can read the tool from a critical rather than a 
purely technical vantage point. In its speedy transfor-
mation of character rigs and other nonbinary attrib-
utes, MetaHuman Creator’s ability to blend between 
characters highlights the potential fluidity and open-
ness of data. Y et most commercial demonstrations 
of the tool focus on how quickly an end result can 
be reached and reinforce status quo representations. 
The image library, which is a complex data set, must 
behave in plausible ways and according to certain con-
straints to produce believable outputs. That intent is 
grounded in Epic’s software documentation, training 
modules, and examples of fully formed MetaHumans 
that are informed by the forms and functions of video 
gaming and draw from many common gaming poses 
such as gun stances.
Although MetaHumans are designed intelli-
gently, with plausible geometries, they would need an 
AI subsystem to imbue them with agency as semiau-
tonomous contextually driven and motivated char -
acters. But that is exactly the prompt posed by Epic 
Games in its early MetaHuman promotional videos: 
“Y ou create the narrative.” Although MetaHumans are 
assets in need of a narrative, we can still read them 
as meaningful traces of a particular industrial process 
that grounds these representations in the aesthetics 
and applications of video game development. With 
a corporate strategy extending beyond video game 
play, Epic is looking to leverage Unreal, its online game 
Fortnite, and other proprietary assets and tools to claim 
territory in the metaverse, a persistent bridge between 
the physical and virtual worlds that can be populated 
with human-like assets, communal events, and every-
day experiences.
Building a Better Human?
In the field of character creation, “meta” implies 
building a higher order human that is both better 
and beyond human. MetaHumans may look like us, 
but they are enclosures for code. Their high-
 fidelity 
bodies ar
e built from large-scale data processes 
such as photogrammetry, a technique for creating 
3D models from detailed images of discrete human 
subjects. By surveilling and mastering the body 
through technology, 3D content generators offer 
up an inscrutable objective truth. Within this visual 
register of truth, the cultural politics of race, gen-
der, class, and other poles of identity are displaced 
by the sheer volume of visible evidence of material 
bodies. Image capture technologies, code, and data 
are intended to render objectively as they reproduce 
the exquisite details of the surface of things. The 
specter of identity, of race, and politics, for example, 
that grounds how we see and understand the world, 
remains buried. The data-rich 3D photographic 
techniques of photogrammetry allow race to be 
captured, analyzed, and quantified, not as a social 
construct but as a phenotypically precise attribute 
that can be transposed to a variable shader.
The pursuit of hyperrealism in AAA video game 
production is influencing visuality in nongame media 
and is being furthered by certain assumptions about 
the inevitable alignment and seamless integration of 
the physical and the virtual world. Video game studios 
have developed sophisticated 3D engines and mas-
tered the technical art of representation, but bodies 
and politics are often cleaved in the design process.
Software studies tells us to consider how systems 
of representation, increasingly grounded in computa-
tion, are informed by deep cultural legacies that deter-
mine how software performs in the world. Software 
has a disposition that is largely linked to the conditions 

298 Production
of its ownership, production, and operation. Software 
and its underlying algorithms perform transformative 
and generative operations on their collocated data 
and, in turn, inform how we see, understand, and act. 
The MetaHuman Creator is a computational practice, 
focused on efficiency, rational problem-solving, and 
high-fidelity 3D character generation, but it is also a 
representational practice, a social practice, and an 
industrial process. It generates playful possibilities 
through long data trails and through a series of trans-
actional relationships between the developer and con-
sumers. It functions through artful data governance 
and is undergirded by rich and unwavering computa-
tional analyses of human subjects.
MetaHumans are both individualized and gen-
eralized character bodies; they are interoperable 
cross-platform subjects that can be inserted into a 
wide range of computationally driven environments. 
Distinct bodies, pulled from the library, can be blended 
together to make custom assets, while retarget-
ing allows a common set of animation data to pass 
between characters with the same underlying skeleton.
With that understanding of MetaHuman produc-
tion and performance, we can move to consider what 
these characters are asked to do. When AAA game 
studios and software developers promote their prod-
ucts, tools, and engines, they commonly foreground 
the naturalism of their material effects, the realness of 
their characters, and the authenticity of their environ-
ments over what these assets are tasked to perform. 
Game engines and artifacts are defined by a series 
of ever-
 expanding t
echnical horizons that support 
and realize the promises of photorealistic rendering, 
dynamic physics and effects, lifelike character ani-
mations, and deeply immersive worlds. By charting 
a more expansive path through critical media studies 
and holding onto both data and image in our examina-
tions of playable media, we can more forcefully exam-
ine the signaling processes of software development.
Epic’s multiethnic, multiracial, transgender 
MetaHuman Creator is a design tool and not a nar-
rative engine. Its transitions are simple and seamless, 
and follow the competitive demands of a marketplace 
dominated by efficient plug-and-play build, edit, and 
design systems. The traces of nonbinary and non-White 
identities are simply part of a larger palette of various 
ethnicities (and genders) in a robust database. The 
MetaHuman Creator has mastered cosmetic human 
diversity alongside the organic and inorganic diversity 
of the material world, and the quick fabrication of mul-
ticulturalism seems to suggest that technology can be 
color blind and embrace a certain in-betweenness by 
offering up a high degree of consumer-driven custom-
ization. The rapid transition between subject positions 
is a masterful visual spectacle, but it seems incompati-
ble with any genuine concern for the difficulties of lived 
and experienced body boundaries, although Epic’s 
developers suggest that the quality and fidelity of its 
MetaHumans (which is defined as a matter of their 
plausible facial geometries) can create player empathy. 
MetaHuman creation is a feat of 
 bodil
y governance, 
of regulating the flow (more precisely, the blending) 
of otherwise discrete bodies; the power and privilege 
associated with the tool are tied to Epic’s proprietary 
systems of data and design.
The MetaHuman system parameters are woven 
into the creative process, and although users can cus-
tomize their outputs, the application’s algorithms con-
sistently conform selections from the central image 
database to a series of normative human geometries. 
Features, such as facial proportions, are kept within a 
number of system guardrails that guarantee a degree 
of realism that holds true even in the system’s shaders, 
textures, and animation logic. Edge cases, or scenarios 
where the system generates outputs that fall outside 
of convention, have been filtered out of the interface’s 
underlying algorithms. MetaHuman creators are not 
given direct access to the primary scan library and its 
data, but instead begin by choosing a MetaHuman pre-
set from a database of diverse premade characters (a 
library of more than 50 named individuals from Ada 
to Zhen), and can enable the application’s viewport to 
blend together multiple characters. Preset characters 
are built from a number of project files that represent 
distinct parts of each digital body—materials, textures, 
and animation data that define such features as skin 
tone and lighting response—and simplify the computa-
tional complexities of real-time computer graphics. The 
MetaHuman Creator is designed to produce plausible 
results as it outputs custom blends of digital individuals.
Within this software ecosystem, Unreal Engine’s 
Live Link Face app allows developers to capture live 


Media Industries and Producing Media Content 299
f
acial performance with an iPhone or iPad, and map 
that performance in real time to their MetaHuman 
characters. MetaHuman characters can also be linked 
to other full body motion capture workflows and pose 
animations that target each character’s base skeleton. 
These software ecosystems, which include other com-
patible development tools, reveal the dynamic nature 
of data, its rapid movement across development envi-
ronments, its eventual accretion (its full assimilation) 
as part of human-centric characters, and the ease 
of imposing a newly determined subjectivity onto 
an existing character asset. These ecosystems also 
reveal how ownership and authorship are intertwined. 
MetaHumans must be rendered or published in Epic’s 
proprietary Unreal Engine in order to comply with the 
company’s End User License Agreement. Moreover, 
with the release of MetaHuman Creator, Epic has 
foregrounded the value of its Pixel Streaming service 
that allows end-users to run a packaged Unreal Engine 
application through a web portal to a centralized virtual 
machine. MetaHuman developers can rely on Epic’s 
cloud data supports to worry less about their own 
local processing power and storage limits. In this cir-
cuit of relations, Epic is a software developer, a content 
creator, and a cloud service provider; in its acquisition 
of complementary visualization holdings that include 
3Lateral (volumetric facial capture), Cubic Motion 
(facial animation technology), Capturing Reality (pho-
togrammetry software), and Quixel (3D worldbuilding 
assets), it has consolidated a robust suite of 3D content 
creation tools and created a closed data system that 
furthers the purposeful application of computer vision 
techniques.
Working Across Media Studies and 
Software Studies
Critical media studies allow us to interrogate the 
formal and structural properties of a media text 
and understand the production process. We can 
ask whether a tool that can produce multicultural 
subjects can also produce substantive social change 
and create counter-narratives that challenge racial 
and ethnic inequities (Benjamin, 2019). The promo-
tional materials surrounding the release of Epic’s 
MetaHuman Creator focus on what its characters 
look like, and how plausible they are, rather than 
what they do; these representations lack context. 
As the engine-driven traces of the natural world 
continue to move toward greater fidelity and greater 
alignment between physiognomic and mechanical 
systems, the power of Epic’s tool is not simply what 
it does but also how it does it. Computer vision tech-
niques continue to become more integrated, and at 
the same time more expansive, more capable of 
ingesting the world and our bodies and reproducing 
them with great detail. The user interface is designed 
as a direct manipulation tool; end-users can monitor 
their design choices in real time. Is the MetaHuman 
Creator an engine for diversity or simply a spectacle 
of control? Video game technologies have extended 
algorithmic influence into the machinery of a much 
broader media and information economy (Finn, 
2017), and they have succeeded by holding onto 
the humanistic attachments of algorithms that make 
software so welcome and familiar.
I asked at the outset of this essay whether simpli-
fied building tools can democratize the field of digital 
content creation. My prompt suggests that these tools 
might impose certain limits on how characters are 
designed, what they are tasked to do, and how they 
might signify beyond themselves as cultural objects. 
Software studies provides a method for examining the 
role of software in everyday life and helps us consider 
how software shapes social agency. By examining soft-
ware systems, and the technologies and applications 
they support, we can begin to understand the cultural 
power of code as it gets written into specific data 
architectures.
The programming logic of the MetaHuman 
Creator shapes all of its image data into a fixed set of 
material relations that follows the governing industrial 
logic of video game production. MetaHuman creations 
must make sense visually and their bodies must work 
and perform without failure as functional human-like 
assets. The algorithms that undergird the MetaHuman 
Creator are responsible for composing responsive bod-
ies, and naturally blending discrete subjects and charac-
ter properties together. There is a broader lesson here 
in shifting our attention to the deeper architectures of 
game design and development, while not abandoning 
the image altogether (Freedman, 2020), and unpacking 

300 Production
the privilege that comes with machine-based identity 
surfing. MetaHuman developers work on the surface 
of things; they use the program’s interface to sculpt and 
transform physical assets, while the raw data operate 
behind the scenes. MetaHuman assets, like all game 
assets, are hygienic, functional, and understandable 
distillations of the material world (Barnett, et al., 2016); 
they are organized containers for discrete fields of 
information that can be made to perform with ease.
I echo the sentiment expressed by Malkowski 
and Russworm (2017) that code analysis, if taken on its 
own, can silence otherness and reconstitute margins—
it assumes that game programming is purely technical 
and not particularly ideological. As we develop and 
expand our work in media studies, we must try to 
situate computation and representation side by side, 
and understand their interrelated disciplinary histo-
ries and practices. Digital media objects have an outer 
layer and an inner layer; they are representations gov-
erned by code, and they are the provenance of both 
media and computing. The concept of infrastructure, 
of examining what lies beneath the surface of material 
representations—often found when media studies is 
conjoined with science and technology studies—may 
help us understand what is otherwise invisible and 
decode what type of functional and ideological work 
may be happening in the background. The information 
infrastructure of a large-scale technical system, when 
laid as the groundwork for a robust networked plat-
form with integrated software components, is designed 
to solve certain technical challenges (Star, 1999), 
including those associated with interoperable data and 
shareable assets that necessitate common file formats 
and programming languages. But it may in turn create 
social challenges.
The machine algorithms of the MetaHuman 
Creator are invisible actors operating in the spaces 
between the discrete physical scans stored in Epic’s 
MetaHuman database, and are not something we 
can fundamentally see or access. We may understand 
what MetaHumans look like and how our efforts can 
alter their appearances, but we are still left to consider 
what they might do. That question is often left unasked 
in the pursuit of plausibility and photorealism. We need 
to remind ourselves that deep layers of programming 
and data can ultimately determine narrative possibil-
ity, and often amplify existing hierarchies of knowledge 
and power. Our work with MetaHumans is limited to a 
series of surface-level interventions with the user inter-
face. As a counter measure, we need to understand 
how proprietary software environments are built. We 
must strive for deeper computational literacy if we are 
to decode the design biases of imaging systems and 
consider how they might operate in and regulate the 
world at large.

Now that you’ve read these chapters, think again 
about some questions raised in the introduction to 
this book: does the social scientific or the critical/
cultural studies approach seem to make more sense 
to you? Why? What do you think are the strengths 
and weaknesses of each approach? If you were 
going to investigate media effects, how would you 
approach the subject? Which types of questions 
(narrow or broad) do you think are more important? 
Which do you think are easier to answer? Which 
methods provide more valid and valuable results? Is 
it possible to maintain one’s objectivity while study-
ing human beings? What is lost, and what is gained, 
by holding one perspective (social scientific) over 
the other (critical/cultural)? Can researchers bor -
row from both traditions? Should they? If so, how? 
What would be gained? At what cost? The answers 
to these and other questions will influence how you 
interpret the scholarship you engage as you con-
tinue through school, and beyond. As you ask these 
questions, you are being a critical participant in 
our academic system/tradition of scholarship and 
research.
Being a critical participant in our media system 
means constantly asking questions. The readings in 
this book have presented you with a kaleidoscope of 
questions to consider—questions about media pro-
duction, media content, and media audiences. Which 
ones did you enjoy the most? Why? What additional 
questions did you think of ? How have you seen your 
own media literacy increase as you thought about 
the issues presented here, and as you have brought 
the question-asking process to your own media use? 
How have you become a more active and empowered 
member of the media audience? How can you bring 
what you’ve learned to any future media production 
you might undertake?
Ultimately, the media in our lives constitute a 
powerful social institution—not the only one, but the 
one most of us spend most of our time with. What the 
media tell us about our social world has a profound 
effect on our understanding of that social world. Even 
though your time in this class has come to an end, 
never stop questioning the media and the image of 
our world they offer us; the way the messages are con-
structed and by whom; and the way we receive, inter-
pret, use, and are affected by the media. The media do 
matter. And so does your ability to ask questions, to be 
a literate and critical participant in the media system.
For More Information
What follows are some resources you might find 
helpful as you continue your studies of media pro-
duction, content, and audiences. As are all such lists, 
it’s incomplete—in this case, limited by available 
space—but it’s a starting point. For websites, please 
see the links in the preface.

Habiba Ahmed  (MA, Wake Forest University) 
works in communication and government and inter-
national politics. Her research focuses on national 
security, security cooperation, and alliances in 
South East Asia.
Cory L. Armstrong  (PhD, University of 
 W
isconsin-Madison) is a professor and associate 
dean of research and faculty affairs in the College of 
Journalism & Mass Communications at University 
of Nebraska-Lincoln. Her research interests include 
diversity, influences in news content, and the media 
messages about severe weather.
Jennifer Stevens Aubrey  (PhD, University of 
Michigan) is a professor in the Department of Com-
munication at the University of Arizona. With an 
emphasis on gender and adolescent development, 
her research focuses on media effects on emotional, 
mental, and physical health in young people, center-
ing on issues related to sexuality and body image.
Dear Aunaetitrakul (MS, California State Univer-
sity, Fullerton) is a senior program manager for the 
AANAPISI Programs at Oakton College, IL.
Michael L. Austin (PhD, The University of Texas 
at Dallas) is a senior lecturer in music production 
at Edge Hill University (UK). His research interests 
include music and sound in interactive and emerging 
media; the politics of representation and appropri-
ation in media; media aesthetics; and media ethics.
Emilee Baker  (MA, University of Wisconsin Mil-
waukee) is a PhD student in Inclusive Education 
at Syracuse University. Her research focuses on 
social justice and inclusive education, decolonizing 
research and education, feminist thought and the-
ory, and disability/land connections. She is a former 
special education teacher and currently a research 
assistant for CODE^SHIFT.
Madison Barnes-Nelson  (BA, Gonzaga Uni-
versity) is a Master’s student in the Department of 
Communication Studies at Colorado State Univer -
sity. Her research interests include television and 
feminist media studies, comedy and performance, 
and media industries.
Andrew C. Billings  (PhD, Indiana University) 
is the Ronald Reagan Chair of Broadcasting in the 
Department of Journalism and Creative Media at the 
University of Alabama. His research tends to focus 
within the nexus of sport, media, and social issues.
Robert Alan Brookey (PhD, University of Minne-
sota) is a professor of media at Ball State University 
where he also serves as the director of Graduate 
Studies. His research analyzes digital media conver-
gence in video games and social media, as well as 
the representation of gender and sexuality across 
media platforms. His most recent work critically 
engages steaming services and closely focuses on 
Disney+.
Dwight E. Brooks  (PhD, University of Iowa) is a 
professor and dean of the College of Communica-
tion and Media Sciences at Zayed University (UAE). 
His research interests include race, gender, class, 
and media; media literacy; and critical race theory. 
He is the author of Earth, Wind & Fire’s That’s the 
Way of the World (Bloomsbury Press: 33 1/3 Series).
 CONTRIBUTORS

 Contributors 317
Jean Marie Brown  (MSJ, Texas Christian Uni-
versity) is an associate professor of professional 
practice and director of student media in the 
Department of Journalism at Texas Christian Uni-
versity. A former newspaper executive, Brown spent 
most of her professional career working for Knight 
Ridder, and later McClatchy newspapers. She is a 
senior Fault Lines trainer for the Maynard Institute.
Patti Brown  (MS, Iowa State University; MSW, 
University of Iowa) is editor of the Estes Park Trail 
Gazette (Estes Park, CO) and a PhD candidate at 
Iowa State University. Her research interests include 
healthcare and social welfare policy and political 
rhetoric. Her dissertation work addresses the rela-
tionship of presidential rhetoric on poverty policy 
from the time of the Great Depression through the 
Great Recession.
Diem-My T . Bui  (PhD, University of Illinois at 
Urbana-Champaign) is a clinical associate professor 
in the Department of Communication and affiliate 
faculty in global Asian studies at the University of 
Illinois at Chicago. Her research interests focus on 
cultural production, cultural memory, and embodi-
ments of difference in racialized and sexualized rep-
resentations in popular culture and media.
Christopher P. Campbell  (PhD, University of 
Southern Mississippi) is a professor in the School 
of Media and Communication at the University of 
Southern Mississippi. He is the author of Race, Myth 
and the News, the editor of The Routledge Companion 
to Media and Race, and the co-editor of Race and 
News: Critical Perspectives and Media, Myth, and Mil-
lennials: Critical Perspectives on Race and Culture.
Gina M. Chen  (PhD, Syracuse University S. I. 
Newhouse School of Public Communications) 
is an associate professor and assistant director 
of the Center for News Engagement, The Uni-
versity of Texas at Austin. Her research interests 
include the emotional responses people have to 
online 
 int
eraction—through social media or online 
 commenting—and the pr
ocess by which these 
emotional responses influence their social, civic, 
and political engagement.
Cynthia A. Cooper  (PhD, University of Ten-
nessee) is Vice Provost for Academic Affairs at 
Towson University. Her research interests include 
communication law and policy; the competing 
rights and responsibilities of the First Amendment; 
and hate speech.
Charisse L’Pree Corsbie-Massay  (Ph.D., Uni-
versity of Southern California) is an associate profes-
sor of communications at the S.I. Newhouse School 
of Public Communications at Syracuse University. 
She investigates how media affects the way we 
think about ourselves and others as well as how we  
use media to affect the way others think about us.
Kiana Cox (PhD, University of Illinois at Chicago) 
is a research associate on the Race and Ethnicity 
research team at Pew Research Center in Washing-
ton, DC. She leads the Center’s research on Black 
American public opinion. Her areas of expertise 
include Black feminism, race, social movements, 
religion, and African American political ideologies. 
She joined Pew after writing this piece.
Carolyn M. Cunningham  (PhD, University of 
Texas at Austin) is an associate professor in the 
Communication and Leadership Studies Depart-
ment at Gonzaga University. Her research interests 
include girls’ studies, digital activism, video games, 
and women and leadership.
George L. Daniels  (PhD, University of Georgia) 
is an associate professor of journalism and creative 
media at The University of Alabama; co-editor of 
Teaching Race: Struggles, Strategies and Scholarship 
for the Mass Communication Classroom, and Faculty 
Fellow for Diversity and Inclusion for the Broadcast 
Education Association. His research focuses on 
issues of diversity in the media workplace and com-
munity engagement.
Dayna Jean DeFeo (PhD, New Mexico State Uni-
versity) is the director of the Center for Alaska Edu-
cation Policy Research at the University of Alaska, 
Anchorage. She studies representation and equity in 
education systems.
Travis L. Dixon  (PhD, University of California, 
Santa Barbara) is the Liberal Arts and Sciences 
Distinguished Professorial Scholar and professor 
of communication at the University of Illinois at 
 Ur
bana-Champaign. He is primarily interested in 
the portrayal of people of color in the mass media 
and the effects of these images on audiences.

318  C ontributors
Magdalayna Drivas (MA, Penn State University) 
is a PhD student at the University of Southern Cal-
ifornia Annenberg School for Communication and 
Journalism. Her research explores the psychologi-
cal effects of human-computer interaction and how 
new media technologies influence users’ health and 
well-being.
Andrea Figueroa-Caballero  (PhD, University 
of California at Santa Barbara) is a user experi-
ence researchers at Meta. Her academic research 
centers on minority representation within the media 
and the impact it has on consumers.
Eric Freedman (PhD, University of Southern Cal-
ifornia) is a professor and dean of the School of 
Media Arts at Columbia College Chicago. He is the 
author of Artificial Intelligence and Playable Media 
and The Persistence of Code in Game Engine Culture. 
His research interests include film and television, 
video game studies, software studies, and artificial 
intelligence.
Barbara G. Friedman  (PhD, University of Mis-
souri) is an associate professor in the Hussman 
School of Journalism and Media at the University 
of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, and an adjunct 
faculty member in the Department of Women’s 
and gender Studies. Her research focuses on gen-
der, race, and class in contemporary and historical 
media. She is the Director of The Irina Project (TIP), 
which analyzes media representations of sex traf-
ficking and advocates for the responsible and accu-
rate reporting of the issue.
Sarah E. Fryett (PhD, Florida State University) is 
an associate teaching professor in the Department 
of English and Writing at the University of Tampa. 
Her work revolves around feminist and queer the-
ory, as well as philosophy, composition pedagogy, 
media studies, and humor.
Issa Galvan  (MA, Texas State University) is a 
nonprofit communications and graphic design 
professional. Her research interests include the 
construction of identity and perpetuation of 
Latino stereotypes in media, political efficacy and 
self-efficacy among minority groups, and media 
inequalities.
Bradley W. Gorham  (PhD, University of 
 W
isconsin-Madison) is an associate professor and 
chair of the Communications Department at the 
S. I. Newhouse School of Public Communications, 
Syracuse University. His research centers around 
the reception and effects of media messages about 
social groups.
Kandice N. Green  (M.A., Southern Connecti-
cut State University) is a doctoral candidate at S. 
I. Newhouse School of Public Communications at 
Syracuse University. Her research interests lie at 
the intersection of media and social psychology, 
primarily examining how people use entertainment 
media to formulate their attitudes, ideologies, and 
identities.
Melissa Greene-Blye  (PhD, University of Ten-
nessee) is an assistant professor in the William 
Allen White School of Journalism & Mass Commu-
nications at the University of Kansas. Her research 
interests include media representations of Native 
American identity, issues, and individuals in journal-
ism past and present.
Rachel Alicia Griffin (PhD, University of Denver) 
is an associate professor of race and communica-
tion at the University of Utah. Her research interests 
span critical race theory, Black feminist thought, 
Whiteness, popular culture, sexual violence, and 
critical communication pedagogy.
Leslie A. Grinner (MS, Syracuse University) is an 
adjunct professor of Gender and Women’s studies 
and Africana studies at Rhode Island College. Her 
research interests include intersectional feminist 
pedagogy, media and cultural studies, power and 
privilege, ideology, and ending oppression.
Aymen Abdel Halim  (MA, San Francisco 
State University) is an independent marketing 
and communications consultant. His research 
interests include the effects of Arab and Mus-
lim representation in US electronic media and 
socio-political aspects of US electronic media. 
He is the former communications director at the 
Council of Islamic Organizations of Greater Chi-
cago and has taught at the University of Phoenix 
and DePaul University.

 Contributors 319
Kyra Heatly (MA, Texas Tech University) is a doc-
toral student at Texas A&M University. Her research 
interests include media representations of women 
in politics and gender and popular politics.
Vanessa de Macedo Higgins Joyce  (PhD, The 
University of Texas at Austin) is an associate pro-
fessor at the School of Journalism and Mass Com-
munication at Texas State University. She teaches 
and researches global, Latin American, and Latino 
media. Her research interests include transnational 
journalism, news and democracy, media effects, and 
consensus building.
Joseph Hoffswell  (PhD, University of Missouri) 
is an independent researcher and communication 
scholar. His research interests include game studies, 
digital media, popular culture studies, social media, 
and social identity theory.
Michael I. Huertas (BA, Pace University) was an 
undergraduate student in the Department of Com-
munication and Media Studies at Pace while work-
ing on this research. His research interests include 
international relations, news media, popular culture, 
and race and diversity studies.
Dina Ibrahim (PhD, University of Texas at Austin) 
is a professor of broadcast and electronic commu-
nication arts at San Francisco State University. A 
former reporter, her research interests include inno-
vative content creation and distribution, Islamopho-
bic content, and audience consumption habits. She 
is the Executive Director of the CSU Entertainment 
Alliance, which connects entertainment and tech-
nology companies to diverse talent from California 
State Universities.
Joshua R. Jackson (MA, Louisiana State Univer-
sity) is a doctoral student in the College of Commu-
nication and Information Sciences at the University 
of Alabama. His research interests include sports, 
race, gender, journalism, and social media.
Natalie Jolly  (PhD, Pennsylvania State Univer -
sity) is an associate professor and coordinates the 
sociology program at the University of Washington 
Tacoma. Her research explores issues of reproduc-
tion and mothering from interdisciplinary perspec-
tives, including sociology, ethnography, and media 
studies.
Christopher S. Josey (PhD, University of Illinois) 
is a faculty fellow and a professor at the University 
of Missouri. His research examines the portrayal of 
marginalized groups within mediated contexts.
Jean Kilbourne  (EdD, Boston University) is 
internationally recognized for her pioneering work 
on alcohol and tobacco advertising and the image 
of women in advertising. She is the creator of the 
award-winning film series Killing Us Softly: Advertis-
ing’s Image of Women and the author of Can’t Buy 
My Love: How Advertising Changes the Way We Think 
and Feel and So Sexy So Soon: The New Sexualized 
Childhood and What Parents Can Do to Protect Their 
Kids. In 2015, she was inducted into the National 
Women’s Hall of Fame.
Zeynep Kiliç (PhD, Arizona State University) is a 
professor of sociology at the University of Alaska, 
Anchorage. She is a cultural sociologist and a 
scholar of food studies.
Seonah Kim  (MA, University of New Mexico) is 
a doctoral candidate in the Department of Com-
munication at the University of Washington. Her 
research interest is broadly in culture, power, differ-
ence, identity, and global popular media.
C. Richard King  (PhD, University of Illinois) is a 
professor and chair in humanities, history, and social 
sciences at Columbia College, Chicago. He has writ-
ten extensively on the colonial legacies and post-
colonial predicaments of American culture, with 
special interest in the racial politics of expressive 
culture.
Jennifer S. Kramer  (PhD, Purdue University) is 
an associate professor of communication at The 
College of St. Benedict & St. John’s University.  
Her research focuses on stigmatizing communi-
cation fat women experience from their medi-
cal providers. She also specializes in intercultural 
communication.
Marina Krcmar  (PhD, University of 
 W
isconsin- 
Madison) is a professor of communication at Wake 
Forest University. Her research focuses on how 
children, adolescents, and families use and are 
affected by media. Recent work has focused on 
the effect  of  social media and media and moral 
reasoning.

320  C ontributors
Ryan M. Lescure (MA, San Francisco State Uni-
versity) is a lecturer of communication studies at San 
Francisco State University and an adjunct instructor 
of communication studies at Skyline College in San 
Bruno, California. His research primarily focuses on 
the intersections between communication, gender, 
sexuality, media, culture, memory, and power.
Rebecca Ann Lind  (PhD, University of Min-
nesota) is an associate professor and director of 
undergraduate studies in the Department of Com-
munication at the University of Illinois at Chicago. 
Her research interests include race, gender, class, 
and media; new media studies; media ethics; jour -
nalism; and audiences.
Rebeca Maseda García (PhD, Autonomous Uni-
versity of Madrid, Spain) is a professor of Spanish at 
the University of Alaska, Anchorage. Her research 
interests include gender and film, trauma studies, 
historical memory, and feminism.
Laura Joy “Anangokwe” Merchant  (AS Lib-
eral Arts and Cert. Ojibwe Language, Lac Courte 
Oreilles Ojibwe University) is the manager of the 
Sustainable Agriculture Research Station at Lac 
Courte Oreilles Ojibwe University where she also 
works as an Extension educator. Her professional 
interests and experiences include Ojibwemowin 
revitalization, Indigenous arts, culture and history, 
K-12 education, environmental action, regenerative 
agriculture, and ethnobotany. She is a former Liai-
son for Native American Student Support Services 
in K-12 education and former Adjunct Instructor 
for Early College Credit Program Ojibwemowin 
and Ojibwe History Continuing Education courses 
offered at Lac Courte Oreilles Ojibwe University.
jas l moultrie  (MS, University of Illinois at 
 Ur
bana-Champaign) is a story holder, filmmaker, 
and graduate student. Her research interests include 
refusal, performance, critical literacy, youth-led 
organizing, speculative fiction, and black visuality.
Greg Niedt  (PhD, Drexel University) is a project 
manager, researcher, and lecturer in Liberal Arts at 
the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts in Phila-
delphia. Greg’s work centers on the visual semiotics 
of diversity, particularly in the contexts of intercul-
tural and gendered communication.
Mary Beth Oliver (PhD, University of Wisconsin, 
Madison) is the Bellisario Professor of Media Stud-
ies at Penn State University. Her research interests 
are in media psychology, with an emphasis on emo-
tion, entertainment, positive media psychology, and 
social cognition.
Laurie Ouellette  (PhD, University of Massachu-
setts) is a professor of Media and Cultural Studies at 
the University of Minnesota. She writes about fem-
inism, television, and cultures of neoliberalism, and 
is the editor of Television & New Media.
Alina Renee Oxendine (PhD, University of Min-
nesota) is a professor in the Department of Political 
Science at Hamline University in St. Paul, MN. Her 
research and teaching interests include American 
politics, political psychology, public opinion, race, 
class, and gender.
Paromita Pain  (PhD, The University of Texas at 
Austin) is an associate professor of journalism at the 
University of Nevada, Reno. Her research interests 
include epistemological concerns raised by emerg-
ing forms of media that are hybrids between old and 
new forms, between citizen and professional news 
practices.
Newly Paul (PhD, Louisiana State University) is an 
assistant professor of journalism at the University 
of North Texas in Denton. Her research focuses on 
journalism processes and effects, particularly how 
supply side factors such as newsroom diversity and 
the presence of women journalists affect media 
content. She also studies cross-cultural reporting, 
particularly how non-Western journalistic norms 
and routines shape news content.
Joshua D. Phillips  (PhD, Southern Illinois Uni-
versity) is an associate teaching professor in the 
Department of Communication Arts and Sciences 
at Pennsylvania State University, Brandywine. He 
teaches courses in rhetoric, interpersonal com-
munication, public address, and communication 
theory. His book Homeless: Narratives from the 
Streets uses narratives of the homeless in an effort 
to improve public policy.
Lea M. Popielinski (PhD, The Ohio State Univer-
sity) applies her love for knowledge and pop culture 

 Contributors 321
to the theme quizzes; she prepares as an associate 
editor for the nationwide pub quiz company Geeks 
Who Drink. She wrote her dissertation on gender 
and embodiment in online graphical virtual worlds, 
with her research focusing on Second Life.
Srividya Ramasubramanian  (PhD, Penn State 
University) is Newhouse Professor and endowed 
chair at the Newhouse School of Public Commu-
nications at Syracuse University. Her scholarship 
focuses on media, diversity, and social justice. She 
is the Director of CODE^SHIFT (Collaboratory for 
Data Equity, Social Healing, Inclusive Futures, and 
Transformation), The Difficult Dialogues Project, 
and Media Rise (a global nonprofit collective for 
meaningful media).
Anthony R. Ramirez  (PhD, Texas A&M Univer-
sity) is an assistant professor of communication at 
the University of Houston-Downtown. His research 
focuses on Latinx and U.S.-Mexico border rep-
resentation in popular culture and media.
Julia C. Richmond  (PhD, Drexel University) is 
an assistant professor in the Department of Public 
Relations and Advertising at Rowan University. Her 
research focuses on the intersection of crisis com-
munication, media studies, and public relations.
Emily Riewestahl  (MA, Texas A&M Univer -
sity) is a scholar-practitioner with transdisciplinary 
training in communication, psychology, and the 
humanities. Her experience focuses on media, cul-
ture, identity, and equity using community-engaged, 
qualitative, computational, and quantitative meth-
ods. She currently works as a Community Powered 
Project Coordinator for Wisconsin Humanities and 
Y outh Engagement Manager for the UCLA Center 
for Scholars and Storytellers.
Frank T . Robinson, Jr. (M.A., Wake Forest Uni-
versity) is a US Air Force Veteran whose research 
focuses on African American Veterans’ reintegra-
tion to civilian life with an emphasis on exploring 
challenges to coping and creating change.
Naomi Rockler-Gladen (PhD, University of Min-
nesota) is a freelance educational writer and chil-
dren’s book author.
Jonathan P. Rossing  (PhD, Indiana University) 
is an associate dean of the College of Arts and 
Sciences and professor of communication studies at 
Gonzaga University. His research interests include 
race and critical race theory, humor, rhetoric, and 
critical pedagogy.
Jené Shepherd (MA, Texas State University) is a 
nonprofit marketing and communications profes-
sional. Her research interests include the intersec-
tion of race and gender in advertising and political 
communication.
Larissa Terán  (PhD, University of Arizona) is a 
lead media researcher at the Geena Davis Institute 
on Gender in Media. With a developmental focus, 
she conducts research on the intersection between 
media consumption, gender, sexuality, and how they 
relate to young people’s behaviors and ideologies.
Anna Grace Usery  (MA, University of Missis-
sippi) is a doctoral candidate at the University of 
Alabama. Her research interests include solutions 
journalism, journalism ethics, and college media 
programs.
Mary Douglas Vavrus  (PhD, University of Illi-
nois) is a professor in the Department of Communi-
cation Studies at the University of Minnesota. Her 
research interests include feminist media studies, 
media and war, political economy of media, and 
journalism.
Melvin L. Williams  (PhD, Howard University) is 
an associate professor in the Department of Com-
munication and Media Sudies at Pace University. 
His research examines the intersections of race, 
gender, and sexuality in popular culture to consider 
the political ramifications of popular culture and 
investigate how historically marginalized communi-
ties use their media to address disparaging media 
representations.
Maria Williams-Hawkins  (PhD, The Ohio 
State University) is an associate professor in the 
Department of Media at Ball State University. She 
researches and teaches in the areas of electronic 
news gathering, video production, diversity, Black 
on Black media, media criticism, scriptwriting, and 
more.

322  C ontributors
Gust A. Yep (PhD, University of Southern Califor-
nia) is a professor of communication studies, core 
graduate faculty of sexuality studies, and faculty in 
the EdD Program in educational leadership at San 
Francisco State University. He has been widely rec-
ognized for his teaching, mentoring, scholarship, and 
community work, nationally and internationally. In 
2021, he received the International and Intercultural 
Communication Division “Distinguished Scholar 
Award” and the Gay, Lesbian, Bisexual, Transgen-
der, and Queer Communication Studies Division 
“Monograph of the Y ear” Award (coauthored with 
Fatima Alaoui and Ryan Lescure), sponsored by the 
National Communication Association.
Bingbing Zhang  (MA, Texas Tech University) is 
a PhD candidate at Donald P. Bellisario College of 
Communications at Penn State. Her research inter-
ests are in media effects and media psychology 
focusing on applying strategic and inspiring media 
messages to improve prosocial, health, political out-
comes, and scientific understanding.
